Even though some people complain that you can't translate British Cockney accent, the German writers still did a very good job. Eliza Doolittle got a Berlin accent, which is not the same as Cockney, but the most important thing is, everybody understood what she was saying / singing, and the message of the movie was not altered or made unrecognizable! Now, take "Moulin Rougea, a recent movie. I happened to watch the German version on TV last night and I got so pissed.. first of all, only talking is dubbed.. the songs are still in English. Don't get me wrong, that's fine with me.. I like the voices of Ewan McGregor and Nicole Kidman and it's perfectly reasonable that no German actor / actress attempts to do better.. plus, I do understand what they're singing, but the thing is, most other Germans don't. So, what would be the easiest solution to this problem? Right, use subtitles for the songs! And what doesn't happen on German TV? Right: there are NO subtitles! Now, this wouldn't be a big deal with movies such as, uhm say, "Greasea or "Saturday Night Fevera or whatever.. but in "Moulin Rougea, the songs are part of the plot.. they add extra information and you can't just leave them out.. the ordinary German viewer wouldn't probably even notice that the songs are important, but of course, the script writers screw that as well.. as soon as there's a spoken word or something that comes close to being spoken, it gets dubbed.. so, there's this duet of McGregor and Kidman in which he wants her to love him but she is afraid the relationship wouldn't work out.. so at some point, McGregor goes like "Come love mea and Kidman sings "You will be meana and McGregor answers "No I wonata. But since he doesn't sing this last line, it gets dubbed ("Nein, werde ich nichta in German).. now, imagine you're watching a movie in a language you don't understand and suddenly one of the characters says "No I wonata in your language. You'll wonder, what the hell it is that he won't do??? And unless you have a native speaker next to you, you'll never find out.. isn't that ridiculous?????? So, as you might have read between the lines, there's a tendency in Germany that everything has to be in English.. especially in business, people seem to think that German things stink and English things are cool.. now again, don't get me wrong.. I do like English things, and I'm far from being a German nationalist.. the thing is, how can I value distinctive English products if some German dorks screw everything? How can I love the English language, if there's incorrect English wherever you go in Germany? I mean, if I had the money, I'd emigrate immediately, and then, those German idiots could do what they want, I wouldn't care.. but unfortunately, this is not an option right now..

I bought myself a living room suite, my daughter some nice clothes and a five-hundred-dollar car. I felt like I was on my way to becoming a productive member of society. All on my own. I stayed single for about three more years, gaining monetarily but not in selfworth. I still felt like a big loser because I couldn't fulfill the obvious dream of catching a man. I learned a lot during this time. I learned how to change the oil in my car, and how to replace sparkplugs and an altenator. I learned how to manage money. I could pay all the bills and still have enough left over to buy things that I needed like toothpaste and shampoo. I could even take my daughter to Wal-mart and buy her a new pair of shoes when she needed them, not when I could scrape the money together. But I wasn't happy. How could I be when there was no man to take care of me? So, once I started having a little extra money, I started going out. I didn't go far, I didn't trust my five-hundred-dollar Nissan too far from town. Mostly, I just cruised around the town I lived in. I knew most of the other kids who were cruising, but I was the only one who cruised with my daughter in the car with me. Sometimes my mom kept her, sometimes I took her with me. Let' face it, I was in the market for a new man. I met several, but none of them wanted to date someone who had a child. Most of them just thought I was easy because it was obvious I had already had sex. They were after one thing and I was after another, and most of the time, they won. I never got what I was looking for. I decided to go back to school. I didn't really know what I wanted to be yet, but they said I could decide that later, after my first two years of college. I was 21, I had two divorces under my belt, I was a single mom, and I was miserable with my life. I knew I had to do something. College was the answer. I signed up at the local Community College for some basic classes. I spent less time going out and more time doing homework. But I knew I was in the right place, because I could meet a college boy now. That's right, it was always about finding a man. Then one day, just before Thanksgiving, I ran into a guy that I had gone to highschool with. Give me your gun." I listened to all that was said in dogged silence. I could not refuse to give up my dearly-beloved weapon; but I did so with a very bad grace; and I am sorry to say that my father's words had at that time little or no effect on my heart. However, simulating subject-specific organ motion using biomechanical modelling efficiently requires specialised software, hardware (such as graphical processing units (GPUs)), and expertise. It is also technically demanding and the need to perform many thousands of simulations for each individual subject becomes computationally expensive, and generating an SSM can take hours in practice even if the degree of manual interaction required can be minimised relatively straightforwardly through the implementation of an automated pipeline process. Furthermore, although there has been considerable methodological progress to ensure the numerical stability of FEM methods, it is widely recognised that such methods can fail to converge under some circumstances, for example due to a poorly configured geometric mesh. Consequently, although integrating such technology into existing clinical workflows is not unsurmountable, there remain a number of significant practical challenges. For this reason, more convenient, computationally efficient, and numerically stable methods for generating subject-specific SSMs of organ deformation - or training data for building them - are highly desirable from the point of view of facilitating clinical adoption. To date, the popular method described by Cootes et al. (1995) for generating low-dimensional, linear SSMs by applying principal component analysis (PCA) to shape or image training data has been used mainly to generate models that describe organ shape variation across a population, e.g. (Onofrey et al., 2013; Perperidis et al., 2005; Thompson et al., 2008). PCA and other statistical techniques have also been applied to generate subject-specific 4D statistical models for organs undergoing respiratory motion (McClelland et al., 2013) or cardiac motion. Examples include models of the lungs (He et al., 2010; King et al., 2012), the liver (Preiswerk et al., 2014), and the heart (Perperidis et al., 2005). Given the considerable effort required to build a model of organ motion for an individual subject, a number of researchers have investigated so-called population-based or cross-population models (McClelland et al., 2013; Preiswerk et al., 2014). These enable subject-specific organ motion to be predicted using learnt information from an independent training set. It is possible to build a population-based SSM by combining training data that is subject to both inter- and intra-subject organ shape variation, but such models are likely to perform less effectively or efficiently compared with a subject-specific SSM for approximating subject-specific shape/motion. In particular, such models usually require additional constraints, such as that provided by an elastic model (Wang and Staib, 2000), to prevent unrealistic or 'over-generalised' instantiation of the model because of shape variation learnt from other subjects. Multilinear analysis (Vasilescu and Terzopoulos, 2003) has been proposed as a method for dynamic modelling of the heart (Zhu et al., 2008) and cardiac valve (Grbic et al., 2012) motion.

Another kind of fowl, an eagle, had built a nest in the bare branches at the summit of an isolated pine tree, of which only the lower boughs were foliaged, and this was higher even than the peak to which Hilary daily repaired for the earliest glimpse of his materialized hopes advancing down the gorge. The pair of birds only of all the denizens of the mountain took heed of his movements and displayed an anxiety and suspicion and a sort of fierce but fluttered indignation. It is impossible to say whether they were aware that their variety had grown rare in these parts, and that their capture, dead or alive, would be a matter of very considerable interest, and it is also futile to speculate as to whether they had any knowledge of the uses or range of the rifle which Hilary sometimes carried on his shoulder. Certain it is, however, the male bird muttered indignantly as he looked down at the young mountaineer, and was wont to agitatedly flop about the great clumsy nest of interwoven sticks where the female, the larger of the two, with a steady courage sat motionless, only her elongated neck and bright dilation of the eyes betokening her excitement and distress. The male bird was of a more reckless tendency, and often visibly strove with an intermittent intention of swooping down to attack the intruder, for Hilary was but a slender fellow of about sixteen years, although tall and fleet of foot. A good shot, too, he was, and he had steady nerves, despite the glitter of excitement in his eyes forever gazing down the gorge. Because of his absorption in this expectation he took no notice of the eagles, although to justify his long absences from home he often brought his rifle on the plea of hunting. How should he care to observe the birds when at any moment he might see the flutter of a guidon in the valley road, a mere path from this height, and hear the trumpet sing out sweet and clear in the silence of the wilderness! At any moment the wind might bring the sound of the tramp of cavalry, the clatter of the carbine and canteen, and the clanking of spur and saber as some wild band of guerrillas came raiding through the country. For despite the solemn stillness that brooded in the similitude of the deepest peace upon the scene, war was still rife in the land. The theater of action was far from this sequestered region, but there had been times when the piny gorges were full of the more prickly growth of bayonets. The echoing crags were taught the thrilling eloquence of the bugle, and the mountains reverberated with the oratory of the cannon - for the artillery learned to climb the deer-paths.

Yet as Ian rides his bike through the hallowed halls of Broadcasting House, managers and producers alike gulp nervously. There's something inherently comic in the juxtaposition of his sunny disposition against the backdrop of swirling bureaucracy. No sooner has he rolled into the building than he's met by his new team-a dazzling array of characters each more delightfully incompetent than the last. At the helm of HR is the ever-enthusiastic but utterly misguided Emma, played exquisitely by Jessica Hynes. Her mission is crystal clear: synergy! As she spins elaborate fables about employee engagement, one can't help but wonder if she even knows what day it is. Perhaps it's a Tuesday she's too busy concepting instead of just dealing. Conversations with Emma tend to drift into the absurd territory of jargon-laden platitudes and misguided zeal, peppered with buzzwords like "leverage" and "drill down". Ian, quick to adopt his signature expression-half confusion, half optimism-nods at her enthusiasm while questioning when the real work might begin. Meanwhile, Ian's feet land squarely in the chaotic realm of a programming director, David, who seems to view his role as more of a theatrical production than a cable broadcast. With rows of Post-it notes plastered onto his office walls, each decorated with bright, almost childish doodles, one can't help but draw parallels between his vision for the BBC and an art installation gone awry. "We need to be edgy," he declares, eyes bright with excitement. "What if we launched a 'Reality Soap Drama' series, centered around the lives of the postroom staff?" Ian merely stares into the middle distance, mentally calculating how soon he can escape to another meeting. Then there's the comedy goldmine that is the technical team, helmed by the unimpressed and perpetually baffled tech wizard, Simon, played with perfect deadpan by the farcical Tim Key. When Ian asks Simon whether they are equipped to handle the upcoming live broadcast of the annual charity gala, Simon's response is reminiscent of Code Red at a spy agency: "We have a backup... and a backup for the backup." In other words, no one really knows if the new technology will work. Spoiler alert: it won't. And every day brings the delightful shambolic consequences of incompetence into riotous focus. The brilliantly diverse cast of characters ensures no two episodes feel the same, with misunderstandings leading to riotous outcomes, whether it's the wrong live feed going out, or a leak in the building purposely misrepresented as an avant-garde art installation. Ian's trademark ability to deliver a workload without the slightest grasp of procedural realities places him at the epicenter of increasingly absurd situations. As he traipses through corporate meetings, mired in an overload of PowerPoints and elaborate pie charts that mean absolutely nothing to anyone, Ian's naive optimism becomes the thread that holds this chaotic tapestry of broadcasting together. Struggling to locate the exit strategy while trying to discover the point of it all, he plows onward, earning chuckles and exasperated sighs. At the heart of W1A lies a delightful examination of the absurdity of modern corporate life through a lens of sharp, irreverent humor. It's a captivating combination-gingerly balancing tragedy with comedy, each misadventure more laughable than the last. In the end, it's clear that Ian's battle against the nebulous forces of bureaucracy is not just for the BBC, but for anyone who's tried to make sense of the nonsense. As he would so eloquently put it, "Let's just get started!"

My father had always believed in my potential, and this meeting was a testament to the promise he saw in me. Chelsea's offer was substantial, a dream for many players: the chance to play in the prestigious Premier League, to adorn the blue kit in one of Europe's grandest stadiums. But for us, it wasn't just about the money or the allure of Europe. It was about making the right decision for my career and my future. As we sat there, Luis Alvaro speaking animatedly about the club's vision, I could feel the weight of the decision pressing down on me. This wasn't just about moving clubs; this was about leaving home, about forsaking the familiar samba rhythms of Brazil for the colder, faster-paced world of the English game. Santos, my club since childhood, held a special place in my heart. It was here that I began weaving the tapestry of my career, where I danced on the pitch and turned my dreams into reality. My father spoke in his deep, calm voice. "Neymar, think about what you really want. It's not just about going to Europe, it's about your legacy." I nodded, understanding him completely. This world, with its flashing cameras and expectant fans, was like a maze, and my father had always been my guide. Amidst the negotiations and discussions, I pondered not only what it meant for me but for Brazilian football. Players like Pele, who once dazzled here, began their artistry in the same sacred grounds I now played. I found solace in that lineage, the pressure transforming into a comforting embrace from the history of Santos. Luis Alvaro broke my contemplative silence, gesturing with an earnest smile. "Stay with us, Neymar. We believe in your vision, your potential to lead this team to glory. We can offer you everything you need to grow." Growing up, I understood the essence of loyalty, about carving out a place in the world that felt truly mine. Rejecting Chelsea was not an easy decision, especially as a young professional eager to prove his worth globally. And yet, something within me told me to persevere here for just a little longer, to weave my story where it began. The memory of that day in 1992 resurfaced faintly. My father's cries, the fear that gripped us at the thought of losing everything. It made me realize that this wasn't just about a transfer; it was about family, about preserving what truly mattered. I was never just playing for myself, but for something greater. I looked at my father, and we exchanged a knowing glance. The contracts, the figures on paper-they were significant but not the defining factors of my choice. Football was about passion, about touching the very soul of the nation I represented every time my foot graced the ball. As we left the meeting, I felt a sense of clarity. My heart was set on staying. This was my journey, and it was just beginning. My father had taught me well: sometimes what seems like the smaller path can lead to the greatest destinations.

The couple will have to decide whether to hire a breast pump or rent a milk bank - where fresh milk from healthy mothers is stored for babies too ill to feed themselves. And if Kate chooses to breastfeed, there will be a media storm when she returns to public life. She may even be asked how many times she feeds the baby a day, although most women don't know themselves. Whether or not Kate decides to return to work soon after giving birth, she'll have to weigh up the pros and cons of breastfeeding. Breastfeeding is recommended by experts because it gives the baby the best start in life. Formula milk is sterile but contains less iron and fewer antibodies than breastmilk. However, Kate could face pressure to give up breastfeeding to resume her royal duties. Although she has no official engagements planned, she will be expected to attend a number of charity events next year. If she wants to go back to work quickly, she may find herself unable to breastfeed. One option open to her would be to express milk and store it for later use, but even that would require someone to help out. She might decide to use a breast pump, which enables her to collect milk at home and then freeze it for future use. But there are problems with pumps. They're expensive and can take up to two hours to fill a bottle. Some women find them uncomfortable. Others say that expressing can cause soreness and bruising. Another option would be to join a milk bank. Mothers donate excess breastmilk to these banks, which then supply it to hospitals for sick children. Using donated breastmilk has its own set of drawbacks. It cannot be guaranteed to be free from infection. Also, it is usually pasteurised, which means that some of the nutrients are lost. The milk is often heated twice, which can mean that the fat separates from the liquid. A third option would be to buy powdered formula milk. While it may seem the easiest solution, it comes with its own difficulties. Most parents find that they have to mix formula milk at least three times a day. Powdered formula milk must be mixed with boiled water, and some brands contain sugar, which can upset the baby's stomach. Whatever she decides, Kate will be a role model for millions of women around the world. The way she copes with her pregnancy and early motherhood will set standards that other women will feel obliged to follow. Our experiment manipulates the cultural organization of the society by varying the level of institutional support for cooperation, specifically the presence or absence of a formal authority that enforces cooperation. We predict that the presence of an authority will increase the prevalence of majority-based social learning, as individuals are more likely to conform to the behavior of their peers when they are aware that deviance will be punished. In contrast, the absence of an authority will lead to a greater reliance on payoff-based social learning, as individuals will be more likely to imitate successful peers in the absence of external enforcement. To test these predictions, we recruited 540 participants and randomly assigned them to one of two treatment conditions: a "strong institution" condition, where participants were told that a third-party authority would monitor and enforce cooperation, and a "weak institution" condition, where no such authority was present. Participants then played a series of cooperative games, where they had to decide whether to contribute to a public good or free-ride on the contributions of others. After each round, participants were shown the decisions of their group members and had the opportunity to adjust their own behavior. Our results show that, consistent with our predictions, the presence of an authority significantly increases the use of majority-based social learning. In the strong institution condition, participants were more likely to conform to the behavior of their peers, even when it meant sacrificing their own short-term payoffs. In contrast, in the weak institution condition, participants were more likely to imitate successful peers, regardless of the behavior of the majority. Furthermore, we find that the cultural organization of the society also affects the dynamics of cooperation in the group. In the strong institution condition, cooperation levels were higher and more stable over time, as participants were more likely to cooperate when they knew that others were doing so as well. In contrast, in the weak institution condition, cooperation levels were lower and more volatile, as participants were more likely to defect when they saw others doing so. Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the role of social learning in human cooperation. They suggest that the cultural organization of a society can shape the way individuals learn from each other and make decisions, and that institutions can play a crucial role in promoting cooperation by providing a framework for social norms and enforcement. Moreover, our results highlight the importance of considering the interplay between individual-level and group-level processes in understanding human cooperation, and demonstrate the value of using experimental methods to study the complex dynamics of social behavior. In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the role of social learning in human cooperation, and highlights the importance of considering the cultural organization of a society in understanding how individuals make decisions. Our findings have implications for a wide range of fields, from economics and psychology to anthropology and sociology, and demonstrate the value of interdisciplinary research in understanding the complex dynamics of human behavior.

It is important to note that for rhythmic coordination tasks, unidirectional informational couplings could account for at least part of the stability of the coordination (Richardson, Campbell, & Schmidt, 2009). However, in contrast to the findings of the previously reported studies, there is also evidence suggesting that instructed or emerging role distributions can be beneficial for joint action coordination. Noy et al. (2011) found that, contrary to improvisation experts, novices achieved better coordination in the mirror game when one of them was instructed to lead and the other to follow, compared to no such role assignment, highlighting the role of expertise in joint action. An example for how an emergent role distribution into leader and follower (Roberts & Goldstone, 2011; Skewes, Skewes, Michael, & Konvalinka, 2015) enables coordination is provided by a recent study by Richardson et al. (2015). They devised a joint action task that required two participants to move stimuli back and forth on crossing paths without colliding. The task was designed such that if both participants moved in synchrony and followed a straight path, they would bump into each other. Nearly all pairs converged on an effective solution where one partner in a pair followed an elliptical trajectory while the other followed a straight path. The partner following the elliptical trajectory was more influenced by the movements of the partner following a straight line than vice versa, indicating that a leader-follower dynamic emerged. This emergent role distribution may be beneficial for coordination because the leader provides a stable and predictable input to the partner who is in charge of compensating and adapting. Indeed, making one's own actions predictable has been identified as a useful coordination strategy in joint tasks (Vesper, van der Wel, Knoblich, & Sebanz, 2011; Vesper, Schmitz, Safra, Sebanz, & Knoblich, 2016). To sum up, on the one hand, some findings suggest that a leader-follower dynamic can be detrimental for interpersonal coordination; such a detriment can be caused by environmental constraints that do not allow for reciprocal information flow (Konvalinka et al., 2010) or by an assigned role distribution that keeps one individual from adjusting to and predicting the other's actions (Noy et al., 2011). On the other hand, other findings indicate that effective role distributions in terms of a leader and follower emerge when some role differentiation is clearly required (Richardson et al., 2015). This raises the question under which conditions role distribution emerges when it is not strictly required by the coordination task, and what makes role distribution beneficial or detrimental to joint action coordination. The current study aims at providing answers to these questions. Our starting point is the important observation that the coordination tasks used in previous studies differ in one key aspect: the congruency of temporal and spatial coordination demands. The joint tapping task used by Konvalinka et al. required only temporal coordination; in the mirror game employed by Noy et al. achieving temporal coordination implied achieving spatial coordination and vice versa, once aligned on a starting position.

In a way, that is why what happened in Paris on Tuesday feels, amid the disgust and shame, like an important step forward. It wasn't a surprise to most observers of the English game. It wasn't anything new. Except for one thing. Except that what happened to Souleymane S is there on video and with audio. Paul Nolan, who shot the footage, performed a great service to English football. The plausible deniability that football exercised time after time, including in San Marino, is gone. This time, there is no denying it. This time, there is no sanitising it. This time, there is no hiding from it. Admitting that race is a real problem in English football again, admitting we have not made as much progress as we thought we had, is a critical first step. Oh, we've made some advances, for sure. Fans do not throw bananas as they used to when Bradford City's Ces Podd ran past in the Seventies. But racial prejudice is on the rise in our society. Somehow, we have reached a point where our Jewish community is, once more, scared for its safety. Xenophobia, in different forms, seems to be multiplying. Look at what happens when articulate men such as Jason Roberts or Stan Collymore speak out about race on Twitter: they are doused with foul abuse. It is time for football to start taking some bold steps. It is not enough to keep playing safe and hoping the problem goes away. The trailblazing Ces Podd (right) runs to training with Bradford manager Bryan Edwards. Stan Collymore (left) and Jason Roberts are routinely abused on Twitter when they speak out about race. This should not be about isolating Chelsea who are in many ways a model of multi-culturalism, owned by a Russian Jew who appointed a Portuguese as manager and a Nigerian as technical director and whose employees have overseen a progressive Asian Star initiative. Chelsea have acted swiftly and strongly. They have been unequivocal in their condemnation of what happened. Jose Mourinho said he was 'ashamed'. But this is not just about Chelsea. This has to go further than merely punishing the scum who repelled Souleymane S from that train and chanted how proud they were to be racist. Prison sentences, banning orders; that's easy. That just scratches the surface. These people are produced by our society, not by our football. There is no quick fix. But there are ways forward; ways that will take courage and perseverance and brave leadership. It's about time, for instance, that the Football League stood up and led the way by introducing a version of the NFL's Rooney Rule for the lower leagues. There is no point involving the Premier League yet. Most aspiring black coaches don't have enough experience to manage in the top flight because they have been denied opportunities lower down the pyramid.

Or maybe not. We reach the border, and the lines are short. A quick exchange of passports, and we are on our way again. And then we see it a the sign welcoming us to Bosnia-Herzegovina! It is now mid-morning, and we are ready for lunch. But where shall we eat? Our Lonely Planet guidebook says that Sarajevo has plenty of restaurants, but we are still an hour away. So we pull off the highway, and find a restaurant a little ways down the road. We order some lamb kebab, which arrives promptly. The waiter is friendly, but he doesn't speak English. We order another round of drinks, and then the waiter comes over and asks us whether we would like dessert. This is unusual in the Balkans, where they don't believe in dessert. I am surprised, but ask him what he recommends. He suggests a Turkish delight cake, so we order one and wait for it to arrive. When it does, the waiter informs me that it costs 5 Euros. Now, the meal itself cost 3.50 Euros, and we thought that the prices were reasonable. But 5 Euros for dessert? I tell him that we are sorry, but we cannot afford such expensive desserts. He looks embarrassed and takes back the plate. We finish our meals, pay our bill, and leave. As we drive along the highway, we see a roadside cafe. We pull in and have a cup of tea and some cakes. The cakes are excellent, and the price is right. Later, we stop at a gas station, and notice that the prices are ridiculously low. Gasoline is less than $1 per liter. We fill up the tank, and continue on our way. Finally, we enter Sarajevo. Sarajevo is divided into three sections a the European section, the Old Town, and the Muslim quarter. The first thing that strikes us is the number of old German cars driving around. Not only do we see Mercedeses and VWs, but also BMWs and Audis. These must be war profiteers who made their fortunes during the war and are now flaunting their wealth. At the same time, the city is not as run-down as I expected. Sure, there are many buildings damaged by artillery shells, and the scars of the war are visible, but the city is not destroyed. It is a city that can recover, given peace and stability. We wander through the Old Town, admiring the architecture and enjoying the shops selling traditional crafts. Sarajevans are known for their metalwork, and we buy a couple of bracelets before continuing on our way. We check into Hotel City, which is near the center of town. It is a nice hotel, with large rooms and clean bathrooms. Dinner is at a local restaurant serving Bosnian specialties. I try the cheese pita, which is delicious. The next morning we take a tour of the city. First we head to the Tunnel Museum, which tells the story of the tunnel built under the airport runway to allow the residents of besieged Sarajevo to receive supplies. It is very interesting, and includes a video showing the construction of the tunnel. Next we head to the Holiday Inn, which served as UN headquarters during the siege. From there we can see the hills surrounding Sarajevo, including Mt. Igman, where the Olympics took place. Then we make our way to the Olympic Stadium, where the games were held. The stadium is impressive, and we admire the view of the mountains behind the stadium. Next we head to the Markale market, site of several massacres of civilians.

Fearing he might have some message for his daughter, whom he did not intend he should see, he started hastily towards him, to intercept him and turn him back before he reached his house. He met Mayall some distance from his house, and forbid his nearer approach. "Look yonder," said Mayall, as he pointed his carbine up the Valley of the Mohawk. "Do you see the smoke and flames that light up the concave of the skies? The use of electronic cigarettes (EC) as a harm reduction strategy for smokers who are unwilling or unable to quit has gained significant attention in recent years. As a non-combustible nicotine delivery device, EC has been shown to be a potentially safer alternative to traditional tobacco products, with levels of toxicants at least an order of magnitude lower than those found in cigarette smoke (Goniewicz et al., 2014; Kosmider et al., 2014). The popularity of EC has been increasing rapidly, with many smokers using them as a means to reduce their cigarette consumption or as a temporary substitute for traditional cigarettes (Beard et al., 2011; Hammond et al., 2008; Levy et al., 2007; Silla et al., 2014). One of the key advantages of EC is its ability to deliver nicotine to the user without the combustion of tobacco, which is the primary cause of cigarette toxicity (Le Houezec et al., 2011). This makes EC a potentially valuable tool for smokers who are looking to reduce their exposure to harmful chemicals found in cigarette smoke. Additionally, EC has been shown to be effective in reducing the number of cigarettes smoked by dual users, with some studies suggesting that it can be used as a bridge to quitting or reducing cigarette consumption (Brown et al., 2014b; King et al., 2013; Vardavas et al., 2014). However, there are still many unknowns surrounding the use of EC as a harm reduction strategy. For example, the long-term effects of EC use on lung function and cardiovascular health are still unclear, and there is a need for further research in this area. Additionally, the regulation of EC products is currently inconsistent across different countries, which can make it difficult to ensure that products are safe and effective for use. Despite these challenges, the use of EC as a harm reduction strategy is likely to continue to grow in popularity. In fact, a recent survey found that nearly 10% of adults in the United States had used an EC in the past year, with many more using them as a means to reduce their cigarette consumption (McMillen et al., 2014). As the scientific evidence continues to accumulate, it is likely that EC will become an increasingly important tool in the fight against tobacco use. In conclusion, the use of electronic cigarettes as a harm reduction strategy is a complex issue that requires further research and regulation. However, the available evidence suggests that EC may be a potentially safer alternative to traditional tobacco products, and that it could be a valuable tool for smokers who are unwilling or unable to quit. As the scientific community continues to study the effects of EC use, it is likely that we will see a continued growth in the use of EC as a harm reduction strategy.

That's why, when a teenage girl commits suicide, her parents often don't see it coming. Boys tend to externalize their emotions, which can result in physical aggression and bullying. Girls also seem better equipped to talk about their emotions. "Girls are given permission to talk about their emotions. He knew every inch of the harbour, every vessel that came and went, and every skipper's habits. He had been a sailor himself, once, on the clipper ships that raced between Sydney and London, but a bad fall from the rigging had left him with a gammy leg, and now he was forced to eke out a living on the waterfront, taking on odd jobs and scrounging for scraps. But Ted had a nose for opportunity, and he could smell it in the air now, as he watched the brig preparing to sail. He knew her type, a sturdy, reliable vessel, built for the rough trade of the Pacific, with a seasoned skipper at the helm and a crew of hard-bitten sailors. She was the kind of ship that could take a man to the farthest reaches of the ocean, to the hidden islands and secret coves that only a few men had ever seen. As the hour ticked by, Ted's eyes never left the brig, his gaze fixed on the skipper, a grizzled old salt with a bushy white beard and a face like worn leather. He was a man of few words, but Ted knew he was fair, and would give a man a chance if he showed willing. The question was, would he take on a man with a gammy leg, and a reputation for being a bit of a troublemaker? Ted's thoughts were interrupted by the sound of footsteps, heavy and deliberate, coming from the direction of the warehouse door. A burly, red-faced man, with a thick, curly beard and a battered top hat, emerged into the rain, his eyes scanning the wharf as if searching for someone. Ted's instincts told him to be wary, but he stood his ground, his eyes locked on the man, as he approached. "You Ted Barry?" the man growled, his voice like thunder on a summer's day. Ted nodded, his heart pounding in his chest, as the man continued, "I've got a message for you, from the skipper of that brig. He wants to see you, down at the ship. Now."

Regarding the female counterpart, the evolution of flowers after anthesis until senescence includes basipetal maturation that starts at the stigma and continues downwardly to the ovary. These changes are developmentally regulated and do not, therefore, depend on the action of pollen tubes (Distefano et al., 2011). The pistil senescence process includes loss of stigmatic receptivity, style abscission and ovule degeneration. The influence of temperature on stigmatic receptivity has been reported in woody species, such as sweet cherry (Hedhly et al., 2003), peach (Hedhly et al., 2005a), and cherimoya (Lora et al., 2011), while the influence of temperature on ovule degeneration has been described in plum, and sweet and sour cherry cultivars (Beppu et al., 2001; Cerovic et al., 2000; Postweiler et al., 1985). Citrus (Citrus spp.) is the leading fruit crop worldwide, whose production amounts to more than 146 million tons (FAOSTAT, 2017) in more than 100 countries with tropical and subtropical climates (between 40 N and 40 S, approx.), and even in colder areas like Japan and the Jeju Island in South Korea. Studies on global climate change predict an increase in average temperatures between 0.3 and 4.8 C in 80 years (IPCC, 2014), and in the temperature range amplitude, which could limit plant cultivation in some areas. The consequences of the global climate change are already affecting phenological plant traits, especially those related to flowering (Hedhly et al., 2009; Springate and Kover, 2014), and also shifts the expected geographical distribution in natural ecosystems (Corlett and Westcott, 2013; Singer et al., 2016). In this context, the environmental conditions of the main citrus production areas will change and citrus-growing areas may be extended. Thus breeding programs based on sexual hybridisations could take into account new environmental conditions. Very few studies have evaluated the influence of temperature on the progamic phase in citrus, especially those related with the female parent. Distefano et al. (2012) showed that temperature variation in this phase has a strong effect on pollen germination in vitro and on the pollen-pistil interaction in detached flowers of three ancestral citrus species. However, new methods based on in planta evaluations need to be implemented to characterise the influence of temperature on the progamic phase in citrus, specifically in a more comprehensive and nature-representative way.

It is therefore very difficult to describe the CPS model of a CNC machine tool in a complete and accurate manner with the use of any single mathematical or physical method. In addition, the massive quantities of parameters in the theoretical model (e.g., friction, rigidity, and the material properties of the machine tool) have high dispersion due to the differences in assembly quality and processing conditions. With the emergence of big data technology, the integration of theoretic modeling with the big data approach makes it possible to improve the completeness and accuracy of the CPS models of CNC machine tools. In recent years, studies on the CPS modeling method based on big data have gained extensive attentions. In 2006, the Association for Manufacturing Technology (AMT) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), both in the US, proposed a communication standard, MTConnectTM [5], for data collection and transmission for CNC machine tools. Kao et al. [6] suggested establishing a CS by providing services via Watchdog Agent(R) tools and establishing a prognostics and health management (PHM) technology directly on the data thus obtained. Wang [7] proposed a CPS scheme in which a plant is set up with a distributed process-planning system, a dynamic resource-planning system, a real-time process-monitoring system, a remote control system, and so on. Lee et al. [8,9] pointed out that collecting and analyzing industrial big data is the key to the establishment of CPS as well as future intelligent-manufacturing equipments. They proposed a 5C (configure, cognition, cyber, conversion, connection) system structure for establishing the CPS of CNC machine tools, under which the status data for CNC machine tools could be collected using radio-frequency identification (RFID) technology, and the machining process and degradation of the CNC machine tools and their components could be identified based on control and inspection data. Wan et al. [10] used the Internet of Things and a multi-sensory network technique to enhance the machine-to-machine (M2M) system for information exchange in order to realize intelligent decision-making and the automatic control of a system, thus upgrading from an M2M system to a CPS of machine tools. Summarizing these studies, we believe that there are three key points in the study of the CPS modeling of CNC machine tools. (1) It is necessary to fully collect and utilize the big data generated from the use of a CNC machine tool over its whole life cycle, and to combine this big data with the theoretical modeling method in order to establish the CNC machine tool CPS model. The whole life cycle of a CNC machine tool includes several stages, such as development, design, manufacturing, installation, usage, maintenance, repair, till scrapping and recycling. During the most important stages of this cycle, those that occur at the user site, there are large numbers of repeated works, including debugging, testing, trial cutting, and production machining.

The suspension technique, also known as slurry washcoating, has been widely employed for depositing catalysts onto microreactor surfaces. This method typically involves a series of steps, including microreactor surface pretreatment, slurry preparation and deposition, impregnation of the catalytically active component, and heat treatment. The pretreatment step involves cleaning the microreactor surface to ensure a uniform and non-reactive surface for the catalyst deposition. The slurry is then prepared by mixing the catalyst support material, typically -Al2O3, with a binder, such as alumina or silica, and a solvent. The slurry is then deposited onto the microreactor surface using various techniques, such as dip-coating, spin-coating, or spray-coating. The impregnation step involves adding the catalytically active component, such as a noble metal, to the slurry. This can be done by mixing the metal precursor with the slurry or by using a separate impregnation step. The heat treatment step involves drying and calcination of the coated microreactor to remove any solvent and binders, and to activate the catalyst. The suspension technique has been shown to be effective for depositing catalysts onto microreactor surfaces, but it is not without its challenges. The rheological properties of the slurry, such as viscosity and particle size, can greatly influence the quality of the coated layer. The adhesion of the catalyst to the microreactor surface can also be affected by the properties of the slurry and the surface pretreatment. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored various methods to optimize the suspension technique. For example, the addition of surfactants or dispersants to the slurry can improve its rheological properties and enhance the adhesion of the catalyst to the microreactor surface. The use of different solvents or binders can also affect the properties of the coated layer. In addition to the suspension technique, other methods have been developed for depositing catalysts onto microreactor surfaces. For example, sol-gel deposition involves the use of a sol-gel precursor to create a thin film of the catalyst on the microreactor surface. Electrophoretic deposition involves the use of an electric field to deposit the catalyst onto the microreactor surface. Chemical vapor deposition and physical vapor deposition are also used to deposit catalysts onto microreactor surfaces. Each of these methods has its own advantages and disadvantages, and the choice of method will depend on the specific application and the properties of the catalyst and microreactor. The development of new methods and techniques for depositing catalysts onto microreactor surfaces is an active area of research, and continues to be an important area of study in the field of microreactor technology.

A number of investigators, notably Levitt and Chothia (1976), Richardson (1981), and Wodak and Janin (1981) recognized the occurrence of recurrent patterns of secondary structure and how these pack together to form compact globules. The first step in this process is the formation of -helices and -strands, stabilized by BB-BB H-bonds. This is followed by their assembly into larger structures stabilized by BS-BS and SS-SS hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions. The next level of organization consists of domains, assemblies of secondary structure elements that fold more or less independently of the rest of the protein. Domains often correspond to functional units such as ligand binding sites. Proteins may contain several domains connected by flexible loops, and the orientation of domains relative to each other may change during function. Finally, individual polypeptide chains associate to form oligomeric complexes stabilized primarily by hydrophobic interactions and salt bridges. As mentioned above, the primary building blocks of protein structure are the -helix and -sheet. Each of these is stabilized by BB-BB H-bonds. The -helix is a right-handed helix with 3.6 residues per turn. The C=O group of residue i forms an H-bond with the NH group of residue i + 4. The distance between successive turns is 5.4 A and the pitch is 1.5 A/residue. The average length of a helical segment is 12 residues. Helices longer than 20 residues are rare. Proline is rarely found in helices because it cannot donate an amide proton for H-bonding. Glycine also occurs infrequently in -helices. Both amino acids increase the flexibility of the polypeptide chain. However, glycines frequently occur at tight bends in the polypeptide chain where an -helix is forced to turn a corner. Such bends are usually stabilized by H-bonds between the O atom of the CO group of residue i and the NH of residue i + 3. Because prolines are unable to participate in BB-BB H-bonding, they disrupt -helices. Nevertheless, they are often found near the ends of helical segments, presumably to cap the helix and protect it from degradation. Another common feature of -helices is an abundance of acidic residues near the N terminus and basic residues near the C terminus. The partial negative charge on the peptide carbonyl oxygen can interact favorably with the positive charge on lysine and arginine side chains located four residues toward the C-terminal end. Likewise, interactions between NH groups and the carboxylate side chains of aspartate and glutamate residues can help anchor the N-terminal end of a helix. Other forces that contribute to the stability of -helices include van der Waals interactions and the intrahelical H-bonds themselves. These collectively overcome the large loss of conformational entropy associated with fixing six chemical bonds for each residue in the rigid -helical structure. The -helix is not the only periodic structure observed in proteins. Linus Pauling predicted that left-handed helices should also exist, but this prediction was never confirmed. Left-handed helices have not been observed in proteins, probably because the side chains are too close to the backbone to fit without straining or distorting the mainchain. However, left-handed helices do occur in synthetic peptides consisting of either D-amino acid residues or -amino acids. In contrast to the -helix, the -sheet is essentially fully extended.

First and foremost, let's talk about the power of gratitude. Each morning, before you even step out of bed, take a moment to reflect on three things that you are grateful for. It could be as simple as enjoying a fabulous cup of coffee or the support of your community, like all of you amazing keto queens out there! This practice is truly transformative because when you focus on what you appreciate, it sets a positive tone for the day. Next up is the importance of mindful eating. Now, I know we all have a tendency to scarf down a meal while scrolling through our phones or binge-watching our favorite shows. But I invite you to turn this around. When you sit down for a meal, take a moment to appreciate the colors on your plate, the aromas wafting up to your nose, and the textures of each bite. Savoring each mouthful not only enhances your eating experience but allows you to cultivate a deeper connection with your food, leading to a more satisfying dietary journey overall. Plus, it's easier to stick to your keto plan when you actually enjoy what you eat! Now, let's chat a little about community, shall we? Being surrounded by like-minded individuals can vastly improve your happiness quotient. So, whether it's our Facebook group or other local meet-ups, tap into that sense of belonging. Share your triumphs, your mess-ups-oh yes, girl, there will be some of those, but that's part of the journey! Create friendships that spark joy and provide encouragement when those paleo cookies start calling your name. We all have those moments, and having someone to chat with-whether it be sharing recipes or just venting about the struggle-can make a world of difference. And let's not forget about movement! Exercise can be such a powerful tool when it comes to happiness. Now, I know some of y'all may think of exercise as a chore, but let's shift that perspective. Think of it as a celebration of what your body can do, rather than a punishment for what you ate. Choose activities that create joy for you! Dance like nobody's watching or sign up for a fun Zumba class. The endorphins you release during physical activity are natural mood boosters and can keep negativity at bay. Finally, please allow yourself to indulge-guilt-free! Part of your happiness on the keto journey is being able to enjoy special treats from time to time. Have a slice of your favorite low-carb pie or whip up some keto-friendly baked goods. It's absolutely crucial to remember that moderation is the key here. Enjoy those treats without the guilt, because life is about balance and enjoyment too, right? As we wrap up this segment of our journey together, remember: Happiness is not a destination; it's a continuous journey, one that you craft every single day. With every choice you make, whether it's about your meals, your mindset, or your relationships, you have the power to create a life filled with joy and satisfaction tailored to you. So, let's commit to bringing more happy into our lives as we navigate our keto paths together. Thank you for listening, beautiful souls! Also, the dynamic role of physical distance and institutional borders may differ significantly across different R&D networks depending upon the type of knowledge that is exchanged (tacit vs. codified) and the nature of the links: arm's length market transactions, hierarchical relations or network forms of coordination (Whittington et al., 2009). Cross-network interdependencies should also be taken into account. For example, international mobility should have a positive impact on regional citation flows as inventor movement is thought to be an important driver of knowledge spillovers (Agrawal et al., 2006). International mobility may, in turn, have a positive impact on large distance collaborations as mobile inventors act as bridges across teams of inventors working for different organizations (Breschi and Lissoni, 2009). Conversely, one could argue that, the more individual inventors and research teams can freely move, the less R&D organizations will feel the need to locate R&D labs abroad or to sign collaborative agreements with foreign partners. In this sense, understanding the extent to which globalization reduces constraints on geographical mobility is important for assessing side-effects in other dimensions of R&D networks. Here we employ a gravity approach to quantify simultaneously the strength of borders and distance on multiple innovation networks constructed from about 2.4 million patents recorded by the European Patent Office (EPO). We analyze a large sample of developed nations over many years to investigate the dichotomy arising from localizing constraints of R&D spillovers and agglomeration economies in R&D clusters vis-a-vis the tendency to expand R&D networks via long-range collaborations. Our study moves beyond previous efforts to understand the geography of research collaboration in many respects. First, we study a large set of developed countries at a low level of spatial aggregation. Second, we analyze a set of interrelated patent networks using the same analytic approach. Third, in our analysis we investigate, jointly, the physical distance effect and the country-border effect on a global scale. Few previous studies have investigated the dynamics of the geographical distance and border-effects simultaneously, focusing either on Europe (Hoekman et al., 2010) or the United States (Singh and Marx, 2013). Fourth, we focus on the evolution of barriers to the internationalization of knowledge networks over two decades, whereas most of previous studies in this field have had to take a static viewpoint. Our more comprehensive analysis allows us to examine and ultimately quantify the effect of European integration efforts in the context of global network evolution trends.1 Beyond scientific relevance of developing methods to quantify R&D network evolution, a better understanding of how distance and borders influence the structure and evolution of R&D networks is important to orient the policy debate. In particular, the European Research Area (ERA) vision of an "open space for knowledge and growth" stands as the most recent in a long line of integration efforts within the European Union (EU).

As he walked, the Dalai Lama's thoughts turned to his childhood, to the visions and dreams that had guided him. He remembered the words of his guru, who had told him that he was the reincarnation of the 13th Dalai Lama, the embodiment of compassion and wisdom. He knew that he had a great responsibility, to carry on the legacy of his predecessor, to continue the work of spreading peace and understanding. The Dalai Lama's journey was far from over. He would face many challenges, many obstacles, but he was determined to persevere, to continue his quest for freedom and justice. He knew that he was not alone, that there were many who believed in him, who supported him. And so, he pressed on, his heart filled with hope and determination, his spirit unbroken.

The discovery of FOXP3 as a critical transcription factor for Treg development and function has led to a deeper understanding of the complex regulatory mechanisms governing immune homeostasis. The Treg-specific demethylated region (TSDR) in the FOXP3 gene plays a crucial role in maintaining stable FOXP3 expression, which is essential for Treg function. The dependence of Tregs on IL-2 production from conventional or effector T cells (Teffs) highlights the intricate interplay between Treg and Teff subsets. For instance, reduction of IL-2 in the pancreatic islets leads to a loss of FOXP3 expression and Treg numbers in a mouse model of autoimmune type 1 diabetes (T1D), underscoring the critical role of IL-2 in Treg function. The identification of ROR t-expressing FOXP3+ Tregs, also known as Th17 Tregs, has added a new layer of complexity to the Treg repertoire. These cells exhibit a unique phenotype, characterized by the expression of the Th17 lineage-specific transcription factor ROR t, and can produce IL-17 upon in vitro activation. The finding that the frequency of ROR t+ FOXP3+ Th17 Tregs in the colon is determined by the composition of the intestinal commensal microbiota suggests that these cells play a critical role in regulating the intestinal Th17 immune responses to commensal and pathogenic bacteria, while preventing inflammation. The adoptive transfer of ROR t+ FOXP3+ Th17 Tregs has been shown to completely abrogate the development of inflammation in a mouse colitis model, and display increased suppressive capacity in vivo compared to conventional ROR t- FOXP3+ Tregs. Furthermore, a subset of FOXP3intROR t+ Tregs has been found to prevent the development of autoimmune diabetes in the NOD model, highlighting the potential therapeutic applications of these cells. The mutually opposing regulatory functions of the FOXP3 and ROR t transcription factors have raised questions regarding the origin and differentiation of Th17 Tregs. The hypothesis that Th17 T effector cells (Teff) and Tregs could share a similar differentiation pathway, and have been selected to ensure immunity at the barrier surfaces and the adaptation of the host to commensal bacteria, provides a framework for understanding the complex interplay between these two cell subsets. The discovery of Th17 Tregs has significant implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for autoimmune diseases. The ability to expand and manipulate Th17 Tregs in vitro or in vivo could provide a new approach for the treatment of conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, type 1 diabetes, and multiple sclerosis. Further research is needed to fully elucidate the mechanisms governing Th17 Treg development and function, and to explore the potential therapeutic applications of these cells.

The challenge of reconciling economic growth with sustainable consumption and production patterns is a pressing issue in the context of climate change mitigation. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has emphasized the need for a significant reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to limit global warming to 2 C above pre-industrial levels. However, recent studies have shown that technical solutions alone may not be sufficient to achieve this goal, and that a broader set of mitigation options, including changes in consumption patterns, is necessary. One approach to reducing consumption-driven GHG emissions is to adopt a "reasonable" consumption strategy, which involves changing consumption patterns and complementing them with "reasonable" production strategies. This can be achieved through a combination of eco-efficiency and consumer efficiency measures. For example, consumers can reduce their energy consumption by adopting energy-efficient appliances and behaviors, while also promoting sustainable production practices through their purchasing decisions. Another approach is to shift the pattern of consumption towards goods and services that are less GHG emission-intensive. This can be achieved through a variety of means, including changes in consumer behavior, product design, and supply chain management. For instance, consumers can choose to purchase products with lower carbon footprints, such as locally sourced and organic food, or products with extended lifetimes, such as durable goods. Companies can also design products with sustainability in mind, such as by reducing packaging waste or using recycled materials. However, changing consumption patterns and production practices is not without its challenges. For example, some studies have found that lifestyle changes can have negative impacts on economic growth, and that consumers may not always make environmentally conscious choices. Additionally, the rebound effect, where consumers re-spend saved money on more GHG-intensive activities, can offset the benefits of reduced consumption. To overcome these challenges, policymakers and businesses must work together to create an enabling environment that supports sustainable consumption and production patterns. This can be achieved through a range of policies and measures, including carbon pricing, subsidies for sustainable products and services, and education and awareness-raising campaigns. In conclusion, reducing consumption-driven GHG emissions is a critical component of climate change mitigation, and requires a comprehensive approach that combines eco-efficiency and consumer efficiency measures. By adopting a "reasonable" consumption strategy, shifting the pattern of consumption towards less GHG emission-intensive goods and services, and promoting sustainable production practices, we can reduce our environmental impact while also promoting economic growth and development.

He used to wonder sometimes what she would do if she ever got ahead of him; but she never did. For Toto was very fond of playing in the woods near the house, and he tore his clothes and broke his things in a way that was perfectly astonishing. However, the old lady never scolded him, no matter how often she had to patch and mend. She would shake her head over his pranks, and say, "Ah, Toto! if I could only see you!" and then sigh, and go back to her work again. But it happened one day that Toto went farther into the forest than usual, and lost himself among the trees. He wandered about for hours, looking for the path home; but it was nowhere to be found. It was growing dark, and he began to be afraid that he should have to spend the night alone in the forest. Just then he heard voices talking. He crept forward softly, and peeped through the bushes. He saw a small clearing in the midst of the trees, and in the middle of it stood a tiny house, built of moss and bark. In front of it sat two little men, with long white beards, smoking long pipes. They looked exactly alike, except that one wore a blue coat, and the other a brown one. They took their pipes from their mouths, and said, "Ough!" first one, then the other. Then they filled and lighted them again, and smoked away vigorously. At last Brown-coat spoke. "Ugh!" said Blue-coat. "So'm I." Then they smoked awhile in silence. "I feel like doing something," said Brown-coat, presently. "So do I," replied Blue-coat. "What shall we do?" asked Brown-coat. Blue-coat shook his head. "Too wet," he answered. "We might play ball," suggested Brown-coat. "That's more fun," assented Blue-coat. So they played tag till they were tired, and then they sat down again and smoked for a while in silence. "There's nothing like a pipe after exercise," remarked Brown-coat. "No," agreed Blue-coat. "How is yours?" "Oh, mine smokes beautifully!" cried Brown-coat, enthusiastically. "Well, I guess I'll have another whiff myself," said Blue-coat. And they smoked away as before. By this time it was quite dark, and Toto began to be frightened. He thought that if he ran past quickly, the queer little men would not notice him, and so he might escape without being seen. Accordingly, he darted out from behind the bushes, and sped across the clearing toward the opposite side. Alas! he had forgotten about the tree-stumps. Over went Toto, flat on his nose. The little men jumped up in surprise. "Hoity-toity!" exclaimed Blue-coat. "What's that?" "It sounded like somebody falling down," replied Brown-coat. "It can't be anybody, because there isn't anybody here but us," said Blue-coat. "But I certainly heard something fall," persisted Brown-coat. At this moment Toto picked himself up, rather bruised and sore, and tried to run away; but he stumbled over another stump and fell again. "There it is again!" cried Blue-coat. "Dear me! how very strange!" exclaimed Brown-coat. "I certainly felt something brush against my leg." "And I felt it too," said Blue-coat. "It must be a catamount." And he picked up a stick to defend himself.

But what I am saying is that you can't let that energy and excitement turn into anxiety and pressure. Because when you make something special, you're putting pressure on yourself. You're putting pressure on your team. And that's when you start to underperform. Let me give you an example. I was working with a tennis player, and she was getting ready for a big tournament. And her coach kept telling her, "This is it. This is the one. You gotta win this one." And I'm like, "Coach, what are you doing? You're putting way too much pressure on her." And the coach is like, "No, no, no. I'm just trying to motivate her." And I'm like, "Motivate her? You're gonna choke her." Because when you make something special, you're taking away from the process. You're taking away from the preparation. You're taking away from the hard work that got her to that point. And then what happens? She goes out there and she starts to think about winning. She starts to think about losing. She starts to think about all the what-ifs. And before you know it, she's tight, she's nervous, and she's not performing at her best. And then what do you do? You start to question yourself. You start to question your training. You start to question your coach. And it's a downward spiral. So, let's flip the script. Let's make every competition important, but not special. Let's focus on the process. Of the possible criminal offences Mr Blair could face in this country, the most likely is misconduct in a public office. It is committed when a public official acting in the course of their duties wilfully neglects to perform that duty, or wilfully misconducts themselves to such a degree that their behaviour amounts to an abuse of the public's trust in them. The offence was used frequently in the phone-hacking scandal to prosecute police officers and other public officials who took money from journalists in return for providing stories. The former Director of Public Prosecutions, Lord MacDonald QC, believes Tony Blair's conduct in the build-up to the Iraq war could amount to misconduct in public office. Speaking to The Times, he highlighted an example of "particularly egregious misconduct" set out in the Chilcot report. It occurred about a week before the war and days before the final legal advice of 17 March 2003 from the then Attorney General, Lord Goldsmith. Through his official, David Brummell, the attorney general informed Mr Blair that it "was an essential part of the legal basis for military action without a further resolution of the Security Council that there is strong evidence that Iraq has failed to comply with and co-operate fully in the implementation of resolution 1441". Lord Macdonald said: "Yet, without seeking any advice whatsoever, or calling for any evidence to determine whether this critical condition was met, Mr Blair simply expressed 'the unequivocal view' that such further breaches had indeed occurred." Sir John said: "It is unclear what specific grounds Mr Blair relied upon in reaching his view. "In his advice of 7 March, Lord Goldsmith had said that the views of (weapons inspectors) UNMOVIC and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) would be highly significant in demonstrating hard evidence of non-compliance and non-cooperation. In the exchange of letters on 14 and 15 March between Mr Brummell and Number 10 [Downing Street], there is no reference to their views; the only view referred to was that of Mr Blair." He concluded: "Senior ministers should have considered the question posed in Mr Brummell's letter of 14 March, either in the defence and overseas policy committee or a 'war cabinet', on the basis of formal advice. Such a committee should then have reported its conclusions to Cabinet before its members were asked to endorse the government's policy."
