The exact contribution of charcoal rot to soybean yield loss remains unclear, particularly in the context of soil moisture stress. Previous studies have demonstrated that charcoal rot severity increases with increased soil moisture stress (Mengistu et al., 2015), but the precise impact of this interaction on soybean yield is still unknown. This knowledge gap is critical to address, as soybean is a vital crop for global food security and charcoal rot is a significant threat to its production. To bridge this knowledge gap, this study aimed to investigate the impact of charcoal rot on soybean yield under varying levels of soil moisture stress. The experiment was conducted in a rain-fed environment, where soil moisture stress is a common occurrence, and charcoal rot is a prevalent disease. The study employed a split-plot design, with soil moisture stress as the main plot factor and charcoal rot inoculation as the subplot factor. Soil moisture stress was manipulated by withholding irrigation at critical growth stages, while charcoal rot inoculation was achieved through the introduction of M. phaseolina spores into the soil. Soil moisture stress was monitored using tensiometers, which measured soil water tension in kilopascals (kPa). The tensiometers were installed at a depth of 30 cm, which corresponds to the root zone of soybean plants. Soil water tension readings were taken daily, and irrigation was applied when the tension reached 50 kPa, which is the threshold for initiating irrigation in sandy loam soils (Smiley, 1999). Charcoal rot inoculation was performed at the V3 growth stage, when soybean plants are most susceptible to infection (Mengistu et al., 2011). The inoculum was prepared by growing M. phaseolina on potato dextrose agar (PDA) plates for 10 days, followed by harvesting and suspending the spores in sterile water. The spore suspension was then applied to the soil around the soybean plants at a rate of 10^6 spores per plant. The experiment was replicated three times, and the plots were arranged in a randomized complete block design. Soybean yield was measured at maturity, and the data were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine the main effects of soil moisture stress and charcoal rot inoculation, as well as their interaction. Preliminary results indicate that soil moisture stress significantly reduced soybean yield, with yields decreasing by 25% under moderate soil moisture stress (50-60 kPa) and by 50% under severe soil moisture stress (70-80 kPa). Charcoal rot inoculation also significantly reduced soybean yield, with yields decreasing by 30% under inoculated conditions. The interaction between soil moisture stress and charcoal rot inoculation was significant, with the greatest yield reduction observed under severe soil moisture stress and inoculated conditions. These findings suggest that charcoal rot has a significant impact on soybean yield, particularly under soil moisture stress conditions. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the contribution of charcoal rot to soybean yield loss and inform the development of effective management strategies for this disease.

We have recently examined the residual effects of recreational cannabis use on brain function in adult and adolescent cannabis users by meta-analytically combining the data from 20 published studies employing functional MRI techniques (Blest-Hopley et al., 2018). While some of these studies investigated cannabis-using participants after a period of abstinence, several others allowed cannabis use up until, as short a period as, 3 h prior to scanning. Therefore, interpretation of the results of these studies may be confounded by residual acute effects of THC and its metabolites that may still be left in cannabis-using participants as well as effects of withdrawal from cannabis. On the other hand, brain functional alteration following a sustained period of abstinence has also been investigated, though the results of these studies are less consistent, with users showing both increased (Chang et al., 2006; De Bellis et al., 2013; Jacobsen et al., 2004; Schweinsburg et al., 2008; Tapert et al., 2007) and decreased (Chang et al., 2006; Schweinsburg et al., 2008) activation compared to controls. Studies comparing cannabis users with different periods of abstinence have found greater activation in the prefrontal cortex and insula in recently abstinent users compared to users with longer (at least 27 days) periods of abstinence, who in turn had greater activation in the precentral gyrus (Schweinsburg et al., 2010). Another study that investigated cannabis users at multiple time-points following abstinence, reported that 28 days of abstinence resulted in reduced activation difference to controls in some regions, but some differences in brain activation persisted (Pillay et al., 2008). Therefore, understanding differences in brain activation between currently using (or non-abstinent) and abstinent cannabis users (ACU), is of particular interest. However, to our knowledge existing evidence in this regard has not been systematically reviewed and summarized using meta-analytic approaches. Hence, we have carried out a meta-analysis complementary to that previously reported by us (Blest-Hopley et al., 2018) to investigate whether altered brain function associated with regular cannabis use persists even after a sustained period of abstinence from cannabis. Consistent with our approach previously (Blest-Hopley et al., 2018), we included fMRI studies that employed a wide range of cognitive activation paradigms engaging various cognitive processes rather than focusing only on task-specific approaches as in other work (Yanes et al., 2018). Our strategy was driven by two key considerations. Firstly, only a limited number of available studies have specifically employed comparable activation paradigms limiting our ability to meaningfully investigate the question of interest here. More importantly, as we have argued before (Blest-Hopley et al., 2018), the effects of cannabis use are unlikely to be limited to only those brain regions that sub-serve cognitive processes examined in studies conducted hitherto. Rather they are more likely to be widely distributed, consistent with ubiquitous distribution of cannabinoid receptors in the brain (Iversen, 2003).

They contented themselves with occasional barbed remarks that echoed through the drawing-rooms of their acquaintance, whisperings of scandal and disapproval that found their way back to John Vavasor, who stoutly declared himself indifferent to their censure. He had what he deemed a superior intellect and a noble spirit, but his poverty was a shackle against the grand aspirations that perpetually roamed within his mind. Thus it transpired that Alice Vavasor grew up amidst an atmosphere of muted grandeur and careworn struggle. The sun-drenched memories of her youth were tinged with shadows of discontent, brightly-lit balls and elegant soirees merely tales told by acquaintances who had chosen the path to affluence that eluded her father's grasp. Yet Alice, perceptive and finely attuned to the reputations woven in the fabric of society, absorbed the lessons of her surroundings with remarkable keen-eyed clarity. She was beloved by the local children for her gentle laughter and grand tales spun from intricate imaginings, and they lauded her enchanting company, but her heart longed for something beyond the simple pleasures of her youth. With an unquenched thirst for the world beyond her father's modest abode, the cobbled streets and horse-drawn carriages of London called to her like siren songs along a perilous shore; enthralling, yet fraught with hidden dangers. As the years flowed gently onward like the slow passage of a river winding its way through a serene landscape, Alice turned her thoughts towards her own destiny. And this burgeoning desire would not remain untethered for long. She moved through her father's modest household in quest of self-definition, her mother's legacy of fervent ambition swelling silently within her breast as she often gazed into the mirror to confront those familiar features, illuminating a latent spirit aflame with aspirations. Alice knew she was destined for more than the joys of pastoral life; more than the insipid gossip of lesser gentlemen or the kind hearted, simple lives of her neighbors. She was determined to seek her fortune amidst the mock silks and gilded mirrors lining the drawing-rooms of those whose social standing seemed to swell like their opulent gowns. Yet as she mused on these lofty aspirations, the reality of her lineage gnawed at her, like an errant fly that besmirches the sweet offerings of dessert. It was on the eve of her coming out that she was approached by a visitor of some note, Mr. Edward Clare, a man from a family of undeniable prominence which firmly secured him within the upper echelons of society. The clever parlance and charming disposition of Mr. Clare dazzled the young Alice, as did his undeniable status, very much in contrast to her own, an innocent prey ensnared by the world she so desperately wished to invade. Their conversations wrapped around delicate subjects-literature, art, and the political climate-each meeting a subtle thrust towards exploring the possibilities of a future that might weave their fates together. Yet, deep within Alice's heart, there lingered an awareness that her mother's shadows played a delicate dance with her own desires; a memory of scorn that could surface at any moment, questioning her right to seek happiness amid the living tapestry of London's elite. And as the night of her debut approached, a quiet dread began to cloud the anticipation that thrummed through her veins. The delicate line between dreams and reality wavered like the flickering candlelight, beckoning her forth into the hurly-burly world that awaited.

He had even acquired a little distinction; not much, not enough to spoil him either for business or society - yet something, enough to enable people to say, "He did very well at Oxford." And he had made some good friends, which perhaps was what his father prized most. One or two scions of noble houses came to Harley Street to see him; he had invitations from a few fine people for their country houses, and ladies of note who had a number of daughters were disposed to smile upon the merchant's son. All these things pleased Mr Burton much, and he had been quite willing to assent to his son's wish that he should end and complete his experiences by a visit to America, before beginning the work which had always been his final destination. He had now just returned from that expedition, and it had been intended that he should step at once into his place in the business - that business which was as good as, nay, much better than, an estate. Up to this time the young man had made no objection to the plan, which he was perfectly acquainted with. So far as his father knew, he was as well disposed towards that plan as Mr Burton himself, and looked forward to it with as much satisfaction. It may therefore be supposed that it was with no small consternation, with displeasure, disappointment, and indignation, one greater than the other, that the father had sat and listened to the sudden and astounding protest of the son. Not go into the business! It was to Mr Burton as if a man had refused to go to heaven; indeed it was less reasonable by far: for though going to heaven is supposed to be the height of everybody's desire, even the most pious of clergymen has been known to say "God forbid!" when he has been warned that he stands on the brink of another world. One would wish generally to postpone that highest of consummations; but to refuse to go into the business was a thing incredible. Mr Burton had raged and stormed, but afterwards he had been brought into partial calm through the evident impossibility of treating his son in any other way. To scold Gervase was practically impossible. To treat him like a child or a fool was a thing that could not be done. His own composure naturally affected all who had to do with him, and his father among the rest. That passionate speaking or abuse, or violence of any kind, should fall dumb before his easy and immovable quiet, was inevitable. He had waited till the outburst was over, and then he had gone on. "And what else then, if not in my office, do you mean to do?" Mr Burton now said. "I suppose, sir," said Gervase, "I am right in believing, as everybody does, that you are a rich man?"

As I walked away from the Hall, the yew-lined path unwinding before me like a dark and foreboding serpent, I couldn't shake the feeling that I was being watched. The silence was oppressive, punctuated only by the soft rustling of leaves and the distant call of a bird. I quickened my pace, my heart beating with an unspoken fear. The trees seemed to close in around me, their branches like skeletal fingers reaching out to snatch me back. I pushed aside a curtain of ivy and emerged onto the bowling-green, the bright sunlight a welcome respite from the gloom of the forest. The green was indeed a sight to behold, the lush grass a vibrant emerald, the rolling hills a gentle undulation of green and gold. The air was thick with the scent of fresh cut grass and the distant tang of the sea. I breathed deeply, feeling the tension in my chest begin to ease. But my respite was short-lived, for as I gazed out across the green, I saw him - Sir Massingberd, standing at the edge of the green, his eyes fixed upon me with an unnerving intensity. I felt a shiver run down my spine as he began to make his way towards me, his long strides eating up the distance. I turned to leave, but my feet seemed rooted to the spot. He reached me, his face a mask of cold calculation, and spoke in a voice that sent a chill down my spine. "Ah, Mr. Long, I see you're enjoying the view. Yes, the bowling-green is one of my favorite spots. The fresh air and the exercise do wonders for the constitution, don't you think?" I nodded, my voice caught in my throat. He smiled, a cold, mirthless smile, and continued, "I see you're not as keen on socializing as I had hoped. Perhaps you're not yet accustomed to the company of the gentry. Fear not, my dear Mr. Long, I shall introduce you to the ways of the aristocracy. You will learn to navigate the intricacies of our little society, and you will find that it is not as daunting as you imagine." I felt a surge of revulsion at his words, but I bit back my retort, knowing that I was no match for his cunning. He turned and walked away, leaving me to ponder the true nature of the man. What secrets lay hidden behind those cold, calculating eyes? What darkness lurked in the recesses of his mind? I shivered, despite the warmth of the sun, and knew that I had to be careful. For in the world of the gentry, one misstep could mean ruin, and I was already walking a tightrope, balancing precariously between respectability and disaster.

"Don't slam the door, Minnie!" Minnie storms into her room, the door thudding behind her like a mini earthquake. She collapses onto her unmade bed, the denim blanket crumpling under her weight. Inside her chest, the thrill of the afternoon intertwines with a nagging sense of doubt. Was she supposed to feel this way? It's just a kiss-it's just a dance. But the memories of those touches linger like the last few notes of a favorite song, replaying in her mind. The walls of her sanctuary, smeared with posters of rock icons, cheerleading trophies, and a few random pieces of art she had hastily taped up, offer no answers. She flips through her record collection, fingers grazing the covers like they're old friends. Abba, Fleetwood Mac, anything that feels alive, electric. But her heart races as she lands on a forgotten gem-David Bowie. She places it on the turntable, the needle crackling to life, and the first notes of "Rebel Rebel" burst forth, seeping into the room. She doesn't want to think about Patty Hearst or the chaotic world her mother channels obsessively from that flickering screen. She wants to escape, to be swept away by glittering dreams and zealous beats. She starts to dance, the rhythm and melody wrapping around her like a warm embrace, coaxing out the little girl who still believes in magic. Her body catches fire as she spins, tapping into memories of her friends in the park-the laughter, the shared secrets, the exhilarating taste of freedom. Each twirl releases a bit of tension, those stupid insecurities-like a bird shaking off rain, or a flower finally reaching toward the sun. She spins until the edges of her vision blur into electric hues, and she allows herself to imagine the world without holds barred. Minnie pauses, the room settling, the music still pulsing gently in the background. She stares at the mirror across from her desk, catching a glimpse of herself. What does she really see? A fierce heart wrapped in uncertainty, hidden behind uncertainty; a face that some see as plain, but she herself sees as a canvas waiting for paint. Her wild, chestnut locks tumble past her shoulders, a tangle of curls refusing order. Those freckles dancing across her nose? More like constellations begging to be connected. She snaps her fingers and winks at the reflection. "You're the star of this show, girl!" Encouraged by her own pep talk, she dives into her closet, rummaging through clothes that scream for attention. A glittery top with long sleeves, a skirt that floats like the clouds, and some bright, mismatched stockings to complete the ensemble. Why not be the outrageous version of herself? No more ordinary for Minnie. She plops down in front of her desk, crafting plans for the following day-a new beginning, a fresh start, a way to be her own rebel. She scribbles notes in an old notebook, her exuberant thoughts spilling over the page. Dance class? Or maybe a protest rally? Everything feels like an invitation, an open door. The door cracks open, and Charlotte peeks in, almost hesitant. "Minnie? You... you okay?" She turns, flashing a bright smile, the kind that paints over cracks like a fresh coat of paint. "Just planning my world takeover, Mom. Want in?" Charlotte chuckles softly, the tension easing slightly. "Sure, let's conquer the world together." With a playful wink, Minnie speeds back into her whirlwind plans. Who knew that life could be this sparkly? Time to channel that rebellious spirit into something brighter. Something out there was just waiting for her to find it.

He was rich now because he had invented a turbine engine, and, because we had helped a little once when some men had gotten his model away from him, he was going to send us all to college, and every little while he did something fine for us-like paying for this vacation trip. "Well," says I, "what next?" "Better climb back into the wagon and make for home," says Plunk Smalley. Mark wrinkled up his nose and looked out at the lake. "D-don't exactly fancy goin' home like this," he says. "Nothin' else to do," says Binney Jenks. Mark turned to the man who drove us out. "Kind of a humorous feller, ain't you?" he says, and the man grinned, not mean, but like he was enjoying himself and wouldn't mind being right friendly. "I calc'late to know a joke when I see one," says he. "This is one, all r-right," says Mark; "but maybe we can pull some of the laugh out of it if we can get a good holt onto it.... Who owns this l-lumber-pile?" "Man named Ames." "What kind of a man is he?" "Takes after you for flesh, and lets folks call him Jim," says the driver. "Live in town?" "Yes." "Guess we better call on Mr. Ames then," says Mark. "Pile into the wagon, f-fellers." "What's the idea?" I asked him. "'Ain't g-got that far yet," says Mark. That was the way with him. You couldn't get anything out of him till he was ready to tell you. You could ask questions all day without finding out a thing. So we got into the wagon and drove back the ten miles to town. The driver stopped in front of a big white house.

Clickety click, clickety clack, went the shining needles all through the long afternoons, when Toto was away in the wood; and nothing answered the needles, except the tea-kettle, which always did its best to make things cheerful. But even in her knitting there were often trials for the grandmother. Sometimes her ball rolled off her lap and away over the floor; and then the poor old lady had a hard time of it groping about in all the corners (there never was a kitchen that had so many corners as hers), and knocking her head against the table and the dresser. The kettle was always much troubled when anything of this sort happened. He puffed angrily, and looked at the tongs. "If I had legs," he said, "I would make some use of them, even if they were awkward and ungainly. But when a person is absolutely all head and legs, it is easy to understand that he should have no heart." The tongs never made any reply to these remarks, but stood stiff and straight, and pretended not to hear. But the grandmother had other troubles beside dropping her ball. Toto was a very good boy,-better, in fact, than most boys,-and he loved his grandmother very much indeed; but he was forgetful, as every child is. Sometimes he forgot this, and sometimes that, and sometimes the other; for you see his heart was generally in the forest, and his head went to look after it; and that often made trouble. He always meant to get before he went to the forest everything that his grandmother could possibly want while he was away. Wood and water he never forgot, for he always brought those in before breakfast. But sometimes the brown potatoes sat waiting in the cellar closet, with their jackets all buttoned up, wondering why they were not taken out, as their brothers had been the day before, and put in a wonderful wicker cage, and carried off to see the great world. And the yellow apples blushed with anger and a sense of neglect; while the red apples turned yellow with vexation. And sometimes,-well, sometimes this sort of thing would happen: one day the old lady was going to make some gingerbread; for there was not a bit in the house, and Toto could not live without gingerbread. So she said, "Toto, go to the cupboard and get me the ginger-box and the soda, that's a good boy!" Now, Toto was standing in the doorway when his grandmother spoke, and just at that moment he caught sight of a green lizard on a stone at a little distance. He wanted very much to catch that lizard; but he was an obedient boy, and always did what "Granny" asked him to do.

He hit double figures in his debut campaign, but just one of those came in the league and he was unable to prevent Boro from dropping into the Championship. Intestinal worms, roundworms, hookworms and tapeworms. These creatures rarely kill, but they will cause discomfort and embarrassment. In more severe cases, they can grow in the brain, causing fits and seizures. Tapeworms are usually contracted when eating under-cooked meat, whereas the larvae of hookworms and roundworms don't even need to be eaten. They can access a body by burrowing through skin, without the victim noticing. Once in your body, roundworms share their victims' ingested food (although they can also block the intestines). The hookworm, however, feasts on the blood. Don't eat under-cooked meat and never walk barefoot in developing or tropical countries because the roundworm ascaris lumbricoides is said to infect 75% of the world's population. 6. Irukandji. The Irukandji jellyfish, considered by researchers to be one of the world's most poisonous creatures, is only the size of a thimble. A tiny jellyfish that is almost invisible, the Irukandji has a painless sting, but can cause massive pain and suffering afterward. The threat is not just for swimmers. It's been reported that a 45-year-old Filipino was stung by an Irukandji while fishing from a bulk carrier. The man, who was airlifted to hospital, was 25 meters above sea level when stung. It's thought that the creature was blown up with sea spray. Jellyfish nets aren't effective either because this tiny animal can slip through. Wearing a "stinger suit" is advised when swimming in Queensland or the surrounding region during Irukandji season, and never swim on beaches without lifeguards with reliable local knowledge. This little beast is most problematic around the east coast of Australia. More: A traveler's guide to eating insects. 5. Wandering spiders. One of the most venomous and dangerous spiders in the world is the Brazilian "wandering spider," or "banana spider," although its bites are also famous for another nasty side effect. The venom can cause involuntary and long-lasting priapism for men. Chances are the victim won't be able to put it to good use before he dies from the other components of this potent toxin. 4. Bloodworms. The very name "bloodworm" sounds macabre. But the damage they can do to the human body, and the sheer scale of the problems caused by these tiny parasites, is far scarier. The larvae (cercaria) of these little animals live in freshwater snails, usually in relatively clear water. But when they sense a warm-blooded host, such as a human being swimming past, they swim towards it, penetrate the skin, move around the body, and finally make their home in the intestines, or the bladder, where they can live and reproduce for up to 12 years gradually destroying the organ that they made their home.

One of them, travelling farther than the rest, led in a way to the end of things for the residents of Pennyroyal as it climbed a hill at the foot of the village, set thick with hardy perennials, evergreens, and small white stones, while encircling this hill was Peter's Creek, that by and by grew up to be a river, but it had a tranquil movement, proceeding slowly on its course by reason of sharing the Pennyroyalian distaste for getting any distance from home. Then the houses in Pennyroyal: although the beautiful open country was all about them, they crowded so close together that they seemed almost to touch elbows, and now and then one of them had appeared to shove the other back in its determination to get the best view of the street. They were mostly cottages, with no front porches, but with sloping roofs and little Gothic wooden fences, and painted white, with green outside blinds, except Ambrose's, and his had been touched with a boy's imagination, its intention being plainly rose colour. Now in a double row along the outside wooden sidewalk this morning the linden trees were dropping fragrant yellow plumes inches deep in the ruts of the clay road, while over the chimneys whirled the last of the spring's apple blossoms. Bees buzzed among the flowers, birds chattered, flying nervously from one tree to another in an effort to be through with breakfast before the disturbing human element should get about; and hitched to a nearby post Ambrose's horse and gig were waiting. The young man surveyed his equipage with the eyes of an idealist. Old Liza had seen service, but her toilet had been made in the spirit of the best foot foremost; her coat had been freshly curried, her gray mane and tail carefully combed, and in her manner there was an air of emotional anticipation. With one foot hovering above the step of his gig, Ambrose suddenly paused. The laprobe inside the carriage was quivering. "Holy Moses!" Reaching underneath, the young man drew forth a small black and brown object whose legs and tail were five upturned points of supplication. Setting it upright on the ground, his face hardened. "Ain't I told you you couldn't come with me, Moses?" he began sternly. "Ef ever there was a crittur, human or otherwise, with a talent for bein' where it wasn't wanted, it's you! Besides, ain't I just locked you in the stable?" The softening in his master's manner, visible in his last question, in the twitching of his eyebrows, in the slight movement of the tip of his long nose, was familiar to Moses. Casually he approached Ambrose's leg, but midway there, sensing defeat and not being an amiable beast, he planted his feet wide apart, barked as loudly as chronic hoarseness permitted, and straightway the young man humbled himself before him.

In this dubious cultural milieu, the true power of feminist narratives seems muted, eclipsed by a cacophony that bellows only one kind of femininity-one that appears eager and endlessly malleable to male whims. It seems that no matter how far we've traveled on the road to gender equality, each new step forward feels punctuated by relentless leaps back. Media portrayals have taken on an astonishingly impressive ability to marry overt sexualization with purported empowerment, leaving viewers tangled in a web of contradictions. Surely, this hybridization stirs unease; after all, nothing screams "progress" quite like the relentless trope of the dumb blonde whose sparkle is matched only by her vapidity. The latest manifestations of this narrative are particularly striking in their audacity, as though they are theatrical expressions of an elaborate tragicomedy wherein female ambition is measured against the frivolity of Instagram likes and Snapchat filters. The modern entertainment landscape, with its glossy sheen, offers a panorama of women who are both tantalizingly approachable yet disappointingly one-dimensional-a baffling concoction of shallow caricatures touted as icons of empowerment. It seems the algorithm governing our cultural output favors images over intellect, spectacle over substance, and style over story. What, then, do we make of the proliferation of shows featuring the same tired motifs? As more networks tune into the frequencies of regressive gender discourse, we find ourselves ensnared in a cycle where 'empowerment' is rendered vacant, becoming merely a brand identity-marketed along with an overpriced fragrance or a dubious diet plan. The ironic twist is that while we celebrate the rise of title-holding women in boardrooms and legislative chambers, prime-time television continues to parade a parade of chaos disguised as progress, where the schadenfreude of watching other women stumble in their endeavors becomes all too irresistible. Consider the curious case of the reality TV star, now seemingly a harbinger of cultural capital, draped in privilege yet stripped of any meaningful narrative. A starlet's rise no longer depends on talent or mastery of craft; instead, it thrives on strategically engineered controversies, spray-tanned appearances, and the gossip columns that diligently chart their rise and fall. This spectacle raises troubling questions: what does it mean when the most celebrated accomplishments are rooted in shock value rather than substance? Why, as women scramble to claim agency, do we find the media more enthralled with the color of their nails than with the color of their ideas? Now we turn to the creators themselves. The writers, directors, and producers who shape these narratives could fundamentally alter this dispiriting trajectory, yet many opt instead to ride the coattails of the timeworn archetypes that assiduously appeal to the lowest common denominator. It would seem that subversive stories, those that break the mold and venture beyond the established norms, struggle to gain traction amidst the endless repetition of 'safe' tropes. Innovators in the industry strive tirelessly, only to find their unique visions drowned out by an industry eager to pounce on the familiar-suddenly it's not just women on our screens who seem uninspired; the creators behind them often appear equally bound by a fear of risking originality. It is a conundrum set against a relentless backdrop of media saturation where true empowerment could flourish, should we dare to let the voices of honest femininity rise above the din. The true challenge lies not simply in resisting the allure of well-trodden pathways, but in cultivating a broadening of the narrative lens-a lens through which women can be seen not merely as objects or caricatures, but as complex individuals refusing to be reduced to hollow stereotypes.

And yet, as we examine the foundational tenets of these Christian principles, epitomized most profoundly by the Sermon on the Mount, we encounter a remarkable dissonance between proclaimed values and practiced policies. The message delivered by Christ in that seminal sermon promoted mercy, peace, and a profound caring for the least among us. "Blessed are the peacemakers," He declared, urging a commitment to resolving conflicts without resorting to force. Yet, when we export our doctrines to foreign realms, it appears that this central Christian teaching of love thy neighbor as thyself is oftentimes lost in translation, buried beneath layers of geopolitical strategies and economic interests. In a world where diplomacy is too frequently cast aside in favor of shows of military might, how do the words of the Sermon resonate today? When we listen to Jesus' call to turn the other cheek, strive for understanding over retribution, and show mercy rather than exacting vengeance, shouldn't these teachings inform the way a purportedly Christian-influenced nation conducts itself internationally? Shouldn't they be guiding the conversations around how we engage with nations we deem adversaries? Yet here we are, steeped in a culture that often celebrates aggression over dialogue, demonstrating power through force instead of enacting the empathy espoused by those we claim to revere. It's an irony that strikes at the heart of the identity we project. As Netpilot astutely points out, this reluctance to embrace these attributes could stem from fear-fear of appearing weak in a world that admires strength only in its most visible forms. There's a peculiar reluctance to embrace the gospel's more challenging commandments, especially when they call for compassion that extends beyond borders and kindness that isn't confined to allies. And this fear pivots us back to the perception of "liberal" as derogatory, a label some twist to suggest a softness unsuited for the hard imperatives of global politics. But isn't there an inherent strength in those qualities that promote negotiation over dominance, patience over fervor, and dialogue over monologue? Perhaps the issue transcends politics altogether, striking instead at the essence of human nature's struggle-an internal battle between the ease of following well-trodden paths of suspicion and hostility, and the challenge of carving new pathways of trust and reconciliation. To embrace teachings that underscore peace and tolerance requires a steadfast courage to challenge existing paradigms and to redefine what it means to be just in a truly inclusive sense. For embracing the so-called liberal ideals should not be construed as a defection from core values but rather as an affirmation of humanity's potential for goodness and grace. Thus, as Boileryard and others like him have patiently endured my rants, they recognize that these musings stem from a yearning-a yearning for an era where ideology no longer stumbles over semantics, and where the commitment to peaceful resolution becomes a shared vision, not an outlier's perspective. So here it is, perhaps less a diatribe and more a declaration: why not let the foundational teachings guide us more fervently, allowing compassion and understanding to be the heralds of our dealings both at home and afar? If that makes me unabashedly liberal, then to therein lies neither shame nor contradiction, but complete conviction. Wouldn't it be refreshing if we all could say the same?

Wayland could no longer deny the truths that thrummed within him. Whether fighting or pondering, engaged with the land he cherished, or deliberating the next step of this new journey she had unconsciously invited him to take, he was moving toward a future where his heart and mind would finally be in accord.

The parents were enraged, and threatened to disinherit their child if she persisted in such conduct. She told them plainly that she could not marry against her will, and live happily with a man whom she despised and hated. At length they proposed to send their daughter to New York city, where she might forget Mayall and find a lover who possessed wealth and merit combined. The young lady agreed to go, and accordingly preparations were made for the journey. It was arranged that the father should accompany his daughter, while the mother remained at home to take care of the farm. The father and daughter started on horseback, attended by two servants on foot, to Albany, from which place they were to sail to New York in an open boat. Mayall watched their movements, and when they left the house on the morning of their departure, he mounted his fleet steed, and followed at a distance. When they reached Johnstown, the father left his daughter in charge of the servants, while he went into the village to transact business. Mayall rode up, and offered his services to escort the young lady to New York. She readily accepted the offer, and mounting behind him, they dashed off at full speed. When the father came back and learned the facts, he sent men in pursuit of the fugitives, and then hastened after them himself. But the lovers kept ahead of their pursuers until they arrived within sight of the Hudson river, when they discovered the father and servants coming up at full speed. In this dilemma, Mayall knew not what course to pursue. His first thought was to fight, but he remembered that he had only a single-shot pistol, and if he killed the father, he would still be obliged to contend with the servants, who were armed. While thus hesitating, his eye fell on the river, and seeing a small boat floating near the shore, he hastily tied his horse, and placing his fair burden in the skiff, pushed off from the shore. By the time the father and attendants arrived, Mayall and his intended bride were half way across the river. The father called to them to come back, but received no answer except a wave of the hand from the lovers. He then discharged his gun, but without effect. The lovers landed safely on the opposite side of the river, and were married before the return of the father. From: William Leete Stone, Reminiscences of Saratoga and Ballston (New York: Virtue & Yorston, 1875), pp. 90-93.

The Fyre Festival was hyped as the ultimate luxury music festival, set against the breathtaking backdrop of a private island in the Bahamas. Influencers flooded Instagram with its promise of sun, sea, and sensational music, enticing festival-goers with a curated FOMO experience like no other. The mastermind behind this grandiose vision was Billy McFarland, a young entrepreneur, alongside rapper Ja Rule. Their dream was to eclipse every festival that had come before, but alas, dreams without groundwork often wilt under the weight of reality. As the event drew closer, the promises began to unravel. What attendees found upon arrival was a far cry from the glitzy promos. Decrepit disaster relief tents replaced luxury villas. Cheese sandwiches served in foam containers stood in for gourmet meals, a stark deviation from what had been marketed. Panic took hold as guests scrambled for food, shelter, and a semblance of order amidst a scene that resembled a Hollywood disaster set more than the paradise they'd been sold. The Netflix documentary "Fyre: The Greatest Party That Never Happened" takes you on an aesthetic journey through the chaos. It delves into the behind-the-scenes blunders with compelling footage, painting a vibrant portrait of unbridled ambition colliding head-on with logistical reality. Key interviews with ex-employees and on-ground staff underscore the sheer scale of mismanagement and deceit. Conversely, Hulu's "Fyre Fraud" pulls no punches, framing McFarland as a con artist extraordinaire. It provides a broader socio-cultural critique, spotlighting the influencer culture and societal obsessions with exclusivity and luxury. They keenly questioned how far one would go to be part of a seemingly elite gathering and unpeeled layers of deception wrapped under glossy social media veneers. The documentary also lands some hard-hitting interviews with McFarland himself, shedding light on his mindset during the entire ordeal. There's a certain poetic justice in the release of these documentaries almost simultaneously. They capture the duality of the disaster from different lenses, one leaning towards narrative immersion and the other towards investigative scrutiny. My personal take? Well, both documentaries deserve a watch. Netflix offers a visceral experience with an excellent narrative arc that grips you, while Hulu delivers a probing analysis into the mind of its orchestrator and the culture that allowed such a fiasco to unfold. To sum it up, their simultaneous release became something of a spectacle, much like Fyre Festival itself, drawing views and stirring debates. Each presents distinct facets of the catastrophic event and, collectively, they offer a well-rounded understanding of what might just be the grandest festival faux pas of our times. So, after binge-watching these, my documentary count is ever closer to that 250 mark. What's in store for the next episode of 200 and Counting? Well, you'll have to stay tuned to join me on this cine-scroll. Who knows which tales of truth we'll explore next? Whether it's scandalous feasts for the eyes or serious soul-searchers, documentaries continue to illuminate, intrigue, and inspire. Until then, keep that popcorn popping, those screens aglow, and your minds curious. Tia Hill signing off, and remember, keep counting and keep exploring.

"He said, 'some people from the intelligence service had come (to our house), and they want you to cooperate,' " Khameneh recalled. "My father said, 'they want your passwords to your Facebook, web blog and e-mail.' " The young man was frightened and felt trapped. First, he didn't manage the page and therefore couldn't take it down. He assumed that the Iranian authorities just didn't understand that. "They came after me maybe because from the beginning, I was very active on the page, and you could tell that I had a close relationship - commenting back and forth - with the manager," he said. He fired off a Facebook message to the manager of the site, explaining the situation and asking that the page be taken down. The manager wrote back, refusing to deactivate the page. It's unclear exactly why the manager chose to keep the site up. But Khameneh thinks there are two reasons, both of them legitimate. Allowing Iran to succeed in taking the page down would be to defeat the very reason it was created: to challenge authority and create a greater sense of free expression. And it's possible that the manager suspected that Khameneh's e-mail was a fake and that the sender was actually someone with the Iranian authority trying to trick the manager into taking the page down, Khameneh said. "At first, I was angry, but I was also emotional" at the news that the page would stay up, Khameneh said. But "I understand that taking the page down, really, wasn't going to help my father." Can Facebook page help Israel, Iran toward peace? Password protection. Khameneh considered whether he should give up the passwords to the accounts he did control: his personal Facebook account and his e-mail. But he decided that wouldn't be wise. The Iranians could go through those accounts and find the names of his friends and other information, he feared. Khameneh seemed to be in an unwinnable situation. So he took the only action he could and deleted his e-mail and personal Facebook account. The page mocking the imam remained up. The day after his father called, Khameneh says, he got a call from his sister and mother in Iran. They were hysterical. They said Iranian authorities had arrested his father and taken him to Evin prison in Tehran, a lockup notorious for torturing inmates. Khameneh's sister begged him to give up his passwords. She pleaded for him to dismantle the Facebook page about the imam. He struggled to explain to her that he didn't control the page and that he had closed all the accounts that he could. He told her he had no options.

In contrast to Asomatognosia or Somatoparaphrenia, BIID manifests before adolescence, is not a product of any apparent brain damage, is not accompanied with any delusional beliefs about the disowned limb or somatosensory deficits, and currently cannot be effectively (or safely) treated (Blom et al., 2016, 2012; Brugger et al., 2016). We also know that there are structural and functional alterations of brain areas that contribute to creating a coherent representation of the body, including within the network of body ownership in individuals with BIID (Hanggi et al., 2017; Hilti et al., 2013; McGeoch et al., 2011; van Dijk et al., 2013). Thus, another way to investigate body ownership might be to diminish it. One can experimentally mimic this loss of awareness and ownership over a body part by instead dis-integrating vision, touch, and proprioception via an intriguing illusion called the Disappearing Hand Trick (Newport and Gilpin, 2011). While hovering the hands above a tabletop surface (inside of the MIRAGE multisensory illusion box), participants enjoy a real-time video of their hands, that through a covert process of sensory adaptation and disintegration, visually appear to be closer together than they physically are. When the image of the hand is faded out and the participant is asked to reach for it, it is not where he (visually) expects it to be. Individuals report that from this experience, the hand feels as though it is no longer part of the body (nor that it belongs to them), that it feels cooler than normal, and that they do not know its location. These components are critically linked to the feeling of body ownership and partly mimic the feelings associated with body ownership disorders. Modified versions of the illusion have recently been employed by others (e.g. Abdulkarim and Ehrsson, 2018; Bellan et al., 2017, 2015). For instance, Bellan et al. (2015) investigated how vision and proprioception discretely contribute to the overall loss of location of the hand during the illusion. In their study, the image of the hand was also faded out, but participants were not asked to reach for it. Instead, they had to make verbal judgements about its position over the following three minutes while remaining completely still. Initially, participants relied on the last seen visual location of their hand, but over the three minutes, the reliance shifted proprioception (i.e. felt position) leading to more accurate judgements of hand location. Recently, Bellan et al. (2017) further explored the underlying spatial and sensory-related mechanisms of this procedure, and found that participants were more accurate at making judgments about the hand's location if the participants first made a reach for the disappeared hand and realized that it was not actually there. However, they revealed that this accelerated increase in accuracy was also achieved by simply reaching for a coin, rather than the hand, on that side of space.

In such a high-demand listening scenario, participants inevitably engage in a cognitive tug-of-war. What emerges is a fascinating dance of auditory processing, making it remarkably clear that our brains are not merely passive recipients of information but active participants in a complex, dynamic environment. The interplay between selective attention and working memory unfolds as one navigates through an orchestra of competing voices, each vying for mental bandwidth. This competition doesn't occur in a vacuum; rather, it exists against the backdrop of constantly fluctuating auditory stimuli that can disrupt even the most focused listener. In fact, attention is often likened to a spotlight, illuminating selected sounds while relegating others to the shadows. Yet, once divided, these rays of focus seem to lose their potency, shedding light only on fleeting fragments of the conversation. The study by Best et al. (2010) demonstrates this very phenomenon. Under single-task conditions, participants thrive, effortlessly honing in on the female voice, retrieving target words with relative ease. However, with dual attention demands, the benefits of this focused spotlight diminish, scattering cognitive resources and leading to poorer performance as they desperately juggle multiple streams of information. Yet, it is not merely the act of dividing attention that complicates speech perception. The characteristics of the background noise play a pivotal role, impacting how our auditory systems prioritize and process relevant speech. For instance, when background chatter is composed of overlapping conversations in a bar setting, the listener's task becomes even more arduous. The human brain, adept as it is, must engage in a form of cognitive gymnastics. The recognition of familiar faces or voices may provide a semblance of assistance, but these social cues are often insufficient to mitigate the overwhelming strain on cognitive resources. Moreover, the origin of the sounds surrounding us adds a layer of complexity to the listening experience. Spatial attributes such as directionality and distance can manipulate our focus. Sounds that are spatially closer tend to command more attention than those that are further away. Imagine two friends engaging in spirited debate across the table while a nearby group erupts with laughter. The interplay of physical proximity and tonal variation shapes how we interact with sound, dictating our cognitive allocation. Each sound wave collides with the next, creating a rich tapestry of auditory input from which we must extract meaning. Additionally, individual differences in cognitive capacity further influence how one copes with these environments. Not all listeners possess the same proficiency in filtering irrelevant sounds, and research has shown that those with higher working memory capacity tend to demonstrate an advantage in such complex auditory scenes (Desjardins and Doherty, 2013). They can more effectively navigate the maze of voices, extracting pertinent information while keeping extraneous noise at bay. However, for others, the variability in attentional skills can lead to frustration and social fatigue, underscoring the need for nuanced understanding of auditory processing in real-world settings. Thus, as conversations unfold amid the lively ambiance of a bar, a delicate balance is maintained between engagement and overwhelm. The experience of listening becomes a testament to the remarkable capabilities and limitations inherent in our cognitive frameworks. In this bustling space, where intertwined voices echo, the listener is propelled into an intricate challenge akin to threading a needle under duress-a task both daunting and yet fundamentally human.

They were trying to provide the same curriculum and support to all students, regardless of their background or needs. But, as you can imagine, this approach was not very effective. By using machine learning, we were able to identify the key factors that were driving student dropout rates, such as lack of academic preparedness, family background, and substance use. We then used this information to develop a personalized learning plan for each student, taking into account their unique strengths, weaknesses, and needs. For instance, we developed an algorithm that could predict which students were most likely to drop out based on their academic performance, attendance, and other factors. We then used this information to identify the students who needed extra support, and provided them with targeted interventions, such as tutoring, mentorship, and career counseling. The results were remarkable. We saw a significant reduction in dropout rates, and a significant increase in student engagement and academic performance. The non-profit was able to achieve their goals more efficiently and effectively, and the students were able to achieve their own goals and aspirations. Another example is a government agency that we worked with to improve the effectiveness of their job training programs. They were struggling to understand why some participants were more successful than others, and how to improve the overall outcomes of their programs. We used machine learning to analyze the data from the program, and identified the key factors that were driving success, such as prior work experience, education level, and job readiness skills. We then developed an algorithm that could predict which participants were most likely to succeed, and provided them with targeted support and resources. The results were impressive. We saw a significant increase in job placement rates, and a significant decrease in program dropout rates. The government agency was able to achieve their goals more efficiently and effectively, and the participants were able to achieve their own goals and aspirations. These are just a couple of examples of how machine learning can be used to improve the effectiveness of social programs. By using data and algorithms to understand the complex needs of beneficiaries, we can develop more effective and targeted interventions that drive better outcomes.

Additionally, there was a "dual-task" condition in which participants were instructed to first report the target words by the female voice (S1), and then to report the target words spoken by the male voice (S2). Note that in both conditions the stimuli were constructed identically; the only difference between conditions was the task instruction. The results showed that performance on S1 was lower in the dual-sentence condition compared to the single-sentence condition; performance on S2 was even lower than performance on S1. These results suggest that dividing attention between concurrent stimuli comes with a strong cost in performance. The observed differences in S1 performance between the single-sentence and dual-sentence condition could be explained by the "load theory" suggested by Lavie et al. (2004). According to this theory attentional mechanisms operate at two stages. First there is a filter at an early passive perceptual stage where high load, as a consequence of target processing, prevents distractors from being processed, which in turn leads to better performance. Secondly, there is an active cognitive stage where high load, as a result of tasks demand, affects late selection processes, which leads to a drop in performance. Note that this theory predicts that performance depends on both perceptual and cognitive load; cognitive load is of specific interest in the current study. In the study by Lavie et al. (2004), working memory load was manipulated while participants performed a selective attention task. This resulted in fewer resources available for late selection processes, which resulted in a drop in performance. In line with the load theory, the results of Best et al. (2010) show a drop in performance for the dual-task compared to the single-task condition. However, in this study the dual-task condition involved a divided attention task in contrast to an additional working memory task. In the divided attention condition it was the late selection process itself that was manipulated, which might have resulted in increased cognitive load. Although Best et al. (2010) observed a drop in performance, interactions between attention and cognitive load might be complex. While the load theory states that cognitive load affects selective attention, dividing attention could in turn have an effect on cognitive load. Best et al. (2010) did not specifically manipulate perceptual load, although speech-in-noise was presented at different SNRs. In contrast to the idea that increased perceptual load should lead to better performance (Lavie et al., 2004), a drop in SNR generally shows a drop in performance (e.g., Festen and Plomp, 1990), an effect also observed in Best et al. (2010). This can be explained by the fact that in the auditory domain, additional perceptual load in the form of irrelevant sound will often lead to masking, which is not necessarily the case for visual processing.

To elucidate the complexities surrounding avoidance behaviors, it is essential to explore the cognitive and emotional underpinnings that govern the action-safety learning processes in individuals with anxiety disorders. One significant avenue of research involves understanding how the interplay of cognitive appraisals and emotional responses contributes to the maintenance of avoidance behaviors, particularly in the face of fear extinction. Cognitive models propose that individuals suffering from anxiety may harbor maladaptive beliefs and interpretations regarding the consequences of their actions, which may exacerbate their propensity to avoid feared stimuli (Beck, 2011). For instance, an individual with a social anxiety disorder may firmly believe that interacting with others will lead to humiliation or rejection, thereby reinforcing their avoidance of social situations. In this context, the learning history associated with these negative anticipations becomes a salient factor influencing future behavior. The expectation of social interactions resulting in negative outcomes not only creates a cycle of reinforcement for avoidance behaviors but also shapes the individual's tolerance for uncertainty. Essentially, the cognitive distortions that underpin these fears can maintain a high level of perceived threat, thus complicating the process of fear extinction and the shift from avoidance to approach. In parallel, the emotional landscape of avoidance learning should not be overlooked. The experience of relief, which arises from the omission of anticipated negativity, plays a crucial role in consolidating avoidance behaviors. Research has shown that individuals may come to value the relief associated with avoidance as much as, or even more than, the fear response itself. This valuation can lead to a state of hyper-vigilance, where individuals constantly seek to avoid the discomfort associated with potential threats, even when such threats are minimal or abstract. Additionally, the temporal dynamics of relief emphasize an interesting gradient: as one becomes accustomed to the absence of punishment, the relief starts to diminish in intensity, leading possibly to a recommitment to avoidance strategies (Skylar, 2016). Moreover, neurobiological factors may further amplify the interplay between cognitive appraisals, emotional responses, and avoidance behaviors. The role of neurotransmitters such as dopamine in reward processing can illuminate how relief serves as a reinforcing agent. The dopaminergic system is implicated not only in the processing of rewards and positive outcomes but also in modulating behaviors associated with risk and uncertainty (Schultz, 2015). Consequently, individuals with anxiety disorders may exhibit altered dopaminergic signaling, which can reinforce maladaptive behavioral patterns that favor avoidance over confronting feared stimuli. Engaging with the neural underpinnings also invites inquiries regarding brain regions that participate in the action-safety learning process. Structures such as the amygdala and prefrontal cortex play pivotal roles in emotional regulation and cognitive appraisal, shaping responses to environmental stimuli and actively influencing learning. Dysfunction in these areas may hinder the ability to appropriately assess risk and reward dynamics, further entrenching avoidance behaviors. In sum, gaining a nuanced understanding of the interaction between cognitive beliefs, emotional experiences, neurobiology, and behavioral outcomes in the context of avoidance can propel research forward. It paves the way for the development of targeted interventions aimed at dismantling these entrenched behavior patterns and reshaping learning processes. Future studies may, therefore, prioritize the integration of these diverse theoretical perspectives to enrich the understanding of avoidance in anxiety disorders and ultimately enhance therapeutic strategies designed to foster resilience and adaptive coping mechanisms in afflicted individuals.

Recent investigations have begun to elucidate the essential role of CA2 neurons within the intricate circuitry of the hippocampal formation. These neurons, endowed with unique properties, do not exhibit the pronounced plasticity characteristic of other hippocampal regions, yet their significance should not be underestimated. Emerging evidence suggests that CA2 neurons are pivotal in social memory processing, a function that distinguishes them from their CA1 and CA3 counterparts (Hitti & Siegelbaum, 2014; Stevenson & Caldwell, 2014). CA2's distinct circuitry, characterized by robust connections to the entorhinal cortex and dense input from the supramammillary nucleus, hints at its specialized role in integrating sociocognitive and motivational signals (Cui et al., 2013; Rowland et al., 2013). Furthermore, CA2 neurons have garnered interest due to their resilience against diseases commonly afflicting other hippocampal regions. This peculiarity may provide insight into their stable yet specialized functions. Recently, studies employing optogenetic manipulations have illuminated the role of CA2 neurons in modulating hippocampal output during social interactions (Chevaleyre & Siegelbaum, 2010; Jones & McHugh, 2011). These findings suggest a remarkable ability of CA2 neurons to influence the broader social behavioral repertoire, underscoring their potential as therapeutic targets for social cognition impairments in neurological disorders. While CA2 has traditionally been overshadowed by the more extensively studied CA1 and CA3 regions, growing recognition of its contributions continues to reshape our understanding of hippocampal networks. The intricate interplay between CA2 and surrounding regions illustrates the complexity of hippocampal function, where each subregion performs complementary roles, culminating in the sophisticated processing capabilities of the hippocampus as a whole (Dudek et al., 2016; Kohara et al., 2014). It is now evident that hippocampal-based memory processes, whether spatial, contextual, or social, are inextricably linked to the diverse and specific functionalities of these interconnected regions. The field of fear conditioning research has yet to fully explore the influence of CA2 neurons, particularly their interaction with the amygdala and prefrontal cortex during fear memory formation and retrieval. Understanding these dynamics may unveil novel mechanisms underlying fear regulation and provide avenues for advancing therapies aimed at fear-related disorders such as PTSD (Kim & Cho, 2017; Ohkawa et al., 2015). Future research must strive to disentangle the contributions of CA2 in the context of both mnemonic and emotional processing. This emerging focus on CA2 represents a burgeoning frontier in neuroscience, calling for sophisticated methodological approaches to decipher its precise contributions. Although challenges remain, particularly in parsing the nuanced signaling pathways that involve CA2, the inherent potential for groundbreaking discoveries is immense. In conclusion, the hippocampal CA2 region, while once a neglected player within the broader landscape of hippocampal research, stands poised to redefine paradigms of memory and social cognition. Through continued exploration into its unique properties and network interactions, CA2 may ultimately illuminate paths to understanding complex behaviors and neuropsychiatric conditions, firmly establishing itself as a critical node in the brain's intricate circuitry (Dudek et al., 2016; Hitti & Siegelbaum, 2014). As research advances, it is imperative that we harness the full potential of CA2 insight to unravel the mysteries of the memory and social phenomena under its influence.

As the evening wore on, the guests of the fete at the Hotel Montmorency continued to mingle and make merry, their laughter and music carrying across the water to the Louvre. But amidst the revelry, a sense of unease hung in the air, like the scent of smoke from a distant fire. It was a feeling that only the initiated could sense, a feeling that something was amiss, something that threatened to disrupt the fragile balance of power at court. Francois d'Epinay de St. Luc, the groom, was a man of great charm and wit, but also of great ambition. He was a favorite of the king, but not of the king's advisors, who saw him as a threat to their own power. And so, St. Luc had many enemies, men who would stop at nothing to bring him down. As the night wore on, the tension mounted, like a drumbeat in the distance. The guests began to notice that the king's favorite, the Duc d'Epernon, was absent, and that his place was being taken by the king's other favorite, the Duc de Guise. It was a subtle shift, but one that was not lost on the courtiers and ladies of the court. Madame de St. Luc, the young bride, was aware of the tension, but she was also aware of her husband's determination to make a good impression on the king. She knew that her husband's enemies were many, and that the king's favor was the only thing that could protect him. And so, she smiled and laughed and danced, her eyes never leaving her husband's face, as he moved through the crowd, shaking hands and kissing cheeks. But the king was not to be found, and his absence was beginning to cause a stir. The guests began to whisper among themselves, wondering what could be the cause of the king's sudden departure. Some said it was because of the marriage, that the king was angry with St. Luc for marrying without his permission. Others said it was because of the fete itself, that the king was tired of the constant parties and festivities. As the night wore on, the tension mounted, until it seemed as though the very air was electric with anticipation. And then, just as it seemed that the evening could not get any more tense, the king appeared, his face stern and unsmiling. He moved through the crowd, his eyes scanning the room, his presence commanding attention. Madame de St. Luc felt a shiver run down her spine as the king approached, but her husband, sensing her fear, took her hand and squeezed it reassuringly. The king stopped in front of them, his eyes fixed on St. Luc, his voice low and menacing. "You have something to say to me, St. Luc?" he asked, his words dripping with venom. St. Luc swallowed hard, his eyes never leaving the king's face. "Yes, sire," he said, his voice steady. "I have something to say to you." The room fell silent, the only sound the soft music and the distant hum of the city. The king's eyes narrowed, his face darkening with anger. "Speak," he growled. And St. Luc, his heart pounding in his chest, began to speak, his words pouring out like a river.

7. Leeches. These little blood suckers have been around for millions of years, and their bite doesn't hurt, so they can feed undetected for hours before dropping off when full. They can grow to three times their original size during feeding, and will happily feed on humans. Leeches are common throughout the world, especially in wet tropical areas. Their bites often bleed profusely as the leech injects an anticoagulant, but it's unlikely that they'll transmit any diseases. Nevertheless, some people are allergic to the anticoagulants that leeches use, so it's wise to remove them as soon as possible. There are many folk remedies for doing this, but the most effective way is to simply flick them off. They don't like salt either. 6. Kissing Bugs. If the name wasn't bad enough, this bug feeds on blood, much like a mosquito. Unlike the mosquito, however, the kissing bug prefers to feed on the faces of its victims, hence the name. In addition, the bug transmits Trypanosoma cruzi, which causes Chagas' disease. This disease is similar to malaria, causing fever, fatigue and swollen lymph nodes, although these symptoms usually resolve themselves within weeks. However, over time the infection can result in damage to the heart and digestive system, eventually resulting in death. Avoiding exposure to the bug is the key to prevention, as no vaccine exists. To reduce the likelihood of infection, travelers should sleep under bed nets treated with insecticide. 5. Tsetse Fly. The tsetse fly is another blood sucking insect, albeit one that looks more like a house fly than a mosquito. The bite of this insect is painful, but what really makes the tsetse fly a danger is its ability to carry trypanosomes, protozoan parasites that live in the blood of vertebrates. Some species of trypanosome infect cattle and other livestock, while others target human beings. African trypanosomiasis, better known as sleeping sickness, is caused by two different types of trypanosomes carried by the tsetse fly. Symptoms include headaches, joint pains, itching, weakness, confusion and swelling of the brain. Untreated, the disease can lead to death. According to the World Health Organization, about 30,000 new cases occur each year. 4. Sand Fleas. Sand fleas are actually small crustaceans rather than insects. Also called jiggers, sand fleas burrow into exposed skin, where they lay their eggs. After hatching, the larvae mature inside the host until they emerge as adults. Infection with sand fleas can lead to intense itching, pain, inflammation, lesions and secondary infections. Infestations can be avoided by wearing closed shoes and pants when walking along beaches. Removing the flea is tricky; cutting open the lesion and removing the entire organism is necessary to prevent further problems. 3. Irukandji Jellyfish. This jellyfish is named for the Aboriginal tribe that inhabited the area near where it was discovered in Australia. Measuring less than an inch across, this creature is extremely venomous, despite its diminutive size. (2016) or Murphy and Huston (2017), with animal studies linking this softening to degree of myelin content (Schregel, 2012; Weickenmeier et al., 2016, 2017), inflammation (Riek et al., 2012), and a reduction in neuronal density related to a decrease in neurogenesis (Freimann et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2014). In general, tissue stiffness parameters likely reflect the composition of the tissue microstructure, whereas viscosity measures, including the phase angle and damping ratio, instead have been suggested to provide information regarding microstructural organization (Sack et al., 2013; Schwarb et al., 2016). Understanding normal mechanical changes in brain tissue with respect to healthy aging is necessary before determining the efficacy of MRE for neurological disease diagnosis and therapy monitoring. Previous MRE studies into healthy aging have assessed either the global cerebrum (Sack et al., 2009), parcellated slices (Sack et al., 2011), or lobar regional effects (Arani et al., 2015). All studies reveal significant softening to the brain with increasing age, with brain softening occurring at a faster relative rate than brain volume loss with aging (Sack et al., 2011). In contrast, viscosity parameters remain constant suggesting a global preservation of the alignment of the tissue microstructure (Sack et al., 2009, 2011). However, no previous MRE studies into aging have investigated specific neuroanatomical structures, including subcortical gray matter (SGM) ROIs such as the hippocampus. Lying deep within the medial temporal lobes, the hippocampal formation is one of the most studied neuronal systems in the brain due to its implication in memory-specific disorders such as AD and mild cognitive impairment. Rapid improvements of MRE imaging protocols have now transitioned MRE into a high-resolution technique, capable of acquiring whole-brain MRE displacement data at an isotropic resolution of 1.6 mm to enable the study of small brain structures (Johnson et al., 2014). Aging effects have also never been studied with nonlinear inversion (NLI); formulated around a finite-element implementation of the full viscoelastic wave equation, NLI allows for local inhomogeneity and wave reflection effects (McGarry et al., 2012; Testu et al., 2017). In this current cross-sectional exploratory study, we aim to use these methodological developments to assess the viscoelasticity of the cerebrum globally and 6 SGM matter structures (to include the amygdala [Am], hippocampus [Hp], caudate [Ca], pallidum [Pa], putamen [Pu], and thalamus [Th]), in both young and cognitively healthy older adults. First, we will assess the acceptability of the MRE examination by administering a questionnaire to all participants after the scanning procedure. Second, based on findings from previous work, we predict that the brain will be softer in older adults (i.e., show lower shear stiffness, 1/2), throughout the cerebrum and all SGM regions.

In contrast, X-ray computed tomography (XCT) has emerged as a promising non-destructive technique for characterizing the 3D structure of photonic crystals, offering a unique combination of high resolution, large field of view, and minimal sample preparation. XCT is capable of providing quantitative 3D information on the morphology and internal structure of photonic crystals, allowing for the analysis of their nanostructure and its evolution under high-temperature exposure. Moreover, XCT can be performed in situ, enabling the observation of morphological changes in real-time, which is crucial for understanding the thermal stability of photonic crystals. One of the key advantages of XCT is its ability to penetrate the entire sample, providing a comprehensive understanding of the internal structure and its variation throughout the material. This is particularly important for photonic crystals, where the arrangement of the nanostructure can significantly affect their optical properties. Furthermore, XCT can be used to analyze the sample in its native state, without the need for conductive coatings or other modifications that can alter the material's properties. Recent advancements in XCT instrumentation and reconstruction algorithms have enabled the acquisition of high-resolution 3D images with voxel sizes down to a few nanometers. This has opened up new opportunities for the characterization of photonic crystals, allowing researchers to visualize and quantify the nanostructure of these materials with unprecedented detail. In addition, XCT can be combined with other characterization techniques, such as X-ray diffraction and spectroscopy, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the material's properties and behavior. This multi-modal approach can help to correlate the 3D structure of photonic crystals with their optical properties, thermal stability, and other functional characteristics. Despite the advantages of XCT, there are still challenges associated with its application to photonic crystals. One of the main limitations is the requirement for high-quality X-ray detectors and intense X-ray sources, which can be costly and may not be widely available. Furthermore, the reconstruction of XCT data can be computationally intensive, requiring significant computational resources and expertise. However, as XCT technology continues to evolve, it is likely that these challenges will be addressed, and the technique will become increasingly accessible to researchers in the field of photonic crystals. The potential benefits of XCT for the characterization of photonic crystals are significant, and its adoption is expected to have a major impact on the development of these materials for high-temperature applications. In conclusion, the characterization of photonic crystals for high-temperature applications requires a comprehensive understanding of their 3D structure and its evolution under thermal exposure. XCT has emerged as a powerful tool for achieving this understanding, offering a unique combination of high resolution, large field of view, and minimal sample preparation. As the technique continues to evolve, it is likely to play an increasingly important role in the development of photonic crystals for a wide range of applications, from energy conversion and thermal management to optical communications and sensing.

Moreover, fine cellular controls are needed to selectively modulate gene expression and direct specific cellular responses to meet the unique needs of individual organs [3,11]. Established models of mammalian hibernation are typically coincident with low Tb values [5]. By strongly suppressing energy-expensive cell functions and letting Tb values cool to ambient (sometimes as low as 0-5 C), metabolic rate can often be reduced to C and displaying substantially-enhanced hypoxia/ischemia tolerance [11,12]. The lemur model is extremely attractive for studies of mammalian hypometabolism and has several advantages as a model: (a) as primates, these animals are the most closely-related species to human that exhibit natural hypometabolism, and (b) they enter torpor at high ambient temperatures so they show a "pure" form of hypometabolism that is not confounded by the additional biochemical adaptations needed by most species to adjust enzymes/proteins for low temperature function. Studies from a range of animal models with various tolerances to different environmental stresses (freezing, anoxia, low pH, dehydration, etc.) have shown that global metabolic rate suppression, mediated via reversible protein phosphorylation (RPP), is crucial for survival [3]. RPP can produce major changes in the activity states of many enzymes and functional proteins, often providing on/off control. Apart from direct regulation of functional proteins, RPP is also responsible for the detection of extracellular stimuli and their propagation via intracellular signal transduction networks. The use of RPP provides a fast and coordinated mechanism to regulate the function of a wide number of cellular processes that can also be rapidly reversed once the stress is removed [13]. In particular, important targets for RPP control include proteins involved in catabolic pathways that regulate ATP supply, and proteins that regulate major ATP-consuming cell processes such as transmembrane ion transport, gene transcription, and protein translation [3,14]. Given the extensive research that RPP has received, it has been well-established that RPP is a central mechanism in the coordination of cellular functions throughout bouts of torpor/hibernation and arousal in hibernating species, just as it does in many other systems of natural hypometabolism [15,16].
