Carbonaceous materials demonstrated high durability in long terms operations with losses identified in 15-30% over one-year operations [49,55]. In parallel, application of PGM-free materials has risen significantly mainly due to the relatively affordable cost of the high performing catalysts that are made out of transitional metals such as Fe, Mn, Ni and Co. Three types of PGM-free materials were recently used in MFCs [16,42,43]. The first type is based on the utilization of transitional metal oxides such as Fe, Co, Ni, etc [56-61]. The improvement compared to AC is certainly important, but still, there are obvious limitations in performance [56-61]. The second type is based on the use of non-pyrolyzed macrocyclic organic compounds such as porphyrins, phthalocyanine, etc. with the incorporation of the metal center such as Fe, Co, Ni [62-70]. Despite the high performances achieved, the main limitation is the high cost of the macrocyclic organic compounds that hinder their introduction in the commercialization world [62-70]. The third type is based on the high-temperature synthetic method in which metal salts and an organic rich in nitrogen precursors are pyrolyzed at a temperature above 900 C [71-77]. The last type is the most adopted for fabricating catalysts utilized in MFCs [26,42,43]. Fe-based catalysts seem to be the most promising since they perform better than Co-based catalysts [17,18]. Mn-based [17,18] and Ni-based [17,18] had high performances compared with bare AC but their performances were lower compared to Fe- and Co-based catalysts. The method we adopted to produce our catalyst is based on a technique named Sacrificial Support Method (SSM) [79,80]. This method was used to create catalysts that were previously tested in MFCs [37,38,47,71,74-76,78]. SSM technique consists of mixing metal salt and organics precursors with monodispersed silica acting as a template. The etching of the silica using aggressive acidic conditions allows creating a three-dimensional structure. In this work, a catalyst was prepared using SSM technique following six steps. The organic precursor (Nicarbazin, N-C source) was mixed with the metal salt (iron nitrate, metal source) and the templating silica particles (step 1). The mixture was then pyrolyzed in reducing atmosphere (step 2). After pyrolysis, the mixture was ball-milled (step 3) and then silica was etched (step 4). The second pyrolysis was applied to the sample (step 5) and then the obtained material was further ball-milled (step 6). Three separate batches were used to fabricate the catalysts. A small quantity of material was saved after every synthesis step. The electrocatalytic activity toward ORR of the catalyst produced after each step in three different batches was evaluated using rotating ring disk electrode (RRDE) in neural media. Those measurements allowed measuring the disk and ring current and identifying the H2O2 produced as well as the electron transfer mechanism involved.

"Not dead, massa," replied the black, with a knowing chuckle, "but dey'm gettin' ready for a fun'ral." "What funeral?" I asked. "Why, dey'm gwine to shoot all de boblition darkies at de Norf, and hab a brack burying; he! he!" and the sable gentleman expanded the opening in his countenance to an enormous extent, doubtless at the brilliancy of his wit. I asked him to take my portmanteau, and conduct me to the best hotel. He readily assented, "Yas, yas, massa, I show you whar de big-bugs stop;" but at once turning to another darky standing near, he accosted him with, "Here, Jim, you lazy nigga, tote de gemman's tings." "Why don't you take them yourself?" I asked; "you will then get all the pay." "No, no, massa; dat nigga and me in partenship; he do de work, and I keeps de change," was the grinning reply, and it admirably illustrates a peculiarity I have observed to be universal with the negro. When left to his own direction, he invariably "goes into partenship" with some one poorer than himself, and no matter how trivial the task, shirks all the labor he can. The silent darky and my portmanteau in the van, and the garrulous old negro guarding my flank, I wended my way through the principal street to the hotel. On the route I resumed the conversation: "So, uncle, you say the people here are getting ready for a black burying?" "Yas, massa, gwine to bury all dem mis'able free niggas at de Norf." "Why? What will you do that for?" "Why for, massa! you ax why for!" he exclaimed in surprise. "I don't know," I rejoined; "I'm a stranger here." "Well, you see, massa, dem boblition niggas up dar hab gone and 'lected a ole darky, dey call Uncle Abe; and Old Abe he'se gwine to come down Souf, and cut de decent niggas' troats. He'll hab a good time - he will! My young massa's captin ob de sogers, and he'll cotch de ole coon, and string him up so high de crows won't scent him; yas, he will;" and again the old darky's face opened till it looked like the entrance to the Mammoth Cave. He, evidently, had read the Southern papers. Depositing my luggage at the hotel, which I found on a side street - a dilapidated, unpainted wooden building, with a female landlord - I started out to explore the town, till the hour for dinner. Retracing my steps in the direction of the steamboat landing, I found the streets nearly deserted, although it was the hour when the business of the day is usually transacted. Soon I discovered the cause. The militia of the place were out on parade.

Just another typical Friday evening at the store, full of the usual antics and friendly shenanigans. Once the doors were closed for real, Stacy, Chrissie, and I began our ritual of tidying up. There's something oddly comforting about the routine-the muted hum of the fluorescent lights above, the soft rustle of the broom against the tiles, and the clatter of misplaced inventory being sorted on shelves. Stacy started humming to herself, some random tune that was vaguely familiar but just out of reach in my memory. Chrissie had taken to swaying while sweeping, adding an impromptu dance to our closing routine. I couldn't help but chuckle as she twirled with the broom, laughing when Stacy joined in, her voice growing louder in song. It felt like being part of a sitcom; the store was our stage, and for those brief moments, the trivialities of life were left at the door. Then, in the midst of refilling the candy displays, it hit me-an end-of-week revelation. It was in these small hours with friends where life's stressors seemed to melt away. Like layers of an onion peeled back, revealing the sweet, pungent truth that what I truly cherished wasn't just success or accomplishments. It was this-the camaraderie, the shared looks of understanding, and the silliness that made even the most mundane tasks enjoyable. But, as with all good things, our night of frivolity was drawing to a close. We traded our usual jabs and playful insults until the final tasks were completed. The store was now clean, silent, and ready for another day of commerce and customer chatter. Chrissie grabbed her coat and mentioned something about a late-night diner breakfast, a tradition we often indulged after our shifts. Stacy clapped her hands together in excitement, as if pancakes were the single greatest invention known to man, which on an empty stomach, was entirely plausible. We locked up the store, the cool night air greeting us as a reminder that summer was waning fast. The town was quiet, just a few scattered cars driving by and the distant hum of some early autumn crickets. Heading down Main Street to the all-night diner, we passed familiar haunts and hangouts. The marquee at the old theater was promoting some indie film festival, reminding me of the plans I had to catch up on the latest releases. Each step was accompanied by Stacy and Chrissie's chatter, punctuated by moments of laughter that echoed into the night. As we sat in the cozy confines of the diner, with steaming mugs of coffee and syrup-laden plates in front of us, it felt like the world had been reduced to this single booth. Surrounded by friends, with the vibrant neon glow from the sign outside casting colorful patterns on our table, the moment crystallized-a reminder of the beauty found in ordinary nights, between work and home, music and quiet, and friendship and laughter. In those fleeting hours post-work, everything felt right, tethered, and wonderfully simple. Such is the curious comfort found at the intersection of mischief and familiarity, a Friday night well spent.

In the former situation, the machines would tend to take care of themselves and their own survival, and consequently, human history would end.... In the latter situation, the human race would reach the nebulous goal of an ever-lasting conflict with intelligence. In either case man would ultimately be superseded. -Alan Turing, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," Mind, October 1950 When Turing wrote these words in 1950, he could not have imagined the advances that would follow in the decades ahead. Today, the prospect of creating intelligent machines is far less remote, and the pace of development is accelerating. Already, we are handing control of entire sectors of society to machines. Machines choose which products we see when we shop online, which news stories appear on our Facebook feeds, which videos we watch on YouTube. They drive our cars, recommending routes based on real-time traffic conditions. More and more tasks are being automated: stock trading, paralegal research, even writing articles like this one. These developments are all good, but what happens if artificial intelligence eventually surpasses human intelligence? As Turing noted, in that case, there are only two possibilities: either the machines will take control, in which case it makes no difference whether we like it or not, or they won't, in which case we may face extinction. Both scenarios are horrifying, but as a scientist I find the second more likely. If you think about it, the idea of machines taking over the world is implausible. Machines don't want anything except what they're programmed to want - they lack free will. In contrast, people can act irrationally and unpredictably, which is why we often fail to accomplish our goals. So while machines may be more capable than us in many ways, they still need us to tell them what to do. This means that any takeover attempt would require us to willingly relinquish control. Why would we do that? For one thing, we might feel threatened by the superior capabilities of our creations. After all, we've always feared whatever we didn't understand. And once machines become smarter than us, we'll probably never understand them completely. This fear is compounded by the fact that most of us aren't well informed about AI. We don't know how the machines really work, so we can't assess their trustworthiness. Moreover, the very notion of building intelligent machines challenges our belief system. It threatens the idea that humans are special, that we're somehow different from animals and plants. That's a scary thought, so we may try to avoid it altogether by suppressing AI research. That's the Luddite option, and it's unlikely to succeed. Given how rapidly technology is advancing, it's inevitable that machines will soon outperform us in many areas. Once that happens, we'll have little choice but to accept their help. The question then becomes: How can we harness their power while retaining control? One approach is to make sure that the machines serve us, rather than the other way around. That requires us to design them carefully, making sure they're built for cooperation instead of competition. Another approach is to set up checks and balances within the system. We could build multiple competing systems that monitor each other, just as we have different branches of government monitoring each other. Finally, we could educate ourselves about AI so that we can keep tabs on its progress. All of these approaches are important, but none of them guarantee success. Ultimately, it comes down to us as individuals. We must be vigilant, constantly questioning our assumptions and challenging the status quo. Only then can we hope to avoid the pitfalls of artificial intelligence and ensure a bright future for humanity.

This mysterious set of islands remains mostly untouched by modern tourism, with raw beauty that influenced Herman Melville and Robert Louis Stevenson. In Ohio, a crucial battleground state, Obama is holding a series of events in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati, while Romney is focusing on the western part of the state. The president's campaign is touting its efforts to turn out African American voters, who are a key demographic in the state. Meanwhile, Romney's team is trying to win over white working-class voters in the state's rust belt. Obama is holding rallies in Miami and Tampa, while Romney is focusing on the state's central and northern regions. The president's campaign is trying to win over Hispanic voters, who are a crucial bloc in the state. Romney's team, on the other hand, is trying to win over white voters in the state's more conservative areas. The president's campaign is trying to win over independents and moderate Republicans, while Romney's team is trying to win over conservative voters who are skeptical of the president's policies. The president's campaign is trying to win over suburban voters, while Romney's team is trying to win over rural voters. As the campaigns wind down, the focus is shifting from swing states to get-out-the-vote efforts. Both sides are trying to mobilize their supporters to get to the polls on Election Day. The Obama campaign is using social media and text messaging to reach out to its supporters, while the Romney campaign is relying on its get-out-the-vote operation to turn out its voters. In the final days of the campaign, the stakes are high. The winner of the election will not only determine the direction of the country for the next four years, but will also set the stage for the next presidential election in 2016. As the campaigns enter the homestretch, one thing is clear: this election will be decided by a narrow margin, and every vote will count.

This disjunction between self-perception and physicality poses profound existential questions about the nature of identity and embodiment. It prompts one to ponder how intricately our self-concept is interwoven with the corporeal form we inhabit. Notably, while some individuals manifest a desire for disownership in a seemingly healthy limb, others engage in complex narratives regarding their 'true' selves. Such narratives often diverge sharply from societal norms, leading to feelings of alienation, confusion, and ultimately, a search for acceptance within both personal and social contexts. The striking difference between conditions like Somatoparaphrenia and Body Integrity Identity Disorder underscores a continuum of experiences surrounding body ownership, revealing the multifaceted relationship we maintain with our own bodies. For instance, individuals with Somatoparaphrenia may insist that a limb, physically severed from their sense of self, is owned by someone else, often leading to rich, albeit irrational, autobiographical stories concerning the lost appendage. In contrast, those with BIID articulate an intrinsic drive for congruity between body and self-concept, driven by an overwhelming belief that their physical form does not reflect their true identity. They harbor profound discomfort regarding their intact limbs, some reporting their existence as a constant source of distress and discord. Furthermore, both conditions challenge the traditional perspectives held within psychological and medical frameworks. The medical community often grapples with the contentions wrought by these disorders; they must navigate the delicate interface of ethical, medical, and psychological implications of amputation desires. For practitioners, recognizing these conditions requires a paradigm shift, where the understanding of body ownership transcends mere physiological integrity to encompass the psychological fabric of personal identity. This, in turn, invites important discussions concerning autonomy, informed consent, and the nuances of mental health treatments. Such views prompt a reconsideration of the boundaries of therapy and rehabilitation. For individuals grappling with BIID, the quest for surgical solutions might not only serve as a physical alteration but as a critical step toward mental congruence and relief from psychological burdens. Conversely, in instances of Somatoparaphrenia, emphasis on developing sensory integration therapies can facilitate improved body awareness. Here, the role of rehabilitation morphs into a dance of understanding and restoration-paving pathways toward reintegrating disowned body parts into the self-concept. Additionally, recent research into neuroplasticity suggests that the brain retains an incredible capacity to adapt, reshape, and alter its representations of bodily self-raising intriguing possibilities for both affected populations. Variations of therapeutic interventions, including sensory enhancement techniques and virtual reality environments, may foster a renewed sense of ownership and connectedness. The power of embodied experiences-leveraged in therapeutic settings-holds promise for helping individuals reclaim their narratives, restore agency, and navigate the complexities inherent to their unique journeys. As we continue to illuminate the intricate psychology of body ownership and its disorders, we also unearth broader implications not just for clinical practice but also for our societal understanding of selfhood. The exploration of body ownership intricately intertwines with how we perceive disability, identity, and the deeply embedded narratives that shape our realities. Thus, a dialogue unfolds, taking its rightful place at the intersection of philosophy, neuroscience, psychology, and ethics-inviting never-ending negotiation of what it means to inhabit a body, to feel ownership over that space, and the fundamental quest for self-identity in a world that relentlessly seeks categorization.

This was a result not only of the sterling efforts of the crystallographers themselves, but also of the combined work of many curators and analysts of the corpus of protein crystal structure data which led to the establishment of systematic protein structure databases, in particular CATH (Orengo et al., 1997) and SCOP (Murzin et al., 1995). Both of these databases make clear that proteins are built up of domains, defined as individual folding units which are linked by stretches of relatively unstructured polypeptide chain. A given protein consists of one or a number of domains, these may be identical (arising perhaps by a gene duplication event) or similar (a gene duplication event followed by mutation) or they can be entirely different (gene fusion). In this work the domain is the structural unit being considered. In the context of fibrous proteins which are constructed from repeating sequence fragments one may perhaps refer to these as "repeating elements", or just "elements" (we shall encounter one such example in the case of a connective-tissue protein). The discussion that follows will focus on globular protein domains but it will be shown that these fibrous protein elements actually have the same properties of closure as defined above. Globular protein domains are often described in terms of local structures along the polypeptide chain made up of so-called secondary structure elements (SSEs), within which stretches of polypeptide form a regular structure with repeating values of the, backbone torsion angles. The two principal SSE types are the well-known -helix and pleated-sheet, which have been qualitatively described (Branden and Tooze, 1999) and quantitatively defined (Kabsch and Sander, 1983) in the literature. Recent work (Bywater and Veryazov, 2015) has highlighted the preferences that different residue types have for these and other SSE classes. There are many possible types of intramolecular interaction in protein domains (Dill, 1990; Cooper, 2006). Apart from covalent crosslinks such as disulfide bonds, these include salt bridges, hydrogen bonding and Van der Waals interactions. These can all contribute toward stabilizing the structure (Dill, 1990; Cooper, 2006). All make some enthalpic contribution (salt bridges are probably strongest in this regard but they are relatively uncommon) and all make entropic contributions (Bywater, 2013a, b), because desolvation is involved in all of these interactions, regardless of the intricacies of the physical mechanism behind the interaction. What ultimately stabilizes the protein is a fine balance between these forces, with the overall free energy for the folded structure being negative of the order of only 5 1/210 kcal/mol (Pace et al., 1996). Of all the possible interactions, hydrogen bonding is deemed to be highly significant (Dill, 1990; Cooper, 2006; Bywater, 2013a, b; Ben-Naim, 1990; 2011) in terms of energy and contribution to stabilization. Unlike salt bridges and "hydrophobic interactions", hydrogen bonding is, as stated above, a result of dipolar interactions and quantum mechanical orbital overlap both of which restrict bending modes.

China has emerged as a formidable leader, notably reshaping the landscape through significant investments and technological advancements. The nation has witnessed unprecedented growth in solar power installation, boasting the largest capacity of solar photovoltaics worldwide (IEA, 2020). China's commitment to achieving carbon neutrality by 2060 has propelled extensive research and development, focusing on not only renewable energy sources but also on enhancing energy storage solutions and grid efficiency (Xie and Fan, 2020). Concurrently, India has carved a niche for itself within the renewable sphere, spearheading initiatives aimed at solar and wind energy proliferation. The country's expansive solar parks, backed by the Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission, reflect its earnest dedication to elevating its renewable energy capacity to combat climate change while meeting its burgeoning energy demands (IREDA, 2019). The transformation of the energy sector is intertwined with technological innovation, policy implementation, and societal engagement. Nations like Denmark have revolutionized wind energy, setting an example of how strategic government support, coupled with public-private partnerships, can effectively drive renewable energy development (DEA, 2019). Denmark's commitment to producing all energy from renewables by 2050 emphasizes the crucial role of innovation and sustained investment in realizing such ambitious targets (Lund and Mathiesen, 2019). Alongside these efforts, technological breakthroughs, such as advancements in battery storage and smart grid technology, are pivotal in ensuring the stability and reliability of energy systems increasingly reliant on intermittent renewable sources (IRENA, 2021). Despite notable progress, the path to a comprehensive sustainable energy transition is fraught with challenges encompassing political, economic, and social dimensions. Balancing the economic realities of transition with the imperatives of sustainability remains a formidable challenge. The vested interests in fossil fuel industries, along with economic considerations in developing regions, often obstruct the seamless integration of renewables (Sovacool and Geels, 2016). Furthermore, the equitable distribution of renewable resources and technology across diverse geopolitical landscapes is vital to avoid exacerbating existing inequalities (Cameron, 2020). International cooperation emerges as an indispensable factor in overcoming these obstacles, facilitating knowledge exchange and fostering global partnerships. Initiatives such as the International Solar Alliance, co-led by India and France, and the Mission Innovation initiative exemplify collective global efforts aimed at accelerating clean energy innovation and deployment (ISA, 2018). Moreover, financing mechanisms, including green bonds and climate investment funds, play a crucial role in supporting large-scale renewable projects, particular in developing economies, enabling a just transition that is both inclusive and equitable (World Bank, 2019). Public perception and community involvement are equally crucial in this transformative phase, as the success of implementing renewable energy solutions is inherently tied to societal acceptance and participation. Educational campaigns, local community projects, and transparent policymaking are essential to cultivating a sustainable energy culture, inspiring individuals and entities alike to adopt cleaner practices (Seyfang et al., 2013). As global warming continues its relentless march, the urgency for transformative action has never been clearer. The collective endeavor to transition to renewable energy offers a beacon of hope-a testament to human ingenuity and cooperation in facing one of the most pressing challenges of our time. The path is arduous but surmountable, holding the promise of a resilient and sustainable future for generations to come.

It's true; attractiveness is a subjective measure, and yet here, amidst the sea of laughter and the clinking of glasses, Eva finds herself assessing the beauty of every woman she sees. There's a freshness to their allure, a charm woven with confidence, smiles that light up entire rooms. "I should get out more," Eva reflects silently, seeking the familiar comfort of a casual conversation rather than staring at the parade of polished perfection. "Oh look at that," she remarks, pointing at a cluster of guests huddled together, animatedly discussing something decidedly boring. "They're either discussing the latest home renovation trend or who's having an affair." Letting out a chuckle, Marianne follows her gaze. "You might be onto something there. I can't tell you how many times I've polled my friends to gossip about the 'renovated' lives of others." Marianne's tone is light, teasing, drawing Eva in. "That pool house? Faux. Celebrity dreams? All fake. It's like a Shakespearean play in-house form. Who doesn't love a little scandal?" "What's a party without a bit of gossip, right?" Eva replies, feeling more at ease. The connection between them sprouted like a wildflower since their first handshake. "Tell me, Eva," Marianne leans closer, as if sharing a state secret. "Do you believe poetry is like a massage? You find the hidden knots, the words trapped beneath layers of meaning?" "That's interesting," Eva muses, intrigued. "I think they share a certain intimacy, but my hands don't do much talking. I find release in physical tension, while you... you seem to bring feelings to the surface, right?" "Well, yes. I attempt to. The last thing I want is to create verses meant to rot on a shelf. Oh, forgive my literary snobbery! Sometimes the poet in me needs a good shake." Marianne's sincerity resonates with Eva, easing the nerves she didn't realize she had. It feels refreshing to engage openly without veils or pretension. "You're not a snob at all; rather, it's refreshing. We both tap into the human experience just differently." Before they can delve deeper into the realms of art and personal stories, Sarah swoops back in, frustration etched on her face. "Eva! There you are! I thought I lost you." "Lost? In this sea of fantastic company?" Marianne laughs, raising an eyebrow playfully. Sarah rolls her eyes. "You can't even find the bathroom in this place without a map." "Speaking of which," Marianne interjects, glancing at her phone discreetly, "I ought to check in on a few things. Business doesn't run itself. It's a pleasure meeting you, Eva." She gives a jaunty wave, then slips gracefully into the crowd, leaving a play of electric energy in her wake. "Who is she?" Sarah asks curiously, her previous annoyance fading. "Marianne? A poet, apparently. We were just talking about... things, you know," Eva replies with a shrug, still basking in the interaction. "Things? What sort of things?" Sarah digs, intrigued. "Love, life. Art, whether poetry or massages, they touch the heart." She sounds like she's a sage in training now, the words rolling off like honey. "Sounds lovely." Sarah's mood lightens, and she nudges Eva, "This, my friend, is why you need to talk to more people. You're good at it." "Am I? Or do I just pretend very well?" Eva laughs lightly, the tension she didn't realize she harbored dissipating like the last traces of dusk as the party settles deeper into evening. "Hey, you've got it. Whether you want to or not!" Sarah preens mischievously, her playful bravado igniting a new connection, leaving Eva with the sense that perhaps the night was only just beginning.

The question now is, how did Cosby manage to keep his dark secrets hidden for so long? Was it his fame and power that allowed him to silence his victims, or was it something more sinister? As the allegations continue to mount, it's clear that Cosby's legacy will be forever tarnished by his alleged crimes.

Beachum swallowed hard, contemplating the journey that had landed him here, each moment a choice, each choice a consequence. The clock read 10:19 now, unyielding in its march. Outside the walls of this sterile fortress, the world turned, the lives of the uninitiated carrying on unaffected by the horrors of justice. The doctor moved again, shifting his gaze downward at the laptop perched on a corner table, the screen filled with data, notes transferred from paper to pixels, a cold analysis of a man reduced to nothing more than a series of readings. "Anything you want to tell me, Frank?" Dr. Waters asked, a hint of intention behind the sterile tone. Beachum's eyes darted left, then right, searching for momentum in this moment between breaths. "No. Just... just do your job," he murmured, attempting bravado but knowing that beneath the iridescent bravado lay a storm of regret, anger, and the paralyzing terror of impending doom. Plunkitt shifted his weight, the creak of his leather shoes reverberating in the silence. "We need to wrap this up, Doc. Years behind his desk had polished away the empathy, leaving behind a pragmatism that felt wearisome. "Of course," Dr. Waters acknowledged, a slight nod toward the warden. (2015) reported that spring freeze (8 C lower than ambient temperature for 5 days) at jointing significantly decreased gas exchange rates and the maximum quantum efficiency of PSII in wheat leaves, causing a 5%-14% reduction in grain yield. Previous studies have primarily focused on the effects of low temperature on wheat photosynthesis and yield (Fuller et al., 2007; Subedi et al., 2010; Venzhik et al., 2011), with less focus on wheat biomass production and the relative importance of biomass production to grain yield. Additionally, previous studies have primarily investigated the effect of either low temperature level or low temperature duration alone on wheat production (Al-Issawi et al., 2013; Whaley et al., 2004), whereas the combined effects of low temperature level and duration have rarely been reported. Furthermore, the temperature regimes in most previous studies were based on fixed day/night temperature treatments (Li, et al., 2015; Venzhik et al., 2011), which are not consistent with the natural daily temperature dynamics. In the actual environment, the impact of low temperature on crop growth and development is often affected by the combination of low temperature intensity and duration under the daily temperature variation pattern (Shimono et al., 2007). Accumulated cold degree days (ACDD, C d), which includes both duration and intensity of low temperature, has been used to quantify the effects of low temperature on the growth, development and yield formation in rice (Roel et al., 2005; Shimono et al., 2005) and wheat (Ji et al., 2017). Godwin et al. (1994) introduced ACDD into the CERES-Rice model to improve the simulation accuracy under low-temperature environments, suggesting that ACDD could effectively quantify the chilling injury effect in an extensive field experiment. Shimono (2011) employed ACDD to quantify the effects of low temperature on rice yield in northern Japan during the past fifty years and found that for each 1 C d increase in ACDD, rice yield was predicted to decline by 0.86%. Ji et al. (2017) used accumulated cold degree days (ACDD) to analyze the relationship between low-temperature stress and grain yield and yield components of wheat and observed significant negative linear relationships between ACDD and grain yield per plant, spike number per plant, grain number per spike and 1000-grain weight. Although several studies have quantified the effects of low temperature on the yield of rice and wheat with ACDD, few similar studies have been conducted on wheat biomass production. In the present study, two years of environment-controlled phytotron experiments were conducted with different cold-sensitive winter wheat cultivars under different low temperature levels and durations at two growth stages.

Among these, human urine is a good feedstock because it contains a high concentration of organics and nutrients (Ieropoulos et al., 2012). Moreover, human urine possesses high solution conductivity, which is beneficial for lowering ohmic resistance and increasing power output. Urine has been used successfully as fuel for MFCs in several applications and field trials (Ieropoulos et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2018). Considering that MFCs generate low power, a number of strategies need to be addressed to ensure that the electrical output can be used in real world applications (Ieropoulos et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2015). As already mentioned, these strategies include improvement of component materials and optimising reactor configuration as well as operational parameters; all this needs to be pursued with cost in mind. The current study addresses all these areas by developing paper-based MFCs and assessing the capacitive features of their electrodes in order to determine whether they can deliver high pulses of power compared to the lower power real-time output. Researchers are realising that low cost, natural materials such as paper can be a viable replacement to conventional materials used in MFCs. Such materials will not be suitable for long term, large scale operation, such as wastewater treatment, but they can be suitable for special, short-term applications, e.g. diagnostics (Fraiwan et al., 2013), biosensors (Fraiwan et al., 2014), biodegradable robots (Rossiter et al., 2016), wearable electronics (Taghavi et al., 2015) and emergency power supplies in remote locations (Winfield et al., 2015) where an 'expiry date' is desirable. Are we to discuss matters of reputation in front of a man like him, a mere laborer and a drifter?" Lafe felt his cheeks burn. In his mind, he'd steadfastly reaffirmed his position as neither drifter nor anything less, yet, faced with the scorn of Mrs. Tracey, any self-assurance dissipated like steam on a chilly day. He attempted to shift the tension with some gallantry, "Ma'am, I reckon I ain't here to listen to any palaver, just to support a friend," he mumbled, awkward and shy. But Mrs. Tracey merely arched an eyebrow, her gaze like a hawk surveying its prey, and turned her attention back to Mrs. Floyd. "And what of you, Sally? You think you'll cleanse the air by accusing me of whispering behind your back? A woman of my standing has little time for adolescent squabbles." "Consider me an adolescent then," countered Mrs. Floyd hotly, "if that means I stand here and challenge the filth you've spread about me. You treat your friends like gossamer, delicate until the wind blows, and then they become the very things you wished to keep at a distance." "Goodness!" Lafe thought, feeling the temperature of the exchange rise like a summer thunderstorm, thick with fervor and heat. He wanted nothing more than to retreat from the escalating verbal duel. He half-turned in his saddle, preparing to ease the tension, but Mrs. Floyd's following words kept him riveted. "You, Lafe," she said, "you can just sit there and listen-as if your presence bears the weight of judgment! Can't you see that while you gallivant about these hills with no conscience, I battle daily against her claws that dig into what little reputation I have left?" "Your reputation?" Mrs. Tracey rolled her eyes, a theatrical gesture of exasperation. "What good is reputation, Sally, when you know the truth? And the truth of the matter is, you are simply insufferable." Lafe could feel the situation spiraling beyond any hope of resolution. "Ladies, let's not-" he began, but his intervention was drowned out by the tumbling torrent of voices. "To think!" Mrs. Tracey continued, her voice laced with scorn and melodrama. "You presume to teach me about standing? Oh, the irony of that statement! Would you have me wallow in your misgivings?! I never thought you'd stoop so low." "For every gossamer thread you weave, I shall count a truth, lest your fabric of lies continue to hold water!" Mrs. Floyd's voice rose to a crescendo. "Enough!" Lafe exclaimed suddenly, the weariness of conflict choking the air. The two women turned to him, their expressions shifting from anger to surprise. "We ought to leave this spitting match behind, and talk sense instead of sin." The tension lingered in the air, unyielding; both women, frustrated by Lafe's summation, seemed caught in the moment as though the looming confrontation had shifted into something foreign-sudden, unexpected, and on the cusp of unraveling a deeper narrative altogether.

This finding implies the existence of alternative binding modes for SH3 domains, which might extend their functional repertoire beyond the classical PxxP interactions (Barnett et al., 2000; Kiel et al., 2005). The ability to engage in diverse binding interactions underscores the evolutionary adaptability of the SH3 domain, facilitating its participation in a wide array of cellular processes. Moreover, ScFus1 illustrates a departure from typical SH3 domain behavior by interacting with the unconventional non-proline-rich sequences, suggesting that other determinants may contribute to SH3 domain specificity (Ahn et al., 2005; Mitra et al., 2008). In light of these peculiar interactions, it becomes essential to address how SH3 domains can exhibit such versatility. One hypothesis is that the structural plasticity inherent within the SH3 domain may allow subtle conformational changes, enabling the accommodation of distinct ligands. Studies utilizing nuclear magnetic resonance and site-directed mutagenesis have illuminated the role of flexible loop regions that can adapt their conformation to fit diverse binding partners (Schueler-Furman et al., 2005; Songyang et al., 1997). This plasticity may be a cornerstone in explaining the numerous non-canonical interactions observed, which do not strictly comply with previously defined motifs. The kinetic and thermodynamic parameters of SH3-ligand interactions also provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanics of these versatile domains. High-affinity interactions are often characterized by rapid association and dissociation rates, indicating that transient interactions are critical for dynamic cellular signaling events (Wu et al., 2003; Zarrinpar et al., 2003). This rapid turnover might be advantageous for cellular processes needing quick and reversible modifications, allowing SH3 domains to act as finely tuned regulatory modules within intricate signaling networks. Innovative techniques such as peptide phage display and computational docking have expanded our comprehension of SH3 binding specificity. Through these approaches, researchers have been able to screen vast libraries of peptide sequences to discern novel SH3-interacting sequences, thereby unveiling new potential interaction partners (Wiesner et al., 2005; Kesti et al., 2007). Such techniques not only highlight the adaptability of SH3 domains but also reveal the expansive potential of the human proteome to interact via these modules in ways previously unconsidered. This growing complexity poses challenges and opportunities for drug discovery, particularly in targeting aberrant SH3-mediated interactions associated with disease states. By designing molecules capable of selectively disrupting specific SH3 interactions, researchers aim to modulate dysfunctional signaling pathways implicated in cancer and neurological disorders (Yuzawa et al., 2001; Zarrinpar et al., 2004). Despite technical challenges, these strategies hold promise for novel therapeutic interventions predicated on the nuanced manipulation of protein-protein interactions. In conclusion, the SH3 domain exemplifies a highly versatile and adaptive module, integral to numerous protein-protein interactions underpinning essential cellular functions. Its ability to engage with a wide variety of ligands, including those deviating from the canonical PxxP motifs, illustrates an evolutionary refinement ensuring functional diversity. Future studies equipped with advanced structural, biochemical, and computational tools will undoubtedly continue to unravel the multifaceted roles of SH3 domains, offering deeper insights into cellular complexity and informing therapeutic strategies that exploit their unique interaction capabilities.

What do you mean, Bad Luck? I mean, sometimes I wonder if the universe just picks on certain people, you know? Like, why does a whole lifetime get turned into a series of unfortunate events? I'm not special-who wants to be? But I guess I drew the short straw. My husband, bless his soul, he was a good man, but it never stopped raining when we were together. That's just how it felt, like we were caught in a storm without an umbrella. Every blessing was followed by a mishap, every good intention thwarted by the wayward winds. No offense to him, but it was like we were constantly navigating through quicksand. Two of everything, Uncle Bobo, two of everything always seemed to happen, and what did we ever get to show for it? All those plans! Vacations shattered by an unexpected bill, a new car that broke down the very next week-cursed, I tell you. And in the end, he left me, just like that. Not voluntarily, mind you; he just slipped away, quite literally to the other side, but still, that's a type of leaving, don't you think? I'm not bitter, of course. At least, I try not to be. I just recognize the irony in life being the punchline of a joke I never asked to hear. "You're too pretty to be alone," said a woman once at the bakery, trying to find solace in my blue eyes. But pretty doesn't fill the silence late at night. It's the laughter you don't have around the dinner table; it's the stories left untold. I got memories, sure, jog them now and again, but they don't paper over the empty space. So, Mr. Johnny, you want to marry me? Have you sat alone with your own thoughts? Do you know what you're getting into? Bobo slid the dessert cart closer, brimming with sweets and pastries, and like a sorcerer revealing his magic wares, I pushed aside my musings for a moment. "What's on the cart tonight?" I inquired with a crooked smile, half my thoughts still lingering on the matter at hand. Flirting with absurdity, that's what we do, the dance of whimsy and fancy just to postpone reality. Chocolate mousse piled high and mini cheesecakes twinkling as if they could potentially save me from the gravity of this moment. "You could do worse than marry a fine man like Mr. Johnny," Bobo chimed, adeptly positioning himself as both confidante and matchmaker. But marriage! That word sat heavy, as if wrapped in iron chains. I don't know. A leap into something unknown, perhaps it was like jumping from a high place, uncertainty lurking beneath. And it's not just me! It's whoever rides the rollercoaster, takes on that thrill. I mean, people look at love through rose-colored glasses without realizing that the notion can simultaneously offer such warmth while, in truth, it bears thorns. But Mr. Johnny, well, he's sweet. He knows good bread, he knows good coffee, and there's that spark between us, or maybe just the heady scent of cocoa swirling around. Does that count? So it's like I have to stop and ask myself, do I really want to turn this love into something more? After all, life is unpredictable enough already without adding wedding bells into the mix. It's like tossing a dice labeled "Either way, it could go wrong." "Alright!" I finally say, "Why not? Let's see where this all leads." And there it is again, the spark, only this time it flickers, a little brighter than before.

Previous investigations have found electrophysiological correlations of CFs in DLB patients. Early work using quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG) has shown a correlation between epoch-by-epoch DFV and CFs in DLB patients compared with healthy controls (Walker et al., 2000). Later work also showed that DLB patients with CFs had greater DFV compared to AD patients in posterior brain regions, and used the DFV together with other QEEG measures to classify AD, PDD-CFs, PDD-without CFs and DLB patients and controls (Bonanni et al., 2008). More recently, a multi-centre cohort analysis has verified these results (Bonanni et al., 2016). The aforementioned findings of QEEG signatures in DLB in addition to the fact that the QEEG measures were shown to be correlated with the clinical phenotype of DLB and specifically with CFs, suggest that the QEEG could be utilised to investigate for a neurophysiological divergence between DLB and other dementias. The QEEG investigations performed so far have not yet managed to identify differences (Engedal et al., 2015; Garn et al., 2017) between DLB and PDD. Generally, these Lewy body dementia (LBD) subtypes demonstrate great similarities in neuropathological processes, symptom manifestation and treatment. However, DLB is typically characterised by greater executive dysfunction, more psychiatric symptoms, poorer response to levodopa (L-DOPA) and greater amyloid burden compared to PDD (Edison et al., 2008). Moreover, the onset of motor symptoms precedes that of dementia in PDD while in DLB, dementia appears concurrently or before motor symptoms (McKeith et al., 1992). These discrepancies may indicate differences in the spatio-temporal sequence of pathology, with a predominant brain-stem start and rostral progression in PDD and a cortical inception in DLB (Beyer et al., 2007). Potential QEEG differences between PDD and DLB are of research interest, as they could provide insight for better understanding these LBD subtypes. Earlier QEEG studies focused on investigating the capacity of such measures in aiding DLB differential diagnosis in clinical settings. Hence, they utilized methods such as assessment by visual observation (Bonanni et al., 2008), or attempted to develop an online method that performs analysis during and right-after EEG acquisition (Garn et al., 2017). Here we took a less clinically-orientated approach, as our primary goal was to characterise and compare the resting EEG rhythm in AD, DLB and PDD patients and in relation to healthy controls, and to investigate for DLB specific signatures of CFs. Thus, we performed extensive pre-processing analysis of the EEG signal and a thorough analysis for differences in QEEG measures within different frequency ranges and brain regions, between diagnostic groups. Based on the literature, we hypothesized that dementia patients will exhibit a differential pattern in the distribution of QEEG measures of power and DF within different frequency ranges compared to healthy controls, and that these QEEG measures in addition to DF variability in time (DFV) will also differ between the dementia groups.

For example, the Mississippi River watershed drains a large portion of the United States' agricultural lands and delivers a substantial amount of nutrients into the northern Gulf of Mexico (Mitsch et al., 2001), contributing to the formation of one of the world's largest hypoxic zones (Rabalais et al., 2002). The Chesapeake Bay watershed is home to a dense population of more than 18 million people, and receives high amounts of nutrients from both point and non-point sources (Kemp et al., 2005). In addition, climate change is likely to exacerbate many problems facing coastal environments, such as increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, storm surges, and flooding (Scavia et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2013). Agricultural land use accounts for nearly 50 percent of total land area in the conterminous U.S. (USDA Economic Research Service, 2016). Agricultural production provides essential food, fiber, and fuel for the country but also results in adverse impacts on the environment. Nutrients and pesticides applied to agricultural fields often make their way into rivers, lakes, streams, and groundwater, degrading water quality and threatening human health. Excess nutrients flowing down the Mississippi River have contributed to the formation of a dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico (Rabalais et al., 2002). Conservation practices implemented on farms help prevent soil erosion, improve soil health, conserve water, and mitigate water quality impacts. Water quality is an important factor in determining whether or not water is suitable for human consumption, recreation, or supporting aquatic life. While natural processes affect water quality, human activities can cause severe impairment. Human activities that can degrade water quality include agriculture, construction, industrial discharge, and municipal wastewater effluent. Water quality monitoring programs exist at local, state, regional, and federal levels. These monitoring efforts track changes in water quality and help determine if water bodies meet designated uses such as drinking water, swimming, fishing, or boating. The USGS National Water Quality Assessment Project (NAWQA) collects data on surface- and ground-water chemistry, hydrology, stream habitat, and aquatic life across the nation to assess current water-quality conditions for each region and how those conditions have changed over time.

Front-end (FE) desaturases are capable of introducing carbon-carbon double bonds into unsaturated lipid substrates at positions between an existing double bond and the terminal carboxyl group [4]. It was found that the varied substrate preference of the front-end desaturases is the root cause of the substrate dichotomy bottleneck in the 3-LCPUFAs biosynthesis pathway [20,63,64]. This is because some 6 desaturases utilize acyl-PC substrates, whereas the elongases at the next step utilize acyl-CoA substrates [20]. Thus, for acyl-PC-specific 6 desaturases, the product of the 6 desaturation has to be converted into an acyl-CoA molecule by an acyltransferase, which limits the metabolic flux in the recombinant 3-LCPUFA biosynthesis pathway in plants [20]. Second, first desaturases (FDs), typically catalyze the formation of the first C = C bond at the 9 position of an acyl group. It has been postulated that the 9 desaturases are the most ancient desaturases among the three groups because of their universal distribution in organisms [24]. The FDs utilize acyl-CoA as substrates except for the FDs of plant plastids [8]. Third, the methyl-end (ME) desaturases are responsible for introducing a CC between a pre-existing CC and the methyl end of the acyl group [26]. ME desaturases are known to utilize PL substrates [27,28]. Finally, the 4 sphingolipid desaturases ( 4-SPs) are particularly important for cellular signalling [29]. This classification was based on a previous limited phylogenetic analysis of eukaryotic membrane-bound desaturases [25]. For a very diverse protein family, such as the membrane FADs, constructing a high-quality multiple sequence alignment can be challenging [30], which limits our ability to obtain evolutionary information from phylogenetic analysis and to annotate the possible functions for identified genes with confidence [30]. Protein sequence similarity networks (SSNs) were developed in 2009 by Babbitt and co-workers to facilitate functional annotation based on known sequence data [31]. SSNs can illustrate the global sequence-structure-function diversity of protein superfamilies [32-34], because they are based on many pairwise alignments of proteins instead of the entire alignment of a large protein datasets, so that the inaccuracy of a large protein alignment is largely eliminated. A SSN presents the level of similarity between members in a protein family in a graphical way in which proteins sharing high sequence identities are clustered. In the SSNs, the edges represent all-vs-all BLAST E-values and each node represents a protein or a group of highly similar proteins. The information about their organism of origin and structural understanding can be mapped and visualized in the network manually or automatically [35]. This method can be combined with other computational or biochemical techniques to annotate and characterize the function-structure relationships of protein subfamilies.

In addition, there have been reports in the fields of oral hygiene and food sciences of using of actual human whole saliva as dissolution media (Saxegaard et al., 1988; Buettner, 2002; Manarelli et al., 2017). To use human saliva in a reliable and reproducible manner for purposes of dissolution, pooling methods were previously employed to reduce inter-individual variability (Schipper et al., 2007). In addition, for a better prediction of the formulation performance in the oral cavity, dissolution media volumes were adjusted to realistic volume to better reflect resident volume of saliva in the mouth (Lagerlof and Dawes, 1984; Rudney et al., 1995). In this study, dissolution exposure time was set to 10 min to be used as a formulation screening trade-off time end point for various orally retained formulations, such as ODTs and taste-masked formulations. While this exposure time is longer than the average disintegration time of ODTs (European Pharmacopeia, 2014; United States Pharmacopeia, 2014), it is shorter than the time required to prevent dissolution for effective taste masking (Lopez et al., 2018). Saliva is composed of 99% water, therefore compounds with poor aqueous solubility will require dissolution enhancement strategies for successful ODT development. There are various techniques available for increasing drug solubility and therefore dissolution (Savjani et al., 2012; Sharma and Baldi, 2016; Bavishi and Borkhataria, 2016; Al-kassas et al., 2017; Khames 2017; Repka et al., 2018). The solubility enhancing techniques used in this study included: particle size reduction, solid dispersions, and inclusion complexes. Firstly, cryomilling was used to enhance dissolution by reducing particle size and by creating amorphous drug particles. Then a polymeric solubilizer, Soluplus(R) was used to aid the solubilisation of poorly soluble drugs in aqueous media and to stabilise the amorphous milled drug material. Lastly, complexation with cyclodextrins was used as it can improve the aqueous solubility of lipophilic compounds. ODTs have been shown to be attractive dosage forms due to their ease of use for the patient. Another benefit to dosage forms fated for dissolving or disintegrating in the oral cavity is that it allows for direct absorption through the oral mucosa allowing drugs to reach systemic circulation bypassing the gastrointestinal tract and hepatic first-pass metabolism. For some compounds, the ability to decrease irritation to the subsequent compartments of the gastrointestinal tract can be advantageous, for example, piroxicam can be used in an ODT formulation to avoid its side effect of gastric irritation (Lai et al., 2011). ODTs have also shown potential when rapid onset of drug action is required, for example, headache relief and freedom from pain with rizatriptan ODTs (Cameron et al., 2015). There have been a number of lipophilic compounds that have been formulated as ODTs for commercial use, such as: loratadine, ondansetron, tepoxalin, loperamide, and cisapride (Fu et al., 2004). In the present study felodipine was used as a model lipophilic compound to assess the suitability of biorelevant human saliva dissolution as a screening tool to guide the development and optimisation of an ODT formulation.

By identifying and analysing these implicit communications associated with resource efficiency initiatives, different routes towards sustainable resource governance may be demonstrated, and their relative merits debated. Consequently, the objective of this paper is to develop and a use a framework for investigating the 'small p' politics of activities undertaken within three linked household resource efficiency initiatives. To achieve this analysis we draw on two conceptual tools. First, we use ideas about the 'imagined public', originating from research on expertise and lay knowledge (Maranta et al., 2003), and applied to the field of renewable energy (Walker et al., 2010). As suggested by Gordon Walker and colleagues: '[T]he potential influence of public subjectivities on sociotechnical change is realized not only through moments of active participation and protest, but also through 'the public' being imagined, given agency, and invoked for various purposes by actors in technical-industrial and policy networks' (Walker et al., 2010: 931). Hence, renewable energy professionals' ideas about public reactions to potential energy projects create a phantom actor, 'the imagined public', who have "agency and political significance" and are "available to be invoked in... decision-making processes" (ibid.: 933). In the same way, we suggest, the organisers of domestic resource efficiency initiatives imagine the public, for example, in determining whether when and how water and energy should be conserved. Moreover, this imagined public shapes resource professionals' practices, for example, in the selection of localities suitable for retrofit initiatives, in how resource demand management interventions are designed, and in how communication with householders occurs. These assumptions and imaginings about the public are therefore pivotal in identifying and shaping the governance approach adopted for resource efficiency initiatives. Ultimately, they also determine the outcomes and perceived 'success' of such interventions. Our understanding of imagined publics is positioned through Mary Douglas' cultural theory (Douglas and Wildavski, 1982; Douglas, 1985; Douglas et al., 2003), our second conceptual tool. Cultural theory has been widely utilised to understand how societies achieve collective action (for example, Hood, 1998; Rydin et al., 2004; Tansey, 2004; Baxter and Greenlaw, 2005; Seyfang, 2007; Thompson, 2008; Entwistle, 2010). This conceptual approach promises to be particularly suitable for studying initiatives seeking to mitigate societal risks associated with unsustainable resource consumption. We use an interpretive version of cultural theory as a heuristic to highlight variations between resource efficiency initiatives (Tansey, 2004). This is achieved by linking the design and planned implementation of particular initiatives to associated organisational assumptions about the public. What is at stake here is whether and how society organises to achieve greater resource efficiency in the domestic sphere. While our focus is on the seemingly small issue of the design, implementation and outcomes of a set of local resource efficiency initiatives, our argument is that these apparently small issues matter for sustainability more broadly.

Each step taught me about precision, discipline, and the unspoken dance that happens in a bustling kitchen. I remember the first time I seared a perfect steak on the grill. It was a simple task, but for me, it was transformative. The sound of the steak hitting the hot surface, the sizzle, the aroma filling the air-it was like composing a symphony, and I was the conductor. But the journey wasn't all glamour and glory. The kitchen can be a merciless place. It's hot, hectic, and sometimes downright brutal. There's no room for error when 50 patrons are waiting, and you can't let the pressure get to you. There were nights when I felt like quitting when the orders just kept coming, and my body ached from the relentless pace. Yet, each time I reached that breaking point, I found something within me that pulled me back up, a resilience I didn't know I had. Becoming a chef was more than just learning recipes or how to wield a knife with precision; it was about embracing a culture. The camaraderie amongst cooks is unlike anything I've ever experienced. It's a bond forged in fire, literally and figuratively. It's about knowing your fellow cook has your back, understanding each other's rhythms in the dance of the evening rush. The friendships I've built in the kitchen are some of the strongest I've ever known. It's funny, really-how different people, from all walks of life, are united by the common language of food. We share stories over the last meal of the night, laugh about the night's blunders, and celebrate the little victories that come with each service. Those bonds go beyond the kitchen doors, and I consider many of those I've worked alongside to be my family. As I progressed to head chef, I learned that the role isn't just about cooking. It's about leadership-mentoring the younger cooks, teaching them the skills they'll need to succeed, and instilling in them the values of passion and perseverance. It's about creating an environment where creativity can thrive and mistakes are seen as learning opportunities rather than failures. I've seen the shyest dishwashers blossom into confident line cooks and watched as talented cooks ventured out to start their own culinary journeys. The culinary world is constantly evolving, influenced by new techniques, global flavors, and the ever-changing tastes of diners. And that's part of what keeps this career so exhilarating. You're always learning and being challenged. The moment you think you've mastered it all, there's something new on the horizon. Whether it's a new cuisine to explore, a modern technique to master, or a unique ingredient to experiment with, curiosity fuels our growth as chefs. So, as I look back over the years, I see not just a career but a passionate adventure. Each day brings its own rewards and challenges, and there's never a dull moment. The kitchen has become a stage where art, science, and passion meet-a place where I've found my voice and my calling. And this is just the beginning.

The dynamics of innovation networks thus manifest a duality marked by both the diminishing boundaries of distance and the persistent allure of geographic proximity. In essence, while technological advancements provide an apparatus for the decoupling of knowledge exchange from its spatial constraints, the rich tapestry of social interactions continues to weave itself within local contexts. This phenomenon invites a further examination of how established knowledge clusters endure, adapt, and even flourish amid the rapid winds of globalization. The emergence of digital platforms has transformed traditional paradigms of collaborative innovation, creating a virtual landscape where distance becomes less salient. Scholars have begun to recognize that these platforms not only facilitate the transference of codified knowledge across borders but also foster new forms of connectivity and interaction among disparate innovators. The rise of open innovation models exemplifies this shift, wherein organizations harness external ideas and paths to market, leading to an expanded collective of knowledge producers who contribute to a burgeoning global pool of intellectual resources (Chesbrough, 2003). Nevertheless, the persistence of localized knowledge spillovers cannot be overlooked. Networks rooted in geographic proximity still demonstrate robust advantages in fostering informal social ties that allow for the nuanced exchange of tacit knowledge, often eclipsing the efficacy of digital interactions alone. The serendipitous conversation in a cafe or the impromptu meeting at a conference can ignite ideas and spark collaborations in ways that digital interactions struggle to emulate. This reality underscores the importance of understanding how geographical clusters evolve, how they respond to technological changes, and how they maintain their critical role in innovation ecosystems. In addition to the interplay of codified and tacit knowledge, the role of policy and institutional frameworks emerges as a key determinant in shaping the configuration of innovation networks. Innovations do not occur in a vacuum; they are heavily influenced by government support, intellectual property rights policies, and the overarching regulatory environment. Regions endowed with favorable policies and institutions are more likely to attract and retain talent, stimulate entrepreneurial activities, and foster collaboration among firms, universities, and research institutions. Such conducive environments can amplify the centrifugal forces enabling knowledge dissemination while simultaneously reinforcing the centripetal dynamics that draw innovators to established hubs. Thus, the question arises: how can emerging regions effectively navigate the complexities of this dual dynamic? To cultivate vibrant innovation networks, they must not only embrace the opportunities afforded by digital technologies to reach far-flung collaborators but also invest in local capacities that enhance interpersonal connections. Creating supportive infrastructures-incubators, co-working spaces, and networking platforms-can catalyze interactions within the local ecosystem and connect it more seamlessly with the global network. Moreover, as new generations of innovators enter the landscape with different expectations and professional paradigms shaped by digital native experiences, their preferences for work and collaboration will undoubtedly influence the evolution of these networks. Emerging professionals are likely to prioritize flexibility, individuality, and varied forms of collaboration, thus reshaping traditional norms of engagement and knowledge sharing within innovation clusters. In summary, the landscape of innovation networks is one that remains deceptively simple yet profoundly complex, characterized by the intertwining forces of globalization and the enduring relevance of local contexts. Given these multifaceted dynamics, a more nuanced understanding of innovation networks necessitates continuous exploration of emergent patterns and behaviors as both spatial and technological dimensions evolve. By appreciating this interplay, policymakers, business leaders, and academic institutions can actively shape more resilient and productive innovation ecosystems.

Perhaps the only drawback to the geographic make-up of Pasadena is its location in a natural valley. The mountains which practically surround the city tend to trap not only the marine layer, which is good, but also pollution and stagnant air, which is bad. For Pasadena, smog is not a 20th century phenomenon. They are several well-documented reports of pollution in the San Gabriel Valley prior to the pre-industrial era. Rain in the winter, drought in the summer, fertile soil, Mediterranean climate, earthquakes, floods, smog, fabulous homes, annual fires that burn those homes, booze, wealthy socialites... Pasadena truly was the creation of nature and mankind. INDIANS IN THE VALLEY Before the Europeans came to Southern California the area now known as Pasadena was inhabited by a clan of Shoshone Indians who called themselves the Hahamongas (a park in present-day northwest Pasadena, in homage, bears their name). The Hahamongas, a notably moral and spiritual clan of indians, lived in harmony with the land and with neighboring tribes. They were a small tribe (California never had any of the large indian confederations often found on the east coast) and were somewhat nomadic. However, archeologists have found remnants of six villages scattered from the foothills to what is today South Pasadena. They established a village near every viable water source. The Hahamongas were hunters and gatherers (no agriculture of which to speak), mostly they gathered, mostly the women gathered. Their diet consisted of the occasional rabbit or squirrel, some berries, some seeds, and a heavy helping of a mushy acorn creation common to most indian tribes of Southern California. On January 17, 1770, in present-day South Pasadena, the Chief of Hahamongas, Chief Hahamovic, smoked a peace pipe with the Spanish governor, a man named Portola (again, if one wants to drink or smoke, South Pasadena is the place). Just one year later, Father Junipero Serra established a mission on the edge of the San Gabriel River and the Hahamonga would never again live as they wished or as they pleased. Within a few years, their culture began to die, asphyxiated by European ways. The Spaniards taught them the ways of agriculture, labor, punishment, disease, and Catholicism. Eventually, Chief Hahamovic married a European woman and, symbolically, put a period at the end of the story of the indians in the valley. But, for the moment, everything was plain: - the sky, full of light, and filmy grey cloud, the fells with their mingling of wood and purple crag, the shallow reach of the river beyond the garden, with a little family of wild duck floating upon it, and just below her a vivid splash of colour, a mass of rhododendron in bloom, setting its rose-pink challenge against the cool greys and greens of the fell. But Bridget Cookson was not admiring the view. It was not new to her, and moreover she was not in love with Westmorland at all; and why Nelly should have chosen this particular spot, to live in, while George was at the war, she did not understand. She believed there was some sentimental reason. They had first seen him in the Lakes - just before the war - when they two girls and their father were staying actually in this very lodging-house. But sentimental reasons are nothing. Well, the thing was done. Nelly was married, and in another week, George would be at the front. Perhaps in a fortnight's time she would be a widow. Such things have happened often. 'And then what shall I do with her?' thought the sister, irritably, - recoiling from a sudden vision of Nelly in sorrow, which seemed to threaten her own life with even greater dislocation than had happened to it already. 'I must have my time to myself! - freedom for what I want' - she thought to herself, impatiently, 'I can't be always looking after her.' Yet of course the fact remained that there was no one else to look after Nelly. They had been left alone in the world for a good while now. Their father, a Manchester cotton-broker in a small way, had died some six months before this date, leaving more debts than fortune. The two girls had found themselves left with very small means, and had lived, of late, mainly in lodgings - unfurnished rooms - with some of their old furniture and household things round them. Their father, though unsuccessful in business, had been ambitious in an old-fashioned way for his children, and they had been brought up 'as gentlefolks' - that is to say without any trade or profession. But their poverty had pinched them disagreeably - especially Bridget, in whom it had produced a kind of angry resentment. Their education had not been serious enough, in these days of competition, to enable them to make anything of teaching after their Father's death. Nelly's water-colour drawing, for instance, though it was a passion with her, was quite untrained, and its results unmarketable.

While these findings highlight the potential for HDAC inhibitors in modulating immune responses and fostering regulatory cells, their role extends beyond mere immunosuppression. The complexity of MS necessitates a multifaceted approach where HDAC inhibitors might serve to not only dampen aberrant immune activity but also promote cellular resilience and repair mechanisms. Emerging evidence suggests that HDACis may influence neurogenesis, angiogenesis, and synaptic plasticity, fundamental processes for CNS repair and rejuvenation (Hsieh et al., 2004; Jessberger et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2009). By promoting chromatin remodeling and facilitating transcription of neuroprotective genes, these compounds could potentially mitigate the effects of ongoing neurodegeneration in progressive MS stages, presenting a dual approach of protection and repair. However, the therapeutic application of HDACis in MS is not without challenges. The broad impact of these inhibitors on gene expression poses significant risks of off-target effects, potentially disrupting essential cellular functions and leading to adverse outcomes. As such, discerning the specific HDAC isoforms involved in MS pathogenesis becomes imperative to minimize unintended consequences and enhance therapeutic specificity. Isoform-selective HDAC inhibitors represent a promising avenue for research, presenting the opportunity to refine treatment modalities while preserving the nuanced balance of immune regulation and neural integrity (Kazantsev and Thompson, 2008; Marks, 2010). Furthermore, the cross-talk between immune and neural cells facilitated by HDACis underscores the necessity of a systemic perspective in understanding and treating MS. The CNS is intricately linked with systemic immune responses; thus, therapeutic interventions must account for these dynamic interactions. Recent advances in multi-omic technologies and systems biology offer powerful tools to unravel the complex networks involved in MS and guide the development of targeted therapies (Francesconi et al., 2008; Hood et al., 2004). In clinical practice, translating HDAC inhibitor research into effective MS treatments demands rigorous trials to evaluate efficacy and safety. Preliminary studies have shown promise, yet robust clinical evidence is required to substantiate their utility in varied patient populations and across different stages of the disease. Personalized medicine approaches, leveraging genetic, epigenetic, and environmental data, may prove invaluable in optimizing treatment plans and maximizing therapeutic outcomes for individual patients (Collins and Varmus, 2015). In conclusion, while MS remains a formidable challenge in the realm of neurology, advances in our understanding of its pathogenesis and the potential role of HDAC inhibitors offer hope for novel and effective therapeutic strategies. By targeting both immune and regenerative pathways, these compounds stand at the forefront of a new paradigm in MS treatment. Continued research and collaboration across disciplines are essential to unlocking their full potential and transforming clinical care for patients with this debilitating disease. As we forge ahead, it is imperative to maintain a delicate balance between innovation and caution, ensuring that breakthroughs not only advance scientific knowledge but translate into tangible benefits for those battling MS.

Many authors have demonstrated the capability to detect faults using the EIS by recording impedance spectra during fuel cell operation and analysing these data using the ECM approach with diagnostic purposes ([11,12]). The paper of Narjis et al. [13] provides the main references for the development of Fault Detection and Isolation (FDI) based on EIS [7]. Also the use of more physical-based modelling representation of fuel cell impedance has been thoroughly accounted for in the literature. For example, Kulikovsky proposed the analytical model of a the impedance of a PEMFC cathode catalyst layer under poor oxygen transport ([14,15]) and at Open Circuit Voltage in addition to the Gas Diffusion Layer impedance [16]. The work of Cruz-Manzo et al. [17] describes the PEMFC impedance spectra subject to Pt oxidation and H2 peroxide formation at cathode side, also with the combined use of physical and circuit modelling. On the same line, Cruz-Manzo et al. [17] and Niya et al. [18] developed an impedance model combining physical and ECM approaches, particularly aiming at describing a PEMFC impedance at different operating conditions, varying current densities, temperature and humidity levels. Physics-based PEMFC impedance models were also developed by Setzler and Fuller [19], with the implementation of an oxide growth oxygen reduction reaction kinetic model, and Chevalier et al. [20,21], aiming at PEMFC state-of-health and degradation analysis. The analysis of the cells Output Voltage Signal with Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) has been also proposed for fuel cells FDI in the recent literature ([22,23]). The EIS methodology, however, has its drawbacks. The traditional EIS equipment is costly and cumbersome and requires several minutes to record a single impedance spectrum. Moreover, the diagnosis can be performed once some metrics are derived through EIS signal treatment. This is not a simple task because, in many cases, different operating conditions could lead to the same impedance spectrum; thus, a deep analysis based on analyst experience is necessary. On the other hand, for on-field (i.e. unattended) operations suitable algorithms, such as those based on the ECM [24] or on FOM approaches [10], can be built to process the EIS to derive useful metrics for monitoring and diagnostic applications. The scientific contribution of the present work is the development of a fast model capable of simulating PEMFC impedance spectra. The model is based on non-dimensional parameters defined by exploiting the Buckingham's Theorem, which is a key method in the similarity theory field. Particularly, it allows suitably describing the relationships linking the physical variables involved in the process under-study to the fundamental dimensions [25]. The definition of non-dimensional parameters allows reproducing the impedance of different types of system operating at different conditions, thanks to the high generalizability of the model.
