We need to look at the impact of fathers on children and how they can have positive impacts in children's lives. FATHERS AND MOTHERS ARE NOT SYMMETRICAL Fathers and mothers make different contributions to the lives of their children. Both parents are needed. Fathers and mothers are not interchangeable parts. There is a difference between being a parent and being a mother or a father. We need to recognize and appreciate these differences. FATHERS HAVE UNIQUE STRENGTHS TO OFFER THEIR CHILDREN Fathers provide something different from mothers. As one expert said, "Dads give kids permission." Mothers tend to teach girls about themselves while dads teach boys about their world. Dads are able to get boys to talk about things they would not tell mom. Boys can learn from dads about masculinity and self esteem. Fathers can help boys become responsible adults. Boys learn by doing, especially in the physical arena. Dads can serve as coaches, mentors and guides for their sons. Fathers can teach their sons about manliness and respect. One study showed that boys who had a strong relationship with their fathers were less likely to use drugs than those who did not. Fathers are important because they provide a sense of security to children. They are often seen as protectors and providers. Sons want to be like their fathers. Dads can provide a sense of continuity, especially to boys. It is important for dads to be present during the early years of a child's life, including pregnancy. Dads are important in helping young children develop their identities. When fathers are involved, children feel secure. This helps them to develop into healthy individuals. FATHERS CAN BE IMPORTANT FOR DAUGHTERS TOO Daughters also benefit from having fathers in their lives. Girls who grow up without fathers are more likely to be promiscuous and to marry too early. Fathers can help daughters develop healthy sexual attitudes. Fathers can also help girls develop healthy relationships with males. Girls need both moms and dads. Moms are great nurturers. Dads can help girls to learn to be independent and to take risks. They can encourage girls to be adventurous and to try new things. FATHERS SHOULD PARTICIPATE IN PREGNANCY AND BIRTH DADS CAN HELP MOMS BE GOOD PARENTS Studies show that dads who participate in pregnancy and birth are better fathers after the baby is born. If dads are not there for the first few months of a child's life, they may never connect with the child. Dads can be very supportive of moms during pregnancy and childbirth. Dads should support moms in their parenting decisions. This includes supporting them through the hard times and not being overly critical. FATHERS WHO WORK FULL-TIME SHOULD NOT FEEL GUILTY ABOUT SPENDING TIME WITH THEIR CHILDREN Being a full-time worker does not mean you cannot be a good parent. Full-time work can actually be beneficial to families. It gives parents time away from each other. Parents need to balance their own needs with those of their children. FATHERS DO NOT ALWAYS KNOW WHAT THEY ARE DOING Fathers are often unsure of what to do when they are with their children. Many dads feel guilty about spending time with their kids instead of working. They think they don't know enough to be good parents. However, most dads are not afraid to ask for help. They just don't always know where to go for assistance. It is important for fathers to find out what kinds of resources are available to them. FATHERS AND MOTHERS MUST COOPERATE FOR CHILDREN TO SUCCEED Dads and moms must cooperate for children to succeed. Mothers and fathers are partners in raising children. They need to share the responsibility of parenting.

To be sure, Google's numbers are impressive; when Facebook first launched, the company had 6.7 million monthly users and 400,000 daily users. And while Google's stats may not be as impressive as Facebook's, the search giant has only been actively promoting Google+ since June 2011, whereas Facebook was pushing its service starting in September 2006. So, where does Google+ go from here? How will the company try to boost engagement among its existing users, and convince skeptics to sign up? Here are five ways that Google can make Google+ a must-have service. 1. Make Circles More Useful. The biggest hurdle for Google+ right now is that most people don't understand what Circles are, or why they should care. Even those who understand the concept feel like they're using them incorrectly. For example, I have a Circle called "Work Friends" that includes people I know from past jobs and internships. But what happens when someone leaves my company? Do I take them out of the circle, or leave them there? What if I want to reach out to them later? Should I create another circle, or find a way to group them with my current work colleagues? These questions are enough to make anyone throw up his hands and give up on the idea of organizing friends in groups. "I think we've done a pretty good job of explaining what Circles are," Horowitz tells Mashable. "The challenge is how to explain how to use them." Well, let's start with the basics. The whole point of Circles is to organize your contacts into groups based on common interests. You might put your family members in one Circle, and your co-workers in another. In fact, Google has already made a huge step toward making this easier by creating auto-Circles for family and co-workers, as well as providing suggestions for new groups. Now, Google needs to take things a step further. It needs to provide a way to easily share content across multiple Circles, and a way to customize posts for each group. For instance, I could post an announcement to everyone in my "Family" Circle, and then send a message to my "Friends" Circle letting them know about a party I'm throwing next weekend. Or I could share photos from my recent trip to Europe with my "Traveling Buddies" Circle, and then send a note to my "Foodie Friends" about a great restaurant I found in Rome. Another big problem with Circles is that they're currently tied to Google+, so you need to be logged in to access them. But Google needs to allow you to view and edit your Circles even if you're not signed into Google+. That way, I can share a link with a colleague outside of work, and he'll still be able to add me to his "Co-worker" Circle without having to log into Google+. Once that's taken care of, Google can then start experimenting with sharing content across multiple platforms. If I share something with my "Foodie Friends" Circle, perhaps Google can automatically share that post with Twitter, or Instagram, or Pinterest. That way, I don't have to worry about posting the same thing twice. 2. Integrate With Gmail. One of the biggest problems with Google+ is that people don't realize it exists until they start using Google's other products. When you sign up for a Google account, you have to choose between signing up for Google+ and signing up for Gmail. Because Gmail is so popular, many people opt to skip Google+ altogether. But Google needs to change that. It needs to make Google+ an integral part of Gmail.

It was of the American type that approximates to the Red Indian, and you guessed the power that lay behind it by the set of the cheek-bones, the breadth of the chin and the restfulness of the eyes. Like the Red Indian, Paul Quincy Adams was slow of speech. A silent man with his tongue. He entered the hospital and passed down a long corridor to the cloakroom, where he left his overcoat and from there, by another corridor, he found his way to the swing-door of the lecture theatre. It wanted five minutes to the hour. He peeped over the muffing of the glass; the place was nearly full, so he went in and took his seat, choosing one at the right hand end of the first row of the stalls - students' vernacular for the lowest row of the theatre benches. The theatre was lit with gas. It had whitewashed walls bare as the walls of a barn; a permanent blackboard faced the audience, and the air was suffocatingly hot after the crisp, cold air of the streets. It would be like this till about the middle of the lecture, when Alphonse the porter would pull the rope of the skylight and ventilate the place with an arctic blast. This room, which had once been an anatomical theatre, and always a lecture room, had known the erect form of Lisfranc; the stooping shoulders of Majendie had cast their shadow on its walls; Flourens had lectured here on that subject of which he had so profound a knowledge - the brain; the echoes of this room had heard the foundations of Medicine shift and change, the rank heresies of yesterday voiced as the facts of to-day - and Adams, having opened his notebook and sharpened his pencil, sat listening to the gas sizzling above his head; then he turned for a moment and glanced at the men behind him: the doctor from Vienna in a broadly braided frock-coat with satin facings, betraying himself to all men by the end of the clinical thermometer protruding from his waistcoat pocket; the two Japanese gentlemen - brown, incurious, and inscrutable - men from another world, come to look on; the republican from Liberia, and the rest. Then he turned his head, for the door on the floor of the theatre had opened, giving entrance to Thenard. Thenard was a smallish man in a rather shabby frock-coat; his beard was scant, pointed, and gray-tinged; he had a depressed expression, the general air of a second-rate tradesman on the verge of bankruptcy; and as he entered and crossed to the estrade where the lecture table stood and the glass of water, he shouted some words vehemently and harshly to Alphonse, the theatre attendant, who, it seemed, had forgotten to place the box of coloured chalks on the table - the sacred chalks which the lecturer used for colouring his diagrams on the blackboard.

Fieldwork has shown that the average yield of green biomass on the riverbank was around 13 t/ha. The average dry matter (DM) content in the riverbank grass was 37% which gives the dry mass yield of around 4.8 t/ha. The overall results pointed to the conclusion that the energy recovery of grass biomass could decrease the dependency of the AD supply chain on the energy crops while obtaining a positive energy return (Meyer et al., 2014). Antagonistic and synergistic effects on biogas and methane production from batch anaerobic co-digestion of cattle and pig slurries with grass silage have shown that the replacement of cattle slurry with grass silage increased the biogas and methane yields (Himanshu et al., 2018). Besides several experimental works on the AD, various studies based on mathematical modelling of the AD have been performed. Mathematical modelling of the AD of biodegradable matter describes the interactions between physical and biological mechanisms (Lauwers et al., 2013). Typically, Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 (ADM1) is applied for the mathematical description of the process. ADM1 describes the reactions occurring in an AD by assuming a perfect mixing and consequently homogenous reactor mixture. The components in the process are expressed regarding their Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) or molar concentrations. Recent studies on modelling of the AD using ADM1 have been applied to several substrates: blackwater and rotten vegetable (Feng et al., 2006); grass silage (Koch et al., 2010); a mixture of municipal waste and grease (Nordlander et al., 2017); microalgae (Mairet et al., 2011) and many others. ADM1 is available in Matlab and Simulink and water-related simulation software such as WEST, BioWin and AQUASIM. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is an useful tool for improving the biogas production chain, with the main focus on the environmental performance and eco-efficiency (Huttunen et al., 2014). There have been several LCA studies on biogas production, such as LCA study on co-digestion of fresh algae with animal manure (Cappelli et al., 2015). LCA-based mixed integer programming (MIP) mathematical model has been applied to investigate sustainability of the biogas production from environmentally harmful raw materials where it was shown that the integrated biogas production with included auxiliary facilities led to a significant eco-profit in the large-scale applications (Cucek et al., 2011). Evaluation of replacing energy crops with macroalgae at a real biogas plant has been performed using the LCA approach where sustainable energy production and lower environmental effects have been obtained compared to energy crops, but only if microalgae are regionally accessible (Ertem et al., 2017). The focus of this study is on the use of residue grass as a replacement for maize silage in the AD. The grass samples have been collected from the areas that do not compete with the food production: uncultivated land, the Sava riverbank in the city of Zagreb and highway verge.

But if you are an asthma sufferer, you can, through natural means, considerably reduce the number of asthma attacks you get. A placebo study has shown that asthmatics who consume 1 gram of vitamin C per day had 4 times fewer attacks. When they stopped taking vitamin C, the attacks resumed with the same frequency as before. The placement of fielders, deliberately positioned to catch the ball from batsmen protecting themselves from short, fast deliveries aimed at the ribs and throat, was entirely legal at the time, but seriously threatened the code of sportsmanship that is so central to cricket. That said, the Australian administrators - who made such a meal of Jardine's tactic at the time - were noticeably quiet when their own fast bowlers Dennis Lillee and Jeff Thomson were terrifying batsmen with short-pitched bowling in the 1970s. The authorities acted swiftly after the Bodyline tour to limit the placing of fielders in catching positions on the leg side in an attempt to deter a repeat of the tactic, and also brought in a restriction of the number of bouncers that can be bowled in a single over. But after Lillee and Thomson, the West Indies' formidable pace attack of the late 1970s and 80s also proved that skilful, intimidatory fast bowling is every bit as effective as Bodyline, even with field restrictions and after the introduction of helmets. Complaints about the tactic quickly appeared. As the bruises and wickets mounted, the disquiet turned to anger, with claims batsmen were being physically targeted. Despite Australia levelling the series at the second match in Melbourne, the repeated blows to lightly protected players attracted outraged headlines. Some batsmen endured hours of punishment and even Bradman looked unsettled. Mr Studham said: "The tactics employed by Jardine roused intense passions, as they were so out of accord with anything that had previously happened on the cricket field. "Targeting the bowling along the line of the batsman's body was regarded by the Australian crowds as vicious, unsporting and especially after repeatedly battering the batsmen, 'hitting a man when he was down and certainly no part of cricket'." With everything to play for, and feelings running at fever pitch, the Adelaide match opened in front of packed stands. Cricket bible Wisden would later call it "probably the most unpleasant Test ever played". Australian captain Bill Woodfull was left staggering after being struck just above the heart by Larwood. The booing lasted for three minutes, despite the fact England had not yet deployed Bodyline tactics in the match. That would change though, moments later, when Jardine called out to Larwood: "Well bowled Harold," and set the fielders in the hated Bodyline formation. Police had to be deployed on the boundary. The next day, Oldfield had his skull cracked and Larwood had to be escorted from the ground. Source: BBC Religion & Ethics Is fair play important in sport? The line between gamesmanship and cheating Can cricket teach children fair play? It was almost inevitable the problems would overflow from the playing field. But no-one could have predicted it would lead to three events then unthinkable in cricket. MCC tour manager Pelham Warner, seeking to smooth relationships, was sent packing by the normally placid Woodfull with what were, for some years, the 25 most famous words in sport.

"We're going to stay right here until we get you to talk."

That year, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 174 (II), which stated that "the general and complete disarmament of the world involves, in addition to the prohibition and elimination of atomic weapons and of all other major weapons adaptable to mass destruction, the establishment so far as possible of effective international controls and safeguards." By the early 1960s, the phrase "weapons of mass destruction" was being used routinely in political debate. In January 1961, President Dwight D. Eisenhower gave his farewell speech, warning against the rise of the "military-industrial complex." Then he added: "A vital element in keeping the peace is our military establishment. Our arms must be mighty, ready for instant action, so that no potential aggressor may be tempted to risk his own destruction." His successor, John F. Kennedy, told Congress in February 1963 that "we seek no wider sphere of conflict; we seek only the removal of threats to our security and freedom." In May 1985, Ronald Reagan spoke about the need to eliminate nuclear weapons, telling an audience in Moscow that they should not be considered "merely instruments of military power" but rather "instruments of death." A year earlier, Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader who presided over the end of the Cold War, had spoken about "the danger of unleashing uncontrollable processes of a thermonuclear war which could lead to the destruction of civilization itself." In March 1994, Bill Clinton said he wanted to see a world free of WMDs. "I believe that the ultimate goal of our foreign and defense policies is the total elimination of all weapons of mass destruction," he said. After the September 11 attacks in New York and Washington, the Bush administration began using the term "war on terror." But the phrase "weapons of mass destruction" continued to appear regularly in speeches and statements. In November 2001, Colin Powell, the secretary of state, said the Taliban regime in Afghanistan was "protecting terrorists and training terrorists, supplying weapons of mass destruction to terrorists, giving safe haven to terrorists." A year later, he said the U.S. would continue to look for evidence of WMDs in Iraq. "We are going to find them," he said. "It's going to take time." On October 14, 2002, the House of Representatives passed the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002. It stated: "Whereas members of al Qaida, an organization bearing responsibility for attacks on the United States, its citizens, and interests abroad since the 1990s, are known to be in Iraq." And, "Whereas Iraq continues to aid and harbor other international terrorist organizations, including organizations that threaten the lives and safety of American citizens." The Senate followed suit the following month. On February 15, 2003, millions of people around the world took part in anti-war demonstrations protesting the impending invasion of Iraq. On March 20, 2003, the invasion began. The last U.S. combat brigade left Iraq in August 2010. In a 2013 interview with CNN, David Kay, who headed the Iraq Survey Group, said that the intelligence community had been wrong about WMDs. "There wasn't any," he said. "We never found anything." # Recommended ### Comments The views expressed are not those of this site, this station or its affiliated companies. But he persevered, and they married in 1948. Diana gave up her career to raise their family: they had two children, Jeremy and Marc, both actors. In a 19-month run during the late Forties at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in The Heiress, he never missed a show. The management gave him an engraved silver ashtray to mark his achievement of giving more consecutive performances than any other actor in the theatre's history. The ashtray was appropriate - despite his asthma, Sinden would for much of his life puff through two or more packs a day. His cinema breakthrough came in 1953 with an adaptation of The Cruel Sea, Nicholas Monsarrat's novel about the battle between the Navy and German U-boats hunting Atlantic convoys during World War II. Jack Hawkins, then the country's biggest star, was the commander of a sub-hunter, and newcomer Sinden was his brave but inexperienced junior, in a father-son relationship that many film buffs believe would have earned them Oscars for Best Actor and Best Supporting Actor, had the movie been made in Hollywood. The honours went to On The Waterfront with Marlon Brando, the mumbling, slurring antithesis of everything Sinden stood for. His loathing of 'Method' acting won Sinden an unexpected admirer, Marilyn Monroe. Their dressing rooms at Pinewood studios were four doors apart while she was filming The Prince And the Showgirl, and he another movie, and Sinden mocked her attempts at Brando-style naturalism. He hung a sign on his door advertising his own drama classes, guaranteed to out-do the Method: 'You too can be inaudible! "Ums" and "Ers" rendered obsolete!' Monroe saw the joke and started dropping in, not for acting lessons but to offload her troubles. 'She popped in for a natter and a giggle,' Sinden said. 'Of course as a sex symbol she was stunning, but sadly, she must be one of the silliest women I have ever met.' Accolades were heaped on him for Twelfth Night and Much Ado About Nothing, in which he acted with Judi Dench, and for his King Lear. The Cruel Sea was followed by another war classic, Above Us The Waves, as well as lighter films, like The Captain's Table, You Know What Sailors Are and the romantic farce Doctor In The House. Sinden played Tony Benskin, the eternal medical student who spends his time boozing and chasing nurses. When he saw a girl he liked, Benskin, instead of wolf-whistling, would emit a gutteral growl.

However, the problem with this approach is that the coefficients of friction need to be known so that the thermal aspects of the model during phase 1 can be replicated accurately. Also, models of this type show that the two workpieces never truly merge - as happens in reality for many materials [2,26,27] - meaning that the mechanical mixing of the separate workpieces is not considered. The second approach [7,9,10,14-16,18,22,25] is to model only one workpiece, which is oscillated against a non-deformable surface, as shown in Fig. 2(b). This approach allows for quicker computational times as only half of the geometry is modelled. Many of the problems with this approach are the same as the first. The third approach [1,11,12], as shown in Fig. 2(c), was developed by Turner et al. [1], who noticed that prior to sticking friction taking place there is negligible macroscopic plastic deformation, at least for the titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V. Once sticking friction begins the process may be modelled as a single body due to there being approximately 100% true interface contact. A temperature profile needs to be mapped onto the single body model to account for the heat generated during sliding friction. The high temperature at the weld interface allows the material at the centre of the model to be highly viscous, thus allowing the single body to represent two individual workpieces. Due to the adhesion of the interface material being modelled this approach considers the mechanical mixing of the separate workpieces and produces much better replications of the flash morphology for Ti-6Al-4V workpieces [1,12]. The limitation of this approach is that the stages prior to sticking friction occurring are not modelled. Surface contaminants, such as oxides and foreign particles, at the weld interface affect the properties [26,28] and possibly the service life of a weld [1]. Oxides are generated during phase 1 when the hot interface material reacts with the atmosphere [29]. It is also possible that some surface oxides may remain at the interface due to insufficient pre-weld cleaning. The foreign particles may constitute oil or grease from workpiece machining which were also not removed during pre-weld cleaning. At the start of phase 2 the contaminants become trapped at the interface during adhesion of the viscous material. Many authors suggest that a weld is likely to be free from contaminants if all of the initial contacting interface material is expelled into the flash [28,30-32]. Wanjara and Jahazi [26] have shown that for the same burn-off distance, contaminants were present at the interface if lower values of frequency, amplitude and applied force were used, whereas if higher values were used the interface was free from surface contaminants. Therefore surface contaminant removal appears to be critically dependent on the combination of process inputs used. However, the reasons why the process inputs affect surface contaminant removal are not understood.

The ruckus drags on, echoing off the bare wooden walls and filtering through the dank, smoky air, twisting into a cacophony of desperate cries and punctured flesh. In the corner of the room, the dying candlelight flickers wildly, casting jagged shadows that dance with a frenetic energy, as if they too are caught in the frenzy. Alice, wrestling with Mike's bulk, feels his breath slick against her neck, the pitiless whiskey-tinged fumes burning her nostrils and filling her mind with violence. She does what she can, clawing at his back, grasping for anything she can get, desperate to turn the tide. "You want her, you pig?" she gasps, teeth gritting in a grimace. "Try me first." Davey trembles behind Delilah, heart hammering like a loose board in a storm. He's paralyzed between instinct and nauseating dread, eyes wide but dulled by a haze of disbelief. This isn't how things were supposed to go. He met Alice in a dusty saloon, years before a bitter wind sent him racing northward with dreams of a better life, only to find himself backing into a nightmare. Gasps slip from his lips as he wrestles with the weight of the scene unfolding before him. Then there's a rustling, a breath beneath the chaos-a whispered prayer clinging to the walls. It's Little Sue, still trembling in the doorway, her innocence barely clinging to her frame like a moth-eaten shawl. She shifts, eyes darting toward the gun wrangled at Skinny's waist; it's a fleeting glimmer of hope too fragile to hold onto for long. "Get the hell out of here," Alice snarls, foreboding in her stare, as if she can hoist Sue's soul from this wretched place with a mere glance. "You're too young for this." But there's no escaping it, not ever. Sure enough, Mike heaves Alice off of him like she's nothing more than a feather, and she crashes into the wall. The thud reverberates through the space, ricocheting off their assembled fears. Fresh blood seeps into the floorboards as Delilah screams anew, a sound so raw it shatters the air, drawing forth an echo of hopelessness. "I'll skin you, Mike," Davey finally finds his voice, the words stumbling out like drunk men. He clutches the trembling hands of Delilah, anchoring her amid the madness. She's strangely calm; there's a tired acceptance in her dark eyes, even as the blood seeps from her scars. "I swear it." "What'll you do, boy?" Mike sneers, wiping spit and rage from his bearded chin. It's a challenge, a beckoning, and all the whiskey in him flares to life. "You're just a pup in this game. You think you got the guts?" In that moment, Alice rises, murder in those scarred cheeks and fire coursing through her veins. "He's got more guts than you have heart," she retorts, spitting venom. "You're nothing but a coward wearing a dead man's skin." Amidst the clattering chaos, Skinny finally arrives, her entrance a baleful tempest, breathless and bent with urgency, gun drawn, steady but trembling. She doesn't hesitate; it's all part of the deal, playing the game or succumbing to it. "Step back, you cretin!" she warns, leveling the barrel at Mike's chest. Time freezes for just a heartbeat, tension like a coiled snake ready to strike. "It's over, Mike." The words drape heavy in the air, tethering this moment on the brink of annihilation.

But the work was too much for him; and his health having suffered, he has been permitted by his father to join the expedition now on foot. His father is a wealthy colonist, who owns large tracts of land, and herds of cattle, in the district of Graaf Reinet. He has given his son permission to spend some time in hunting and travelling; and Hans, being fond of both, has taken advantage of it, and here he is. Hendrik has also left school - not college, however, for he has never been there - but an academy for training youth up in the knowledge of useful things. He has learnt to be a smith, a carpenter, and a saddler; and he expects soon to set up shop on his own account, near the town of Beaufort, which is his native place. But before doing so, he has determined to go out on a grand hunt; and when invited by Hans to accompany him, he gladly accepted the offer, and here he is. He, too, has shot up considerably since we last met him, and looks like a man of twenty. Little Jan is the same little Jan he always was, except that he is somewhat older and stouter. He, too, has left school - the village school of Beaufort, which had taught him nearly all it knew - and is now apprenticed to a shoemaker. But his apprenticeship is not yet complete, and he has obtained leave to join his friends Hans and Hendrik in their proposed expedition. So here he is - little Jan - with a face as round and rosy as ever, and eyes as blue and twinkling as ever. He is the jester of the party, and his jokes keep everybody in constant laughter. But who are those other three young fellows? One of them - the tallest of the lot - seems to be a stranger among them. You may know he is by the way the others treat him. He is evidently regarded as their superior; and although they address him familiarly, it is easy to perceive that they hold him in high respect. This young man, tall, handsome, and well-proportioned, with dark hair and black eyes, is a true type of the Dutch South African. His name is Arend van Wyk. He is the son of a rich farmer, who resides in the district of Graaf Reinet, near the town of Somerset East. He is about nineteen years of age, and has just returned from Europe, whither he went to finish his education. He was educated partly in Holland, and partly in Germany; and while in the latter country he became acquainted with natural history. He made such progress in this branch of science that he resolved to devote his life to it. On returning home, he found that his father did not approve of this resolution. Mr van Wyk wanted his son to assist him in managing his estates and flocks; and, as he was getting old, desired Arend to remain at home. Arend was unwilling to disappoint his father, and so gave up his favourite pursuit. But after a few months spent in superintending the farm and sheep-folds, he grew weary of this sort of life, and again expressed his desire to travel and study natural history. His father at length yielded to his entreaties; and it was arranged that Arend should make an excursion into the interior, accompanied by a guide and servants. At the same time he heard that his old playmate, Hans Marais, was going out on a grand hunting-trip; and it occurred to him that he might combine business with pleasure by joining company with Hans and his companions.

"What? A crown, you say? You must think me a bonnie lad, indeed, to pass off such a sweet tidbit!" he retorted, still flipping the beefsteaks languidly. "But do not squander your coin so thoughtlessly; there's no wealth in proving a fool, even if he could claim the title of groom quite rightly." Long Ned narrowed his eyes, seeking to pierce through the banter that hung like smoke in the air. "And who speaks of proving fools? By all accounts, you're lined with more folly than an alehouse on a Sunday morn, MacGrawler!" he laughed heartily, before fetching himself a tankard of ale. "Aye, 'tis true," said Tomlinson, shifting to rest his elbows upon the worn table of ragged wood. "But mind you, t' mere fools may construct better schemes than the wise in haste. Now, what's this concerning our journey, gentlemen? Shall we risk that cursed Wattleton Pass again?" "But soft!" interrupted Augustus, as a glitter of mischief sparked in his eyes. "I do believe the shadows dance upon the path of those who tread recklessly. Better perhaps we sway to the harbor, and drink as sailors before encountering fate." "Ah, a wise thought, my dear Augustus!" cried Ned. "For what better rise can there be before the enmity of the world than the sweet, heady brew of good rum and cheer?" He poured a generous measure into the cup and handed it round, all agreeing heartily, for they were none save men of mirth. Their spirits buoyed, the heroes translated their misfortunes into joyous jest, laughing away the fading sorrows that had turned their fates upon a thin, precarious line. "Tell me, MacGrawler," began Tomlinson slyly, "does one find wisdom in the base notes of spirit? Or is all wisdom fermented within the barrels from the Highlands?" "The only wisdom you might glean from such spirits is to know when to unsheathe your sword and when to sheathe your tongue," retorted MacGrawler, his expression a mask of feigned seriousness. "These unholy concoctions only serve to embolden the miscreant and embolden the coward, mark my words." "And yourself, then, MacGrawler?" questioned Long Ned, keen to provoke. "Are you edges sharper for abstinence, or merely rusting from lack of use?" With a sly smile, MacGrawler fixed his gaze on Ned. "Sharp as a dagger, my friend! But beware, for an edge too keen may carve its own master." And thus their words turned to barbs, each jest another feather in their fraying cap. A moment's reprieve took them, each man resting upon the primitive pleasures of companionship and flames crackling again to life. The pensive quiet was pierced only by the rhythmic echoes of the rain against the earth, as though the heavens wept for the souls knit together in schemes of mirth and mischief. "But alas, dear comrades," broke Augustus pragmatically. "We must, in the end, return to our grim task-the world may spin on jests and merriment, but those who wander in gleeful circles soon find the path leads straight into the jaws of peril." "I pledge," proclaimed Long Ned, "that we shall slice through our adversities as surely as we carve a roast!" With that, a fresh resolve ignited, a determination forged anew in the flickering light of camaraderie-under the watchful gaze of stars yet concealed by misty clouds. Each man, taught by temperance and folly alike, steeled himself for the adventures still unwritten, bound to the fervent cycle of jest and endeavor. For there lay a world awaiting their return, and within it, destinies tangled like the threads of a fine tapestry.

He and his wife, the old lady who had received me, looked at each other in a frightened sort of way. He mumbled out that the money had been sent in a letter, and that was all he knew. When I asked him if he knew Count Dracula, and could tell me anything of his castle, both he and his wife crossed themselves, and, saying that they knew nothing at all, simply refused to speak further. It was so near the time of starting that I had no time to ask anyone else, for it was all very mysterious and not by any means comforting. Just before I was leaving, the old lady came up to my room and begged me with tears in her eyes to wear a string of beads around my neck. She threw herself on her knees and implored me to take them off myself when I got to the hotel, and not to say a word about them to my future host. They were "for my protection," she said, and again she solemnly enjoined me to take them off before I went to sleep. I tried to arouse her curiosity, but she appeared to wish to say nothing, so I dropped the subject, and wished her good-bye. She said she would pray for me, and again she warned me to take care of myself about wearing the beads. She gave me some holy candles to put in my window at night, and a crucifix blessed by the Pope. Now, these things I fear, would savour of Romanism. But then, as the Count is not of that creed, he will probably not mind them. I shall carry them with me in case. My luggage was ready, and there was nothing to remain for; so, thanking them for their kindness, and promising to show them my beautiful home in Whitby, I drove off. All day long we seemed to dawdle through a country which was full of beauty of every kind. Sometimes we saw little towns or castles on the top of steep hills such as we see in old missals; sometimes we ran by rivers and streams which seemed from the wide stony margin on each side of them to be subject of great floods. It takes a lot of water, and running strong, to sweep the outside edge of a river clear. At every station there were groups of people, sometimes crowds, and in all sorts of attire.

I think it's interesting that we're even having this conversation, because it speaks to the fact that there's no one-size-fits-all approach to design interviews. I mean, every company, every team, every designer has their own way of doing things, and that's what makes this topic so contentious. Some people swear by design exercises, while others are adamant that design challenges are the way to go. For me, the key difference between the two is the level of guidance and support provided. With a design exercise, you're typically working within a set timeframe, and you've got someone guiding you through the process, asking questions, and providing feedback in real-time. It's a more collaborative experience, and it gives the interviewer a chance to see how you think on your feet, how you respond to feedback, and how you iterate on your ideas. On the other hand, design challenges are more of a solo affair. You're given a problem, and you're left to your own devices to come up with a solution. This can be intimidating, especially if you're someone who thrives on feedback and collaboration. But at the same time, it's a great way to showcase your skills, your problem-solving abilities, and your attention to detail. One thing that I've noticed is that some companies use design exercises as a way to weed out candidates early on in the process. It's like a screening test, to see if you've got the basic skills and knowledge to move forward. And then, if you pass that hurdle, you might be given a design challenge to complete on your own time. This can be a more comprehensive assessment of your skills, and it gives the company a chance to see how you approach a problem, how you prioritize your time, and how you communicate your ideas. But here's the thing: both design exercises and design challenges can be flawed. I've seen exercises that are too easy, too vague, or too focused on trivial things. And I've seen challenges that are too open-ended, too complex, or too time-consuming. So, it's not just about whether you're doing an exercise or a challenge - it's about how you're doing it, and what you're trying to achieve. I think what's most important is that the company is clear about what they're looking for, and that they're transparent about the process. If you're going to ask someone to spend hours on a design challenge, you'd better be willing to give them feedback that's just as thorough. And if you're going to put someone through a design exercise, you'd better be prepared to provide guidance and support throughout the process. Ultimately, it comes down to what works best for the company, and what works best for the candidate. And that's what makes this topic so contentious - there's no one right answer. But I think that's what makes it so interesting, too. It's a chance to explore different approaches, to learn from each other, and to figure out what works best for us as designers. So, what do you think? Do you have a preference for design exercises or design challenges? Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences with either one? Let's keep the conversation going!

We took the midnight train together for our vacation trip down here, and since then we've been inseparable. We'll stick together, won't we?" "Sure!" agreed Ardmore heartily, putting out his hand. "But let's cut loose from the crowd for awhile. I've had enough of their everlasting chatter. Let's go down to the beach by ourselves and enjoy the rest of the season in peace." "All right, old man; whatever you say goes. When shall we start?" "To-morrow. I'll telegraph them to-day." As he turned away to send his message, Ardmore saw a young girl who had come into the station with an elderly lady and gentleman, and was standing near the door, glancing nervously about her, while she waited for the porter to bring her trunks. Her face attracted him instantly. He had seen hundreds of girls, thousands of them perhaps, yet none like this one. She was not beautiful - he could see that even across the room - but she possessed a charm which beauty seldom has. He wondered vaguely who she might be, and why she had come to Atlanta. Perhaps she lived here. Then he remembered that the town was full of strangers at this time of year, and that she might only be passing through. He lingered to watch her as she moved toward the door, and his eyes followed her wistfully until she disappeared. "She looks like a nice girl," remarked Griswold, coming back with the tickets. "What girl?" demanded Ardmore, turning quickly. "That girl over there, with the big hat and the blue suit." "Oh, yes; did you notice her too?" "Couldn't help it. She came in just after you went out." "And you noticed her?" "Certainly. I told you so. She looks like a nice girl." "Yes, she does, doesn't she?" "We must hurry now if we catch this train." They hurried, but Ardmore could not forget the girl in the blue suit. A half-hour later, when they reached their hotel, he found himself still wondering who she was, and why she had come to Atlanta. CHAPTER II THE GIRL IN BLUE Ardmore sat moodily smoking in the veranda of the hotel, listening to the orchestra playing inside. The music was good, but he scarcely heard it. His thoughts wandered far away. He had tried to interest himself in the talk of the men around him, but without success. Their conversation seemed trivial and unimportant. Presently he rose and strolled out into the garden, where he found a seat beneath a palm-tree. The moonlight lay softly about him, and the air was heavy with the scent of flowers. Insects hummed drowsily among the shrubbery, and a mocking-bird sang its weird song in the distance. There was a sense of peace and restfulness everywhere. It was a perfect setting for romance. Suddenly he became conscious of voices close beside him. Two people were walking slowly along the path, evidently unconscious of his presence. They passed within a few feet of his chair, and he recognized the girl whom he had seen in the station that morning. Her companion was a young man, tall and broad-shouldered, with dark hair and a short, pointed beard. They stopped a moment at the end of the path and stood talking earnestly. The moonlight fell full upon them, and Ardmore could hear every word distinctly. "This is the end," the girl was saying. "I cannot bear any more. I must tell father." "Tell him nothing," replied the man harshly.

While some studies have investigated the role of social capital and collective action in facilitating risk management in the face of cyclones [5,7,31,38,39], few have looked at how farmers' groups might facilitate this process or whether they are effective in reducing the impacts of cyclones on rural households. This study investigates the effectiveness of farmer-led organizations (FLOs) in helping smallholder farmers in the Mahajanga region of northwestern Madagascar cope with and adapt to cyclones. FLOs are non-governmental organizations (NGOs), associations or cooperatives formed and led by farmers themselves and generally focus on improving their livelihoods through increasing their knowledge and skills, improving their market access, strengthening their bargaining power, gaining access to inputs and services, securing land tenure rights, managing natural resources and/or promoting community-based development projects. Although FLOs are not new in Madagascar, there has been a rapid increase in the number of FLOs in recent years, especially since the early 1990s when a series of laws were passed to encourage and support their formation [27]. Today there are over 800 FLOs registered in Madagascar [16] and many others operating without registration. The FLOs in our study area are located in a rural area where the main economic activities are subsistence farming, animal husbandry and fishing. They vary greatly in size, composition, structure, objectives and degree of success, but generally aim to improve the members' livelihoods by increasing their incomes and well-being. Most FLOs are involved in various types of collective actions related to agriculture, livestock, fisheries, forestry, wildlife conservation, energy production, and tourism, among others. Our research questions were: (i) What type of collective actions do the FLOs in the study area undertake? (ii) How do the FLOs help their members to cope with and adapt to cyclones? (iii) Are FLOs successful in reducing the negative impacts of cyclones on their members?

"Ah, yes, good old Uncle Bernard," Geoffrey replies with a chuckle, as he continues to scratch the terrier's ears. "The quintessential eccentric, wasn't he? Always had a knack for the extraordinary-like that peculiar castle in Spain he dreamed of owning, yet never bothered to visit. It seems he had a penchant for collecting properties he could enjoy more in his imagination than in reality." "Well, I suppose Coolnagurtheen will suit you," Lady Rodney declares, dismissing further discussion of her late brother's proclivities with a flick of her slender hand. "You were ever the dreamer, Geoffrey-not unlike him. Let us hope your dreams are a little less confounding." "They remain dreams until one ventures forth to realize them," Geoffrey retorts, rising to his feet and crossing the room to gaze out of the tall window at the somnolent garden beyond. The terrier, feeling slightly neglected, hops down and trots after him, its tail wagging in earnest appreciation of his presence. "The thought of traveling there stirs something-a curiosity, perhaps. It's been too long since life offered any semblance of adventure." "It is a risk," responds Lady Rodney, more sharply. Her thin brows furrow momentarily, as if considering the full weight of her son's ambitions. "If not from the infamous pikes and pitfalls, then from becoming quite the recluse in so remote a location... You might even meet some peculiar locals who speak with that melodic peculiarity you find so amusing." "Or it could be a golden opportunity to refine my own brogue," Geoffrey counters with a grin. "Think of it, Mother-a grand escape from the ennui of balls and social minutiae that haunt every season here. No need to present oneself in endless, stifling drawing rooms." "In one of which, I might add, your interests might be better served," Lady Rodney notes with a certain pointedness, although her tone remains listless. "Think of the charming Helen Montrosse; a connection with her family would be most advantageous. They, of course, are conveniently settled in England-not that you seem to care." "You forget, dear Mother, I am not quite a pawn in matrimonial chess," Geoffrey states, his voice light, though underscored with firmness. "Besides, I doubt Helen Montrosse longs for such a rustic abode as Coolnagurtheen-nor the company of a chimerical fellow such as myself, fixated as I am on fleeting notions of adventure." Lady Rodney sighs, unconvinced yet unwilling to press more. "Just do not forget your obligations here, Geoffrey," she ventures softly. "Even dreamers must wake to reality eventually." "Reality follows wherever one goes," he reassures her, retreating from the window and reclaiming his seat, the terrier hopping upon his lap, settling into a cozy curl. "Rest assured, Mother, I have all intention of returning, stories to tell and everything." Her half-closed eyes settle upon him again, skepticism tinged with maternal affection. "With you, my son," she ventures, "such promises seem elusive as dreams themselves." Yet there is a glimmer of amusement in her gaze-an acknowledgment that in Geoffrey's world, dreams drive the narrative, surreal, just as enticing.

In the context of bacterial mutagenicity assays, the incorporation of varied methodologies in laboratory protocols has gained prominence. This evolution reflects a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying mutagenesis, as well as the necessity for a diversified approach to address the myriad of compounds that may exhibit genotoxic potential. Moreover, as the landscape of pharmaceuticals and chemical agents expands, researchers face an increasing challenge in discerning mutagenic properties, prompting the evolution of experimental designs that not only adhere to regulatory expectations but also push the boundaries of scientific inquiry [11]. The inclusion of novel mutant strains, for instance, has catalyzed discussions surrounding their efficacy in capturing a broader spectrum of mutagenic events. Consequently, the assessment of additional strains capable of elucidating mutagenic potential through different mechanisms has emerged as a topic of considerable interest [12]. Such strains may serve to enhance sensitivity and specificity, thereby allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of complex substance interactions within microbial genomic frameworks. The potential for modified strains to yield differential responses to specific mutagens, as seen with the E. coli WP2 uvrA pKM101, underscores the importance of stratifying testing paradigms according to chemical structure and mechanism of action [2,13]. Furthermore, advancements in forward-genetic techniques, such as whole-genome sequencing and CRISPR-based methodologies, offer illuminating frameworks for dissecting mutational landscapes. These technologies facilitate not only the identification of mutated loci but also the mapping of mutation pathways, providing richer context to established assays. Thus, their integration into routine protocols could radically shift the paradigm toward a more mechanistically-informed approach to mutagenicity testing [14]. Indeed, the application of such innovative strategies may lead to the identification of novel biomarkers of genotoxicity, which could transform our understanding of dose-response relationships and threshold effects [15]. During the recent IWGT conference, participants underscored the critical need for harmonizing methodologies across international laboratories. Disparities in experimental design and interpretation have often led to varied outcomes in toxicity assessments, raising questions about the reproducibility of results-a situation that not only complicates regulatory decision-making but also threatens public health initiatives [16]. Standardization efforts would not only bolster confidence in the reliability of results but also foster collaborative dialogues aimed at refining mutagenicity assessment techniques. Moreover, special attention was directed toward emerging alternatives to traditional mutagenicity assays, such as in vitro techniques utilizing human cell lines. While these may reduce reliance on animal testing, they also pose challenges in terms of translating findings to in vivo systems. The debate continues regarding the extent to which in vitro assessments can predict human outcomes, as metabolic pathways inherently differ between species [17]. Nevertheless, refining these approaches stands to enhance ethical practices while aligning with global regulatory shifts towards humane testing methods. In essence, the future of bacterial reverse-mutation assays hinges upon an amalgamation of traditional methodologies reinforced by cutting-edge technological innovations. As genetic toxicology progresses, so too must the frameworks guiding mutagenicity testing, evolving in tandem with scientific advancement and societal expectations. The commitment to continuous dialogue among stakeholders will be pivotal in ensuring that the tools employed are not just adequate, but exemplary, thereby safeguarding public health through rigorous and credible scientific inquiry.

Larry paced the small apartment, each step echoing his inner turmoil. "Even if I could keep them quiet, you know Brown an' Lawson are always snoopin' around. "You honestly think my sister's child is going to raise such a hullabaloo that people'll be slobberin' to tell tales on us? She's a quiet girl, Larry. Barely makes a peep. All those up there making fuss and bother-it's all nonsense! Half of them thoughtless gossips wouldn't know charity if it reached out and bit them." Larry sighed, his broad shoulders slumping just a bit. "The world's not built on charity, is it, love? It's built on contracts and deals and negotiations. The lease... it's a contract. You break it, and suddenly life's like a runaway horse you can't rein in." Kate's eyes softened. She reached a hand towards him. "And we've reined in plenty of wild horses, haven't we? Remember when we first moved to the city? Had just about as much as could fit in a case? Ate beans outta the tin for weeks." Her voice softened, coaxing memories of their shared past into the present. "We got through that. We'll get through this too." Larry, hardened by years of struggle, felt a quiver of that old resolve in his heart. A fleeting smile touched his lips. "Aye, you're right. We did alright for ourselves, didn't we, Kate?" He gazed around the modest room, imagining the small figure of Mary Rose bringing life and laughter where there was now only silence. "She'll be a blessing," Kate murmured, voice filled with conviction. "An' maybe, just maybe, she'll soften the edges of this harsh world for a few folks livin' under this very roof. They got no childern themselves most of them-can't imagine the change one young girl could bring." Larry pondered her words. The kindness Kate so effortlessly gave to the world sometimes had a way of turning even the hardest of them around. Could it be the same with those living in the building? Could Mary Rose be the light in the often dark, narrow corridor of their lives? "Alright, Kate," Larry said at last, the battle in him finding some peace. "Let's bring Mary Rose home. We'll figure it out, somehow. I'd rather lose the steam of this gig than the warmth of a family's heart." Kate beamed, and for a moment, the room seemed much brighter than before. "You won't regret it, Larry. That's a promise." As Larry stepped out the door, ready to return to his duties with a new resolve, Kate murmured softly, "The good Lord works in mysterious ways, remember that. They all say it, even those above us who pretend not to believe it." And as the door closed behind him, a peculiar feeling of hope settled over their small world. Maybe the world wasn't just contracts and deals after all. Maybe, just maybe, it was about more than the words in a lease.

I don't remember what else was in the plate, but I do remember eating so much of it that I almost exploded. After that we went to the famous old school shop for some 'Pulut Tai' and 'Tau Fu Fa'. For those who don't know, Pulut Tai is basically glutinous rice cooked with coconut milk and sugar, then wrapped in banana leaves and steamed till done. Tau Fu Fa is basically tofu pudding. They serve it cold and covered with gula melaka syrup. After that, we took off for the Thai border. In Thailand, I had the most delicious meal of my life. It was a deep-fried chicken leg marinated in ginger sauce, served with white rice and vegetables. I ate the entire thing and washed it down with an icy glass of fresh fruit juice. After lunch, I decided to take a nap. We were supposed to be going to Haadyai and I wanted to sleep. So I lay back in my seat and closed my eyes. About an hour later, I woke up to a startling discovery. My bladder was full. Not just full, but FULLER than it has EVER been. I mean, I had never felt anything like this before. I sat up and tried to feel around for the zipper of my jeans, hoping against hope that I could hold it until we reached our destination. No such luck. I got out of the van and ran over to a nearby tree, where I squatted and tried desperately to relieve myself. Nothing happened. I stood up and tried again. Still nothing. I tried several more times. All to no avail. It was like my bladder had become a solid block of ice, refusing to let loose even the tiniest drop. As the hours ticked by, I became increasingly desperate. I walked back and forth, squatting every few minutes, trying to get the juices flowing. I started getting worried. What if I couldn't hold it in? What if it burst? What if I died? What if I pissed myself in front of everyone? The thought of the latter made me want to cry. I imagined the scene. Me standing next to the van, pants around my ankles, peeing away while everyone looked on in horror and disgust. I shuddered at the thought. Then I remembered that I had brought along a book with me. So I opened the book, flipped to a random page, and began to read aloud. "The sky is blue. The grass is green." I repeated this sentence over and over again, trying to distract myself from my predicament. To my relief, the pressure gradually subsided and I finally managed to empty my bladder. But it wasn't over yet. I still had to face the rest of the trip. So I did the only thing I could think of. I picked up the book again and resumed reading. "The sky is blue. The grass is green." I kept repeating the words over and over again, trying to distract myself from the uncomfortable situation I was in. To my surprise, it worked. I found myself lost in the story and completely oblivious to everything else around me. I was so focused on the book that I didn't realize how long I'd been sitting there until someone tapped me on the shoulder. It was my aunt. She said she needed to talk to me. Experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) has been widely used to study pathogenic mechanisms shared with MS and to develop therapies and biomarkers (Steinman and Zamvil, 2006). Chronic HDACi treatment has been reported to prevent clinical signs of EAE in rats (Zhang et al., 2012) and mice (Camelo et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2013; Lv et al., 2012). HDAC inhibition targets the immune system resulting in the reduction of IFN- -producing Th1 and IL-17-producing Th17 CD4 + T helper lymphocytes in the periphery (Ge et al., 2013; Lv et al., 2012) and CNS (Lv et al., 2012) in murine EAE. HDACis also induce changes in T helper cytokine expression in rat EAE (Zhang et al., 2012). While HDACi effects are significant when aggressive daily preventive treatments are given (Ge et al., 2013; Lv et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), treatments after the onset of disease, as would occur in MS, demonstrate only mild amelioration in Lewis rats (Zhang et al., 2012) and still require continuous daily HDACi use for efficacy in mice (Lv et al., 2012). HDACs can be evicted from specific loci at the chromatin by thyroid hormone (T3) treatment. T3 can bind to specific HDAC-bound nuclear receptors, inducing allosteric modifications and HDAC release (Perissi et al., 2010). Interestingly, an acute therapeutic treatment with l-thyroxine (T4), which is converted in target tissues to the active compound T3, leads to mild EAE amelioration in Lewis rats, but not in Dark Agouti (DA) rats (Fernandez et al., 2004). T3 appears to target directly the CNS instead of the immune system, with increased expression of markers for oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) and accelerated remyelination (Fernandez et al., 2004). Remyelination can be induced in demyelination models in rodents (including EAE) and in MS by recruitment of adult OPCs of the CNS and/or neural stem cells (NSCs) from the subventricular zone (SVZ) of the brain, followed by differentiation into OLs and myelination (Fancy et al., 2011; Nait-Oumesmar et al., 2007; Tepavcevic et al., 2011; Zawadzka et al., 2010). SVZ NSCs and OPCs are recruited to the sites of lesions in MS, where they differentiate and promote remyelination in early stages of disease. However, OPCs eventually fail to remyelinate leading to disability progression. Interestingly, we have recently shown that exposure of embryonic NSCs to HDAC inhibitors in the absence of T3 leads to neuronal differentiation, while they promote increased OL differentiation and expression of myelin genes in the presence of T3 (Castelo-Branco et al., 2014). In addition, knockdown of HDAC2 in the presence of T3 in NSCs and OPCs also leads to spontaneous OL differentiation (Castelo-Branco et al., 2014). Thus, HDAC inhibition and T3 can synergize for terminal oligodendrocyte differentiation in the CNS. In this study, we investigated the effects of combinatorial HDAC inhibition and thyroid hormone treatment on the immune system and CNS in the context of EAE.

These men belonged to the class of individuals who could neither read nor write, yet who could wield a sword with skill, or throw a dagger with deadly precision; whose hands were hard and calloused from years of manual labour, but whose hearts were filled with hatred towards all men, and who looked upon women as things made solely for their pleasure. For, indeed, such men were common enough in Paris, and especially in the Marais. They were the sons of the peasants who had come to Paris to seek work and found none, or rather, who came to Paris to do nothing, having left their homes and lands to find themselves unable to return to them. The sons of these men had grown up in the streets of Paris, among thieves and cut-throats, learning little save how to steal, how to fight, how to live by their wits, and to hate all men who wore ruffs and doublets, hose and shoes, and who were known as gentlemen. Some few of them became brigands in the country, and roamed over France like wolves, living by plundering travellers and wayfarers, and by stealing cattle. Others, more fortunate, had become soldiers, and served in the armies of the King, either as pikemen or musketeers, and had learned to use arms with wonderful accuracy and rapidity. Yet others had remained in Paris, and formed bands of desperadoes, who infested the dark, narrow, tortuous streets, and lay in wait behind doors or in dark corners for any one whom chance threw into their path, whether a rich merchant returning home late at night, or a poor artisan hurrying homeward after a weary day's work. These men were known as "the scum of the earth," and they carried on a regular warfare against the police, who hunted them unceasingly, and against the citizens, who were continually falling victims to their ferocity. Sometimes they attacked parties of travellers coming into or going out of Paris, and robbed them of everything they possessed. At other times they fell upon pedestrians who were passing along the streets, and stripped them of all their clothing, leaving them naked and bleeding, if they did not kill them outright. And so fierce were they, so terrible was the repute they bore, that even the bravest citizens feared to cross their paths alone, and avoided them if possible. These men were known as "mouchoirs," because they always carried a large white pocket-handkerchief about them, which they used to bind up wounds and dress the hurts they received in battle. They never went abroad without this pocket-handkerchief, and it was said that they never laid it aside until they were dead. Hence they were called mouchoirs, and, although it may sound strange to us, this name was given to them in derision, as though implying that they were but mere poltroons and cowards. And yet, brave as these men were in battle, and fierce as their natures were, they were not lacking in certain characteristics which rendered them interesting. They were fond of poetry, for instance, and were frequently seen in the evenings at the theatres, listening to the recitations of the poets. They knew all the verses of Agrippa D'Aubigne, of Malherbe, of Charron, and of many others, and sometimes joined in the choruses, singing lustily and tunefully, and often improvising verses of their own, which were far superior to the compositions of many of the poets of that time. They were also very fond of music, and whenever a band passed through the street they stopped to listen to the strains.

Specifically, the carriers of the low-expressing 5-HTTLPR short allele have elevated risk for depression, particularly in the context of social adversity (Caspi et al., 2003; Eley et al., 2004; Kendler et al., 2005), and also tend to have increased anxiety and stress reactivity, as demonstrated in healthy samples (Canli and Lesch, 2007). In comparison, carriers who are homozygous for the long 5-HTTLPR allele have increased transcriptional activity, and reduced risk for depression, anxiety, and stress reactivity (Canli and Lesch, 2007) as well as heightened levels of optimism (Fox et al., 2009). A more recent meta-analysis, however, failed to find support for increased risk of depression following childhood adversity in short allele carriers of 5-HTTLPR (Culverhouse et al., 2018). In fact, the Culverhouse et al. meta-analysis, which included 31 studies totaling 38,802 individuals of European ancestry, did not replicate the widely-published finding of increased risk of depression following a stressful event for short allele carriers of 5-HTTPLR compared with long allele carriers (Ancelin and Ryan, 2018). The gene encoding the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) has also been closely linked to depression. As a member of the neurotrophin family, BDNF plays a critical role in regulating cellular structure and plasticity in the adult brain (Bramham and Messaoudi, 2005; Lu, 2002; Kovalchuk et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2008). Located on human chromosome 11p13, the BDNF gene contains a guanine-to-adenine SNP at nucleotide 196 (rs6265), which results in an amino acid substitution of valine (Val) to methionine (Met) at codon66. This SNP, known as the val66met, changes the 5-prime pro-domain of the human BDNF protein reducing BDNF protein secretion in the brain, and leading to increased vulnerability to depression (Egan et al., 2003; Groves, 2007). In fact, data have suggested that the Met allele of the BDNF gene moderates the relationship of childhood adversity and depressive symptoms in adulthood (e.g., Aguilera et al., 2009). In line with these findings, other studies have linked the Met allele with cognitive difficulties in contrast to protective properties of the Val allele (e.g., Egan et al., 2003). However, similar to 5-HTTLPR research reviewed above, another set of findings examining the role of BDNF in depression has come to a diametrically opposite conclusion regarding risk and protective properties of Val and Met alleles. For example, in a sample of 441 Caucasian Americans, carriers of the Val allele had significantly higher scores on neuroticism, a well-established personality risk factor for depression, than did carriers of the Met allele (Sen et al., 2003). Similarly, another study showed that carriers of the Val/Val allele had higher scores on self-reported anxiety, which often accompanies depression, than did participants with Val/Met or Met/Met genotypes (Lang et al., 2005).

Laboratory studies have shown that anxiety patients are generally impaired in safety-signal learning, namely, learning which stimuli predict safety (Briscione, Jovanovic, & Norrholm, 2014; Duits et al., 2015). If these impairments generalize to action-safety learning in avoidance, omissions of punishment (i.e., safety) would remain somewhat unexpected and continuously trigger a 'pleasant surprise' PE. We propose that these continuous reinforcements give way to a habitization of the avoidance action, by which it becomes a behavioral routine that is disconnected from current goals and motivational states and is therefore more resistant to change (Gillan et al., 2014). In particular, we hypothesize that impaired learning of the action-safety association produces continuous reinforcements that promote the development of an association between the CS and the action instead. This association does promote repetition of the avoidance action to minimize future punishments, but in an inflexible manner that may develop into the unproductive/unnecessary avoidance behaviors that characterize anxiety disorders. This type of stimulus-response learning may be intact in anxiety patients, as it does not relie on an ability to learn to predict safety. In summary, we propose that safety-learning impairments may push adaptive, goal-directed avoidance into maladaptive, habitual avoidance through a dysregulation of PE signaling. Current avoidance paradigms are not designed to study the interplay between safety learning and PE signaling in avoidance (but see Eldar, Hauser, Dayan, & Dolan, 2016, for a decision-making study that focused on neural PE signaling in avoidant decision-making). Some avoidance paradigms track emotional learning processes before each avoidance action (at CS onsets), which focuses on the role of CS-induced fear and/or expected controllability, but not on avoidance-induced safety or relief (e.g., van Meurs, Wiggert & Lissek; Delgado, Jou, LeDoux, & Phelps, 2009). Other paradigms do not signal the US (e.g., Collins, Mendelsohn, Cain, & Schiller, 2014), use very brief CS presentations (Gillan et al., 2014), or terminate the CS upon avoidance actions (mostly used in animal studies, e.g., Moscarello & LeDoux, 2013). These procedures make it difficult to disentangle avoidance-induced safety from omission-induced relief. Hence, although these paradigms contribute importantly to the study of avoidance, they are not ideally suited for detailed examination of the temporal dynamics of relief. In addition, most avoidance studies have focused on the conditioning of avoidance per se, leaving the extinction and recovery of avoidance behavior relatively unexplored in human research (but see Vervliet & Indekeu, 2015; Schlund, Brewer, Richman, Magee, & Dymond, 2015; Cameron, Schlund, & Dymond, 2015). The current study tested in healthy individuals a newly developed protocol to track the temporal dynamics of relief and to probe the recovery of fear and avoidance. For that purpose, we integrated an avoidance protocol previously developed by Vervliet and Indekeu (2015) with a well-established fear extinction /recovery paradigm (Milad, Orr, Pitman, & Rauch, 2005), and added subjective ratings of relief pleasantness on a trial-by-trial basis (Leknes et al., 2011). Of note, CS durations were always fixed, irrespective of avoidance actions.

His dress was simple, being in the American manner, of well dressed buck-skin. He however still clung to his sombrero, which, instead of being cocked jauntily on the side of his head, was drawn down over his eyes to shield them from the hot sun. His whole equipment was that of a mounted ranger, and this style of dress has so often been described as to be familiar to all. Instead of the short carbine which a Mexican habitually carries, he sported a long, elegant rifle - a very witch to charm a hunter's eye. Then he had a brace of silver-mounted revolvers, each firing five times without reloading. Like the rifle, they were costly, and fatally precise and true, models of expensive and beautiful workmanship. But in his belt was that which, however captivating to the eye they might be, cast them into the shade. It was a long dagger, double-edged, sharp as a razor, with a basket handle of rare workmanship. This last was gold (the handle) - pure, yellow gold, chased and milled into all manner of quaint and droll devices. It hung jauntily in its ornamented sheath at his belt, and his hand was forever caressing its beautiful handle. Why should this man, forty years of age, rough, plainly dressed, riding with the stealthy air of one who is at war - with a ragged saddle and plain, even homely steed, have such elegant and costly weapons? They cost a large sum, evidently, and should be the property of a prince. While he is caressing his dagger, as the weapons and their history are the subjects of this narrative, let us go back a year for a brief space. The name of the Mexican was Pedro Felipe, the old and tried servant of a wealthy and kind master, also a Mexican. A year ago his master, Senor Martinez, had occasion to cross a vast, sterile wilderness, lying a hundred or more miles north of the Gila river. While on that plain, in a remote part of it, called the Land of Silence (a ghostly, spectral plain, considered haunted), his only daughter, a beautiful young girl, was abducted by a robber chief, and carried away to a rendezvous - a hollow hill in the plain. Here she was rescued by Pedro, disguised as a black savage. The hillock had an aperture in it, and Pedro, on hearing a noise, looked out and saw the lieutenant of the band, a fierce man called the "Trailer," approaching. Knowing he must take his life or be discovered by the whole band, he shot him dead, from off his horse. From the Trailer's body he took the weapons we have described, and then left the body to be devoured by wolves and birds of prey. He was certain that in the hillock a large treasure was secreted, but fearing to be discovered by the band, whom he expected to arrive every hour, he left without searching for it.

I think that's where the line gets blurred, right? Between authenticity and selling out. And it's hard to know where that line is, especially when you're trying to make a living off of your passion. I mean, we've all seen those Instagram influencers who start out with a genuine message, but then they start promoting detox teas and waist trainers, and you're like, "Wait, what happened to the real you?" And I think that's where the skepticism comes in. We start to question the motives behind the message. And it's not just the influencers, it's the wellness industry as a whole. I mean, have you seen the prices of some of these wellness retreats? Thousands of dollars for a weekend of yoga and meditation? It's like, who can afford that? And it's not just the financial aspect, it's the exclusivity. It's like, wellness is only for those who can afford it, and that's just not true. Wellness should be for everyone, regardless of your socioeconomic status. And then there's the language, right? The way we talk about wellness. It's all about "self-care" and "mindfulness" and "manifesting your dreams." It's like, what does that even mean? Is it just a bunch of buzzwords to make us feel good about ourselves, or is there actual substance behind it? And I think that's what we need to start questioning. We need to start looking beyond the surface level and really examine what's being sold to us. I mean, take the concept of mindfulness, for example. Mindfulness is a beautiful thing, don't get me wrong. But it's been commodified to the point where it's just another product to be sold. You can buy mindfulness apps and mindfulness journals and mindfulness retreats. It's like, can't we just be mindful without having to buy something? Can't we just take a few deep breaths and focus on the present moment without having to shell out money? And then there's the pressure to constantly be "on." To constantly be producing content, to constantly be inspiring, to constantly be motivating. It's exhausting. I mean, can't we just have a bad day without having to post about it on social media? Can't we just have a moment of weakness without having to turn it into a teachable moment? It's like, we're human beings, not robots. So, yeah, I think that's where the skepticism comes in. We need to start questioning the motives behind the message, and we need to start looking beyond the surface level. We need to start examining what's being sold to us, and we need to start being honest with ourselves about what we're really buying into. Because at the end of the day, it's not about the products or the services or the influencers. It's about us. It's about our own growth, our own development, and our own well-being.

He was surrounded by the unknown, apprehensive of what might happen, ignorant of what he should do, aware that he walked and bore himself awkwardly, fearful that every attribute and power of him was similarly afflicted. He was keenly sensitive, hopelessly self-conscious, and the amused glance that the other stole privily at him over the top of the letter burned into him like a dagger-thrust. He saw the glance, but he gave no sign, for among the things he had learned was discipline. Also, that dagger-thrust went to his pride. He cursed himself for having come, and at the same time resolved that, happen what would, having come, he would carry it through. The lines of his face hardened, and into his eyes came a fighting light. He looked about more unconcernedly, sharply observant, every detail of the pretty interior registering itself on his brain. His eyes were wide apart; nothing in their field of vision escaped; and as they drank in the beauty before them the fighting light died out and a warm glow took its place. He was responsive to beauty, and here was cause to respond. An oil painting caught and held him. A heavy surf thundered and burst over an outjutting rock; lowering storm-clouds covered the sky; and, outside the line of surf, a pilot-schooner, close-hauled, heeled over till every detail of her deck was visible, was surging along against a stormy sunset sky. There was beauty, and it drew him irresistibly. He forgot his awkward walk and came closer to the painting, very close. The beauty faded out of the canvas. His face expressed his bepuzzlement. He stared at what seemed a careless daub of paint, then stepped away. Immediately all the beauty flashed back into the canvas. "A trick picture," was his thought, as he dismissed it, though in the midst of the multitudinous impressions he was receiving he found time to feel a prod of indignation that so much beauty should be sacrificed to make a trick. He did not know painting. He had been brought up on chromos and lithographs that were always definite and sharp, near or far. He had seen oil paintings, it was true, in the show windows of shops, but the glass of the windows had prevented his eager eyes from approaching too near. He glanced around at his friend reading the letter and saw the books on the table. Into his eyes leaped a wistfulness and a yearning as promptly as the yearning leaps into the eyes of a starving man at sight of food. An impulsive stride, with one lurch to right and left of the shoulders, brought him to the table, where he began affectionately handling the books. He glanced at the titles and the authors' names, read fragments of text, caressing the volumes with his eyes and hands, and, once, recognized a book he had read. For the rest, they were strange books and strange authors.
