The London Metropolitan Boroughs (LMBs) provide a unique opportunity to examine the impact of suffrage rules on the political budget cycle. Prior to the First World War, the LMBs were governed by a system of taxpayer suffrage, where only those who paid a certain amount of taxes were entitled to vote. This meant that the majority of the population, including women and working-class men, were excluded from the electoral process. In contrast, after the war, the LMBs adopted a system of universal suffrage, where all adults over the age of 21 were entitled to vote, regardless of their economic status. Using a dataset of LMBs' budgets and election outcomes from 1900 to 1925, we find that the political budget cycle is present in both the taxpayer suffrage and universal suffrage regimes. However, the nature of the cycle varies systematically with the suffrage rules. Under taxpayer suffrage, the budget cycle is characterized by a strong emphasis on spending on public goods and services that benefit the wealthy, such as infrastructure and transportation projects. This is because the pivotal voter, who is the taxpayer, is more likely to be a member of the upper class and is more likely to benefit from these types of projects. In contrast, under universal suffrage, the budget cycle is characterized by a greater emphasis on spending on social welfare programs and public services that benefit the working class, such as education and healthcare. This is because the pivotal voter, who is now a broader cross-section of the population, is more likely to be a member of the working class and is more likely to benefit from these types of programs. Our results suggest that the suffrage rules have a significant impact on the political budget cycle, and that the type of spending that is prioritized by politicians varies systematically with the rules of the game. This has important implications for our understanding of the relationship between democracy and public finance, and highlights the need for further research on the impact of suffrage rules on the political budget cycle in other contexts. One potential limitation of our study is that it is limited to a single city and a relatively short period of time. Future research could seek to replicate our findings in other cities and time periods, and could also examine the impact of suffrage rules on the political budget cycle in other types of governments, such as national governments or state governments. Additionally, future research could examine the impact of other factors, such as the level of economic development or the presence of interest groups, on the political budget cycle and the suffrage rules. In conclusion, our study provides evidence that the suffrage rules have a significant impact on the political budget cycle, and that the type of spending that is prioritized by politicians varies systematically with the rules of the game. This has important implications for our understanding of the relationship between democracy and public finance, and highlights the need for further research on this topic.

It was therefore not strange that when, shortly before Paddy's arrest, it became known that Sevier was about to take up his defence, there should have been a general assumption that the case was hopeless. In the crowded court-room, however, the atmosphere had grown tense. The spectators' attention had gradually shifted from the prisoner to the young lawyer, who had taken his place beside him, and they watched him eagerly, ready to applaud any move on his part, to jeer at a slip, to murmur approval or disapproval of his every word. For hours he had kept them waiting, while the old judge had hammered out his summing-up with a judicial obstinacy that was beginning to tell on the patience of the spectators. Finally, however, the jurymen had filed in and the trial had ended. The crowd had surged forward, but Sevier had risen slowly to his feet, and, taking the prisoner's arm, led him to the centre of the court-room. There he paused, looking round for a moment, then spoke: "Gentlemen of the jury, I ask you to listen to me." His voice was low and clear, and its tone made itself heard above the stir of the throng. "I shall not detain you long. I know what you are thinking, and why you have brought in this verdict. You think my client is guilty. But you have no proof against him. All your evidence has shown is that he was drunk, and that some money disappeared from a certain drawer in the night-house. Now, gentlemen, there is a good deal more than this to show. My client is not only innocent, but he did not even go near the house that night." The spectators began to press forward, craning their necks to see better, and there was a loud murmur of surprise. Sevier continued, "You must remember that he was in jail at the time." Again there was a murmur, and one of the jurymen rose to his feet. "If we could have seen the man who arrested him, sir!" he cried angrily. "He was a detective from New York City, sent here by the police department because he knew something about the case." Another murmur broke out, and the judge, rising, said sharply: "Order! Order!" The jurors were whispering together excitedly. One of them turned to Sevier. "What do you mean?" he asked. "I will explain later," answered Sevier. "Meanwhile, if you will look at the record, you will find that the officer testified that he arrested my client because he saw him steal the money. Well, that is simply untrue. The witness did not see the prisoner take anything, nor did anybody else. That is the whole point of the case. Gentlemen, it is possible that the real thief may be sitting here listening to us now." Again there was a murmur of astonishment, and a woman screamed. The judge banged his gavel violently, crying: "Silence!" "You needn't get excited, your honour," said Sevier coolly. "All I am doing is showing how much weight to attach to the testimony of the witnesses. I submit that they have none whatever, and that the charge against my client should be dismissed." He stopped speaking abruptly, and the courtroom was still. The judge was leaning back in his chair, staring at the speaker, and the jurymen were sitting silent, looking at each other. Suddenly one of them sprang to his feet. "I'm afraid there is something wrong about this business," he said. "Yes," assented another. "It looks fishy."

What did I do in retreat? It's a question that flits around like a curious butterfly, yet it's difficult to pin down with a straightforward answer. The essence of retreat isn't always in the doing-or, more precisely, it's in the un-doing of constant doing. It's about slowly, gently unwinding the tightly coiled springs of expectation and obligation. I spent silent hours simply being, gazing inward as if watching the changing colors of a sunset; there's a profound beauty in observing your thoughts come and go, much like weather patterns passing through a valley. In those timeless moments in solitude, the rivers of consciousness run deep, carving their way through the bedrock of the mind. You discover reservoirs of patience you didn't know existed and catch glimpses of the heart's true nature, unadorned and unfettered by the trappings of the world outside. It's transformative, to say the least. But there's a danger in trying to quantify or qualify these experiences with mere words. Language, while beautiful in its own right, is often an inadequate vessel for transmitting the subtleties of internal change. As these experiences soaked into the marrow of my being, the world outside continued unabated, each day marked by the rhythmic cadence of practice and presence. It's a lesson in itself-the realization that the world spins on its axis regardless of how much we try to steer it. Progress in practice is not always visible, like a plant growing underground before breaking the surface. Sometimes just sitting, breathing, and letting the world rush past is the most profound practice of all. The purpose of retreat is also to cultivate an inner resilience, a stoic calm that doesn't waver in the face of life's unpredictability. The still space becomes a crucible, burning away the dross of ego and attachment. In retreat, the mind learns the art of letting go-not in resignation, but in liberation from the clinging that yields only suffering. When the bustling life resumes, you emerge with a clarity as if seeing with new eyes, and a spirit fortified by the fires of introspection. Returning from retreat is no abrupt awakening but a gentle reentry-a transition from a space of focused simplicity to the rich, complex tapestry of everyday existence. The challenge, and the goal, is to integrate the stillness and insights gained into the ordinary tapestry of life, weaving serenity into every interaction and task. Engines owner, a gracious host and facilitator of this solitude, fosters a sacred space where one is encouraged to explore the inner landscape without the usual distractions. You learn to appreciate the luxury of uninterrupted thought and the rare gift of silence in a world clattering with noise. The talk, then, becomes not just a recount of days spent but a sharing of the distilled wisdom that retreat offers-a guide of sorts, though not of explicit instructions. Instead, it serves as an invitation to each soul to find its path to solace and self-discovery. In this way, our gatherings become a collective meditation, where each individual's stillness contributes to a greater harmony and shared understanding. As I conclude this journey of reflection, I realize that retreat is not merely an escape but a return to the essence, a homecoming. So, my gratitude extends beyond words, for the time granted and for the humans, and perhaps something greater, that made this retreat an indelible chapter of being.

His visits to his affianced were frequent, and his protestations passionate; but he had effected nothing substantial towards a happy union. Miss Bliss's guardian grew impatient; and, although there is no evidence to prove that the young lady's affection for Vaughan was otherwise than deep and sincere, yet even she began to lose confidence in him. His excuses were evidently evasive, and not always true. The time fixed for the wedding was fast approaching; and Vaughan saw that something must be done to restore the young lady's confidence. About three weeks before the appointed Easter Tuesday, Vaughan went to his mistress in high spirits. All was right - his certificate was to be granted in a day or two - his family had come forward with the money, and he was to continue the Aldersgate business he had previously carried on as a branch of the Stafford trade. Vaughan then produced twelve twenty-pound notes; Miss Bliss could scarcely believe her eyes. She examined them. The paper, she remarked, seemed thicker than usual. So far from letting any living soul know he had placed so much money in her hands, Vaughan exacted an oath of secresy from her, and sealed the notes up in a parcel with his own seal - making her swear that she would on no account open it till after their marriage.

Mr. Richwine also holds a doctorate from Harvard in public policy, with a concentration in political science. His thesis was entitled "IQ and Immigration Policy." In his introduction, Mr. Richwine writes that there is a "large body of research" showing that different ethnic and racial groups have significantly different average IQs. He goes on to argue that such differences help explain the economic performance of immigrants from different countries. For example, he notes that the Irish and Italians, two of the largest immigrant populations in the early 20th century, had lower average IQ scores than other European immigrants. This helped account for their high rates of poverty. Mr. Richwine's thesis also reviews the extensive literature on the relationship between family structure and academic achievement. He finds that children raised without fathers do worse in school than children raised with fathers present in the home. Then Mr. Richwine applies this insight to contemporary America, arguing that welfare programs designed to support single mothers have worsened the educational outcomes of minority children. There's no question that Mr. Richwine's thesis is controversial. Some readers will find it offensive. And yet it's hard to see how any serious scholar can dismiss it out of hand. Consider Mr. Richwine's work on the link between IQ and income. The idea that IQ matters is not new. Nor is the notion that IQ varies among different ethnic groups. These claims have long been made, and they have always been controversial. But they are hardly fringe ideas. For instance, the late Christopher Jencks, a prominent liberal sociologist at Northwestern University, once argued that IQ tests "are too strongly related to social background variables to be used as measures of innate ability." " But Mr. Jencks conceded that IQ tests are valid predictors of academic success. And he concluded that "the relation of IQ to income is probably stronger than the relation of income to anything else." Mr. Richwine's views on IQ and education are similarly mainstream. They may not be popular, but they are certainly not radical. For example, the U.S. Department of Education reports that black students score 14 points lower on standardized tests than white students, and Hispanic students score 13 points lower. These gaps persist even when the test-takers' socioeconomic backgrounds are controlled for. The department concludes that the gaps reflect real differences in cognitive abilities. Similarly, the U.S. Census Bureau reports that children raised in single-parent homes are far likelier to drop out of high school than children raised in two-parent households. Again, the bureau attributes the difference to the impact of parental absence on children's development. Why then all the fuss about Mr. Richwine? Because he combined his scholarly findings with political conclusions. Specifically, Mr. Richwine argues that the U.S. should stop allowing unskilled immigrants to enter the country. After all, if unskilled immigrants do worse in school, and earn less money, and depend more on government services, why bring them here? Instead, we should admit highly skilled workers who will contribute more to society. But that means turning away many Hispanics and blacks. Indeed, Mr. Richwine recommends limiting legal immigration to 300,000 per year. That's fewer than half of today's inflow. And it's well below the levels of the 1920s and 1930s, when the U.S. economy grew rapidly despite relatively tight restrictions on immigration. So, according to Mr. Richwine, if you care about poor minorities, you should oppose increasing immigration.

When Arthur Reeves was in England, he lived in a bungalow not far from the Frazers' home at Shoreham, where he was a frequent and welcome guest. He was six feet in height, of fairly light build, long-limbed and thin-featured. He was partially blind in his left eye and nearly deaf in his left ear, but in spite of these defects he succeeded in passing the doctor in an examination for the Accountant Branch of the Navy. How he did it could never be satisfactorily explained, though he strongly asserted that it was sheer bluff. But he was "ploughed" in the educational examination, and took to journalism. By another supreme piece of bluff he succeeded in getting a post as war correspondent in one of our petty border wars. This was his bent. He did so well getting his "copy" through a good two hours before his rivals that his success was assured. In the Boer War he made the circulation of his paper increase by leaps and bounds, succeeding by more bluff in gaining exclusive information and adding to his fame. He came home with a splendid reputation, a touch of enteric, and a Mauser bullet wound in his left leg; but in spite of the fact that the left part of his anatomy was seriously crippled, his energy, resource, and marvellous descriptive powers made him in great request as a special correspondent. In this capacity he had been dispatched to the ends of the earth, often at a few hours' notice, always adding to his laurels; and, being a born linguist, he had a thorough knowledge of French, German, and Italian, and more than a smattering of Turkish, Arabic, Hindustani, and Swahili. Ten days previously he had been enjoying a brief but well-earned rest at Shoreham, after an exciting time in a revolution in Central America; then, like a bolt from the blue, came the news of Italy's high-handed declaration of war against Turkey. Reeves was ready within an hour of receiving a telegram from his chief. Wearing a worn yet serviceable suit of khaki, and light, strong boots and puttees, and carrying a small portmanteau containing his trusty Mauser pistol, fifty rounds of ammunition, writing materials, and a change of linen - the old war correspondent knew the importance of carrying but little impedimenta - he caused no small sensation amongst the scribes of Fleet Street. His visit to the editorial offices was also of brief duration, and, having secured his letters of introduction, and drafts upon the Bank of Italy, he caught the boat train from Victoria by just thirty seconds. Two days later he was in Rome, presenting his credentials to the Minister of War. That high official was most urbane, and gave the correspondent permission to embark on any of the transports, "if convenient to the exigencies of military service".

Being constantly on edge meant that even our moments of joy were tinted with a sense of caution. We spent a lot of time exploring the local markets, where vendors would set up booths selling everything from handcrafted trinkets to fresh produce. Those markets, bustling with the kind of chaotic energy you'd only find in Romania, presented a different kind of thrill-one steeped less in fear and more in the simple exhilaration of new discoveries. Koren and I made a game out of bargaining, something we both realized we'd need to learn quickly. Negotiating prices was expected and became a social ritual of sorts. A smile appeared here and there amidst the exchanged banter, dispelling, even if temporarily, the wary glances and stone-faced seriousness we were advised to adopt. We brought back some beautiful carved wooden boxes and embroidered tablecloths, mementos tainted, and yet made more vivid, by the lively interactions and haggles that birthed them. Despite the underlying tension, we were captivated by Romania's natural beauty. We took a couple of weekends to roam the countryside, renting an old car to embark on our own little adventures. The landscape was a stunning tapestry of rolling hills, ancient forests, and sprawling fields of sunflowers that seemed to stretch endlessly towards the horizon. Every so often, we'd stumble upon small villages where life seemed paused, unaffected by the frenetic pace of city life. In these villages, the ever-present sense of caution eased slightly, and the residents were often more welcoming, providing us with stories and occasionally a warm meal. One memorable stop was the Bucegi Mountains, where we decided to hike despite Toni's protests about our safety. For once, we felt safe enough to embrace the warmth of the sun on our faces without worrying about who might be following us. The mountains had a mystic aura, and being up there among those ancient peaks, we experienced a strange sense of peace. It was a reminder that even amidst uncertainty, it's possible to find moments of tranquility. Our trip wasn't just about experiencing Romania's natural beauty, though. The history and culture were no less enthralling. Bran Castle, with its Dracula legends, was a place we had to see. Despite the hordes of tourists like us, the air buzzed with a palpable sense of the past, making myths feel nearly tangible. We wandered through the dimly-lit corridors, letting ourselves be enveloped by the haunting atmosphere, aware once again of the layers of history pressing in. Leaving Romania was bittersweet. It may not have felt entirely safe, but I'd learned how to adapt, and that adaptation became almost a part of me. Back in Canada, I find myself missing those vivid mornings at the market, the contrast of ancient landscapes against urban sprawl, and even the heightened sense of awareness that made every encounter, every moment, sharper and more real. Koren and I have vowed to go back someday. Next time, we'll arm ourselves with what we've learned and maybe even show others how to traverse this fascinating land with both caution and curiosity.

At his core lies the need for acceptance-not just from others, but from himself. In his quest for redemption, he seeks out fairness amidst relentless chaos, where the threads of empathy weave into the very fabric of his existence. Each bullet dodged, every scuffle survived, speaks to the resilience of his spirit-a testament to a life lived boldly, mirroring the love he harbors for all.

The intricate dynamics of coral reef ecosystems are underscored by a plethora of interactions between species. These interactions, often niche-specific, contribute significantly to the resilience and functionality of the reef as a whole. Coral reefs do not merely represent a physical structure; they embody vast networks of biological interactions that depend on the delicate balance between different species. The high species richness on coral reefs supports a complex web of ecological interactions, with each organism playing a distinct role that shapes the overall health of the ecosystem (Worm et al., 2006). Within the multitude of organisms that inhabit coral reefs, the role of polychaetes, a class of annelid worms, cannot be overlooked. Recent studies indicate that polychaete diversity may rival that of known crustaceans, with an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 species inhabiting reef environments (Martins et al., 2018). Although often overlooked in favor of more charismatic megafauna, polychaetes are essential players in nutrient cycling and contribute to the structuring of benthic habitats. Their burrowing activities aerate the substrate, facilitating the movement of essential nutrients and enabling other organisms to thrive (Rhoads and Young, 1970). Shifting the focus to the microbial realm, the implications of microbial dynamics in coral reef ecosystems reveals yet another layer of complexity. Microbes, particularly bacteria and archaea, play vital roles in nutrient cycling, often serving as foundational members of the food web. Notably, the microbiomes associated with reef organisms, such as corals, can influence the health and resilience of the entire reef ecosystem (Shannon et al., 2020). Coral health is highly dependent on the balance of beneficial and harmful microbial populations, and disturbances to this balance-whether through pollution, climate change, or disease-can have dire consequences. Recent work elucidates how certain microbial communities can confer resistance to coral bleaching events, a phenomenon exacerbated by rising ocean temperatures (Hartmann et al., 2019). Oceanographic processes also uniquely influence the biodiversity and distribution of species across coral reefs. Factors such as water temperature, salinity, and nutrient availability, along with ocean currents, dictate not only which species can inhabit a particular reef but also how populations interact with one another (Hughes et al., 2007). Variations in these parameters can result in shifts in community composition, often tilting the balance towards less desirable, fast-growing species that can threaten the integrity of coral habitats. Furthermore, the advent of modern molecular methods has greatly enhanced our understanding of marine biodiversity, allowing for the differentiation and identification of cryptic species previously undetected through traditional morphological approaches. This advancement highlights the necessity of employing integrative taxonomic practices to more accurately quantify biodiversity and assess community structures (Meyer et al., 2008). As methods evolve, it is crucial that efforts to protect coral reefs continue to adapt, driven by an understanding that the conservation of these ecosystems hinges upon the preservation of their myriad inhabitants, both known and yet to be discovered. As the threats to coral reefs grow increasingly dire due to anthropogenic influences, the importance of comprehensive biodiversity assessments becomes ever more paramount. The intricate relationships between species not only underscore the importance of each organism within the ecosystem but also illustrate the potential cascading effects that arise from species loss. Protecting coral reefs requires ensuring the integrity of every member of this diverse community, highlighting a critical relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem health.

When you're in the midst of a breakup, it's essential to remember that your emotional state can fluctuate like a pendulum, swinging from hope to despair in a matter of moments. This emotional turbulence can leave you feeling on edge, questioning your own worth, and wondering where things went wrong. Many people experience these ups and downs as they navigate the aftermath of a breakup, often finding it hard to maintain a clear perspective. The reality is that healing is not a linear process; you may take two steps forward and then find yourself retreating back one step. You see, relationships are complex, filled with layers of emotions and dreams that often color our perceptions. When your ex-partner moves on or makes a statement that seems final, it feels like an avalanche crashing down on your sense of self. You might ask yourself, "Why wasn't I enough?" or "What did I do to deserve this?" These questions can echo in your mind, becoming a relentless chorus that hampers your ability to focus on your healing journey. It's critical to recognize that this turmoil, while painful, is a normal part of the healing process. It's okay to feel hurt and confused. Give yourself permission to experience these emotions; don't suppress them. The sorrow and frustration you feel are valid and signify that you're human. Allow yourself some space to grieve the relationship and to process the loss. It's part of moving forward, even if it doesn't always feel like progress at the moment. You may find solace in understanding that breakups serve as a catalyst for change and growth. Reflecting on what you learned about yourself during the relationship can provide you with valuable insights going forward. Perhaps it made you realize what you truly desire in a partner or highlighted certain patterns you'd like to avoid in your next relationship. Engaging in self-reflection can truly be transformative, allowing you to emerge from this experience wiser and more robust. Consider also surrounding yourself with supportive individuals who uplift you and reaffirm your value. Leaning on friends, family, or a therapist can be incredibly beneficial during this tumultuous period. They can offer fresh perspectives and remind you that you are not defined by your relationship status. Building connections with those who genuinely care for you can serve as a powerful reminder of your worth and the beauty of potential new beginnings. The struggle of wanting to move on while still feeling tethered to your past can be challenging. You may wrestle with the impulse to check in on your ex's social media, curious about their new life. It's important to establish boundaries for yourself. Sometimes, a break from their online presence is necessary to foster your healing. Letting go of the urge to keep tabs can empower you and allow for space to heal without continually reopening wounds. Lastly, be kind to yourself. Understand that healing takes time, and it may require you to fortify your emotional resilience. Take small steps each day towards creating the life you want. Reestablish routines that bring you joy, explore new hobbies, or revisit past passions that were set aside. As you start to fill your life with positivity and pursuits that enrich your soul, you'll begin to find a renewed sense of self, independent from your past relationship. Remember, there's no timeline for healing, and that's perfectly okay. Although it may feel insurmountable now, every day is an opportunity for growth and rediscovery. Before long, you'll find that light begins to seep back into your life, illuminating the path ahead with new possibilities and endless avenues for love and connection. And who knows? One day, you may look back at this moment and realize how far you've come.

I left Sirte back in early December. Islamic State fighters took over the city in February 2015. It wasn't an invasion per se. It was a combination of local jihadi fighters (Ansar Al-Sharia) declaring their allegiance to the Islamic State group and later being joined by fighters fleeing or beaten by the forces of General Khalifa Haftar in Benghazi. There are also other nationalities in the ranks of IS that we either noticed from their accents or looks. They included Tunisians and Egyptians. They were not just Arabs. In April 2015, there was a special parade welcoming people they said were Boko Haram fighters from Nigeria. IS was quite laid back at the start in terms of implementing their harsh interpretation of Sharia, or Islamic law. You get the feeling that they were focussing on building loyalty and allegiances from the tribal society of Sirte. It was only in August when Islamic codes of dress and behaviour began to be implemented more noticeably. It was also then when crucifixions and lashings began to be meted out to anyone convicted. These usually take place after Friday prayers. Until I left in December with my family, going in to and leaving the city was quite routine. The only people experiencing problems when it comes to their freedom of movement is anyone associated with other fighting groups or suspected of being a "spy". Most foods and items at the shops are slightly more expensive. But there hasn't been any petrol available for a year and a half. People who still receive their public sector salaries from Tripoli choose to stay. Leaving simply does not make economic sense for most people. Leaflets and letters have been distributed to shopkeepers and public sector workers inviting them to "re-education" courses run by Islamic State. IS have their command centre next to the domed, marble-clad Ougadougou Conference Centre - built by Muammar Gaddafi to host pan-African summits. The centre is now used for courses where IS members instruct employees in the importance of adhering to their version of Islamic law. The letters warn: "Whoever does not attend will be liable to questioning." I'm originally from Sirte. I was self-employed but I left the city with my family on 17 July last year, some time after the arrival of IS. I was of course also scared for my family. We still have relatives and friends inside the city. We now live in Misrata. When we escaped, they left people alone to come and go as they please. I'm hearing from friends people can still leave if they wish to. We're also hearing that medicines at hospitals are almost non-existent. Food is available, but via 'war profiteers'.

They snubbed herself and her chosen husband; but they did not so far separate themselves from her and her affairs as to give up the charge of her possessions. Her four hundred a year was settled very closely on herself and on her children, without even a life interest having been given to Mr. Vavasor, and therefore when she died the mother's fortune became the property of the little baby. But, under these circumstances, the big people did not refuse to interest themselves to some extent on behalf of the father. I do not suppose that any actual agreement or compact was made between Mr. Vavasor and the Macleods; but it came to be understood between them that if he made no demand upon them for his daughter's money, and allowed them to have charge of her education, they would do something for him. He was a practising barrister, though his practice had never amounted to much; and a practising barrister is always supposed to be capable of filling any situation which may come his way. Two years after his wife's death Mr. Vavasor was appointed assistant commissioner in some office which had to do with insolvents, and which was abolished three years after his appointment. It was at first thought that he would keep his eight hundred a year for life and be required to do nothing for it; but a wretched cheeseparing Whig government, as John Vavasor called it when describing the circumstances of the arrangement to his father, down in Westmoreland, would not permit this; it gave him the option of taking four hundred a year for doing nothing, or of keeping his whole income and attending three days a week for three hours a day during term time, at a miserable dingy little office near Chancery Lane, where his duty would consist in signing his name to accounts which he never read, and at which he was never supposed even to look. He had sulkily elected to keep the money, and this signing had been now for nearly twenty years the business of his life. Of course he considered himself to be a very hardly-used man. One Lord Chancellor after another he petitioned, begging that he might be relieved from the cruelty of his position, and allowed to take his salary without doing anything in return for it. The amount of work which he did perform was certainly a minimum of labour. Term time, as terms were counted in Mr. Vavasor's office, hardly comprised half the year, and the hours of weekly attendance did not do more than make one day's work a week for a working man; but Mr. Vavasor had been appointed an assistant commissioner, and with every Lord Chancellor he argued that all Westminster Hall, and Lincoln's Inn to boot, had no right to call upon him to degrade himself by signing his name to accounts.

No confirmed wreckage from Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 has been found since it vanished from air traffic control screens off Malaysia's east coast early on March 8, less than an hour after taking off from Kuala Lumpur for Beijing. 'I can confirm we have a new lead,' Malaysian Transport Minister Hishammuddin Hussein told reporters in Kuala Lumpur, where the investigation into the missing airliner is based. Another official in Malaysia said investigators were 'hopeful but cautious' about the Australian discovery. This is the agonising moment that families are anxiously awaiting news of the missing Malaysia Airlines flight were told two large objects bobbing in a remote part of the Indian Ocean had been found. Chinese relatives of passengers from the missing Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 react as they wait for news at the Metro Park Lido Hotel. The fate of Flight MH370 has been baffling aviation experts for nearly two weeks. Investigators believe that someone with detailed knowledge of both the Boeing 777-200ER and commercial aviation navigation switched off the plane's communications systems before diverting it thousands of miles off its scheduled course. Exhaustive background checks of the passengers and crew aboard have not yielded anything that might explain why. An Australian air force AP-3C Orion plane was already at the scene, John Young, general manager of the emergency response division of Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), told the news conference in Canberra. Three more aircraft were also on their way, including a New Zealand Air Force Orion and a U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon, the world's most advanced maritime surveillance plane. A merchant ship diverted for the task was also arriving in the area, Young said. A Royal Australian Navy ship equipped to recover any objects was also en route, but was still 'some days away'.China, whose citizens made up about two-thirds of the passengers on board the flight, said it was also sending ships to the area of the sighting, but it was not clear how long it would take for the vessels to reach the scene. Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) general manager John Young is seen next to an AMSA graphic map during a press conference on the search for the Malaysia Airlines flight MH370. The huge potential breakthrough in an investigation that had appeared to be running out of leads was revealed by Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott, who told parliament the objects had been located with satellite imagery. 'New and credible information has come to light in relation to the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 in the southern Indian Ocean,' Abbott said. He added that he had already spoken with his Malaysian counterpart, Najib Razak, and cautioned that the objects had yet to be identified. 'The task of locating these objects will be extremely difficult and it may turn out they are not related to the search for MH370,' Abbott said.

Economic output in the 17-nation single currency area fell 0.3 per cent in the fourth quarter from the third, official data showed yesterday as the sovereign debt crisis crushed a recovery and looked set to push the bloc in to a mild recession. The Italian economy joined Belgium, Greece and Portugal in formal recession having already shrunk in the third quarter of 2011. Purchasing data from Markit for January showed a slight improvement for the Spanish manufacturing and services industries, but it may not be enough for an economy that has been in recession or close to stagnation for almost five years. Spain had been growing at an above-average rate since the country entered into the eurozone monetary union 12 years ago, but the boom was largely due to the housing expansion fuelled by cheap loans and has been struggling since the 2007 crash. Experts say the government's new provisions for real estate holdings will almost certainly prompt the banks to sell holdings at firesale prices, forcing property values down much more than the 22 per cent that they have dropped since the financial crisis hit Europe in 2008. In Sesena and other ghost developments around Spain, some banks are already trying to unload finished apartments at discounts of up to 50 per cent of their original prices. But that is hurting untold numbers of Spaniards who invested savings and took out big loans to buy property they thought they would be able to sell for more money or rent. Satellite cities that never ended up with populations are not Spain's only problem. Around Madrid and across the country, there are vast subdivisions carved out of farmland complete with paved roads and streetlights but only weeds where houses were supposed to be built. Half-built apartment buildings stand idle in suburbs rich and poor. With unemployment at a eurozone high of 23 per cent, there are simply fewer buyers - and young Spaniards are increasingly trying to find work abroad. In December alone, sales were down 25.3 per cent compared to the same month in 2010, the government reported last Friday. 'This is the problem: Who is going to buy these homes?' said Jose Luis Alvarez Arce, head of the economics department at the University of Navara. It could take years for the banks to clean up their assets and relieve a growing credit crunch affecting individuals and businesses, some of whom never got caught up in the Spanish real estate craze in which most citizens bought real estate as an alternative to savings accounts, investment funds and retirement plans. The boom and bust has been so profound that the impact is changing the Spanish mentality about real estate, said Fernando Encinar, head of research at Spain's most popular real estate website, Idealista.com.

I was at the right end of my file, and at my shoulder was a boy from Morrownest, a slim, white-faced lad, his weak chin trembling from fear, and his eyes staring about so pleadingly I spoke a word of courage to him, whispering in his ear, lest the guard behind might strike. He glanced aside at me, but with no response in the depths of his eyes, in which I could perceive only a dumb anguish of despair. Beyond him marched Grover, one time butcher at Harwich, a stocky, big-fisted fellow, with a ghastly sword wound, yet red and unhealed on his face, extending from hair to chin, his little pig eyes glinting ugly, and his lips cursing. The man beyond was a soldier, a straight, athletic fellow, with crinkly black beard, who kept his eyes front, paying no heed to the cries. The guard pressed the people back as we shuffled along, but there was no way of keeping them still. I heard cries of encouragement, shouts of recognition, sobs of pity, and occasionally a roar of anger as we passed. "Good lads! God be with yer!" "Thet one thar is sore hurted - it's a damn shame." "Thar's Teddy - poor laddie! Luck go with yer, Teddy." "Ter hell with Black Jeffries, say I!" "Hush, mon, er ye'll be next ter go - no, I don't know who sed it." "See thet little chap, Joe; lots ther lad bed ter do with the war." "They all look mighty peaked - poor devils, four months in gaol." "Stand back there now. Stand back!" The guards prodded them savagely with the butts of their musketoons, thus making scant room for us to shuffle through, out upon the far end of the wharf, where we were finally halted abreast of a lumping brig, apparently nearly ready for sea. There were more than forty of us as I counted the fellows, and we were rounded up at the extremity of the wharf in the full blaze of the sun, with a line of guards stretched across to hold back the crowd until preparations had been completed to admit us aboard. As those in front flung themselves down on the planks, I got view of the brig's gangway, along which men were still busily hauling belated boxes and barrels, and beyond these gained glimpse of the hooker's name - ROMPING BETSY OF PLYMOUTH. A moment later a sailor passed along the edge of the dock, dragging a coil of rope after him, and must have answered some hail on his way, for instantly a whisper passed swiftly from man to man. "It's Virginia, mate; we're bound fer Virginia." The ugly little pig eyes of the butcher met mine. "Virginia, hey?" he grunted. "Ye're a sailorman, ain't ye, mate? Well, then, whar is this yere Virginia?"

The MODIS bi-directional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) product (MCD43A1) and the albedo product derived from it (MCD43A3) provide continuous BRDF and albedo time series starting from year 2000. For each day of interest, the BRDF at each of the seven MODIS bands is estimated by fitting a semi-empirical BRDF model to multiangular MODIS surface reflectance data (Schaaf et al., 2002). In case the main algorithm inversion is not of sufficient quality, magnitude inversion (a back-up algorithm) is used instead. Spectral albedo at any illumination geometry can be computed from the fitted BRDF model. Shortwave albedo is computed from the spectral albedos by using band-specific weights. Recently, a new version (V006) of the MODIS BRDF and albedo products was released. It provides several improvements over the previous version (V005). These improvements contribute to better quality and more retrievals at high latitudes (Wang et al., 2018). Most importantly, the albedo is produced daily, compared to the 8-day interval in V005, improving the ability to track rapid seasonal changes. The daily V006 MODIS albedo product has been previously used in studying albedo dynamics in the boreal forest by e.g. Bright et al. (2015) and Hovi et al. (2017). The MODIS albedo product is provided in sinusoidal projection with a nominal pixel size of 463 m. The effective spatial resolution of the product, i.e. the actual footprint area generating the reflectance signal(s) received by MODIS, is however coarser. This is because the original satellite observations are assigned to each MODIS pixel (in sinusoidal projection) to which they contribute the most, and because the area seen by the MODIS sensor increases towards large view zenith angles (Campagnolo et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2006; Xin et al., 2013). A recent analysis by Campagnolo et al. (2016) quantified the effective spatial resolution of MODIS nadir reflectance (MCD43A4) product that is, similarly as the albedo product, also derived from the BRDF product. Nominal pixel size of the MODIS albedo/BRDF product has usually been applied in studies focusing on forest structure albedo relations. To our knowledge the effect of ignoring the effective spatial resolution on the obtained results has not yet been quantified. Another important aspect that has received less attention is the effect of the albedo quality (main algorithm vs. magnitude inversion) on the results. This is particularly important in the high latitudes where good quality data are often difficult to obtain and thus use of the magnitude inversion data will result in better temporal coverage. The relatively coarse spatial resolution of MODIS albedo sets also special requirements for the field reference data used in the interpretation. Finding spatially extensive (wall-to-wall) field reference may be difficult particularly in remote areas. A relevant option nowadays is to use airborne LiDAR data.

Assuming that reading and spelling rely on the very same word-specific orthographic representations, the existence of marked dissociations between reading and spelling skills is not obvious. Investigating such dissociations provides an excellent opportunity to gain important insights into the role of orthographic knowledge during reading. For isolated spelling deficits, two explanations have been suggested; both assume that individuals with isolated deficits in spelling have problems in building up well-specified orthographic representations, but they differ in their explanation as to how this deficit is compensated for in reading. Frith (1980) argued that underspecified representations are sufficient to recognize words during reading even if they are not exact enough for spelling. Based on that, Frith assumed that isolated poor spellers rely on a partial cue reading strategy, that is, reading words by sight based on degraded orthographic representations without considering the exact letter-by-letter structure. In line with this interpretation, isolated poor spellers showed good performance when reading high-frequency words but made substantially more errors than typical readers in nonword reading. A different explanation was presented by Moll and Landerl (2009) based on German-speaking children. In their study, isolated poor spellers showed age-adequate reading performance for words as well as nonwords. More important, they did not show the typical advantage of real words over corresponding pseudohomophones (i.e., unfamiliar letter strings that sound like real words, e.g., rane for rain in English), which is taken as an indication of lexical access of the real word spelling (see also Francuz & Borkowska, 2013). Interestingly, they nevertheless showed adequate reading latencies compared with age-matched typically developing children even for words they could not spell. Therefore, it was assumed that they relied on highly efficient decoding strategies2 to compensate for their deficient orthographic knowledge, which is possible in an orthography with high consistency of grapheme-phoneme correspondences such as German. The current study went one step further by analyzing eye movement patterns in order to investigate to what extent children with isolated spelling deficits apply lexical processes during reading. In contrast to isolated deficits in spelling, isolated reading fluency deficits are hardly described in the literature, especially for opaque languages (but see Lovett, 1987). The phonological deficit view of dyslexia assumes that deficits in reading fluency result from slow and effortful grapheme-phoneme decoding compensating for lack of orthographic representations (Vellutino et al., 2004). However, recent findings suggest that poor readers do use lexical strategies during reading and do not simply rely on decoding (e.g., Gangl et al., 2018; Paizi, De Luca, Zoccolotti, & Burani, 2013). An alternative suggestion was presented by Wimmer (1993), who argued that dysfluent reading may result from inefficient visual-verbal access that affects both sublexical and lexical reading strategies. According to this view, dysfluent readers may have intact orthographic representations available and may even access them during reading, but in an inefficient way.

No pen could describe, no brush convey, any idea of the vivid crimson, western clouds, and the flood of blinding golden light, that bathed the hills, the far-away islets, the tangled mangroves, and the glassy sea. To the cool dispassionate northern eye, which may have first opened on a leaden sky, snow-capped hills, pine woods, and ploughed lands, there was a general impression of wildly gaudy, south sea scenery, of savage silence, and lawless solitude. Soon that scarlet ball will have plunged below the horizon, a short-lived grey twilight have spread her veil over land and sea, the parrots' noisy pink bills will be tucked under their wings, and the turbulent peacocks have gone to roost. Close to the flagstaff (which was planted on a kind of large, flat mound, at the highest point of the island), one human figure stood out in bold relief against the brilliant sunset; an elderly gentleman with grizzled hair and beard, a careworn expression, and mild, brown eyes,-eyes that were anxiously riveted on the at present sailless sea. He carried a small red telescope in his hand, and divided his time between pacing the short grass plateau, and spasmodically sweeping the horizon. For what was he looking so impatiently? He was looking for the smoke of the Calcutta steamer, that brought mails and passengers to Port Blair once in every six weeks. Think of but one mail in six weeks, ye sybarites of Pall Mall, revelling in a dozen daily posts, scores of papers, and all the latest telegrams from China to Peru! Imagine reading up forty days' arrears of your Times or Post; imagine six Punches simultaneously! Gladly as Colonel Denis usually hailed his letters, and especially the Weekly Gazette, yet it was neither news nor promotion that he was so restlessly awaiting now-his thoughts were altogether centred on a passenger, his only daughter, whom he had not seen for thirteen years, not since she was a little mite in socks and sashes, and now she was a grown-up, a finished young lady, coming out from England by this mail to be the mistress of his house! He was glad that this long anticipated day had dawned at last, and yet he scarcely dared to analyze his own feelings-he was ashamed to own, even in his inmost heart, that mingled with all his felicity, there is a secret dread-a kind of stifled misgiving. This girl who is to share his home within the next few hours, is in reality, as far as personal acquaintance goes, as much a stranger to him as if he had never seen her before, although she is his own little Nell, with whom he used to romp by the hour in the verandah at Karkipore, thirteen years ago. Those thirteen years stand between him and that familiar merry face, dancing gait, and floating yellow hair; they have taken that away, and what are they going to give him instead?

As you stroll along the Rue St. Gingolphe, the aroma of freshly baked bread wafts from the bakery, enticing you to enter and sample a crusty baguette. The baker, a jovial man with a bushy mustache, greets you with a warm bonjour and offers a taste of his latest creation, a delightful pastry filled with sweet, caramelized fruit. You linger for a moment, savoring the treat, and observe the lively atmosphere of the street. The cafe, situated next to the bakery, is bustling with activity. Patrons sit at small, marble-topped tables, sipping coffee and engaging in lively conversations. The sounds of clinking cups and saucers, accompanied by the murmur of hushed tones, create a sense of conviviality. You notice a group of artists, easels and canvases in hand, gathered at a corner table, debating the merits of Impressionism versus Realism. Across the street, the bootmaker's shop beckons with its enticing display of handcrafted leather goods. The proprietor, a skilled artisan with nimble fingers, busies himself repairing a delicate kid glove. He looks up, catches your eye, and smiles, inviting you to enter and peruse his wares. You browse through the selection, admiring the exquisite craftsmanship, and perhaps, if you're so inclined, commission a custom-made pair of shoes. The tobacconist, situated at the far end of the street, seems an unlikely hub of activity. Yet, as you approach, you notice a queue of patrons waiting to purchase their daily allotment of cigarettes and cigars. The vendor, a wily individual with a keen eye for profit, dispenses his wares with a knowing smile, aware that his goods will soon find their way into the pockets of unsuspecting tourists. You can't help but chuckle at the irony, as the government reaps its profits from the sale of these dubious products. As you continue your stroll, you notice the eclectic assortment of residents who call the Rue St. Gingolphe home. There's the elderly madame, who tends to her window box with loving care, coaxing vibrant blooms from the soil. Next door, a young couple, newlyweds by the look of them, busily furnish their tiny apartment, their laughter and chatter carrying out into the street. The street itself, with its worn cobblestones and faded facades, exudes a sense of history, a testament to the countless lives lived and stories told within its narrow confines. You feel the weight of time, the accumulated experiences of generations past, as you walk along the Rue St. Gingolphe. And yet, amidst the nostalgia, there's a sense of vitality, a vibrant pulse that beats in rhythm with the city's eternal heart. As you reach the end of the street, you glance back, taking in the sights and sounds one last time. The Rue St. Gingolphe, a microcosm of Paris itself, has left an indelible mark on your imagination. You know that, no matter where your travels may take you, this charming street will remain etched in your memory, a reminder of the beauty and charm that lies just beyond the Seine.

The admiral's exclamation was a thunderclap in the stillness of the chamber, and Gower, though prepared for some astonishment, felt the force of it. The old sailor's eyes blazed like beacons in a storm, and his voice, though weakened by illness, still commanded attention. 'Greengrocer?' he repeated, as if the word were a challenge to the universe. Mrs. Carthew, who had been watching the scene with a mixture of anxiety and curiosity, hastened to intervene, her hands fluttering like birds in distress. 'Oh, dear Admiral Fakenham, pray, do not excite yourself! The young gentleman is here to tell us about the countess, not to disturb your rest.' But the admiral was beyond consolation. His mind, long accustomed to the discipline of the sea, had been stirred by the news, and now it was as if the waves themselves were crashing against the shores of his understanding. 'Greengrocer?' he muttered again, his eyes fixed on some distant horizon, where the memories of his past were anchored. Gower, sensing the turmoil in the old man's breast, waited patiently for the storm to subside. He knew that the admiral's reaction was not merely a response to the news, but a culmination of all the emotions that had been simmering beneath the surface. The silence that followed was oppressive, heavy with the weight of unspoken thoughts. Mrs. Carthew, still fluttering about the room, tried to distract the admiral with offers of tea and gentle words, but he waved her away, his gaze fixed on Gower. 'You say she's in Whitechapel?' he asked, his voice low and husky, like the growl of a beast awakened from its lair. Gower nodded, his eyes locked on the admiral's, and in that moment, he felt the weight of his mission, the burden of the countess's story, and the responsibility of being the messenger. 'Yes, sir,' he replied, his voice steady, 'she's in Whitechapel, and she needs our help.' The admiral's eyes narrowed, his face set in a determined expression, and Gower knew that the old sailor was already charting a course, navigating the treacherous waters of his own past, to reach the shores of redemption.

The significance of understanding the impact of human factors and organisational energy management policies on building energy consumption cannot be overstated. Despite the abundance of research on the technical aspects of building design, the role of occupants and management practices in shaping energy usage patterns remains understudied. This knowledge gap is particularly concerning, given that buildings are increasingly being designed with advanced energy-efficient systems, yet their actual performance often falls short of predicted levels. One of the primary challenges in accurately predicting building energy consumption is the complexity of human behaviour. Occupants' actions, such as adjusting thermostat settings, using lighting and appliances, and operating building systems, can significantly influence energy usage. Moreover, these behaviours can vary greatly depending on factors such as cultural background, personal habits, and organisational culture. For instance, a study by Azar and Menassa [18] found that occupants' comfort levels and energy-saving habits were influenced by their perceived control over the building's thermal environment. Organisational energy management policies and practices also play a crucial role in shaping energy consumption patterns. The implementation of energy-efficient practices, such as regular maintenance of HVAC systems, optimising lighting schedules, and encouraging energy-saving behaviours among occupants, can lead to significant energy savings. However, the lack of clear policies, inadequate training, and insufficient resources can hinder the adoption of such practices. A study by Rohdin et al. [19] found that energy management practices in commercial buildings were often inadequate, with many buildings lacking a dedicated energy manager and relying on informal energy-saving initiatives. To bridge the gap between predicted and actual building energy performance, it is essential to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between human factors, organisational energy management policies, and technical design parameters. This requires a multidisciplinary approach, incorporating insights from fields such as psychology, sociology, and organisational behaviour, in addition to building physics and engineering. Several studies have employed innovative methods to investigate the impact of human factors on building energy consumption. For example, the use of sensors and monitoring systems to track occupants' behaviour and energy usage patterns has provided valuable insights into the dynamics of building energy consumption [20]. Additionally, the application of data analytics and machine learning techniques has enabled the identification of patterns and trends in energy usage data, which can inform the development of targeted energy-saving strategies [21]. In conclusion, the energy efficiency of commercial buildings, particularly office and university buildings, is a critical issue that requires a multifaceted approach. While advances in technology have improved the energy efficiency of building systems, the actual performance of buildings often falls short of predicted levels due to the complex interplay of human factors and organisational energy management policies. To achieve significant energy savings, it is essential to develop a deeper understanding of the impact of occupants' behaviour and management practices on building energy consumption, and to develop targeted strategies that address these factors.

Therefore, there is a need to find a solution that would replace the need to perform the work of treating the substrate, and therefore to improve the pull-off strength of epoxy resin coatings. Resin floors require greater financial expenses when compared to cementitious floors [1], and thus the solution should also reduce the costs of their execution. In [13], the results of research on the evaluation of the effect of texturing the surface of a concrete substrate on the pull-off strength of an epoxy resin coating are presented. In this work, it was found that grinding, cleaning and applying a bonding agent can be substituted by texturing the surface. It has been found that surface texturing has a particularly beneficial effect on the pull-off strength of the epoxy resin. However, this method has also some disadvantages: it is hard to apply it on site due to the fact that the texturing should be performed on fresh and liquid surface. This makes this method to be not cost-effective. In [14], it was highlighted that recent innovations in civil engineering cannot be made without considering sustainable development. Thus, it therefore seems reasonable to look for a different method, including modifying the composition of the epoxy resin coating. It can be done for example by applying the addition of waste material. One recent research direction is to modify the composition of epoxy resin coatings using different additives. Article [15] presents the results of investigations on the impact of the addition of carbon nanotubes on the increase of the tensile strength (improvement of 2.25 times in relation to the control sample) and deformation (improvement of 3.27 times in relation to the control sample) of epoxy resins. In [16], the effect of adding polymers on the basic properties of self-leveling industrial floor mortars, such as density, flow, consistency change and adhesion, was investigated. The results were almost equal when compared to conventional floors finished with epoxy or polyurethane resins. In paper [17], the influence of the addition of diacrylate monomers on the bond strength of polymer concrete on the wet, dry, smooth and rough substrate was investigated. The study concluded that calcium diacrylate improves epoxide binding strength. Interesting research was also presented in works [18,19]. In [18], the influence of silica dust and metakaolin on the bond strength of interfacial adhesives to the repaired concrete was investigated. The improvement of bonding strength was observed in samples with the addition of metakaolin. In the subsequent studies [19] of the same authors, the effect of treatment the concrete surface on the bond strength of an overlay, containing metakolin, to the concrete substrate was evaluated. From this research it was concluded that adhesion depends mainly on the method of surface treatment and the addition of metakaolin. According to the authors, a potential additive that may positively affect the properties of epoxy resin coatings may be glass powder sourced from industrial wastes.

But that's the way it goes. The governing bodies, the clubs, the players, they all pay lip service to the fight against racism, but when it comes down to it, they're more concerned with protecting their own interests than taking a stand. They're more worried about being seen to be doing something than actually doing something. And so the problem persists. It persists because it's allowed to persist. Because those in power are more interested in maintaining the status quo than in rocking the boat. And so we get the same old platitudes, the same old empty words, the same old gestures. We get the "Kick It Out" campaign, with its catchy slogans and its token gestures. We get the players wearing "No to Racism" armbands, as if that's going to make a difference. We get the clubs releasing statements condemning racism, but only after they've been forced to by public outcry. And we get the fans, the fans who claim to be outraged, but who are really just outraged that they've been caught out. But the truth is, racism is endemic in English football. It's a cancer that's been allowed to spread, unchecked and unchallenged. It's a cancer that's been ignored, downplayed, and excused. And it's a cancer that's going to take more than just words and gestures to eradicate. Souleymane S knows that. He knows that he's not just a victim of racism, but a symbol of it. He knows that he's not just a black man who was refused entry to a Metro carriage, but a representation of all the black people who've been refused entry to the game. He knows that he's not just a statistic, but a reminder that racism is real, and it's here, and it's now. And so he stands, implacable and angry, defiant and unbowed. He stands because he has to, because he knows that if he doesn't, no one else will. He stands because he's tired of being told that racism doesn't exist, that it's just a fantasy perpetuated by the politically correct. He stands because he's tired of being told that he's overreacting, that he's being too sensitive. He stands because he knows that racism is not just about words, it's about actions. It's about the actions of the Chelsea fans who refused to let him on the train. It's about the actions of the governing bodies who turn a blind eye. It's about the actions of the clubs who don't take it seriously. And it's about the actions of the players who stay silent. Souleymane S stands because he knows that it's time for action. It's time for more than just words, more than just gestures. It's time for change. And it's time for those in power to take responsibility, to take a stand, and to take action. Because until they do, until we all do, racism will continue to haunt English football.

Only once for a few moments she had seemed to understand something about it, when little Fritz Adler, her great friend, going by riding on a stick with a horse's head attached to it, shrieked up to her from the street beneath in great pride, - "Ha, ha, Violet! look at me how I can prance; thou couldst not do so if thou triedst." "I could," she shouted. "By-and-by, when I can run like thee, I will ride too." "No, no, thou never wilt," screamed Fritz, giving his wooden horse a lash with his leather whip. "I wanted to give thee this horse, this very one; Ella had bought thee this very whip; but mother said 'No,' it would be folly to give thee such a present." "Why?" asked Violet. "Why, Fritz, did she say that?" "Ah! thou knowest thou art not like other children." "Why am not I like other children?" "Because thou canst not run or even walk about like me and Ella. Mother says thou art a little hunchback, and it would hurt thy poor back to ride and prance like this;" and Fritz, again lashing his horse, began to plunge violently up and down on the pavement opposite. "Fritz, what didst thou say? I am what?" but he could give no answer, for his mother, who lived in the little baker's shop across the road, rushing out, promptly secured the offender, and having given him a smart slap across the face, dragged him back into the house. "Mother, what did he say I was? and why did his mother slap him? He called me a little hunchback. What does that mean, mother?" Violet's mother had not been attending to the conversation. She had been working at a little white frilled pinafore for her daughter at a table near the stove, and she had just taken the crimping irons from the heart of the fire, red-hot and smoking; but when she heard these words she dropped them suddenly on the floor, and in a moment she was on her knees in front of little Violet's chair, and covering the child's thin white hands with kisses. "What does it signify what it means; he is a cruel boy to call thee such a name. Thou art my darling, my treasure, my sweetest Violet. Thou art the most precious little girl in all the town." Somewhat amazed at her mother's sudden anguish of mind, and at the passionate way she kissed her cheeks and stroked her hair, Violet gazed at her with eyes which widened and dilated, and then she seemed for a few moments lost in thought; after which she said, in her usual quiet voice, with only the faintest tinge of trouble in it, - "Mother, dear, is this a hump I have on my back? and is that the reason why I sit in this chair and cannot walk?"

Their anticipation swelled as the bell rang repeatedly, hinting at imminent departure, the oars eagerly dipping into the Seine, each stroke melding with the laughter of those aboard. Like playful sprites, the young ladies in their flowing gowns flitted about the deck, each fabric shimmering under the soft caress of the sun. Anchored amidst the vibrant colors was Prince Andras himself, an imposing figure draped in impeccable attire, his presence both magnetic and commanding. His dark hair, slightly tousled by the gentle breeze, framed a face defined by both nobility and an underlying mirth that eluded formalities. As the steamer slowly left its moor, the gathered crowd on the quai swelled with intrigue. "There goes a wedding party fit for royalty!" whispered an elderly lady, her hands clasped tightly upon her cane. "Such opulence," she continued, nodding towards the elaborate floral arrangements that bobbed playfully in tune to the waves. Her companions echoed her sentiments, their eyes gleaming with curiosity as they followed the boat's progress down the river, losing the vessel within the lush tapestry of trees lining the Seine's banks. "Monsieur, it is a grand occasion indeed," piped a young man nearby, addressing a fellow onlooker who was struggling to capture the scene on canvas. "You must do justice to this masterpiece!" The painter merely chuckled, his brush pausing momentarily to assess the twinkling waters that reflected the joyous chaos before him. Words of joy continued to filter through the crowd, with each remark weaving together the threads of anticipation and admiration. He knew - perhaps Blessington, perhaps a sister, perhaps his mother had told him - that it was Christmas Eve, and he saw that when Blessington spoke to him she steamed delightfully at the mouth, as if there had been a hot bath just inside her lips. At her suggestion he found he could do it, too, and his sisters also; whereafter they played hot-baths all the way home. But of the Christmas Day that followed he had no recollection whatever. His observation became a little less detached; he began to form in his mind an explorer's map of the places where these phenomena occurred, to be dimly aware that he was taking some sort of part in them, and was not a mere spectator, and one summer evening he definitely knew that the day-nursery and the night-nursery and the room beyond where his sisters slept were all part of the red-brick house which he and others inhabited, just as, according to Blessington, the rabbit which he had seen pop into its hole in the wood beyond the lawn, had a home within it. He had already had his bath, on a patch of sunlight that lay across the nursery-floor, and escaping, slippery as a trout, from Blessington's towelling hands, had run with a squeal of delight across to the window. Outside was the lawn, which hitherto he had thought of as a thing apart, a picture by itself, and beyond was the wood where the rabbit had a house. On the lawn was his mother, playing croquet with his two sisters, and of a sudden it flashed upon him that the wood and the rabbit, the lawn and the croquet-players, the night-nursery, Blessington, the shine of the sun low in the west, and his own wet self were all in some queer manner part of the same thing, and made up that to which he and Blessington went back when, at the limit of their walk, she said it was time to go home. "Oh, there's mummy," he cried. "Mummy!" And he danced naked at the window. Blessington caught him in the towel again. "Well, I never!" she said. "That's not the way for a young gentleman to behave. There, let me dry you, dear, and put your night-shirt on, and you shall say good-night to your mamma out of the window." This was duly done, and it struck Archie as a very novel and delightful discovery that he could say good-night to his mother when she was on the croquet-lawn and he up in the night-nursery. It shed a new light on existence generally, and coloured with a new interest the few drowsy moments which intervened between his being put into bed and falling asleep. Blessington still moved quietly about the room, emptying his bath, and putting his clothes tidy, and he just remembered her kissing him when she had finished.

I continued to operate under the misguided notion that romance in real life mirrored the movies for a while longer. I mean, why wouldn't it? I had seen it work a million times on screen. The grand gestures, the swooning declarations of love, the happily-ever-afters. It was only natural to assume that this was the way it was supposed to go. But, as I soon discovered, reality had a way of punching me in the gut and setting me straight. My next major crush was on a girl named Rachel. She was a senior, and I was a junior, and I thought I was being so bold by asking her out on a date. I mean, I was basically a nobody, and she was a queen bee. But I was convinced that my boldness would pay off, that she would be swept off her feet by my charming words and dashing good looks. So I asked her out, and to my surprise, she said yes. Or, at least, she said yes, but only because she felt sorry for me. I mean, I was a awkward, gangly kid who couldn't even talk to her without stumbling over his own words. But I didn't know that at the time. I thought I was being suave, that I was pulling off some kind of romantic magic. So I took her to the movies, and we sat in the back row, holding hands and making goo-goo eyes at each other. But as the credits rolled, I realized that something was off. Rachel wasn't giggling and blushing like I thought she would. In fact, she looked kind of bored. And when I tried to kiss her, she politely declined. I was devastated. I mean, I had been so sure that this was it, that I had finally found my Kayden. But as I walked her home, feeling like a total reject, I started to realize that maybe, just maybe, romance in real life wasn't like the movies. A figure on the deck detached itself from the group and waved a beckoning hand to the rowboat. The rower hesitated, frowning. Then he shrugged his shoulders and pulled out and alongside. The deck crew lowered a set of steps. "Take a couple of us ashore, will you?" He was addressed by a short, stout man. He was very round and pink of face, very well dressed, and by the manner in which he spoke to the others, and the glances he cast ashore, a person of some consequence in great impatience. The young man laid his rowboat against the steps. "Climb in," he said briefly. "You, Smith, come along," the round-faced one addressed a youth in tight blue jersey and peaked cap. The deck boy climbed obediently down. A girl in white duck and heavy blue sweater put her foot on the steps. "I think I shall go too, papa," she said. Her father nodded and followed her. The rowboat nosed in beside the end of a narrow float that ran from the sea wall. The boy in the jersey sprang out, reached a steadying hand to his employer. The girl stepped lightly to the planked logs. "Give the boy a lift on that boat to the chuck, will you?" the stout person made further request, indicating the white boat bottom up on shore. A queer expression gleamed momentarily in the eyes of the boatman. But it passed. He did not speak, but made for the dinghy, followed by the hand from the yacht. They turned the boat over, slid it down and afloat. The sailor got in and began to ship his oars. The man and the girl stood by till this was done. Then the girl turned away. The man extended his hand. "Thanks," he said curtly. The other's hand had involuntarily moved. The short, stout man dropped a silver dollar in it, swung on his heel and followed his daughter, - passed her, in fact, for she had only taken a step or two and halted. The young fellow eyed the silver coin in his hand with an expression that passed from astonishment to anger and broke at last into a smile of sheer amusement. He jiggled the coin, staring at it thoughtfully. Then he faced about on the jerseyed youth about to dip his blades. "Smith," he said, "I suppose if I heaved this silver dollar out into the chuck you'd think I was crazy." The youth only stared at him. "You don't object to tips, do you, Smith?" the man in the mackinaw inquired. "Gee, no," the boy observed. "Ain't you got no use for money?" "Not this kind. You take it and buy smokes." He flipped the dollar into the dinghy. It fell clinking on the slatted floor and the youth salvaged it, looked it over, put it in his pocket. "Gee," he said. "Any time a guy hands me money, I keep it, believe me."

Moreover, this year has been a terrible one for technology companies new to the stock market. Two dozen technology-related companies have gone public in 2004, Mr. Peterson said; collectively they were down more than 10 percent as of Friday's stock market close. That compares with a gain of about 1 percent in the share price for the nontechnology companies that have gone public this year Google is hardly just another company seeking to sell shares on the stock market. But, then, that is already reflected in the share price, which is expected to be the highest ever for an initial public offering. In Monday's filing, Google said it expected its shares to sell for $108 to $135 each. Even assuming that Google sells initially for $108 per share, that would make the company worth 150 times its last four quarters of earnings. By contrast, its Internet rival, Yahoo, is valued at 105 times earnings, and Microsoft 39 times earnings. Still, Barry Randall, a mutual fund manager, is among those thinking about taking the plunge. The company's balance sheets, at least at quick glance, he said, are compelling. According to Google's most recent filing, it has a gross profit margin "in the high 80 percent range," said Mr. Randall, who runs the First American Technology Fund, which specializes in technology stocks. "Your average tech stock," he said, "has gross margins of 40 percent." Still, it seems legitimate to ask if any company, no matter how extraordinary, should trade at such sky-high multiples. As even Google acknowledges in its S.E.C. filings, competitors threaten its dominance in search, from Yahoo and Microsoft to any number of lesser-known rivals. Moreover, Google can maintain its torrid rate of growth - which it must do to justify so extravagant a stock market valuation - only if it increases traffic on its site. That is no easy task given that it's already the default search engine for much of the world. (That explains recent initiatives like Gmail, a free e-mail service from Google that challenges offerings by Yahoo and Microsoft.) "The company's valuation is clearly based more on the hype factor than business fundamentals," said Ashok Kumar, a technology analyst at Raymond James & Company. Unlike many of the Internet companies that came to life at the end of the last decade, Google turns a sizable profit ($79 million in the second quarter of 2004, up 147 percent from a year earlier). But Mr. Kumar nonetheless concluded that its pricing "harkens back to the late 90's boom." As many people learned the hard way after the bubble burst in 2000, the stock market value of a technology company is not based as much on its intrinsic worth as on an assessment of its future earning power.
