My lunches are typically composed of lean proteins, like grilled chicken or turkey, paired with a hefty serving of kale or spinach, sprinkled lightly with olive oil and balsamic vinegar. Snacks are minimal, often just a handful of almonds or an apple, to maintain energy without straying from my path. Evenings aren't much different; dinner is another round of lean proteins, sometimes tofu if I'm feeling adventurous, alongside a medley of steamed vegetables. Water is my constant companion, never sweetened beverages or sodas. When people hear about my routine, they often react with surprise or even disbelief. They think it sounds intense or perhaps even extreme, but for me, it's a lifestyle choice, one carefully crafted over years of understanding what my body needs and how best to care for it. Each bead of sweat in the gym feels like an affirmation of my commitment, each healthy meal yet another step towards my goals. My journey is not about vanity or societal pressure; it's about health and self-respect, about knowing that I'm doing everything in my power to maintain a body that supports me in all my endeavors. There were times at the beginning when I felt tempted to revert to my old habits, to indulge in things I knew weren't beneficial for me. But every single time those cravings crept up, I reminded myself of the progress I had made, of the renewed energy I felt, and the self-discipline I had forged through consistent effort and patience. Of course, not every day is perfect. There are evenings when stress makes the couch look more inviting than any treadmill could. Sometimes, social gatherings pose a challenge to my strict regime, but I've learned to navigate those waters with balance and grace. I allow myself the occasional treat, a small slice of cheesecake, a glass of wine, reminders that life is also about enjoyment and celebration. In terms of my workout regimen, the gym is my second home. I've come to love the rhythm of my exercises, the repetition, and the tangible measurement of my strength increasing day by day. I've even started adding new disciplines into my routine, like yoga and pilates, which offer a counterbalance to the high-intensity training. They teach me to slow down, to breathe, to find a different kind of strength in stillness and flexibility. The decision to maintain such a comprehensive regime stems from an understanding of how crucial physical health is to mental and emotional well-being. Every time I pass the one-mile mark or lift a heavier weight, I feel a surge of accomplishment, a mental note that translates into confidence in other areas of my life. In truth, it's not simply about longevity or statistics; it's about living fully, freely, and embracing the best version of myself. This journey is not something I'm merely enduring; it's a path I've consciously chosen, because every day that I commit, every choice I make is a step towards not just looking better, but feeling resilient, empowered, and truly alive.

As I walked through the dusty streets of Mororo, I couldn't help but notice the bright smiles of the girls I met. Despite the hardships they faced, they radiated a sense of hope and determination that was truly inspiring. I met Jane, a 12-year-old girl who dreams of becoming a pilot one day. She told me about her daily routine, which starts at 5 am with fetching water from the nearby well. She then helps her mother with household chores before rushing off to school. "I want to fly high in the sky and see the world," she said, her eyes sparkling with excitement. "I want to show my community that girls can do anything they set their minds to." I also met Sarah, a 15-year-old who has already faced immense challenges in her young life. She was forced to drop out of school when her parents couldn't afford the fees, and was subsequently married off to a man more than twice her age. But Sarah refused to give up. She escaped her abusive husband and returned to her parents' home, where she is now determined to continue her education. "I want to be a lawyer," she said, her voice firm and resolute. "I want to help girls like me who have been forced into marriage and denied their right to education." As I listened to their stories, I was struck by the common thread that ran through them all - the desire for education and the determination to overcome the obstacles that stood in their way. These girls are the future leaders of their communities, and it's imperative that we support and empower them to reach their full potential. I met with a group of girls who had formed a club to support each other in their pursuit of education. They called themselves the "Strong Girls' Club," and their motto was "Education is our power." They met weekly to discuss their challenges and share their successes, and they had even started a small savings scheme to help each other with school fees. It was a testament to the power of community and the impact that girls can have when they come together to support each other. As I prepared to leave Mororo, I couldn't help but feel a sense of hope and optimism. Despite the challenges that these girls face, they are determined to succeed, and they are not alone. Organizations like Compassion UK are working tirelessly to support girls like Jane and Sarah, providing them with access to education and empowering them to become leaders in their communities. As I said goodbye to the girls, I knew that I would never forget their stories and their determination. They are the embodiment of the phrase "strength enables us to choose education over marriage," and they are a testament to the power of education to transform lives and communities.

The history of our land, as tangled and thorny as the wild brambles in the fields, had always been a cause for contemplation and caution. The Shannon flowed with its eternal grace, perhaps the only constant in our changing world. "Here ye go, Major, fresh coffee and warm water!" he exclaimed, placing the tray carefully on the dresser. "Biddy says she's on her way with breakfast soon enough." Larry and I trod the corridor silently, a shared sense of purpose in our stride. Outside, Ballinahone greeted us anew with its age-old charm, its stone walls and verdant gardens a testament to endurance and legacy. Today felt different, subtly but distinctly so. Perhaps it was the promise of change carried on the morning breeze, a hint of new beginnings whispered by the murmuring Shannon, as the castle sighed in sync with the rhythm of unfolding histories.

The thud of heavy footsteps, the distant shouts of men, and the grinding of machinery sent shivers coursing through Shaggycoat. His grandfather's strong yet trembling voice had quickly urged him away from their icy sanctuary, away from the small world they had known. "Stay close, young one," his grandfather had instructed, his tone both firm and gentle. "Keep your wits about you." Now, as they crept through the underbrush, Shaggycoat's wide eyes searched the darkening woods for any sign of danger, his ears perched and alert for any hint of the hostile intruders. The shadows stretched and yawned, mingling with the darkening sky as the daylight began to retreat, ushering in the night that felt both foreign and foreboding. Eventually, they found a small thicket of willows, their branches dipping low and draping like a curtain-a sanctuary of sorts. They settled down momentarily amidst the soft rustling leaves. The warm memories of home contrasted sharply with this new reality-a life of caution governed by the threat of those who traversed the land, their seeming dominion inexplicable and overwhelming. As the first stars appeared like scattered diamonds on the velvet sky, Shaggycoat felt a flicker of resilience ignite within him. They had lived under the ice, hidden from the harshness above, twisting and navigating the waters in cunning ways that ensured their survival. "Then we must be resourceful," he declared bravely, rubbing his damp paws together to keep warm against the chill of night. "We can find a way back, can't we?" With renewed determination, Shaggycoat listened attentively as the older beaver began telling stories of other beavers who had faced danger bravely, who had outsmarted their foes through ingenuity and teamwork. Each tale began to weave a thread of courage into the very fabric of his heart, igniting a flicker of hope amidst the shadows. The night was long and fraught with uncertainty, but in the belly of despair, a sense of purpose began to emerge-an unyielding desire to reclaim their home and defend what was rightfully theirs.

Thus, the subfamily features many endemic species (Graf et al., 2008; Malicky, 2005; Kucinic et al., 2011; Olah, 2010, 2011). The last exhaustive treatment of this group was conducted by Schmid (1956), who identified 7 genera of Drusinae and 6 species groups within the largest genus Drusus. He defined the subfamily mainly by venation characteristics of the male wings, and the presence of specialized A2 and A3 veins in the male hindwings, which form a pouch that harbors long vein bristles of unknown function (Schmid, 1956). Schmid (1956) examined 37 out of a total of 41 then known species, of which 35 are still valid. Since then, 1 new genus and many new species have been described, resulting in roughly 100 known extant species (Graf et al., 2008; Malicky, 2004, 2005; Kucinic et al., 2011; Olah, 2010, 2011; Olah and Kovacs, 2013; Previsic et al., 2014a; Sipahiler, 2002). A first molecular phylogenetic study on the subfamily Drusinae revealed the prevalence of three distinct evolutionary lineages, reflecting feeding ecology of larvae (Graf et al., 2009; Pauls et al., 2008): (1) carnivorous filterers (developing toothed shredder-like mandible edges, modifications of head capsules, and additional filtering spines on legs and the first abdominal sternum), (2) omnivorous shredders (exhibiting toothed shredder mandibles, but lacking additional spines and filtering bristles), (3) epilithic grazers (developing spoon-shaped mandibles without teeth and lacking additional spines and filtering bristles). Further, Pauls et al. (2008) rejected most of the generic concepts and species groupings that Schmid (1956) had proposed based primarily on the morphology of adult male terminalia. In particular, the monotypic genus Cryptothrix was found to be closely related to the filtering carnivorous Drusinae, whereas the genus Drusus was identified as paraphyletic with Anomalopterygella, Metanoea, polyphyletic Ecclisopteryx, and Cryptothrix nested within (Pauls et al., 2008). The genus Drusus was found to comprise members of all three larval feeding types (Graf et al., 2009; Pauls et al., 2008). Taxonomic knowledge enabling larval identification were hitherto presented for 47 Drusinae species only (references in Previsic et al., 2014a; Vitecek et al., 2015a; Waringer et al., 2013a,b). Larval stages of Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera and Trichoptera are crucial quality elements for contemporary biological water quality monitoring approaches (AQEM consortium, 2002; Barbour et al., 1999; Barbour and Yoder, 2000; Graf et al., 2002). Particularly the differential sensitivity of caddisfly species to minute environmental changes renders them ideal to monitor pollution or anthropogenic disturbance (Graf et al., 2002), particularly at species level (Waringer et al., 2013c). As all identifiable members of Drusinae are used as bio-indicators and sensitive species in biological monitoring (Moog et al., 2002), larval keys to this highly diversified group are crucial. Currently available larval keys cover roughly 50% of all known species, and need to be extended in order to exploit the full bioindicative potential of Drusinae. In this study, we examine whether adult apomorphies exist for the feeding groups sensu Pauls et al. (2008).

The most common approach to measuring SES is to use income or wealth indicators. However, these variables may not capture adequately the effect on health of early-life experiences (Case et al., 2005; Case and Paxson, 2001; Lynch et al., 2000; Sastry, 2005). Education has been proposed as a better indicator of lifetime SES because it provides a more direct measure of the resources available to individuals over the course of their lives and because it can be measured retrospectively (Bartley and Plewis, 1997; Feinstein, 1993; Marmot et al., 1978; Palloni, 2006). Education is highly correlated with income but its effects on health are not always mediated through income (Bartley and Blane, 1994; Breeze et al., 2004; Deaton, 2002). Education may influence health via different pathways: through greater knowledge about healthy behaviours, access to health-promoting goods and services, access to information, skills needed to deal with illness and stress, the ability to cope with stressful events and the capacity to make better decisions about health (Adler and Rehkopf, 2008; Case and Paxson, 2001; Diez Roux, 2012; House et al., 1988; Kawachi et al., 1997; Lynch et al., 1997; Marmot, 2006; Marmot et al., 1978; Ruhm, 2000; Schoeni et al., 2008; Smith and Egger, 2000). The aim of this study was to examine trends in disability prevalence among men and women aged 60-74 years between 1995/96 and 2010/11 using data from three cross-sectional surveys in England. We focused on disability rather than disease prevalence to provide a better estimate of the potential need for care services. Our main objective was to investigate whether there were differences in disability prevalence between successive birth cohorts within each survey year. We also investigated whether any cohort differences persisted after adjusting for age and other individual characteristics including education and household income. Finally, we examined whether any cohort differences varied according to educational level. The data come from the first three waves of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). ELSA is a nationally representative panel study of adults aged 50 and above living in private households in England. It began in 2002/03 when respondents completed a baseline interview followed by two further interviews in 2004/05 and 2006/07. Wave 4 fieldwork took place in 2008/09 and Wave 5 in 2010/11. The sampling frame comprised all residents of private households who were registered with a general practitioner in England and Wales and had been identified from computerised lists provided by general practices. Each wave consists of both a core sample and an oversample of people aged 70 and above. For Wave 1, 12,099 people participated in the baseline interview and 10,917 responded to the follow-up interview in Wave 2. For Wave 2, 10,370 participants responded to the Wave 3 interview. Of these, 9,851 returned a response in Wave 4 and 8,853 in Wave 5. Full details of the design and implementation of ELSA are given elsewhere (Barbiere et al., 2012; Steptoe et al., 2006).

A number of studies have suggested that it is possible to identify QTLs for grain yield under DS (Saxena et al., 2006; Cavanagh et al., 2013; Upadhyaya et al., 2013b). However, there is a lack of information regarding the genetic control of phenology-related traits in chickpea. These traits play a significant role in determining the adaptation of plants to environmental stresses like drought (Gaur et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2011; Yadav et al., 2012). This study was carried out at the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA), Syria during 2013-2014. Seeds of 95 advanced lines derived from 21 cross combinations involving 17 exotic parents were used for evaluation. All the 95 lines along with their respective parental lines were evaluated in three replications each under both well-watered and water-stressed regimes at ICARDA's field station, Tel Hadja, located at latitude 35 40' N and longitude 38 10' E with altitude of 530 m above mean sea level. The soil type was calcareous clay loam with pH 8.2 and electrical conductivity of 0.48 dS/m. Average temperature ranged between 25.3 C and 30.5 C. The experimental design was a split-plot randomized complete block design with two replications. Plot size was 12 m long and 2 m wide, consisting of four rows spaced 20 cm apart. Lines were sown in row pairs, leaving one row empty between them. Each plot consisted of 80 plants. The first irrigation was applied before sowing and subsequent irrigations were given at 15 days interval to ensure proper plant growth and development till the onset of flowering stage. Thereafter, irrigation was withheld until the end of the experiment, which resulted in terminal drought. The experiment was conducted in accordance with the good agricultural practices followed in the region. Fertilizer application was done as per the recommended dose, i.e., 120 kg ha-1 N +60 kg ha-1 P2O5 +120 kg ha-1 K2O. The seeds were treated with fungicides (Bavistin(R) 250 g kg-1 seed) before sowing. Weeds were removed manually whenever necessary. Data were recorded on 16 different morpho-agronomic and phenological characters, including days to 50% flowering, days to maturity, plant height, stem thickness, leaf area index (LAI), dry matter accumulation, harvest index, biomass, pods per plant, seeds per pod, thousand-seed weight, biological yield, grain yield, and straw yield. Days to 50% flowering was defined as the time taken by 50% of the plants in a plot to flower. Plant height was measured from ground level to the tip of the longest fully expanded leaf. Stem thickness was measured at the base of the plant by holding the stem between the thumb and forefinger and noting the maximum distance between the two fingers. LAI was estimated by measuring the length and width of five representative leaves from the middle of the canopy and then calculating the leaf area from the formula: leaf area = length * width * 0.75. Dry matter accumulation was calculated by harvesting a 0.25-m2 area at the base of the plant at 30, 45, 60, 75, and 90 days after emergence (DAE). Harvest index was calculated as the ratio of grain yield to total biomass. Biological yield was obtained by adding together the grain and straw yields.

However, the Committee's challenge does place a particular, and acute, focus on the difficulty of applying the legally 'neat' concepts of the functional model of mental capacity across the full complex spectrum of human life. Further, it is undoubtedly the case that there are situations in which determinations of mental capacity are reached which any fair-minded observer would consider to be problematic. Against this backdrop, a large multi-disciplinary2 and multi-jurisdictional3, project is underway, one of its aims being to produce educational tools to enable more satisfactory determinations of mental capacity in difficult cases in health and social care contexts. Its first stage has consisted of a detailed review and analysis of the resolution by the Court of Protection in England & Wales of capacity disputes presented to it in the first 10 years of its life, from October 2007 to October 2017. In focusing this review on cases in which there is an explicit dispute as to the capacity of P, the subject of proceedings, whether between P (or P's family) and the health or social care professionals involved in P's care, or between professionals or expert witnesses called to give evidence, we aimed to shine a spotlight on those cases in which the onus is highest upon the judiciary to apply a statutory formulation of the functional model of capacity so as to achieve a satisfactory resolution of the case before them. This paper, drawing upon the initial fruits of that review, first outlines how capacity cases came to be in the Court of Protection and examines the role of the Court of Protection in determining capacity. This goes into some detail because (1) many readers will not necessarily be familiar with the workings of the court; (2) there is no readily accessible equivalent overview of the historical developments and the current practice of the court - the closest is Baker J's book (The Hon Mr. Justice Baker, 2018) to which Ruck Keene contributed; and (3) because the court is unusual in being a specialist court charged with the determination of capacity, publishing judgments upon capacity delivered by senior judges, and thus meriting a detailed explanation of the context within which those judgments come to be delivered. The paper then describes legal and clinical characteristics of disputed capacity cases and asks the question as to how the Court of Protection, now ten years in existence, is doing in complying with its own statutory parameters. The preliminary analysis we present suggests that it is still on a learning curve and has room for improvement. It does, however, highlight the complexity of decision-making capacity in specific contexts, and shows what taking capacity seriously looks like in the court-room, as well as suggesting pointers for future practice. This is the first in-depth study looking specifically at disputed capacity cases before the Court of Protection.

The voice came from the bed and was marked by that peculiar tone noticeable when persons extremely cold try to speak without chattering. "I can't help it, mother. I'm cold, so cold, and I'm hungry, too. I only had half a potato, and Maggie says they're all gone." "Poor child!" said the mother with a sigh. "Here, Maggie, give him this," and she drew from under the pillow a small potato which she held toward the girl. But the girl did not stir until the hungry boy made a move in the direction of the bed. This movement aroused her as his overdose of coal had roused his other watchful sister a moment previous. "No! No! Johnnie. Do not take it. Our mother will starve. She has not eaten anything for two days." "Let him have it, Maggie. I cannot eat it. Perhaps your father will come soon and bring some tea. I think a good cup of tea would make me better." "And, mother," said Cora, "we will take the money we were going to spend for shoes and get a bit of flannel for you and the baby. You must have it or you will freeze. Surely father will come soon. He said he would." "Nearly everyone has gone home now. Hardly a person passes," Cora observed, with her nose pressed against the frosty pane. "That is because it is so cold. It is not late yet. We will wait a little longer, and then Maggie - " "O, mother! Do not ask me to go. It is so cold, and suppose - suppose I had to go into a saloon again. It nearly kills me to go about such places." "You might meet him, Maggie, and keep him from going in." "If my pa don't come tonight, he's a big liar, that's all!" broke in Johnnie, hotly. His mother did not answer him. She was watching the face bent low over the tiny baby. She noted the careworn look and the nervous pressure of the hand held over the tiny one to keep it warm. Presently the girl lifted her eyes to her mother. Those tender pleading eyes of the mother would have melted a harder heart than hers. She went to the bed and put the baby in, close to its mother's side. Then she threw her arms around the haggard woman's neck and kissed her passionately. "Dear mother," she said, "I would do anything for you. I will go for father, and before it gets any later." "Pray, child! Pray every breath you draw! Pray every step you take that you may find him before it is too late. If you do not - I cannot imagine what is to become of us. Pray! God is not cruel. Surely he will hear us in our misery." Would you see the drunkard's daughter dressed for a walk this bitter night?

The first step in the motor process is to select the appropriate allograph, which according to Van Galen (1991) is the activation of the motor programme (retrieval of an allograph action pattern from long-term motor memory). Following the activation of the motor programme the module of size control and speed is activated (Van Galen, 1991). The muscle synergies from both the agonist and the antagonistic muscles are then recruited during the muscular adjustment module, which results in the real time movement of the pen (Van Galen, 1991). Van Galen's model of handwriting, although the most complete in the literature, is not without limitations. According to Kandel and Spinelli (2010) it fails to account for parallel processing at different levels of the model, which results in an increased duration of the handwriting movements. In addition, research by Kandel, Soler, Valdopis and Gros (2006) in French writers has demonstrated that letters are not programmed individually, but rather in chunks, and the temporal profile is determined by the number of syllables in the word. This emphasises the relationship between the production of handwriting and the cognitive and linguistic aspects of writing and must be accounted for when examining pausing behaviour in more detail. The definition of a pause in writing is inconsistent in the literature. Rosenblum and Livneh-Zirinski (2008) defined a pause as a pen lift from the writing tablet. However, it was not clear as to how long the pen needed to be raised from the surface in order to be classified as a pause. In the writing literature Alamargot, Chesnet, Dansac, and Ros (2006) and Alamargot, Plane, Lambert, and Chesnet (2010) defined a pause as a period of 15 ms or more with the pen not in contact with the tablet. The rationale for such a short pause threshold was to include all writing events that occurred; including raising the pen to think of an idea or briefly to dot an 'i'. Other authors have omitted to define a pause and made reference only to the fact that pauses occurred during the writing task (Accardo, Genna, & Borean, 2013). In addition to the debate on how pauses are classified, it is also unclear even in the literature on writing what exactly a pause represents. Thus, the pause thresholds used in the current study are grounded in evidence where possible, while some aspects of the analysis are exploratory in nature. In relation to pausing in children with DCD, Rosenblum and Livneh-Zirinski (2008) proposed anomalies in the lower level processes of handwriting, such as between stroke muscular adjustments, as reasons for excessive pausing. Alternative explanations for the excessive pausing include physiological factors such as fatigue (Rosenblum & Livneh-Zirinski, 2008).

For our sins or for the sins of our fathers?' 'Be it far from me to presume to set forth the ways of Providence!' returned her guest. 'I meddle not, like some that should be wiser, with the calling of the prophet. It is enough for me to know that ever and again the pride of man will gather to "a mighty and a fearful head," and, like a swollen mill-pond overfed of rains, burst the banks that confine it, whether they be the laws of the land or the ordinances of the church, usurping on the fruitful meadows, the hope of life for man and beast. Alas!' he went on, with a new suggestion from the image he had been using, 'if the beginning of strife be as the letting out of water, what shall be the end of that strife whose beginning is the letting out of blood?' 'Think you then, good sir, that thus it has always been? that such times of fierce ungodly tempest must ever follow upon seasons of peace and comfort? - even as your cousin of holy memory, in his verses concerning the church militant, writes: "Thus also sin and darkness follow still The church and sun, with all their power and skill."' 'Truly it seems so. But I thank God the days of my pilgrimage are nearly numbered. To judge by the tokens the wise man gives us, the mourners are already going about my streets. The almond-tree flourisheth at least.' He smiled as he spoke, laying his hand on his grey head. 'But think of those whom we must leave behind us, master Herbert. How will it fare with them?' said the lady in troubled tone, and glancing in the direction of the window. In the window sat a girl, gazing from it with the look of a child who had uttered all her incantations, and could imagine no abatement in the steady rain-pour. 'We shall leave behind us strong hearts and sound heads too,' said Mr. Herbert. 'And I bethink me there will be none stronger or sounder than those of your young cousins, my late pupils, of whom I hear brave things from Oxford, and in whose affection my spirit constantly rejoices.' 'You will be glad to hear such good news of your relatives, Dorothy,' said the lady, addressing her daughter. Even as she said the words, the setting sun broke through the mass of grey cloud, and poured over the earth a level flood of radiance, in which the red wheat glowed, and the drops that hung on every ear flashed like diamonds. The girl's hair caught it as she turned her face to answer her mother, and an aureole of brown-tinted gold gleamed for a moment about her head. 'I am glad that you are pleased, madam, but you know I have never seen them - or heard of them, except from master Herbert, who has, indeed, often spoke rare things of them.'

As the summer solstice approached, the days grew longer, the sun hanging low in the sky like a burning ember, casting a golden glow over the landscape. At this prodigious moment her father came in from his ride, saw the governess cowering and wringing her hands in the corner, and the Hope of Rhodope flicking the ash off her cigarette with the apparent mastery of habit. His face expressed no surprise, though he cast one furious glance at Mademoiselle Fifine, and dismounting from his horse, he walked to where his daughter was sitting. She had not seen him till he had well turned the corner into the yard, and knew that he must have observed her employment; and convinced of this, she had not resorted to what would have been the ordinary young lady's pitiful subterfuge on such an extreme occasion, and either dropped her cigarette, or handed it behind her back to the groom. She was far too defiant and proud for such paltriness of conduct, and she smoked quietly on, a slight patter of fear in her heart, but outwardly calm. Her father approached in silence, and as he drew near Sophia respectfully got up. Still in silence he sat down on the horse-block, and Sophia stood beside him. If he had only boxed her ears and called her a 'dirty, vulgar little cat,' she would have drawn a sigh of relief, but this silence was intolerably ominous. She was the first to break it. 'I am smoking a cigarette, papa,' she said frankly, 'and I find it excellent.' He did not look at her, but only took out his own cigarette-case and laid it by his side. 'So I see,' he said; 'and when you have finished that, you shall have another. These, too, are excellent cigarettes; I have plenty of them.' 'Thanks; you are very kind, but I think one will be enough,' remarked Sophia. 'It may be, but you will have another if it is not.' Then turning to the stablemen: 'Stop where you are, all of you,' he said. 'I wish you to see the Princess Sophia smoking till she has had enough.' Sophia understood, and her small spirit was up in indignant revolt. Already she had had nearly enough, and the cigarette was yet only half consumed. Each puff became a more palpable pang. Meantime Mademoiselle Fifine had approached. 'Oh, sir,' she said tremulously, 'Princess Sophia has been very naughty, and I could not stop her. But make her stop; perhaps she will obey you. If she smokes any more, she will die of it, for already she is growing very pale.' The Prince turned to the distressed governess with a malign light in his eye. 'As you say, you could not stop her,' he said. 'You had better get home and pack your boxes. I do not choose to retain the services of one who cannot govern my daughter. You a governess!' he cried, his voice rising suddenly to a tone that the late Princess Fedora well knew. 'Great and merciful God!' Sophia turned to her father.

The game wore on, the weight of the evening settling more heavily upon the shoulders of each man present. The cards continued to shuffle and deal, falling limply in the dim lamplight like leaves abandoned by the reluctant hands of autumn. Lieutenant Spurrier, with his youthful face shadowed with a hint of wistfulness, surveyed the room. His gaze flitted over each of his comrades in arms, resting briefly on Captain Comyn before skipping to the commander whose brow was furrowed with concentration. Within Spurrier, a thought burgeoned, cloaked in the apprehension of youth suddenly aware of the fragility of sanity in this oppressive heat. Major York, the battalion commander, sat reclined with an air of practiced indifference, trying to ignore the night that wrapped them all in a humid embrace. Even now, as his eyes peered over his hand, punctuated by taps of his forefinger on the table's worn edge, the lines of responsibility etched themselves into his features, adding years to a soul wearied by the demands of leadership. He lost and won with the same stoic demeanor, as if each round of poker was another battle in the endless campaign against the jungle beyond their encampment. The tension in the air was a palpable entity, an invisible vine coiling tighter around their assembled circle. Major York finally spoke, his voice cutting through the dense atmosphere, "We're all a bit on edge, gentlemen. Perhaps it's time we consider adjourning for the night. The heat is not the only thing that tires a man." A murmur of agreement, a collective sigh of relief passed through the gathering-except for Captain Comyn, whose battling thoughts were not so easily silenced. His fingers twitched around the base of his whiskey glass, distilling his nervous energy into the cool, comforting solidity of its form. He knew the signs too well, having faced darker shadows in quieter battles. "Just one more hand," Comyn urged, casting a pleading glance towards the major. In that moment, it was not just the game he wished to prolong but the fragile thread of normalcy that it stitched into their fracturing world. This plea, simple yet profound, met with sympathetic understanding. The cards were dealt once more, their corners creased with the many beseechings they'd borne over this campaign of companionship. And as the hands were laid bare upon the scarred tabletop, the assembled soldiers exhaled together, a breath fraught with the mingling of camaraderie and solitude. The night crept further, shadows lengthening and entwining with the whispers of trees outside. In the near distance, a faint rustle carried the song of the untamed wilderness that surrounded them. They were each its captive and its protector, bound to the challenges it wove so seamlessly into their daily discourse. With the final hand played in reverent silence, Captain Comyn felt a semblance of peace, however fleeting, before the shadows returned with their gnawing persistence. He knew that come morning, the Sun would rise with the same relentless intensity, that he would still face the labyrinth of his own thoughts, yet for now, he sat among friends, and together they faced another nightfall in the ever-seething subconscious of the jungle.

There could be glitches and pitfalls, but if they're going to learn geography, why not try it this way? "Just drilling them, that's not always the best in my mind, as far as teaching pedagogy," Bedley said. "I wanted to expose and connect them with kids all over the United States." Each time they run the exercise, students are assigned particular jobs: Among them, a "think tank" tracks maps, fact-checkers confirm what's said, note-takers and runners make sure everyone has the information they need, and "on-camera talent" asks and answers questions. A student supervisor watches the whole process and looks for ways they can improve next time. A reporter-blogger documents the process. "Organized chaos," Bedley calls it. He rarely appears on camera. The whole thing takes about 20 minutes and touches on critical thinking and problem-solving his students need, not to mention geography know-how. Students' questions have gotten better as they've practiced more, and they've actually added new rules to make it tougher: No more Googling and guessing based on a city name they spotted in the other classroom. So far, it's working. "They'll go home and research on their own, without assigning homework or anything," Bedley said. His students just finished their 17th state, Minnesota. As a reward for all their hard work, they've recently earned a class pet. (A huge, sometimes smelly, risk, any educator will agree.) It's a tan hamster. Bedley's students named him Hashtag. Don't call him a 'techie' Bedley can understand why teachers and schools are wary of the latest-and-greatest technology: They've heard it all before. "The technology that was being provided for schools to use to help kids learn was disastrous. We were limited to word processing or 'Oregon Trail,' " he said of his early years in education. "The tools available for teachers now are what I wish I would have had my first year teaching." Now, he's got BYOD (bring your own device) classrooms where students can use cell phones, iPods, tablets or laptops from home, as long as they've passed a course on how to use them appropriately. They have access to a few school computers, and Bedley has raised money or landed grants for big-ticket items, such as iPads, netbooks, a webcam and a desktop computer for the classroom. "I know (my district) would want to provide the funds, they just don't have them," he said. Like a lot of teachers, he relies on free tools, too. He first tried using Skype in 2009, when budget reductions cut back on arts education for his students. He connected his classroom with working artists in other parts of the country, so they could still had a chance to learn. Last year, his students Skyped with docents from Fort Meigs, a War of 1812 battlefield in Ohio. When they revealed the armory, "the kids just gasped," he said.

Major Rockford permitted himself a slight smile, an acknowledgment not lost on those standing near. The unknown results hanging in the balance gnawed at Dick's resolve, urging patience he alone could muster. With the resilience of one who has faced many adversities, he let the flicker of a smile pass over his otherwise stoic features, knowing without certainty that his cadets had given their utmost. As the officers continued their rounds, moving on to yet another glistening company, Dick Hamilton allowed himself a moment of quiet reflection. Whatever outcome awaited, he knew the bond among his comrades had only strengthened, a chain forged in loyalty and shared ambition.

These pioneering studies highlighted not merely the physiological responses of pollen tubes to thermal variations, but also the cascading effects that temperature could have on reproductive success and, ultimately, seed set. To further elucidate the complexities of this interaction, contemporary research has begun employing advanced imaging techniques and molecular analyses. Techniques such as fluorescence microscopy and gene expression profiling afford a more nuanced understanding of the mechanisms governing pollen tube growth under varying thermal regimes (Liu et al., 2020; Rojas et al., 2021). In addition to the physical and mechanical challenges imposed by high temperatures, it is critical to consider the biochemical alterations that occur within the pollen grain itself during the progamic phase. Elevated temperatures can induce stress responses that may alter the metabolic pathways responsible for energy production and cellular integrity (Lopez et al., 2016). Such stress responses can result in a reduction of ATP availability, ultimately impairing the motility and viability of the pollen tube as it traverses the pistil in search of the ovule. Under scenarios of heat stress, the synthesis of heat shock proteins becomes paramount, as these molecules play a significant role in maintaining protein homeostasis and mitigating damage to cellular structures (Zhang et al., 2018). As the challenges associated with climate change become increasingly clear, the interplay between temperature and reproductive success in plants assumes urgent significance. The ongoing rise in global temperatures could lead to alterations in flowering phenology, with potential mismatches between the timing of pollinator activity and the flowering periods of plants (Hegland et al., 2009). Such mismatches could have detrimental effects on pollination success, ultimately impacting fruit and seed yield. Moreover, the concept of thermal thresholds emerges as an essential consideration in the dialogue concerning temperature effects on plant reproduction. Each species exhibits varying degrees of tolerance to temperature extremes, often shaped by local adaptation and evolutionary pressures (Kearney and Porter, 2009). For example, studies suggest that some temperate species may have evolved mechanisms to cope with transient heat stress during reproductive phases, while subtropical species may be less resilient (Hedhly and Hormaza, 2016). This variability emphasizes the need for focused research on specific genotypes, particularly those that exhibit promising traits for climate resilience. In the context of horticulture and agriculture, understanding these dynamics also paves the way for strategic breeding programs aimed at developing cultivars that better withstand temperature variations. Selection for traits associated with pollen tube growth and ovule fertilisation under elevated thermal conditions could prove instrumental in securing stable yields against the backdrop of a changing climate. Such investigations should also encompass the genetic underpinnings of thermal acclimation in key species, delving into the role that specific alleles may play in conferring resilience to thermal stress during critical reproductive windows (Pulawska et al., 2014). The collaborative efforts among molecular biologists, ecologists, and horticulturists would undoubtedly yield groundbreaking insights, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of plant reproduction in an era marked by climatic uncertainty. The ramifications of temperature on plant reproduction extend beyond ecology and agriculture, prompting inquiry into the broader implications for ecosystems and biodiversity. Shifts in successful reproductive strategies may alter species distributions, prompting cascading effects throughout trophic levels. As such, addressing these intricate relationships requires an interdisciplinary approach, highlighting the interconnectedness of all biological systems in the face of environmental change.

Simultaneous with the universal application of solar modules and the increasing number of installations research and development activities focusing on avoiding and solving the short-term and long-term efficiency decrease mentioned above become more of an issue. There's no expectation that a person has attained full sobriety before offering support. Instead, the power lies in shared experiences, mutual understanding, and the knowledge that no one walks alone. In the same vein, Christians are called to support one another, to learn and grow together, embracing imperfections as part of the journey. Consider how liberating it could be if we embraced our vulnerabilities and recognized that our struggles, failures, and imperfections are integral to our testimonies. The very act of being honest about our shortcomings can serve as a powerful tool for connection, for fostering empathy, and for highlighting the transformative power of faith. It's in the authenticity of our human experience that we find the threads that connect us. True vulnerability allows others to see Christ's work in us, not as a confounding magic act, but as a series of small, meaningful changes that illuminate the soul. But society's fixation on perfection, fueled by a superficial understanding of faith, keeps us locked in silence and riddled with self-doubt. We consider ourselves inadequate spokespeople for the Gospel, placing our personal imperfections on a pedestal where Christ is meant to stand. This is not only detrimental to our faith journey but also diminishes opportunities to positively influence those around us. By holding back, we inadvertently contribute to the very notion of exclusion we fear-retreating into silence when we should be a testament to the grace and redemption Christianity promises. Now, let us pivot to consider the societal pressure that stamps this hypocrite label as an inevitable consequence of speaking one's faith. The truth is that each encounter, each candid admission of one's struggles in the light of faith, is an invitation for camaraderie, for shared exploration. In this way, we cultivate an environment that values authenticity over perception, collective growth over individual perfection. Isn't this a more credible witness to what it means to live a life of faith-being real, broken, yet hopeful and redeemable? In our fear of inadequacy, we forget the fundamental tenet that the Gospel is for all and that no one stands exempt from its redeeming love. Speaking our truth doesn't demand an unblemished history; it requires an open heart and an honest voice. Imagine the ripple effect if we all pursued this genuine expression of faith. The more we speak openly, balancing our humanity with our beliefs, the more we demystify the myths around Christianity, making it accessible, relatable, and profound to others. Therefore, let us reject the notion that perfection precedes ministry. Instead, just as Christ did with his disciples, let us come as we are, willingly sharing our growth and our setbacks. Let's turn the fear of being labeled a hypocrite into an opportunity to invite others into the journey of faith. In doing so, we not only honor the spirit of community that our faith extols but also step towards a profound communal grace. Our imperfection is not a barrier; it is the very testament of the transformative power of God's love.

With a swift motion, Arno hurls the bra over his shoulder, darting toward the changing room as the MERCS break through the entrance of the store. The STORE CLERK's jaw drops, eyes wide as she witnesses the chaos unfolding. Arno doesn't look back. He slides through the narrow door, the sounds of chaos beginning to unfold beyond the fabric walls. Inside the changing room, Arno's mind races, calculating his next move. The MERCS are close, too close. A quick glance reveals a window at the end of the cramped space. With little time to spare, he aims his gun upwards-it's now or never. The shot reverberates, stunningly loud in the tight quarters. The window shatters, raining down shards of glass as Arno leaps up, pulling himself through the jagged frame. Outside, he lands on a roof, the cool air rushing past him as he regains his footing. Below, the thrumming heartbeat of the mall continues, oblivious to the turmoil that had just erupted. He takes a moment to get his bearings, his pulse thumping wildly in his ears. He scans the horizon, spotting an exit ramp leading to a parking lot. 'That's the way,' he tells himself, and he takes off. With each leap over the edges of rooftops, memories flash before him-unsanctioned jobs, tight squeezes, bleeding for survival. This was just another day in the relentless grind, but today felt different, electric. Something was off, and Arno swore he felt elements of an unseen force hot on his tail. Suddenly, he hears the telltale CRACK of gunfire splintering the air behind him. The MERCS had regrouped, their coordination sharp as they pursued him across the rooftops like wolves on a hunt. The lead MERC-a tall guy with a scar running from his brow to his jaw-raises his weapon. Arno ducks just in time; the bullet zips past him, but it's not just aimed at him anymore-it's a warning. He quickens his pace, adrenaline fueling every muscle in his body as he leaps from building to building. In the distance, he sees the PARKING LOT, now a chaotic battleground. Shoppers scamper to their cars, confusion gripping the remains of tranquility. Arno yells to the crowd, "Get down!" He lunges towards two unsuspecting MEN, thrusting them aside just as a volley of bullets whirls past them. The sound of shattering glass echoes again as the MERCS begin to infiltrate the area, their shooters now taking aim at the commotion. Arno spots a vehicle parked askew-its door ajar. He rushes towards it, a sleek black SUV that looks untouched by the chaos. No time for niceties; he dives inside, fumbling for the ignition as bullets continue to chip at the SUV's frame. With a metallic roar, the engine springs to life, and Arno slams the accelerator down. The tires screech, and he pushes the SUV into motion, plowing through the parking lot, barely missing a cluster of terrified shoppers. His heart pounds as he swerves toward the exit, only to see a blockade of MERCS forming ahead. A plan emerges in his mind-this may be insane, reckless, but as they say, fortune favors the bold. With a fierce determination, Arno takes aim at the barricade, bracing himself as he speeds up, tightening his grip on the wheel. A split-second decision drives him to push through a nearby drift of concrete barriers, and he feels the thrill of speed surge through him-their eyes wide with shock-the MERCS' faces blur together as he makes his escape.

In front of this car were other cars, ranged close together in a row. All were stripped of their top works, and bore numbers. "What is this place?" gasped the Dutch boy. "The 'Automobile Club,'" replied the cowl. "The club of the real automobile men of Denver." "I've heard of it," muttered the Dutch boy. "But I never knew there was such a thing." "You should have known. We are the most important body of men in Denver. We control the police, the courts, and everything else. We can make or break any man we choose." "Why didn't you tell me about this when you met me at the corner?" asked the Dutch boy suspiciously. "We did not know whether you would be worthy to join our ranks. You may yet prove unworthy." "Well, if I am, why not let me go? What do you want with me?" "That will be explained presently. First we must see how well you stand the test. Do you know anything about automobiles?" "Yes, sir. I'm a mechanic myself." "Do you know anything about racing them?" "Not much, but I've seen some races." "Have you ever driven an auto yourself?" "Once." "And how did you drive it?" "Very carefully, for fear I'd break something." "How many speeds has your car got?" "Two. And they're pretty slow ones, too." "How many speeds does this car have?" "Three. But I haven't tried them yet." "Try them now." The Dutch boy obeyed. He threw in the clutch and stepped on the accelerator. The engine began to purr softly; the wheels spun around rapidly. Then, as he pressed harder on the accelerator, the purring changed to a roar, and the car shot forward. "Stop!" cried the cowl. The Dutch boy obeyed instantly, and brought the machine to a halt. "Go backward," ordered the cowl. "Yes, sir," said the Dutch boy, obediently reversing the car. "Now go forward again." Once more the car sped ahead. "Backward again." Again the car reversed itself. "Forward again." This time the Dutch boy kept the speed down, and drove slowly across the room. "Very good," approved the cowl. "You have passed the first test. Now we'll try you in another way. Take off your clothes and put on these overalls." The Dutch boy hesitated. "Don't delay," warned the cowl. "Take off your clothes." Reluctantly the Dutch boy complied. As he slipped off his coat and vest, he saw that the floor of the room was strewn with articles of clothing - shirts, trousers, hats, coats, vests, shoes, etc. When he had taken off his boots and socks and laid aside his underclothes, the only garments left upon his person were his union suit and his underwear. The cowl handed him a suit of blue overalls, which he hastily drew on. "Now," said the cowl, "we shall see if you are equal to the second test. There are five hundred dollars in gold lying on that table yonder. Bring it to me." The Dutch boy stared. Five hundred dollars! Why, that was enough money to buy a horse and wagon, and still leave enough over to pay for a trip to Europe! He looked at the cowl suspiciously. Was this a trap? If so, he could easily escape from it. The Dutch boy had no conscience whatever. He had often stolen things, and had always gotten away with it.

Consequently, detailed information on how smallholder farmers in particular landscapes are already responding to climate shocks is needed to inform the development of strategies and policies to their vulnerability to climate shocks and to enhance their adaptive capacity [4]. In Madagascar, smallholder farmers are known to be at great risk from cyclones [19], but to date there have been no studies on the specific impacts they experience and how they cope with these impacts. An estimated 71% of Malagasy farmers are smallholders [23,29], with a national average upland rice area per farmer of only 1.28 ha [54]. Most Malagasy smallholder farmers practice subsistence farming, depending on agriculture both for food security and for household income, and are seasonally food insecure [5,13,14,19,37]. Most smallholder farmers are also extremely poor, with an estimated 87% of smallholder farmers falling below the national poverty line [23]. As a consequence, Malagasy smallholder farmers are extremely vulnerable to extreme weather events that reduce agricultural productivity or cause crop loss. The overall objective of our study was to understand how Malagasy smallholder farmers prepare for and cope with the impacts of cyclones, using a case study of how smallholder farmers reacted to cyclone Giovanna that hit Madagascar in February 2012. Cyclone Giovanna was a category '4' cyclone (on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Intensity Scale of 1-5, where 1 is the weakest and 5 the strongest [27]; with winds of up to 269 km per hour and a total of 355.6 mm of rainfall occurring over three days [18]. The cyclone is known to have affected at least 246,000 people, destroyed >44,000 houses, damaged >27,000 houses and damaged at least 12,517 ha of agricultural land across Madagascar, but the real impact was likely greater given that information on impacts was only reported by 250 of the 697 municipalities in Madagascar [7]. We conducted surveys of 200 farmers to: a) explore how farmers prepared for cyclone Giovanna and how effective their preparations were in reducing vulnerability; b) document the specific impacts of the Giovanna cyclone on agricultural production and farmer livelihoods (including impacts on income, health, housing and food security); and c) examine how farmers coped with the impacts of cyclones on their farming systems and livelihoods and how effective these coping strategies were in reducing their vulnerability. While there are existing government assessments of the overall impacts of individual cyclones (including cyclone Giovanna) at the district, regional and national levels [7,17], to our knowledge, this is the first study in Madagascar to collect detailed household-level data on the specific impacts of cyclones on smallholder farmers and to examine the coping strategies used by farmers to deal with these impacts.

Besides this shared position, diagnostic morphological characters of bilaterian apical organs are rather limited: in general, a tuft of long cilia emerging from mono- or multiciliated cells is present, accompanied by flask-shaped receptor cells, often positive for serotonin or FMRFamide immunoreactivity and connected to the larval nervous system by a plexus of neurites (Byrne et al., 2007; Hay-Schmidt, 2000; Nakajima et al., 1993; Richter et al., 2010). The morphology, number and arrangement of nerve cells associated with apical organs can vary considerably (e.g. Altenburger and Wanninger, 2010; Dickinson and Croll, 2003; Hay-Schmidt, 2000; Kempf et al., 1997; Temereva and Wanninger, 2012; Voronezhskaya et al., 2002). In deuterostomes, the cell bodies of the apical organ-associated neurons are typically located in or close to the apical portion of the ciliary bands and can be organized into bilaterally arranged ganglia (Byrne et al., 2007; Nielsen, 2012). Generally, larvae swim with their apical organs pointing forward, prior to settling on a substrate and undergoing metamorphosis-at which point the apical organ degenerates (Gifondorwa and Leise, 2006; Hinman et al., 2003; Nielsen, 2005b). Since Cnidaria are the sister group to Bilateria, their apical organs are particularly relevant for evolutionary comparisons (Hejnol et al., 2009; Philippe et al., 2009). Based on similarities in the genetic control of the development of the bilaterian anterior/apical pole and the aboral pole of Nematostella vectensis homology of these two domains has recently been proposed (Marlow et al., 2014; Santagata et al., 2012; Sinigaglia et al., 2013), suggesting that apical organs in a cnidarian and in bilaterians develop from homologous territories. However, these studies addressed the homology of the apical organ itself only to a very limited extent. Cnidarian apical organs with a ciliary tuft have only been identified in anthozoan, and not in medusozoan planulae. They have been described as a set of columnar cells with basal nuclei, with a cytoplasm filled with various undetermined vesicles, and an underlying plexus of neurites (Chia and Koss, 1979; Nakanishi et al., 2012) but, in contrast to bilaterians, distinct nerve cells associated with the apical organ have not been identified. In addition to the long cilia-bearing cells, the apical organ of N. vectensis contains two types of gland or secretory cells (Nakanishi et al., 2012). Clearly, the paucity of comparable morphological characters both in bilaterians and cnidarians complicates inferences about the homology of apical organs. Moreover, possible homologies may not be found at the level of the whole apical organ, but rather at the level of individual cell types (Arendt, 2008; Marlow et al., 2014) Accordingly, a molecular characterization of the cells constituting the apical organ is necessary in order to improve our understanding of this structure from both a functional and evolutionary perspective. Ideally, such a molecular characterization would include genes which control the development of the apical organ cells (i.e. signalling molecules and transcription factors), and genes that define specific cellular structures and processes (e.g. cytoskeletal components or metabolic genes).

We shall all see better." She removed the hat from a small head that was very prettily overgrown with brown, thick, cropped curls. The bright eyes with which she blinked at first in the strong sunlight were of the colour of the flying-ground before them: earth-brown and turf-green mixed. "I will hold your hat, since it is for me that you take him off," said the girl whom they called Baker. Her real name was Becker; Ottilie Becker. She worked at the German correspondence of that London office where the other two girls, Gwenna Williams and Mabel Butcher, were typists. It was one of the many small jokes of the place to allude to themselves as the Butcher, the Baker, and the Candlestick-maker. All three were excellent friends.... The other two scarcely realised that Gwenna, the Celt, was different from themselves; more absent-minded, yet more alive. A passer-by might have summed her up as "a pretty, commonplace little thing;" a girl like millions of others. But under the ready-made muslin blouse of that season's style there was ripening, all unsuspected, the dormant bud of Passion. This is no flower of the commonplace. And her eyes were full of dreams, innocent dreams. Some of them had come true already. For hadn't she broken away from home to follow them? Hadn't she left the valley where nothing ever went on except the eternal Welsh rain that blurred the skylines of the mountains opposite, and that drooped in curtains of silver-grey gauze over the slate roofs of the quarry-village, set in that brook-threaded wedge between wooded hillsides? Hadn't she escaped from that cage of a chapel house sitting-room with its kitchen-range and its many bookshelves and its steel print of John Bunyan and its maddening old grandfather-clock that always said half-pastt two and its everlasting smell of singeing hearthrug, and never a window open? Yes! she'd given her uncle-guardian no peace until he'd washed his hands over Gwenna's coming up to London. So here she was in London now, making fresh discoveries every day, and enjoying that mixture of drudgery and frivolling that makes up the life of the London bachelor-girl.

His face was covered by a thick, dark beard, which concealed his features. His clothes were worn out, and he carried a brace of revolvers, a bowie-knife, and a rifle. After sitting a few moments, he turned his horse back, and started slowly along the river-banks, keeping a sharp lookout. Presently he came to a halt again. He listened intently for a while, then threw himself down on the ground, and began to dig furiously. In a short time he uncovered a small tin box, containing some papers. Opening them, he found they contained a letter written in English. It was addressed to "Miguel de la Cruz," and signed "Rosa." The letter read as follows: - "DEAR MIGUEL: I am writing you this note, that you may know what has become of me, if ever you hear of my death. We are still in Arizona, but our money is all gone. Your father sold out last month, and we are living on the proceeds of the sale. All the rest we lost gambling. You know how reckless your brother is. Last night he gambled and lost every cent of the money. He did not want us to go without anything, so he gave us the money he won yesterday. This morning the cards went against him, and he lost it all. If he had not been generous, we would have enough to get through on till your return. Now we can hardly make it, unless you come soon. There is no use talking about going back. Our credit is all gone, and we cannot borrow another dollar. So we must stay here until you come. Do not forget us. Your loving sister, ROSA." The reader will observe that Miguel de la Cruz was a Spaniard, and the name of his brother was Antonio. The reader will also observe that the name of Rosa was Spanish. Miguel read the letter carefully, and then tore it into pieces, and put it into his pocket. He seemed much troubled, and finally mounted his horse, and rode slowly onward. At intervals he would stop and listen, and scan the country ahead. When he reached a certain point, he halted again. Here the river bent sharply round a high cliff, and ran almost parallel with itself for some distance. It was a fine spot for a camp. He tied his horse to a tree, and walked up to the top of the bluff, looking cautiously about him. Then he returned to the river, and took off his coat, and, folding it carefully, laid it down on the grass. Then he walked back to the bluff, and brought three heavy stones, which he placed upon his coat. This done, he pulled off his boots, and took his hat in his hand, and walked quickly into the river. He walked straight across to the opposite shore, swimming strongly, though he was encumbered with his clothes. Reaching the other side, he walked up the bank, and stood listening. Not hearing any noise, he walked back to the river, and climbed the bank. He stepped on his coat, and the stones fell into the river below. The coat was instantly inflated, and floated buoyantly on the surface of the water. Then Miguel walked swiftly down the river, and soon left the vicinity of the bluff behind him. He made his way cautiously along the banks of the stream, stopping frequently to look and listen. He traveled thus for two hours, when he arrived at a point where the river curved suddenly to the right, forming a deep bend.

In the end, I came away believing that almost everyone deserved to be there. But what I did not expect was the extent to which these men's humanity remained intact. They spoke with eloquence about their families, their faith and their hopes for the future. Even Fredrick Baer, who has spent much of his adult life in prison, spoke movingly about his love for his wife and children. He showed me pictures of his family and told me about his struggle to maintain contact with them. And although he described himself as a 'bad seed', he also talked about how much he loved his cat. He said: 'She is everything to me. She is my heart, soul and world.' A number of inmates said they hoped for redemption through God. One of the few women on Death Row told me she had found peace by forgiving her victim's family. Others believed they might eventually be exonerated. All of them seemed to want to believe they could somehow escape the system that had condemned them to die. Their resilience surprised me. After all, we tend to associate prisons with despair. The reality is very different. Prisons are full of hope, however misplaced. When I asked why he was still fighting for his freedom after 20 years behind bars, one inmate replied: 'Because I'm innocent!' Another told me: 'I'll tell you what I do know. I know I've got more time than anybody else in here.' These men and women are locked up but not locked down. They are allowed to read, watch television and listen to music. Many work in the prison laundry, library or kitchen. Some are studying for degrees, and several have started businesses selling goods made in prison to the outside world. In short, they are not living in isolation. I met one inmate who had a computer in his cell and another who had a guitar. I saw prisoners playing basketball and volleyball and going to church. They had friends and enemies. One inmate told me he was a 'snitch' because he was giving information to the authorities. I watched as other prisoners spat at him and threatened to kill him. Not only are they not isolated, but they are able to communicate with each other and with people on the outside. This means they can plan and organise. While I was there, the prison was put into lockdown following a riot. Inmates had seized control of parts of the facility, barricading themselves inside. They had set fire to mattresses and thrown furniture out of windows. They were demanding better food and threatening to burn down the whole prison unless their demands were met. The atmosphere in the prison was tense. Guards carried guns and wore body armour. One inmate told me that there were often fights between rival gangs. On one occasion, he said, three prisoners had died during a single incident. Another prisoner told me about being held hostage by armed robbers during a daring break-out attempt. Despite these dangers, the majority of inmates appeared relaxed. They knew I was making a programme and wanted to talk to me. One man, convicted of killing a police officer, told me he was planning to appeal against his conviction. He was convinced he was innocent. Another explained how he had become involved in crime after his father was killed in a drive-by shooting. He said he had no regrets about his actions. 'It's just what happens,' he shrugged. 'You're either a part of it or you're not.' The only person who seemed genuinely afraid was Fredrick Baer. He was concerned that someone would try to take revenge on him. He told me: 'There are certain things you don't talk about in prison.

We had been branded, scourged, starved, kept in darkness, loaded with irons, and treated worse than beasts. Some of them were mere boys, others gray-haired men, hardened criminals; while there were a few of better birth and education, whose faces showed traces of refinement. All were suffering from wounds, or the effects of ill-usage, and none of us had ever been permitted to see the light of day since being condemned to banishment. Yet, vile, hopeless wretches as we were, we felt the thrill of that fresh morning air sweeping up from the sea, and breathed it in deeply, with new life. Even the sight of those masts ahead gave promise of freedom, of escape, of a chance once again to fight for liberty. The very uncertainty of our future made us reckless, and we laughed and joked coarsely among ourselves as we tramped forward, cursing the guards and struggling desperately against our bonds. We were not Englishmen, most of us, but adventurers from every country of Europe, and our crimes were committed mostly aboard ship, or on the high seas. Not one of us would have hesitated to sell his soul to Satan if thereby he could have obtained release. The mere fact that we were about to be taken away from England, and placed beyond reach of the gallows, inspired hope. As we neared the dock, and could distinguish the outlines of the vessel awaiting us, the mob pressed closer, held in check by a cordon of soldiers, yet eager to get nearer, and howl derision at us. I could hear women shrieking insults, and the shrill cries of children, mingling with the hoarser yells of the men, and the curses of the sailors. Those waiting on the dock, already on board the vessel, were prisoners also, and as we came into view they broke into a wild uproar of welcome, shaking their chains defiantly above their heads, and shouting words of encouragement. I caught glimpses of white, pinched faces, and glaring eyes, and noted that nearly all were stripped to the waist, their bodies glistening in the sunlight. A sudden burst of cheering greeted our appearance, and we responded with a yell of defiance. Then the lines broke apart, the guards forming a hollow square about us, and we were driven roughly forward, stumbling over each other, and cursing loudly, to where a gang-plank led from the dock to the deck of a brigantine lying alongside. She was a trim craft enough, her yards squared, and pennants flying aloft, with a great press of seamen crowding her rails, and staring curiously at us. There was a hubbub of noise everywhere, the blare of trumpets, the rattle of drums, the shouts of officers, and the tread of hurrying feet. All around us, and out across the water, the ships lay thickly anchored, their decks black with people, and gay with fluttering colors. The scene was one of wild confusion, a babel of sounds, the air filled with dust, the heat almost unbearable.

Left an orphan at an early age, he had inherited a comfortable property and the income of a city block, and he spent the money judiciously, if lavishly. His Panhard was the swiftest car in town, as his offices were the most sumptuous, though ostentatiously simple in appointment. He had a Japanese valet, and the "at homes" which he occasionally gave in his bachelor apartment, though they might be dominated "pink teas" by the envious unbidden, were affairs to which an entree was a hallmark. He maintained also a shooting-box on an upper slope of the Blue Ridge - a comfortable bungalow set in a hundred acres of wilderness - whither of autumns he and a dozen other choice spirits were wont to fare for a fortnight's tramping and fishing, sleeping on pungent hemlock boughs and eating homely food cooked by the single negro servant who lived there as caretaker. He had a gift for private theatricals - he was in constant demand of the Amateur Dramatic Club - and had more than a dilettante appreciation of music and art. As regards his profession, he had injected into the somewhat cut-and-dried legal life of the old Capital an unusual and winning element of personality and a method at variance with established usage. His very eccentricities had set him apart from the mass, who were so glamoured with the sordid things of life; and the apparent contempt for material reward with which he defended poor and unknown clients as readily as rich and influential ones had its appeal to a class which possessed imagination and ideals. There had seldom been a case in which he had not successfully employed a curious subterranean logic - an apparently wilful insistence upon what seemed at first glance the unvital and immaterial - as a preliminary to a swift volte-face by which he turned the evidence at a new and unexpected angle of inference, and drove home the doubt with a brilliant display of oratory which captivated and - for the moment - convinced. In the four years in which he had stamped his individuality upon the town, not only had he never lost a criminal case, but he had created a certain conviction that a trial in which he figured would offer unmistakable elements of surprise and entertainment. So that the Criminal Court had come, in a way, to be the fashion, and the sombre chambers of justice saw many an assemblage that would have graced another sort of gathering. Seldom, however, on this day had Harry's glance through his gold-rimmed eye-glasses wandered to the benches. With many there he had danced and golfed and bridged a hundred times. That, however, had been play; this, which had come to furnish another and quite as fascinating a sort of entertainment for them, was what he had chosen to make the more serious business - in so far as anything had been serious to him - of his life.

I still have the disquieting fear that my uncle did not modify his opinion of me until I was thoroughly over being a senior. You will note that I do not say he changed his opinion. Modify is the word. His original estimate of me, as a freshman, of course, - was uttered when I, at the age of eighteen, picked out my walk in life, so to speak. After considering everything, I decided to be a literary man. A novelist or a playwright, I hadn't much of a choice between the two, or perhaps a journalist. Being a journalist, of course, was preliminary; a sort of makeshift. At any rate, I was going to be a writer. My Uncle Rilas, a hard-headed customer who had read Scott as a boy and the Wall Street news as a man, - without being misled by either, - was scornful. He said that I would outgrow it, there was some consolation in that. He even admitted that when he was seventeen he wanted to be an actor. There you are, said he! I declared there was a great difference between being an actor and being a writer. Only handsome men can be actors, while I - well, by nature I was doomed to be nothing more engaging than a novelist, who doesn't have to spoil an illusion by showing himself in public. Besides, I argued, novelists make a great deal of money, and playwrights too, for that matter. He said in reply that an ordinarily vigorous washerwoman could make more money than the average novelist, and she always had a stocking without a hole to keep it in, which was more to the point. Now that I come to think of it, it was Uncle Rilas who oracularly prejudged me, and not Uncle John, who was by way of being a sort of literary chap himself and therefore lamentably unqualified to guide me in any course whatsoever, especially as he had all he could do to keep his own wolf at bay without encouraging mine, and who, besides teaching good English, loved it wisely and too well. I think Uncle Rilas would have held Uncle John up to me as an example, - a scarecrow, you might say, - if it hadn't been for the fact that he loved him in spite of his English. He must have loved me in spite of mine. My mother felt in her heart that I ought to be a doctor or a preacher, but she wasn't mean: she was positive I could succeed as a writer if I set my mind to it. She was also sure that I could be President of the United States or perhaps even a Bishop. We were Episcopalian.

In May 2002, the then U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Disarmament Affairs, Jayantha Dhanapala, told the American Bar Association that WMD "today consist of nuclear, biological, and chemical arms - they all share one deadly trait: they are indiscriminately lethal." Dhanapala went on to say: "They are neither lightly nor inappropriately called 'weapons of mass destruction.'" Reichart and Carus said they had identified "more than 50 WMD definitions issued by a government or international organization." The definition in the U.S. Criminal Code included high explosives and was "inconsistent with most national guidance and with the usage preferred by the State Department and the international community," they said. "Almost all crimes" prosecuted under this definition could be prosecuted under other provisions of the U.S. criminal code, they suggested. Bombs, grenades, rockets "having a propellant charge of more than four ounces, a missile having an explosive or incendiary charge of more than one-quarter ounce" and mines, are among the explosives covered by the criminal code's definition of WMD. Robert Chesney - professor of law at University of Texas - said the statute Tsarnaev had been charged under - U.S. Code title 18, section 2332a - defined WMD "far more broadly than that phrase is normally understood." "At the bottom, it is simply a statute that makes it a felony to set off bombs in public places, which certainly applies in this case. Unless the government were to try to take advantage of the WMD language to try to convince the public that this defendant was using a WMD in the usual narrow and scary sense of that phrase, there's really no harm in the situation in my view," he said. Chesney noted that in order for a prosecution for using WMD within the United States to be successful, at least one of four conditions relating to interstate or foreign commerce also needed to be proved against the defendant. In the case of the Boston bombings "the easiest one to prove would be the impact-on-commerce condition - there's just no real doubt that the bombing had a tremendously disruptive impact on interstate commerce," he said. Harvard Law School's Alan Dershowitz told CNN'S Becky Anderson he was surprised the WMD charge had been used against Tsarnaev. "Everybody thought that the indictment would be under the federal terrorism statute," he said. "Instead they charged him under a very rarely used statute involving explosion of weapons of mass destruction that result in the death of an individual." Dershowitz said the charge put less emphasis on the intention behind the attack. "Under the terrorism statute, you would have to, in effect, charge a jihadist or extreme Islamic motivation. Here you don't have to show any motivation at all," he said.
