In understanding the intricacies of microbial fuel cells (MFCs), it becomes clear that the separation and optimization of the anode and cathode processes are paramount. The membrane serves as a crucial component when aiming for long-term stability and efficiency, despite its propensity to introduce heightened internal resistance. Advanced research has demonstrated that choosing an appropriate membrane material can mitigate these resistive losses while still ensuring effective compartmentalization and selective ion transport (Cheng et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2007). Nafion, a perfluorinated polymeric composite, has been extensively utilized because of its superior ionic conductivity and chemical resistance, although its high cost and susceptibility to biofouling remain challenges (Rozendal et al., 2008). Recent innovations are directed toward developing more cost-effective and robust alternatives, such as composite membranes and biopolymers, which promise lower environmental impact and enhanced fouling resistance (Liu et al., 2014a; Yuan et al., 2015). These advancements complement the evolution of microbial electrochemical technologies, which are increasingly integrating into a broader ecological and industrial framework. For example, MFCs stand at the forefront of waste-to-energy technologies, offering a dual solution of wastewater treatment and bioelectricity production (He et al., 2009; Pant et al., 2010). This aligns with the global mandate for sustainable development, as these systems not only reduce the carbon footprint but also potentially recover resources from waste streams (Kumar et al., 2013). To maximize the performance of MFCs, strategic inoculation with electroactive microbial communities is critical. The use of robust, electroactive bacterial strains, isolated from diverse environments, can greatly enhance power outputs (Choi et al., 2011; Kiely et al., 2011). These microbes facilitate efficient electron transfer processes at the anode, thriving in the metabolically diverse and dynamic milieu of the cell (Logan and Regan, 2006). Recent studies have highlighted genetic and metabolic engineering strategies to fine-tune and augment the electron transfer capabilities of these microorganisms (Lovley et al., 2008; Rabaey et al., 2004). Additionally, the scale-up of MFCs from laboratory prototypes to viable commercial systems necessitates addressing challenges related to hydraulic and operational scalability, economic viability, and system integration (Aelterman et al., 2006; Ieropoulos et al., 2010). Industrial applications often require bespoke designs tailored to specific waste characteristics and treatment requirements, demanding constant innovation in cell architecture, material science, and process engineering (Rabaey and Verstraete, 2005). Future directions in MFC research explore hybrid systems combining multiple bioelectrochemical processes, expanding the functional versatility of these technologies (Pant et al., 2011; Zhang and Angelidaki, 2014). Such integrations could potentially enable the simultaneous treatment of multiple types of waste or the recovery of diverse resources, thus broadening the applicability and environmental impact of MFCs. Conclusively, the progress in microbial fuel cell technologies reflects a broader shift towards sustainable, decentralized, and integrated systems for resource recovery and waste management. Continued interdisciplinary research and development will likely propel MFCs into mainstream utility, underlining the potential of bioelectrochemical systems as pivotal components of future green infrastructure (Logan et al., 2019). Looking ahead, concerted efforts in policy, academia, and industry are essential to cultivate the conditions conducive to the wide-scale adoption and adaptation of MFCs, ensuring a sustainable legacy for future generations.

To shed more light on the role of gold nanoclusters in cyclohexane oxidation, our group has conducted a systematic study on the size-dependent catalytic activity of Au nanoclusters supported on TiO2. We synthesized a series of Au nanoclusters with precise atomic numbers (n = 25, 38, 55, and 76) and characterized their structures using high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The catalytic performance of these nanoclusters was evaluated in the oxidation of cyclohexane to KA oil. Our results show a clear size-dependent trend in the catalytic activity, with the smallest nanoclusters (n = 25) exhibiting the highest activity and selectivity towards KA oil. The turnover frequency (TOF) of the Au25 nanoclusters was found to be 3.5 times higher than that of the Au76 nanoclusters. Furthermore, the selectivity towards KA oil increased from 85% to 95% as the nanocluster size decreased from 76 to 25 atoms. These findings suggest that the unique electronic structure and geometric properties of small Au nanoclusters play a crucial role in the catalytic oxidation of cyclohexane. To gain insight into the reaction mechanism, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations on the adsorption of cyclohexane and oxygen on the Au nanoclusters. The results indicate that the smaller nanoclusters have a higher binding energy for cyclohexane and oxygen, leading to an increased reaction rate. Additionally, the DFT calculations revealed that the Au25 nanoclusters have a higher density of states near the Fermi level, which facilitates the charge transfer between the reactants and the catalyst. The size-dependent catalytic activity of Au nanoclusters in cyclohexane oxidation has significant implications for the development of more efficient and selective catalysts for this reaction. The ability to control the size and structure of Au nanoclusters at the atomic level offers a new degree of freedom in catalyst design, enabling the optimization of catalytic performance for specific reactions. Further studies are needed to explore the potential of Au nanoclusters in other oxidation reactions and to develop a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms. However, the current results demonstrate the promise of atomically precise Au nanoclusters as a new generation of catalysts for sustainable chemical processes.

In our update in May 2018, we searched PsycINFO and Embase for randomised controlled trials published between June 12, 2012, and May 15, 2018, that reported on care home interventions targeting agitation for people with dementia of any severity and how to sustain an intervention, using the terms: (agitation OR restless* OR irrita* OR aggression OR "aberrant motor behav*" OR "psychomotor activity" OR "challenging behav*" OR pacing OR sundowning OR wander* OR "walking about" OR "safe walking") AND (dement* OR alzheimer OR "vascular dement*" OR "pick's disease" OR huntington OR creutzfeldt OR cjd OR binswanger OR lewy) AND ("randomised control* trial*" OR RCT"), with no language restrictions. Our search identified 49 trials, of which 16 measured agitation as an outcome. Three studies reported clinically significant reductions in agitation. Successful interventions were intensive and multicomponent. The first intervention comprised staff training, increased social interaction, antipsychotic review, physician review of medical history, all medications and physical examination, assessment of pain, a doctor and nurse-led reflective case conference developing individualised treatment plans using a problem-solving model and a 3 h educational lecture, and role play for 8-12 weeks. This intervention reduced agitation at the end of the intervention. The second intervention included training and support of care home staff by a physician and specialist nurse for two 4 h blocks on behavioural symptoms in dementia using standardised assessments, non-pharmacological and pharmacological interventions, case conferences using standardised case vignettes, and activities delivered twice per week by activity co-coordinators or occupational therapists, for residents not already attending. This intervention was effective at 10 months for agitation. The third intervention combined training for staff and managers in person-centred care and the promotion of tailored person-centred activities and social interactions by a psychologist or occupational therapist working in the home for a month. Further training was provided for two champions (one training day per month) with coaching, supervision, and regular review with the therapist during the 9 month period. The intervention also included, if appropriate, triggering doctor's review of antipsychotic medications, and for individuals who did not participate in activities, implementation of activities. This intervention was effective at 9 months. One intervention was costed, but no cost-effectiveness analyses were done and we identified no reports of intervention effects being sustained. A separate systematic review found that interventions were sustained by interactive training, individual staff support after group training, retention of training materials, incorporating interventions into routine care, and nearly all staff attending. Added value of this study Our Managing Agitation and Raising Quality of Life (MARQUE) intervention, which comprised six sessions of staff training, was less intensive than some multicomponent interventions that have had positive outcomes and was primarily delivered by non-clinical staff. The intervention did not reduce agitation or affect secondary outcomes.

The consultation room seemed to transform into a miniature battlefield where logic and emotions clashed. Dr. Godbole's manner was as brisk and thorough as a drill sergeant's, his words precise and deliberately constructed to fortify my understanding of the gravity of my situation. Each piece of paper represented a lifeline, the key to maintaining a semblance of normalcy amidst this medical upheaval. I scribbled notes frantically, trying not to let the cascade of information drown me. "Remember," he emphasized, locking eyes with me as if to ensure the gravity of his message penetrated the fog of my apprehension, "Your pancreas has effectively resigned. It's now your responsibility to manage what it no longer can." The words landed with a thud. This was no temporary affliction but a lifelong companion, tethered to me like an invisible shadow. I fought back rising despair, knowing it served no productive end. The focus had to be on strategy, adaptation, and resilience. He explained basal-bolus insulin regimes, the intricacies of blood glucose monitoring, the vital importance of maintaining stable sugar levels to avoid both the pitfall of hyperglycemia and the sudden plummet into hypoglycemia. What astounded me was his ability to forecast the emotional phases I would traverse-denial, frustration, acceptance-as though he had watched this same play unfold countless times before. "You must allow yourself patience," he advised, not unkindly, "patience to adjust and patience to learn. Your life is no longer about avoidance, but adaptation." In those hours, under harsh fluorescent lights, I was initiated into a world of relentless vigilance. Diabetes demanded attentiveness, a constant dialogue with one's own physiology-meals transformed into calculated decisions, physical activity into a factor to be meticulously synced with insulin doses. Dr. Godbole guided me through self-injection techniques, correcting my novice clumsiness with rare patience and mechanical precision. Each successful practice shot emboldened me, as if mastering the needle was a small victory over the unruly tide of uncertainty. As I left his office, my mind swirled with the information imparted, yet amidst the chaos dwelled a burgeoning resolve. Life in Colorado awaited, a place as foreign as the tasks now at hand, but also a canvas for a newer, stronger self to emerge. I would board the plane armed with insulin, meters, and an emerging understanding of dietary algebra, but what I clung to most was a shard of hope, polished through the hard edges of a reality I was learning to own. Outside, the January air was cold but invigorating, filling my lungs with a bracing reminder that life continued unabated. As I walked away from Dr. Godbole's office, his words echoed-a reminder that control, though elusive, was a pursuit worthy of every effort. The endeavor around mastery over this unpredictable companion was now my singular focus as I set my sights toward the impending journey, determined to navigate the throes of change with tenacity and fortitude.

The study of TRD can be traced back to a 1962 pioneered work on energy balance (Monteith and Szeicz, 1962). Further in time, the concern moved progressively to the area of thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing applications, like the assessment of directional variability of TIR radiance for various vegetation canopies (Kimes et al., 1980). In the last 40 years, several models have been proposed to simulate the directional brightness temperature (DBT) distribution or LSE distribution over different surfaces. Usually, these surfaces were assumed to be unique thematic surfaces. More recently, the DBT distribution of mixed pixels has been addressed (Cao et al., 2015; Shi, 2011). The TRD models were aimed at mimicking the observed thermal radiance with consideration of canopy structure, component emissivities and temperatures, and energy budget processes. For inland water bodies (3.56% of land surface, according to FROM-GLC dataset (Gong et al., 2013)), barren lands (16.51% of land surface) (Garcia-Santos et al., 2012; Sobrino and Cuenca, 1999), and snow and ice (12.81% of land surface) (Cheng et al., 2010b), most of the models are trying to simulate the emissivity directionality, as this is the main source of directional effects on LST over relatively homogeneous surfaces. The structure of such surfaces is simpler when compared with those of vegetation and urban surfaces. The TRD attributed to emissivity is also a main concern for sea surfaces (Masuda et al., 1988; Wu and Smith, 1997). Although the proportion of urban landscapes is the smallest (0.66% of land surface), many models were developed to simulate the urban surface DBT (Fontanilles et al., 2008; Lagouarde et al., 2010) because the thermal environment directly links to the human life in cities, where an increasing larger share of the world's population now resides More DBT models have been developed for vegetation canopies (including croplands, forests, grasslands, and shrub lands), which cover 64.72% of the world land surface (see the review by Sobrino et al., 2005). These models can be classified into four main categories: 1) radiative transfer models (RTM), such as S&WVM (Snyder and Wan, 1998), FRA1997 (Francois et al., 1997), FRA2002 (Francois, 2002), REN2015 (Ren et al., 2015a), CE-P (Cao et al., 2018b) and 4SAIL (Verhoef et al., 2007). 2) geometric optical models (GOM), such as MGP (Pinheiro et al., 2004; Rasmussen et al., 2010). 3) hybrid model (HM), such as SLEC (Du et al., 2007). 4) 3D models, such as DART (Gastellu-Etchegorry et al., 2017) and TRGM (Liu et al., 2007).

Continuing this journey across the great lakes of North America, we draw nearer to the heart of the British Canadian territories, meandering through landscapes resplendent with natural grandeur. Beyond Lake Erie, as our course flows steadily onward, the waters find their way into the picturesque Lake Ontario, crafting a path through the renowned Niagara River, where the cascading falls roar tirelessly in a spectacle of mist and thunder, rivaled by few other natural wonders. Here, the land speaks a language older than the colonial claim, murmuring through leaves and streams the tales of peoples long past. Upon leaving the magnificent splendor of these cascades, the river narrows, drawing us into the embrace of Lake Ontario's expansive stretch, a jewel among the constellation of lakes guarding the eastern approaches of Canada. It is in these waters that the St. Lawrence River gathers its force, gradually swelling as it courses onward, embracing tributaries and ferrying forth the histories of lands touched by its flow. The banks of the St. Lawrence, dotted with settlements burgeoning with the resilience of frontier life, offer a juxtaposition of wild beauty and burgeoning civilization. As we retrace our path from the farthest reaches of Michilimackinac towards the more charted territories along the St. Lawrence, our narrative soon veers toward the cities that have sprung along these lifelines of water. Kingston, a sentinel at the eastern tip of Lake Ontario, greets navigators with its storied fortifications and echoes of past skirmishes, standing proudly as a testament to a colonial past. Its streets carry whispers of strategies deliberated and alliances forged, hallmarks of a time when the canvas of the continent was yet being painted in broad strokes of destiny. My suspicions are directed towards this man Hammerton." "Towards Captain Hammerton!" I repeated in amazement; "why? What possible motive could he have to open this despatch-box?" "I'll tell you afterwards," he answered abruptly. "Here is something for you to read meanwhile," and he handed me a thick blue envelope, stamped with the Privy Council Seal. It contained a copy of a report made by the Military Attache to the English Embassy at Vienna, who, having received information through the Austrian Secret Service Bureau, communicated with Sir Philip Emden, asking whether he desired further investigation. The reply was affirmative, whereupon the Vienna authorities gave their consent to the transmission of an agent to Berne, where the matter was found to have its origin. The document, therefore, was forwarded direct from the Austrian Minister at Bern to Sir Philip Emden, at Berlin, and thence to London. It ran as follows: - To His Excellency the Ambassador of Great Britain at Berlin. Sir, - I have the honour to inform Your Excellency that, according to information recently obtained by the Imperial and Royal Secret Service Bureau here, a certain person named Robert Zilcher, now residing in Switzerland, was, during the latter part of the year 1880, employed as confidential clerk in the offices of Herr von Schiller, then Secretary of the German Embassy in Paris. During the years 1879-80, Herr von Schiller acted as intermediary between the French Government and the Russian Grand Duke Alexis Michaelovitch, and was entrusted by the former with the conveyance of important secret documents to the Grand Duke. These communications were always transmitted to him by M. de Seze, formerly First Secretary of the French Embassy at Berlin, and subsequently First Secretary of the French Embassy at St Petersburg. He, however, soon became aware that the German Government were cognisant of his connection with the Grand Duke, and, consequently, that he was being watched, and, fearing discovery, resigned his post at the Embassy, and took up his abode at Lucerne, where he remained until his death, which occurred in March, 1892. In the autumn of 1881, owing to his dissatisfaction with his position, Herr von Schiller applied for and obtained leave of absence for three months, and proceeded to Paris, ostensibly for the purpose of purchasing books for the German Library at Berlin, but really with the object of arranging matters with the Grand Duke. On arriving at Paris, he called upon M. de Seze, and, on showing him a letter from the Grand Duke, stating that he had received a communication from the Emperor Alexander III., intimating that he wished to confer with him personally, requested M. de Seze to forward the same to him at Berlin, which request was complied with. Herr von Schiller left Paris shortly afterwards, and returned to Berlin. Shortly prior to his departure from Paris, Herr von Schiller had become acquainted with a young lady named Henrietta Mary Fox, the daughter of Mr John Fox, a retired merchant, living at No. 4 Rue de la Ville-l'Eveque, Paris, and, as she was considered by her father to be somewhat imprudent, he consented to her marriage with Herr von Schiller, which took place in September, 1881. The couple resided together in Paris for several weeks, and during this time Herr von Schiller frequently met M. de Seze, who, having become suspicious of him, informed Baron de Tschudi, then Counsellor of the Austro-Hungarian Legation at Paris, of all he knew concerning him.

It was Tanya, calling from her hotel room to say hello, to ask where I was, and then to tell me where to find her. A few minutes later I was standing before her, holding her close and breathing in her scent, telling her how happy I was to see her. And now I'm sitting here in my hotel room, the sun gone, the day dimming, the weather turning cold again. In a few short hours I will meet with my editor and we will discuss the book, the process of making it happen. Then we will eat dinner and talk more, and then tomorrow I will sit down with my laptop and write. And on Sunday morning I will leave this place and fly back home, back to the land of dreams and nightmares, back to the land of the living dead. 28 May 2004 My flight leaves in less than twenty-four hours and I have yet to pack anything. This is not unusual for me, but it does seem odd, given that I have been thinking about packing since yesterday afternoon. I have a lot of stuff here, a lot of clothes, books, magazines, CDs, DVDs, all sorts of things. All the things that fill my life, all the things that define me, all the things that make me feel whole, are sitting here around me, mocking me. They want to come with me, they want to get packed into suitcases, they want to be crammed into backpacks, they want to go on tour with me, they want to come along for the ride. They want to be on stage with me, they want to be the voice of my poetry, they want to be heard by others, they want to become a part of something bigger, they want to be immortalized. They want to live forever. But I canot take them all with me. I cannot carry everything with me. I cannot bring every single thing that makes me me with me, and I cannot allow myself to be defined by the things I bring with me. So I must choose carefully, I must select only those items which are important to me, those items which I need to survive, and those items which I want to share with others. Those items which I want to give to others. There are many things that I have here, many things that I have acquired over the years, things that I have collected, things that I have bought, things that I have received, things that I have stolen. These things, these objects, these artifacts, these treasures, these memories, they all represent me, they all show who I am, they all show the history of my life, they all show what I value. Some of them are beautiful, some of them are ugly. Some of them are worthless, some of them are priceless. Some of them are old, some of them are new. Some of them are mine, some of them belong to others. Some of them are made of wood, some of them are made of plastic. Some of them are made of metal, some of them are made of stone. Some of them are sharp, some of them are dull. Some of them are strong, some of them are fragile. Some of them are heavy, some of them are light. Some of them are useful, some of them are useless. Some of them are clean, some of them are dirty. Some of them are full, some of them are empty. Some of them are wet, some of them are dry. Some of them are hot, some of them are cold. Some of them are broken, some of them are fixed. Some of them are dead, some of them are alive.

Xu et al. [23] fabricated a reusable glass capillary device by assembling glass capillaries and needles in a three-dimensional printed holder. These devices were designed for generating simple emulsions, but not complex multiple emulsions. Here we present a novel design of a reusable glass capillary device that can be assembled and disassembled without the use of adhesives. The device consists of four coaxially arranged glass capillaries, which can be used as an assembly tool for other applications requiring precise alignment of small objects. It can be easily cleaned and reused after each experiment. We demonstrate its performance by producing double emulsions using water and liquid paraffin as dispersed phases and Span(R) 80 dissolved in hexadecane as continuous phase. The glass capillary device was made of four borosilicate glass capillaries (Fig. 1b). The first capillary (outer diameter: 0.7 mm; length: 100 mm) had one end tapered to an inner diameter of ~30 1/2m using a pipette puller (P-97 Flaming/Brown Micropipette Puller, Sutter Instrument Co., USA), while the second capillary (outer diameter: 0.7 mm; length: 50 mm) was tapered to an inner diameter of ~200 1/2m. The third capillary (outer diameter: 0.3 mm; length: 25 mm) was inserted into the second capillary, while the fourth capillary (outer diameter: 0.7 mm; length: 150 mm) was inserted into the first capillary. All capillaries were purchased from Hilgenberg GmbH, Germany. The capillaries were cleaned with acetone, rinsed with deionised water, dried with nitrogen gas, and stored in a dust-free environment until needed. The first capillary was glued onto a microscope slide (76 * 26 * 1 mm) using UV-curable adhesive (Norland Optical Adhesive 81, Norland Products Inc., USA) and cured under UV lamp (365 nm wavelength, 8 W power, Thorlabs Inc., USA) for 10 min. The second capillary was then inserted into the first capillary so that it protruded approximately 300 1/2m out of the tip of the first capillary and held in place by friction. The third capillary was inserted into the second capillary and the fourth capillary was inserted into the first capillary. Finally, a 27-gauge needle (BD PrecisionGlide cent, Becton Dickinson, USA) was connected to the third capillary using Tygon tubing (Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics, France). Figure 1. Schematic diagram of (a) conventional glass capillary device and (b) novel glass capillary device. To prepare double emulsions, water (deionised water, VWR International Ltd., UK) was injected through the fourth capillary, liquid paraffin (Sigma-Aldrich Company Ltd., Ireland) was delivered through the third capillary, and hexadecane (Sigma-Aldrich Company Ltd., Ireland) containing 5 wt% sorbitan monooleate (Span(R) 80, Sigma-Aldrich Company Ltd., Ireland) was injected through the second capillary. The capillaries were connected to syringe pumps (NE-4000 Programmable Syringe Pump, New Era Pump Systems Inc., USA) via Teflon(R) PFA tubing (Cole-Parmer Instrument Company Ltd., UK).

Somerset watches from a distance, his eyes narrowed as Mills, now composed but still visibly seething, secures the second thug in the back seat of the car. Mills shuts the door with a grim finality and leans against the battered vehicle, wiping a hand across his brow as if trying to erase the encounter from memory. Somerset approaches cautiously, the gravel crunching beneath his well-worn shoes. There's a moment of silence between them, the air thick with unspoken questions. Mills meets Somerset's gaze, a reluctant camaraderie forming in the shared understanding of what's just transpired. Without a word, Somerset nods, as if acknowledging the necessity of Mills' violent actions. "Think these guys have learned their lesson?" Somerset asks, breaking the silence. His tone is dry, but there's a faint hint of wry humor. Mills shrugs, casting a glance toward the thugs, now unconscious and crumpled inside the car. "Doubt it," he replies, crossing his arms. "But I didn't really give them much choice." Somerset lets out a low chuckle, shaking his head. "You always did have a way with people," he observes, patting Mills on the shoulder with a certain rough fondness. The camaraderie, though tinged with violence, offers a sense of belonging in this chaotic setting. The wind picks up, rustling through the nearby trees, stirring the loose leaves that gather by the roadside. There's something oddly calming about it, a reminder that life revolves outside the violence and the uneasy dealings with unscrupulous men. "So, what's the plan now?" Somerset inquires, redirecting the conversation to more pressing matters. "We can't just leave them here." Mills nods slowly, eyes drifting toward the horizon where the sun is beginning its slow descent. "We take them to the station," he decides aloud, his voice firm with resolve. "Let them sleep it off in a cell. Maybe they'll think twice before pulling another stunt like this." There's no disagreement from Somerset, whose own experiences lend him a cynical understanding of human nature. Partial redemption through hard-earned lessons-or lack thereof-is a theme all too familiar in their line of work. They both move with a practiced efficiency, loading into the car. Somerset takes the wheel, and Mills settles into the passenger seat, glancing back at the thugs one last time with a weary sigh. It's not the first time they've found themselves in such a situation, and it certainly won't be the last. Yet, it somehow still feels surreal-like an out-of-body experience lived through gritted teeth and adrenaline. As the car rumbles into motion, the rhythmic hum of the engine complements the steady beats of Mills' heart, letting the adrenaline slowly ebb away. Somerset navigates the winding streets, the town bathed in the late afternoon glow, shadows growing long and ominous around them. For a brief moment, there's peace in the shared silence, much more profound than any conversation could offer. The sun casts its fading light through the windshield, a warm farewell to the day's tumult. Mills leans back against the seat, content to let Somerset steer them into a yet uncertain future, guided only by the unwavering resolve that the right thing is never easy, but always necessary.

Larry was, I must own, as odd-looking an individual as ever played the part of valet. His shock head of hair was unacquainted with comb or brush; his grey coat reached to his calves; his breeches were open at the knees; his green waistcoat, too short to reach the latter garment, was buttoned awry; huge brogues encased his feet, and a red handkerchief, big enough to serve as the royal of a frigate, was tied loosely round his neck. He stood waiting for further orders, when the major, turning round to take a sip of coffee, by a sign bade him begone, and he vanished. Major McMahon, my mother's uncle, was an old officer, who, having seen much service for the better part of half a century, - his sword being his only patrimony, - on retiring from the army had come to live with us at Castle Ballinahone when I was a mere slip of a boy. Knowing the world well, - having been taught prudence by experience, though he had never managed to save any of his pay or prize-money, and was as poor as when he first carried the colours, - he was of the greatest service to my father, who, like many another Irish gentleman of those days, knew nothing of the world, and possessed but a small modicum of the quality I have mentioned. The major, seeing the way matters were going at Castle Ballinahone, endeavoured to set an example of sobriety to the rest of the establishment by abstaining altogether from his once favourite beverage of rum shrub and whisky punch, although he had a head which the strongest liquor would have failed to affect, and he was therefore well able to manage everything on the estate with prudence, and as much economy as the honour of the family would allow. My father was an Irish gentleman, every inch of him. He delighted to keep up the habits and customs of the country, which, to say the best of them, were not calculated to serve his own interests or those of his family.

Of course they were not expensive, since the Queen had so many, but still they cost enough to make Rosa Merry quite rich. As for the Kimble boys, they were as gay and jolly as the girls. Every morning at daybreak they would start out from the castle gate with their baskets of buttons and cry: "Buttons, Buttons!" So loud and shrill was their call that it echoed far across the fields and brought every Gilliken farmer running to buy buttons. For Kinda Jolly sold only the best buttons and never took more than two bits for a basket full. It was hard work, this gathering buttons in the fields and pastures and along the roadsides, but the boys loved it, and always came back laughing and singing merrily. "Buttons, Buttons, and nothing else," cried the Kimble boys, and none of the farmers ever bought anything else. One day Kinda Jolly called his court together and said solemnly: "My dear people, my castle is too small for me." The people murmured, for they knew how fond Kinda Jolly was of his castle. "I must build another castle," continued the King. "This is a great mistake," remarked the Prime Minister, a solemn fellow named Pompous. "You are getting old, Sire," observed the Captain of the Guard, a pompous person named General Guffaw. "You need rest and quiet," added the Royal Tutor, a pompous gentleman named Professor Sniffle. "We will build a second castle, and I shall retire there," declared Kinda Jolly, paying no attention to these remarks. "It will take a year or more to find the right place for such a building." "Oh, let us stay here," cried the Princesses and Princes. But Kinda Jolly shook his head. "The castle must be near the sea," he decided. "Yes, yes! We'll go to the sea shore!" shouted the children. "Then we shall see ships and boats and sailors, and learn how to swim," cried the Princesses and Princes. "And we shall catch fish," said the Kimble Boys. "And grow fruit and vegetables," said the Kimble Girls. "And gather shells," cried the little ones. "And eat ice cream," said the big ones. "All those things and more, my dears," promised Kinda Jolly. "But what about me?" asked Rosa Merry, coming in at that moment. "Don't I count?" "Of course you do, darling," answered Kinda Jolly. "How would you like to live beside the sea?" "I'd love it," replied Rosa Merry, clapping her hands. "Then we're all agreed," announced Kinda Jolly. "Let us move to the sea shore." "I'm sure we'll enjoy ourselves," said the Queen, smiling happily. "Well, well, well!" grumbled General Guffaw. "What next?" "I don't know why you want to leave your own country," complained the Prime Minister. "There are no mountains nor rivers nor deserts here," said the Royal Tutor. "Just button woods and button hills and button streams," laughed Kinda Jolly. "True; true; but there are no foreign countries to visit," objected the Prime Minister. "That is just what we want," cried Kinda Jolly, impatiently. "We are tired of visiting other countries. Let us build our castle on the edge of the Great Gulf and keep our treasures safe forever." "How nice!" cried the Queen.

Wood ants (Formica rufa), when far from a goal, use landmarks like beacons, or divert around them, or use them to inform directional choices (Graham et al., 2003). They typically follow a sequence of visual landmark memories to find their way between the nest and a foraging area according to their feeding state (fed or unfed) (Harris et al., 2005). Previous studies have examined the impact of removing certain landmarks, with for example the removal of trees affecting the natural visual environment (Narendra and Ramirez-Esquivel, 2017). Sequential landmark retrieval can be understood as operating within a mechanism of panoramic image matching, whereby ants move to fit a memorised 2D image of the goal's surroundings to their current view (Lent et al., 2010; Woodgate et al., 2016). This image matching process can be understood as operating like a terrestrial visual compass (Graham et al., 2010; Zeil, 2012). The navigation literature has tended to discuss edge following, proximal landmarks, visual beacons, and distant panorama as distinct sources of navigational information and hence navigational strategies. However, recognition of the panoramic surround can be understood as a navigation strategy which aggregates all of these informational sources both near and far. Indeed, evidence suggests that for insects with relatively poor visual resolution, like the Temnothorax ants studied here (Ramirez-Esquivel et al., 2017), the ability to isolate landmarks from the rest of the scene may be both lacking and functionally unnecessary (see for example studies of the Australian desert ant Melophorus bagoti, (Wystrach et al., 2011b; Schultheiss et al., 2016)). Therefore, the influence of similar or dissimilar landmarks is perhaps most likely to be through its impact on a navigating ant's perception of the panoramic surround. One scenario where visual navigation can be of critical importance for animals is in the emigration to a new nest site. In the case of T. albipennis ants emigrating to a new nest, the goal orientation of the ants is clear: toward the new nest and away from the old one. Therefore, as in the studies of Pratt et al and McLeman et al (Pratt et al., 2001; McLeman et al., 2002) the emigration procedure of the ants is an excellent opportunity to observe how the ants make use of multiple visual landmarks in their visual panoramas. When T. albipennis has learnt a route toward a new nest using a horizontal landmark to guide its way toward the goal, it stays a constant distance from the wall as it walks along by maintaining it at a persistent retinal position. This has been demonstrated by raising the wall, inducing the ants to shift away from it (because it appears bigger, or closer) and lowering the wall, inducing a shift toward it (because it appears smaller, or further away) (Pratt et al., 2001).

These changes to the Earth's surface and subsurface have been driven by a range of anthropogenic processes, including the extraction and use of natural resources, the construction of infrastructure, and the alteration of ecosystems. For example, the widespread deforestation and land degradation that has occurred in many parts of the world has led to increased soil erosion, landslides, and flooding (Liu et al., 2014). Similarly, the extraction of groundwater and fossil fuels has caused subsidence and sinkholes, while the construction of dams and reservoirs has altered river flows and increased the risk of flooding (Kundzewicz et al., 2014). The impact of human activity on the Earth's systems is not limited to these direct effects. Human-induced climate change has also led to changes in the frequency and intensity of natural hazards, such as heatwaves, droughts, and storms (IPCC, 2013). For example, a study by Mora et al. (2013) found that the frequency and duration of heatwaves are increasing in many parts of the world, with significant impacts on human health and ecosystems. In addition to these changes, human activity has also led to the creation of new hazards, such as the risk of oil spills and chemical leaks from infrastructure (Gao et al., 2016). The construction of pipelines and other infrastructure has also increased the risk of subsidence and sinkholes (Gao et al., 2016). Furthermore, the extraction of minerals and other resources has led to the creation of new hazards, such as the risk of mine collapses and landslides (Kumar et al., 2014). The interactions between human-induced hazards and natural hazards are complex and multifaceted. For example, the construction of infrastructure in flood-prone areas can increase the risk of flooding, while the extraction of groundwater can lead to subsidence and sinkholes (Gao et al., 2016). Similarly, the alteration of ecosystems can lead to changes in the frequency and intensity of natural hazards, such as landslides and floods (Liu et al., 2014). In this paper, we will examine the interactions between human-induced hazards and natural hazards in a multi-hazard context. We will focus on the intra-and inter-actions within and between natural hazards and anthropogenic processes, and discuss the implications of these interactions for disaster risk assessment and management. We will also examine the role of human-induced climate change in shaping the frequency and intensity of natural hazards, and discuss the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between human and natural systems.

The darkness of the cellar seemed to loom around them like a thick cloak, smothering the faint glow of the lamp in a blanket of stifling air. "Why must we always come to this dreadful place? I refuse to let these vermin rule my kitchen!" She straightened herself, attempting to regain some semblance of dignity, brushing off imaginary dirt from her immaculate frock, her expression a mixture of annoyance and exasperation. Marianna, her maid, watched without a trace of sympathy etched onto her face, offering a grin that seemed cruel in its amusement. "Would it not be better to find fresh cabbage than to rummage around this odorous pit? Perhaps one of the neighbors would lend us a few heads? Surely no one's cooking on such a wretched evening." But Mrs. Tiralla's fierce spirit returned, fueled by indignation. "No! I need that cabbage, and I require it now! I won't be bested by a few scuttling pests!" With a defiant snort, her the glare transformed the darkness surrounding her into something manageable, something she could conquer. But with each creak of the old wooden stairs above, Mrs. Tiralla's resolve began to wane. To distract herself, she turned her attention back to the cellar, its secrets and shadows beckoning her with an unwholesome allure. Each of the wretched items stored there had a story, a rekindling of the vivid past of her family. She leaned against the cool stone wall and mused aloud, "This house has stood for generations-yet it remains locked in this disrepair. Would my ancestors be proud of their lineage, huddled amongst such filth?" "Maybe they'd be pleased, Pani," Marianna suggested with a hint of malice, "to see their descendants keeping this charming mess intact." "But one must admit, the rats may truly be distasteful, but they do seem to know how to survive in places where you and I dare not tread." Just as her fingers brushed against the aged surface of the cabbage tub, a sudden skittering sound broke the silence, harsh and jarring. Mrs. Tiralla's heart lurched. "Marianna! Did you hear that?" Her voice was now a mere whisper, the hint of panic returning with a vengeance. Stationary video cameras have consequently illuminated the previously unknown, yet crucial functional roles of species that tend to be rare in visual surveys (Hoey and Bellwood, 2009; Plass-Johnson et al., 2015). Conventional reef status assessments thus risk providing a superficial level of information that does not convey functionality and ecosystem robustness, and hence may not provide enough support for adaptive management decisions. Essentially, although conventional measures of abundance can provide an idea of the system's current state, they do not consider whether the system is most likely to improve or deteriorate over time and overlook important components of system resilience. The likelihood of coral reefs changing over time and in response to disturbances is a product of many factors. In an attempt to improve predictions of these complex systems, several important ecological processes have been identified and alternative monitoring tools proposed (e.g. McClanahan et al., 2012). Benthic assessments are increasingly encouraged to consider more dynamic indicators that respond quickly to changes and drive system resilience, such as coral recruitment success, turf height and coral-algal interactions (Anthony et al., 2015; Flower et al., 2017). Furthermore, conventional benthic monitoring often applies broad categories such as 'dead coral' or 'rock' to describe seemingly 'free space' in the reef available for colonisation, while in reality very little space is actually free of benthic organisms. Rather, such substrate tends to be overgrown by a diverse assortment of early colonisers such as turf algae, benthic cyanobacteria or crustose coralline algae, which differ in their suitability for stony coral larvae to settle and survive, but are often not adequately captured in monitoring. To evaluate settlement dynamics on free space, hereon referred to as biotic substrate colonisation, surveys would benefit from refining the level of detail in which different benthic categories (e.g. algal turfs, crustose coralline algae, cyanobacterial mats) are recorded. One of the fastest colonisers of available substrates are algal turfs (Diaz-Pulido and McCook, 2002), yet their cover and intrinsic properties are often neglected in surveys (Harris, 2015; Flower et al., 2017). While algal turf cover itself may not be very informative, it can be a strong predictor of coral recruitment and subsequent development when combined with turf height (Birrell et al., 2005; Mumby et al., 2013). For coral reef fish communities, efforts are increasingly invested towards monitoring key functional groups separately (Green and Bellwood, 2009) and quantifying herbivory (Fox and Bellwood, 2008; Rasher et al., 2013). Spatial, temporal and surveyor-related discrepancies, as well as differential species wariness (Kulbicki, 1998), imply that visual fish biomass surveys should be supported by: (i) remote video surveys, and (ii) parameters that reflect longer-term fish functions. The latter can include algal traits and prey behaviours in response to predatory fish (e.g. Vermeij et al., 2015). Here we evaluate the effectiveness of local management using conventional reef status metrics in combination with a set of complementary metrics that have implications for system resilience.

Moreover, modularity analyses make it possible to identify the brain connector hubs, i.e. the regions that are responsible for the integration of the activity of different modules, and to assess the effects of disease on these hubs (van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013; Crossley et al., 2014). Indeed, there is growing evidence that abnormalities in nodes characterized by high topological centrality and connectivity are implicated in several neuropsychiatric disorders, and that connector hubs may present increased vulnerability to brain disease (Crossley et al., 2014). Several studies have investigated the modular structure of resting state functional connectivity networks derived from functional MRI in schizophrenia patients compared to healthy controls (Alexander-Bloch et al., 2010; Alexander-Bloch et al., 2013; van den Heuvel et al., 2010; Fornito et al., 2012; Lo et al., 2015; Lerman-Sinkoff and Barch, 2016; Yu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2008). Reduction in Modularity, a measure of segregation of functional modules within an integrated network, was found in Childhood Onset Schizophrenia (Alexander-Bloch et al., 2010). However, no strong evidence of group differences in the dispersion and structure of brain modules was found in that study (Alexander-Bloch et al., 2010). Reduced Modularity was associated with a proportional increase in inter-cluster edges and decrease in intra-cluster edges in patients (Alexander-Bloch et al., 2012). Lerman-Sinkof et al. (Lerman-Sinkoff and Barch, 2016) reported similar modular structures in adult schizophrenia patients and healthy subjects under stringent control of potential sources of imaging artifacts, with small but significant alterations of node community membership in specific patient networks. Yu et al. (2012) found reduced overall connectivity strength and a larger, even though very limited, number of communities in the patients' group (6 in SCZ subjects vs 5 in healthy controls). Disturbances in modularity were also observed in subjects with 22q11.2 deletion, a condition associated with cognitive impairment and high risk of developing schizophrenia (Scariati et al., 2016). These pioneering investigations provide important indications that the strength of division of resting-state functional connectivity networks into modules may be altered in patients affected by schizophrenia. However, the partitions per se, i.e. the clustering of different brain regions into modules, appear very coarse, comprising only a few, broad modules that are similarly distributed in patients and controls. Hence, it remains unclear whether schizophrenia affects specific functional modules and how defective connectivity translates into cognitive dysfunction and other symptoms. Graph theory as applied to the study of brain networks is still in its infancy, and several methodological and conceptual issues that are still open may have affected early studies. An important finding in complex network theory is that most community detection methods, like those applied in previous studies in schizophrenia patients, suffer from a resolution limit (Fortunato and Barthelemy, 2007), as they cannot resolve clusters of nodes that are smaller than a scale determined by the size of the entire network.

I was hurrying to catch up on my tasks, trying to make up for lost time, when I tripped on a stray pallet in the stockroom. My ankle twisted in an awkward angle, and I felt a sharp pain shooting through my leg. I let out a loud "Ow!" as I hobbled to the nearest shelf to grab onto it for support. My friend, who was nearby, rushed over to help me, asking if I was okay. I nodded, trying to brush it off, but he could see the pain etched on my face. He offered to get me some ice, and I gratefully accepted. As I sat on the floor, elevating my ankle and icing it, I couldn't help but think about how this was not the first time this had happened. I've sprained my ankle so many times, I've lost count. It's like my ankles are made of glass or something. My friend came back with some ice wrapped in a towel and handed it to me. I thanked him and began to gingerly apply it to my ankle, wincing at the initial cold shock. The rest of my shift was a blur. I hobbled around, trying to do my tasks while favoring my injured ankle. My friend helped me out as much as he could, but I still had to do some heavy lifting (literally). By the time my shift ended, I was exhausted and in pain. I clocked out and hobbled out of the store, grateful to be going home. As I walked home, I couldn't help but think about how this was going to affect my plans for the rest of the weekend. I was supposed to go to the picnic tomorrow, but now I wasn't so sure. I didn't want to be a burden to anyone, and I didn't want to risk making my ankle worse. I sent a text to the person organizing the picnic, apologizing and explaining my situation. They were understanding, but I still felt bad about it. When I got home, I collapsed onto my bed, exhausted. I elevated my ankle and continued to ice it, hoping that it would heal quickly. I spent the rest of the evening watching TV and feeling sorry for myself. I was supposed to be having a fun weekend, but instead, I was stuck at home with a sprained ankle. Oh well, at least I had my music to keep me company. I put on some "U Got It Bad" by Usher and let the smooth melodies soothe my pain.

But with Slack, they've finally hit the jackpot. And it's not hard to see why. The company's offices in San Francisco's financial district are a hive of activity, with rows of desks stretching as far as the eye can see, each one cluttered with laptops, notebooks, and the occasional yellow emoji balloon. The atmosphere is lively, with the sound of chatter and clinking coffee cups filling the air. It's a far cry from the humble beginnings of the company, which started life as a small team working out of a rented house in San Francisco's Mission District. Despite the company's success, Henderson is keen to stress that it wasn't always easy. "We've had our fair share of setbacks and failures," he says. "But we've always been driven by a desire to build something that people love to use." And it's clear that they've achieved that with Slack. The company's users are fanatical about the product, with many taking to social media to sing its praises. But Henderson's comments about the UK's tech scene are a sobering reminder that not every country has the same level of support for start-ups. "The UK has a lot of talented people, but it's just not set up to support companies like Slack," he says. "The funding, the talent, the infrastructure - it's all just not there in the same way that it is in the Valley." It's a sentiment that's echoed by other British entrepreneurs who've made the move to San Francisco. "I love the UK, but it's just not the same as being here," says one founder, who wished to remain anonymous. "The energy, the excitement, the sense of possibility - it's all just so much more intense here." But it's not all doom and gloom for the UK's tech scene. There are still plenty of success stories, from companies like DeepMind and TransferWise to entrepreneurs like Richard Reed and Brent Hoberman. And there are efforts underway to try and replicate the Valley's success in the UK, from initiatives like Tech City to programmes like Seedcamp and Entrepreneur First. However, as Henderson's comments make clear, there's still a long way to go. "The UK needs to be more ambitious," he says. "It needs to think bigger, to aim higher. Because right now, it's just not competing at the same level as the Valley." It's a tough message to hear, but one that needs to be heard. The UK's tech scene has come a long way in recent years, but it still lags behind the Valley in terms of funding, talent, and infrastructure. And until that changes, companies like Slack will continue to thrive in San Francisco, rather than in London or Manchester or Edinburgh. As I leave Slack's offices and make my way back to the BBC's San Francisco bureau, I can't help but feel a sense of frustration. The UK has so much potential, so much talent, but it's just not being realised. And until that changes, the UK will continue to lose out to the Valley, and companies like Slack will continue to thrive in San Francisco, rather than in the UK.

We find the ranch without too much trouble, even though it is way back off the main road. We arrive at 2:45, so we wait around in the car and look through brochures of things to do in the area. At 3:15, we go knock on the door of the office. No answer. Knock again. Still no answer. Look at each other and shrug. Look around and notice a small sign on the side of the building pointing down a path. Decide to follow the path and hope we don't get lost. Follow path and come across a small cottage that looks like it belongs in the Swiss Alps. Go up to the door and knock. A man answers who looks like he has been sleeping. He says he's sorry he didn't hear us knocking earlier and that he had fallen asleep. We ask him if this is where we check in and he says yes. We introduce ourselves and tell him we have reservations. He tells us to make ourselves comfortable while he goes to get our key. We sit down on the couch and look around. The room is full of books and knickknacks. The walls are covered in paintings and drawings. There is a large bookshelf filled with books and a basket of magazines. It smells wonderful. When he comes back, he asks us what kind of wine we prefer - red or white? We both love red wines and tell him so. He says he'll bring us a bottle later. We fill out paperwork and he shows us to our cottage. It is beautiful. I feel like I'm in Switzerland. Our cottage is decorated beautifully and has everything we need. It's so quiet here. All we can hear are birds chirping. I am so excited. This is the perfect place for us. We unload the car and then head back into Wimberley. We walk around downtown and poke our heads into shops. It's quaint and cute. We buy a couple of souvenirs. We then head over to the River Road Ice House for dinner. We eat inside because they have live music starting soon. We order beer and appetizers and relax. The band starts playing and they sound good. The crowd seems friendly. We order burgers for dinner and they are excellent. The atmosphere is fun. After dinner, we wander around the grounds and check out the stage outside. It looks like a lot of people are setting up lawn chairs in front of the stage. We go back inside and dance a bit before heading back to the ranch. Back at the ranch, we discover that our host brought us a bottle of wine. It's a nice Zinfindel from California. We drink most of it sitting on the porch listening to the crickets and frogs. We talk about our lives together and our plans for the future. Day 2, Saturday (April 10) We wake up late and have breakfast in our cabin. We've decided to go to New Braunfels today. We pack up the cooler and head out. On the way, we pass the Wimberley Market Days, which is a huge flea market. We decide to stop. It is crowded and hot, but we have fun looking at the junk. We spend about $12 total on a few items. We then continue on to Gruene Hall. We park behind the hall and walk to the river. It's low and rocky. We wander around the shops and have a beer at the Gristmill restaurant overlooking the river. The food looks good, but we decide to try something else for lunch. We walk next door to the Gruene General Store and get sandwiches to go.

Prince Bandar's explanation, that His Majesty, the King of Saudi Arabia, didn't want them to be inconvenienced, makes the whole matter even less clear. Why should His Majesty have a say in this at all? As Moore points out, what would have happened if Clinton had arranged to have all of Timothy McVay's family flown out of the country within days of the Oklahoma bombing. Surprising Factoid: The idea that the Saudis own 6-7% of the country was interesting. There seemed to be a little slippage between ownership of the country and ownership of equity in the stock exchange. I think the 6-7% refers to the stock exchange, which is still a surprising figure. Funniest pop culture allusions: well, there are actually quite a few. For starters, framing Afghanistan as an episode of Bonanza, was very cleverly done. But I think I liked the hip use of the Talking Head's "Shiny, Happy People" as background for the footage of the Bushes and the Sauds and the Bin Ladens socializing, and "Come On, Party People, Put Your Hands in the Air" as background to the anti-American demonstrations in Iraq. Deconstructive moments: As many critics have noted, at the beginning of the film, we see outtakes of Bush White House officials getting prepared for television appearances and at the end we see them taking off their microphones. This does seem to underscore the theatricality, the constructedness of politics. The constant references to pop culture that show both the Bush team and Moore and his audience relying on culturally produced precedents to respond to current events again shows how the "real world" of politics and even war is affected by art. Interestingly, there is a moment where someone accuses Moore's movie of being staged - and at that moment, and that moment only, we see one of the cameras from Moore's film. It's as though Moore is inviting us to think about what it would mean for his movie to be staged. Moments showing the documentary filmmaker's skill: A lot of people find Lila Lipscomb's story the most moving part of the movie. She's the working class woman whose son died in Iraq. Filmically, her story is also very well done. We meet her first in the context of unemployment in Flint and the attraction of the military. Only later do we learn that her son is in the military and it is even later that we learn that he has died. Now, when Moore is putting together his documentary, he obviously already knows that her son is dead. So he consciously structures it so that we gradually learn about Lila Lipscomb's story. (Similarly, we learn somewhat early that she wears a multicolored cross because she supports multiculturalism - later we meet her family and realize that her husband is Black.)

The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea. "It's nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time," he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house. "I had not thought there was any particular strain," I answered. "It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty." "Strain!" he snorted. "Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!" He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. "How about this here tide that's rushin' out through the Golden Gate?" he demanded, or bellowed, rather. "How fast is she ebbin'? What's the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we're a-top of it! See 'em alterin' the course!" From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog. "That's a ferry-boat of some sort," the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. "And there! D'ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell's a poppin' for somebody!" The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion. "And now they're payin' their respects to each other and tryin' to get clear," the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. "That's a steam-siren a-goin' it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat-a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin' in from the Heads against the tide." A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

Miss Birch, with an air of authority that seemed to fill the room with shadows darker than her hair, rose from her seat and pointed an accusing finger towards me. "Mr. Warton," she began, her voice as firm as the oak paneling adorning the walls, "Lucille has failed in her lessons today, both in spelling and arithmetic, despite repeated instructions." She turned those penetrating eyes toward me, her presence as commanding as ever. "Such negligence cannot go unchecked, especially for a young lady of her standing. I fear it is a reflection of deeper languor and indiscipline." My father, standing with arms crossed and face a mask of paternal disappointment, nodded solemnly. "Indeed, Miss Birch, I share your concern. Discipline is the cornerstone of any noble upbringing. What course of action do you propose?" I stood there, my heart pounding erratically within the confines of my small chest, feeling cornered and misunderstood. The room felt cold despite the warm sunlight streaming through the high windows, casting long strips of light upon the polished wooden floors. With bated breath, I awaited Miss Birch's verdict, the shadows cast upon me as both judge and jury. Miss Birch, maintaining her ironclad poise, declared, "In times past, a gentle reminder from the birch rod has served to correct many a fledgling soul." Her words fell like stones, heavy and immovable, yet her countenance betrayed no malice, merely a belief in the righteousness of her methods. She gestured towards the corner cupboard, within which lay instruments of correction that had, until now, existed only in the murky recesses of my fears. "Very well," responded my father, his voice like distant thunder. "If you believe it will aid in her education and comportment, then so be it." My heart sank further, touching upon an abyss I did not know could exist within one so young. I watched as Miss Birch retrieved a slender bundle of dreaded twigs from their hidden sanctuary. She approached with a meticulous calm, every stride echoing the finality of the situation. "Lucille," she intoned, "come forward." With wavering resolve, I stepped with trepidation, each movement hesitant as though a puppet guided by uncertain strings. The room seemed suspended in a breathless anticipation. I could feel the weight of their eyes upon me-one of duty, the other of regret. Bending to her will, I was guided by Miss Birch's hands, firm yet unexpected in their non-hostility, to assume a posture apt for the correction. My father's presence faded to the periphery, yet I was ever aware of his disapproving stance like a looming indictment. The first strike landed with a searing clarity that left no space for composure nor pride, igniting a rawness unfamiliar and all-consuming. Tears sprang unbidden to my eyes, a release I had fought to delay, battlement breached by the twin forces of shock and sting. With each further stroke delivered in resolute measure, the intensity mounted, a crescendo of discomfort under the orchestration of Miss Birch's unwavering demeanor. Time seemed to lose definition, each passing moment a stretched eternity until the rite of correction concluded, leaving behind a tender lesson engraved upon mind and skin alike. As I returned to stand before them, tears now silent harbingers of submission, Miss Birch offered a gentle nod-unspoken acknowledgment that the ordeal was over. Though chastened, I emerged with a nascent understanding, etched not just in pain but with clarity wrought from it-a harbinger of the discipline expected within noble circles.

He stooped over and picked up one of them and read the label. A good brand, too. He straightened up and tucked the bottle under his arm. Someone, he told himself, had gone to a lot of trouble. Had brought the stuff from Earth or Mars. At least a hundred miles away, perhaps considerably farther than that, loomed the towering mass of Pluto, hanging in the sky like an enormous globe. A world of utter desolation, a place of bitter cold and darkness and howling gales of poison gas. West turned back toward his ship and the sight of it gave him a little shock. He had forgotten what it looked like. Forgotten? No, not forgotten, but rather his mind had refused to accept its appearance. He had tried to tell himself that he had imagined the changes, that the ship was just as it always had been. But now, seeing it against the background of the rocks, he knew that he had not imagined it. It was squat and ugly now. The lines had changed. It seemed somehow alien. As if it had become something other than a spaceship. Almost as if it had taken on some characteristics of the creatures who had attacked it. He shuddered at the memory of the attack. How long ago had it been? A week? A month? Two months? Time meant nothing in space. One lost track of time. And there was no time here, either. There never had been time. This was a place where time had stopped eons ago. The ship had been a beauty once. Picked it up cheap, he recalled. Cheap because it was old and battered and obsolete, but sound enough mechanically, needing only a coat of paint to make it look like new. And he'd done better than that. He'd fixed it up inside. He'd made it into a home instead of a machine. And he'd painted it - he remembered the pride and pleasure of painting it. A bright red body and the wings and tail assembly chrome yellow and the nose blue and the fins canary yellow. Bright colors, pretty colors, like the ones they used in pictures advertising holiday cruises. He'd picked up the idea from one of the ads. Now it was squat and ugly and there was no color left. Just grayness. Grayness everywhere. Grayness covering everything. And it was hard to see the shape within the grayness. It was as if the ship were wrapped in fog. Fog, hell! he thought. That isn't any fog. It's something else. Something that crawled out of Jupiter. Something that clung to us and followed us, eating its way through metal, plastic, glass, rubber, fabric. Eating its way through anything we had aboard the ship. Eating its way through the ship itself. Maybe it is alive, he thought. Although it didn't seem to be. Not alive as man knows life. Just a sort of - well, maybe a sort of protoplasm. A protoplasm that moved slowly, flowing over things and digesting them, incorporating them into its own structure. And the funny thing about it was that it did not add to its bulk as it flowed over and digested things. It stayed the same size it had been when it first hit the ship. It grew thinner as its area widened until it finally reached a point where it broke contact with itself. Then it pulled together once again and became its normal size, a huddled, quivering blob of protoplasm resting on the hull. When it got too big, it split apart into two separate entities and each of those two grew bigger and then split once again.

And Mynors playfully snatched the book from her arms. 'Oh no! Give it me!' she cried, laughing, and reaching up to him. He was six feet high, and as broad as he was long. His face was large, fleshy, and red; his hair black, short, and bristly. In repose his features wore a look of coarse sensuality, but this passed away when he smiled, leaving only a simple benevolence in its place. He wore a pepper-and-salt suit, with a fancy waistcoat. His collar was low, and his necktie very wide and loose. On his head was a hard felt hat, slightly brownish in hue. 'No,' said he, holding the volume above her reach. 'You mustn't have it till I know whether you've earned it or not. Have you been attentive all the afternoon? Now tell the truth.' 'Yes, Mr. Mynors.' 'And have you learned your verses nicely?' 'Yes, Mr. Mynors.' 'Then you shall have your book,' he replied, giving it to her with mock solemnity. 'Thank you, Mr. Mynors,' said Agnes, smiling. 'Now, what are you waiting about here for? You ought to be gone home long ago. What do you mean by stopping behind everybody else?' 'Please, mother told me to wait for her.' 'Your mother! Where is she?' 'She's in there.' And Agnes pointed to the lecture-hall. 'In there! What next? I didn't know we'd got any mothers in our class. Well, go and fetch her out, my dear.' 'But please, Mr. Mynors, she doesn't want me to come in.' 'Oh, indeed!' said he, lifting his eyebrows. 'Perhaps she thinks she's too old to learn anything more.' Then, turning to his companion: 'What do you think of that, Willie? Mrs. Naylor doesn't want Agnes to interrupt her.' 'Why shouldn't she come in, though?' asked Willie Price, with a puzzled air. 'I don't see why she shouldn't.' He was twenty-one years of age, and looked younger. He was five feet eight inches high, thin, and loosely jointed. A pair of steel-rimmed spectacles magnified his pale blue eyes, and gave him a dreamy and rather helpless appearance. His clothes were shabby, ill-fitting, and out of fashion. 'Come along, my dear,' said Mynors. 'We'll just peep inside and see what your mother's doing.' But Agnes hesitated, looking at them doubtfully. 'Never mind,' continued Mynors, catching hold of her hand and drawing her gently forward. 'It will be quite right. We're both members of the class, so we can go in whenever we like. Come along, Willie.' They entered the lecture-hall together, and found Mrs. Naylor seated near the stove in conversation with two other ladies. The room was long, lofty, and dim, and contained thirty or forty chairs arranged in rows. It was used for meetings of various kinds, and also served as a vestry to the chapel. At the far end was a platform, with a harmonium upon it, and over the platform hung a dusty green curtain, which was now drawn back and pinned to the wall. The class was evidently over, and the remaining scholars had departed. When the three newcomers appeared in the doorway Mrs. Naylor rose quickly, with a gesture of annoyance. 'Agnes!'

He sprints down the corridor, the sound of his footsteps echoing off the cold metal walls. The ship's alarm system begins to wail, a piercing shriek that cuts through the darkness. Walter's eyes dart from one console to the next, his mind racing to assess the damage. "Mother, what's the status on the terraforming bay?" he calls out, his voice firm but laced with a hint of urgency. "Severe damage reported, Walter," the computer responds, her voice calm and detached. "Life support systems are failing. We're experiencing a toxic gas leak in sector three." Walter's face sets in a grim determination as he rushes towards the terraforming bay. He bursts through the door, his eyes scanning the room for any signs of survivors. The air is thick with the acrid smell of smoke and ozone, and the once-pristine equipment now lies twisted and mangled. He spots a figure slumped against a console, a young woman with a look of shock frozen on her face. Walter rushes to her side, gently turning her over. Her eyes flicker open, and she gazes up at him with a mixture of confusion and fear. "W-what happened?" she stammers. "We were hit by a neutrino burst," Walter explains, his voice low and urgent. "We need to get out of here, now." He helps the woman to her feet, and together they stumble out of the terraforming bay, the ship's alarm system growing louder with every step. They make their way to the bridge, where the rest of the crew is slowly coming online, their faces pale and drawn. Captain Lewis, a grizzled veteran of deep space, takes charge, his voice firm and authoritative. "Alright, let's assess the damage. We need to know what we're up against." The crew begins to report in, their voices overlapping as they detail the extent of the damage. Walter's eyes scan the room, his mind racing with the implications. They're 239 light-years from Earth, with limited resources and a ship that's barely holding together. As the reports continue to come in, a sense of dread begins to settle over the crew. They're not just fighting to survive - they're fighting to stay human. The vast expanse of space stretches out before them, a cold and unforgiving void that's waiting to claim them. And then, on the edge of the nebula, a strange signal begins to pulse, a faint beacon calling out to them like a siren's song...

But he never shows the same kind of passion for Patroclus (Orlando Bloom), the man whose death will drive him to slaughter. That's not just wrong, it's criminal. It also ignores the fact that Achilles himself dies after the war ends, from an arrow shot by Paris through the heel which the gods have made invulnerable except for that spot. In Homer's epic, Achilles' heel becomes a metaphor for human vulnerability; it symbolizes how much the gods can influence our lives. Without this, there is no reason why Achilles should die. Then there's Odysseus, the smartest guy around. We learn nothing about him, except that he likes to trick people and has a plan to trick the Trojans. There are no stories of his famous cunning, no witty repartee, no charming banter. They didn't even make him look clever! Why did they bother casting Sean Bean, then? He plays a sort-of Sir Guy of Gisborne without the coolness factor. The other Achaean leaders don't fare much better. Menelaus, king of Sparta and brother of Agamemnon, is supposed to be the brains behind the whole operation. Here he's just another big dumb fighter who wants his wife back. Agamemnon is supposed to be the toughest, fiercest fighter of them all. Here he's just a weak-willed bully. Diomedes is supposed to be the second strongest fighter next to Achilles. Here he's just a minor player. Nestor, the old wise counselor, is just a grumpy old man. Ajax, the second strongest fighter next to Achilles, is just a generic bad-ass. Antilochus, the son of Nestor, is just a kid. Teucer, the archer, is just a guy with a bow. Phoenix, the old mentor of Achilles, is just a crazy old man. The women aren't much better. Briseis, Achilles' captive concubine, is just a girl who cries a lot. Chryseis, daughter of Chryses and priestess of Apollo, is just a girl who cries a lot. Hecuba, Queen of Troy, is just a worried mom. Cassandra, Priam's daughter, is just a weirdo. Helen, Queen of Sparta, is just a nagging wife. The other women are just extras. You see the pattern yet? All these people were so much more than this. They were complex, multi-faceted, psychologically rich individuals. These characters are cardboard cutouts. They're stereotypes. They're generic. They're dull. As a result, the story lacks drama. I'm sorry, but if you don't feel anything for the main characters, it's hard to really enjoy the movie. Then there's the setting. In the original, the Trojans and Achaians live in wooden palaces. There are no walls, no towers, no battlements, no fortifications. It's a pretty place, not a fortress. The Trojan horse is built out of wood. The Achaians attack by land and sea, but they're not equipped with catapults and battering rams. They don't have siege engines, trebuchets, or any of the heavy equipment used by medieval armies. They have arrows, swords, spears and shields. The city is sacked by fire and burning torches. The actors wear togas. Yes, yes, I know that this is a fantasy, and that it takes liberties with history. I don't mind that. But why couldn't the filmmakers have chosen a different mythic story to retell?
