Furthermore, the shifting landscape of legal frameworks surrounding mental capacity necessitates a thorough interrogation of not only the theoretical underpinnings but also the practical ramifications on the lives of individuals. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities fervently emphasizes the importance of inclusivity in both legal discourse and assessment methodologies, suggesting that any framework addressing mental capacity should prioritize the lived experiences of those it is intended to serve. In this regard, the emphasis on social and political contexts is not merely an academic point, but a clarion call for genuine engagement with the realities faced by individuals who navigate these complex systems. The contention that mental capacity is influenced by societal norms brings into sharp focus the question of who gets to define capacity. Different cultural and social contexts can yield vastly different interpretations of mental competence, reflecting, as the Committee argues, biases inherent within the structures designed to protect rights. For instance, societal notions surrounding aging, disability, or mental health can frame perceptions and consequent evaluations of an individual's abilities, often leading to a prescriptive rather than a descriptive understanding of capacity. Additionally, the argument for a re-evaluation extends beyond legal bounds; it permeates into educational, healthcare, and community systems. As the disciplines tech and implement assessments and frameworks, there is an urgent necessity to train professionals to recognize their own biases and assumptions when determining mental capacity. The dialogue initiated by the Committee must resonate in training practices, ensuring that those engaged in assessing mental capacity are not merely following a checklist but are dynamically interacting with individuals in an empowering and respectful manner. Moreover, the emergence of person-centered approaches champions the validity of subjective experiences over purely objective assessments. By placing individuals at the heart of decision-making processes, we illuminate the multifaceted nature of mental capacity. This approach serves to honor the rights of those deemed to have diminished capacity by recognizing that capacity can be contextual and fluid, rather than a fixed trait. The implication of this perspective is significant, as it necessitates legal reforms capable of supporting dynamic and nuanced understandings of autonomy and agency. Yet, as the debate unfolds, it becomes clear that the challenge is not simply a matter of reformulating legal definitions but also addressing deeper societal attitudes that often dehumanize those presumed to lack capacity. Efforts must extend beyond mere advocacy; there is a critical need for a shift in public perception to foster an environment that celebrates diversity in decision-making processes and recognizes the intrinsic worth of every individual, irrespective of their cognitive abilities. Thus, the legal discourse surrounding mental capacity stands at a crucial juncture, echoing broader societal currents that prioritize autonomy while grappling with the moral imperatives of care and protection. Moving forward, the convergence of legal theory, social psychology, and human rights discourses will be essential in crafting a holistic understanding of mental capacity. Such a synthesis has the potential not only to redefine legal capacities but also to reshape our collective views on competence, dignity, and the recognition of agency in a world that too often sidelines the voices of those with mental impairments. The encroaching landscape of these discussions holds promises of deeper engagement, where advocacy aligns with lived experiences, fostering systems that respect and uphold the rights of all individuals, resolutely and unflinchingly.

The cognitive layer of the CPS architecture is responsible for the integration of human and machine intelligence, and the development of intelligent control strategies that take into account the capabilities and limitations of both humans and machines. The development of a CPS model of a CNC machine tool is a complex and multidisciplinary task that requires the integration of expertise from various fields, including mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, computer science, and cognitive science. George steps out of the shower, his eyes adjusting to the dim light of the bathroom. He wraps a towel around his waist and makes his way back to the bedroom. He picks up the stack of letters and envelopes, running his fingers over the addresses, his mind wandering. He sets them down on the bed, his gaze drifting to the window. The curtains are still drawn, but the faint light of dawn is creeping in, casting an eerie glow over the room. George's thoughts are a jumble of memories, fragmented and disjointed. He tries to piece together the events of the past eight months, but his mind is a fog. He remembers the pain, the darkness, the feeling of being trapped. He remembers the faces, the voices, the sounds. But it's all a blur. He walks over to the window, pulling back the curtains to reveal the ocean outside. The waves crash against the shore, the gulls crying out in the distance. George feels a pang of longing, a sense of longing for something he can't quite grasp. He stands there for a moment, lost in thought, the sound of the waves washing over him. Suddenly, he's back in the present, standing in his own bedroom, the letters and envelopes still scattered on the bed. He picks one up, his eyes scanning the address. It's from his brother, Jim. He sets it back down, his heart heavy with a mix of emotions. George's thoughts turn to his brother, to their conversations, their arguments, their laughter. He remembers the way Jim used to make him feel, like he was the only person in the world who truly understood him. But that was before. Before the war, before the pain, before the darkness. George's eyes fall on the empty scotch bottle on the floor. He remembers the nights, the endless nights, the whiskey and the tears. He remembers the feeling of being lost, of being alone. He remembers the sound of his own voice, whispering in the darkness, "I'm still here." The sound of the waves outside seems to grow louder, more insistent. George feels the weight of his own mortality, the weight of his own regret. He looks around the room, at the chaos, the mess. He knows he needs to clean it up, to start anew. But for now, he just stands there, frozen, lost in the past, lost in the present. The camera lingers on George's face, his eyes sunken, his skin pale. He looks like a man who has given up, a man who has lost his way. The sound of the waves continues to wash over him, a constant reminder of the passage of time, of the fragility of life.

To reconcile these nuanced findings, it is essential to consider the multifaceted nature of action observation and the cognitive processes involved. While familiarity undoubtedly plays a significant role in the activation of the AON, other factors-including contextual cues, the complexity of the observed action, and the observer's experiential background-can influence neural responses. For instance, an unfamiliar action might draw greater attention due to its novelty, prompting a deeper engagement of cognitive resources aimed at understanding and predicting the actions of a social partner (Voyer et al., 2015). This heightened observation may be linked to the observer's potential need to adapt behavioral strategies in response to novel stimuli, thereby inciting an amplification of AON activity. Furthermore, the socio-emotional context within which actions are perceived cannot be overlooked (Tremblay, 2006). The intentions behind actions, combined with the emotional significance attributed to them, can shape our neural responses. When witnesses observe someone engaging in an intricate or potentially hazardous behavior, the inherent risk associated with that action may lead to increased AON activation, underscoring the observer's need to anticipate consequences and prepare appropriate social responses (Adolphs, 2002). Such a dynamic underscores the importance of distinguishing between an observer's mere familiarity with actions and the contextual richness that imbues those actions with meaning. In addition, the observer's own motor experience may modulate their neural response even in the presence of unfamiliar actions. For example, an individual with a background in athletics might exhibit greater AON activation when watching a complex athletic maneuver, regardless of personal experience with that specific action. This concept aligns with the simulation theory, suggesting that past motor experiences-whether directly related to the observed action or not-create a reservoir of motor knowledge that can be recruited during action observation (Wilson and Knoblich, 2005). Thus, it becomes evident that familiarity must be viewed through a wider lens, encompassing not only direct familiarity but also the broader context of an observer's lifetime of experiences. Moreover, considering the evolution of the AON itself opens further avenues of understanding. The engagement of the AON may have evolved as an adaptive mechanism to foster social interconnectedness and cohesion-capabilities vital for survival in social species. This evolutionary perspective invites inquiry into the mechanisms that underpin empathic responses and social learning, as AON activation during action observation may promote the encoding of social norms and expectations (Tooby and Cosmides, 1992). Furthermore, an augmented understanding of action patterns-whether familiar or unfamiliar-may facilitate the transmission of knowledge across generations, ensuring the perpetuation of culturally significant behaviors and skills. In sum, while the interplay between familiarity and AON activity remains a core area of research, the narrative is undoubtedly more intricate. The relationship is not merely a straightforward increase in response correlating with familiarity; it encompasses an array of influences including attention, emotional context, and past experiences. Such insights remind us that human interaction is not merely about the actions we see but also about the connections we forge through understanding. Consequently, for future investigations into the functions of the AON, it may be beneficial to adopt more nuanced approaches that consider a wider spectrum of contextual and experiential factors that contribute to the rich tapestry of social cognition.

The incorporation of inclined exits on circular coaxial nozzles, as a means to modulate jet-mixing characteristics, warrants a comprehensive examination of the underlying flow dynamics. In this context, the present study aims to elucidate the effects of inclined exits on the flow behaviour of circular coaxial jets, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between the nozzle incline-angle, secondary-to-primary jet area-ratio, and velocity-ratio. A detailed experimental investigation was conducted using a combination of flow visualization, hot-wire anemometry, and particle image velocimetry (PIV) techniques to elucidate the mean and turbulent flow characteristics of inclined circular coaxial jets. The experimental setup consisted of a circular coaxial nozzle with an inner diameter of 10 mm and an outer diameter of 20 mm, which was inclined at angles of 15, 30, and 45 with respect to the horizontal plane. The secondary-to-primary jet area-ratio was varied between 0.25 and 1.0, while the velocity-ratio was maintained at a constant value of 0.5. The flow visualization experiments revealed the formation of complex vortex structures in the near-field region of the jet, which were influenced by the nozzle incline-angle and secondary-to-primary jet area-ratio. The hot-wire anemometry measurements showed that the mean velocity profiles were significantly affected by the incline-angle, with a greater degree of asymmetry observed at higher incline-angles. The PIV measurements provided further insight into the turbulent flow characteristics, revealing a significant increase in turbulent kinetic energy in the near-field region of the jet with increasing incline-angle. The turbulent flow structures were found to be highly anisotropic, with a greater degree of turbulence intensity observed in the direction perpendicular to the nozzle axis. The results also indicated that the secondary-to-primary jet area-ratio played a crucial role in modulating the turbulent flow characteristics, with a higher area-ratio resulting in a more pronounced degree of turbulence anisotropy. The findings of this study demonstrate the potential of inclined exits on circular coaxial nozzles as a means to control jet-mixing characteristics, and highlight the complex interplay between the nozzle incline-angle, secondary-to-primary jet area-ratio, and velocity-ratio. The results of this study have important implications for the design of jet-mixing systems, and provide a foundation for further research into the use of inclined exits as a means to enhance jet-mixing performance. Future studies could focus on the application of inclined exits to other nozzle geometries, such as elliptic or rectangular nozzles, as well as the use of active control techniques to modulate the jet-mixing characteristics. In addition, the effects of inclined exits on the noise characteristics of circular coaxial jets could be investigated, as previous studies have shown that the incline-angle can have a significant impact on the noise levels generated by jet flows. Furthermore, the use of inclined exits could be explored as a means to enhance the stability of jet flows, which is critical in a range of industrial applications, including combustion systems and propulsion systems. Overall, the present study demonstrates the potential of inclined exits as a means to modulate jet-mixing characteristics, and highlights the need for further research into the underlying flow dynamics and potential applications of this technique.

Despite the growth in the literature on the relation between the CDS market and other markets, empirical evidence on the lead-lag relation between the stock and the CDS markets is still unclear (e.g., Hilscher et al., 2015; Longstaff et al., 2003; Forte and Lovreta, 2015; Forte and Pena, 2009; Marsh and Wagner, 2015; Norden and Weber, 2009, 2004; Flannery et al., 2010; Bystrom, 2008). Thus, the motivation for our study is to add to the literature by using a large data set that covers nine main economic sectors in North America, Europe, Asia, and the UK. Our study uses the highly liquid Thompson Reuters CDS indices and manually constructs the underlying stock portfolios to examine whether default risk is priced equally fast by the CDS and the stock markets. We use a bivariate vector autoregression system to examine the relation between the daily stock returns and changes in the daily CDS spreads. Specifically, we address the following two questions: (i) Is there a lead-lag relation between the CDS and the stock markets? And (ii) is the lead-lag relation between the CDS and stock markets different across different geographical regions and economic sectors? We find that the daily stock returns lead the daily CDS spread changes. We also find weak and mixed evidence that the changes in the daily CDS spreads lead the daily stock returns. This asymmetric relation holds in all of the geographical regions and economic sectors. We also find weak evidence that the documented lead-lag relation is not regime-dependent and that is stronger for negative stock market news. Overall, the results indicate that the stock market prices changing default risk faster than the CDS market. Thus, it seems that the stock market is relatively more efficient in processing information than the CDS market and therefore leads the price discovering process. Similar to Hilscher et al. (2015), our results are consistent with the theories on market selection according to which informed traders participate mostly or only in one market. Hence, our results also support the view that the stock market is dominated by informed traders of default risk, while uninformed traders of default risk (i.e., liquidity traders) participate mostly in the CDS market. Our paper makes several contributions. First, we examine which market leads the price discovery process by using the highly liquid Thomson Reuters (TR) CDS indices rather than firm-level CDS. Indeed, most previous studies use firm-level data of usually a low number of obligors.3 The use of the TR CDS indices helps to mitigate any adverse effects due to nonsynchronous data, stale quotes, and extreme differences in the liquidity of single-name CDS that could affect the interpretation of the observed lead-lag relations.4 The possible nonsynchronous data in the CDS and the stock markets may lead to cross-autocorrelation between the CDS spread changes and the stock returns, and to spurious results related to the lead-lag relation of the CDS and stock markets.

"This is the reason that people nowadays are jumping up and saying, 'The antidepressant drugs don't work,'" Carroll said. "If you take this broad category, it's difficult to even show why they don't work." "There's a great deal of a concern, so we are hardly voices in the wilderness," said Dr. Allen Frances, author of the book "Saving Normal: An Insider's Revolt Against Out of Control Psychiatric Diagnosis, DSM-5, Big Pharma and the Medicalization of Ordinary Life." He is largely credited with spearheading anti-DMS-5 efforts. "A petition regarding DSM-5, signed by 50-plus associations, was presented to the (psychiatric association), asking for an independent scientific review. The association brushed it aside," said Frances, a Duke professor emeritus and former psychiatric department chairman. The psychiatric association says the DSM-5 was independently reviewed for 18 months but that those findings will not be made public. Also, the reviewers' identities will not be disclosed until the manual is released. "The development of DSM-5 began with an unprecedented process of research evaluation that included a series of white papers and 13 scientific conferences supported by the National Institutes of Health," wrote Dr. David Kupfer, chairman of the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, who oversees the entire DSM-5 task force, in an e-mail. "This preparation brought together more than 400 international scientists and produced a series of monographs and peer-reviewed journal articles. DSM-5 is the product of the most extensive discussion and debate - as part of the most transparent process - of any DSM." Mental illness in children: Know the signs. Frances contends that the process, though conducted with volunteers, has been somewhat secretive and did not sufficiently consider objections to what the manual will contain. Frances led the task force that produced the DSM IV in 2000. "What motivates me is the experience of having inadvertently contributed to fads and psycho-diagnosis that have resulted in over-diagnosis and over-treatment," Frances said. "Some of this happened during DSM IV, even though we were more conservative with that document than they've been with DSM-5, with its many changes that are unsupported and, in some cases, quite reckless."

Upon Hendrik there is a decided change. He has outgrown his elder brother both in length and breadth, and comes very near looking like a full-grown man. He is yet but eighteen years old, straight as a rush, with a decided military air and gait. The last is not to be wondered at, as Hendrik has now been a cornet in the Cape Mounted Rifles for more than a year, and still holds that commission, as may be learnt by looking at his forage-cap, with its golden embroidery over the peak. So much for our old acquaintances the "Bush-boys!" But who are the other three that share with them the circle of the camp-fire? Who are their companions? for they are evidently on terms of companionship, and friendship too. Who are they? A word or two will tell that. They are the Van Wyks. The three sons of Diedrik Van Wyk. And who, then, is Diedrik Van Wyk? That must also be explained. Diedrik is a very rich boor - a "vee-boor" - who every night shuts up within his spacious kraals more than three thousand horses and horned cattle, with five times that number of sheep and goats! In fact, Diedrik Van Wyk is accounted the richest vee-boor, or grazier, in all the Graaf Reinet. Now the broad plaatz, or farm, of Diedrik Van Wyk lies contiguous to that of our old acquaintance, Hendrik Von Bloom; and it so chances that Hendrik and Diedrik are fast friends and inseparable companions. They see each other once a-day, at the least. Every evening Hendrik rides over to the "kraal" of Diedrik, or Diedrik to that of Hendrik, to enjoy a smoke together out of their ponderous pipes of meerschaum, or a "zoopje" of brandewyn distilled from their own peaches. They are, in fact, a pair of regular old comrades, - for Van Wyk in early life has seen military service as well as Von Bloom, - and, like all old soldiers, they love to repeat their camp stories, and "fight their battles o'er again." Under such circumstances it is not to be wondered at, that the children of both should be intimate acquaintances. But, in addition to the friendship of their fathers, there is a tie of relationship between the two families, - the two mothers were cousins, - so that the children are what is usually termed second cousins, - a very interesting sort of affinity. And it is not an unlikely thing that the relationship between the families of Von Bloom and his friend Van Wyk may one day become still closer and more interesting; for the former has for his daughter, as all the world knows, the beautiful flaxen-haired cherry-cheeked Truey, while the latter is the father of the pretty brunette Wilhelmina - also an only daughter.

Recent measures of empowerment, such as the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index (WEAI) (Alkire et al., 2013), operationalize Kabeer's (1999) definition of empowerment as the process by which people expand their ability to make strategic life choices, particularly in contexts in which this ability had been denied to them. In Kabeer's definition, the ability to exercise choice encompasses three dimensions: resources (defined to include not only access but also future claims to material, human, and social resources), agency (including processes of decision-making, negotiation, and even deception and manipulation), and achievements (well-being outcomes). Filling a niche unaddressed by existing metrics, the WEAI measures women's empowerment in the agricultural sector directly through a focus on women's agency using individual-level data collected from male and female household members in a household survey designed for this purpose. The WEAI is an aggregate index, reported at the country or sub-national level and comprised of two sub-indices. The first sub-index assesses the degree to which respondents are empowered in five domains of empowerment (5DE) in agriculture, namely, decisions about agricultural production, access to and decision-making power about productive resources, control of use of income, leadership in the community, and time allocation (Alkire et al., 2013). It reflects the percentage of women and men who are empowered and, among those who are not, the percentage of domains in which they achieve a pre-defined threshold for adequacy in empowerment. The second sub-index, the Gender Parity Index (GPI), measures gender parity. The GPI reflects the percentage of women who are empowered or whose achievements are at least as high as the men in their households. For those households that have not achieved gender parity, the GPI shows the empowerment gap that needs to be closed for women to reach the same level of empowerment as men in their households (Alkire et al., 2013). The WEAI's focus on women's empowerment in the agricultural sector is important, given that agriculture remains the basis for the livelihoods of most rural people in low- and middle-income countries. Originally, the WEAI was intended as a monitoring and evaluation (M&E) tool for the US Government's Feed the Future (FTF) initiative to track changes in women's empowerment in agriculture over time and assess differences across countries, regions, and population subgroups. The WEAI was suited to this purpose, given its broad applicability and transparent design, and its original domains were chosen based on the areas that United States Agency for International Development (USAID) aimed to affect directly in FTF programming. More than a single number, the WEAI provides an "information platform" (Alkire, 2018) for measuring women's empowerment in agriculture. It includes multiple sub-indices and indicators that provide complementary, yet unique, pieces of information.

In most species each cell of the outer layer of the periderm has a central silicon papilla from a basal Si-plate (Haines and Lye, 1983). The fruit wall or pericarp is made up of three layers, (1) a one cell thick epicarp with cells usually wider than high, (2) a middle layer (mesocarp) 2-15 cells thick and (3) an inner layer (endocarp) usually consisting of a fibrous layer with or without vessels. The conical papillae of the epicarp are often named silicon phytoliths. In a comparative study of development of the pericarp and seed coat Shah (1968) found that in Carex wallichiana the inner 3-5 layers of the pericarp (the endocarp) develop into sclerenchymatous fibers placed at right angles to each other, and in Bulbostylis barbata (Rottb.) C.B.Cl. the innermost cells enlarge, become vacuolated, lose their cytoplasm and strech radially only to collapse. Similarly, before fertilization the outermost cells (the epicarp) are thin-walled and contain starch grains; only following fertilization the inner tangential walls are thickened (Shah, 1968). Sections of young ovaries are also illustrated by Vrijdaghs et al. (2005, 2011). The chemistry of the fruit wall of Cyperaceae is almost unknown except for the assumption that the papillae in epidermis cells are made of silicon (Schuyler, 1971). The fruits of all genera in tribe Trilepideae are small, narrow and light with numerous basal hairs (Fig. 1A, D and F), and are thus well adapted to dispersal by wind. The ripe fruit projects above the rest of the spikelet and narrows to a beak without any sharp demarcation between the ovary and style. It superficially resembles that of a Carex fruit with its utricle since there is a wide air space between the fruit wall and the seed (Haines and Lye, 1973). von Nees (1842) described the fruit wall of Trilepis lhotzkiana as a utricle "perigynium femineum utriculiforme rostratum, ore ad stylo cohaerente". However, Bentham (1883) and Gilly (1943) recognized Nees' perigynium as part of the ovary. Nelmes (1953) again described the fruit wall of Coleochloa as a "sac-like membranous utricle from the apex of which the 3 stigmas are only just exserted, the style being situated in the upper beak-like portion of the utricle". Raynal (1963) found that the vessels at the corners of Nees' and Nelmes' supposed utricle continued directly into the 3 style branches and thus proved that the supposed utricle is the outer ovary wall. Despite Raynal's convincing work, Koyama and Maguire (1965) again described the fructifications of Trilepis and other Cryptangieae "not a fruit of true achene type" but "a compound structure of an achene and a utricle". Haines and Lye (1973) also found the vascular bundles of the three ribs of the fruit wall to continue directly into the style branches, thus again showing that the fruit wall is not a utricle surrounding and separate from the pistil.

So, with that said, let's dive a bit deeper into the fascinating world of conceptual art. It's a territory ripe for exploration, full of nuance, contention, and-dare I say-intellectual playfulness. When we consider the titanic shifts in art movements during the 20th century, which led to what we now call conceptual art, one cannot overlook the context in which these artists operated. The 1960s were a tumultuous time, with societal upheavals, political unrest, and emerging countercultures all influencing creative expressions. It was a time when artists were beginning to ask critical questions about the very nature of art itself. Now, Tricia, I want to poke at that a little. When you think about the evolution of conceptual art, who do you see as particularly pivotal? Oh gosh, there are so many! I'd have to say Marcel Duchamp, for starters. His 'Fountain' is a quintessential example, not just of conceptual art, but of how the very definition of what art could be was challenged. He took an ordinary urinal, signed it, and presented it as art. It wasn't even about the object itself, but more about the context, the dialogue it provoked, and the audacity of subverting traditional artistic sensibilities. Exactly! That audacity is essential, right? And Duchamp set the stage for countless artists after him. This idea that art could exist primarily as an intellectual exercise rather than a produced object was revolutionary. But that leads me to ask, how do you both reconcile more traditional forms of art with conceptual approaches? Doesn't the technical skill still matter to some extent? In my opinion, they're not mutually exclusive. The technical prowess that artists may have cultivated can enhance the conceptual underpinning of a work. But yes, there's a tension there, particularly when considering the preferences of the traditional art world that often prizes craftsmanship. There's this thought that if it doesn't have 'skill' behind it, does it really count? I'm not here to dismiss those sentiments, but at the end of the day, isn't art meant to provoke thought and emotion? Totally! I think that's where it gets tricky, especially in today's art climate. Traditionalists may scoff while younger generations embrace the fluidity of what art can mean and be. It's an exciting time fueled by accessibility brought on by the internet-so many new voices and perspectives! Like, it makes me think of contemporary artists who utilize social media platforms to reach audiences-like Banksy and his street art. What does everyone think about that? Such a cool point! Taking art to the streets and to the masses allows for a democratization of access. Banksy embodies the spirit of conceptual art wrapped in a social commentary package. It's not just about the art-it's about who gets to determine its value or meaning. But here's a cheeky thought: Are we now teetering on the edge of becoming so conceptual that we risk diluting what art can do? What's your take, Athera? Ah, good question! We do run the risk of oversaturation, sure. But art will always adapt and evolve, responding to societal needs. Perhaps it's an experiment within an experiment. At the core, it seems our job-curators, artists, and even audiences-is to foster conversations, even if they make us uncomfortable. And isn't that what ultimately enriches the art experience? Right? But let's not shy away from that discomfort. Conversations can get awkward, but there's so much depth to be uncovered! Alright, folks, that feels like a good spot to pause. Let's take a moment to breathe here, collect our thoughts, and maybe grab a cup of coffee before we dive back into this artistic rabbit hole-what do you think?

The process then translates into the activation of motor programs, ultimately leading to the neuromuscular execution of these handwriting movements. Every stage is pivotal, and disruptions at any level can compound to affect the final output, which, in children with DCD, is seen as increased pausing. The intricate dance between cognitive planning and motor execution is delicate, and in the case of DCD, this choreography becomes halted by interruptions, characterized by the pauses that distinguish their handwriting from that of their typically developing peers. These pauses can be understood as the visible manifestation of underlying challenges faced by children with DCD: moments where cognitive or motor processes lag or stall entirely. It is, therefore, natural to question the origins of these hesitations. One theory posits that pausing could be a compensatory technique, an adaptive strategy employed to allow for more time to reconcile cognitive demands with the physical act of writing. For instance, the task of retrieving the correct word from memory, processing its spelling, and then translating it into a sequence of hand movements demands considerable cognitive resources. In children with DCD, this process may require more time and intentional breaks to bridge the gaps between thought and action. Further investigation into the underlying cognitive functions, such as working memory and executive function deficits, might lend insight into why these pauses are necessary. Executive functions, which include processes like planning, attention, and cognitive flexibility, are often implicated in children with DCD, suggesting that the pauses seen might be a direct reflection of delays and bottlenecks at these higher-order cognitive stages. These cognitive processes are involved before the pen ever touches the paper, and if inefficiencies exist here, the smoothness of writing is inevitably compromised. There is also likely an interplay between cognition and the motor system that necessitates pausing. The timing of pausing, whether prior to letter formation or during transitions between letters, might provide further clues. Different types of pauses may point to varied challenges at different stages of writing. For example, longer pauses before writing a word or letter could suggest difficulties with planning and retrieval, while intermittent pauses between strokes might highlight issues within motor control itself. To elucidate these aspects of handwriting in children with DCD, a multifaceted approach that integrates cognitive, neurological, and educational perspectives is essential. Advancements in technology, such as digital tablets and motion capture techniques, offer promising avenues for real-time analysis of handwriting kinetics, which can further unravel the complexities of the pausing phenomenon. Ultimately, understanding these pauses is not merely academic; it holds profound implications for intervention. By unveiling the root causes of pausing, tailored interventions can be designed that more effectively address the specific needs of children with DCD, enhancing their educational experiences and overall quality of life. The journey to unwind the mysteries of DCD and its impact on handwriting is as intricate as the dance of pen on paper but holds the potential to transform the challenges faced by these children into newfound abilities.

The custom has died out of residing above, or even trading above, the ground-floor, till, in the great towns at least, if the nuclear family dwell or carry on their business below, they seem to be pariahs - interlopers on floors that none but servants have any business to tread upon; and the rooms below penthouses, and swollen out by due violation of ancient municipal rights into vast plate-glass shops, where the chances are that the unbonneted mistress may call down the iron shutters with her own hands the moment desertion begins, and she finds herself free to lock up her goods. If you would wish to know how people lived in former days, the counties where old customs last the longest must be searched for the patterns or remains of patterns. It sometimes seems as if the dwellings in great towns had absorbed all the conception and capital which the landowners might have spent on their parks and pleasure-grounds. About sixty years ago, soon after the Prince Regent had set the fashion of growing trees in clumps as ornaments in a park instead of planting them in formal lines by the side of straight avenues (the latter style having been carried to excess about a hundred years before, in imitation of the thorough-paced Frenchman, Le Notre), a gentleman stood considering the improvement necessary to throw all his grounds into one estate, thereby adding a thousand pounds or so to his rental; he thought such a plan could not fail to increase the value of the place fifty per cent., and determined to spare no expense which might secure durability as well as good taste. He employed a celebrated landscape gardener of the new school to form the clumps; and the man selected for this purpose had so much taste, that I have heard those now living say, that he chose every spot admirably, and with a keen appreciation of what would look well forty or fifty years hence, as well as at the time when his labours were to be completed. But unfortunately he died in the midst of his undertakings, without having made any plan or memorandum as to what trees he meant to plant in certain places, reserving them meanwhile by a wooden peg, on which was inscribed such remarks as "Cedar," "Larches," etc.; and as most of these pieces of wood became rotten and the inscriptions undecipherable, the improver found himself suddenly placed in a dilemma, whether to employ some one else to decide upon species, or trust to his own judgment. His own judgment would have done extremely well, could he have obtained all the sorts of trees he wanted from the same nursery garden; but some few of unusual kinds were only to be had of another gardener of repute, living nearly a hundred miles distant. Rather than acknowledge his ignorance, and apply to some brother gardener for assistance, he preferred sending off post-haste to this distance for the requisite number of trees, with no other instruction than that they were to be shrubs of some kind, and of various sorts. Of course, the person applied to executed the order according to his own fancy. My father remembered helping to plant them in my grandfather's absence from home. When they arrived, they proved to be laurels and rhododendrons. The former have grown to immense trees, which shade out a great part of the grass beneath; the latter have spread far and wide, and are considered as dainties by the neighbouring donkeys. The next generation will find out their mistake.

The enamel cubes studied in our preliminary experiments could not withstand high external load applied by direct compression between the platens. Without the protection of the epoxy disk, samples were likely to develop local stress concentrations and/or microcracks that reduce the accuracy of measuring the mechanical behaviour of enamel. Furthermore, due to its birefringent properties, epoxy offers the possibility of deducing information about the stress distribution around the sample using photoelastic techniques. Photoelasticity is a non-destructive, whole-field method widely applied in stress distribution analysis. A number of different models of composite deformation have been previously used to describe the elastic response of mineralized biological tissues that arises through the interaction between different constituent phases [11]. However, these models mainly focused on the analysis of deformation in only one direction (loading direction) and therefore were not able to provide adequate consideration of the elastic anisotropy. Recently, a multiscale Eshelby inclusion model has been established and successfully applied for the evaluation of the mechanical response of human dentine [12] and of the enamel subjected to compression along the longitudinal direction of the rods [19] by capturing the relationship between the nanoscale structure and the macroscopic loading. The multiscale modelling approach was shown to capture the micromechanical response reasonably well using the two-level hierarchical description of the structure of dentine and enamel, with each level consisting of an isotropic matrix and a group of anisotropic inclusions. In this study, in situ photoelasticity and synchrotron WAXS techniques were applied simultaneously to measure the applied stress, the internal HAp crystalline orientation distribution and the elastic lattice strain for three samples of human enamel.

WHAT THE RESEARCH SHOWS CHILDREN NEED CONSISTENCY AND SENSITIVITY FROM BOTH PARENTS Children need a continuing relationship with responsible, sensitive and caring parents, regardless of the structure of the family. It has been shown that children can have healthy development in divorced families, gay and lesbian families, and other types of family structures. It is the quality of the relationship that the parents have with the child that most influences that child's development. Research has not fully addressed the special challenges that children may face in alternative family structures and the strategies that will help children deal effectively with those challenges. Research shows that when mothers get strong emotional, financial, and other support from fathers, children are more likely to be healthier. This effect holds true even in divorce situations. A general conclusion from many studies is that father absence can cause adverse effects in boys, particularly if father absence occurs before age 5. Boys show poor school performance, poor relationships with peers, problems with impulse control and have a variety of adjustment issues. The effects of father absence show up later for girls. Adolescent girls have difficulty in establishing relationships with other men. Discussion on where research is lacking: RESEARCH ON PARENTING MUST INCLUDE FATHERS Too few studies consider the role of fathers; research on parenting usually only includes mothers. Furthermore, for highly porous materials an infiltration step with epoxy or conductive material is required, in order to avoid excessive sample drift, which would cause variations in the prescribed slice thickness and even loss of information in the z-axis direction (anisotropic resolution) [6]. Alternatively, X-ray computed tomography is a powerful non-destructive technique to investigate the inner structure morphology of porous materials [7-9], such as the inverse opal photonic crystals, in a multi length scale approach. In case of the samples studied herein, the resolution of microtomography (micrometer scale) is not enough, but synchrotron tomography, more specifically, ptychographic X-ray computed tomography (PXCT), can image different structural features from the micrometer to the nanometer scale with high resolution, even in air at atmospheric pressure [10,11]. The fabrication process defines the final structure and composition of a photonic material, and therefore, its photonic properties. Inverse opal photonic crystals are usually produced by the infiltration of a polymeric template, also referred to as a direct photonic crystal, which can be assembled by a variety of routes [12]. Infiltration techniques include sol-gel [13], colloidal routes [14,15], chemical vapor deposition (CVD) [16] and atomic layer deposition (ALD) [17]. Inverse opal photonic crystals can also be fabricated in a single-step approach, described as co-deposition [18,19]. Depending on the chosen fabrication technique, a variety of ceramic inverse opal photonic crystal materials can be produced, such as silica [19], titania [17], alumina [14], zirconia [15] and yttria stabilized zirconia (YSZ) [18]. When ranking the techniques, ALD is by far the one with the highest capability for uniform coating of such high aspect ratio structures, by which very high filling fractions and infiltration homogeneity are reported [20]. Moreover, ALD bases on successive, alternating reactions between precursors and substrate, with excellent film thickness control (on the Angstrom-scale) and compositional control [21], even for complex systems such as ternary and quaternary oxides [22]. By ALD, tailor-made atomically mixed systems can be realized, such as mullite, a known refractory ceramic system with high-temperature stability. Deposition of mullite films on planar substrates, not photonic structures, has already been demonstrated by CVD [23], electron beam physical vapor deposition (EB-PVD) [24] and plasma spraying [25]. However, all these processes run at considerably high or very high temperatures, i.e. 600 C [24], 1200 C [23] or even higher (>1800 C) [25], which makes them unviable for infiltration of polymeric templates. In our previous work [26], we demonstrated the possibility of infiltrating Al2O3 inverse opal photonic crystals with mullite by ALD super-cycles performed at 150 C. This deposition temperature is already considered low for ALD [21], however still too high for possible infiltration of polymeric templates, usually based on polystyrene or polymethylmethacrylate latex particles with glass transition temperatures of around 100 C [27]. At temperatures usually used in ALD, polymeric templates may not only decompose, but also be oxidized during oxidant exposure [28], especially in case of ozone [29].

The connections between dragons and prehistoric creatures extend far beyond the regions initially explored by Mayer. In many cultures, dragons have taken on symbolic meanings that surpass their physical representations. They are often depicted as guardians of treasure, representing both the fearsome challenges and grand rewards that life can offer. This dual representation can be seen in ancient mythology, where dragons were fierce protectors of sacred lands or divine secrets, making them both revered and feared. One interesting facet of dragon lore is how its narrative has evolved in literature and entertainment. In medieval Europe, dragons became emblematic of chaos and evil, foes to be vanquished by noble knights. This portrayal consolidated with stories like that of St. George and the Dragon, where the dragon represents the ultimate adversary requiring heroism and virtue to overcome. The narrative suggests not only a literal battle but a metaphoric one against life's innate challenges and internal struggles. Yet, the adaptability of dragons doesn't stop there. As we shift into modern pop culture, dragons often shed their ominous exteriors to take on more complex roles, showcasing attributes like wisdom, companionship, and even benevolence. They appear as wise advisers or misunderstood creatures, urging an exploration of themes like misunderstood identities and prejudice. Iconic modern portrayals like Smaug in Tolkien's "The Hobbit" reinforce the dangerous allure of dragons, while simultaneously instigating dialogues on greed and power. In Eastern traditions, especially in Chinese culture, dragons have long been revered as symbols of potency, strength, and good luck. You'll often see the dragon linked with water, believing it to have control over rain, rivers, lakes, and seas. During the Chinese New Year, dragon dances are performed to summon prosperity, health, and happiness. This positive association provides a stark contrast to Western representations, where dragons are often harbingers of chaos or malevolence. Eastern dragons, unlike their Western counterparts, are celebrated for their benevolence and ability to grant blessings. This divergence in perception reiterates the importance of cultural context in mythology. It reminds us that folklore develops from unique societal values and geographical circumstances-a dragon feared in one culture may be treasured in another. Moreover, the depiction of dragons continues to evolve as we uncover more about our own world and the history of life on Earth. As theoretical ties between dragons and dinosaur fossils continue to provide material for speculation, the awe-inspiring nature of these creatures persists in capturing human imagination. The dragon, whether a celestial being or a monstrous antagonist, serves as a reminder of both the creative depths of human storytelling and the intricate ties to nature's mysteries we seek to understand. In closing today's exploration of dragons, one cannot ignore the universal threads of fear, wonder, and curiosity these mythical creatures weave through our civilizations. Dragons, those enigmatic creations of cultural narrative and ancient lore, retain a timeless place in our collective consciousness. Whether soaring high above in tales of fantasy or lying dormant in our fears and dreams, dragons remain the ultimate emblem of humankind's enduring fascination with the extraordinary.

We all burst out laughing again at that, and this time Mark joined in, his stutter getting worse with every word. "W-w-well, I g-g-guess I got t-t-taken in," he said, wiping his eyes with his sleeve. We laughed so hard we had to hold our sides, and I think we would have laughed ourselves sick if we hadn't been so hungry. As it was, our laughter was mixed with groans and growls from our empty stomachs. Finally, we got ourselves under control and looked around for a way to get some food. The hotel, of course, was no good, but we spotted a little general store down the road and decided to try our luck there. Mark, still chuckling, led the way, and we trooped after him, our feet kicking up dust on the deserted road. The store was a tiny place, with a porch that creaked under our weight, but it looked like it might have some food inside. We pushed open the door and stepped into a dim, musty smell that made our noses wrinkle. The owner, an old man with a long white beard, looked up from behind the counter and eyed us like we were a bunch of vagrants. "What can I do for you young fellas?" he asked, his voice as gruff as the mountains themselves. Mark, still grinning, stepped forward. "W-w-we're l-l-looking for s-s-some grub," he said. "We came to stay at the hotel, but it seems to be c-c-closed." The old man's face creased into a thousand wrinkles as he laughed. "You boys must be the ones from Michigan," he said. "I heard you were coming. I've been expecting you." We exchanged a puzzled glance, but the old man just winked and said, "I'll get you fixed up. You boys must be starved." He disappeared into the back room and came out with a big basket of sandwiches, some apples, and a jug of milk. We fell on the food like wolves, and for a few minutes, the only sound was the crunch of bites and the gurgle of milk being poured into cups. As we ate, the old man told us that the hotel had been closed for years, and that the advertising book we'd seen was just a leftover from better days. He said the town had been waiting for us, and that we were the best joke that had come to those parts in a long time. We laughed again, feeling a little silly but also relieved that we weren't going to starve to death in the mountains. And Mark, well, he just shook his head and said, "I g-g-guess I'll have to be more c-c-careful with my r-r-research next time." As we finished up and prepared to leave, the old man handed us a note. "This is from the folks in town," he said. "They want to invite you to a big supper tonight, to make up for the hotel being closed." We looked at each other, and I could see the wheels turning in our heads. We might have gotten taken in by a fake hotel, but it looked like we were going to get a vacation out of it after all. And Mark, well, he was already grinning, ready to take on whatever else Vermont had in store for us.

I have not spoken harshly to you, nor have I punished you; but remember that I have power to do both." "I will try to be better, father," I replied. "I promise you, I will." "And remember that if you again offend, you will receive a severe chastisement," he rejoined. "Now, go back to the house and give up these guns and dogs to the care of one of the servants." I left him, deeply affected by his words, and resolved to mend my ways. Indeed, I felt ashamed of myself, and determined not to expose my parents to the disgrace which their son's misdeeds would bring upon them. As I walked slowly homeward, I thought of the scenes I had witnessed since leaving home. I had shot three wild geese, five partridges, and four rabbits. One of the latter I had killed with my knife, having missed him with my gun. I thought, moreover, of the many other birds and beasts which I had slain during the past year. I remembered that my father had repeatedly warned me against continuing the practice. He told me that it was wrong, and that it would end in my destruction, either by imprisonment or transportation. He advised me to give up hunting altogether, and to devote myself to study. But I paid little heed to his counsels, and often went forth alone to shoot whatever game I met with. I sometimes acted as a guide to young gentlemen who came down to stay at the neighbouring seats. They were generally eager to bag some game, and I gladly undertook to assist them. In addition to the above, I was frequently employed in beating the woods and fields, and driving the game towards the shooters. I considered that I was entitled to the greater part of what I killed, and to the whole of what I caught with my snares. Sometimes I sold the game to a butcher in the village, who bought it cheaply and resold it at high prices. To him I gave the names of the gentlemen to whom the game belonged. I kept the proceeds of my labours to myself. Thus, by degrees, I became a thorough poacher. During the last autumn I had made several attempts to trap a fox, but had failed. I had also tried to snare a hare, but without success. This morning, however, I had taken both. The fox had fallen into one of my traps, set under a hedge; and the hare had been entangled in another placed in the corner of a field. I had just secured them when my father came up. I had intended to hide the animals, but it was too late.

Conventional studies on drawing robots have applied a model that can convert captured images into sets of trajectories of the robot's hand. Calinon et al. [7]proposed a humanoid robot system for drawing human portraits. First, this system extracts the main lines of an image using the Canny edge detector [8]. In addition, the model creates a backup of the image in order to maintain the face details, which could disappear after the edge detection. Finally, the model produces the trajectory of the robot's hand, and the robot follows that trajectory. Kudoh et al. [9]explicitly divided the drawing process into developing the shape model of the target object and producing a series of lines that form a hand-drawn-like picture. When the thickness of the lines is not uniform, e.g., when a brush is used, it is necessary to simulate the drawn lines and update the generated trajectory in order to produce a natural order of strokes [10-12]. These studies have a common "top-down" approach in the perception of the visual information on the target and the conversion into a trajectory of the robot's end effector by a well-designed strategy. Although this approach contributes to understanding artistic expression by representing drawing styles [13], it is difficult to compare with human's drawing-related cognitive studies, because the characteristic of the model directly depends on the experimenter's policy. In contrast, a few recent studies have utilized a "bottom-up" approach. Cognitive developmental robotics [14]attempt to develop a corresponding computational model that replicates this set of complex cognitive skills. Mohan et al. [15]proposed a learning model based on the catastrophe theory that uses primitive features of shapes, called "critical points". Their model learns to draw a sequence by decomposing shapes and generates drawing motions by synthesizing the primitive features. Mochizuki et al. [16,17]proposed a dynamical learning model that acquires skills of drawing simple shapes through incremental learning with human-robot interactions. In their study, a robot learns the relationships between the pen's position and the joint angles by moving its right arm randomly. Afterward, the robot develops its drawing skills through incremental learning by adding pause phases at the edge of shapes. Although the "bottom-up" approach was adopted by some studies, they have not considered both temporal drawn images and motion, which mainly forms the robot's drawing experiences.

As we trudged through the snow, the biting wind whipping our faces, I couldn't help but think about the absurdity of it all. A popsicle on the ice? It was a joke. A cruel, cruel joke. But, of course, I had to play along. I had to humor Professor Sapperstein's wild goose chase, just in case it was more than just a prank. "So, what's the plan, Professor?" I asked, trying to keep my tone neutral. "Ah, Marshal Stetko, always the pragmatist," he said, his eyes twinkling with excitement. "We're going to follow the trail of clues, of course. We'll start with the pilot who spotted the popsicle, Delfy. He might remember something useful." I raised an eyebrow. "Useful? What could a popsicle possibly have to do with anything?" Sapperstein chuckled. "Ah, but that's the beauty of it, Marshal. We don't know what it has to do with anything. Yet. But sometimes the most seemingly insignificant things can lead to the most extraordinary discoveries." I sighed, resigned. "Fine. Let's get moving. But if this is some kind of prank, Sapperstein, I'm going to make sure you regret it." He grinned. "Oh, I'm shaking in my boots, Marshal. Now, let's go find that popsicle." As we made our way to the hangar, I couldn't help but think about the strange occurrences that had been plaguing the base lately. Equipment malfunctioning, strange noises in the night, and now a popsicle on the ice. It was all starting to feel like some kind of bizarre dream. But I pushed those thoughts aside, focusing on the task at hand. I had a job to do, and I was going to see it through. Even if it meant chasing after a frozen treat on the ice. As we arrived at the hangar, I spotted Delfy, the pilot who had spotted the popsicle. He looked nervous, fidgety, like he was trying to get out of there as fast as possible. "Hey, Delfy," I said, trying to sound friendly. "What's going on? What did you see?" Delfy hesitated, then spoke in a rush. "I-I saw something, Marshal. A popsicle, just lying there on the ice. It was... it was weird. I mean, I've never seen anything like it before." I raised an eyebrow. "Weird how?" Delfy shrugged. "I don't know. It was just... it was just there. And then it was gone. I didn't see anyone around, but I could've sworn I saw something moving out of the corner of my eye." I exchanged a look with Sapperstein. This was getting weirder by the minute. "Okay, Delfy," I said. "We'll take a look. Let's get the plane ready to go out there and investigate." As we prepared for takeoff, I couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. What were we getting ourselves into? And what did it have to do with the strange occurrences on the base? But I pushed those thoughts aside, focusing on the task at hand. I was a United States Marshal, and I would see this through to the end. Even if it meant facing whatever was out there on the ice.

For example, NVB302 has completed Phase 1 clinical trials and MU1140 is in preclinical development, both for treatment of C. difficile infections.11 Nisin is the most widely studied member of the lantibiotics (Fig. 1). It has broad spectrum antimicrobial activity, notably against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and vancomycin resistant enterococci (VRE). Despite widespread use as a food preservative12 over a period of decades few nisin-resistant strains have been reported (via mechanisms such as nisin-degrading enzymes and modification of the cell wall13). It binds with high selectivity to lipid II, a key biosynthetic precursor of the bacterial cell wall, with the resulting 8:4 nisin:lipid II complex leading to the formation of pores in the bacterial membrane.14,15 NMR studies have revealed key interactions between rings A and B of nisin and the pyrophosphate moiety of lipid II.16 Although the nisin(1-12) fragment, which just comprises rings A and B, has little or no antibacterial activity,17,18 it is able to antagonise the activity of full-length nisin, suggesting that this fragment recognises and maintains affinity for lipid II.17 After binding to lipid II, the C-terminal moiety, nisin(23-33), comprising the DE rings, inserts into the bacterial membrane to form the pore structure.19 The structural role of ring C and the "hinge region" (nisin(20-22)) is not completely understood, but are clearly important for the activity of nisin. Flexibility in this region is one key factor. Mutagenesis studies have shown reduced activity when Pro residues are introduced at positions 20 and 21;20 although binding to lipid II is still possible, the assembly and membrane insertion of the nisin:lipid II pore complex is prevented by these mutations.19 In support of this, screening of a library of mutants of all three hinge positions identified sequences such as Ala-Ala-Ala and Ala-Ala-Ser, with small, chiral amino acids, as leading to improved activity.21 Shorter hinge region mutants showed greatly reduced activity but mutants with two extra amino acids were well tolerated,22 and mutations in this region were also found to increase activity against significant pathogens such as MRSA and VRE.23 The total synthesis of nisin using a segment synthesis approach24 and the solid-phase peptide synthesis of fragments and analogues of nisin25-30 as well as of other lantibiotics31,32 has been reported.

However, there is no effective implementation of this legislation. Under international law, it is the duty of the state to protect people from torture and other ill-treatment. This includes preventing torture and punishing those responsible. The UN Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment requires governments to take appropriate measures to ensure that acts of torture do not go unpunished. In addition, under the ICCPR, individuals whose rights have been violated by agents of the state are entitled to an effective remedy before competent national authorities. They must also be able to obtain compensation if they have suffered material loss. In practice, however, the Iraqi judiciary fails to provide an effective remedy for the victims of torture. Relatives of victims who are prepared to speak publicly about their ordeal often face threats and harassment. 2 THE REPORTING OF TORTURE AND OTHER ILL-TREATMENT BY AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL Amnesty International has documented widespread torture and other ill-treatment in Iraq since 1985. The organization has received reports of torture and ill-treatment from former detainees who were arrested during the Gulf War, from political detainees, from people detained for religious reasons, and from people detained in connection with criminal offences. Reports of torture and ill-treatment have come from all over Iraq. Amnesty International has also received reports of torture and other ill-treatment of people detained after demonstrations. Such detentions took place during the demonstrations against the Gulf War in February 1991, the demonstrations in support of the uprising in southern Iraq in March 1991, the demonstrations in support of the uprising in northern Iraq in September 1996, and the demonstrations against the arrest of Shi'a leader Ayatollah Muhammad Sadiq al-Sadr in February 1999. Amnesty International has sent delegates to visit Iraq on several occasions but has never been granted permission to enter the country. The organization has, however, received reports from independent sources within Iraq about torture and ill-treatment in Iraqi prisons and detention centres. These reports have included detailed descriptions of the methods used. Most reports have come from former detainees, some of whom have fled the country, others of whom remain inside Iraq. Some of them have submitted written statements to Amnesty International describing their experiences. Others have spoken to the organization via telephone. Many reports have come from Iraqi refugees living in neighbouring countries, particularly Jordan and Syria. Amnesty International has also received reports from diplomats stationed in Iraq and from foreign nationals who have visited Iraq. In addition, Amnesty International has received reports from the families of people who have disappeared into Iraqi custody, sometimes after being taken away by members of the security forces. 3 TORTURE IN IRAQ The following section describes torture techniques that have been reported to Amnesty International. All of these techniques violate the absolute prohibition against torture under international law. A. Beatings Beatings are among the most common torture techniques. People are beaten with fists, sticks, whips and cables. They may also be kicked repeatedly until they lose consciousness. The beating may last hours. Sometimes beatings continue until the victim dies. B. Suspension and flogging Suspending a detainee upside down by the feet or hands is another common method of torture. Detainees are suspended either from hooks or bars or tied up. Their hands and legs may be bound behind their backs or they may be tied up with ropes. During suspension, they may be beaten or shocked with electric current. When the detainee loses consciousness, he or she is lowered back onto the floor where they may be further beaten.

I tell my college freshman when we talk about The Will of God as a Way of Life that I've never experienced the will of God as a path - or even the clear blazes on trees spaced evenly apart. What always happens to me is that anytime that my to-do list abates enough for me to take stock of where I am, make a decision, decide to follow God, or try to make sense of my life - that I look around me and I find that I'm at the deepest place imaginable in the woods. Nothing is recognizable. There are no clearings in the distance. But I hear a whisper - "over here." But by the time I turn around, there's no voice. Maybe even there never was a voice. But *now* there's something about *this* direction which makes a bit of sense so I move... But to you, reader, this woodsy metaphor seems to offer irational hope. A "feeling of peace" emerging from...what? A confidence which doesn't make sense out of any particular past. It doesn't offer promise about what's come before.... But you weren't lucky enough to have grown up at Treasure Island with me, either. Every summer, our family pilgrimaged North to the Upper Peninsula of Michigan where we wound down a two lane highway to a dirt and gravel road, hewn out of the woods by my grandfather. You didn't feel the surge of endorphins that we all did as we peered through the windshield and through the dense pine forest and strained at the curves in the road, the whole station wagon engulfed by a rollicking chorus of "Around the Corner's the Cabin!" (to the tune of "for he's a jolly good fellow". There - that's all you needed to sing it - because there are no other lyrics - "and now we're almost there" - sometimes).

After much deliberation and a few well-deserved chuckles, we reluctantly came to the conclusion that the ladder simply wasn't going to fit. I knew the ladder was a bit long-but in our defense, we weren't entirely prepared for the stubbornness that would ensue when we attempted to maneuver that pesky contraption into the trunk. So, there we were, wedged in what felt like a comedy sketch-Jeff and I, turning the ladder every conceivable way and adjusting our approach multiple times as if we could somehow cheat physics with sheer determination. Cinder eagerly wagged her tail, completely oblivious to the growing chaos around her. She seemed quite pleased with all the attention and the occasional pats on her head, blissfully enjoying the errand, which was, to her, just another adventure. Finally, after what felt like an eternity of wrestling with the ladder and trying to mold it to our will, we laughed and decided to take a slightly more desperate approach. Jeff suggested we try strapping part of the ladder to the roof of the car using a spare tie-down cord we had in the trunk. This would not only allow us to transport the ladder but would also add a touch of intrigue to our small-town drive-who wouldn't appreciate a car with a ladder strapped precariously to the roof? With our adventure finally set in motion, we carefully loaded Cinder back into the car, ensuring she had a clear view of the outside world. There was something delightfully freeing about driving through our neighborhood with flair and folly. As we navigated back home, I turned up the music and we sang along, creating a joyful atmosphere that overshadowed any annoyance from our previous shenanigans. Once we made it home with the ladder successfully (if not aesthetically) attached, we made our way inside and tackled the task at hand. As Jeff climbed up the rungs, I played the supportive role on the ground, handing him tools and holding the chandelier as he delicately positioned it above our staircase. He sweat and strained, taking careful consideration of each adjustment and bolt, while I worried audibly that he was going to topple over in his haste and ambition. But Jeff is a determined fellow, and after some maneuvering that rivaled a Cirque du Soleil performance, he finally had the chandelier hanging gracefully-final touches included, of course. We stepped back, looking up at our labors and admired our handiwork. The old, broken chandelier was now gone, replaced by a beautiful new piece that boasted delicate crystal accents that shimmered in the light. We decided to call over William and Marie to see the end result, so they could also catch a glimpse of our handiwork. When they arrived, Cinder bounced happily around them and we all took a moment to marvel at the transformation of our stairwell. Conversation flowed easily, full of laughter and the comfortable cadence of good friends. Marie, always keen to share a lighthearted moment, began recounting a story about how William had almost dropped a chandelier when they had done theirs a few years ago. The evening was turning out to be funnier and more rewarding than we had anticipated. It was these moments that reminded us of the strong bonds we've formed in our community, even in the face of challenges. Whether it was fixing a tire or hanging a chandelier, everything was always a little easier when friends were by your side.

However, the effect of local haemodynamics on plaque initiation has been poorly studied in the literature. Only a few studies focus on the effect of local haemodynamics on the distribution of lesions along the artery, and those studies are limited to the carotid arteries [29-32]. The aim of the present work is to investigate the effect of local haemodynamics on the distribution of atherosclerotic lesions along the coronary artery tree. To achieve this goal, we use a statistical approach based on a large database of patient-specific computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. We simulate the blood flow in 300 patient-specific models of coronary arteries using CFD and compute the haemodynamic parameters WSS, OSI and RRT. Then, we perform principal component analysis (PCA), which is a dimensionality reduction method, to extract relevant information about the spatial distribution of the three haemodynamic parameters along the coronary artery tree. PCA allows us to build a correlation matrix between the different locations of interest and the three computed haemodynamic parameters. We analyse the data obtained through PCA using a specific methodology inspired by the literature on gene expression data analysis. This methodology, called 'significance analysis of microarrays' (SAM), allows us to identify significant correlations between the different locations of interest and the three computed haemodynamic parameters. We finally compare our results with the location of the atherosclerotic lesions observed in patients undergoing coronary angiography. Our study demonstrates that the local haemodynamics influence the location of atherosclerotic lesions in the coronary artery tree. It also shows that there exists a good agreement between the predicted lesion locations and the ones observed in patients. 2.1 Data acquisition To construct our database, we used a set of 100 clinical cases of left coronary artery stenosis acquired during routine cardiac catheterization procedures. All patients were referred for elective percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA). They presented with a single de novo stenosis located in one major epicardial vessel. Stenoses were considered de novo if no previous PTCA was performed at the same site and if the lesion was visible on both the pre- and post-dilatation angiograms. In case of multiple lesions, only the most severe was considered. Patients suffering from congenital heart diseases or valvular abnormalities were excluded from the study. We then constructed a three-dimensional (3D) geometrical model of each coronary artery using the angiographic images. Each 3D model consisted of a set of contours extracted manually from the angiogram series. The contours were connected together to obtain the corresponding 3D geometrical mesh, which was then discretized into tetrahedral elements using the software ICEM-CFD (version 11.0, ANSYS Inc., Canonsburg, PA, USA). In order to get a larger database, we chose to increase the number of cases rather than increasing the resolution of the mesh. Indeed, the resolution of the meshes used here is high enough to capture the flow features and to accurately predict the haemodynamic parameters of interest. Moreover, the choice to keep the resolution constant allows us to avoid any possible bias when analysing the data using PCA. Thus, the resolution of the meshes was chosen to be fine enough to ensure convergence of the numerical solution and to provide accurate predictions of the haemodynamic parameters. More precisely, the average size of the elements is equal to 200 mu m, while the maximum element size does not exceed 400 mu m. An example of the mesh used in our study is given in figure 1. Speed forward to the general election of 2005, where Huhne is fighting the Tory-held marginal of Eastleigh, Hampshire, and we find his election literature desperately gushing: 'Family matters to me so much. Where would we be without them?' Affair: Chris Huhne, right, arrives at court for his hearing, with Carina Trimingham. Pre-election leaflets shoved through voters' front doors showed pictures of his wedding with the caption 'Getting married does not seem like 26 years ago', and another picture of him feeding a baby, with the caption, 'I took to becoming a father so seriously I gave up smoking'. Just how important family matters really were to Chris Huhne became crystal clear in June, 2010 when it emerged that, for perhaps two years, he had been having a secret affair with his former press officer, Carina Trimingham, who was in a civil partnership with a woman. He had even been using his Hampshire constituency home for trysts with Miss Trimingham, now 45, and 13 years younger than his wife. Disclosure of the affair in two Sunday newspapers produced an almost comic response from the Cabinet Minister, showing how easily he dismissed moral issues. In a carbon copy of that other Cabinet rank politician, Labour's late Robin Cook, another dedicated family politician caught bang-to-rights in an affair with his secretary, Huhne immediately issued a statement saying: 'I am in a serious relationship with Carina Trimingham and am separating from my wife.' (Cook was actually at the airport about to go on holiday with his wife when he was forced by Alastair Campbell to decide - wife or mistress.) Ms Pryce, a thoughtful figure, is best remembered that difficult day for despatching her son Peter to the newsagents to buy all the papers. But it was a full 11 months later that the allegation which would destroy him first appeared in a Sunday newspaper. Imagine Huhne's horror at this exposure, the loss of face over something, in retrospect, so ludicrously trivial. Fleeting victory: Chris Huhne and Vicky Pryce celebrate his 2010 election win, but Huhne is now contemplating a prison sentence for perverting the course of justice. This is a man used to brushing awkward inconveniences aside, a millionaire politician whose expenses included receipts for bus tickets, milk and loo rolls, as well as 119 for a Corby trouser press, but who had the temerity to declare with typical passion on his (now former) constituency website that 'MPs should spend the taxpayers' money more carefully.' Huhne and Trimingham were living together and he had been hoping that his domestic troubles were behind him. He was even quietly eyeing the party leadership again - despite having thrown his hat twice into the ring and lost - as Nick Clegg struggled to maintain party support within the Coalition. The first time he had lost to Sir 'Ming' Campbell in 2006 - impudent, really, for an MP who'd been in the Commons less than a year.

I don't worry about sources of oil; I love mayo, butter, etc. It does add up, so I tend to eat most oils in the form of salad dressing and grill my meat as opposed to pan-fry it. b) Carbohydrates cause cravings. It's tough, but once you cut out bread, potatoes, rice, pasta, and sugar, after 3-5 days you quit craving it. As long as you are on it you will desire it. c) Staying away from such carbs means insulin levels will be level. You will feel better overall. I never realized how moody I got until I stopped (well, almost stopped) eating all that crap. I have more energy and get more accomplished. d) Good carbs are vegetables; your body takes a while to digest them. Some fruit is okay, like melons and berries, but eat them sparingly. I eat at least one salad a day plus one cooked veggie, like broccoli, snow peas, greens, or stir-fry. Sometimes I eat 2 salads. e) Your ratio of protein to carbs to fat should (roughly) be: 30%5%65%. Or, eat at least 1 gram of protein per pound of lean body mass(if you weight train). Do not skimp out on fat! Again, this will help you maintain the muscle you have. f) If you weight train, invest in whey protein. Find a brand that tastes good. Take a certain amount (I take enough to give me 20g of protein, more than enough) after a workout so your body won't chew on its own muscle. Rule 3: Diets can be boring. Vary them; find good cook books (at LEAST the Joy of Cooking). Rule 4: Tupperware (in the generic sense; that stuff's expensive)! a) I eat 3 of my meals at work. I buy the cheap stuff so that if I lose one or have to throw it away because it was left in the hot car for 3 days I don't stress. b) Try to prepare things ahead of time.
