Crucially, the control of metabolic rate can be linked not only to temperature regulation but also to energy balance and hormonal fluctuations that are intimately tied to seasonal changes [12]. The many adaptive strategies displayed by the Microcebus species highlight the intricate relationship between physiology and environmental pressures, showcasing the evolutionary significance of torpor and hibernation mechanisms. In most mammals, the switch into a torpid state is marked by the secretion of specific hormones, particularly melatonin and cortisol. These hormones facilitate the adjustment of the circadian rhythm and metabolic functions, enabling a temporary shutdown of daily physiological activities without compromising the organism's overall fitness [13]. For the mouse lemurs, studies reveal that the hypometabolic state can manifest within hours, yet the ability to sustain such states for extended periods hinges on various preconditioning factors. Such preconditioning encompasses adequate fat storage in the lead-up to winter months, a clockwork-like preparation that is both physiological and behavioral in nature [14]. The seasonal dynamics experienced by mouse lemurs are a critical aspect of their life history strategy. As summer days wane, these small primates engage in a preparatory phase termed "hyperphagia," characterized by increased foraging and energy intake to accumulate lipid reserves for the impending scarcity of sustenance [15]. The efficiency with which they convert food into energy reserves is, in part, dictated by their gastrointestinal functionality, which demonstrates plasticity in response to diet composition across seasons [16]. Once these reserves are adequately built during the autumn months, lemurs initiate their torpor cycles in response to environmental cues such as dwindling daylight and dropping temperatures [8]. What makes this adaptation particularly fascinating is the emergent evidence suggesting that these adaptations are not merely passive responses but are actively regulated by a suite of genes involved in metabolic reprogramming. Recent genomic studies have identified gene expression changes associated with metabolic pathways that facilitate energy conservation during torpor, including shifts in mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, and thermal protection mechanisms [17]. This intricate orchestration of genetic responses elucidates how mouse lemurs, despite their small size, exhibit remarkable resilience and adaptability in the face of ecological unpredictability. Moreover, the evolutionary trajectory that has led to these adaptations raises intriguing questions about the ancestral states of torpor in mammals. Given the phylogenetic evidence indicating a common lineage for torpor-capable primates, the implications for understanding human evolution and physiology become profound. The potential parallels between the metabolic flexibility exhibited by mouse lemurs and the adaptive qualities of early hominins rush into view, suggesting that the ancestral lineage may have also harnessed these physiological tools during periods of environmental volatility [18]. In conclusion, the remarkable abilities of mouse lemurs to navigate seasonal hardships through metabolic modulation offer a compelling glimpse into the resilience inherent within mammalian life. Future research endeavors focused on the molecular underpinnings of these processes will further clarify not only the physiological nuances of torpor and hibernation but also the broader implications for biodiversity conservation as climate change continues to reshape the environments in which these species exist. As scientists delve deeper into the genetic and biochemical intricacies of these remarkable adaptations, the future of understanding mammalian survival strategies remains as dynamic and intriguing as the species at the heart of this exploration.

They were evidently going out for a stroll in the cool sea breeze before dinner. "You are well acquainted with the city?" said Don Jose de Mendoza, addressing one of the officers. "Perfectly," replied he addressed, "I have been stationed here three years." "I thought so," returned the other, "and I am glad to find it confirmed. You know how fond my daughter is of sight seeing, and she has never been here before." "Oh! yes, indeed," replied the officer, "we shall take great pleasure in showing you everything worth seeing, especially if we may be permitted to do so under your guidance." The old gentleman bowed assent, and the party moved on. "How many years is it since you came to Cuba, Don Jose?" asked the younger officer. "It is now just six years," replied the other. "But I am thinking of leaving it soon. My affairs require me to go to Spain." "And what will become of your estates?" asked the first speaker. "They will remain here," replied Don Jose, "under the care of a steward, until I come back again. I shall leave them in good hands, and hope to find them safe when I return." "But suppose you should never come back," suggested the young man, "what would become of them?" "That is easily told," answered the father, glancing affectionately toward his fair companion; "they would belong to yonder child. She is the only heir I have, and she would inherit everything I possess." "So much the better!" cried the elder of the two officers, "for she is already rich enough to set up half a dozen husbands!" Don Jose smiled at the remark, but did not reply. "I wonder if she would ever think of marrying a poor fellow like myself!" continued the speaker, gazing tenderly into the dark eyes of the lady, who blushed and looked down, but made no answer. "What would be the use of such a match?" asked the young man, laughing; "you would only get enough to pay your debts, and then you would be as bad off as ever." "Not quite as bad off," returned the other, still regarding the lady, "for I should have a wife, and that would make me happy." "Ay, for a time," remarked Don Jose, smiling, "but not always. A woman is like a flower - beautiful while fresh, but fading and worthless when plucked." "That depends upon circumstances," said the other; "there are flowers that bloom forever, and women who grow lovelier as they advance in life. I have seen both." "No doubt," responded the old gentleman, "but they are rare exceptions to the rule. But come, let us turn our attention to something else. Yonder, Senora, is the Moro Castle. What do you think of its appearance?" The lady raised her eyes to the massive pile, whose gray battlements frowned down upon the bay, and gave utterance to an exclamation of surprise. "Is it really built of stone?" she asked. "Yes, of solid masonry," replied her father. "It is one of the strongest fortresses in the world, and contains a garrison of five hundred men. If it should ever fall into the hands of the enemy, the city must follow." "The walls of Havana are also strong," observed one of the officers. "Yes," replied Don Jose, "but not so strong as the castle. Still, they are impregnable to any force that could possibly assail them. There is nothing to fear from an attack either by land or water."

The second characteristic of the proposed model involves recognizing and reproducing drawings. This allows robots to effectively associate the visual representation of a picture with the corresponding motor actions needed to reproduce it. In essence, this process mimics the human ability to interpret visual stimuli and convert them into coordinated motor activities that result in accurate drawings. By leveraging the association capability, robots can not only recognize a wide range of hand-drawn pictures but also replicate them with high fidelity. This association is an emergent property of the complex interplay between visual perception and motor execution, deeply rooted in the mechanisms governing visuomotor integration within the cortex. Moreover, implementing this model requires rigorous training through iterative learning processes. Robots undergo extensive training sessions, where they are exposed to a variety of hand-drawn shapes and tasked with replicating them. Throughout this training, the model refines its internal representation of visuomotor memory, thereby enhancing its ability to recognize and reproduce increasingly complex patterns. The training process involves feedback mechanisms, which evaluate the accuracy of each drawing task, and adjustments are made accordingly to optimize performance. This mirrors the way humans refine their drawing skills over time through practice and feedback. A crucial aspect of developing the proposed model is ensuring its adaptability to novel stimuli. The model is designed to generalize learned information and apply it to new, unseen shapes, thereby demonstrating cognitive flexibility akin to human creativity. This adaptability hinges on the model's ability to dynamically adjust its visuomotor associations in response to new perceptual experiences. By facilitating generalized learning, robots can navigate diverse drawing scenarios autonomously, enhancing their utility across varying applications, from art creation to technical drafting. In advancing this research, there is a substantial emphasis on understanding the neural correlates of visuomotor memory in humans. Insights gained from cognitive neuroscience contribute to refining the computational model, ensuring its alignment with biological processes. Investigations into areas such as the premotor cortex and parietal lobe, which play pivotal roles in the integration of sensory and motor functions, provide valuable guidance in scaling computational models towards human-like capabilities. Ultimately, the development of a robust computational model for robot drawing based on visuomotor memory has far-reaching implications. Not only does it enhance the field of robotics by endowing machines with sophisticated perceptual and motor skills, but it also enriches the understanding of human cognition. By serving as a bridge between human neuromechanics and artificial intelligence, this research fosters advancements in both domains, facilitating the creation of machines capable of seamlessly interacting with the artistic aspects of human culture. Continued exploration in this area will likely yield further insights into the fundamental processes underlying creativity and motor coordination. As models become increasingly sophisticated and neurobiologically plausible, the boundary between human creativity and robotic interpretation continues to blur. This convergence promises a future where robots not only execute predefined motions but also contribute creatively to human endeavors, offering novel perspectives and enriching the artistic landscape. The ultimate aim is to cultivate an intricate tapestry of shared understanding between humans and machines, rooted in the timeless art of drawing and the boundless potential of cognitive interplay.

In this context, these guidelines and frameworks have played a pivotal role in addressing the vulnerabilities inherent in SCADA systems. As the digital landscape evolves, so do the threats, necessitating a layered defense strategy to shield critical infrastructure. One such approach is the Defense-in-Depth (DiD) strategy, which incorporates multiple security controls and safeguards distributed across various layers of an ICS. This approach not only mitigates risks but also ensures that even if one control fails, others will provide the necessary protection (Stouffer et al., 2011). Further emphasizing the need for robust security measures, the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) developed the IEC 62443 series of standards. These are tailored to various facets of ICS security, ranging from establishing security program requirements for industrial automation and control systems to defining security levels and zones (International Electrotechnical Commission, 2013). Such standards act as comprehensive guidelines for companies aiming to fortify their SCADA networks against potential threats. As SCADA systems continue to integrate with IT networks, they no longer remain isolated. This amalgamation has greatly benefited operational efficiencies but simultaneously expanded the attack surface for adversaries (Byres et al., 2004; Weir et al., 2008). In recent years, the threat landscape has witnessed the emergence of sophisticated cyber threats, including Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) explicitly targeting SCADA systems. These threats are often orchestrated by well-resourced adversaries, including nation-states, who aim to disrupt the functionality of critical infrastructure for strategic gains (Stuxnet Report, 2011). Notable incidents, such as the Stuxnet worm discovered in 2010, underscore the potential devastation that well-coordinated cyber-attacks can wreak on SCADA systems. This particular malware demonstrated unparalleled sophistication, explicitly targeting Siemens PLCs and exemplifying how vulnerable industrial control systems can be when lacking adequate protections (Langner, 2011). Consequently, it became a wake-up call for governments and industries worldwide, leading to intensified efforts in bolstering SCADA security and resilience. Developing a culture of security awareness and incident preparedness within organizations managing SCADA systems is crucial. Training personnel to recognize and respond to potential security incidents can drastically reduce the impact of cyber-attacks (Ten et al., 2008). Moreover, conducting regular security audits and vulnerability assessments ensures the identification and rectification of potential security loopholes. Another essential aspect of enhancing SCADA security involves implementing real-time monitoring and anomaly detection systems. These systems not only provide visibility into network activities but also facilitate prompt responses to unusual behavior indicative of possible intrusions (Goldenberg and Wool, 2013). Addressing these challenges requires a collaborative effort between governments, industries, and cybersecurity experts to create a resilient environment equipped to withstand diverse cyber threats. The future of SCADA systems relies heavily on ongoing advancements in technology and security practices. With the emergence of IoT and Industry 4.0, SCADA systems must adapt, incorporating new technologies while maintaining rigorous security standards. By fostering innovation and maintaining vigilance, SCADA systems can continue to play a crucial role in safeguarding national infrastructure and ensuring the uninterrupted delivery of essential services.

With respect to disgust stimuli, activation in the TPJ might reflect the redirection of attention away from a disgusting stimulus location. We therefore expect that validity effects in the TPJ reverse when targets are cued by disgust stimuli; that is, greater activity is expected in the TPJ for valid target positions compared to invalid target positions. Other brain areas might also show an interaction between emotion and validity. FMRI studies investigating spatial cueing effects with emotional cues different from disgust such as fear or anger (Pourtois et al., 2006; Reeck et al., 2012; Carlson et al., 2009) found increased activity in extrastriate visual cortex for validly versus invalidly cued targets. This is similar to studies that used emotionally neutral cues (fMRI: Santangelo et al., 2009; Zimmer and Macaluso, 2007; EEG: Eimer, 2000), as well as to studies that used crossmodal paradigms with neutral cues (Macaluso et al., 2000). Another brain area sensitive to the direction of spatial attention due to cueing is the inferior parietal lobule (IPL). Using fearful facial cues followed by neutral targets, Pourtois et al. (2006) found increased activity in the IPL for validly versus invalidly cued targets. Likewise, in a crossmodal spatial cueing paradigm with neutral cues, Macaluso et al. (2000) found also increased brain activation in inferior parietal cortex next to extrastriate visual cortex. However, it remains to be seen whether the validity effects observed in these areas for neutral stimuli as well as negative emotional cues (anger or fear) reverse in the case of disgust. In the present fMRI-study, we presented three auditory cues of neutral, disgusting and fearful content intermixed in an event-related spatial cueing design. During fMRI, each of these three sounds was presented equally often to the right or left ear and was followed by a neutral visual target on the same (valid) or opposite (invalid) side of space where the cue was presented. The target was a white arrow, pointing up- or downwards. Participants were required to press one of two buttons indicating whether the arrow pointed up- or downwards. After fMRI-scanning, participants rated all sound cues for emotional valence and arousal as well as their motivation to turn towards or away from a person making such sounds. With regard to the behavioral results, we hypothesized a typical cueing effect for fear and neutral sound cues: a validly cued target should be detected faster than an invalidly cued target. In the case of the disgust cues, however, we expected the reverse pattern: Here, an invalidly cued target should be detected faster than a validly cued target. This would indicate that disgust sounds direct attention away to the opposite side of space, whereas the other two cues should direct attention towards the same side of space. Taken together, the results for fear and disgust should result in an interaction of emotion by validity.

Recently, we showed that chronic intermittent AAS treatment induces significant changes in the expression of genes involved in neuroplasticity, stress response and energy metabolism in the frontal cortex of mice (Mikkelsen et al., 2016). However, whether and how these gene expression changes translate into functional changes in brain activity remains unknown. Here, we investigated the effect of chronic intermittent AAS administration on the functional connectivity of the mouse brain using resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI). rs-fMRI is an imaging technique based on spontaneous low-frequency ( C, 50% humidity, lights on from 07:00 h to 19:00 h) with free access to food and water. Mice were randomly assigned to either the control group (n = 10) or the chronic intermittent AAS group (n = 13). Mice were injected intraperitoneally once daily with either vehicle (corn oil) or AAS (Nandrolone Decanoate, 25 mg/kg body weight, Schering AG, Berlin, Germany) for 28 days. The dose and duration of AAS treatment correspond to those previously used to induce robust and reproducible behavioral and biochemical effects in rodents (Cohen et al., 2015; Mikkelsen et al., 2016). On day 29 all mice were sacrificed by decapitation and the brains were extracted. One mouse from the AAS group died prior to sacrifice due to technical complications. Therefore, data from 12 AAS-treated mice were included in the analysis. Resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging Functional MRI scanning was performed on a 7 Tesla Bruker PharmaScan scanner equipped with a 30 mm inner diameter gradient coil providing a maximum gradient strength of 400 mT/m and a rise time of 120 1/2s. A birdcage radiofrequency coil (Bruker Biospin, Ettlingen, Germany) was used for transmission and reception. Each animal was anesthetized using isoflurane (induction 4%, maintenance 1.5%) and placed inside the magnet. Body temperature was maintained at 37 C using a warm air blanket (SA Instruments Inc.).

The irony is that Martinez's detractors are the same ones who were thrilled when he brought a sense of flair and adventure to Goodison Park. They were the ones who celebrated his commitment to playing attractive football, who revelled in the free-scoring wins and the swashbuckling style that brought a sense of excitement to the blue half of Merseyside. And yet, now that the results have taken a dip, they're suddenly clamouring for a more cautious approach, as if the principles that brought success last season are no longer relevant. It's a knee-jerk reaction, driven by the fear of relegation and the pressure of the Premier League's ruthless environment. But it's a reaction that ignores the very essence of Martinez's philosophy. This is a manager who has built his reputation on playing attacking football, on trusting his players to express themselves and take the game to the opposition. To ask him to suddenly abandon that approach and adopt a more defensive mindset is to ask him to compromise his values, to sacrifice his identity as a coach. And what's the guarantee that it would even work? Moyes's success against Manchester City was built on a solid defence, but it was also built on a team that was well-drilled, well-organised and well-motivated. You can't simply transplant that approach onto a team that's been built to play a different way. The players would need to adapt, the system would need to change, and the whole dynamic of the team would need to shift. It's not a simple fix, and it's not a guarantee of success. Moreover, what about the players? Lukaku, Naismith, and the rest of the squad were recruited to play a certain way, to express themselves on the pitch and to take risks. If Martinez suddenly asks them to play a more cautious game, he risks stifling their creativity, stifling their confidence, and stifling the very essence of what made them successful in the first place. And let's not forget, Martinez has been here before. He's faced criticism, he's faced pressure, and he's come out on top. He's a manager who's been through the wars, who's been tested and proven himself. He's not a novice, he's not a rookie, and he's not someone who's going to be swayed by the whims of the fans or the media. So, no, I don't think Martinez needs to change. I think he needs to be given time, to be given trust, and to be given the freedom to implement his vision. He's the manager, he's the one who knows the players, and he's the one who knows the game. Let him do his job, let him make the decisions, and let him take Everton forward in the way that he sees fit. Because, at the end of the day, that's what he was hired to do.

As the news spread, Emmanuel, then 25, joined the mob that descended upon Alice's village. He was one of the many who had been convinced that the Tutsis were a threat to their very existence. The hate speech and propaganda had done their job, and he was convinced that the Tutsis were to blame for all their problems. Alice, 28 at the time, was at home with her baby daughter, Jeanette, when Emmanuel and the mob arrived. She remembers the sound of machetes chopping, the screams of her neighbors, and the smell of smoke and blood. Emmanuel, fueled by a toxic mix of fear and hatred, attacked Alice, slicing off her right hand and killing her baby girl. The memories of that day still haunt her, and the scar on her left temple is a constant reminder of the brutality she endured. Despite the unimaginable pain and trauma, Alice's story is one of resilience and forgiveness. After the genocide, she was left to pick up the pieces of her shattered life. She received medical treatment for her injuries and eventually started rebuilding her life. She remarried and had four more children. But the memories of that fateful day never left her. She often wondered about the man who had taken her hand and her child. Who was he? What drove him to commit such atrocities? And, most importantly, could she ever forgive him? The answer to that question came years later, when Alice and Emmanuel met at a community reconciliation program. The program, set up by the Rwandan government, aimed to bring together perpetrators and victims of the genocide to facilitate healing and reconciliation. It was a daunting task, but one that was necessary for the country to move forward. Alice was hesitant at first, but something about Emmanuel's demeanor struck a chord. He was remorseful, genuinely sorry for his actions, and willing to make amends. Over time, they began to talk, to share their stories, and to understand each other's perspectives. The road to forgiveness was long and arduous, but Alice eventually came to a place of acceptance. Today, Alice and Emmanuel are more than just acquaintances; they are friends. They work together, live near each other, and shop at the same market. Their friendship is a testament to the power of forgiveness and reconciliation. It is a beacon of hope in a country still grappling with the aftermath of the genocide. As Rwanda marks the 20th anniversary of the genocide, Alice and Emmanuel's story serves as a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there is always a way forward. It is a story of the human capacity for forgiveness, of the possibility of redemption, and of the power of love to overcome even the most profound evil.

The Cherohala Skyway, North Carolina and Tennessee. The route: 43 miles. The name may be a mouthful, but the Cherohala Skyway is actually a straightforward route connecting Robbinsville, NC, with Tellico Plains, TN, via the Cherokee and Nantahala national forests. As the scenic highway climbs past 5,000 feet above sea level, it offers panoramic views of the Smoky Mountains. On the western side of the Unicoi Mountains, enjoy the sight of flowering dogwood trees and redbud shrubs. Where to stop: Stretch your legs on one of the many hiking trails, including the 2.6-mile Turkey Creek Trail, where you'll find mountain laurels. Or keep your eyes peeled for black bears near the Hooper Bald picnic area. Travel + Leisure: Best places to travel in 2013. Wisconsin Lake Superior Scenic Byway. The route: 70 miles. The Apostle Islands, a group of 22 forested islands off the Bayfield Peninsula, are home to a rare collection of lichens, plus orchids and aster flowers. The Lake Superior Scenic Byway, which runs parallel to the lake, connects several state parks and recreational areas. These reviews showed LEZs do not consistently improve air quality, and effects are small. Few studies addressed health impacts, and these have tended to rely on modelled predictions of air quality improvements. Added value of this study We exploited the comprehensive monitoring network in London, UK, to evaluate the changes in air pollution following the introduction of the LEZ. Our study covered the tightening of emission controls within the LEZ in 2012, which occurred alongside national, regional, and local policies to improve air quality. We based our study in four inner-city London boroughs, which were identified as non-compliant with EU annual NO2 limit values at the start of study. Despite the problems associated with vehicle non-compliance with European class emission standards over this period, we have provided evidence of improvements in air quality. We also confirmed the previously reported association between pollutant exposures and reduced children's lung volume. We observed some evidence of a reduction in rhinitis, but not asthma symptoms or the proportion of children with small lungs over the study period. Implications of all available evidence Large-scale LEZs can deliver improvements in urban air quality and these can be linked to changes in childhood respiratory health. However, more ambitious schemes than those evaluated here are required to meet legislative limits and deliver improvements to respiratory health in many European cities. Low emission zones (LEZ), areas where the entry of polluting vehicles is restricted or penalised on the basis of European class emission standards, are often used as the major component of emission control strategies. London, UK, introduced the world's largest citywide LEZ in 2008 (appendix 1 p 4). Across Europe, about 200 LEZs are now in operation, with others in use in Asia, including Singapore and Tokyo. Despite the widespread application of LEZs to improve air quality, evidence that LEZs reduce pollutant concentrations or improve health is scarce.20-27 Holman and colleagues26 concluded that LEZs in operation in European countries had inconsistent effects on PM10 and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentrations. Wang and colleagues28 found only six studies that addressed impact of traffic LEZ-type emission control interventions on health.29-33 Of these, only one31 gathered health data directly from individuals, finding negligible effects on respiratory symptoms. The other studies relied on modeling the effects of predicted (not necessarily achieved) emission reductions on health. Health equity has been assessed in only two studies, with opposing conclusions.20,30 The phased introduction of London's LEZ, beginning in 2008, provided the opportunity for a natural experiment to evaluate the effect of this emission-based mitigation strategy. A description of the various phases of the LEZ is presented in appendix 1 (p 4), with the early phases in 2008 (phases 1 and 2), followed by a further tightening of emission controls in 2012 (phase 3).

Stonewall, a man of unassuming appearance, with a mop of unruly brown hair and piercing blue eyes, had spent years pouring over dusty tomes and crumbling manuscripts in his quest for the ultimate secret. He was a recluse, a hermit, a man consumed by his own obsessions, and yet, he was about to unlock the door to a world beyond the wildest dreams of his contemporaries. As the clock struck nine, Stonewall emerged from his humble abode, a small cottage on the outskirts of town, and made his way to the local general store. The proprietor, a gruff but kind-hearted man named Jacob, looked up from behind the counter as Stonewall entered, his eyes narrowing slightly as he took in the intensity of the man's gaze. "Evening, Stonewall," Jacob said, his voice low and gravelly. "What brings you out tonight?" Stonewall's eyes seemed to bore into Jacob's very soul as he replied, "I've come for the package, Jacob. The one you've been holding for me." Jacob's eyes flickered, and for a moment, Stonewall thought he saw a glimmer of something there, something almost like fear. But then, the proprietor's expression smoothed out, and he nodded curtly. "Ah, yes, of course. Right here." He reached beneath the counter and produced a small, unassuming box, adorned with intricate symbols and markings that seemed to shimmer in the dim light of the store. Stonewall's eyes lit up with an unholy excitement as he took the box from Jacob, his fingers closing around it like a vice. "This is it," he whispered, his voice trembling with anticipation. "This is the key to it all." And with that, Stonewall turned and disappeared into the night, leaving Jacob to wonder what he had just witnessed, and what secrets lay hidden within the small, mysterious box.

The warmth he collected around him was tangible, a magnetism that drew people to his tailoring shop tucked away between the apothecary and the bookman's residence. As the sun slipped into the horizon's embrace, casting a dim golden hue on the cobblestone streets, the news of Mr. Mel's passing began to spread its wings amongst the townsfolk, taking flight from the lips of gossiping matrons sipping tea to the eager ears of restless children. Whispers of his great exploits-of horseback jaunts to the hills beyond Lymport and invaluable advice offered to aspiring gentlemen-resonated like church bells tolling in unison for a revered figure. Tears began to glisten even in those presumed indifferent to the petty affairs of tailors and their yokes of fabric; indeed, he had transcended the walls of mere profession. At the corner of the lane, Old Man Farquhar tugged at his grizzled beard, squinting beyond the sharp edges of twilight, recalling a time he had found himself in dire need of a fitting suit. "That was one man you could count on!" he remarked to anyone who would listen, albeit no one was truly present to engage. "Last time I asked him for a tailor's measure, he brought a bottle instead! A long drink and a rowdy song, mind you! Ah, where will I find a new suit that comes with such grand accompaniment?" Despite the growing shadows, the pub began to busier as patrons huddled together, nursing pints and exchanging sentiments towards their now-gone friend. With every mug raised in tribute, tales amplified in ridiculousness-the time he had raced a horse against the rising tide, the evening caper when he apparently entered a dance hall clad only in a bathrobe to prove a point on frivolity, the incessant borrowing of tools that were sometimes never returned. Yet, for all the laughter, a stout undercurrent of remorse prevailed. The specter of loss lingered, visited by the spectres of what the town might miss-even the echoes in the street where Mr. Mel's cheer had sewn a sense of community and camaraderie. "We may all wear black," an emotionally charged Miss Bountree piped up, straining against the murmurs of the crowd. "But who will stitch together the fabric of our kindness without his expert hands?" Across the room, the candlelight shimmered in the glasses as toasts flowed like the sea lapping against the pebbled shore. Each man and woman embraced the collective grief, rekindling a truth known to the every heart of the town-mortal lives, however cloaked in the winds of time, inevitably weave an undying tapestry of affection, vitality, and indomitable spirit. For in the threads that had composed the life of Mr. Melchisedec Harrington, Lymport was resolute in knowing it was not only the tailor who would be missed, but the exceptional man who had tailored the very essence of their lives.

In 2008, the Centre for Protection of National Infrastructure (CPNI) produced a Good Practice Guide for Process Control and SCADA Security (CPNI) encapsulating best security practices. In 2008, NIST released a comprehensive guidance on a wide range of security issues, and technical, operational and management security controls. The guide was updated in 2011 (NIST, 2011). In 2013, the European Union Agency for Network and Information Security (ENISA) released the recommendations for Europe on SCADA patching (ENISA, 2013). Currently, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) actively works on the development of a wide range of standards covering many aspects of CNI cyber security (NERG, 2014). More extensive overviews of SCADA-related security standards and initiatives are provided in Igure et al. (2006) and Nicholson et al. (2012). Modern day SCADA systems are highly sophisticated, complex and based on advanced technology systems. The escalating sophistication and modernisation as well as real-time continuous operation and distributed, multi-component architecture underpin the growth of cyber threats to SCADA systems. SCADA systems are exposed to a wide range of cyber threats also because of the standardisation of communication protocols and hardware components, growing interconnectivity and legacy. (All these aspects we discuss in greater detail in Section 2.) Over the last several decades we already saw a range of cyber attacks on CNI and SCADA. In 1982, the first recorded cyber attack on CNI took place at the Trans-Siberian pipeline and resulted in an explosion visible from space (Miller and Rowe, 2012). Over the last decade there was a number of cyber attacks on SCADA systems and ICS. In 2003, a slammer worm penetrated a network at the Davies-Besse nuclear plant in Ohio (Guan et al., 2011; Patel et al., 2005) and a computer virus named Sobig shut down train signalling systems in Florida (Miller and Rowe, 2012). In 2006, a hacker penetrated the operation system of a water treatment facility in Harrisburg, USA (Guan et al., 2011; Patel et al., 2005) and the Browns Ferry nuclear plant in Alabama was manually shut due to the overload of network traffic (Nicholson et al., 2012). In 2007, a dismissed employee installed unauthorised software on the SCADA system of the Tehama Colusa Canal Authority (Miller and Rowe, 2012). In 2010, the Stuxnet computer worm struck the Iranian nuclear facility causing the failure of almost one-fifth of all centrifuges (Miller and Rowe, 2012). Stuxnet was a game-changer, it attracted the world's attention to cyber threats to CNI by drawing a vivid and horrifying picture of the consequences of a cyber attack on CNI. In 2011, five global energy and oil firms were targeted by a combination of attacks including social engineering, trojans and Windows-based exploits (Miller and Rowe, 2012). In 2012, a malware named Flame was discovered to have been operating in many sites in the Middle East and North Africa for at least two years (Miller and Rowe, 2012).

The sight of those majestic elephants basking in the dusk was nothing short of surreal. Their colossal forms stood out against the backdrop of the pink facades that Jaipur is so famous for. I couldn't help but imagine the tales these gentle giants could tell, having traversed the same bustling streets for centuries, carrying weight far greater than their own physical burdens. Camels, with their swaggering gait, gracefully sidled up to the curb, intermingling with scooters and auto-rickshaws, creating a colorful chaos that felt oddly harmonious. "This is India," I thought, and Joel echoed my sentiment, tilting his head back with a grin that illuminated his face. As we ventured deeper into the city, the aroma of spices wafted through the air, beckoning us to dive into the local culinary scene. Our driver, sensing our yearning for proper sustenance, skillfully maneuvered through narrow alleyways, dropping us off in front of a small, unassuming eatery. The kind of place that didn't boast ornate decor but radiated authenticity. Adorned with vibrant marigold garlands, the entrance was flanked by an old brass bell that tinkled as we stepped inside. The warmth of the place enveloped us, much like the spice-laden air that filled our lungs. Inside, the clamor of voices mingled with the clattering of dishes, creating a symphony of sounds that resonated with the pulse of the city. Before we could even make sense of the menu, a bevy of dishes emerged, served with generous portions and heartfelt smiles. Cumin-scented curries, crisp naan, and fragrant biryanis beckoned us from every corner of the table. Joel, ever the adventurous eater, insisted we try everything. "When in Jaipur!" he declared, slightly muffled by a mouthful of paneer tikka. I couldn't argue; we were basking in the vibrant tapestry of flavors that danced on our taste buds. With our bellies full and our spirits lifted, we decided a stroll was in order. The streets of Jaipur are a living canvas of artistry and culture. We ambled past street vendors hawking bright bangles, kaleidoscopic fabrics, and intricate handicrafts; each stall a treasure trove begging to be explored. The shopkeepers, ever friendly, engaged us in conversation, eager to share stories about their wares. We practically glided from one stall to another, enchanted by the vivid colors and sounds around us. Our aimless wander took us to Hawa Mahal, the Palace of Winds, its pink sandstone facade catching the last rays of sunlight. The intricate latticework mesmerized us, a stunning fusion of art and architecture, allowing royal women to observe life on the streets without being seen. Camera clicks echoed as tourists jostled for the perfect shot - and here we were, two more souls entranced by the allure of this city. As the sun dipped behind the horizon, a tapestry of stars emerged, twinkling like diamonds scattered across a velvet drape. We paused at a small rooftop cafe, illuminated by soft lanterns, where we enjoyed sweet masala chai. The warmth of the tea was a comforting contrast to the evening breeze, which whispered stories of Jaipur's past. And thus, under the vast Indian sky, we sipped our tea while listening to the bustle of the city. In this magical place, we felt an inexplicable connection to a world so rich in history, culture, and warmth. The allure of elephants, camels, and the laughter of monkeys hung in the air like a lingering melody, the kind that stays with you long after the music has faded.

When external food aid is introduced into local markets, particularly in areas self-sufficient in grain production, it can significantly disrupt local agricultural dynamics. The infusion of subsidized or free grains creates an artificial supply, leading to lower prices for locally produced grains, which in turn demotivates local farmers from planting crops. As the price of their produce declines, farmers face decreased income, forcing many to abandon agricultural practices altogether in favor of off-farm employment or migration - a trend that, while offering temporary relief, can threaten the sustainability of their households in the long term (Lentz et al., 2005). This cycle invariably results in a reliance not solely on food aid but also on external income sources that are inherently volatile, often dictated by urban economic fluctuations beyond their control. Moreover, aid recipients may come to rely on the consistency of food transfers, leading to a decline in self-sufficiency and a growing belief that assistance is a permanent feature of their livelihoods (Edkins, 2000). This perceived permanence can erode community norms around mutual support and cooperation, as people may feel less inclined to engage in reciprocal agricultural practices when they perceive relief as a substitute for self-reliance. Such a shift risks dismantling social ties that reinforce communal resilience and adaptive capacity to climatic or market shocks. Over time, the intricate web of interactions between farmers, local policies, and global markets becomes increasingly frayed, with food aid at its center perpetuating dependency rather than fostering agency. One of the most concerning aspects of food aid interventions is their inconsistency in terms of delivery and quality, which further complicates farmers' ability to plan effectively (Harvey & Lind, 2005). When aid distributions are irregular or insufficient, communities often face feast-and-famine cycles that can lead to crises of food insecurity when assistance falls short. These experiences entrench a perspective of aid as the dominant solution to food scarcity rather than the development of robust agricultural practices that prioritize resilience and sustainability. In light of these adverse outcomes, it becomes essential to interrogate the underlying assumptions that inform current food aid structures. Far from being a one-size-fits-all remedy, food aid must adapt to the unique realities of diverse agricultural environments, and, crucially, it must consider the potential ramifications on local economies and social fabrics. If the intention is to assist developing communities and enhance food security, approaches to aid must incorporate methodologies that empower rather than undermine local agricultural systems and knowledge. In practice, this may mean reorienting food aid from mere sustenance towards more nutritionally and culturally appropriate support. Programs might incorporate training for local farmers in sustainable agricultural practices, creating ways to improve productivity while maintaining market viability. Linkages with local cooperatives or farmer associations can bolster community capacity and ensure that any interventions align with existing local strategies for overcoming food insecurity. Such a shift allows for dignity, agency, and innovation to flourish within affected communities, fostering an active rather than passive role in their endeavor for food security. Ultimately, the conversation around food aid and dependency must evolve into one that prioritizes holistic, inclusive solutions. By recognizing the complex interplay of social, economic, and agricultural factors, we can begin to dismantle the dependency trap and cultivate sustainable pathways toward food sovereignty in the world's most vulnerable populations. The road ahead requires a redefined commitment to agriculture and a nuanced understanding of how external assistance can, if not applied with caution, inadvertently replicate the very challenges it seeks to resolve. Adjustments must go beyond monetary inputs, thoughtfully weaving together a rich tapestry of local knowledge, cultural relevance, and genuine empowerment into the framework of food aid.

A comprehensive overview of these considerations was presented by Leary et al. [20], who identified four categories of constraints: (i) geometrical, (ii) mechanical, (iii) thermal, and (iv) functional. Geometrical constraints relate to the inherent properties of the AM system and include layer thicknesses, maximum overhang angles, minimum feature sizes, and maximum part dimensions. Mechanical constraints relate to the mechanical properties of the manufactured part and include the effect of support structures, build orientation, and post-processing operations. Thermal constraints relate to the effect of the thermal environment during the manufacturing process and include residual stresses and distortion. Functional constraints relate to the final application of the manufactured component and include fatigue life, impact resistance, and corrosion resistance. The aforementioned categories of constraints represent a non-exhaustive list of the numerous challenges that designers face when designing for AM. For example, additional constraints related to the specific material properties and processing parameters of the chosen AM system must be taken into consideration. This highlights the importance of understanding the underlying principles of AM techniques to enable informed decision-making during the design phase. One of the earliest works in this area was conducted by Khajavi et al. [21], who developed a framework for estimating the costs of producing a single part using laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF). Their work considered two types of costs: direct costs and indirect costs. Direct costs included the cost of the raw material, the cost of energy consumption, and the cost of maintenance. Indirect costs included the cost of the building platform, the cost of the building chamber, and the cost of labour. They concluded that the most significant factor influencing the total cost of LPBF was the cost of the raw material, followed by the cost of energy consumption. Other studies have focused on developing cost models for other AM technologies, such as electron beam melting (EBM) [22], selective laser sintering (SLS) [23], and fused deposition modeling (FDM) [24]. A thorough tester executes a particular test scenario with different sets of data, and conducts boundary testing to ensure that an application would not be deployed into production with overlooked problems. A suggested question to discern a candidate's testing meticulousness is to have a candidate provide use cases and test cases for a commonly used machine, or a self service application. In addition, a test script provides information about the test execution results for "passes/failures" and mapped requirements for the test step. The test manager can have the tester provide information as to how test cases and test scripts were documented at the previous project. What level of detail was presented for the test cases and test scripts? What exactly was documented for the test cases and test scripts? Another suggestion is to have the tester send a sample test case and test script that he/she documented at a previous project for review. ECs have also been demonstrated to increase cessation rates in clinical trials (McRobbie et al., 2014) and some population studies (Biener and Hargraves, 2015; Brown et al., 2014a), but not all observational studies have detected an effect (Grana et al., 2014), and more research is needed to confirm EC effectiveness, using an appropriate methodology to distinguish between the impact of EC use on cessation when used as part of a quit attempt vs. when it is used for any general purpose (Hajek et al., 2014). Although some concerns remain in the population regarding the safety of prolonged use of non-combustible nicotine delivery devices (Black et al., 2012; Dockrell et al., 2013), the evidence indicates that long-term NRT use is safe in terms of levels of nicotine delivered (Shahab et al., 2014) and associated toxicity (Benowitz and Gourlay, 1997; Hubbard et al., 2005) and growing data on EC would suggest the same (Hajek et al., 2014). This, combined with the known toxicity of combustible nicotine use, further supports the idea of harm reduction, shifting smokers towards non-combustible nicotine delivery devices and away from smoked tobacco. However, relatively little is known about the processes which underpin a smoker's transition to sole use of non-combustible nicotine delivery devices and whether long-term use of such products aids cessation or maintains smoking in the long run. One universal mechanism worth investigating in the context of understanding this transition is "smoker identity", the self-concept that being a smoker is an essential constituent of one's identity (Shadel and Mermelstein, 1996; Shadel et al., 1996). It has been posited that identity influences behaviour by creating strong wants or needs, such as wanting to be a non-smoker, which compete with external impulses, such as the desire to smoke, and may therefore reinforce or undermine shifts in behaviour (West and Brown, 2013). Studies have observed a weakening in smoker identity during cessation as smokers distanced themselves from an unwanted smoker identity (Johnson et al., 2003; Vangeli and West, 2012), and liking being a smoker has been identified as an important barrier to smoking cessation (Tombor et al., 2013; van den Putte et al., 2009). Another important factor in the transition from smoker to non-smoker is the physiological impact of cessation. The role of mood and physical symptoms in relapse is well-documented (West et al., 1989), and even after long periods of abstinence the presence of withdrawal symptoms has been shown to predict return to smoking (Piasecki et al., 2003). In line with existing theory (West and Brown, 2013), it is therefore important that such symptoms are minimised to ensure the motivation not to smoke remains stronger than the motivation to smoke. For this reason, effective harm reduction should treat negative mood and physical symptoms.

So when the stakes are higher for survival, we're more individualistic than group-oriented? De Waal: Oh no, we very much survive by group life. Humans are not able to survive alone. For example, solitary confinement is one of the worst punishments we can give. We are not really made to live alone, we would not survive, and so when things get tough we would actually come together more and be more social when things get tough. CNN: Can you talk about how being nice to another individual helps you? De Waal: Sometimes people put that in a very narrow sense, and they say that everything that humans do or that animals do needs to have a payoff, but that's not true. The example... of adoption of children, I basically think it's a costly act with no payoff, and these things happen in animals also. Animals sometimes help each other even between species. Dolphins may help human swimmers, and I don't think the dolphins get much out of it. So individual acts don't necessarily need to have a payoff. So they are not selfishly motivated. They are really altruistic, but you have the tendency to help, and to have empathy for others in general, on the average, is beneficial. Because you live in a group, you depend on these others, so you need to care about these others also because your survival depends on group life, and so there is some sort of general payoff, but people often think in terms of each individual act needs to (reap) some benefit but that's not necessarily true. CNN: Tell us more about the origins of empathy. De Waal: We think that the origin of empathy, in the mammals at least, has to do with maternal care. So a female, whether you're a mouse or an elephant, you need to pay attention to your offspring, you need to react to their emotions when they're cold, or in danger, or hungry, and that's where we think the sensitivity to others' emotions come from. That also explains why empathy is more developed in females than males, which is true in many animals, and it's true for humans, and it explains the role of oxytocin. Oxytocin is a maternal hormone. If you spray oxytocin into the nostrils of men and women, you get more empathic (empathetic) reactions from them, and so the general thinking about empathy is that it started in the mammals with maternal care, and then from there it spread to other relationships. So men can definitely have empathy, but they on average have a little bit less of it than women. CNN: By empathy, you mean that they feel each others' pain? De Waal: Well, feeling someone else's joy is also empathy. Being affected by the laugh, as humans are, is a form of empathy.

11-14 The first lantibiotic to enter Phase III clinical trials was NVB302,15 which is currently being developed by Novacta Biosystems Ltd for treatment of Clostridium difficile infection. NVB302 is a derivative of the lantibiotic deoxyactagardine B,16 a compound that was originally isolated from Actinoplanes liguriensis17 and has recently been shown to inhibit cell wall biosynthesis through inhibition of lipid II synthesis.18 The structure of deoxyactagardine B differs significantly from the type I lantibiotic nisin in that it contains only two Lan rings and no MeLan rings. It also does not contain any d-amino acids and all of its lanthionines are C-terminal to dehydroamino acids. These structural differences mean that deoxyactagardine B is relatively stable compared to most lantibiotics, making it an attractive candidate for further development. Deoxyactagardine B itself showed promise in animal models of C. difficile infection19 but was unsuitable for clinical development due to the difficulty of producing large quantities of pure material. To overcome this problem, Novacta carried out a comprehensive programme of semi-synthetic optimisation20,21 leading to the discovery of NVB302,22 a hybrid molecule containing the N-terminus of actagardine23 and the C-terminus of deoxyactagardine B. NVB302 is produced by fermentation of a recombinant strain of Streptomyces coelicolor followed by purification and partial semi-synthesis. This process allows production of multi-gram quantities of pure NVB302. In vitro, NVB302 shows good potency against a broad spectrum of Gram-positive pathogens including MRSA, VRE and Clostridia spp.,24 and demonstrates low propensity to select for resistance.25 NVB302 has completed a successful phase I trial26 and is currently in Phase II clinical trials. Other lantibiotics currently under investigation include duramycins,27 mucopeptides28 and microbisporicin29 which have reached Phase I clinical trials for the treatment of various infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria. Although these lantibiotics show promising in vivo efficacy, they suffer from poor solubility and stability which limits their potential for oral delivery.30 Furthermore, the current route to these lantibiotics relies on fermentation which makes scale-up difficult and costly.31 These limitations highlight the need for alternative approaches to access lantibiotics and lantibiotic analogues. Structures of the naturally occurring lantibiotics nisin Z (A) and deoxyactagardine B (B). Lan = lanthionine, Dha = dehydroalanine, Dhb = dehydrobutyrine. Synthesis of Lantibiotics Chemical synthesis provides the opportunity to produce modified lantibiotics and lantibiotic analogues that are inaccessible using standard fermentation-based routes. Chemical synthesis would allow direct control over the stereochemistry of the lantibiotic, thus allowing access to unnatural stereoisomers and diastereomers. Additionally, the inclusion of unnatural amino acids and/or protecting groups could lead to compounds with improved pharmacokinetic profiles.32 Finally, chemical synthesis provides a means to prepare large amounts of lantibiotics without relying on fermentation.33 The major obstacle to the chemical synthesis of lantibiotics is the presence of several thioether bridges within the core structure.

So there we were, an odd little band of jesters, prancing through the woods with our shirts flapping in the warm breeze like flags of rebellion. It felt liberating, this spontaneous burst of camaraderie amidst the towering trees and the chorus of chirping birds. The trail wound its way deeper into the lush, green heart of Huntsville, and as we trampled over rocks and roots, it became a race of sorts. Kerri, Sebastian, and Steven darted ahead, daring each other to hop over gnarled branches while I trotted behind, attempting to catch my breath and wiping the sheen of sweat from my brow. You see, while it was all merriment and playful ribbing, I couldn't help but ponder the absurdity of it all. Who were we but a couple of misfits, underprepared and overenthusiastic, hiking our way through a Saturday morning like we were on some grand adventure? As I caught up to the front of the pack, I noticed Steven pausing, barely catching his breath - perhaps his plan to show off how fit he was had backfired. We all rallied around, offering motivational cheers, which, of course, quickly turned into mocking commentary about his "athletic prowess." After a particularly steep climb, the trees parted, and we found ourselves standing before a stunning vista. Seriously, it was postcard-worthy-the kind of sight that makes you pull out your phone, snap a few pictures, and then realize you've forgotten to actually take in the moment. The sprawling landscape stretched out before us, with verdant hills rolling away into the horizon. Kerri's eyes lit up, and she whipped out her phone, turning our little gathering into an impromptu photo shoot. We struck goofy poses-half-formed jazz hands, finger guns, and the classic awkward jumping shot we all played along with, shrieking with laughter as we tried (and failed) to synchronize. The air was filled with an infectious energy, and for a split second, all worries melted away. Who cared about deadlines, responsibilities, or any of the pesky things that had been nagging at the back of my mind? It was just us, the forest, and the promise of a fun-filled day ahead. But, as you might expect, that euphoric moment didn't last long. Remember how I said I was sweating? Well, it reached a critical point. As the group of merry hikers resumed our trek, I found myself struggling to keep pace. My enthusiasm soon gave way to an unfortunate realization: hiking is hard work. Hot, sweaty, and slightly winded, I began to lag behind. It was only when Kerri noticed she had sprinted ahead without me that she turned back, a concerned look on her face. "Hey, are you okay?" she called, her voice echoing through the trees. Breathing heavily, I managed a thumbs-up, albeit a little more sarcastically than intended. "Yeah, just... you know... contemplating the meaning of life." Sebastian chimed in from ahead, "If by meaning you mean the snacks at the bottom, I hear those are top-tier!" Laughter rang out, and I couldn't help but smile, despite my fatigue. The trail turned rougher, rocks jutting up underfoot like the universe was throwing obstacles just for kicks. But trudging along with my friends, I felt a sense of belonging-this was my lot, and their teasing was just part of the love. Eventually, we stumbled upon a clearing with a small, still lake, shimmering in the midday sun. The atmosphere became quiet as we caught our collective breath, and as I looked around, I realized that somehow, this blissful chaos had turned into something special, a tapestry woven from shared laughter, friendly jabs, and the unwritten rule that we were all in this together.

These changes are leading to rapid growth in both digitised and 'non-purpose-oriented' data. In particular, there is increasing availability of large quantities of data that either: (i) were not specifically captured for transport applications but which have relevance to its understanding; or (ii) have been archived to preserve historical 'pictures' of transport patterns, but without an analytical method in mind. This process completely contradicts classical methods of statistical inference: experimental design, random sampling, even (it might be claimed) 'the scientific method' (Mazzocchi, 2015; Kwan, 2016). It seems clear that something quite fundamental is happening beyond data-sets simply increasing in size and becoming digitised. Considering these issues from the perspectives of transport system analysis and planning, this paper seeks to achieve three goals: to try to identify what is truly 'special' about big data in this particular context; to provoke debate on the future relationship between transport planning and big data; and to try to identify promising themes for research and application. As authors we approach this topic from a background in transport modelling and have a particular interest in the opportunities, threats and permissive impacts that these emerging data sources may have for travel, and for our ability to understand and predict it in support of planning and decision-making. The focus of our paper is on medium-term transport planning and not on providing real-time system or personalised information, analytics and control, which have been covered elsewhere and which lead to a very different set of considerations (e.g. Zheng et al., 2013; Kitchin, 2014a, 2014b; Mori et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2015). The paper will also avoid focussing on a single type of big data and its detailed applications, such as mobile phone records which have been covered quite extensively elsewhere (Bohte and Maat, 2009; Calabrese et al., 2014; Steenbruggen et al., 2015; Rojas IV et al., 2016). Instead, the paper will consider any kind of 'big data' (in the senses we shall define) and will discuss: how it differs from more traditional transport data sources; what those differences mean for the information it can provide; how different information has an impact on the analytical techniques that make use of it (from the perspectives of both analysing past data and devising predictive models), and what the implications of all this are for the practice of transport planning. Our ultimate aim is to try to identify what we believe are key questions and areas for debate, which might suggest foci for research regarding the potential impact of big data on the future of transport planning and policy assessment. Our starting point is a simple conceptual understanding of the relationship between data about the transport system and the practical discipline of transport planning. Our proposition is that, in the transport sector, analytical approaches-most of which could be referred to as models-have traditionally played a vital role in linking observable phenomena to decision-making.

I think of Lisa, her laughter like a sudden summer storm, brief and cleansing, an understanding too profound for comfort. Her influence so potent it could knock the air from your lungs, leave you panting for more or struggling to regain your footing. But there is also Pinta, caught between a world wanting to devour her innocence and another desperate to preserve it, a tug-of-war with no victor. I pondered then, the meaning of protection-its weighty promises, its costly veneer. In this urban jungle, bodyguards became more than shield-bearers; they transformed into actors in this macabre play, their presence a mask to the world's callousness. The stage was set, the script unwritten. And the currency for this performance? Risk. The very air buzzed with unwritten contracts, silent exchanges made in glances and gestures. Samuel, dear Samuel, your voice echoes in my mind like the distant clang of temple bells, ringing through the cacophony with questions that have no easy answers. Safety? Assurance? In this world, they are as elusive as the horizon, always just beyond reach. And yet, hope persists-a stubborn flame refusing to be extinguished. We barter, we gamble, finding solace in hollow assurances, in the frail armor of an insurance policy nearing its expiration. We cling to these tokens as if they could truly stave off the shadow that lurks in every alley, every heartbeat. What is it to be strong? Rivers flowing power masked by their deceptive calm. A bodyguard stands, a sentinel, an iron door in the storm. Not a superman, but perhaps something rarer-a symbol of what we wish we could be. How much would it cost to turn back time, to unsee, unfeel, unlive what we have suffered? And on it goes, this cycle, this maddening dance, partnering with fear and obsession in steps that neither uplift nor destroy. It just is, a measured expression in a world that demands perfection etched from imperfection. For a moment, I entertained the thought that perhaps, somewhere past the swirling miasma of doubt and deception, lay peace-a dull, quiet haven where the weight of armor need not be worn. But here, in the clangor of this room, I realized peace flows not from absence of threat but from courage to face it unflinching. As I await my rescue, the dance continues around me, relentless. I know that soon enough, another tale will begin, threaded through with the same desires and fears, the heartbeat of this relentless city that-ironically-never sleeps. It is here, in this unrelenting rhythm, I find a kindred spirit, holding his breath just under the surface, waiting. For life always finds a way, and even through the darkest valleys, we shepherd the fragile light of hope.

Mr. Novak's eyes scanned the colorful array of sweets on the shelves, his mind momentarily distracted from the disappointment of the coin shop's closure. "Ah, yes," he said, his eyes settling on a jar of golden-hued caramels. "A quarter pound of those, please, Petersen." As the confectioner scooped out the treats, Mr. Novak's gaze wandered to the antique scales on the counter, their brass surfaces polished to a warm sheen. He recalled the countless times he'd watched Petersen weigh out precise portions of sweets for the townspeople, the scales' gentle balance a testament to the shop's commitment to quality. Petersen handed Mr. Novak his treats, and he paid with a few crumpled bills from his pocket. As he turned to leave, his eyes caught on a small, leather-bound book lying open on a nearby shelf. The pages, yellowed with age, displayed intricate drawings of locomotives and railroad tracks. Mr. Novak's curiosity piqued, he reached out to touch the book's worn cover. "Ah, what's this?" he asked Petersen, his voice tinged with nostalgia. Petersen smiled, his eyes twinkling. "Just an old railroad enthusiast's journal, Mr. Novak. Found it in the back room when I took over the shop. Thought it might interest you, given your... background." Mr. Novak's eyes lingered on the drawings, memories of his years on the rails flooding back. He felt a pang of longing, a sense of connection to a bygone era. As he stood there, lost in thought, the silver bell above the door jingled again, and a young woman entered the shop. Her bright pink hair, styled in a punk rock pompadour, was a stark contrast to the old-fashioned charm of the candy store. She eyed Mr. Novak warily, her gaze flicking to the journal in his hand. "Uh, hi," she said, her voice laced with a hint of awkwardness. "Just looking for some... candy." Petersen, ever the salesman, launched into a enthusiastic description of his latest creations, but Mr. Novak's attention remained fixed on the journal, his mind whirling with the possibilities hidden within its yellowed pages.

A mid-market rate (MMR) based P2P energy sharing models was proposed in [14], but the flexibility in DERs were not considered. A discriminate pricing technique using game theory was adopted in [15]. This technique allowed participating energy users to decide their energy use (consumption or supplying energy) based on the price per unit of energy. Fairness between energy users were optimized by using Pareto optimality. The game theoretic approach was also adopted for P2P energy sharing in [16-18]. All these works have one thing in common that is, these P2P sharing mechanisms do not need a central control system, but a local market operator is required to collect the bidding/offering information and provide the pricing signal to individuals in the community Microgrid. This required intensive computational power and communication infrastructures. Moreover, divergence problem exists in the bidding and pricing iterations. In [10], two techniques (i.e. step length control and learning process involvement, and a last-defence mechanism) were proposed to facilitate the convergence in determining the trading prices in the local energy market. Broadly speaking, P2P energy sharing does not necessarily mean prosumers directly control their DERs, and prosumers may get use of a third party entity (e.g. an aggregator, or an energy service company) to manage their resources. Several works carried out P2P energy sharing via a third party entity [19-21]. Battery energy was shared between two groups of electric vehicles (EVs) that have different driving characteristics (divided by the journey distance, and daily re-charging habit) [19]. The EV aggregator, was used as a third party to define the P2P energy sharing price, and to schedule the EV discharging and charging. The paper concluded that the proposed P2P energy sharing took place in workplaces, and the number of EVs able to participate in P2P energy sharing was limited. In [20], a localized P2P electricity trading model was proposed for locally buying and selling electricity among hybrid EVs. Aggregators were used as the market operator. The social welfare was considered as the optimization objective function. However, the social welfare is an index for all the population, and using this index would be likely to result in inequality between customers, and some customers might be worse off comparing to the case when these customers did not participate in P2P energy sharing. To solve this problem, a Pareto optimality method was used in [21]. This work proposed an optimal P2P energy sharing model for smart homes, where a centralised control of all the appliances were carried out to minimize the energy cost of the community Microgrid as well as each individual customers. A cloud controller was considered as a third party entity. This method requires a central processing unit/centre (i.e. a cloud infrastructure) to collect and process the information of all households, which is challenging in the power distribution network.

As she gazed out at the tranquil scene, Miss Cookson's thoughts were far from the picturesque view. Her mind was preoccupied with the upcoming arrival of the new lodgers, and the prospect of having to tolerate their presence in the house. She had never been one for small talk or frivolous conversation, and the thought of having to make polite conversation with a young couple, fresh from their wedding and newly arrived from the city, filled her with dismay. Just then, the sound of footsteps echoed up the stairs, and Miss Cookson turned to see Mrs. Weston, the landlady, descending into the room. Mrs. Weston was a stout, comfortable-looking woman, with a warm smile and a kind face. She was a native of the district, and had lived in the house for many years, having taken it over from her mother. "Ah, Miss Cookson, I see you're still admiring the view," Mrs. Weston said, her voice warm and friendly. "It's a lovely spot, isn't it? I never tire of it myself." Miss Cookson nodded curtly, her expression unchanging. "Yes, it's very pretty," she said, her voice devoid of enthusiasm. Mrs. Weston smiled, undeterred by Miss Cookson's lack of warmth. "I'm glad you like it," she said. "I was thinking of having a little party to welcome the new couple. What do you think?" Miss Cookson raised an eyebrow. "A party?" she repeated, her tone skeptical. "Why on earth would we want to do that?" Mrs. Weston laughed. "Oh, just a little get-together, you know. A few cups of tea, some sandwiches and cakes. It's always nice to make the new people feel welcome, don't you think?" Miss Cookson shrugged. "I suppose it's up to you, Mrs. Weston," she said. "But I don't see the point of it myself." Mrs. Weston's smile faltered for a moment, but she recovered quickly. "Well, I think it's a lovely idea," she said. "And I'm sure the new couple would appreciate it. They're a lovely young couple, I've heard." Miss Cookson's eyes narrowed. "What have you heard?" she asked, her tone sharp. Mrs. Weston's smile grew wider. "Oh, just that they're very nice people. The bride is a sweet girl, and the groom is a brave young man, off to fight for his country soon." Miss Cookson's expression darkened. "Yes, well, I'm sure they're very brave," she said, her tone dripping with sarcasm. Mrs. Weston's smile faltered, and she looked at Miss Cookson with a hint of surprise. "I'm sorry, Miss Cookson," she said. "I didn't mean to upset you." Miss Cookson's expression softened slightly, and she looked away, her eyes gazing out at the view once more. "It's all right, Mrs. Weston," she said, her voice a little softer. "I'm just not very good at...social things." Mrs. Weston nodded understandingly. "I know, Miss Cookson," she said. "But you're very good at other things. You're an excellent housekeeper, and you're very efficient." Miss Cookson's eyes snapped back to Mrs. Weston's face, and for a moment, the two women locked eyes, the tension between them palpable. Then, Miss Cookson turned away, her expression once more closed and reserved.

[23] used two commercial PEEK cent chromatography tees to align two round glass capillaries inside a square glass capillary. The device was easy to dismantle and assemble and allowed adjustment of the distance between inner round capillaries during operation by pulling or pushing the capillaries inside the outer capillary. The device was able to generate monodisperse O/W or water-in-oil (W/O) emulsions with a droplet size down to 20 1/2m. Chang et al. [24] inserted two coaxial capillaries inside two T-junction connectors and used the device to make core-shell monomer droplets via two sequential co-flow drop generation steps. Martino et al. [25] fabricated a glass capillary device by 3D printing acrylonitrile butadiene styrene. The device consisted of a rectangular platform with a square observation hole in the middle and two sliding connectors holding coaxial assembly of round and square capillaries. The distance between inner capillaries could be adjusted during drop generation by moving the connectors along two rails made at both sides of the platform. After 3D printing, the support material must be removed by sonicating the parts with isopropanol. Herranz-Blanco et al. [26] fabricated a glass capillary device with a round-capillary-inside-round-capillary geometry using Shapeways 3D printed steel. The device was used to prepare polymeric nanoparticles by nanoprecipitation and core/shell droplets. Shapeways 3D printed steel is corrosive and non-biocompatible, since it contains 40% bronze, and the printing resolution of 3 mm is relatively poor [27]. Both devices mentioned above are fed with the fluids using hypodermic needles. Micromilling has advantages over 3D printing in terms of the broader choice of materials that can be used for fabrication, precision, speed, and cleanliness of the finished product [28]. The main disadvantage of all subtractive manufacturing methods including micromilling is the generation of waste during fabrication compared to 3D printing which uses the exact amount of material to make the desired part [29]. Both processes employ computer numerical control (CNC) machining that automates the process and enables direct conversion of CAD models to finished parts, thereby improving repeatability and precision. In this work, novel, cheap, easy to dismantle and assemble, and reusable glass capillary devices have been fabricated using micromilling (Fig. 1d). Glass capillaries are held between two interchangeable bespoke plastic blocks that can be easily joined together and separated using Lego(R)-inspired stud-and-tube coupling system (Fig. S1). Three different blocks were combined in different manners to obtain three different flow configurations. The design allows a round-capillary-inside-round-capillary geometry (Fig. 1e) in contrast with round-capillary-inside-square-capillary geometry used in the conventional device (Fig. 1b). Self-alignment of the capillaries was achieved by precise drilling of the mounting holes in both blocks.
