FOM was applied to PEMFCs in the past [11], but it has not been widely employed yet. The aim of this work is to develop an accurate model of a real PEMFC able to predict its behavior under variable operative conditions. In order to achieve this goal, a series of experimental tests were carried out on a 12-cells PEMFC stack at the University of Genova laboratories. The stack was tested under different operating conditions, including steady-state and dynamic tests. A Fractional Order Model (FOM) was developed starting from the results obtained through the EIS technique. The FOM was implemented in Matlab/Simulink(R) environment and validated against experimental data. Analysis of the fractional order modeling of a PEMFC RIZZI, FRANCESCO;BERRUTO, ROLANDO;CHIESA, MATTEO;GIANELLE, STEFANO;PRINA, MASSIMO GIUSEPPE Among the environmentally friendly energy conversion technologies, one of the most suitable solutions to cope with pollutant emissions and global warming issues are fuel cells, which have attracted the interest of many researchers in the last decades. In particular, the Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC) has proved to be the most suitable for applications between 0.1 and 1000 kW [1]. The main advantages of PEMFCs are the high performance, modularity and potentially pollution-free operation. However, this technology has to meet specific technical requirements to become commercially competitive. US Department of Energy (DOE) and European Institutions have set clear technical targets to be achieved by PEMFC systems with costs and lifetime being the main issues; for stationary and automotive applications 40.000 h and 6000 h of operations are required, respectively ([2,3]). In order to enhance FCS reliability and lifetime, control and diagnostics must be improved thanks to advanced monitoring algorithms, which must be fast enough to operate on-field to obtain effective advantages. Advanced techniques are required to analyze performance losses caused by degradation mechanisms and the impact of the current operating conditions. The most effective methods used to characterize the performance of a fuel cell are electrochemical techniques, such as Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS), polarization curves, cyclic voltammetry, AC impedance and current interruption techniques [4]. Among these techniques, EIS is the most suitable to recognize the individual contributions related to voltage drops caused by membrane, charge transfer and mass transfer resistances, both for single cells and overall stack [5]. The EIS technique is used to measure the frequency dependence of the impedance of a fuel cell by applying a small sinusoidal AC voltage (or current) as a perturbation signal to the fuel cell and measuring the current (or voltage) response. This is done at different frequencies for each load to obtain the overall system impedance, often plotted as Nyquist diagram [6]. The applications of EIS in PEMFC studies allows providing electrochemical information about the FCS, which can then help in fuel cell structure optimization and selection of the most appropriate operating conditions. The EIS appears to be the most suitable method for fuel cells on-field monitoring and control, thanks to its peculiar characteristics [7]. Indeed, the main advantage of using EIS resides in the possibility to recognize the contributions of each physical phenomenon (i.e. ohmic losses, charge-transfer and diffusion limitations) to the full impedance thanks to the Equivalent Circuit Modelling (ECM), which consists in modelling the cells using equivalent circuits. Therefore, each contribution can be identified since each circuital parameter represents a physical phenomenon occurring inside the fuel cell [8].

In addition, a longitudinal study using immunisation stress in 2 month old infants found antenatal maternal depressive symptoms to be predictive of cortisol reactivity, but the relationship was complex, with both low and high levels of depressive symptoms predicting greater reactivity (Fernandes et al., 2014). In contrast to studies of infants and young children, investigations of older samples have the advantage that standard paradigms exist which reliably provoke a cortisol stress response (Kirschbaum et al., 1993), although few studies have examined cortisol reactivity in youth or adults at risk for depression. One study examining the at-risk offspring of parents with bipolar disorder did not find cortisol responses to stress to distinguish them from controls (Ellenbogen et al., 2006). Moreover, in contrast to the pattern of findings deriving from infants and young children, a second study examining parental retrospective self-reports of "depressive problems" found that these were associated with reduced cortisol stress reactivity in adolescent girls, and were not associated with cortisol responses in boys (Bouma et al., 2011). The limited availability of robust evidence for enhanced cortisol reactivity to stress in the offspring of depressed parents is significant, as elevations in basal cortisol levels that have been observed in this group have been proposed to reflect HPA axis dysregulation linked to increased vulnerability to stressors (Ostiguy et al., 2011). Further investigation is warranted. Here, we report on cortisol stress reactivity in a longitudinally studied sample of young adults. Participants in the study were recruited shortly following birth based on the presence or absence of maternal depression during the postnatal period; and maternal depression was repeatedly assessed throughout the 22-years of the study, providing a clear profile of offspring exposure to depressive disorder. In the same sample, we previously identified elevations in basal morning cortisol secretion in the 13-year old offspring of mothers who experienced postnatal depression (PND) versus control group offspring (Halligan et al., 2004). In the current study, offspring cortisol reactivity in response to a standard social stressor (Trier Social Stress Test: TSST) was measured at age 22-years. We used hierarchical linear modelling (HLM) to model changes in cortisol concentrations over the course of the TSST in relation to PND group status, and to test the hypothesis that PND versus control group offspring would show enhanced cortisol stress reactivity as young adults. We controlled for gender, history of offspring depressive or anxiety disorder, current offspring depressive or anxiety symptoms, and incidences of negative life events in our analyses, given their potential relationship with cortisol reactivity (Burke et al., 2005; Petrowski et al., 2010; Allen et al., 2014). Since elevated basal cortisol concentrations have previously been interpreted as a marker for HPA dysregulation or increased reactivity to daily stress (Goodyer et al., 2000; Kunz-Ebrecht et al., 2004; Ostiguy et al., 2011), we also specifically tested whether basal morning cortisol levels at 13-years predicted the TSST reactivity profile at 22-years.

Indeed, advanced service provision entails a more relational approach because it requires greater involvement of customers and ecosystem partners in value creation processes (e.g., Lusch, Vargo, & Gustafsson, 2016; Parida et al., 2019; Petri & Jacob, 2016). Thus, the servitization literature would benefit from studies that provide evidence of viable alternative governance strategies for firms to capture value from advanced services because a range of strategies can lead to optimal financial outcomes (Forkmann, Henneberg, Witell, & Kindstrom, 2017). For example, one governance strategy could be to tie customers into long-term binding contractual commitments, whereas another could be to adopt a more trust-based relational approach, conceivably leading to different performance outcomes. Second, our understanding of the governance of relationships in servitization is still limited (Petri & Jacob, 2016; Reim et al., 2018; Tuli et al., 2007). Ideally, advanced services would allow superior value creation in provider-customer relationships by leveraging complementary assets, maintaining high levels of informal trust and knowledge sharing, and making customized investments in each partnership (Dyer et al., 2018; Ronnberg Sjodin, Parida, & Kohtamaki, 2016; Ronnberg Sjodin, Parida, & Wincent, 2016). However, this is not always the case. There appear to be important tradeoffs in governance depending on market conditions (Huang & Chiu, 2018; Reim et al., 2018). Yet these tradeoffs have not been systematically studied. By focusing on the performance effect of alternative governance strategies for advanced service providers under varying conditions, we can identify important choices that advanced service providers make not only to create value but also to capture value (Baines & Lightfoot, 2013; Huikkola, Ylimaki, & Kohtamaki, 2013). Third, there is a need to advance the servitization literature beyond overly simplistic, linear explanations and show that multiple pathways can lead to successful servitization (Forkmann et al., 2017; Kowalkowski et al., 2017; Parida et al., 2019; Rabetino et al., 2018). A suitable way to do so is to adopt a configurational approach (e.g., Goduscheit & Faullant, 2018; Ronnberg Sjodin, Parida, & Kohtamaki, 2016; Ronnberg Sjodin, Parida, & Wincent, 2016), which has several advantages when exploring how different configurations of governance conditions facilitate the performance of advanced service providers. The configurational lens enables the capture of three types of causal complexity (Greckhamer, Misangyi, Elms, & Lacey, 2008; Ragin, 2008): conjunction (i.e., different conditions do not act in isolation but rather work in combination), equifinality (i.e., there are multiple paths to the desired outcome), and causal asymmetry (i.e., low-performing configurations are not necessarily a mirror image of high-performing configurations). A configurational approach would thus enable greater potential of uncovering complexity and different paths in the servitization-performance relationship (Kowalkowski et al., 2017). This study uses a configurational perspective to address the aforementioned gaps. Against this background, the purpose of this study is to identify diverse configurations of relational governance strategies and their effect on the financial performance of advanced service providers.

As the minutes ticked by, the young man's impatience grew. He glanced about him at the quiet, moonlit landscape, his eyes lingering on the dark, motionless trees and the silent, still water of the brook. The air was filled with the sweet scent of wild thyme and heather, and the nightingales sang their soft, melancholy songs in the distance. But the young man's thoughts were not of the beauty of nature; he was too occupied with his own thoughts of Cynthy, and the promise she had made to meet him. He sighed and rose to his feet, his eyes scanning the darkness as if he expected to see her appear at any moment. But as the minutes passed, and there was no sign of her, his patience began to wear thin. He paced up and down the bank, his footsteps quiet on the soft earth, his eyes fixed on the darkness beyond the trees. "Ah, Cynthy, Cynthy, why dost thou tarry?" he muttered to himself, his voice low and impatient. "Art thou not as good as thy word? Doth thy heart not beat with the same eagerness as mine?" As he spoke, a faint rustling sound came from the darkness beyond the trees. The young man's heart quickened, and he stood still, his eyes fixed on the spot where the sound seemed to come from. And then, out of the darkness, a figure emerged, a figure that was as lovely as the moon, with skin as pale as the stars, and hair as dark as the night. The young man's heart leapt with joy, and he took a step forward, his eyes drinking in the sight of her. But as he looked into her face, he saw that it was not Cynthy, but another girl, a girl with a face as lovely as a flower, and eyes as bright as the stars. "Who art thou?" the young man asked, his voice low and husky, his eyes fixed on her face. The girl smiled, and her eyes sparkled with mischief. "I am a traveler," she said, her voice as sweet as honey. "I came to the brook to drink, and I heard your sweet singing, and I followed the sound." The young man's face fell, and he felt a pang of disappointment. But the girl's smile was so radiant, and her eyes were so bright, that he forgot all about Cynthy, and his heart began to beat with a new and exciting rhythm. "Come," he said, taking her hand, "let us sit by the brook, and I will sing to you, and tell you the story of my love for Cynthy."

As we delve further into the practice of scenario analysis, it becomes imperative to recognize the essential role of stakeholder engagement in shaping and refining these scenarios (Rounsevell and Metzger, 2010). Engaging stakeholders from diverse sectors, including government, academia, private industry, and local communities, allows for a more holistic understanding of how land-use drivers may evolve and interact in the future. This inclusive approach aids in validating scenarios by integrating varied perspectives and insights, thereby ensuring that the scenarios are not only scientifically grounded but also contextually relevant and socially acceptable (Biggs et al., 2007; Reed et al., 2009). Incorporating local knowledge and values can particularly enrich scenario-building processes, as stakeholders bring nuanced understandings of local ecosystems and socio-economic dynamics that are often overlooked in broader analyses (Reed et al., 2013). This participatory approach helps democratize the scenario development process, fostering ownership and buy-in, which are crucial for subsequent policy implementation and adherence (Stringer et al., 2006). Moreover, the integration of both qualitative and quantitative data provides a robust platform for scenario analysis, enabling a comprehensive assessment of potential pathways. Qualitative insights, often derived from stakeholder consultations and workshops, can illuminate the motivations, beliefs, and behaviors that underpin land-use decisions, while quantitative models can simulate the biophysical and economic impacts of various scenarios over time (Harrison et al., 2013; Swart et al., 2004). The complexity and interconnectivity of land systems underscore the necessity of employing systems thinking in scenario development. By recognizing and mapping the linkages among social, ecological, and economic components, we can better anticipate the cascading effects of changes in one domain on others. This systems perspective is crucial for identifying critical leverage points where interventions can yield significant benefits, as well as for recognizing potential unintended consequences that might arise from well-meaning policies (Meadows, 2008; Schluter et al., 2012). As we look towards the future, the role of technology and innovation in scenario analysis becomes increasingly salient. Advances in remote sensing, geographic information systems, machine learning, and data analytics offer unprecedented opportunities to enhance our understanding of land-use dynamics and improve the predictive power of our models (Verburg et al., 2015). These tools enable the real-time monitoring of environmental changes and can facilitate more dynamic and adaptive scenario planning. Finally, scenario analysis not only informs policy but also empowers adaptive management practices. By continuously monitoring environmental indicators and comparing them with scenario projections, policymakers and land managers can respond more nimbly to emerging trends and surprises. This adaptive approach, characterized by iterative learning and flexibility, is fundamental to navigating the uncertainties of future land-use and sustainability challenges (Folke et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2002). Scenario analysis thus serves as a bridge connecting rigorous scientific inquiry with practical policy and management decisions. It provides a structured yet flexible framework to explore and prepare for multiple possible futures, helping societies to chart pathways towards sustainable land management in the face of uncertainty and change. Through interdisciplinary collaboration and stakeholder engagement, scenario analysis charts a path to a more resilient and informed stewardship of our planet's land resources (Wackernagel et al., 2002; Carpenter et al., 2009).

We focus on 'collectivism-individualism', a society-wide set of values that govern the role of the individual relative to the group (Greif, 1994; Hofstede, Hofstede, & Minkov, 2010; Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Schwartz, 1994). Collectivist and individualist values have been shown to mold human cognition and social behavior in a range of domains such as thinking styles (Nisbett, 2010), everyday dishonesty (Gachter & Schulz, 2016), and the inclination to trust others (Yamagishi, Cook, & Watabe, 1998). The central role of the group in collectivist societies plausibly modulates the relevance of social information in people's everyday interactions. In collectivist societies, people tend to see themselves primarily as part of a collective; they tend to value fitting-in and harmony and to derive their own identity from their relationships with others. By contrast, people from individualist societies are inclined to see themselves as independent, to emphasize uniqueness and autonomy, and to regard others as points of social comparison (Markus & Kitayama, 1991). More than individualist societies, collectivist societies emphasize conformist values in upbringing, schooling, and daily life (relying on rote learning and valuing obedience to parents and teachers; Mesoudi, Chang, Murray, & Lu, 2015; Schwartz, 1994). Psychological studies indicate that people from collectivist societies are more likely than people from individualist societies to conform to majority behavior among their peers (Bond & Smith, 1996). Moreover, recent behavioral experiments suggest that collectivist values may enhance individuals' reliance on social learning in solving complex individual tasks (Glowacki & Molleman, 2017; Mesoudi et al., 2015; Toelch, Bruce, Newson, Richerson, & Reader, 2014). Based on these observations, we predict that people from collectivist societies rely more on social information in cooperative interactions, and are more inclined to follow majority behavior than people from individualist societies. We use a behavioral experiment to assess basic propensities for social learning in cooperative decision making across two very different societies, China and the United Kingdom. We ask to what extent people from a collectivist (China) and an individualist (United Kingdom) society use social information in making cooperative decisions, and whether they use payoff-based or majority-based social learning strategies. Native Chinese (in Ningbo and Shanghai, n = 320) and native British participants (in Norwich and Nottingham, n = 220) completed a series of tasks (Molleman, van den Berg, & Weissing, 2014; van den Berg et al., 2015) in which they interacted anonymously via web browsers. Participants were placed in groups of five to make a series of simultaneous binary decisions. If societal background matters, we expect similar behavior within a country, but differences between countries. Participants faced three interaction settings in sequence (Fig. 1): a social dilemma, a coordination game, and a 'best choice' setting. In the social dilemma, one option ('cooperate') increased the average payoffs of all group members, while the other option ('defect') improved one's own payoffs in a given period. In the coordination game, the expected payoffs of either option increased with the number of group members choosing it.

Additionally, while the U.S. offers comprehensive upper secondary education, Japanese high schools are institutionally stratified in the form of between-school tracks (e.g., LeTendre et al., 2003; Matsuoka, 2015b)2: ninth-grade students in Japan take high school admission examinations at the end of their junior high school education and then go on to high schools that match their demonstrated academic performance. Thus, unlike the U.S., the first critical education selection's timing is the end of the lower secondary education for most students (i.e., those attending neighboring public junior high schools) in Japan. Importantly, studies (e.g., Yamamoto and Brinton, 2010) have repeatedly found that the high school a particular student attends greatly shapes that individual's future educational attainment in the society. This means that the high school (track) attended is highly consequential as it significantly influences the student's educational trajectory in the education system. Given these vast differences between the Japanese context of a highly standardized compulsory education system with a highly consequential educational selection event in ninth grade, and the U.S. context of a highly de-centralized education system with comprehensive high school education, college-educated parents in Japan and the U.S. possibly practice concerted cultivation in different ways. Specifically, some studies hint at potential specific characteristics in middle-class parenting in the Japanese context, while the U.S. study (Potter and Roksa, 2013) indicates that disparities between parental education levels concerning children's participation in extracurricular leisure activities such as art and sports do not significantly change between third and fifth grades. Using cross-sectional data on parents with elementary school children from first to sixth grade, Suzuki (2010) provides descriptive statistics of children's participation in EAs and states that children's main activities outside the school system shift from sports to academics including juku, a major form of shadow education services (e.g., Entrich, 2015; Matsuoka, 2015b, 2018; Ono, 2001; Rohlen, 1980; Stevenson and Baker, 1992; Tsukada, 1991), offering additional enrichment and/or remedial learning opportunities for improving children's academic performance in school in exchange for tuition. The same data show that participation rates in EAs in the sports and arts categories gradually increase from first grade, peak in third and fourth grade (having equivalent rates) for sports and fourth grade for arts, then gradually decrease from fourth to sixth grades (Kataoka, 2010; Nishijima et al., 2012; Suzuki, 2010). Meanwhile, the participation rate for academic activities, including juku attendance, consistently increases from first to sixth grade. Although these reports used cross-sectional data gathered from different children in each elementary school grade rather than longitudinal data following the same children over several years, the data suggest that, on average, parents shift their strategies regarding EAs around fourth grade.

I remember those bright green apples vividly-crisp, refreshing, and almost a badge of honor in a world swirling with food angst. It's interesting how food can morph into a symbol of accomplishment or failure over time. The more I engaged with Weight Watchers, the more my relationship with food transformed into an obsession-a complex dance that felt more like a competition against myself than a nourishing experience. I had traded meals for numbers, replaced hearty lunches with strategic choices to maximize points, and yet, paradoxically, I still felt lost in a loop of self-judgment and guilt. At home, I was often surrounded by family gatherings, celebrations filled with laughter and, of course, food. But my mind would frequently wander back to my points system, dividing my attention between enjoying the moment and calculating caloric sacrifices. I now realize how each meal became an internal battle, and with every weigh-in came a swell of anxiety. It wasn't enough to just be present; I felt the weight of my worth hinging on that little scale. As I moved through the years, my struggle transformed. Binge eating crept into my life like a shadow-sometimes it knocked on the door softly, and other times it barged in uninvited. It often filled the void left by restriction, a backlash against a regime that was meant to liberate me. I now understand that this pattern was not just about food itself. It was about control, emotions, and seeking comfort in the mundane chaos of life. I bounced from one extreme to another-rigorously counting calories one week, then succumbing to two or three days of indulgent rebellion another week. It felt cyclical, like I was on a relentless treadmill, running but never quite arriving. As I ventured into adulthood, my professional life blossomed, but the cycle continued to haunt me. I qualified as a personal trainer, pouring my newfound knowledge into positive change. I felt empowered to help others navigate their wellness journeys, but within me, the tumult swirled, often unnoticed amid the drive to succeed. It was such an ironic twist; in teaching others about healthy living, I found myself grappling with conflicting ideas of health and worthiness. Over time, and with reflection, I began to recognize something crucial: My relationship with food was not solely about what I consumed, but how I engaged with myself. It involved deep-seated beliefs about body image and self-esteem that warranted consideration, far beyond a mere dietary overhaul. My binge episodes began to shed light on my emotional landscape, revealing the discomfort, stress, and anxiety that often lay beneath the surface. Conversations with friends and family unearthed secrets I once held tight. They welcomed me into a vulnerable space where shame started to dissipate, and validation bloomed. I sought help from professionals who helped me navigate these complexities. It became clear that healing wasn't a linear journey but a nuanced exploration, an ever-evolving dance toward understanding. There's this profound liberation in simply being honest with myself about my struggles-the acknowledgment that it's okay to have slip-ups, that it's possible to learn and grow alongside missteps. Embracing this process has undeniably changed my perspective on wellness as a whole. It has made me curious about the intersection of food, emotions, and self-worth. Now, I feel driven to unpack this journey alongside you, dear listeners, as we uncover the layers of our relationships with food together. The aim is to foster a community of support, understanding, and shared experiences, allowing us to thrive in our complexities. So hold tight; we're just getting started.

Emerging research suggests that MRE could revolutionize the way we assess and understand neurodegenerative conditions by offering insight into the microstructural integrity that traditional MRI does not capture. Unlike volumetric measures that simply quantify size, MRE provides data on tissue stiffness that correlates with the microenvironment's cellular matrix and integrity. Studies have indicated that certain pathological changes, such as those found in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, manifest as distinct alterations in brain viscoelastic properties before significant atrophy becomes apparent on volumetric MRI (Schwarb et al., 2016). This ability to detect changes earlier could pave the way for interventions that prevent significant progression of these diseases. Furthermore, MRE's sensitivity to microscopic changes underscores its potential as a non-invasive diagnostic tool that could be employed in routine screening, especially for populations at high risk for neurodegenerative disorders. As the understanding of viscoelastic changes associated with early pathological processes expands, it may allow for the development of specific mechanical biomarkers tailored to different diseases. For instance, ongoing studies are exploring the specific patterns of viscoelasticity alterations associated with various dementia subtypes, with the aim of differentiating them with higher precision compared to current methodologies (Hiscox et al., 2019). However, while MRE holds promise, there are challenges that must be addressed before widespread clinical adoption can be realized. The technical complexity of MRE, including the generation and control of mechanical waves, requires specialized equipment and expertise that may not be readily available in all clinical settings. Moreover, the interpretation of MRE results requires a nuanced understanding of both normal viscoelastic properties across different age ranges and how these properties may be influenced by other factors such as hydration status, blood flow, and intracranial pressure. Standardization of MRE protocols is paramount, similar to the processes that allowed MRI to become ubiquitous in clinical practice. This includes the refinement of wave generation techniques, improved algorithms for data inversion, and consensus on normative datasets that can serve as references. Collaboration among research institutions is crucial for advancing these goals, fostering a collective understanding of MRE's potential impact on neurological diagnostics. In parallel with technical advancements, research must also strive to elucidate the biological underpinnings of viscoelastic changes observed with MRE. This requires interdisciplinary efforts that integrate insights from biomechanics, neuroscience, and clinical neurology. As the biological significance of MRE findings becomes clearer, correlations between mechanical properties and pathology can be systematically explored, potentially unveiling novel therapeutic targets. Ultimately, the future of MRE in neurodegeneration rests on its ability to offer actionable insights. Detecting disease earlier and understanding disease progression in greater detail will be pivotal in not only refining diagnostic criteria but also in crafting more effective treatment protocols. As the field progresses, MRE may emerge not merely as an adjunct to existing imaging technologies but as a cornerstone of neurological assessments, reshaping paradigms of patient care from early detection through to management and monitoring. As with any burgeoning technology, the promise of MRE as a transformative tool in neurological imaging brings with it the responsibility to carefully validate its capabilities, ensuring that its integration into clinical workflows enhances the accuracy, efficiency, and efficacy of neurodiagnostic and treatment strategies.

John, the second, still remained with her, assisting, by his unceasing toil, to earn a supply for their daily wants. Henry, the third son, a bright-eyed youth of sixteen, had attracted the notice of his pastor, and by his advice and assistance, had been placed on the list of the beneficiaries of the American Education Society, and was now at an Academy, preparing for College. James was living with a farmer in the neighborhood, and was now on the green with Arthur. These changes had already taken place, and now, could she part with Arthur, - her sweet-tempered, gentle Arthur? That was the question which agitated and saddened her. An offer had been made her, by Mr. Martin, who lived in an adjoining town, and whom she knew to be an excellent man. He wished to take Arthur, and keep him till he was twenty-one; would clothe him, send him to school, and treat him as one of his own family; training him to habits of industry and economy. Could she hope any thing better for her darling boy? There was a younger brother and two sisters still remaining at home, and embarrassed as she was, ought she not to be grateful for such an opening, and thankfully avail herself of it? Such was the view another might take of the subject, but to her it was unspeakably painful to think of the separation. Arthur was ten years old; but he was a modest and timid boy, whose sensitive nature had led him to cling more closely to his mother's side than his bolder and more active brothers. Mrs. Hamilton knew that this was no time for the indulgence of sentiment; she knew that duty must be done, even though every chord of her heart quivered with agony. After much consideration and earnest prayer, she had concluded to let him go, and the thought of sending him away from her, and all he loved, among entire strangers, was what made her so sorrowful. She strove to calm herself by the reflection, that she had done what seemed to be right, and by remembering the blessed promises of God's Holy Word to the fatherless, and to all those who put their trust in Him. With a cheerful voice, she called the boys, telling James it was time for him to go home, as Captain L., with whom he lived, was a very particular man, and would be displeased if he staid out beyond the proper time. Mrs. Hamilton's sons had been trained to obedience, and James never thought of lingering and loitering for half an hour, as I have seen some boys do, after being told to go. He just gave Rover a good pat on the back, and saying a hasty "good-night" to his mother and Arthur, he ran home. Arthur was alone with his mother, and she told him of the arrangement she had made for him, and the reasons for it.

What do you think is the biggest misconception about evolution? De Waal: That it's always competition, red tooth and claw. The reason that is such an easy thing to say is because nature documentaries always show animals fighting over food and females. But actually, in everyday life, cooperation is much more important than competition. If you look at chimpanzees, they spend most of their time grooming each other, playing together, sharing food. All these things that we usually don't film as much, and yet those are the building blocks of primate societies. CNN: Is this why you believe humans are naturally empathetic? De Waal: Yes, and empathy is part of our biology. We share it with all mammals, and probably even birds. It's just one of these capacities that we have that is very ancient. It's a mammalian capacity, and we can recognize ourselves in the emotions of others. And sometimes we take action based on that recognition. CNN: Can you tell me about some examples of animal empathy? De Waal: One example that I give in the book is about a bonobo - a female named Kuni. She was in a zoo in England, and she found a starling that fell into her enclosure. And she picked up the bird and started walking around with it. Then she took it to the highest point in the enclosure, unfolded its wings and spread them wide open, and sent the bird down to see if it could fly. It didn't fly, so she went back down and tried again, until eventually she got the bird to fly away. Now that's an example of empathy.... Another example I talk about in the book is a capuchin monkey who lost a fight with another male and ended up sitting all by himself, whimpering. A little juvenile came over and put an arm around his shoulder, like a friend. These are the kinds of behaviors that we see that make us think that they understand the emotions of others, and sometimes will respond to them. CNN: Do you think animals have a sense of spirituality? De Waal: It's very hard to know because we cannot ask them. They cannot tell us. But we do know that they have many of the same emotions as we have. They get angry; they get jealous; they feel love; they feel compassion. So I assume there must be some sort of spiritual feelings associated with that. But then the next question is, do they believe in invisible agents, spirits, things like that? So I mean first of all just kind of giving some definitions because I feel like sometimes these terms can get used interchangeably and people aren't really sure what they mean. And so bribery is using a reward to try to stop an unwanted behavior while it's happening. So let's take the example that Hillary gave us if instead of having a conversation with the younger siblings ahead of time about what's expected during the hockey game. If instead you're at the hockey game and your younger siblings are being disruptive maybe running around screaming throwing stuff whatever it may be and then you pull them aside and you say hey guys if you sit down and you listen and you behave yourself then you can have a treat after the game. That would be bribery because you're trying to stop the unwanted Behavior as it's happening and you're offering a reward. Whereas reinforcement is providing a reward after an appropriate Behavior occurs. So again in our example, if you're having a conversation ahead of time, you're letting them know what's expected and then they follow through with that. Then yeah, you could provide a reward afterwards which would be reinforcement not bribery. So I hope that makes sense. And I also wanted to mention too that bribery is often used to get someone to do something that they wouldn't normally do whereas reinforcement is used to increase the likelihood that a desired behavior will occur in the future. So for example, let's say your kid doesn't typically like to clean their room and you want them to do it. So you say okay, I'll pay you $20 if you clean your room that would be bribery because you're offering money to get them to do something that they probably wouldn't do otherwise. But if your kid does like cleaning their room and you want to encourage that behavior, then you might say Hey, every time you clean your room without me asking you can pick a prize from the prize box or something like that. So that would be reinforcement because you're trying to increase the likelihood that the desired behavior will happen again in the future. This approach would necessitate a comprehensive understanding of both the biological characteristics of invasive species and the ecological contexts of the environments they invade. A multi-faceted evaluation of numerous habitats would yield valuable insights into patterns of invasibility, thereby allowing researchers to identify commonalities and divergences in ecological responses to invasions (Crawley et al., 1999; Macdougall et al., 2009). Such comparisons could encompass a variety of metrics: environmental variables such as soil composition, climate patterns, and hydrology must all be factored in, alongside biological metrics that assess the richness and identity of resident communities. Furthermore, temporal dynamics play a crucial role in the success of invasive species. Studies have shown that invasions can take years to manifest, with initial appearances often giving way to exponential growth and significant ecological impacts later down the road (Davis et al., 2000). In this regard, understanding the temporal nature of invasive species-how their impacts and community interactions evolve over time-offers another dimension to our comprehensions of biological invasions. Management strategies, too, must evolve in tandem with our understanding of invasions. Effective management requires an integrated approach that combines prevention, early detection, and rapid response (Hulme, 2009). Many invasive species are notorious for their ability to escape control once established, prompting the need for preemptive measures in susceptible areas (Zavaleta et al., 2001). The development of predictive models that incorporate environmental data and biological characteristics of potential invaders is critical in striving for a proactive stance. Additionally, sociocultural factors contribute significantly to both the success of invasions and the effectiveness of management plans. Human behaviors, such as the introduction of ornamental species that later escape cultivation, interact fluidly with ecological factors, creating complex scenarios that challenge simplistic ecological models (Levine and D'Antonio, 1999). Local policies, educational outreach, and collaboration among stakeholders can greatly influence both awareness and actions taken against invasive species. The intersection of biology and sociocultural dynamics suggests a need for interdisciplinary approaches, engaging fields from ecology and biology to sociology and environmental policy (Simberloff, 2013). Moreover, examining the genetic adaptations of invasive species can yield further insights into their resilience and competitive abilities. Research into phenotypic plasticity, for example, reveals how certain invaders can acclimate to diverse environmental conditions, further complicating their management (Richardson and Pysek, 2006). Genetic variability within invasive populations may grant them a selective advantage, enabling rapid responses to environmental changes, thereby reinforcing the importance of incorporating genetic perspectives into invasibility assessments. In summary, the challenge posed by biological invasions warrants a holistic view that encompasses ecological, biological, sociocultural, and genetic dimensions. The quest to understand and manage invasive species must consider all of these facets in order to devise robust strategies and responses. As such, the synthesis of interdisciplinary research will lead to the construction of a coherent framework that facilitates not only the mitigation of current invasions but also the prevention of future incursions, fostering resilient ecosystems capable of sustaining their native biodiversity in an ever-changing world.

But he is sometimes rather slow; he is not as quick and clever as Blanche, and she often puts him down at first, though she generally comes round to his way in the end. She answered for him now, though I hadn't spoken to her. 'How can there not be something the matter?' she said sharply. 'If Peterkin has been half-an-hour or an hour, perhaps, wandering about the streets, it shows he has at least lost his way, and who knows where he's got to. I wish you wouldn't ask such silly questions, Giles.' Then, all of a sudden, Elf burst out crying. It may have been partly Blanche's sharp tone, which had startled her, and made her take more notice of it all. 'Oh, Clem, Clem,' she wailed, 'could he have been stolened?' 'No, no, darling,' said Clement, dabbing her face with his pocket-handkerchief. 'There are kind policemen in the streets, you know. They wouldn't let a little boy like Peterkin be stolen.' 'But they does take little boys to pison,' said Elf. 'I've see'd them. It's 'cos of that I'm frightened of them for Peterkin.' That was not quite true. She had never thought of policemen till, unluckily, Clem spoke of them in his wish to comfort her. She did not mean to say what was not true, of course, but there never was such a child as Elf for arguing, even then when she was only four years old. Indeed, she's not half as bad now that she is eight, twice as old, and I often tell her so. Perhaps that evening it wasn't a bad thing, for the talking about policemen stopped her crying, which was even worse than her arguing, once she started a good roar. 'It's just because of that, that I'm so frightened about dear sweet little Peterkin,' she repeated. 'Rubbish, Elf,' I began, but Clem looked at me and I stopped. 'You needn't be frightened that Peterkin will be taken to prison, Elfie,' he said in his kind, rather slow way. 'It's only naughty little boys that the policemen take to prison, and Peterkin isn't naughty,' and then he wiped Elf's eyes again, and she forgot to go on crying, for just then nurse came upstairs. She was not actually crying, of course, but she did look very worried, so Clem and Blanche's faces did not clear up at all. Nor did mine, I suppose. I really did not know what to think, I was waiting to see what the others thought, for we three younger ones looked up to Clement and Blanche a good deal, and we still do. They are twins, and they seem to mix together so well. Blanche is quick and clever, and Clement is awfully sensible, and they are both very kind, though Clem is the gentlest.

As you ponder these profound insights, consider how often you may have found yourself feeling trapped by the weight of your circumstances. Perhaps it was a challenging job, a difficult relationship, or even the daunting prospect of financial instability. It's easy to succumb to the belief that your situation dictates your mood, your actions, and your future. Yet, in those moments of darkness, I urge you to remember Dr. Frankl's journey-his unyielding assertion that the power to choose remains intact even in the most oppressive conditions. So, how do we begin to harness this power of choice in our own lives? First, we must cultivate awareness. Awareness of our thoughts, our emotions, and the choices that stem from them. This presents an opportunity for reflection: do we often fall into patterns of negative thinking? Are our choices guided more by fear and resignation than by hope and possibility? Often, our autopilot mode leads us down a path of least resistance, making decision-making a passive activity rather than an intentional one. By practicing mindfulness-the art of being present with our thoughts and feelings without judgment-we can start to recognize these patterns. Acknowledge that feeling overwhelmed or defeated is a normal human experience. Then shift your focus back to choice. In every moment, no matter how dire, you have the option to alter your perspective. One powerful technique is reframing your mindset. Instead of seeing challenges as roadblocks, view them as opportunities for growth. This subtle, yet transformative shift can lead to profound realizations. Now, let's take a practical step. Write down three areas in your life where you feel dissatisfied or constrained. Next to each area, note the choices you have made that contributed to your current situation. Then, brainstorm alternative choices that you could make moving forward-choices that align with your values and aspirations. For instance, if you feel stuck in a job that does not fulfill you, consider the choice of pursuing further education or networking in a field that excites you. Empower yourself with the knowledge that every choice creates a ripple effect, setting off a series of events that can lead you in a completely different direction. Ultimately, change is not a monumental leap but rather a collection of small, conscious decisions. Every day, from the moment we wake until we close our eyes at night, we are confronted with choices that shape our reality. Will you hit that snooze button again or rise to embrace the day? Will you engage in conversations that uplift, or will you indulge in those that bring you down? Every choice counts. And here's the valuable takeaway: when you realize that you are never truly at the mercy of your circumstances, empowerment begins to swell within you. The simple mantra of "make better choices" can remind you of your agency. Commit to seeing potential instead of obstacles, and transform those three words into a daily practice. As you do so, reflect on the lessons of Dr. Frankl and consider what kind of attitude you wish to embody-one marked by resilience, courage, and hope. So, as we wrap up today's discussion, I challenge you to step back and evaluate your life through the lens of choice. Reflect on the freedom you possess at this very moment. The power to create change lies within your grasp. And remember, while life may present challenges that can feel insurmountable, it is your choices-the conscious, deliberate choices-that ultimately set the course for your journey ahead. What will you choose today?

As the summer heatwave continues to bear down on the UK, the residents of Cornwall Drive are bracing themselves for yet another long, hot summer of living in the shadow of the 40ft high rubbish mountain. The once-peaceful suburban road has been transformed into a toxic wasteland, with the constant threat of fire and the stench of rotting garbage hanging in the air. Despite the efforts of the London Fire Brigade, the mountain of rubbish continues to smoulder away, emitting a noxious cloud of smoke and fumes that wafts through the streets and into the homes of the residents. The fire service has been called to the site more than 650 times since 2011, at a cost of over 650,000, and yet the problem remains unsolved. For Alan Cowburn, 74, who has lived on the road for 50 years, the constant threat of fire and the putrid stench of rotting litter is taking a toll on his health. "I'm at my wit's end," he said. "I'm fed up with living in this toxic environment. I'm fed up with the rats, the flies, the smell, the constant fear of fire. It's a nightmare." The residents of Cornwall Drive are not alone in their frustration. The local council has been criticized for its handling of the situation, with many calling for the rubbish tip to be moved to a more suitable location. But despite the mounting pressure, the council remains silent on the issue, leaving the residents to suffer in silence. As the summer heatwave shows no signs of abating, the residents of Cornwall Drive are left to wonder when their nightmare will finally come to an end. Will the council take action to move the rubbish tip, or will they continue to ignore the problem, leaving the residents to suffer in this toxic environment? Only time will tell.

Not far from the house there were a few cottages, apparently of the same date as the keep, probably built for some retainers of the family, who sought shelter - they and their families and their small flocks and herds - at the hands of their feudal lord. Some of them had pretty much fallen to decay. They were built in a strange fashion. Strong beams had been sunk firm in the ground at the requisite distance, and their other ends had been fastened together, two and two, so as to form the shape of one of those rounded waggon-headed gipsy-tents, only very much larger. The spaces between were filled with mud, stones, osiers, rubbish, mortar - anything to keep out the weather. The fires were made in the centre of these rude dwellings, a hole in the roof forming the only chimney. No Highland hut or Irish cabin could be of rougher construction. The owner of this property, at the beginning of the present century, was a Mr. Patrick Byrne Starkey. His family had kept to the old faith, and were staunch Roman Catholics, esteeming it even a sin to marry any one of Protestant descent, however willing he or she might have been to embrace the Romish religion. Mr. Patrick Starkey's father had been a follower of James the Second; and, during the disastrous Irish campaign of that monarch, he had fallen in love with an Irish beauty, a Miss Byrne, as zealous for her religion and for the Stuarts as himself. He had returned to Ireland after his escape to France, and married her, bearing her back to the court at St. Germains. But some licence on the part of the disorderly gentlemen who surrounded King James in his exile, had insulted his beautiful wife, and disgusted him; so he removed from St. Germains to Antwerp, whence, in a few years' time, he quietly returned to Starkey Manor-House - some of his Lancashire neighbours having lent their good offices to reconcile him to the powers that were. He was as firm a Roman Catholic as ever, and as staunch an advocate for the Stuarts and the divine right of kings; but his religion almost amounted to asceticism, and the conduct of those with whom he had been brought in such close contact at St. Germains would little bear the inspection of a stern moralist. So he gave his allegiance where he could not give his esteem, and learned to respect sincerely the upright and moral character of one whom he yet regarded as an usurper. King William's government had little need to fear such a one. So he returned, as I have said, with a sobered heart and impoverished fortunes, to his ancestral house, which had fallen sadly to ruin while the owner had been a courtier, a soldier, and an exile.

Both Ba(OH)2, and any residual Na2SO4 that has not reacted with the Ba(OH)2 to precipitate BaSO4, aid the activation and therefore control the reaction of the slag. An increased content of Ba(OH)2 promotes a higher degree of reaction, and the formation of a cross-linked C-A-S-H type gel. Alkali-activated slag cements are produced via a chemical reaction between a source of alkalis (i.e. alkali activator) and blast furnace slag, producing hardened solids, if properly formulated and cured [10]. These binders have the potential to encapsulate radioisotopes and reactive metals, and when produced using sodium carbonate or sodium sulfate as alkali sources, develop a relatively moderate alkalinity compared with Portland cement based wasteforms [11]. In Na2SO4-activated slags, ettringite (Ca6Al2(OH)12(SO4)3 26H2O) forms as a major crystalline reaction product, which chemically binds SO42- present in the system, and can act as a host for a number of positively and negatively charged ions as isomorphous substituents within its structure [12], including various radionuclides. As cementitious wasteforms are exposed to ionising radiation throughout their lifetime service, it is essential to understand the effects of radiation, and determine if they can withstand such service conditions. Gamma irradiation is the focus of the present study, being the most penetrating ionising radiation and more difficult to shield than alpha and beta radiation. Most of the studies evaluating gamma irradiation resistance of cementitious wasteforms [13,14] focus on hardened cements and concretes based solely on Portland cement (PC), and assess the effects of gamma irradiation on mechanical properties and physical deterioration. The most significant interaction of gamma rays with cementitious materials is the radiolysis of pore water, resulting in H2 gas as a primary product and H2O2 as a secondary product [15]. The process of radiolytic dehydration can cause pressurisation, spalling and micro-cracks in the cement matrix [16,17]. In PC-based materials, increased formation of calcite has been observed in the aged concrete samples exposed to high doses of gamma radiation samples [18,19]. This is a consequence of the reaction of the radiolysis product H2O2 with calcium-rich phases formed upon hydration of PC, such as portlandite (Ca(OH)2), to form calcium peroxide octahydrate (CaO2 8H2O), which can then be converted to calcite (CaCO3) in presence of CO2. The specific chemistry of slag-blended cements can also lead to distinct behaviour under irradiation when compared to plain PC materials. Richardson et al. [20] evaluated the microstructure of a BFS-PC (9:1) cement at a dose rate of 10 kGy/h to a total dose of 87 MGy, over two years at 50 C. The formation of additional ettringite in the irradiated samples was observed when compared to the control samples, indicating that gamma radiation may accelerate the oxidation of the sulfide (S2-) supplied by the slag, to form sulfates (SO42-) and promote further formation of ettringite.

No, and the stock's feelin' it, too," grunted Pete, digging his big, blunt-roweled spurs into his buckskin cayuse. Followed by Jack on his Firewater, the professor on his queer, bony steed as angular as himself, Ralph on Petticoats - of exciting memory, - and Walt Phelps on his big gray, they pushed on. The heat was blistering. In fact, to any one less accustomed to the arduous intensity of the sun's rays in this part of the country, it would have proved almost insupportable. But our party was pretty well seasoned by this time. All of them wore the broad, leather-banded sombreros of the plainsmen except Professor Wintergreen, who had invested himself in a gigantic pith sun-helmet, from beneath which his spectacled countenance peered out, as Ralph said, "Like a toad peeking out from a mushroom." For the rest, the boys wore leather "chaps," blue shirts open at the neck, with loosely knotted red handkerchiefs about their throats. The latter were both to keep the sun off the back of their necks and to serve as protection for their mouths and nostrils against the dust in case of necessity, - as for example, when they struck a patch of burning, biting alkali. Of this pungent stuff, they had already encountered one or two stretches, and had been glad to muffle up the lower part of their faces as they rode through it. As for Coyote Pete, those who have followed his earlier experiences are pretty familiar with that redoubtable cow-puncher's appearance; suffice it to say, therefore, that, as usual, he wore his battered leather "chaps," faded blue shirt, and his big sombrero with the silver stars affixed to the stamped leather band. In a holster he carried a rifle, as did the rest of the party, as well as his well-worn revolver. The others had provided themselves with similar weapons, although theirs glittered in blatant newness beside Pete's battered, but well-cleaned and oiled, "shootin' iron." While they are pressing onward, with the Hachetas lying like a dim, blue cloud far behind them, let us tell the reader something about the quest that brings our party into the midst of this inhospitable place. As readers of "The Border Boys on the Trail" know, Professor Wintergreen had accompanied Jack Merrill and Ralph Stetson from Stonefell College, some weeks before, to spend a vacation on the Agua Caliente Ranch, belonging to Jack's father. The professor, as well as being on a vacation, was in a sense on a mission, for he bore with him the commission of a well-known institute of science in the East to investigate some of the mesas of this part of the world, and also to procure relics and trophies of the vanished race that once inhabited them, and accurate measurements of the strange formations. Since their arrival at the ranch, some weeks before, events had so shaped themselves as to render the immediate undertaking of his mission impossible.

The quest for efficient and sustainable energy production from waste has led to the development of bioelectrochemical systems (BESs), which harness the power of microorganisms to generate electricity or valuable chemical compounds. The past decade has seen significant advancements in this field, with researchers exploring various configurations and applications of BESs (Liu et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2014; Escapa et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2017). One of the most promising applications of BESs is the microbial electrolysis cell (MEC), which uses microorganisms as catalysts to produce hydrogen or other valuable chemicals. MECs have been shown to be effective in treating wastewater while simultaneously generating energy, making them an attractive solution for wastewater treatment and energy production (Kadier et al., 2016). However, the development of MECs has not been without its challenges. Early laboratory experiments using membrane separators to isolate the anode and cathode chambers suffered from drawbacks such as increased internal resistance and electrical charge imbalance (Liu et al., 2005; Rozendal et al., 2006). To address these issues, single-chamber membraneless MECs were introduced, which eliminated the need for membrane separators and improved energy efficiency (Call and Logan, 2008). Despite the advantages of single-chamber MECs, they also had their limitations. The production of hydrogen at the cathode can undergo diverse pathways, leading to the formation of low-value products that can negatively impact overall system performance (Lee and Rittmann, 2010). Additionally, the anode can re-oxidize hydrogen, reducing the electrical current and efficiency (Ruiz et al., 2013). Furthermore, the proliferation of homoacetogenic or methanogenic microorganisms can reduce hydrogen production and accumulation in the system, converting it into acetate or methane (Ruiz et al., 2013). To overcome these challenges, researchers have been exploring novel configurations and operating conditions for MECs. For example, some studies have investigated the use of different types of electrodes, such as biofilm-based electrodes, to improve the efficiency of hydrogen production (Kumar et al., 2017). Others have explored the use of alternative microorganisms, such as halophilic microorganisms, to enhance the stability and performance of MECs (Liu et al., 2015). In addition to MECs, other types of BESs, such as microbial fuel cells (MFCs), have also been developed to harness the power of microorganisms for energy production. MFCs use microorganisms to oxidize organic matter and generate electricity, making them a promising solution for wastewater treatment and energy production (Ketep et al., 2013; Rivera et al., 2017). Overall, the development of BESs has the potential to revolutionize the way we produce energy and treat wastewater. However, further research is needed to overcome the challenges and limitations associated with these systems and to optimize their performance and efficiency.

"Well, we meant to give them a concert out of the council tree," said Jack. "But this will be better. Wonder we didn't think of it before." Will he handle it all right?" Frank smiled confidently. "When I give him the signal," he said, "Matse will do his part, never fear. He'd undertake anything in order to save Wimba. But we're not out of the woods yet, Jack. We don't know what's going on. Oh, if we only had another boy who could speak English and could translate this for us." Jack gripped his companion's arm. "Look, Frank, the trial is over. Now Chief Ruku-Ru is about to pronounce sentence. See. Wimba is staring hard at us. Poor fellow, he believes his end has come and what a look of dumb appeal. Despite the growing uncertainty surrounding the Gospel of Jesus's Wife, Professor Karen King has remained steadfast in her initial presentation, emphasizing the importance of ongoing scholarly analysis and dialogue. In a statement to The Guardian, she noted, "While the questions about the papyrus's authenticity are serious and demand thorough examination, the dialogue they provoke regarding the historical understanding of early Christianity and its texts is equally valuable." Her stance has invited both criticism and support from the academic community. On one side, scholars argue that her initial endorsement may have granted undue legitimacy to a potentially fraudulent document, thereby misleading the public and muddying historical discourse. On the other, some commend her courage in inviting scrutiny and fostering an environment where academic debates can flourish, viewing this as an essential component of historical inquiry. The broader implications of this controversy extend beyond academia, weaving into public discourse and affecting religious narratives globally. For adherents of Christianity, particularly those with conservative leanings, any suggestion that Jesus might have been married could challenge longstanding theological doctrines and interpretations of the Gospel. This is precisely what makes the meticulous examination of such artefacts all the more critical - the stakes extend far beyond scholarly curiosity; they touch upon the foundational beliefs of millions. The scientific community, however, emphasizes the importance of objectivity in determining the veracity of ancient texts. In particular, the fields of paleography and radiocarbon dating play pivotal roles in peeling back the layers of history to reveal the truth buried within. While radiocarbon dating suggests the material itself might be ancient, this does not necessarily authenticate the text it bears. Scholars like Professor Askeland caution against taking such findings at face value: "Age of material alone cannot confirm the age of the text inscribed upon it. Forgeries can be and often are, inscribed on ancient materials to add a veneer of legitimacy." The scrutiny has not dissuaded some experts from advocating for further tests on the papyrus, utilizing advanced technologies to analyze the ink compositions and compare them with known samples from the period purportedly in question. Moreover, calls for transparency regarding the papyrus's provenance have grown louder - understanding the artefact's journey through time could be instrumental in assessing its authenticity. Meanwhile, media outlets continue to dramatize the unfolding saga, drawing interest from those both within and outside the religious and academic arenas. Documentary filmmakers have begun chronicling the controversy, interviews with key figures dramatizing the tension between discovery and authenticity. In this age of instant information, the narrative of the Gospel of Jesus's Wife has captured a curious public, eager to witness history and faith potentially redefined or reaffirmed. As debates wage on, the Gospel of Jesus's Wife serves as a reminder of the delicate, intricate dance between faith, history, and science. It underscores the necessity for rigorous scholarship and open dialogue in unraveling the mysteries of the past while highlighting the impact such findings could have on the world's understanding of one of history's most significant figures. The saga continues, with the scholarly world holding its breath, awaiting the results of further investigations that may finally uncover the truth. Until then, this enigmatic piece of the past remains a topic of fervent discussion, symbolic of the eternal quest for knowledge and understanding.

This systemic failure cannot be merely swept under the rug or dismissed as isolated incidents. It demands a comprehensive examination that extends beyond the individuals involved; it necessitates an investigation into the very frameworks that govern the Veterans Administration and its operations. The gauntlet has been thrown down, and now it is imperative that Congress seizes this moment to implement transformative reforms that will not only rectify the current deficiencies but also lay a robust foundation for the future of veteran care. Could it be that our service members, who so gallantly defend our freedoms, are consigned to navigate a labyrinth of inefficiency, red tape, and bureaucratic neglect upon returning to civilian life? It is an unforgivable travesty that those sent to combat foreign foes should encounter even greater battles in securing the care and benefits they have so rightly earned upon their return. The tragic irony of our situation cannot be overlooked: the individuals who risk everything for our nation must then endure a second fight against a system designed to assist them but instead ensnares them in a web of failure. The American public is beginning to wake up to this startling reality. Community outrage simmers, growing ever louder as veterans' stories emerge to highlight the indignities they suffer: the reams of paperwork, the unending phone calls, the lost records, and the staggering waits for appointments. More importantly, these stories expose a lack of accountability that underscores the urgent need for a complete overhaul of the VA. What would a modern VA look like? It would prioritize accessibility and transparency, fostering a culture of respect and dignity for those who have sacrificed so much for our collective well-being. Imagine a scenario where veterans can log into an intuitive portal that seamlessly integrates all their health records, eligibility information, and appointments-all at their fingertips with real-time updates and notifications. An efficient system would not only promote accountability among VA employees but also empower veterans by giving them direct, immediate access to their care. Veterans would be met with staff trained not merely to process requests but to understand the unique challenges faced by service members transitioning back to civilian life. Training should encompass compassion as much as technical proficiency, ensuring that staff are not just bureaucrats but true advocates for those they serve. Such a transformation in mindset could dramatically shift outcomes, leading to a more responsive environment where veterans are treated as allies rather than mere numbers in an online system. To achieve such a paradigm shift, Congress must wield its responsibility effectively, demanding accountability from leadership at the VA while simultaneously fostering genuine dialogue with veteran communities. It is time to create an environment where veterans' voices are heard, not just co-opted for positive press releases. When drafting policy, lawmakers must actively seek input from those who truly understand the trials and tribulations of navigating the current VA system-those whom it is meant to serve. Let this be the moment when we break the cycle of apathy and neglect that has plagued the VA for generations. We owe it to our veterans, to the too-long silenced voices demanding change, and to the national integrity that hinges on how we treat those who have fought for our freedom. As Dellinger has poignantly stated, "we do this because of people who have been failed by the system." It is high time we turn the tide and build a Veterans Administration that, rather than failing, fulfills its promise: honoring the sacrifices of our veterans with the dignity and respect they deserve.

As the investigation into the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 continues, authorities are still trying to piece together the events leading up to the plane's disappearance. One crucial piece of information that has emerged is a mystery phone call made by Capt. Zaharie Ahmad Shah, the pilot of the missing plane, just minutes before takeoff. The call was made to an unknown number, and investigators are now racing against time to identify the recipient. The Malaysian authorities have refused to comment on the investigation, but sources close to the inquiry have revealed that the call was made from the cockpit of the plane. The exact contents of the call remain unknown, but it is believed to have lasted for several minutes. The discovery of the phone call has sparked hopes that it could hold the key to unlocking the mystery of the plane's disappearance. Investigators are now working to trace the call and identify the person who received it, in the hopes that they may have information about the plane's final moments. In the meantime, search teams are continuing to scour the southern Indian Ocean for any signs of debris from the plane. Hutus started killing Tutsis, who ran for their lives and flooded Alice's village. Three days later, local Hutu leaders told Emmanuel, then 23, that they had a job for him. Emmanuel severed Alice's right hand and sliced her face. Emmanuel turned himself in and confessed to his crimes in 1996, and his prison term lasted from 1997 until 2003. They took him to a Tutsi home and ordered him to use his machete. A Christian who sang in his church choir, Emmanuel had never killed before. But inside this house he murdered 14 people. The next day, April 12, Emmanuel found a Tutsi doctor in hiding and killed him, too. The day after, he killed two women and a child. 'The very first family I killed, I felt bad, but then I got used to it,' he says. 'Given how we were told that the Tutsis were evil, after the first family I just felt like I was killing our enemies.' In the meantime, Alice's family took refuge in a church, just as they had done before, crammed in with hundreds of others. But this time, Hutu attackers threw a bomb inside and set the church on fire. Those who fled the fire inside died by machetes outside. Alice lost some 26 family members, among the estimated 5,000 victims at the church. Alice, then 25, escaped with her 9-month-old daughter and a 9-year-old niece into Rwanda's green countryside, moving, hiding, moving. She hid in a forested swamp. 'There were so many bodies all over the place,' she says. 'Hutus would wake up in the morning and go hunting for Tutsis to kill.' By late April rebel Tutsi fighters led by Kagame had reached the capital and chased Hutus out. Hutu troops began to flee to neighboring countries, and the violence spread, with killings carried out by both sides. On April 29, Emmanuel joined Hutu soldiers searching the countryside for Tutsis. The attackers blew a whistle whenever they found a Tutsi hiding. The murders began at 10 a.m. and lasted until 3 p.m. Alice had been hiding in a swamp for days, keeping out only the top of her face so she could breathe. That was where the Hutus found her. They surrounded the swamp. Then they attacked. After she was attacked, Alice was left for dead, fell unconscious and was found three days later by other survivors. Emmanuel recognized Alice at a group for both genocide killers and survivors, who still meet weekly. Though he first avoided her, Emmanuel eventually kneeled before Alice to ask for forgiveness. First they killed the girls. When that was done, they came after Alice. She was sure she would die, but instinctively put up her arm up to defend herself. (2008) explored cleavage of ether bonds present in the lignin structure during reductive depolymerisation of lignin with hydrogen [23]. In this study, birch wood sawdust was converted to four main monomers, namely guaiacylpropane, syringylpropane, guaiacylpropanol, and syringylpropanol using an organic solvent and a series of active carbon supported catalysts, such as Ru/C, Pd/C, Rh/C, and Pt/C, at 523 K and 4 MPa H2 pressure for 0.5-2 h. The maximum monomer yields were 46% relative to the initial lignin mass for Pt/C catalyzed conversion in dioxane. Production of value-added chemicals from lignin requires the simultaneous depolymerisation of the lignin structures with subsequent hydro-deoxygenation of the lignin monomers and alkylation of aromatic rings, and is thus very complex [11,15,24]. Several studies have shown that the use of formic acid as a hydrogen donor enhances the depolymerisation of lignin. In 2008, Kleinert and Barth reported an innovative conversion method for valorization of lignin termed lignin to liquid (LtL). The LtL-process can be considered as a thermochemical solvolysis process in a liquid or near-critical reaction medium at high temperature and high pressure. Lignin to liquid conversion involves the use of a hydrogen donor solvent instead of molecular hydrogen. A well-known hydrogen donor is formic acid. At the given conditions, the formic acid acts not only as an in situ hydrogen source, but also as assists in the depolymerisation of the lignin molecule, and thus results in higher oil yields than comparable reactions with H2 as reductant. A recent study reported by Oregui-Bengoechea et al. (2017) has revealed that the decomposition of formic acid and the chemical reaction between lignin and formic acid are competing reactions, and based on this study, a formylation-elimination-hydrogenolysis mechanism for the formic acid aided lignin conversion has been proposed. Commonly used solvents are water and ethanol [8,11,26]. The reaction product consists of a well-separated mixture of an organic top layer and an aqueous bottom layer with a total liquid yield of up to 90 wt%. The liquid organic phase is an oil with a high H/C and a low O/C ratio relative to the lignin input. GC-MS analysis show that the liquid organic fraction mainly consists of phenols and aromatic compounds, and this makes it a potential source of components for blending in motor fuels, or for utilization in fine chemical production. The isolated phenolic fractions were reported to be within 25-35 wt% of the lignin input and are quite high compared to the reported values from pyrolysis of similar feedstocks at the same reaction severities [8,9,12,13,24,25].

"This is much ado about nothing," said Ed Whelan, a former law clerk to Scalia and a fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center. "Justice Scalia has been a frequent guest at the vice president's ranch, and this trip was simply a continuation of their friendship. In a statement released yesterday, he said, "I have been a judge for over 20 years, and I have always been able to separate my personal relationships from my judicial duties. The task force, which was established in 2001, was composed of top administration officials and energy industry executives, and its meetings were closed to the public. Environmental groups and lawmakers have been seeking access to the documents, arguing that they may reveal conflicts of interest and undue influence by the energy industry on the administration's energy policy. The Supreme Court's decision in the case could have far-reaching implications for the balance of power between the executive and legislative branches of government. As the controversy surrounding Scalia's hunting trip continues to swirl, many are calling for greater transparency and accountability from the Supreme Court. In the meantime, Scalia's decision to remain on the case has sparked a heated debate about the role of the judiciary in American democracy. As the Supreme Court prepares to hear the case, one thing is clear: the stakes are high, and the outcome could have far-reaching implications for the future of our democracy.
