This sorption process is an essential mechanism affecting the bioavailability and mobility of MPs, as it can significantly reduce the concentration of such compounds in infiltrating water due to their binding to particulate and dissolved organic matter. The interplay between adsorption and microbial degradation is, therefore, crucial to determining the overall fate of MPs during riverbank filtration (Davis et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2015). As river water passes through the aquifer, the dynamic equilibrium between these processes allows for the gradual attenuation of contaminants. The degradation kinetics of MPs within the hyporheic zone often depend on the specific microbial communities present, their metabolic pathways, and the availability of electron acceptors, which can vary significantly depending on local hydrological and geological conditions (Ferguson and Muir, 2011). Moreover, the spatial heterogeneity of the riverbank increases the complexity of these interactions. Infiltration rates can vary dramatically along a river stretch, influencing the residence time of water within the hyporheic zone, ultimately impacting the extent of natural attenuation processes. For example, areas with high sediment permeability tend to exhibit faster flow rates and shorter retention times, thereby lessening the exposure of MPs to microbial action and sorption (Boulton et al., 2010). Conversely, lower permeability zones may lead to prolonged water residence times and enhanced attenuation potential, enhancing removal efficiencies (Starr et al., 2018). Consequently, understanding these intricate dynamics is pivotal for the protection of water resources, especially in the context of diverse land uses and climate challenges that influence river water quality. Field studies of riverbank filtration systems have revealed significant variations in MP concentrations and attenuation efficiency, underscoring the critical role of hydrological and environmental variables in driving these processes (Hughes et al., 2019; Regnery et al., 2015). For instance, fluctuations in river discharge can dramatically alter the hydraulic gradients, affecting the rates of infiltration and the mixing of surface and groundwater. Additionally, seasonal changes in temperature and organic matter input can further modulate microbial activity, thereby influencing the overall degradation of MPs (Schwarzenbach et al., 2006). Understanding these seasonal dynamics is vital for implementing effective management practices that ensure safe drinking water without excessive reliance on advanced treatment processes. Another aspect to consider is the role of anthropogenic influences on the natural attenuation potential of MPs in riverbank filtration systems. The presence of emerging contaminants, such as microplastics and nanomaterials, poses new challenges to traditional sorption and degradation pathways. Research has shown that such micro-pollutants can interact with organic matter and alter the behavior of other MPs, potentially leading to unforeseen consequences for both aquifer stability and drinking water quality (Besseling et al., 2013; Mazia et al., 2021). As societies strive to combat water scarcity and ensure sustainable resource management, it is imperative that future research is aimed at elucidating these interrelationships and developing innovative solutions that leverage the multifaceted mechanisms of riverbank filtration. In summary, while riverbank filtration offers a promising method for enhancing water quality and preserving natural resources, a deep understanding of the underlying processes affecting MP attenuation is essential. Potential alterations in hydrological patterns, varying land use practices, and the emergence of novel contaminants necessitate a comprehensive approach to managing riverbank filtration. Prospective frameworks must incorporate advanced monitoring techniques and predictive modeling to better anticipate effluent composition and optimize treatment outcomes, effectively safeguarding against the threats posed by today's complex array of micro-pollutants. Thus, concerted efforts towards research, management, and public education will collectively foster resilience and sustainability within water supply systems worldwide.

However, existing analytical solutions are restricted to simplified fracture geometries in homogeneous rock masses, and are typically constrained to a set of fixed boundary conditions. Standard geometries include the PKN fracture (Perkins and Kern, 1961; Nordgren, 1972; Mathias and van Reeuwijk, 2009), the KGD fracture (Geertsma and de Klerk, 1969; Spence and Sharp, 1985; Adachi and Detournay, 2008), and radial (penny-shaped) fractures (Savitski and Detournay, 2002; Bunger et al., 2005; Kovalyshen, 2010). Moreover, analytical solutions do not exist for cases that are not at the corners of this parameter space. Numerical models that attempt to simulate hydraulic fracturing include the boundary integral method (Peirce and Siebrits, 2001), the boundary element method (Simpson and Trevelyan, 2011), the distinct element method (Marina et al., 2014), the finite element method (Carrier and Granet, 2012), discrete fracture network (Fu et al., 2013), the embedded fracture model (Norbeck et al., 2015), the lattice approach (Grassl et al., 2015) and the extended finite element method (Dahi-Taleghani, 2009; Mohammadnejad and Khoei, 2013; Salimzadeh and Khalili, 2015a). However, in the majority of available models, flow through the rock matrix, and fluid exchange between fracture and rock matrix, are either ignored by assuming an impermeable rock formation (e.g. Dahi-Taleghani, 2009), or simplified by using a one-dimensional analytical leakoff model (e.g. Zhou et al., 2015). Substantial field evidence has proven the impermeable matrix assumption to be an unrealistic assumption (Economides and Nolte, 2000; Adachi et al., 2007). In one-dimensional leakoff models (Carter, 1957), fracture-to-matrix flow is represented as a sink term in the mass balance equation for fracture flow. This approach has several shortcomings, such as the assumption of one-dimensional flow, time-dependency of flow instead of pressure-dependency, and more importantly, this approach cannot model matrix dilation. Although flow from the fracture into the rock matrix is by definition locally one-dimensional at the fracture wall, where the flux vector must be normal to the fracture wall, in a global sense it is three-dimensional, unless the permeability in the direction normal to the fracture plane is significantly higher than in other directions (Hagoort et al., 1980). As time elapses, the leakoff rate predicted by Carter's model, at each position along the fracture, decreases proportionally to square-root of time; consequently, a scenario of fracture arrest is not possible (Mathias and van Reeuwijk, 2009). Finally, this model does not account for the fact that seepage of the fracturing fluid into the rock formation increases the fluid pressure in the matrix, causing dilation of the rock matrix. A dilated matrix applies stresses back onto the fracture, referred to as 'back-stresses' in the hydraulic fracturing literature, which tend to close the fracture (Kovalyshen, 2010). These factors also affect the available semi-analytical solutions for leakoff-dominated regimes that use a simplified one-dimensional leakoff model in their formulation.

For a while, online dating seemed like the answer. Friends had recommended it, telling me stories about soulmates found in chat windows and true love blossoming in digital meadows. At first, the novelty was refreshing. Profiles filled with witty bios and hobbies that ranged from rock climbing to knitting eclectic scarves promised excitement and intrigue. I crafted my own profile meticulously-photos that captured the light in just the right way, descriptions highlighting my penchant for baking and an appreciation for art museums, and an assurance that I could never say no to a good book or a great cup of coffee. My inbox gradually filled, and the digital conversation flowed like a gentle stream. There was excitement in anticipation, as messages dinged on my phone, moments of human connection tucked in between the monotony of daily life. Some interactions fizzled out after the initial introductions, others lingered a little longer but never quite took off. I stayed hopeful, reminding myself of the success stories-I could be one of them. Then came Mark. Like a character stepping right out of a romantic comedy, he seemed charismatic and attentive. We chatted for weeks, exchanging stories and dreams, building the foundations of something genuine, or so I thought. When we finally decided to meet, I had butterflies-those hopeful, naive creatures fluttering with expectation. We chose a quaint little cafe, somewhere cozy and intimate, hoping the ambiance would match the promises of our text threads. I arrived early, as I often do, settling into a corner booth with a view of the entrance. Minutes ticked by, the cafe filling with the rhythmic hum of espresso machines and the soothing strum of acoustic guitar. My phone buzzed-a message from Mark, saying he was parking his car. I watched the door with anticipation, sipping nervously at my latte. The minutes stretched longer, my fingers drumming unconsciously against the table. Then came another message-an apology, a sudden emergency, a rain check. It was peculiar, the mundanity of being stood up didn't pierce me the way it might have before. Instead, it left an empty space, a void where disappointment should have settled, but instead was filled with the faint sting of deja vu. The barista gave me a sympathetic smile as I left. I walked aimlessly for a while, the city lights blurring as the night air wrapped itself around me. At home, my sister's cat, Octavius, nuzzled against me-a comforting ritual, his purring a soothing balm to my vexed heart. Each missed connection was but another thread in the tapestry of my life, weaving its way into my narrative, shaping who I was becoming. Even as doubts brushed against the fringes of my mind, I returned to the dating apps, ever hopeful that somewhere behind a glowing screen, a connection was waiting.

The former interaction requires the canonical hydrophobic pocket of the SH3 domain while the latter interaction involves a region that is structurally separated from the PxxP binding pocket and located at the opposite surface of the domain (Barnett et al., 2000; Bottger et al., 2000; Douangamath et al., 2002; Pires et al., 2003). In the case of ScFus1, a secondary binding pocket was identified that in combination with the primary hydrophobic binding pocket of the domain can alter the strength of the interaction with peptides that have a PxxP motif in their N-terminus followed by a R(S/T)(S/T)SL consensus motif (Kim et al., 2008). Other examples of non-canonical SH3-ligand binding are the interaction of the Fyb c-terminal SH3 domain with Skap55 via the RKxxY294xxY297 motif, which is devoid of proline (Kang et al., 2000; Duke-Cohan et al., 2006) and the binding of murine and human Esp8-SH3 to PxxDY motifs (Mongiovi et al., 1999). These examples emphasize that binding of non-canonical motifs by SH3 domains is more common than previously thought. SH3 domains are ubiquitously expressed in species ranging from yeast to humans, and are implicated in various cellular processes such as cell signaling and endocytosis. One family of SH3-containing proteins we have studied in more detail is the Rvs167 family. Rvs167 proteins are characterized by a membrane binding BAR (Bin-Amphiphysin-RVS) domain in their N-termini and an SH3 domain in their C-termini (Wigge and McMahon, 1998; Ren et al., 2006), and are involved in the final steps of the endocytic process (Kaksonen et al., 2005; Kukulski et al., 2012). The genome of S. cerevisiae encodes a single Rvs167 protein, ScRvs167, whereas the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans has three Rvs167 paralogs: CaRvs167, CaRvs167-2 and CaRvs167-3 (Douglas et al., 2009; Reijnst et al., 2010; Gkourtsa et al., 2015). There is compelling evidence for a role of CaRvs167 in endocytosis; however, the function of the other two proteins, CaRvs167-2 and CaRvs167-3, remains largely unknown (Reijnst et al., 2010; Gkourtsa et al., 2015). In a previous genome-wide study involving four different yeast species, S. cerevisiae, Ashbya gossypii, C. albicans and Schizosaccharomyces pombe, we studied the evolution of the SH3 domain specificity landscape (Verschueren et al., 2015). This study revealed that SH3-binding specificity was largely conserved within SH3 families, in particular when SH3 domain sequence identity among family members was high. Interestingly, the SH3 domain of CaRvs167-3 was a domain that, despite a high SH3-sequence conservation, appeared to have a binding specificity that was distinct from that of the other Rvs167 family members (Fig. 1 and Verschueren et al., 2015). In contrast to the Type II specificity as found for the other Rvs167 family members, its binding preference showed a non-canonical Type I specificity in which the first proline residue in the PxxP motif is replaced by a hydrophobic residue ( xxP, where stands for a hydrophobic residue).

It explores how these strategies can help in overcoming the identified service paradox and in addressing the noted variability in performance outcomes (Gebauer et al., 2005; Kowalkowski et al., 2017). By leveraging relational governance, firms aim to build trust-based relationships with their clients, thus securing long-term engagements that are mutually beneficial (Dyer & Singh, 1998; Reim et al., 2018). This is particularly crucial in handling the dynamic complexities associated with advanced service solutions, which often necessitate a high degree of collaboration and alignment between service providers and customers. Such relational governance mechanisms-rooted in mutual understanding and shared objectives-are argued to be more resilient against market fluctuations and uncertainties, allowing companies to better manage risks and enhance service delivery effectiveness (Morgan & Hunt, 1994; Vesalainen & Kohtamaki, 2015). Institutional theory presents another layer by highlighting how institutional logics can shape and guide the strategic actions of firms in the servitization process (Powell & DiMaggio, 1991; Scott, 2008). By adopting institutional logics that align company goals with those of stakeholders, firms can legitimize their actions and gain broader support for servitization initiatives. This alignment is essential when the transition involves extensive organizational changes needed to support advanced service offerings. Accordingly, institutional pressures can act as enablers or barriers to servitization success, depending on the degree of regulatory, normative, and cultural-cognitive alignment with the firm's strategic objectives (DiMaggio & Powell, 1983; Scott, 2008). Moreover, the interplay between relational governance and institutional theory suggests that firms can benefit from developing hybrid governance structures that integrate both formal contracts and informal relationship-based mechanisms (Reim et al., 2018; Rindfleisch & Heide, 1997). This dual approach allows for flexibility in dealing with unforeseen circumstances while maintaining a structured plan for service delivery (Huang & Chiu, 2018). It empowers firms to be adaptable and responsive, crucial traits in a competitive marketplace where customer needs continuously evolve (Tuli et al., 2007). As firms increasingly embrace servitization, a robust understanding of these governance frameworks can guide strategic decision-making, enhancing value creation for both companies and their customers (Kohtamaki et al., 2013). Importantly, by fostering deep partnerships through effective relational governance and leveraging appropriate institutional frameworks, firms can mitigate the risks associated with the servitization journey, transforming challenges into opportunities for innovation and growth (Baines et al., 2017; Martinez et al., 2017). This study not only adds to the burgeoning field of servitization research by identifying and exploring critical governance strategies but also offers practical implications for managers seeking to navigate the uncertainties of transitioning from product-centric to service-centric business models. By charting these strategies, managers can better anticipate potential hurdles and design interventions that align with both organizational capabilities and market demands, thus positioning their firms for sustained success in a rapidly changing industrial landscape (Parida et al., 2019; Kowalkowski et al., 2017). Future research should continue to explore these dual perspectives-relational and institutional-alongside examining other potential influences on the servitization-performance relationship, such as technological advancements, market variations, and global economic shifts (Luoto et al., 2017; Rabetino et al., 2018). This multilayered exploration promises richer insights into how manufacturers can effectively harness the full potential of servitization, achieving not only enhanced competitive advantage but also deeper customer satisfaction and loyalty in an ever-evolving market environment.

Twenty years after Clark's review, Basell (2008) presented a synthesis of chronometrically dated MSA assemblages accompanied by a qualitative overview of assemblage composition. This overview clearly illustrated the diversity of stone tool use, highlighting considerable overlap between assemblages, and again stressing the absence of any single fossil directeur of the eastern African MSA. Extending Clark's focus on the interactions between ecology and behaviour, Basell (2008) highlights the placement of MSA sites within ecotonal settings, permitting access to wooded ecologies, in contrast to the previously assumed central importance of savannahs. Furthermore, the roles of volcanism and tectonics are also recognised alongside patterns of climate change as affecting the habitability of the region and permitting the identification of potential regional refugia. In conclusion, Basell (2008) hypothesised that following contraction of MSA occupations during the high aridity of Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 6, regional expansion and movement into new environments in MIS 5 corresponded with increased mobility and changes in stone tool use, promoted by climatic, volcanic and tectonic push and pull factors. Tryon and Faith (2013) augment the description of patterns of stone tool technology with the introduction of a quantitative appraisal of the presence/absence of a range of artefact types. Again, descriptions of stone tool technologies broadly echo earlier suggestions for considerable diversity across eastern Africa within different artefact types and the absence of a single unifying type. Notably, these authors suggest that the lack of regionally distinct and derived typological traits is likely to hamper efforts to identify human expansions from the region. Tryon and Faith (2013) evaluated the presence and absence of a range of stone tool and other artefact types using correspondence analysis from dated assemblages, differentiating early (MIS 6 and earlier) from later (MIS 5 and later) assemblages. Alongside considerable overlap between early MSA and some later MSA assemblages, they identify a subset of later MSA assemblages that appear distinct, associated with the presence of blades and backed pieces, as well as beads, grindstones, ochre and anvils. These latter categories appear critical in resolving between earlier and later assemblages (Tryon and Faith, 2013: Fig. 4). In addition, Tryon and Faith (2013) demonstrated a weak but significant negative relationship between geographic distance and assemblage similarity, suggesting that geography does have some effect on the observed patterning. Whether this is due to geographic distance per se, or to habitat differences within the region, remains an open question. These three reviews highlight a number of common themes in their appraisal of eastern African MSA sites, such as the lack of clear intra-regional structure in behaviour, the importance of ecotonal site locations, and the absence of regionally specific stone tool use. Typology remains a key means to evaluate variability across the breadth of the MSA record, although it is not entirely unproblematic.

In previous work we have shown that fouling is indeed mitigated by the introduction of air bubbles in the feed channels of a RED stack, however, the effect was limited (Vermaas et al., 2012a,b, 2014). Therefore, the objective of this study is to investigate the effect of two-phase flow on the performance of a RED stack operated under real conditions using natural feed waters, i.e. seawater and river water. To this end, experiments were performed with synthetic feed solutions containing model foulants, i.e. kaolinite clay particles and sodium alginate, and with natural feed waters, i.e. seawater and river water. ## Materials and methods ### Materials The RED stacks used in these experiments consisted of Fujifilm Type I membranes, having a thickness of 170 \(\mu\)m and an area of 10 cm\({}^{2}\)(Tufa et al., 2015). These membranes consist of a polyethylene backbone structure, where sulfonic acid groups are introduced to obtain the negatively charged CEMs, and quaternary ammonium groups are introduced to obtain positively charged AEMs. The spacer material used was made of polypropylene with a thickness of 100 \(\mu\)m and a mesh size of 1 mm \( imes\) 0.9 mm. The electrodes used were made of platinum coated titanium mesh (thickness: 1 mm). The open circuit voltage (OCV) was measured using an Agilent U1252B multimeter. The current-voltage (I-V) curves were recorded using a Keithley 2400 sourcemeter. For the I-V measurements, the current density was increased stepwise from zero to a value corresponding to the maximum power point (MPP) according to Vermaas et al. (2014). At each current density step, the corresponding voltage was recorded after stabilization, typically within 30 s. The MPP was determined from the I-V curve by multiplying the current density (\(J { ext{cell}}\)) and the corresponding cell voltage (\(U { ext{cell}}\)). The power density (\(P {d}\)) was then normalized per unit of membrane area. For the experiments with artificial feed waters, sodium chloride (NaCl, VWR chemicals, purity \(>\)99%), sodium sulfate (Na\({} {2}\)SO\({} {4}\), Merck KGaA, purity \(>\)99%) and calcium chloride dihydrate (CaCl\({} {2}\cdot\)2H\({} {2}\)O, VWR chemicals, purity \(>\)98%) were used. The pH of the solutions was adjusted by adding sodium hydroxide (NaOH, Sigma Aldrich, purity \(>\)97%). The concentration of NaCl and CaCl\({} {2}\cdot\)2H\({} {2}\)O was analyzed with a conductivity meter (WTW Cond 3210) and the concentration of Na\({} {2}\)SO\({} {4}\) was analyzed with an ion chromatograph (DIONEX ICS-1100). Kaolin (Sigma-Aldrich, particle size \(<\)5 \(\mu\)m) was used as a model compound for colloidal fouling and sodium alginate (Sigma-Aldrich, medium viscosity) was used as a model compound for organic fouling.

It's crucial to remember that asking the right questions can often unlock the best insights. Understanding the underlying challenges a project faces is pivotal for success, and this all begins with thoughtful inquiry. Often, designers rush towards solutions without taking the time to truly understand the problem landscape, which can lead to misaligned expectations and ultimately, project failure. So Ryan, what are some of those go-to questions you find yourself asking that help set the stage for effective research? Absolutely, Brendan. One of my top questions is, "Who are the end users?" It may sound basic, but you'd be surprised by how often teams underestimate the diversity of their user base. Identifying the different user personas early on helps inform not only design decisions but also guides the entire research process. Understanding demographics, pain points, and user contexts can shape our approach tenfold. Another question I like to delve into is, "What problem are we trying to solve?" This prompts stakeholders to clarify their objectives. By breaking down the problem into specifics, we not only facilitate better user-centric solutions but pave the way for deeper discussions on user needs. This also encourages us to think critically about measurement-how will we know if we've succeeded? Yes! And that leads perfectly into my next question, which is, "What success metrics are we working with?" It's vital to define what success looks like for the project right from the beginning. What does winning mean to our stakeholders? Is it an increase in user satisfaction, more completed transactions, or perhaps greater user engagement? By being clear on what we are measuring, we ensure that our research focuses on the variables that matter most. Another good question is, "What can we learn from previous projects?" Whether they were successes or losses, projects from the past contain invaluable lessons that can guide current efforts. I always advocate for a retrospective analysis before we forge ahead. Our field is ever-evolving, and acknowledging prior experiences can help us create a roadmap that avoids common pitfalls. Absolutely! And then we can't forget about the importance of context-we should ask, "What are the constraints we need to consider?" This opens up the conversation to discuss technical, budgetary, or timeline limitations. Recognizing constraints can help set realistic expectations for the outcome and can guide the design team in making informed, tactical decisions throughout the project lifecycle. Moving on, let's not overlook the impact of user input. I always like to include, "How will user feedback be integrated into our process?" Designing iteratively with user input can help refine our solutions and catch potential issues before they escalate. For instance, through usability testing or A/B testing, we can validate our assumptions, modifying our approach based on real-world behavior instead of hypotheticals. And as we gather insights, it's vital to continuously assess our own biases. So another question could be, "How can we remain objective in our findings?" Awareness of our biases allows us to approach user research with a clearer lens and ensure that we are genuinely listening to users rather than projecting our own preferences onto the design. In the end, these questions serve as a guiding framework for uncovering insights and fostering discussion among team members. They not only empower designers but also strengthen collaboration across the board. As we dive deeper into these considerations, we pave the way for innovative and inclusive designs that resonate with users on a profound level.

IL-6, which is a potent driver of inflammatory disease, is instrumental for the commitment to the Th17 lineage, by inhibiting FOXP3-mediated suppression of ROR t, thereby promoting the differentiation of the Th17 Teff lineage in mice [28-30]. In addition, studies in mice have also shown that IL-6 signalling is an established factor to inhibit the suppressive function of Tregs [31], although this effect has been shown to be Treg extrinsic, through the activation of Teffs, which are able to escape Treg suppression [32]. Furthermore, in the presence of IL-6, Tregs have been reported to induce IL-17 production by Th17 Teffs cells and have been shown to be themselves capable of producing IL-17 [33]. The effects of IL-6 in studies of human CD4+ T cells differ from those reported using cells from mice in several aspects. For example, IL-6 does not contribute to the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells to the Th17 lineage as it can in mice, although IL-1 and IL-6 together induce IL-17A secretion from human memory CD4+ Th17 cells [34]. Furthermore, the exact role of IL-6 signalling on human Treg function remains uncertain. In psoriasis patients, elevated IL-6 production in affected skin has been suggested to promote the differentiation of IL-17-producing pathogenic Th17 cells and reduce the suppressive capacity of Tregs, although this latter effect is likely to be indirect [35]. Evidence from Bhela et al. also supports the hypothesis that Tregs are not the direct target of IL-6 for its ability to elicit resistance to Treg-mediated suppression [36]. In contrast, Bending et al. have reported that IL-6 provides pro-regulatory signals directly to human Tregs [37]. Previously, a genetic variant in IL6R (rs2228145 A > C; Asp358Ala) has been associated with human inflammatory diseases, including T1D [38], ankylosing spondylitis [39] and rheumatoid arthritis [40], presumably due to a greater expression of the IL-6 receptor and therefore a higher IL-6 signalling capacity in CD4+ Teffs expressing the common Asp358 susceptibility allele compared to Ala358 [38]. Furthermore, IL-6 signalling is increased in T1D patients owing to increased IL-6R expression [41]. These results indicate that inhibition of IL-6 signalling could be a therapeutic approach in T1D, as it is in other human inflammatory diseases [42,43]. Nevertheless, blockade of IL-6, which is a key pathway in immune defence, could raise the risk of serious infections in T1D patients and hence targeting the therapy to a specific cell type could offer advantages in therapy. In the current study we show that a portion of the memory IL-6Rhi CD127lowCD25+ T cells (here designated as Tregs) lack TIGIT and HELIOS expression and have a constitutively elevated expression of the effector Treg marker CTLA-4, and contain a heterogeneous group of cells that as a total population are highly suppressive, with portions expressing a Th17 signature, a demethylated FOXP3 TSDR and the FOXP3 transcription factor protein.

The seconds stretched into infinity, and the walls themselves seemed to lean in, closing me into this cocoon of perplexity. The mirror was both my prison and my escape, a gateway into understanding my own disarray. The light in the room, a dull, cold luminescence, flickered slightly, casting long shadows that twisted and melded into shapes my mind tried desperately to decipher. In the mirror, my reflection's eyes bore into mine with an unsettling intensity, like a sentinel guarding the secrets lurking just beneath coherence. I blinked, and it blinked back, a silent, synchronized dance of confusion and recognition. It was as if I was split between two worlds, the me trapped in glass and the me trapped in flesh, both equally lost. Minutes, or perhaps hours, ticked away-time had diluted itself into an abstract notion, mocking my ineptitude at grasping the abstract. Questions tumbled relentlessly through my mind like leaves caught in a gust of wind. Who am I? Why am I? Such simple inquiries with weight unbearable. My gaze inadvertently turned toward the room's sole window, behind which the world existed in stark clarity. Yet even that world held its mysteries: the leaves on the trees, the distant hum of restless civilization, each a riddle wrapped in the mundane. I sensed a pull towards the window, a primal need to push beyond the constraints of my surroundings, to touch the tangible tapestry that lay beyond the pane. But the mirror called me back, unavoidable, insistent. It whispered of truths I was terrified to confront and lies that had perhaps become my sanctuary. Leaning closer to it, the apparition before me grew increasingly vivid, detailing every imperfection and every story etched upon my skin. My face, though familiar, now seemed like a collection of tales untold, echoes of a past I couldn't touch. A memory began to claw its way upward through the murk of obscurity. A flicker of recognition, the soft, lilting laughter of a child-my own youthful cackle lost in time. The vision sharpened and waned, slipping away just as my mind grasped its edge. Frustration mounted, pressing against my temples with a fierce tenacity. I couldn't shake this pervasive sense that something vital was missing, something ripped from my being, leaving behind only the shadowy vestiges of its presence. My reflection's eyes appeared to shimmer with the same unshed tears that threatened to spill over my own lashes. Was this reflection an ally or adversary? Hope and hopelessness warred within my chest, each battling for domination in an eternal cycle. If only there was someone who might help untangle the chaotic threads of my existence. I struggled to remember-was there once a mentor, a guide, a companion who might cast light onto my path? Yet, the mirror remained my solitary confidante, my silent companion. And in its depths, beneath layers of distortion and despair, perhaps lay a spark-a sliver of truth that might rekindle the dormant embers within me. As I exhaled a deep, shuddering breath, I resolutely locked eyes with myself once more. The shadows breathed around me, alive with untold possibility, and I knew I had but to reach out and claim my own story from their grasp.

The main aim of this paper is to advance on this front, and consider both the composition of finances and its potentially nonlinear impact. We incorporate both the sources (bank financing, debt securities financing, and stock market financing) and the recipients of finances (households, non-financial corporations, and financial corporations). We believe that it is important to include them in this analysis for a number of reasons. First, there is already evidence that the type of financing may matter. Different sources of finances (bank-based versus market-based financing) can have an uneven impact (see e.g. Beck and Levine, 2004; Cournede and Denk, 2015; Demirguc-Kunt et al., 2013; Gambacorta et al., 2014; Langfield and Pagano, 2016; Mishra and Narayan, 2015). At the same time, fund recipients (users of finance) might also matter nontrivially for the outcome. For instance, Chu and Cozzi (2014) develop a model in which the nature of liquidity constraints (whether they affect consumers or firms more) matters for the performance and optimality of macroeconomic policies. Beck et al. (2012) stress that a substantial household credit expansion might be hurting economic growth. In parallel, Bezemer et al. (2014) point out that the share of credit to nonfinancial business credit decreased sharply since 1990, while it had a significantly positive effect on growth. Along these lines, although warning for a small sample size, Arcand et al. (2015) indeed find that the non-linearity of household credit is more significant than that of firm credit. Second, the analysis of the importance of financial structure is currently quite limited. The impact of different components of financing is mostly analyzed individually or looking only at a few of them (see e.g. Cournede and Denk, 2015), thus creating potentially an omitted variable bias. Even when the analysis is performed including several subcomponents together (see e.g. Gambacorta et al., 2014), the difference between their individual and joint impact (e.g. that of total financing) is not investigated. Besides, though the dependence of economic growth rates on bank credit financing and stock market financing is often analyzed, the influence of debt securities is rarely considered. Moreover, when it is, like in Langfield and Pagano (2016), the stock market and debt securities financing is often merged, which might impose an incorrect restriction and lead to biased inference. Finally, to our knowledge there is no study that jointly and not individually investigates the impact of both the sources (bank financing, debt securities financing, and stock market financing) and the recipients of finance (households, non-financial corporations, and financial corporations), not to mention also the non-linearity.

As I stood on the quarterdeck, gazing out at the endless expanse of blue, I couldn't help but feel a sense of excitement and anticipation. The Congo River, with its dark and mysterious waters, held a certain allure that was hard to resist. I had heard tales of the treacherous currents and hidden shoals that lay in wait for the unwary, but I was confident in the Barracouta's ability to navigate its dangers. Our captain, Commander Stopford, was a seasoned veteran of the slave-squadron, and I had every faith in his judgment. As the morning wore on, the sun climbed higher in the sky, casting a golden glow over the waves. The air was thick with the scent of salt and tar, and the sound of the gulls crying overhead added to the sense of excitement that was building within me. I could feel the tension in the air, a sense of expectation that something was about to happen, something big. Mr. Young, our first lieutenant, stood beside me, his eyes fixed intently on the horizon. He was a tall, lanky man, with a mop of curly brown hair and a quick wit that had earned him the respect and admiration of the entire crew. I had always found him to be approachable and kind, and I valued his counsel and guidance. "What do you think we'll find, Mr. Young?" I asked him, my voice low and conspiratorial. He turned to me, his eyes glinting with a hint of mischief. "I'm not entirely sure, Henry," he replied, "but I have a feeling that we're in for a surprise. The Governor of Sierra Leone was adamant that we investigate the Congo, and I suspect that we'll find something worth our while." I nodded, my mind racing with possibilities. Could it be a slaver, hiding in the shadows, waiting to pounce? Or perhaps a hidden cove, teeming with contraband and illicit goods? Whatever it was, I was determined to be a part of it, to play my role in bringing the perpetrators to justice. As the morning wore on, the cry of "Land ho!" was repeated, this time with more urgency. The lookout in the crow's nest was pointing to a dark smudge on the horizon, a smudge that was growing larger by the minute. I felt a shiver run down my spine as I realized that we were approaching the mouth of the Congo, and that our adventure was about to begin. The crew was stirring now, men scrambling to their stations as the captain's voice rang out across the deck. "All hands, prepare to drop anchor! We'll take a boat in to investigate!" I felt a surge of excitement as I joined the throng, my heart pounding in my chest. This was it, the moment we had all been waiting for. We were about to embark on a journey into the unknown, a journey that would test our courage and our resolve. And I, Henry Dugdale, was ready for whatever lay ahead.

And let me tell you, the transformation has been nothing short of magical. Goals, my friends, replace the stagnant resolutions that often fade away like last night's glitter. Instead of creating unattainable high bars for myself, I crafted small, digestible bits of awesomeness here and there that I could actually achieve. Tracking progress became my new best friend. Now, I'm all about affirmation and reflection. I take time each week to check in with myself, reassess my goals, and bask in the joy of accomplishments, no matter how small. Whether it's simply enjoying a well-deserved cup of coffee without interruption or finally getting around to that DIY project I had been putting off, I celebrate life! I relish those seemingly insignificant moments. It's in these little victories that I find joy and motivation to push forward. One of my favorite techniques is the practice of gratitude journaling. Sounds a bit cliche, right? But hear me out! Each evening, I jot down three things I'm grateful for. It can be anything from the warmth of my blanket on a cold night to the laughter of my kids echoing through the house. This simple act shifts my focus from what's lacking to what's abundant in my life. And let me tell you, it works wonders. My perspective shifts, negativity fades, and suddenly I'm in a space where creativity flows like honey! Then, there's the power of community! Surrounding myself with like-minded, positive people has been a game changer. Friends who challenge me to explore new ideas, share my dreams, and encourage me to reach for the stars. Whether it's a weekly brunch with my girlfriends or a spontaneous game night, these interactions fuel my spirit. The good vibes are infectious, and before you know it, I'm buzzing with ideas and motivation like never before! Combining these unique perspectives fosters an endless supply of creativity and fresh takes on the mundane. So, as we stand at the beginning of this exciting new year, I encourage you to seize the opportunity to craft your narrative. Paint your world with robust colors of joy, inspiration, and positivity. Forget about the baggage that was dragging you down-let it go. Make your goals, not resolutions. Take those small, actionable steps toward everything you've envisioned for yourself. Whether you aspire to travel more, nurture those relationships, or simply cultivate a happier mindset, remember that progress is progress, no matter how small. It's time to prioritize YOU! Let go of the negativity and infuse your life with positivity, laughter, and creativity. Share your awesomeness with the world because, darling, you have a voice that deserves to be heard. So buckle up for this wild, beautiful ride called life! And keep mindset and spirits high as you leap into the glorious new adventures waiting just around the corner. Here's to a new year of inspiring growth, my friends!

The Alarm-The Flames-The Ladder. As the revelry flourished in the cafe, life thrummed in the very air of San Francisco, a lively metropolis pulsating with youthful vigor and economic promise. The vigor of the city was not merely confined to the chatter and laughter echoing off the walls; it infused itself into the streets, where merchants hawked their wares, and a motley array of humanity jostled for space upon the sun-drenched sidewalks. The aroma of fresh bread wafted through the air, mingling with the salty tang of the ocean breeze, creating a sensory tapestry that was uniquely San Franciscan. Yet, amidst the jubilance, the flicker of unease simmered below the surface, a latent ember waiting for the breath of wind to coax it into a conflagration. It was said that fortune favored the bold, but for every daring venture, there lurked the specter of calamity-a whisper of disaster that loomed over the heads of even the most confident youth. Today, however, it seemed that the atmosphere absorbed that tension into its bustling streets, leaving only the sparkling laughter of youth and their dreams of gold. One could not miss the presence of the formidable Senor de Castro even amid the din of frivolity. He was a man carved from the very essence of the land-stoic, solid, and marbled with the history of his ancestors. Hushed reverence often cloaked discussions of his name, his estate regarded not merely as a domicile but a veritable fiefdom, stirring the imaginations of the ambitious who sought to undermine or align themselves with his power. His eyes, dark and brooding like a tempest over the sea, offered a glimpse of the untold stories that trailed behind him like a fog. On that afternoon, ensconced in the cafe's lively chatter, the stout man who had shattered the glass now warmed to another topic-an animated discussion of the forthcoming horse races, where glory and ruin would dance in tandem upon the very dirt from which fortunes sprang. Young aspirants leaned in close, their enthusiasm accentuated by the promise of wind-swept gallops and the thrill of companionship. The stout man, elaborating upon the prowess of his own equine-an iron muscled beast named El Fuego-gestured wildly, each pronounced syllable punctuated by the sound of chairs scraping against the floor as patrons leaned closer, intoxicated by his exuberance. Just then, a sudden crackle punctured the jovial air-a sound resembling thunder rolling over the hills, sending ripples of uncertainty through the crowd. Eyes darted toward the door, and conversation dwindled to a tentative hush. In that moment, a waft of thick, acrid smoke crept through the gaps, heralding a disturbance that had far more significant implications than the squabble over drinking vessels. "Fire!" A voice exclaimed, rising from among the throng, and before order could be restored, panic ignited within the hearts of men and women alike. The inferno had begun to manifest itself beyond the bounds of the cafe, flames licking greedily at the wooden structures lining the street. The fervor which once defined the cafe erupted into tumult-a baptism by chaos that consumed joyous laughter, replacing it with cries of terror and urgency. "Grab your belongings-there's no time to lose!" the stout man bellowed, his joviality evaporating faster than the burning embers. He clasped the shoulder of the nearest youth, pulling him towards the exit as the crowd surged forth, driven by primal instincts of survival. The streets, which had moments before pulsed with life, now transformed into a frantic scaffold of desperation as people stumbled over one another-hearts racing to escape the tragedy unfolding like a nightmarish vision upon the sunlit cityscape.

Say, you are in the country; in some high land of lakes. Take almost any path you please, and ten to one it carries you down in a dale, and leaves you there by a pool in the stream. There is magic in it. Let the most absent-minded of men be plunged in his deepest reveries-stand that man on his legs, set his feet a-going, and he will infallibly lead you to water, if water there be in all that region. Should you ever be athirst in the great American desert, try this experiment, if your caravan happen to be supplied with a metaphysical professor. Yes, as everyone knows, meditation and water are wedded for ever. But here is an artist. He desires to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting bit of romantic landscape in all the valley of the Saco. What is the chief element he employs? There stand his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as if a hermit and a crucifix were within; and here sleeps his meadow, and there sleep his cattle; and up from yonder cottage goes a sleepy smoke. Deep into distant woodlands winds a mazy way, reaching to overlapping spurs of mountains bathed in their hill-side blue. But though the picture lies thus tranced, and though this pine-tree shakes down its sighs like leaves upon this shepherd's head, yet all were vain, unless the shepherd's eye were fixed upon the magic stream before him. Go visit the Prairies in June, when for scores on scores of miles you wade knee-deep among Tiger-lilies-what is the one charm wanting?-Water-there is not a drop of water there! Were Niagara but a cataract of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, upon suddenly receiving two handfuls of silver, deliberate whether to buy him a coat, which he sadly needed, or invest his money in a pedestrian trip to Rockaway Beach? Why is almost every robust healthy boy with a robust healthy soul in him, at some time or other crazy to go to sea? Why upon your first voyage as a passenger, did you yourself feel such a mystical vibration, when first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the old Persians hold the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it a separate deity, and own brother of Jove? Surely all this is not without meaning. And still deeper the meaning of that story of Narcissus, who because he could not grasp the tormenting, mild image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and was drowned. But that same image, we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all. Now, when I say that I am in the habit of going to sea whenever I begin to grow hazy about the eyes, and begin to be over conscious of my lungs, I do not mean to have it inferred that I ever go to sea as a passenger. For to go as a passenger you must needs have a purse, and a purse is but a rag unless you have something in it. Besides, passengers get sea-sick-grow quarrelsome-don't sleep of nights-do not enjoy themselves much, as a general thing;-no, I never go as a passenger; nor, though I am something of a salt, do I ever go to sea as a Commodore, or a Captain, or a Cook. I abandon the glory and distinction of such offices to those who like them.

He had made no enemies, and had, on the whole, been popular. And yet, as they sat there in the library, Mr. Burton could not help feeling a sense of disappointment, of disillusionment. He had expected more from his son, more dash, more ambition, more of the Burton spirit that had made him, a self-made man, a success. Gervase was too calm, too quiet, too... too gentlemanly. He lacked the fire in the belly that drove men to greatness. Mr. Burton sighed, and leaned back in his chair, his eyes fixed on the ceiling. "You know, Gervase," he said, "I sometimes wonder what's to become of you. You're not like me, not like your mother. You're not like anyone I know. You're... you're a puzzle to me." Gervase looked up from the book he had been pretending to read, his eyes meeting his father's with a quiet intensity. "I'm sorry, sir," he said. "I know I'm not what you wanted me to be. But I'm doing the best I can." Mr. Burton snorted. "The best you can? The best you can is not good enough, Gervase. You have to be better than that. You have to be the best. Anything less is failure." Gervase shrugged, a small, helpless movement. "I don't know what you want me to do, sir. I've done everything you've asked of me. I've got a good degree, I've made friends, I've... I've tried to make you proud." Mr. Burton's face twisted in a scowl. "Proud? Proud of what? Your mediocrity? Your lack of ambition? No, Gervase, I'm not proud of you. I'm disappointed. I'm ashamed." The words hung in the air, heavy with unspoken meaning. Gervase felt a sting of hurt, of resentment. He had always tried to please his father, to make him proud. And this was the result? This bitter disappointment? He stood up, his movements stiff with anger. "I think I'll go out for a walk, sir," he said, his voice tight with control. "I need some air." Mr. Burton nodded, his face still twisted in a scowl. "Go, then. Go and think about what I've said. Think about what you're going to do with your life." Gervase turned and walked out of the room, the door closing behind him with a soft click. Mr. Burton was left alone, surrounded by the trappings of his success, the books, the pictures, the busts. He felt a sense of emptiness, of desolation. He had failed, failed to create the son he had wanted, failed to instill in him the drive, the ambition that had made him a success. He sighed, and rubbed his temples. What was to become of Gervase? What was to become of him?

The prospect of sustained peace seemed almost a distant dream, as the scars of recent violence remained etched deeply within the collective memory of the Gazan populace. Among the rubble of shattered homes and twisted metal, a flicker of hope began to wane, even as small fragments of normalcy attempted to resurface. People lined up for basic necessities at makeshift markets, eager to return to a semblance of routine despite the overwhelming reminders of loss and grief that surrounded them. Each interaction-be it a greeting, a shared meal, or a moment of laughter-was weighed down by the specter of their recent trauma. In the midst of this hesitant return to everyday life, a palpable tension lingered in the atmosphere. Families were divided by ideologies, yet the shared suffering in Gaza proved a unifying thread in the fabric of their existence. The sitting government-chastened by years of external isolation and internal division-sought to fortify its hold over its populace through gestures of unity, preaching messages of resilience that blended seamlessly with the rhetoric of impending hope. Finding signs of reconciliation, families adorned with logos of both factions walked side by side, their voices rising in songs of defiance, a declaration that they would not be easily broken. Outside the mosques, prayers of gratitude mingled with calls for justice, evoking a sense of solidarity among the attendees. As their voices filled the air, it became clear that the line between celebration and mourning was blurred and, in many cases, nonexistent. Each cry for peace, each lamentation for the fallen, was interwoven with calls for action-an invitation to rise from the ashes like the phoenix, stronger and more resilient than before. However, hope was not entirely without hesitation. The harsh realities of life in Gaza loomed large; countless individuals still yearned for the basic freedoms stripped from them over years of conflict. Suffering a slow bureaucratic death, the essence of their aspirations-freedom, dignity, and security-remained tantalizingly out of reach. In private conversations, whispers of discontent grew louder, punctuated by frustrations about leadership and the effectiveness of the continous struggle. "What now?" many found themselves asking in uncertain tones, an unspoken question underscoring the fragile ceasefire and the looming unpredictability of the region. Amidst the complexities of human emotion, relief efforts started trickling into Gaza, like a hesitant stream attempting to thaw the icy grip of deprivation. 13 We found one previous study14 that examined residential segregation by ethnicity and mortality among patients with schizophrenia. Our findings The main finding of this study is that people with severe mental illness who live in neighbourhoods with high proportions of their own ethnic group had reduced mortality rates compared with those in areas with low proportions of their own ethnic group. This finding remained after adjusting for age, sex, and socioeconomic status. We also found that individuals with severe mental illness living in areas with greater deprivation had increased mortality. The association between ethnic density and mortality did not vary according to sex or age group. Strengths and limitations of this study We included only studies that had sufficient data to allow us to estimate adjusted relative risks. By doing so we were able to avoid confounding effects of age, sex, and socioeconomic status. In addition, we restricted our analyses to people with severe mental illness rather than broader mental health diagnoses, which allowed us to capture people with similar underlying severity of disease. We were unable to assess potential moderating effects of diagnostic subtype because the available studies did not report subgroup analyses according to diagnosis. A further limitation of our study is that it is based on observational data, and therefore causal conclusions cannot be drawn. Future research should explore whether interventions targeted at reducing social fragmentation within local communities can improve physical health outcomes in people with severe mental illness. Implications of all the available evidence There is a clear need to shift towards a public health approach to improving physical health in people with severe mental illness, focusing on wider environmental and structural influences. In this study, we found that people with severe mental illness who lived in areas with high proportions of their own ethnic group had better mortality outcomes compared with those in areas with low proportions of their own ethnic group. This suggests that interventions aimed at reducing social fragmentation in local communities could improve physical health outcomes in people with severe mental illness.

I can still hear the dull thud echoing in my ears, a constant reminder of the price paid for vanity in athleticism. I was attempting to show off, no doubt, attempting to impress the always-enigmatic Jasper, who, let it be known, was barely even paying attention. I, of course, was gung-ho, convinced that pulling off a spectacular dive to save the ball would both earn me admiration and a moment of glory. Instead, the ball collided with the pride of my forehead, sending an electrifying zap straight through my neurons and out the other side. Those joys of youthful exuberance? Well, they tend to fade fast when confronted with the realities of bumps, bruises, and that sharp reminder that sports are better left to those with fewer delusions of grandeur. By Thursday evening, I had resorted to carrying around an ice pack like it was a brand new accessory, pausing mid-conversation with friends as if to say, "Oh, this old thing? Just a little something to accompany my newfound chic look." Jade, my ever-quick-witted friend, insisted on calling me "Ice Queen" after that, and I had to admit, it had a certain ring to it - dramatic yet oddly regal. Preening in front of the bathroom mirror became a challenge; not only did I need to navigate the ice, but I also had to conjure up an excuse as to why I was sporting what could only be described as a melon-sized bruise right between my eyebrows. Answering the barrage of "What happened?" became my new part-time job. At some point, I simply accepted that no matter how many times I explained it, the sheer absurdity of the situation just made it all the funnier. Now, let me pause for a moment and discuss the ramifications of this head injury. Walking into school felt like stepping into a hazy dreamscape. The fluorescent lights flickered above like malevolent spirits, and every person who passed by morphed into a caricature of a concerned friend or a bewildered stranger. Each glance turned into a quiz on my unfortunate predicament and eventually dissolved into laughter, laughter that echoed through the hallways as it circled around my unfortunate run-in with a volleyball. My social life, for the most part, hung comfortably in the balance of humor and sympathy, slight nods of "Are you alright?" laced with grinning disbelief. Friday rolled around, ushering in yet another weekend of festivities and perhaps, more questionable decisions. My head was still a fiery mess, but I was determined to not let it slow me down. We had a karaoke night planned, and the prospect of belting out off-key renditions of pop classics was simply too good to pass up, even if it meant risking the wrath of the knot on my forehead. So, I plastered on some makeup, wearing my headband strategically to conceal the evidence of my not-so-heroic exploits. As the night unfolded, the air filled with laughter and enthusiasm while I clutched my ice pack discreetly beneath the table, a secret weapon to combat the thrumming headache. Then, as if chance had conspired to ensure that my night was bound to be memorable, a delightful twist of fate happened when the microphone somehow landed in my hands. With my friends chanting my name, I found refuge in the moment, taking a deep breath and launching into a tepid rendition of "Dancing Queen." Who knew I could channel such diva energy while trying to camouflage my battle wounds? The world felt all sorts of right, even through the haze of my unfortunate head trauma. The night glowed brighter with each laugh, each off-kilter note ringing true in the hearts of those surrounding me. We danced, we sang, and despite the bruises and falls, I was alive. More alive than ever in a sea of camaraderie and ridiculousness. In the end, I reminded myself that life, much like the lyrics that took flight in that karaoke bar, couldn't be anything but a beautiful mess.

For instance, the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index (WEAI) was developed to assess women's empowerment in the agricultural sector, taking into account dimensions such as autonomy in production, access to and control over resources, and participation in decision-making (Alkire et al., 2013). The WEAI has been widely used in agricultural development projects to monitor progress toward women's empowerment and has been adapted for use in various country contexts. Another approach has been to develop project-specific indicators that are tailored to the specific goals and objectives of the intervention. For example, the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) has developed a range of indicators to measure women's empowerment in the context of agricultural value chains, including indicators of women's participation in decision-making, control over income, and access to credit and other resources (Malapit et al., 2019). Despite these efforts, there remains a need for more comprehensive and standardized approaches to measuring women's empowerment, particularly in the context of agricultural development projects. One challenge is the lack of consistency in the way that women's empowerment is conceptualized and measured across different projects and programs. This can make it difficult to compare results across different contexts and to identify best practices in promoting women's empowerment. Furthermore, many existing measures of women's empowerment rely on self-reported data, which may be subject to biases and limitations. For example, women may underreport their levels of empowerment due to social desirability bias or lack of awareness of their rights and opportunities. Additionally, self-reported data may not capture the complex and nuanced ways in which power operates in different contexts. To address these challenges, there is a need for more innovative and robust approaches to measuring women's empowerment, including the use of objective indicators and data collection methods that can capture the complex and multidimensional nature of empowerment. For example, researchers have begun to use machine learning and data analytics techniques to analyze large datasets and identify patterns and trends in women's empowerment (e.g., Yount et al., 2019). Moreover, there is a growing recognition of the importance of intersectionality in measuring women's empowerment, recognizing that women's experiences of empowerment are shaped by multiple factors such as race, class, ethnicity, and disability (Crenshaw, 1991). This requires a more nuanced and contextualized approach to measuring women's empowerment, one that takes into account the diverse experiences and perspectives of women in different contexts. In conclusion, while there have been significant advances in measuring women's empowerment in agricultural development projects, there remains a need for more comprehensive, standardized, and innovative approaches to measuring women's empowerment. By developing more robust and nuanced measures of women's empowerment, we can better understand the complex and multidimensional nature of empowerment and identify effective strategies for promoting women's empowerment and gender equality in agricultural development projects.

Moreover, the relationship between cannabis use and cognitive functioning extends beyond the duration of acute effects and necessitates further scrutiny regarding the long-term implications of cannabis exposure on neurocognitive processes. Longitudinal studies have painted a mixed picture, with some investigations indicating a significant decline in a spectrum of intellectual domains-most notably memory, attention, and executive functioning skills-while others have suggested that these impairments may not be uniformly pervasive and could potentially dissipate over time (El-Mallakh et al., 2019; Gruber et al., 2012). This context leads to an important dichotomy: are the cognitive deficits attributable to cannabis use a direct result of neuroadaptations within the brain, or do they arise from factors such as pre-existing vulnerabilities in certain populations? Several studies scrutinizing the patterns of cognitive decline have also aimed to disentangle the role of confounding variables such as age of onset, duration of use, patterns of co-use with other substances-especially alcohol-and psychosocial influences such as socioeconomic status and educational attainment. The interplay between these factors and cannabis use can complicate interpretations of cognitive performance and its association with cannabis. For instance, adolescent users may exhibit more pronounced neurocognitive deficits due to the critical developmental changes occurring in the brain during these formative years (Gonzalez et al., 2014; Meier et al., 2012), raising the question of whether early initiation correlates with pathological changes that could manifest as long-standing cognitive challenges into adulthood. Neuroimaging research lends additional insights into this multifaceted issue. Functional MRI (fMRI) studies have documented altered activation patterns in cannabis users as they engage in cognitive tasks, indicating a potential compensatory mechanism to counterbalance cognitive deficits (Schweinsburg et al., 2008). For instance, it appears that cannabis users might recruit additional brain regions to maintain performance levels, yet this compensatory response may not be uniformly effective across all cognitive tasks, leading to variability in overall cognitive outcomes post-abstinence (Cousijn et al., 2012; Jager et al., 2006). The significance of the timing of assessment post-abstinence also cannot be understated. Studies suggest that cognitive performance could continue to evolve over extended abstinence periods, indicating a potential for cognitive recovery (Hao et al., 2019). Neuroplasticity-the brain's ability to reorganize itself-may play a vital role in this recovery process, allowing individuals to regain functioning as neural pathways adapt (Zou et al., 2013). Yet, it remains to be established whether all users experience this level of recovery, particularly in populations with a long history of high-quantity cannabis use. Equally important is the need to explore the effects of different cannabis formulations and consumption methods, which could yield divergent impacts on cognition. Concentrated forms of cannabis, such as oils or edibles, may deliver higher doses of THC, and thus could exert more profound effects on cognition than traditional smoked cannabis (Huestis, 2010). Hence, understanding specific formulations and their relative psychotropic potential is paramount as the cannabis landscape evolves with legalization and commercialization. In summary, the intricate tapestry of cannabis use and its cognitive concomitants continues to demand rigorous inquiry. While it is clear that cannabis affects cognitive performance, the nuances underlying these effects-a product of intrinsic biochemical pathways, developmental factors, and individual user variability-remain an area of active investigation, promising to enrich our understanding of cannabis's role in cognitive health.

PDMS can be considered as a reference material for the top layer, but other silicone based polymers (PTMSP [22] and POMS [23]), polyether block amide (PEBA) polymers [24] and liquid membranes [25] were investigated as well. PDMS based membranes are of particular interest as they do not suffer from fouling during more than 27 days of operation, a prerequisite for long-term operations [13,26]. More recently, POMS based membranes proved their superior performance in terms of (solvent) flux and separation factor in comparison to PDMS based membranes during long-term continuous integrated cultivations lasting more than 25 days [27]. A decreased energy consumption is often claimed as an advantage for introducing ISPR, but rarely calculated for the overall process taking into account all process streams [8]. Rigorously calculating the energy consumption for production of bioproducts, particularly of potential biofuels, is an arduous effort, but a necessity to advance emerging technologies that can impact society. Significant savings in steam consumption of 51.7% from fermentation till purified products (from 69.5 MJ kg-1 to 33.52 MJ kg-1 butanol using ChemCAD simulations, excluding pretreatment) in the distillation and evaporator sections of the plant were calculated for a multistage continuous fermentation integrated with organophilic pervaporation (as described in WO2018/015415 A1) in comparison with a conventional continuous fermentation [11,28]. Often neglected aspects in pervaporation are costs associated with maintaining the vacuum and costs associated with cooling the permeate vapors. In most research articles, vacuum pressures are applied from 0.2 to 3.9 mbar [18,29-34]. These are unattainable on an industrial scale (roughly between 10 and 100 mbar [35]) and lead to excessive vacuum pump operating costs due to the presence of the non-condensable gases CO2 and H2 [27]. To reach this vacuum, vacuum traps operated at -72.6 C (liquid nitrogen) are utilized in most of the cases [18,29-34]. Therefore, the use of fluxes and separation factors experimentally obtained at these low vacuum pressures and condensation temperatures leads to irrelevant numbers to predict industrial operating conditions. Furthermore, costs associated with chilling and operating vacuum pumps were never considered in these studies leading to too rosy views on potential energy cost reductions. Finally, pervaporation is frequently studied during short time spans of ca. 20 h [32] up to ca. 120 h [36]. Such a test set-ups have their merits to quickly indicate the usefulness of a particular membrane, but performance and potential fouling issues have to be studied during longer time spans and integrated with running fermentations to generate reliable data for cost engineering. Therefore, the data used in this techno-economic assessment originate from long-term continuous cultivations integrated with POMS and PDMS composite membranes where industrially feasible permeate pressures (10-50 mbar) and condensation temperatures (-2 to 15 C) were applied [27]. While the technical feasibility and advantages of the technology are clearly demonstrated, the economic outlook remains unclear.

This book does not exist in a vacuum; rather, it emerges from the broader context of political scrutiny and the perennial questions surrounding the ethical implications of wealth accumulation by public figures. The narrative Schweizer lays out quickly becomes one of intrigue and potential scandal, tapping into the already fraught relationship many Americans have with the political elite. For some, the allegations may be seen as a legitimate inquiry into a pattern of corruption. For others, it merely feeds into a partisan narrative long cultivated by critics of the Clintons. What remains compelling, however, is the framing of these accusations within a narrative of foreign influence. The book is steeped in the language of quid pro quo, a notion that suggests a transactional relationship between Clinton's public duty and private enrichment. One can't help but think of the stakes involved; if Schweizer's assertions hold any weight, they expose a potential breach of loyalty to the nation, one that could reverberate through the coming election cycle. The figures quoted-whether it is the $500,000 speech fees or the millions received from foreign donors-paint a picture that transcends individual missteps and hints instead at a systemic issue within how political fundraising and influence peddling intertwine. Critically, the book has already garnered attention not only for its content but also for its timing. At the precipice of a presidential campaign, the revelations it contains may well serve as a litmus test for the current political climate, reflecting a populist backlash against the established order. Whether or not Schweizer's claims are substantiated, the mere act of putting these questions out into the public sphere invites a necessary examination of political accountability-and that's where the true impact of texts like Clinton Cash resides. One cannot ignore the effect this book may have on both the Clinton campaign and the electorate at large. As each layer of the narrative is peeled back, the potential ramifications echo far beyond the individuals involved. Voter sentiment can shift dramatically, and the whisper of scandal may serve to energize opponents while simultaneously disheartening supporters. Furthermore, it will be critical to analyze the responses from both Clintons and their allies. Denials, evasions, and counter-attacks are the expected playbook in the face of such allegations. This cyclical back-and-forth could create an atmosphere of prolonged unease for the candidates, one that detracts from their policy proposals and broader campaign messages. In the hyper-PAC finance era, any misstep-real or perceived-can derail an electoral ascent. All of this also asks another question: how do voters reconcile their desire for integrity with their incessant appetite for celebrity and wealth? As citizens demand transparency from their elected leaders while simultaneously consuming media infused with glittering narratives of the rich and powerful, there unfolds a paradox that Schweizer's book invites us to confront. As Clinton Cash continues to ripple through political discourse, one thing remains clear: in an era where trust in government is waning, the challenges of accountability, conflict of interest, and foreign entanglements will likely dominate conversations about candidates, their commitments, and their ghosts from the past. As the primary season heats up, readers and voters will find themselves navigating the murky waters of political allegiance, personal ambition, and public service, ever more wary of the implications that accompany the intersection of money and power in American politics.

This concept singularly resonates with the growing understanding of the brain as an interconnected system, a series of simpler networks organized into increasingly complex networks, undergoing a changing trajectory throughout the lifespan (Power et al., 2010). The application of this theory to understand the developing brain may help answer such questions as: How can the stable and integrated pattern of the adult neural network emerge from the decentralized patterning typical of a child's brain? How can the local community clusters of a child's brain emerge from a single neuron communicating to another? According to dynamic systems theory, the key to understanding these fundamental developmental questions lies within the process of self-organization. Some form of global order or coordination arises out of the local interactions between the components of an initially disordered system. In other words, development of networks may organically emerge as a product of the system's own activity and the relationship between the system's component parts. Connectivity techniques provide a set of tools for researchers to examine interactions between elements of the brain. The current review describes tools to assess functional and effective connectivity and describes a framework for understanding large-scale networks. Although the tools described here do not represent the entirety of available techniques implemented to evaluate functional and effective connectivity, they are widely used and have been selected to demonstrate the power of these approaches thematically. Individually and together, these tools have the potential to offer significant contribution in the methodological and conceptual strides being made toward an understanding of the developing brain as a dynamic system. The reader is directed to reviews discussing methods not discussed here, such as Granger causality (Friston et al., 2013). The general principles of dynamic systems theory may be useful for conceptualizing biological self-organization. The first such principle is the tenet of multicausality, which assumes that the regularities of the mature organism patently emerge from multiple factors, including internal configuration of the system and external changes in the environment that the system responds to. The stable and distributed functional system of the mature brain may be a developmental product of multiple sources, including the system's internal configuration (i.e., intrinsic architecture) and its response to the external environment (i.e., extrinsic architecture). The brain's intrinsic architecture is defined as the spontaneous fluctuations between elements of the neural system in the absence of an explicit task, which can be assessed through the acquisition of functional data such as resting-state. This intrinsic architecture may provide a framework for the moment-to-moment responses that the external world evokes (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Raichle, 2010). Extrinsic networks, defined as in-the-moment coupling of regions in response to external stimuli, may be assessed through task-evoked effective connectivity techniques, such as dynamic causal modeling (DCM). Individually and together, the intrinsic and extrinsic architectures of the brain have the potential to shape the development of functional networks through a shared history of co-activation.
