The machine was drawn back again on to the beach, and his mother came out of it wearing a straw hat and a green cloak, and Blessington took them both by the hands and led them away along the shore. They seemed to be walking very fast, though they were really walking quite slowly, and presently they became quite small and indistinct, and disappeared altogether behind a boat that lay keeled up on the sands. Blessington said "There!" when they got out of sight, and picked Archie up in her arms, and carried him back to their lodging-house for lunch. All these things were isolated memories, like separate pictures in an album, and then, like the leaves of such an album being turned over quickly, there followed a series of snapshots, so to speak, of Blessington's face, sometimes cheerful, sometimes severe, sometimes sympathetic, always loving, and in the background of each of these there was a room with a window opening on to a lawn and shrubberies outside. Sometimes he was sitting in a low chair having his lessons, and sometimes he was standing in front of her, and sometimes lying in bed with his head on the pillow, while she told him stories. Sometimes she scolded him, and once he bit her fingers when she tried to take something away from him, and she slapped him hard, and he howled dismally. And then suddenly there was a great blank in his memory, as if somebody had torn out several pages from the album, and there followed a picture of Blessington sitting in a railway-carriage opposite him, with her eyes shut and her mouth rather tightly closed. She looked extremely cross, and Archie felt vaguely uncomfortable because he knew he had done something which would make her crosser still. There were two portmanteaus in the rack above them, and one of them bore the initials W.A., and the other B. He was aware that these letters spelt his name and hers, and he wondered why she should be taking her portmanteau away, since it was labelled with her own initials. When the train stopped she got out without saying anything to him, and walked off down the platform carrying her bag. He watched her till she passed out of sight, and then began to cry. Somebody came and took him out of the carriage, and gave him a bun to eat, and told him that Blessington had gone away, and that he needn't cry any more. So he ate his bun instead.... It was about this time that Archie's real life began, and he ceased to be merely a spectator of events and became an actor in them. His father and mother had come back from abroad, and had taken him away from the house where Blessington lived, and installed him in another house which he instantly accepted as home, because it contained his father and mother. Here also was his sister Sylvia, who was four years older than he, and his brother Harry, who was two years younger. It is true that neither of them took much notice of him, except to pull his hair and call him names, but that did not matter. The mere fact that they belonged to him was sufficient to give him a sense of proprietorship in them.

'My daughter,' answered the old man, 'the Lord has sent us this judgment because we would not be judged; and he will not take off his hand until we repent.' 'Then must we suffer till we do repent?' 'No doubt of it. But he gives us the grace to endure, and thereby helps us to repentance. We have sinned, my child, grievously. I cannot tell how much you may know of these things, for I have kept you very retired, and you have never been at court, where the light shines most clearly.' 'Alas! father, I am afraid I should not have loved it better!' 'Yet I fear you might, my child. You were born in a bad time. The devil is abroad, and the Lord has withdrawn himself. Our church is in sore straits, and the land is full of lamentation. The king is troubled, and the people are divided amongst themselves. My hope is in God, who can turn their hearts as the rivers of water.' 'Is it true, then,' asked the lady, after a pause, 'that the king is bent upon fighting with his subjects?' 'I fear it is too true. And what is more, I fear he has chosen the wrong side. He ought to have stood by his parliament, and let them purify the church.' 'And yet,' returned the lady, 'they say that the parliament is filled with men that hate the church.' 'That may be. There are always some of those among the reformers. But it does not follow that the king should therefore fight against both. If he would only yield up the bishops, and consent to the establishment of presbyteries instead, all would go well.' 'He would yield up the bishops sooner than the queen would yield up her priests, I think.' 'You speak truly. The queen is a plague to the king and to England. But she is a woman, and may be pardoned.' 'She is a Frenchwoman, and that is worse,' said the lady. 'She cares nothing for England.' 'She is a Romanist, and that is worst of all. It is hard to love her.' 'What is a Romanist?' asked the lady. 'One that follows Rome.' 'Yes, yes; but what does that mean?' 'It means that she believes the bishop of Rome to be the head of the church.' 'What church?' 'The whole church, throughout the world.' 'Does he then rule over your church, father?' 'God forbid! No. That is just the difference between us and the papists. They believe him to be Christ's vicar; we believe he is antichrist.' 'Antichrist! What is that?' 'It means the enemy of Christ - one that pretends to be Christ, and is not. Do you not remember the story of Judas Iscariot, whom Jesus called friend?' 'Oh, yes, yes!' cried the lady, clasping her hands, and turning pale. 'I see now. Oh, the wicked wretch! Why, he is the same as the false prophets that Jesus spoke of, who come in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves!' 'Well done, my daughter! Yes, they are all one. The false prophet is the type of the antichrist.' 'But why does the queen want to bring him here?' 'Because she loves darkness rather than light.' 'Ah, yes! I see now. It is horrible. Crustaceans inhabit all reef microhabitats and are major components of invertebrate assemblages within live corals, dead corals, coral rubble, the epilithic algal matrix (Kramer et al., 2013), and sand (Kramer et al., 2014). Of these microhabitats, dead coral colonies have been identified as the most biodiverse habitats (Enochs, 2012; Kramer et al., 2014). This is probably because of the structural relief of the coral still remaining intact to provide habitat and shelter from predators, in comparison to the lower structural complexity of other microhabitats, such as sand and coral rubble. The heterogeneity of the benthic substrata increases on dead branching coral compared to live coral as sessile organisms, such as Porifera and Ascidiacea, colonise recently dead corals providing a variety of niches for motile cryptofauna (Enochs and Manzello, 2012b), resulting in higher biodiversity through complementarity and facilitative interactions (Hooper et al., 2005). In addition, the productivity of the complete faunal assemblage of dead coral colonies is estimated to be up to 149 g Ash-free Dry Weight (AFDW) m-2 yr-1 (Kramer et al., 2014), suggesting this microhabitat is one of the most productive in the world, surpassed only by Californian macrophyte detritus and mussel beds in the Wadden Sea (Asmus, 1987; Taylor, 1998). The greatest threat to natural biodiversity across all ecosystems is ongoing degradation and loss of critical habitats (e.g., Brooks et al., 2002; Waycott et al., 2009), which is being increasingly caused and compounded by global climate change (Mantyka-Pringle et al., 2012). This is especially acute for tropical coral reefs (Burke et al., 2011) which are impacted by multiple stressors including unsustainable and destructive fishing practices, sedimentation and pollution from coastal and maritime activities, and biological outbreaks of crown-of-thorns sea stars. These direct impacts are taking place against a background of increasing global climate change affects, such as mass coral bleaching events, eroding the resilience of reef ecosystems (e.g. Pandolfi et al., 2003; Harborne et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2017). For instance, the Great Barrier Reef lost over 50% of it coral cover from 1985 to 2012 which has been further compounded by the 2015-2016 global mass bleaching event (D'eath et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2018). Despite the demonstrated importance of coral reef decapod assemblages there is little information on how decapod, or indeed cryptofauna communities, are affected by human-induced stressors (But see Coles, 1980, Tsuchiya, 1999, Idjadi and Edmunds, 2006, Leray et al., 2012). In other ecosystems, pollutants have been shown to impact abundance and diversity of decapods. For example, decapod communities on deep offshore banks suffered a dramatic decrease in both abundance and diversity following an oil spill, hypothesised to be a result of cascade effects from seaweed loss (Felder et al., 2014).

But you know how rumors start in a small town like Shopton. People see a shadow at night, or hear a strange noise, and the next thing you know, a house is haunted," said Ned with a laugh. Tom shrugged, rapidly losing interest in the ghostly gossip. "Well, as long as it keeps curious folks away, I suppose it's all right. I've got enough on my plate without dealing with nosy neighbors or would-be haunters." Ned nodded in agreement. "So, what's your latest invention, Tom? You've been awfully quiet about your projects lately." Ned probed, his curiosity piqued. With a glint of mischief in his eyes, Tom leaned closer, as if revealing a grand secret. "It's not ready yet, Ned, but I think it's going to change things a bit. I've been working on a new type of battery-one that's lighter, charges faster, and holds energy longer." Tom's enthusiasm was evident, his eyes gleaming as he spoke. "Imagine what that could do for our flying machines!" Ned whistled appreciatively. "That sounds incredible, Tom! You always have your mind on something remarkable. Do you think it'll be ready soon?" "Still needs some testing," Tom replied, trying to remain modest despite his bubbling excitement. "I've been running trials, and the results are promising. Just a few more tweaks and it might be ready to show." The two friends walked in comfortable silence for a few moments, the conversation shifting naturally as they strolled towards Tom's workshop. The late afternoon sun cast long shadows across the road, and the autumn leaves crunched pleasantly underfoot. "You know," Ned ventured, "if Andy does come back, maybe he's changed. People do grow up, after all." Tom snorted derisively. "Maybe some people do, but not Andy. Not after everything he pulled the last time. Still, I suppose it wouldn't hurt to give him a chance, as long as he stays out of my business." "Exactly," Ned agreed, slapping Tom on the shoulder. "Besides, we've got bigger fish to fry. We'll be too busy with your grand unveiling to worry about Andy Foger creeping around." As they approached the workshop, Tom keyed in a sequence on the electronic lock, and the heavy door swung open with a whisper. Inside lay rows of unfinished projects and scattered blueprints, a testament to Tom's restless innovation. The place smelled comfortingly of machine oil and possibilities. Tom surveyed the organized chaos with pride. "This," he said expansively, "is where the future happens." Ned chuckled, admiring his friend's boundless ambition. "You always make it sound so grand, Tom. But that's what I like about you. Who else in Shopton thinks big like this?" Tom grinned, then his expression grew serious. "But remember, Ned, it's not just about invention. It's about making things better. For us, for everyone. That's what keeps me going." With this declaration, Tom Swift, ever the visionary, turned his attention to the intricate mechanism sprawled across the workbench. To address these challenges, an integrative assessment approach that combines both traditional metrics with contemporary ecological indicators is warranted. Recent research emphasizes the significance of including functional traits of species alongside mere abundance or diversity counts. Functional traits, which may encompass morphological, physiological, or behavioral characteristics, facilitate a deeper understanding of how species interact with one another and their environment, ultimately influencing ecosystem processes (Diaz et al., 2007). By shifting the focus from simply measuring "who is there" to "what they do," we can attain a nuanced comprehension of the underlying ecological dynamics shaping coral reef ecosystems. Furthermore, developing a dynamic assessment framework necessitates collaboration across multiple disciplines and stakeholders. Ecologists, marine managers, and local communities must coordinate their efforts to gather relevant data forms, which may include citizen science initiatives, remote sensing technologies, and ecological modeling. Such collaborative frameworks can enhance data collection efficiency while also fostering community stewardship and increased awareness of marine conservation issues (Burgess et al., 2017). When communities participate in the monitoring process, they gain a more profound connection to their local ecosystems, often leading to more effective conservation outcomes as they are invested in the health of their marine environments. Moreover, the integration of remote sensing technologies into routine assessments could revolutionize our ability to monitor ecosystem health efficiently. Satellite imagery and aerial drones can provide a wider spatial coverage that allows for high-resolution mapping of coral cover and benthic composition, enabling researchers to capture dynamic changes over time (Moussa et al., 2019). Such technological approaches pave the way for real-time monitoring systems that inform adaptive management strategies, empowering stakeholders to make informed decisions promptly. In light of the rapid environmental changes faced by coral reefs-exacerbated by climate change, ocean acidification, and anthropogenic pressures-there is an urgent need for flexible management frameworks that remain responsive to changing conditions. Implementing adaptive management practices, which entail a cycle of monitoring, assessment, and adjustment based on ecological feedback, can enhance both resilience and sustainability of coral reef ecosystems (Walters, 1986). Engaging with local environmental conditions and recognizing the complexities of inter-species relationships will undoubtedly support more effective strategies for mitigating habitat degradation. Additionally, enhancing our understanding of the connections between biotic and abiotic factors in coral reefs is essential. Various environmental stressors, such as increased sedimentation and nutrient loading, can significantly influence the health of coral populations while simultaneously reshaping community dynamics among reef organisms (Fabricius, 2005). By identifying critical thresholds and feedback loops that may destabilize these ecosystems, we can implement timely interventions designed to reverse negative trends in marine health. In conclusion, adopting a comprehensive approach that emphasizes functional traits, multidisciplinary collaboration, and advanced monitoring technologies will be paramount for the future conservation of coral reef ecosystems. This diversified methodology will not only augment existing knowledge of ecological dynamics but will also empower stakeholders to make data-driven decisions, ensuring resilience and sustainability in the face of unprecedented global changes. As we seek to refine our understanding of these systems, we must also remain cognizant of our responsibility to protect the irreplaceable biodiversity that coral reefs embody, for both their intrinsic value and the essential ecosystem services they provide. The enduring challenge lies in translating this knowledge into actionable frameworks that genuinely reflect the complexities of these incredible ecosystems.

The birth of Pasadena as a thriving oasis was not merely due to its enchanting climate and fertile soil; the city's cultural and social fabric played an equally pivotal role. As we delve deeper into Pasadena's early days, we uncover the intricate tapestry of individuals who embraced this new land. Prominent figures from various walks of life began to gather, drawn by the promise of prosperity and the allure of camaraderie. The city quickly morphed into a melting pot of ideas, arts, and innovations. Wealthy Easterners mingled effortlessly with adventurous pioneers, and the convergence of these diverse minds would erupt into a cultural renaissance that shaped Pasadena's identity. Artistic communities flourished as painters, poets, and musicians found inspiration amid the breathtaking vistas and serene landscapes. Painters like the American Impressionist, Guy Rose, were entranced by the unique light found only in this corner of California. The fair served not only as a testament to Pasadena's agricultural wealth but also as a vehicle to unite the community, fostering the spirit of togetherness that defined the burgeoning city. Education, too, became a cornerstone of Pasadena's evolution. As more families settled in the area, establishing schools became a paramount concern. The founding of institutions, such as Occidental College and the California Institute of Technology, signaled the growing emphasis on academia and research. The establishment of electric railways connected Pasadena to Los Angeles and the broader world, further enabling the influx of settlers and tourists alike. Restaurants, bookshops, and boutiques began to fill the streets, transforming Pasadena into a hub for commerce and culture. The city burgeoned as its reputation as an idyllic destination for escape spread beyond California's borders. Coined as 'new public health' in the 1990s, social scientists problematized its narrow focus on lifestyle related prevention, which places the onus and responsibility on the individual to exercise control, be healthy, and become productive citizens (Lupton, 2003). The population is handed "biological responsibilities [...] embodied in contemporary norms of health and practices of health education" (Rose, 2007, p. 133). Public health agendas have somewhat shifted in recent years towards wider social and structural determinants and a growing recognition that the context of people's lives needs greater consideration to reduce 'lifestyle' disease (Cohn, 2014). The life-course is subject to a range of influences and people are not merely 'blank sheets' awaiting and receptive to health promotion messages (Baum and Fisher, 2014, p. 215). Rather than being unaware of the risk, it is more likely that constraints in people's their lives makes behaviour change difficult (Baum and Fisher, 2014). It is possible that walking groups fit into this more holistic public health agenda by providing structure and opportunities for physical activity rather than narrowly focusing on sports and exercise. For example, within public health and epidemiology, there is an increasing research field on the health benefits of green space, either as opportunities to be physically active in, or more generally as health enhancing spaces. This includes Gesler's seminal work (Gesler, 1992) and more recently, work such as Gatrell (2013), Roe et al. (2013), and Bowler et al. (2010). Without understanding both individual needs and life situations, there are potentially barriers created for those who have the greatest health need (Matthews et al., 2012). For walking, it appears to be particularly important to understand both the physical and social environments in which the behaviour takes place. It may be that for those people from more deprived backgrounds, rather than being a pleasurable leisure activity, walking may be their only available and affordable mode of transport. Consequently, walking may be burdensome or stressful, for example when walking with small children or in unsafe neighbourhoods (Bostock, 2001; Green, 2009). This might partway explain why in the United Kingdom, despite its past history of socialist walking clubs, rambling (walking in the countryside for pleasure) has a particularly middle class identity (Green, 2009). Using a qualitative approach, this study worked with a newly formed walking group as part of a referral scheme in a place of social and health deprivation with participants with multiple health problems. The aim was to add to our understanding of non-participation in walking groups for particular social groups and thus how they can be more effectively promoted to target people in those communities who could benefit most. To do so this study was framed within a social practice perspective which aimed to highlight the social context of walking and walking group participation, rather than understanding it as an individualised health behaviour (Blue et al., 2014).

The main objective of our paper is therefore to establish whether the structure of finances matters for economic growth. We do so by examining the role of various types of finances (credit, bonds, stocks) for the dynamics of real per capita GDP in a sample of 23 advanced economies over the period 1987-2013, while controlling for the impact of other factors affecting the latter, including: human capital, physical capital, labour force, openness, inflation, government expenditures and investments, and quality of institutions. The novelty of our study lies in its focus on the importance of the structure of finances for economic growth. This is not only a natural extension of the existing research, but also crucial given the ongoing debate about the desirability of large financial sectors. Our results show that the structure of finances does matter for economic growth. Not all types of finances contribute positively to economic growth, and the non-linearity found in previous studies is mainly driven by credit. Bonds have a negative linear effect on economic growth, whereas stocks have no significant impact. Given the strong positive correlation between bond and stock markets (see Table 1 in Section 2 below), we argue that the insignificance of the latter stems from the fact that the two markets substitute each other to some extent. In order to account for this substitution, we examine the effects of both markets jointly, i.e. via the ratio of stocks to bonds, and find a positive linear impact of the ratio on economic growth. Our results thus suggest that not only the size of finances but also their structure matters for economic growth, and that policies aimed at stimulating the financial sector should take into account the particular type of finances promoted. 11374 copyright.

Sanchez, rather like Luis Suarez after he became unsettled at Liverpool, has the driven winning mentality that ensures he can block out all outside distractions once he gets on the field. It would be no surprise to see him continue to exert a major influence on Arsenal. Premier League champions Chelsea have brought in real talent in this window in the shape of 60m striker Alvaro Morata from Real Madrid and Monaco's talented midfielder Tiemoue Bakayoko - but there will still be frustration after several failures in the transfer market. Romelu Lukaku was long-touted for a return to his former club but ended up joining Manchester United in a 75m switch from Everton, while a move for Juventus defender Leonardo Bonucci never materialised as he chose to stay in Italy at AC Milan. The Stamford Bridge club agreed a 40m fee with Arsenal for Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain only to discover the midfielder preferred Liverpool, before the steady pursuit of Swansea City striker Fernando Llorente was trumped by a late, swift 15m intervention from Tottenham. Finally, and most bizarrely of all, Chelsea agreed a 35m deal with Everton for Ross Barkley, only for the 23-year-old England midfielder to change his mind on the move. Everton major shareholder Farhad Moshiri said Barkley had even had a medical - a claim denied by Barkley's camp.

As the bartender shuffled off to fill the order, I couldn't help but feel a slight twinge of regret at how quickly I'd folded to their request. The bar was bustling that afternoon, a mixture of locals and tourists seeking respite from the summer sun, and the familiar clatter of glasses and raucous laughter filled the air. With a sigh, I turned my attention back to the crew, sizing up the operation at hand. Mike was already making himself at home, leaning back against the bar as if he owned the place, a self-satisfied grin plastered across his face. His crew was no better-loud and boisterous, completely at ease as if they'd been doing this circuit for years. Their carefree demeanor did little to settle my growing discomfort. The crew dove in with gusto, their girlfriends chatting animatedly among themselves about plans for the weekend. I did a quick mental tally of the bill this would rack up and winced. This wasn't exactly what I'd budgeted for. Watching them dig in, I realized I had no real strategy in place for the rest of the weekend. The fireworks show was supposed to be a hit, a highlight of the summer festivities, and here I was stumbling through preparations half-blind. Other urgent matters called for my attention, but now I was tethered to this makeshift duty until it all blew over-quite literally, in a fireworks burst of light and sound. Determined not to let my growing exasperation show, I pasted on a smile and decided to make this work, somehow. "So, Mike," I started, taking a sip from my own drink, "what's the plan for the evening? Anything specific you need to get done?" Mike, seemingly caught between a slice of pepperoni and a swig, shrugged nonchalantly. "Oh, we'll enjoy the town a bit tonight. No rush, we got it covered," he said, as if this would all sort itself out magically. "Tomorrow, though," he continued, "We'll get the speakers set up. Can you have that CD ready by then? Straightening up, I nodded solemnly. "Not a problem. I'll make sure it's good to go for you." The afternoon wore on into the evening, a lazy hue settling over the waterfront. Despite my rising concerns, the infectious, carefree attitude of the crew was almost, dare I say, comforting. Amidst their laid-back revelry, I found myself slightly more at ease, albeit with the nagging worry of the weekend's impending chaos nipping at the edges of my consciousness. There was nothing left to do but see where it all led-firework displays, music, pizza, and all. After all, sometimes you just had to go along for the ride and hope the view was worth the journey.

As I grew older, my father, in his zeal to instill in me a sense of morality and righteousness, would often regale me with tales of the Quibble family's storied past. He would speak of Great-Aunt Hepzibah, who had bravely defied the British during the War of Independence, and of Great-Uncle Silas, who had made a small fortune in the China trade. But I fear that these stories only served to instill in me a sense of restlessness, a feeling that I was destined for greater things than the humble life of a small-town pastor's son. My mother, on the other hand, was more practical in her approach. She taught me the importance of thrift and frugality, skills that would serve me well in later life. She would often take me on walks through the town, pointing out the various landmarks and sharing stories of the people who lived in the houses we passed. I remember in particular her tales of the old Lynn Athenaeum, where she had spent many an hour as a young woman, poring over the pages of Dickens and Thackeray. As I entered my teenage years, I began to feel the stirrings of ambition. I devoured books on every subject imaginable, from the sciences to literature to history. My father, seeing my interest in learning, encouraged me to pursue a career in the ministry, but I had other plans. I was drawn to the law, with its promise of power, prestige, and financial reward. A long gabled front of red brick, with the complexion of which time and the weather had played all sorts of pictorial tricks, only, however, to improve and refine it, presented to the lawn its patches of ivy, its clustered chimneys, its windows smothered in creepers. The house had a name and a history; the old gentleman taking his tea would have been delighted to tell you these things: how it had been built under Edward the Sixth, had offered a night's hospitality to the great Elizabeth (whose august person had extended itself upon a huge, magnificent and terribly angular bed which still formed the principal honour of the sleeping apartments), had been a good deal bruised and defaced in Cromwell's wars, and then, under the Restoration, repaired and much enlarged; and how, finally, after having been remodelled and disfigured in the eighteenth century, it had passed into the careful keeping of a shrewd American banker, who had bought it originally because (owing to circumstances too complicated to set forth) it was offered at a great bargain: bought it with much grumbling at its ugliness, its antiquity, its incommodity, and who now, at the end of twenty years, had become conscious of a real aesthetic passion for it, so that he knew all its points and would tell you just where to stand to see them in combination and just the hour when the shadows of its various protuberances which fell so softly upon the warm, weary brickwork - were of the right measure. Besides this, as I have said, he could have counted off most of the successive owners and occupants, several of whom were known to general fame; doing so, however, with an undemonstrative conviction that the latest phase of its destiny was not the least honourable. The front of the house overlooking that portion of the lawn with which we are concerned was not the entrance-front; this was in quite another quarter. Privacy here reigned supreme, and the wide carpet of turf that covered the level hill-top seemed but the extension of a luxurious interior. The great still oaks and beeches flung down a shade as dense as that of velvet curtains; and the place was furnished, like a room, with cushioned seats, with rich-coloured rugs, with the books and papers that lay upon the grass. The river was at some distance; where the ground began to slope the lawn, properly speaking, ceased. But it was none the less a charming walk down to the water. The old gentleman at the tea-table, who had come from America thirty years before, had brought with him, at the top of his baggage, his American physiognomy; and he had not only brought it with him, but he had kept it in the best order, so that, if necessary, he might have taken it back to his own country with perfect confidence.

He sat his horse as one born to the saddle; his hands were firm, his whole frame full of physical force, energy, and endurance - a man who would act promptly and with decision, probably a good man to have as a friend, most certainly an awkward one to have as an enemy. "We delayed too long at our last halt, Seth. I doubt whether we shall see Paris to-night," he said presently, but made no effort to check the pace of his horse. "I've been doubting that for an hour past, Master Richard," was the answer. The grizzled man was Seth, or sometimes Mr. Seth, to all who knew him. So seldom had he heard himself called Seth Dingwall that he had almost forgotten the name. Born in Louisiana, he believed he had French blood in him, and spoke the language easily. He had gone with his mistress to Virginia when she married Colonel Barrington, and to him Broadmead was home, and he had no relation in the wide world. "Is it so necessary to reach the city to-night?" he asked after a pause. "I had planned to do so." The answer was characteristic of the man. As a boy, when he had made up his mind to do a thing, he did it, even though well-merited punishment might follow, and the boy was father to the man. Save in years and experience, this was the same Richard Barrington who had dreamed as he watched sunlit sails disappear in the haze over Chesapeake Bay. "I was thinking of the horses," said Seth. "I reckon that we have a long way to travel yet." "We may get others presently," Barrington answered, and then, after a moment's pause, he went on: "We have seen some strange sights since we landed - ruined homes, small and great, burned and desolated by the peasants; and in the last few hours we have heard queer tales. I do not know how matters stand, but it looks as if we might be useful in Paris. That is why we must push on." "Master Richard," he said slowly. "Yes." "Have you ever considered how useless a man may be?" "Ay, often, and known such men." "You do not catch my meaning. I am talking of a man who is full of courage and determination, yet just because he is only one is powerless. A lion might be killed by rats if there were enough rats." "True, Seth, but there would be fewer rats by the time the lion was dead, and a less number for the next lion to struggle with." "A good answer," said Seth, "and I'm not saying it isn't a right one, but I'm thinking of that first lion which may be slain." A smile, full of tenderness, came into Barrington's face which, in the gathering darkness, his companion could hardly have seen had he turned to look at him, which he did not do.

No wonder so many women seek the maternal embrace of Oprah's and Katie's book clubs. When I first came to the Weekly in the 1980s, I wrote alongside Helen Knode, the house bad girl, whose reviews frequently pointed out how movies debased women by portraying them as bimbos, psychos, whores and corpses a or ignoring them altogether. Each time she did so, she received furious letters from men saying, "Spare us your feminist politics and just review the moviea a as if it's not part of a film that the female characters are all vacuous, skanky or dead. After fighting the good fight for several years, Helen eventually abandoned film criticism and wrote a crime novel, The Ticket Out, about the many ways that Hollywood kills women. Although the degradation of women remains the often-unmentioned elephant in the home entertainment center a and let us not forget the "bitches" and "hos" of pop music a it hasn't gone unnoticed. I recently asked a well-known film critic how often she sees movies she finds demeaning. "Every fucking week," she replied. "But I only write about it now and then, when something really bothers me. If you do it all the time, you become boring. You don't want to seem relentless." Sad to say, it's easy to be thought relentless if you're a female critic writing about pop culture. When a male reviewer like me points out that Starsky & Hutch displays a disgustingly puerile attitude toward women (wasn't Ben Stiller once thought to be smart?), this proves I'm a sensitive guy, a hero. When a woman makes the identical observation, she's considered a strident bitch. If I seem peculiarly fascinated by the tribulations of women critics, this is because, in my formative years, I was enthralled by two of them: The New Yorker's late, great film critic Pauline Kael and Susan Sontag, now 71, who has given herself the groovy description of "freelance intellectual." I clearly wasn't the only one. In his enjoyable new book Sontag & Kael: Opposites Attract Me, Craig Seligman offers a personal riff on the two most visible American critics of the last 40 years. Not only were they hugely influential a their work has been strip-mined and embarrassingly mimicked by countless other critics a but their vast differences in taste, style and image (one was "Pauline," the other "Sontaga) marked the boundaries of popular criticism. Like Mary McCarthy before them, Kael and Sontag presumed to an authority that was routinely thought of as a masculine prerogative. If they have been more praised and reviled than their male counterparts, this isn't simply because their work was better at capturing the joys of Jean-Luc Godard or modern styles of eroticism; the fact of their being women induced a protracted frisson in an America that has always found it easy to find the bitch lurking in the goddess.

For American readers, do a thought experiment in which armed Mexican drones were routinely killing members of drug cartels living in Texas, but they were also sometimes killing a number of ordinary Texans and you get a sense of how the average Pakistani thinks about this issue. In Yemen, the U.S. drone campaign has also become increasingly controversial because drones continue to kill Yemeni civilians - as they did last month in a strike that targeted members of al Qaeda's Yemeni affiliate. In that strike on April 19, at least nine militants were killed but so were three civilians. Even with these issues, drones present features that make them appealing to political and military leaders. Drones are not simply pieces of artillery that happen to fly. They have four characteristics that mean they are likely to reshape warfare at a tactical level. First, armed drones are different from any previous form of artillery because they can linger over and assess a target for many hours. That capability can quite dramatically lower the civilian casualty rates that have been typical of earlier eras of warfare. The smallest bomb dropped by the U.S. Air Force is typically 500 pounds. Such a bomb cannot, of course, distinguish between a civilian and a combatant. A drone can do so. And it can also shoot much smaller missiles, such as the 100-pound Hellfire missile. In that sense there is a case to be made that armed drones presage a more ethical form of warfare that kills fewer civilians. But that doesn't mean of course that drones and the people who operate them won't kill civilians in the future. The U.S. drone campaigns in Pakistan and Yemen have killed hundreds of civilians over the past half decade. Second, armed drones also make it possible to wage war against particular individuals. In a sense drones are flying assassins that target particular people. It is not an accident that the rise of drone warfare has coincided with America's unconventional war against al Qaeda and its allies. In conventional wars, armies wearing uniforms attack each other. But in the kind of drone warfare that the United States has conducted since 9/11 outside of conventional war zones in countries such as Pakistan and Yemen, drone strikes are not directed at someone because of his status as a uniformed member of another military force, but rather because of the individual's suspected connection to al Qaeda or an allied group. Bergen: Target an American with drones? Third, there is a lower threshold for the use of force when armed drones are an option. In many ways the use of armed drones is akin to the use of cyberwarfare. Both tactics greatly reduce or eliminate the number of deaths that would result from a conventional armed conflict. And whoever launches a drone attack or a cyberattack pays no costs of the kind that would typically take place on a conventional battlefield.

These children, untouched by the cynicism of adulthood, represent the purest form of love for the game-a love untainted by statistics, contracts, or scandals. For them, baseball is not just a game but a realm where myths are crafted, and legends are born. As these youngsters grow, and the real world imposes its labyrinthine choices and consequences, baseball remains a tether to simpler times. It is a constant in an ever-evolving landscape-a lighthouse guiding wayward souls back to a place of familiarity and peace. It is well known that all of the exotic plants that successfully invade a new country or area must establish, grow, reproduce, and colonize, becoming a population that can maintain itself independently and then subsequently invade native ecosystems. Therefore, it is useful to investigate the mechanisms of successful biological invasions by identifying and analyzing all of the invasive plants of a country or region (Ordonez, 2014). Furthermore, invasion rules for all of the invasive plants of a country or an area in the context of the three main issues related to invasive plants need to be established. First, we need to analyze the characteristics that determine the invasive capacities of all of the invasive plants in a region, including their life forms, reproductive strategies, and morphological and taxonomic characteristics. Second, we need to analyze the characteristics of those habitats that support a high proportion of invasive plants to identify the environments or regions that are more likely to be invaded by exotic species (Menuz and Kettenring, 2013). Regional or biome-scale assessments can indicate the relative susceptibility to invasion of certain larger units within a region (e.g., climatic zones) (Reichard and Hamilton, 1997). Landscape-scale assessments of the spread of alien species can also indicate when and where mechanical control could be used effectively (Guido et al., 2016; Higgins et al., 2000). Third, the histories of alien species from their introductions to invasion, the purposes and processes of introduction, and the management processes applied should provide important information. These factors are often important in facilitating the naturalization and invasion of an alien species. Therefore, this information is useful in the management of invasive species at the landscape scale (Higgins et al. 2000, 2001), and it is also particularly helpful in planning long-term strategies at regional and national levels (Rouget et al., 2002). Different areas or countries differ in aspects, such as climate, geographical environment, human activities, and laws, and thus the biomes of invasive species are diverse. However, just as there are certain traits associated with the invasive capacities of these plants, there are also universal similarities in the ways that alien species are introduced, and in their management and control. When an alien species is introduced into a new area, its success in becoming established and breeding successfully depends upon the similarity between its region of origin and the invaded area in parameters, such as the climatic and ecological environments, and these factors must be within the tolerance range for the growth and breeding of the invasive alien plant (Haeuser et al., 2017). Therefore, information about the region of origin and the invaded area of an invasive alien species is helpful in identifying the areas that are vulnerable to that particular invasive species. This information is also important in resisting or supervising a biological invasion. For example, China and the USA are generally located at the same latitudes and have similar types of climates.

He flexed his fingers, feeling the familiar shape of his hands, and a spark of recognition flickered to life in his mind. Even into their sheltered nook the sun, far down in the south, throws but cold and watery gleams from a steel-colored sky, and as the northern blast eddies around the sheltering buildings the poor creatures shiver, and when their morning airing is over are glad to return to their warm, straw-littered stalls. Even the gallant and champion cock of the yard is chilled. With one foot drawn up into his fluffy feathers he stands motionless in the midst of his disconsolate harem with his eye fixed vacantly on the forbidding outlook. His dames appear neither to miss nor to invite his attentions, and their eyes, usually so bright and alert, often film in weary discontent. Nature, however, is oblivious to all the dumb protests of the barnyard, and the cold steadily strengthens. Away on every side stretch the angular fields, outlined by fences that are often but white, continuous mounds, and also marked by trees and shrubs that, in their earlier life, ran the gantlet of the bush-hook. Here and there the stones of the higher and more abrupt walls crop out, while the board and rail fences appear strangely dwarfed by the snow that has fallen and drifted around them. The groves and wood-crowned hills still further away look as drearily uninviting as roofless dwellings with icy hearthstones and smokeless chimneys. Towering above all, on the right, is Storm King mountain, its granite rocks and precipices showing darkly here and there, as if its huge white mantle were old and ragged indeed. One might well shiver at the lonely, desolate wastes lying beyond it, grim hills and early-shadowed valleys, where the half-starved fox prowls, and watches for unwary rabbits venturing from their coverts to nibble the frozen twigs. The river, which above the Highlands broadens out into Newburgh Bay, has become a snowy plain, devoid, on this bitter day, of every sign of life. The Beacon hills, on the further side, frown forbiddingly through the intervening northern gale, sweeping southward into the mountain gorge. On a day like this the most ardent lover of Nature could scarcely fail to shrink from her cold, pallid face and colder breath. Our return to the home, whose ruddy firelight is seen through the frosted window-panes, will be all the more welcome because we have been shivering so long without. The grace of hospitality has been a characteristic of the master of the house for over half a century, and therefore the reader need not fear to enter, especially at this Christmas-time, when the world, as if to make amends for the churlish welcome it gave to its Divine Guest, for whom no better place was found than a stable, now throws open the door and heart in kindly feeling and unselfish impulses. We propose to make a long visit at this old-fashioned homestead.

Visual feedback is particularly important when performing difficult tasks requiring high levels of accuracy and dexterity, such as writing with a pen, and when manipulating small objects. In the absence of vision, performance of these tasks deteriorates significantly (Johansson and Westling, 1988). For example, if vision is removed from the grasp phase of handwriting, there is a marked increase in the variability of movement time, movement distance and movement velocity (Liu et al., 2006). Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that disruption of visual feedback by occlusion of one eye results in increased force variability (Kawashima et al., 2001). In the current study we examined the effect of removing visual feedback on the activation of the visuomotor network during a precision grip task. We hypothesized that the removal of visual feedback would result in reduced activation in the cortical areas involved in the integration of visual information into the motor command signals. However, given that the removal of visual feedback could potentially alter the motor strategy employed by participants, we were also interested to examine whether any differences in neural activation patterns were related to changes in the biomechanics of the task. ## Methods ### Participants Twelve healthy right-handed adults (seven females; mean age: 26 years; range: 22-31 years) participated in this study after providing written informed consent. All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological disorders. The experimental protocol was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the University of Sydney and conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki. ### Experimental design During each trial, participants sat comfortably with their arms supported on a table. Their right arm rested in a comfortable position with the elbow flexed to approximately 90\({}^{\circ}\), the forearm pronated and wrist extended. A cylindrical handle attached to a load cell was held by the participant's right hand. A custom-built force transducer (Transducer Techniques, Temecula, CA) measured the force applied by the subject along three axes (anterior-posterior, medial-lateral and vertical). Data were sampled at 500 Hz and stored on a PC computer. Subjects were instructed to maintain a constant contact pressure against the handle throughout the experiment, and to apply a steady force (approximately 10% MVC) in the anterior-posterior direction while holding the handle. They were asked not to move the handle, and to keep their eyes open and fixate on a crosshair placed on the wall directly in front of them. The crosshair was visible through a mirror positioned below the load cell so that the participant could see themselves without being able to see their hand. During some trials, a screen was placed in front of the mirror to block out the view of the participant's hand. The experimental paradigm consisted of two conditions: a "vision" condition where participants performed the task with visual feedback available, and a "no-vision" condition where they performed the task with visual feedback blocked. The order of presentation of the two conditions was randomized across participants. Each session lasted approximately 60 min, and included practice runs before the data collection commenced. Two types of task were performed within each condition: a 'constant force' task and a 'variable force' task. During the constant force task, participants were required to maintain a constant level of force (approximately 10% MVC) over a 30 s period. During the variable force task, participants were required to hold the handle for 30 s and then rapidly increase the force to 50% MVC and then decrease back down to baseline over a period of 15 s. After a pause of 5 s, they then repeated the same pattern of force application.

There is a growing acceptance of being monitored, which may be leading to changes in how people behave. In addition, there is growing awareness among the general population about the way in which their personal data can be used by others. This means that, at least in some countries, there are increasing concerns about privacy and data protection (Gidari, 2012; Custers et al., 2013; Kokolakis, 2017). The objective of this paper is to review the emerging literature on the application of Big Data for transport modelling purposes. It aims to identify the main challenges facing those who wish to exploit these new opportunities and to offer some solutions to them. Big Data and Transport: Understanding and Assessing Options Goodwin P.;Nocera S.;Scheiner J. In recent years there have been enormous technological advances in the capture and storage of data, affecting our potential to monitor both human behaviour and the physical world, and providing possibilities to track and triangulate diverse data sets. A report by the OECD (2013) identified the following types of new data on 'the human condition': Data from government transactions (e.g. tax, social security) Data related to official registration/licensing Commercial transactions by individuals and organisations Internet data from search and social networking activities Image data (e.g. aerial/satellite images, land-based video) All of these are potentially relevant to planning transport systems since they either provide insights into the location, timing and frequency of activities that generate travel (such as employment, shopping or social engagement), or they provide direct evidence of the volume, concentration and direction of person movements or vehicular movements. These opportunities have been explored to varying degrees. Saadi et al. (2016) used social security data to infer trip patterns. Chatterton et al. (2015) used annual vehicle test data to understand social variations in vehicle use. De Montjoye et al. (2015) used credit card data to reconstruct individual movements. Smart card data has been widely used by many researchers (e.g. Pelletier et al., 2011; Tao et al., 2014; Tamblay et al., 2016), with a range of applications in public transport planning. Location-based, social media check-in data from services such as Foursquare and Twitter has been used by a range of researchers (e.g. Hasan and Ukkusuri, 2014; Liu et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014; Abdulazim et al., 2015; Hu and Jin, 2017) to attempt to estimate travel activity patterns, while Jestico et al. (2016) have investigated the potential of the activity tracking app STRAVA for measuring cycling volumes. Social media data have also been used to examine unexpected situations and special events (Pender et al., 2014; Pereira et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2016). Automatic vehicle identification has been used to understand complex travel activity patterns (Ozbay and Ercelebi, 2005; Siripirote et al., 2014). Perhaps most widely exploited for understanding travel/mobility patterns has been mobile phone data (e.g. Calabrese et al., 2013; Blondel et al., 2015; Widhalm et al., 2015) and GPS data (e.g. Frignani et al., 2010; Lin and Hsu, 2014; Montini et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2015; Gong et al., 2016).

And then there's Nathan Bunce. He runs the largest duck and goose farm in the valley. He's remarkably short, possibly due to some congenital condition, but don't let his stature deceive you. He doesn't eat his birds; instead, he consumes only doughnuts and liverwurst paste, mashed into a sort of grisly paste and washed down with gallons of cider. He's got this bizarre obsession with developing what he calls 'the perfect dunk,' where the pastry holds just the right amount of moisture without dissolving. It's a grotesque spectacle that I've witnessed once, and once was plenty. Lastly, we've got Franklin Bean. The man brews cider from apples of dubious origin. He's lean as a rake, drinks his product exclusively, and somehow manages to remain sober enough to oversee one of the largest orchards you've ever seen. Rumor has it, he hasn't consumed solid food in years. His skin has the eerie pallor of a man who drinks more than he eats, and his eyes glint like shards of glass in the sunlight. Honestly, there's more scarecrow than man to him, but don't be fooled-his wits are sharper than his sickle. These three farmers have an unholy alliance of sorts. They might not see eye to eye on everything, but they hate one thing more than anything else: us foxes. They've been trying to outsmart us for years, setting traps, hiring guards, and concocting outrageous schemes. Despite all their efforts, we always find a way around them, at least up until now. We're not alone in our plight either; countless other creatures find themselves threatened by their ever-encroaching ambition. The stories our grandparents told about plentiful resources and peace among the fields have started to fade into myth. That's why I can't simply remain underground. The world is changing. Maybe it's time we change with it. I suppose I should've mentioned the cub sooner, but a father's life is filled with contingencies. A blend of apprehension and excitement courses through me as I think about the future. Our family is growing; we must find a way to thrive amidst the shifting tides. Perhaps the answer isn't in hiding or skirting the edges of danger anymore. Perhaps it's time for a plan so audacious, so utterly unexpected, that even Bunce, Boggis, and Bean won't see it coming. But first, we should take stock of our allies. Badger should be on the list, despite his apparent irritation. Rabbit, too, for all the rumors that circulate around his judgment, has a keen sense of tunnels. Kylie, of course, never hesitates to provide support when buckets of minnows are involved. These companions might just have the skills we need to orchestrate something as grand as the coup I envision. Let's convene at twilight and devise our next move. We'll use the very traps set against us as stepping stones. Because if there's one certainty in this endlessly unpredictable world, it's that a fox with enough determination and wit can overcome anything-even the combined might of those greedy farmers. As the stars begin to prick the velvet sky, promising guidance, I smile at the challenge ahead.

This work is a continuation of our previous study [59] where we reported that a nitrogen-doped carbonaceous material prepared from a mixture of polyaniline (PANI), carbon black (CB) and iron chloride salt could lead to enhanced ORR activity in neutral media. Herein, we further investigated this material in more detail to clarify the role of each component in the final product, the effect of the heat-treatment temperature on the composition and structure of the resulting materials and the influence of the iron precursor on the electrocatalytic activity of the synthesized composites. Materials preparation Polyaniline (emeraldine base, powder, MW 50000 g/mol) and iron(III) chloride hexahydrate (FeCl {3} 6H {2} O) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and used as received. Carbon black (Vulcan XC-72) was obtained from Cabot Corporation. Deionized water was purified through a Millipore Milli-Q system. Ammonium persulfate ((NH {4} ) {2} S {2} O {8}, APS), sulfuric acid (H {2} SO {4} ), hydrochloric acid (HCl) and ammonium hydroxide solution (28 wt% NH {3} in water) were purchased from VWR International LLC. Synthesis of polyaniline/carbon black composite In a typical synthesis, 0.91 g of aniline monomer was dissolved in 90 mL of 1 mol L ^{-1} aqueous HCl solution under magnetic stirring at room temperature. Then, 20 mL of 1 mol L ^{-1} aqueous APS solution was added dropwise into the above solution. After that, 0.9 g of CB was dispersed in 80 mL of 1 mol L ^{-1} aqueous HCl solution and then added to the above mixture. The polymerization reaction proceeded for 24 h at room temperature. The precipitate was filtered, washed with deionized water until the filtrate became colorless, and dried overnight in air at 60 C. The obtained PANI/CB composite was denoted as PC. Synthesis of FeCl {3} /polyaniline/carbon black composite A similar procedure was used as described above, except that 0.27 g of FeCl {3} 6H {2} O was added to the reaction mixture before adding the APS solution. The obtained product was denoted as FPC. Thermal treatment of the synthesized composites The obtained PANI/CB and FeCl {3} /PANI/CB composites were thermally treated in argon atmosphere at different temperatures ranging between 600 and 900 C for 2 h. However, these studies did not explicitly measure whether there are differences between the way leaders and followers use prediction during interaction. Therefore, we conducted an experiment using a novel paradigm, the joint dot motion tracking task, to investigate how leading and following roles affect the way humans use predictive mechanisms during joint action. We manipulated who had access to visual feedback about the other's actions while they performed the joint dot motion tracking task. Participants performed the task either alone, with full mutual access to visual feedback, or in pairs with restricted access to visual feedback. In the latter case, only one participant saw the dots controlled by the other partner. We expected that participants would be better at performing the task when they could observe each other's actions because they would have a greater amount of information available to make predictions about each other's behavior. Moreover, we predicted that the leader-follower relationship would influence the degree to which participants relied on prediction during interaction. If being able to predict the other's behavior is particularly important for successful joint action coordination, then followers should rely on prediction more than leaders. In this study we show that it is possible to identify neural correlates of different behavioral strategies within a group of healthy subjects. We used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to compare brain activation associated with a control strategy and a prediction strategy while participants performed a simple visuomotor task. In the control strategy, the participants initiated their movements immediately after the appearance of a target. In the prediction strategy, the participants anticipated the movement onset based on a periodicity present in the stimulus sequence. Behavioral results showed that the prediction strategy led to faster response times and lower temporal variability. Imaging data revealed higher activity in supplementary motor area (SMA), presupplementary motor area (pre-SMA), left dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), right ventral premotor cortex (PMv), and bilateral inferior parietal lobules (IPLs) when comparing the prediction and control strategies. Activity in SMA, pre-SMA, PMd, and IPL was also correlated with the efficiency of implementing the prediction strategy across subjects. These findings suggest that SMA, pre-SMA, PMd, and IPL may subserve functions necessary for the prediction strategy, such as movement preparation driven by sensory cues, interval timing, and updating of movement parameters. How does the human mind represent abstract knowledge of complex events? Cognitive theories disagree on whether knowledge takes the form of exemplars and prototypes or abstract rules. Recent evidence suggests that people rely on multiple formats of mental representation simultaneously. However, little is known about how people integrate different forms of knowledge, especially when they conflict with each other. Here we report that people flexibly shift between different forms of knowledge depending on the demands of the task. We observed that people spontaneously adopt a rule-based strategy to guide responses when reasoning about complex events, but revert back to similarity-based processes when rules become unreliable. Our results indicate that people possess sophisticated meta-representational abilities that enable them to strategically combine multiple sources of knowledge to support cognition and decision making. Humans excel at learning and exploiting latent structures in sequential sensorimotor tasks. Here we test the hypothesis that the basal ganglia play a critical role in this process by combining computational modeling and neurophysiological recordings in patients undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery. We recorded local field potentials from the subthalamic nucleus and scalp EEG while subjects performed a serial reaction time task that contained an embedded repeating sequence. Computational simulations show that basal ganglia circuits can discover repeating patterns in sequences through reinforcement learning. Local field potential recordings reveal that beta-band power decreases when the task contains a repeating pattern relative to a random pattern. Beta desynchronization is strongest when the repeating pattern is first learned, and its magnitude predicts subsequent performance benefits.

Only one previous study has investigated functional brain networks as measured using functional MRI (fMRI) after prolonged AAS use. Using a seed-based approach targeting amygdala connectivity, it was found that resting-state coupling between the right amygdala and frontal, striatal, limbic, hippocampal, and visual cortical areas, respectively, was significantly lower in 7 users compared to 9 non-users (Kaufman et al., 2015). Further, a recent meta-analysis of fMRI activation studies revealed significant amygdala foci both after testosterone administration and in endogenous testosterone studies (Heany et al., 2016), and higher endogenous testosterone levels have been linked to attenuated resting-state amygdala-prefrontal coupling in adolescents (Peters et al., 2015), and in healthy males during a social approach-avoidance task (Volman et al., 2011), and intranasal testosterone reduced amygdala coupling with the orbitofrontal cortex in females (van Wingen et al., 2011). Supraphysiological doses of AAS may cause apoptotic effects on a variety of cell types including neurons (Basile et al., 2013; Caraci et al., 2011; Cunningham et al., 2009; Estrada et al., 2006; Orlando et al., 2007). In an overlapping sample, prolonged AAS use was associated with smaller gray matter, cortical and putamen volumes and thinner cortex, with stronger effects with increasing exposure, also in users without any other substance abuse (Bjornebekk et al., 2016). Summarized, converging evidence suggests that prolonged AAS use with supraphysiological doses is associated with both structural and functional brain alterations. However, available neuroimaging studies of AAS users are rare and limited by small samples sizes. The aim of the current study was to test the effects of sustained AAS use on resting-state functional connectivity in a sample of male long-term AAS users and non-users. After rigorous denoising of the individual datasets to minimize the impact of motion and other artifacts, spatial maps constituting the nodes in the functional brain network and their associated time-series were estimated using spatial group independent component analysis (ICA) and dual regression. We defined the brain connectivity indices as the between-node partial temporal correlations, yielding a node-by-node correlation matrix for each dataset, where each node pair is referred to as an edge in the network. Next, we tested for associations between AAS status (current user, previous user or control) and connectivity strength using edgewise analysis. In order to further characterize the clinical sensitivity, we tested for associations with AAS dependency, lifetime exposure and AAS cycle state (on vs. off). Since elevated testosterone to epitestosterone (T/E) ratio may indicate use of testosterone, we tested for associations between connectivity and T/E ratios in the full sample (n = 142). Based on existing evidence reviewed above, we anticipated that discriminative connections would implicate regions according to the anatomical distribution of androgen receptors, including the amygdala, hippocampus, and brain stem, and their synchronization with cortical nodes (Kritzer, 2004; Pomerantz et al., 1985; Simerly et al., 1990).

These theoretical constructs serve not merely as academic abstractions; rather, they form the linchpin for practical applications and operational best practices within the industry. As hydraulic fracturing evolves, practitioners increasingly rely on a symbiosis of empirical data and theoretical frameworks to optimize performance and minimize environmental impact (Bour et al., 2016). The implementation of advanced monitoring technologies, such as microseismic monitoring and downhole sensors, allows engineers to glean real-time insights into fracture behavior and fluid migration patterns. This data, coupled with refined mathematical modeling, leads to a more precise understanding of how fractures propagate through heterogeneous geological formations and how they interact with natural stresses present in the subsurface environment (Jaeger et al., 2007). Additionally, the characterisation of fracturing fluid compositions now includes a plethora of biodegradable surfactants and proppants tailored to enhance conductivity and operational resilience. The optimization of these chemical formulations is pivotal in ensuring that the fluid dynamics within the fracture system promote sustained hydrocarbon flow without contributing to long-lasting environmental detriment (Kutasov et al., 2015). In light of the increasing scrutiny surrounding environmental stewardship, the industry has begun to embrace a paradigm shift towards greener methodologies, which involves rigorous risk assessments and compliance with regulatory frameworks meant to safeguard groundwater resources and mitigate surface water contamination. Recent advancements in computational power and algorithmic innovations have propelled the field of hydraulic fracturing simulation forward, allowing for the creation of detailed three-dimensional models that capture the intricate interplay between hydraulic fracturing processes and the geomechanical behavior of the reservoir (Raghavan et al., 2018). These models incorporate aspects of geomechanics, hydrology, and fracture mechanics, thus offering a holistic view of the subsurface landscape. The burgeoning field of machine learning is also making inroads, providing avenues to predict fracture performance based on historical data analyses, unlocking previously unimagined efficiencies in hydraulic fracturing operations (Eidsvik et al., 2019). The significance of integrating geological models with fracture propagation simulations cannot be overstated. Understanding the lithological variations and subsurface stress distributions allows for a tailored approach to fracturing design, optimizing the network of fractures to maximize contact with hydrocarbon resources (Wang et al., 2020). Moreover, the importance of quantifying the mechanical properties of reservoir rock cannot be overlooked, as variations in Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio directly affect fracture initiation and propagation-parameters that are vital in predicting operational outcomes. Simultaneously, the adoption of real-time data feedback mechanisms has forged new pathways in adaptive hydraulic fracturing techniques, where operators can modify fracturing parameters on-the-fly to respond to evolving reservoir conditions (Peirce et al., 2016). This responsiveness enhances operational resilience, promoting sustainability within extraction processes, while reducing the inherent uncertainties associated with fixed fracturing designs. As the landscape of hydraulic fracturing continues to mature, the emphasis on a holistic, data-informed approach will undoubtedly pave the way for advanced methodologies that challenge conventional paradigms. The integration of multidisciplinary insights-from geoscience to engineering and environmental science-will ultimately dictate the trajectory of hydraulic fracturing practices, shaping the industry's ability to harness energy resources responsibly and sustainably for future generations. In summary, the evolution of hydraulic fracturing exemplifies a critical convergence of technology, science, and policy designed to adapt to the multifaceted challenges that lie ahead.

We and others have shown that CA2 neurons display spatial properties, including firing in place fields, and that place fields are remapped with various manipulations to the animal's context (Alexander et al., 2016; Lee, Wang, Deshmukh, & Knierim, 2015; Lu, Igarashi, Witter, Moser, & Moser, 2015; Mankin, Diehl, Sparks, Leutgeb, & Leutgeb, 2015). In addition, mice lacking the GTP-ase activating protein Regulator of G-Protein Signaling 14 (RGS14), a protein that is highly enriched in CA2 pyramidal cells (PCs), learn faster than wild-types (WTs) in the Morris water maze test of spatial memory (Lee et al., 2010). In these RGS14 knock-out (KO) mice, CA2 PCs have increased excitability and a capacity for LTP at synapses in the CA2 stratum radiatum, where LTP normally does not occur (Lee et al., 2010; Zhao, Choi, Obrietan, & Dudek, 2007). These findings further support a role for CA2 neurons in contextual memory. In addition, CA2 neurons project both within the same coronal plane and in the caudal/posterior direction, targeting CA1 neurons in both dorsal and intermediate to ventral CA1 (Tamamaki et al., 1988). As such, CA2 neurons may transmit contextual information from the dorsal hippocampus to more ventral CA1. Ventral CA1 neurons, in turn, project to amygdala and mPFC (Jay & Witter, 1991; Kishi, Tsumori, Yokota, & Yasui, 2006). Although it is unknown how CA2 neuronal activity affects the amygdala, we previously found that modifying CA2 neuronal activity can influence mPFC activity. Therefore, CA2 neuronal activity is capable of influencing neuronal activity of more ventral CA1, as well as at least one target area of ventral CA1 neurons (Alexander et al., 2018; Meira et al., 2018). In addition, CA2 neurons project to CA3 (Mercer, Trigg, & Thomson, 2007) and gate the communication between CA3 and CA1 (Alexander et al., 2018; Boehringer et al., 2017; Kohara et al., 2014). Accordingly, chemogenetic modification of CA2 neuron activity inversely influences sharp wave ripple (SWR) occurrence in both dorsal and ventral CA1, likely by affecting CA3 output to CA1 (Alexander et al., 2018; Boehringer et al., 2017). Interestingly, dorsal and ventral hippocampal CA1 neurons fire together during SWRs (Patel, Schomburg, Berenyi, Fujisawa, & Buzsaki, 2013), and neuronal activity is modulated in a subset of basolateral amygdala (BLA) neurons by SWRs recorded in dorsal CA1, providing a link between dorsal hippocampus and BLA through ventral hippocampus during SWRs (Girardeau et al., 2017). Further, in animals exposed to an aversive stimulus in one area of a linear track, BLA neuron modulation is greater during population SWRs that include place cell reactivation encoding the aversive area and trajectory of the track (Girardeau et al., 2017), which may reflect consolidation of a contextual fear memory. In sum, CA2 neurons transmitting contextual information could connect dorsal hippocampus to more ventral hippocampus, possibly by regulating SWRs to provide a link from dorsal hippocampus to the BLA. As such, CA2 neuronal activity may play a role in context fear conditioning.

As the boy scurried to collect his stray coins he saw one quarter roll toward Mr. Novak who nonchalantly placed a wingtip shoe over the coin. Kenny looked up at the man. "Why aren't you in school?" Mr. Novak said. "S-schools not till next week," Kenny said. The boy stood up accepting the fact that his quarter was no longer his. He counted out eighty-nine cents on the glass counter then put the remainder of his money back into his pocket. Mr. Petersen pushed the coins off the edge of the counter; the coins fell into his hand. "Thanks, Kenny. Say ahia to your mom for me." "Okay," Kenny said. He picked up his bag of goodies. He glared at the coin thief as he left the store. "Enjoying the beautiful day, Mr. Novak? Mr. Petersen said. "I'll have some of your overpriced candy." The confectioner laughed. "Give me four of those," Mr. Novak said, pointing at a glass jar filled with miniature peanut butter cups. "That's all." While Mr. Petersen scooped four peanut butter cups out of the glass jar Mr. Novak crouched to retrieve his ill-gotten gain. "That'll be twenty-one cents please." Mr. Petersen folded the top of the paper sack and handed it to his grumpy customer. Mr. Novak paid for his treat with Kenny's quarter. The old cash register clanged and its drawer opened. "Four cents is your change," Mr. Petersen placed four pennies in the center of Mr. Novak's palm. "Thanks, have a wonderful day." The tinkling of the silver bell was Mr. Novak's reply. Mr. Novak popped a peanut butter cup into his mouth as he watched the traffic pass by. He rolled the candy wrapper into a tight ball and flicked it into the street. He savored the tasty blend of chocolate and peanut butter as he watched the wrapper fall between the slats of a storm drain. A glint of light caught Mr. Novak's attention. He stooped to get a better look into the drain. His bushy eyebrows lifted in surprise when he saw the arc of a golden coin protruding from the debris-riddled sand below. He noted the close proximity of the Coinucopia to the storm drain. His heart rate accelerated as he imagined some poor schmuck unknowingly dropping the coin. In his mind's eye he saw the coin roll across the sidewalk and fall into the storm drain. That's his tough luck, thought Mr. Novak.

His gaze barely lifted from the untouched tray, a flicker of acknowledgment passing through his eyes. "Hello," he replied, his voice thin, as if carried on a whisper from another world. I stepped into the room, observing the cluttered space that seemed to mirror the turmoil of his thoughts. A few photographs adorned the bedside table, their edges frayed and colors faded, yet they radiated stories of love and laughter long past. "How's your day going?" I inquired, hoping to ignite a spark of conversation. But John's eyes turned back to the mushy potatoes on his plate, his expression distant, as though he were gazing into the recesses of memories that brought him joy. "It's... fine," he muttered, still not meeting my gaze. "Just fine?" I prodded gently, "Have you had any visitors today?" My curiosity was genuine; I always sought to connect, to remind these souls that they were more than their pain and their illness. He sighed, a sound that resonated with a weight of loneliness. "My daughter came by this morning but had to leave for work. She's busy, you know? A single mom, can't blame her." His voice faltered, and I could see unspilled tears pooling in the corners of his eyes. "I'm okay, though. Just... tired." The room was thick with silence, punctured only by the distant beeping of machines and the murmurs of nurses passing by. In that moment, my own aches faded to the background, replaced with an intense desire to buoy this man's spirit. "Would you like a bit of a chat? I could tell you about my day, some funny stories..." I attempted, my words coming out warmer than I had intended, a lifeline thrown into turbulent waters. His gaze finally lifted to meet mine, and the corners of his mouth quirked upward, not quite a smile, but a recognition that perhaps he was not being as isolated as he felt. "You're a volunteer, right?" he asked, a spark of curiosity igniting amid his melancholy. "Yeah! I come here to brighten up someone's day, and I figured why not start with you?" I responded, eager yet gentle. "It gets a bit dreary in here, huh?" Slowly, he nodded, tentative at first, then with a mix of nostalgia and warmth. "You remind me of my younger self. Always trying to make others laugh, push through the dreariness." And just like that, we began to talk-two souls sharing the weight of their existence, lost moments picked from the tangled web of life. I told him about my childhood escapades, the antics that had once rolled off my tongue with great fervor. Laughter began to unfold between us-soft at first, then growing stronger, filling the room with the sweet nectar of shared stories. As the minutes turned into an hour, I watched the life return to his eyes-a light that had long seemed extinguished. In that sacred space, his burdens felt lighter, shared between us like a breath of fresh air. Indeed, this was where meaning burgeoned; a simple connection amidst the machinery of life and the chaos of our individual struggles. A reminder that we are all intricately woven into the fabric of one another's journeys. And perhaps that is how we craft a life devoid of regret, one kindness, one shared laugh at a time.

It was a form of masquerade that, tragically, allowed him to continue his heinous appetite for violence, this time without the physical restraints of prison bars. By day, he donned the facade of a reformed author and journalist, but when the sun sank below the horizon, the darkness within him ignited. He returned to his predatory behavior, preying on vulnerable women-often sex workers who roamed the streets of Vienna in search of clients. As he navigated the city's nightlife, under the pretense of being a compassionate writer eager to understand the lives of those he chose to enslave, he reveled in his double life.
