His reign of terror escalated, leading to the death of several young women, culminating in a string of murders that would chart an undeniable pattern. For investigators, the challenge was not merely stopping a killer but tracing the elusive threads binding these tragedies together. The Austrian police were faced with a chilling reality; the very same man who had been celebrated for his literary work was the lethal figure behind the cruelest of atrocities. Yet Jack cunningly evaded suspicion, using his notoriety to cloak himself in safety. In an insidious twist of fate, Jack was invited to cover the very stories that danced around his own crimes; the irony was palpable. Euler's circle, a complex network of guests and victims alike, fed into the narrative he spun-spurred by the belief that he had turned a page on his past. But his demons remained, lurking just out of sight, waiting for the night to cloak their insatiable hunger again. As each body was discovered, panic swelled within the community. The media surged with reports and features on the so-called Vienna Woods Killer, a moniker that sent shivers down the spine of every woman after dark. The police struggled, grappling with the chilling reality that they were dealing not just with a murderer, but a man skilled in both manipulation and evasion-a man no longer bound by the chains of his past. As a chilling pattern emerged, the search for Jack Unterweger was only just beginning, intertwining societal fascination with his artistry amid the horrors he orchestrated. And yet, beneath the veneer of respectability and charm, the truth was becoming increasingly gruesome and undeniable.

Soon his income was insufficient to meet his expenses. Speculation on the Stock Exchange seemed to him to be a quicker road to fortune than a slow-going profession. So this man, morally weak though physically brave, not having the courage to curtail his extravagances, hurried blindly to his destruction. He gambled and lost all his own property; for ill-luck ever pursued him. Even then it was not too late to redeem his position. But he was too great a coward to look his difficulties in the face; therefore, having the temptation to commit so terribly easy a crime ever before him in his office, he began - first, timidly, to a small extent; then wildly, in panic, in order to retrieve his losses - to speculate with the moneys entrusted to him by his clients. He pawned their securities; he forged their names; he plunged ever deeper into crime - and all in vain. When it was too late, he swore to himself, in the torments of his remorse, that if he could but once win back sufficient to replace the sums he had stolen, he would cut down all his expenses, forswear gambling and dishonesty, and stick to his profession. At last it came to this. He sold his yacht and everything else he possessed of value. He realised what remained of the securities under his charge, and then placed the entire sum as cover on a certain stock, the price of which, he was told, was certain to rise. The "bloodhounds" had begun to track their prey. Rounding up, with a skill born of long practice, they drove the diggers before them towards the centre of the Flat. Here they passed from group to group and from hole to hole, calling for the production of licences with an insolence that made its object see red. They were nice of scent, too, and, nine times in ten, pounced on just those unfortunates who, through carelessness, or lack of means, or on political grounds, had failed to take out the month's licence to dig for gold. Every few minutes one or another was marched off between two constables to the Government Camp, for fine or imprisonment. Now it was that it suddenly entered Long Jim's head to cut and run. Up till now he had stood declaring himself a free-born Briton, who might be drawn and quartered if he ever again paid the blasted tax. But, as the police came closer, a spear of fright pierced his befuddled brain, and inside a breath he was off and away. Had the abruptness of his start not given him a slight advantage, he would have been caught at once. As it was, the chase would not be a long one; the clumsy, stiff-jointed man slithered here and stuck fast there, dodging obstacles with an awkwardness that was painful to see. He could be heard sobbing and cursing as he ran. At this point the Commissioner, half turning, signed to the troopers in his rear. Six or seven of them shook up their bridles and rode off, their scabbards clinking, to prevent the fugitive's escape. A howl of contempt went up from the crowd. The pink and white subaltern made what was almost a movement of the arm to intercept his superior's command. It was too much for Long Jim's last mate, the youthful blackbeard who had pluckily descended the shaft after the accident. He had been standing on a mound with a posse of others, following the man-hunt. At his partner's crack-brained dash for the open, his snorts of indignation found words. "Gaw-blimy!... is the old fool gone dotty?" Then he drew a whistling breath. "No, it's more than flesh and blood.... Stand back, boys!" And though he was as little burdened with a licence as the man under pursuit, he shouted: "Help, help!... for God's sake, don't let 'em have me!" shot down the slope, and was off like the wind. His foxly object was attained. The attention of the hunters was diverted. Long Jim, seizing the moment, vanished underground.

Such a high-sounding title as predestination, seems to lose much of its potent charm when we take an interesting existence into our hands, to dissect it, and analyse it, and reduce it to a rational origin. Like decades of heterogeneous pearls, a human career with all its varied details, glides through the fingers of the moral anatomist, each fraction standing out by itself, suggesting its own real or relative importance, yet associating itself ever with the rest, making of the whole a more or less intricate, and, at best, a very uneven chain. When we consider that all the bewildering throng around and about us have evolved into their present conditions of misery or joy from a passive and innocent babyhood, we are mystified and awe-stricken; there is so much inequality among the lots and portions of the children of men, that it comes strangely home to us in our reverie, to realize that the starting-point is, for one and all, the great and the lowly, one and the same. In its cradle, or on its mother's breast, the human creature knows no special individuality, but when the rails of the cradle have been climbed over, and the first foot-print stamped unaided upon the "sands of time," a distinct personality has been established, which is the embodiment of possible, probable, or uncertain influences - a personality which grows and thrives upon internal stimulants administered by an expanding mind and heart, and which leans almost entirely for support upon the external accidents of fate or fortune that may come in its way. Were we as thoroughly penetrated with this conviction as we should be, how different would be the issues of many human careers? Could we accustom ourselves to meditate upon this truth as seriously as we would upon a religious one, to examine our conscience from it as from a reliable standpoint every day of our lives, what a flood of sympathy and Christian charity would be let loose upon the social world from converted hearts? When men and women will thoroughly understand the strange and intimate frame-work of human society, the wail of the pessimist will be soothed and hushed forever: for then will they realize how dependent we poor mortals are upon each other for sorrows or joys: then will it be plain to them that no human life, however obscure, however trifling, is an unfeeling thing, apart from every other, outside the daily contact of every other. Ah! we think, that God's creation, in all its grandeur and unrivalled beauty, would be little worth, to a creature born to live and enjoy it alone: and the infinite Wisdom decreed otherwise, when it gave unto man a friend and companion in the first moments of his existence; but is the world less desolate, less empty to a million hearts, because a million others inhabit it as well?

Some of the most famous names in cricket have played in Ashes Test matches - but there are some which are synonymous with this particular battle. One of those is Ian Botham, widely regarded as England's biggest Ashes hero having had a Test series named after him. "Botham's Ashes" which took place in 1981, produced one of the most spectacular moments ever witnessed in an Ashes series. After resigning as captain just days earlier following an opening Test defeat, England were on the cusp of going 2-0 down in the series. A dismal start to the second Test at Headingley left Australia tantalizingly close to victory - but Botham's heroics defied all the odds. An unbeaten 149 from 148 deliveries gave England hope, forcing Australia to score 130 to win the match. But the tourists only managed 111 - handing the victory to England, which eventually went on to win the series. Australia dominated between 1989 and 2003 - winning eight consecutive series. The undisputed team of the decade in the 1990s and early 2000s, Australia boasted several world class players such as Shane Warne, Glenn McGrath, Ricky Ponting and brothers Steve and Mark Waugh. Then there was wicketkeeper Adam Gilchrist, who scored the second fastest century in Test match cricket during Australia's 5-0 whitewash of England in 2006-7. But Australia's and indeed the world's greatest ever batsman, is widely acknowledged to have been Donald Bradman. 'The Don' scored 5,028 runs in Ashes contests during his career from 1928-1948 and finished with an average of 99.94. Australia have also dominated with the ball with Warne the leading wicket taker in Ashes cricket with 195, while McGrath claimed an impressive 157. Recent history. While, England might be favorites to win this series, it's important to realize it wasn't always this way. When the 2005 series came to England, Australia was hoping to win its ninth consecutive Ashes series. A routine victory in the opening Test appeared to confirm its status as favorite before a narrow two-run defeat at Edgbaston drew England level. A crucial England victory at Trent Bridge in the fourth Test, coming in between two drawn games, gave the host nation its first series win since 1989. It was the series which introduced Kevin Pietersen to the world stage and led to Andrew Flintoff establishing himself as favorite with cricket fans across the world. Flintoff's 24 wickets and 402 runs were integral to England's success. But his next venture did not go so smoothly as he captained England during its tortuous 5-0 whitewash defeat in Australia in 2006/7. That result left a huge scar on English cricket as Australia humiliated its rival in ruthless fashion.

Their courtship, fittingly, was a theatrical affair. Sinden, with his customary flair, would woo Diana with sonorous soliloquies, each word meticulously enunciated, turning every declaration of affection into a masterpiece of language. It wasn't long before they married in 1948, forming a partnership both on and off the stage that would last until her passing in 2004. His early career was filled with an eclectic array of roles in repertory theatre. He thrived in the vibrant post-war London scene, where his deep, plummy voice and distinct presence quickly became hallmarks. Audiences were captivated by his ability to switch from the comedic to the dramatic with seamless versatility. In 1953, he joined the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre (later known as the Royal Shakespeare Company), where he honed his skills alongside contemporaries who would all go on to leave indelible marks on the world stage. Sinden's transition to film was equally impressive. He starred in a string of successful British comedies during the 1950s and 60s, becoming a household name. His performances in movies like "Doctor in the House" and "Mogambo" solidified his status as a leading man capable of melding charm with gravitas. Nevertheless, it was his stage work that remained closest to his heart. He often returned to the theatre, reveling in the immediacy of live performance and the connection it brought with an audience. Television also played a significant role in his career. By the 1970s, Sinden was a familiar face on the small screen, starring in series such as "Never the Twain" where his comedic timing and booming delivery were always on display. Despite his success in multiple mediums, Sinden remained resolute in his dedication to the craft of acting, ever critical of those who he felt disregarded the beauty of language. Off the stage and screen, Sinden's interests were manifold. He maintained a profound affinity for architectural exploration, spending countless hours documenting the intricate designs of England's historic churches. This pursuit not only satisfied his intellectual curiosity but provided a peaceful counterbalance to the fervor of his acting life. Publicly, Sinden was never one to mince words. His disdain for linguistic sloppiness was legendary; he lamented the degradation of the English tongue with an almost Churchillian fervor. Yet, those who knew him intimately spoke warmly of his generosity, wit, and unyielding devotion to his family and friends. In his later years, accolades continued to pour in, a testament to a life rich with achievement and the respect he commanded across the industry. When asked about his secret to longevity, Sinden, ever the raconteur, would quip, "It's all about keeping the syllables in check." Even as age crept upon him, his voice never lost its luster, nor did his passion for performing diminish. Sir Donald Sinden's legacy endures, not only through his extensive body of work but in the echoes of his orations that continue to inspire emerging thespians. As the curtain falls on an illustrious career, the English language stands a little taller for having been articulated by such a devoted custodian.

To catch peach orchards and trees in full bloom, time your drive to late spring or early summer. Where to stop: Hundreds of roadside stands that begin filling with fruit in early June. If a twig snapped, or there was a rustling noise in the underbrush, she was ready in an instant to fling fresh dry sticks on the fire and make it glow red against the black opening of the cave. She knew that no wild animal, however fierce and hungry, would dare come near the leaping flames. Yet watchful as she was, she did not see two children who were creeping stealthily toward her, over the great rocks which sheltered the mouth of the cave. They were a boy and a girl, and from their size they must have been about eight years old. They both had bright twinkling eyes and flaming red hair, and were dressed alike in skins of red foxes of almost the same colour. You could tell at a glance that they were twins, but it would have puzzled any one to tell whether they were both boys or both girls, or one of each kind. They came down over the rocks so quietly that not even the quick ears of the old woman heard the faintest sound. When they had almost reached the ground, they stopped, and at the same instant opened their mouths and howled exactly like two young wolves! The noise was so sudden and so near that the old woman never thought of her fire at all. She simply screamed and fell right over backwards into the cave. Then she rolled over and scuttled on all fours out of sight in the darkness as fast as she could go. The acorns from her lap flew in every direction and rolled down the hillside. The boy and girl jumped to the ground, shrieking with laughter. In a moment the old woman was back again in the door of the cave. She had a stout stick in her hand and she looked very angry. She shook the stick at the Twins and scolded them so fast that the sound of it was like the chattering of an angry squirrel in a tree-top. Now, of course, I cannot tell you just the words she used, but, translated into English, this is what she said: - "You horrid little catamounts, if I catch you, I'll teach you better manners! I'll give you such a taste of this stick that you'll not need more till the river runs dry." The Twins sprang up, still shrieking with laughter, and danced about the fire just out of reach of the woman's stick. "But you can't catch us," they screamed. Their red locks of hair flew about in the wind as they danced, until it looked almost as if red flames were bursting from their heads. The old woman glared at them helplessly. "Dance away," she cried, "dance away, you red-headed rascals! I shan't need to put sticks on the fire while you are here. Your red hair would scare away the sabre-toothed tiger himself!

Getting to know the Thompson clan isn't merely a matter of transcription; it becomes a deep dive into a culture that is, while sometimes brash and exuberant, unequivocally human. In the midst of nonstop shenanigans, there are heartfelt moments enveloped in humorous dialogue that requires vigilance to capture adequately. "It's not just about technicalities; it's about preserving the essence of who they are. Their laughter, their quirks, the way they transition seamlessly from one shouting match to a teary-eyed reconciliation - that's what we strive to encapsulate," Reddy notes with a glimmer of passion in her eyes. It becomes increasingly clear that her role transcends mere transcription; she is, in a way, a custodian of these fleeting anecdotes of everyday life on reality television. Observing the Thompsons during filming is delightful chaos. The family, often submerged in their own joyous pandemonium, juggles everything from spaghetti dinners to spontaneous dance parties. The frenetic pace ebbs and flows; a non-linear blend of rapid-fire dialogue peppered with dramatic pauses. "You never quite know where the next punchline is going to come from," she recalls, fondly shaking her head. The unpredictability is exhilarating, yet capturing it all succinctly, with the accuracy that audiences require, demands skill and an inherently adaptable mindset. To ensure no golden moment goes undocumented, Reddy often parks herself next to the sound engineers monitoring each comedic spat. "We use an array of high-tech gear to try to capture the nuances in the audio. It's an all-hands-on-deck situation," she explains. "Every muffled comment, every excited screech must be cataloged for posterity - it would be tragic to miss a gem." These gems, the warbling exchanges interspersed with contagious laughter, become central components of episodic storytelling. Beyond successful transcription, working with this eccentric family fosters a strange kinship for Reddy. It's not just about professional respect; it's more like protective camaraderie. "They may live in their bubble, but every week I'm immersed with them, piecing together the fabric of their lives. There's a warmth by the end of it - it feels like family," she reflects with a tenderness only the sternest of producers might reserve for a kindred spirit. Yet with friendship comes an acute awareness of responsibility. "I'm always conscious that I'm the one who decides how they come across to the rest of the world. Despite the ridiculousness, the family deserves fairness; there is authenticity in their affection that must shine through no matter how absurd the scene." In this peculiar dance of transcription and entertainment, Reddy deftly embraces the duality of her role, becoming both a vigilant chronicler and a steadfast supporter of the Thompson family's vibrant narrative. Each episode serves as an entry point into a reality that, while at times ludicrous, holds a mirror to the joyful - and often messy - tapestry of human life.

Additionally, the role of habit and routine in shaping route choice has been explored, highlighting the importance of considering the influence of past experiences and learned behaviours on current decision-making (Garling and Axhausen, 2003). Furthermore, the increasing availability of data from various sources, including GPS tracking, social media, and mobile devices, has enabled researchers to develop more sophisticated and data-driven approaches to route choice modelling. For example, machine learning algorithms have been applied to large datasets to identify patterns and relationships between route choices and various attributes, such as traffic conditions, time of day, and weather (Toole et al., 2015). These approaches have the potential to provide more accurate and dynamic models of route choice, which can be used to inform transportation planning and policy decisions. Despite these advances, there are still significant challenges to overcome in route choice modelling. One of the main limitations is the lack of data on the cognitive and psychological processes underlying route choice, which makes it difficult to develop models that accurately capture the complexities of human decision-making. Moreover, the increasing complexity of route choice models can make them difficult to interpret and apply in practice. Therefore, there is a need for further research that integrates insights from multiple disciplines, including transportation studies, spatial cognition, and behavioural geography, to develop more comprehensive and realistic models of route choice. Another area of research that has received increasing attention in recent years is the impact of new transportation technologies, such as autonomous vehicles and ride-sharing services, on route choice behaviour. These technologies have the potential to significantly alter the way people travel, and understanding how they will affect route choice is crucial for transportation planning and policy decisions. For example, research has shown that the availability of real-time traffic information and ride-sharing services can influence route choice and travel mode (Liu et al., 2017), and that autonomous vehicles may lead to changes in route choice patterns and travel behaviour (Fagnant and Kockelman, 2018). In conclusion, the study of route choice is a complex and multidisciplinary field that requires the integration of insights from transportation studies, spatial cognition, and behavioural geography. While significant advances have been made in recent years, there are still many challenges to overcome, including the need for more data on the cognitive and psychological processes underlying route choice and the impact of new transportation technologies on route choice behaviour. So far, Google+ doesn't have anything like Twitter's trending topics (although it has a "What's Hot" stream that's a click or tap away for users) or Facebook's sponsored stories. When asked if we might someday see similar features introduced in Google+, Gundotra wouldn't say, but his change in manner betrays a disdain for how Google's competitors incorporate advertising. I remember my right leg cramped from sudden activity after hours of sitting, but I didn't care. I kept pushing. As I rode, I cried. I got thirsty, and had no water bottle with me so I stopped at a diner owned by my former best friends' family. Their father was glad to see me. He gave me a soda and let me sit for a few since I was red in the face and out of breathe. The fifties nostalgia diner was sea foam green and white, with splotches of pink and coca-cola signs everywhere. I drank down my coke, listening to the jukebox playing, "Daniela by Elton John. "Daniel is leaving tonight on a plane. I can see the red taillightsa.and I can see Daniel waving goodbye Lord it looks like Daniel. Must be the clouds in my eyes." I sat there, my eyes still stinging with tears, and I let my father die. I closed my eyes and I saw the future. My father's funeral, the hundreds of people turning out to say what a brilliant sun of a bitch he was, my immediate family in pain, and my extended family squabbling over everything from the will to the way the priest conducted himself. My siblingsa weddings, occurring in my mind over the next five years, without my father there to make sure the functions happened according to his traditions. My mother in whitea.lots and lots of white. White is such a hard color to clean. I understood then why Hindus wore white as the mourning color. With white, on dusty roads, you must be aware of yourself. You must always be conscious of what you are wearing. You must be careful every time you eat or drink. You never forget the person who died. I saw my high school graduation, my college graduation and every other milestone in my life. I saw the probability of moving to Texas to be closer to more extended family, or Washington DC for the same reason. I saw my mother working. I saw us losing the house I grew up in, or selling it to help my sister pay for graduate school. I saw me and my mother in a cramped apartment in downtown Buffalo. I saw all of this, and I decided it was ok. I resigned myself to the idea that my father was going to die. I gave up on him. I left the diner, after thanking Mr. Harrishburg for the soda, and headed out again. Once again pushing my legs hard, feeling the pain and pushing for more. I whipped past the houses of friends who had known me since the day I was born. I stopped and rang their doorbell, hoping to get a game of catch out of them, or at least a drink of water. No one was home. The tears stopped. I felt empty. I had accepted my father's death, and the inevitability that came with it.

A couple weeks ago, he took home a 4-month-old red chow. The public can also visit dogs in the less flashy kennel rooms. The 22 "kennel runs," each four feet wide and 14 feet long, are significantly larger than standard shelter cages. At the opposite end of the shelter are the individual cat "condos" and three cat "cotillions" - large rooms with open drawers, cubbyholes and climbing poles, where as many as 10 cats live and people can visit. All details are designed to bring out the best in the animals. The floors are soft, waterproof epoxy-finished surfaces and the ceilings are sound-absorbent. The cacophony typical of kennels not only is unpleasant for people but also hurts the animals (dogs can hear frequencies more than 20 kHz higher than humans; cats, more than 45 kHz higher). "When a dog is in pain from the sound, that elevates the stress level," says Emerson Hughes, owner of Holiday Barn Pet Resorts and former chairman of the Richmond SPCA board, who oversaw the project. Although the creature comforts are as much for visitors, Deisler says Mozart really does soothe the savage beast - or confused puppy. In a study conducted at Queen's University in Belfast, psychologists found that heavy-metal music increased anxiety in dogs and caused barking, while classical music alleviated stress and quieted barking. The shelter's classical music is digitally altered to put a damper on the ultrahigh and low frequencies. "If they are too stressed out, that reduces their immune system and that leads to them being sick, and if they are sick we can't adopt them," says Deisler. But what an adoring public sees and hears in the adoption area is just a small part of the center. Only about a quarter of the animals are available for adoption at any one time. The rest are being rehabbed. Behind the scenes, every animal gets a physical and behavioral checkup. Dogs with contagious diseases - like Raspie, a 4-year-old Sheltie with kennel cough - are confined to the Physical Rehab Room for treatment. Staff experts work with personality problems in the Behavioral Rehab Room. Even healthy animals get a three-day adjustment period to acclimate to shelter life. As mentioned above, these general trends are modulated by many parameters such as temperature, discharge, organic carbon content, and the residence time in the riverbank (Massmann et al., 2006; Rauch-Williams et al., 2010; Storck et al., 2012). Recently, organic compounds that have substantial persistence (freshwater half-life >40 days according to REACH definition) and mobility characteristics (log Doc (organic carbon water distribution coefficient) < 4.5 between pH 4-10) to be transported through natural and urban barriers and reach sources of drinking water have been defined as PMOCs (persistent and mobile organic chemicals) and have received more attention (Arp et al., 2017). In general, information on vertical and lateral transport of MPs within surface waters and from surface water into aquifers is scarce. Only few studies have been conducted to evaluate the natural attenuation potential of selected MPs in different aquifer types. For example, the attenuation potential of a rapidly recharging karst aquifer in southern Germany with short residence times was investigated using waste-water specific tracers (Hillebrand et al. 2012, 2015). High attenuation rates with degradation half-lives ranging from 37 h to 90 h were obtained for atenolol, caffeine, ibuprofen, and paracetamol, depicting the high degradability of these compounds. The fate of MPs in the hyporheic zone and the influence of temperature and redox potential on attenuation was also studied at an eutrophic lowland stream (Lewandowski et al., 2011) and a sediment core in the laboratory (Burke et al., 2014). Except for benzotriazole and carbamazepine remaining persistent, degradation rates decreased from warm to cold and oxic to manganese reducing conditions in the laboratory experiments. In another bench scaled flume experiment designed to study hyporheic processes (Li et al., 2015), transformation products (TPs) were detected which were only formed in the sediment but released to the water, hinting at secondary contamination with TPs (Writer et al., 2013). Kunkel and Radke (2012) provided a list of favourable attenuation conditions within rivers located in Central Europe and reported higher attenuation for sunny, dry weather periods during periods of low discharge. In comparison to the above mentioned studies, in Switzerland mostly aerobic conditions prevail in the aquifers, and groundwater usually contains less dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Hence, oxic, redox-independent conditions predominate RBF processes. As a consequence of the predominance of mainly alluvial gravel aquifers, RBF is often highly dynamic with short groundwater residence times. The growing number of river restoration projects that are conducted along Swiss rivers as modern flood protection measures and to achieve a "good ecological status" of rivers as required by the European Water Framework Directive (European Parliament, 2000) might further decrease the average residence times in RBF systems by removal of bank fixation and widening of the river (Schirmer et al., 2014). Swiss legislation for drinking water abstraction requires only a minimum subsurface residence time of 10 days, 5 times less than in the European Union, and about 30% of Swiss drinking water is produced at RBF sites.

With increasing availability of molecular phylogenies and genetic distances within and between populations, our understanding of the processes shaping the current diversity patterns of Drusinae has increased considerably during the last decade. However, many questions remain unresolved, such as the origin of several cryptic species complexes, the number of species hidden under the name Drusus discolor, the position of the monotypic genus Hadimina, the relationships between Monocentra and other Drusinae, or the true taxonomic status of the "subgenus" Leptodrusus. Here we present the first comprehensive molecular phylogeny of the subfamily Drusinae based on sequence data from five nuclear genes and three mitochondrial loci. We used the phylogenetic framework to evaluate the utility of currently applied morphological characters and to discuss possible adaptive radiations of feeding modes and habitat preferences. We sequenced five nuclear (CAD, EF1, ITS1+2, L10P, RpL32) and three mitochondrial markers (COI, COII, ND1) from 85 specimens representing 57 nominal taxa of Drusinae. Sequences were aligned using MAFFT v. 7 (Katoh and Standley, 2013) and edited manually in Mesquite v. 3.04 (Maddison and Maddison, 2011). Bayesian inference was conducted in MrBayes v. 3.2.2 (Ronquist et al., 2012) using four chains for each locus, 10000000 generations and sampling every 500 generations. We combined the results of separate analyses into a single tree file using LogCombiner v. 1.06 (Drummond and Rambaut, 2007) and visualized the result in FigTree v. 1.4.2 (Rambaut, 2009). Phylogenetic reconstruction The final dataset included sequences of 12 loci and 119 terminals (Suppl. material 1: Table S1). The total alignment length amounted to 8842 bp, out of which 163 bp were excluded due to ambiguous alignments and 102 bp were missing in at least one terminal. Our phylogenetic analysis resulted in a well-resolved topology with strong support values for almost all nodes (Fig. 1). All major clades received posterior probabilities (PP) > 95%. The inferred phylogeny corroborates the traditional classification of the subfamily, except for the placement of the monotypic genus Hadimina. It was placed within the genus Drusus as sister lineage to D. moravicus, thus supporting its inclusion into Drusinae. Moreover, our results confirm the validity of the genus Metanoea, which was synonymized with Drusus by Malicky (2002). The remaining two genera of Drusinae, Leptodrusus and Monocentra, could not be resolved as independent groups. Instead, they formed a polytomy together with the remaining members of Drusinae.

Of course, it's always been tough being a teenager. I remember well the shame of being the only girl in the class still wearing Clarks sandals, for example. But I wouldn't want to be a 14-year-old girl in 2015 for all the money in the world. Modern teens have it harder than ever. The pressure to fit in is so much greater. At least when I came home from school in the Seventies, I could escape from the mean-girl chorus of disapproval. But today - thanks to social media - there is no escape from the judgment of others. Today's teenagers don't come home from school and spend an hour on the sofa watching The Waltons. They are too busy sending images of themselves via the online photo-sharing app Snapchat to 50 of their closest friends. Daisy (right) thinks modern teens, like Lydia (left), have it 'harder than ever' with the constant pressures of social media. Lydia's phone is never silent; it cheeps, rings and bellows all day and all night long. At her age I was also in touch with my friends while at home - I used to spend hours on the phone dissecting the events of the day. But going through the minutiae of who said what to whom was a good deal less appealing with my brother and father listening in. For my daughter's generation, there are no such limits. As the person who pays her phone bill, I can see that there have been nights where she's been texting and 'chirpsing' (a kind of digital flirting or chatting up) way into the small hours, which horrifies me. Today's teens are also not restricted, as we were, to spending time with friends only in the flesh; you can have a virtual party with all your closest pals on Whatsapp - a messaging service - whenever you like. Worse, you can chat online with perfect strangers at any hour of the day or night. Daisy (right) is pictured here with her mother, Jocasta Innes (left) and her oldest daughter Ottilie in 1991. Daisy thinks even Ottilie had it easier as a teenager just ten years ago. The problem is that if you are feeling a little bit vulnerable, there is no escape from the feeling of being scrutinised. Of course, plenty of teenagers are supportive of each other, but there are plenty more who fasten on evidence of vulnerability like piranha fish on a gaping wound. Now that I'm at home, I realise just how much time my daughter has been spending in this parallel digital universe, and how badly it can affect her self-esteem. I also realise how hard it has been for her to come back to an empty house for years with nothing to do before her parents get back from work but bare her soul on social media. I have an older daughter, too - ten years older.

While the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) plays an essential role in maintaining order within the broadcasting realm, it finds itself straddling the line between regulation and potential overreach. The crux of the issue lies not only in what constitutes indecency but also in who delineates these boundaries. This brings us to the heart of the conversation: the protection versus restriction of content available to the masses. There exists a fundamental tension between ensuring public decency and protecting the unfettered exchange of ideas. It is vital to recognize that the airwaves are, in effect, public. They are not owned in a traditional sense; rather, they serve as a platform for dialogue and expression. Therefore, the question arises: should the government, through the FCC, wield such power to dictate what is offensive? The contention here hinges on the potential chilling effect that censorship may impose on free expression. Broadcasters, fearful of fines or sanctions, may self-censor, thereby leading to a homogenization of content that stifles diversity in thoughts, opinions, and ideas. Furthermore, the evolution of society's perceptions around decency begs for reassessment. Historical context matters; topics once deemed taboo may now be subjects of critical discussion and artistic exploration. Take, for instance, the evolution of discourse around race, sexuality, and mental health. These very topics, essential to societal growth and understanding, have historically faced censorship in various forms. To relegate these matters to a slipshod definition of indecency seems not only regressive but also detrimental to the progress we strive for as a society. Additionally, many argue that the current approach to indecency lacks nuance. The knee-jerk reactions to offending language or imagery often ignore the broader context. Sometimes, the very materials labeled indecent serve as catalysts for change or vehicles for necessary conversations. For example, a film that exposes systemic injustices may use provocative language or imagery, yet dismissing this art on the grounds of indecency risks negating its impactful message. Furthermore, consider the contrasting frameworks employed by platforms like cable television compared to traditional broadcasting. In cable, viewers often exercise choice, opting in or out of specific channels, suggesting that audiences can self-regulate their consumption of content. However, over-the-air broadcasters are, by nature, accessible to all, including minors. This raises profound questions about the responsibility of broadcasters to consider their content's susceptibility to a younger audience, yet inherently, it also points to parental responsibility in mediating what children consume. Arguments surrounding indecency must, therefore, engage with emerging media forms and societal shifts. The intertwining of digital platforms with traditional broadcasting complicates censorship further. As content increasingly flows across borders on the internet, the very definitions of indecent and acceptable may continue to blur, challenging the efficacy and justification of stringent regulations. Ultimately, the debate must reconcile the need for some form of accountability in broadcasting while preserving the sacred right to free expression enshrined in the Constitution. The necessity for standards should not precipitate the squandering of fundamental freedoms. Society thrives on the clash of ideas, the grappling with difficult subjects, and the ability to express dissent, even if that expression may sometimes offend the sensibilities of others. Policymakers must tread carefully, recognizing the delicate balance that must be struck between safeguarding the public interest and upholding the constitutional rights that form the foundation of American democracy; these rights are not simply privileges granted at the government's discretion but are intrinsic to the very fabric of a free society.

I attended webinars, joined design communities, and surrounded myself with talented designers whose passion was infectious. I consider myself a perpetual student, eager to drink in new knowledge, assimilate it, and then deliver it in a way that resonates with both designers and non-designers alike. Working closely with designers has been both a joy and an invaluable learning experience. I have this incredible opportunity to dive into their world and understand their challenges, triumphs, and visions. It could be the inspiration behind a sleek interface or the persistence required to navigate through a challenging project. By highlighting these narratives, I not only educate our readers but also ignite conversations and connections within the design community. These technologies are reshaping how designers work, offering new ways to visualize and implement creative ideas quickly and effectively. Designers are becoming more conscientious about their environmental impact, focusing on energy-efficient solutions, minimal waste, and even digital sustainability through less data-heavy interfaces. It's an inspiring shift as creatives around the globe strive to meld beauty with sustainability. Last but not least, storytelling through interactive media is capturing much attention. With technology evolving at breakneck speed, designers are exploring novel ways to engage users through immersive experiences. This trend adds an additional layer of interaction, making designs not only visually appealing but also experientially satisfying. In our blog, I aim to delve into these topics, providing our readers with both foresight and insight. By coupling innovative ideas with strategic guidance, we strive to nurture and inspire the design community, spurring growth and creativity. It's truly fulfilling to know that our work, the stories we tell, and the information we share resonate with our audience. My non-designer perspective, rather than being a hindrance, has allowed me to question assumptions, challenge conventions, and ultimately create a dynamic dialogue between design and writing. Being part of Envision and leading our blog has been a wonderful journey. It's about intertwining passion and profession, where I get to meet amazing people, engage with thought-provoking ideas, and continue to explore the exciting world of design. This year, and in the years to come, I envision only growth, community, and endless creativity.

CNN: Let's talk about the real reason you're working with the American Heart Association. Janney: I had a bit of a scary experience with my mother who, like most women I think, ignored the symptoms. She was driving, going to see the grandkids. She was in a motel and probably had what was a very small heart attack - but a warning. She just thought she was having this unbelievable pressure and discomfort in her neck and shoulders. She drove 10 hours to Dayton, Ohio, and drove right to the doctor because she knew something was wrong. He just couldn't believe she drove all that way. She went right into the hospital and had emergency quadruple bypass surgery. I almost lost her. For that reason alone, I'm glad to be part of this campaign. CNN: You mentioned that many women feel like they have to tough it out and just ignore the symptoms. Why do you think that is? Janney: I think, as women, we tend to always put our own needs in the back seat to take care of our family or loved ones. My mother did just that. Women feel they need to take care of everybody, (but) they can't take care of anybody if they don't take care of themselves. Jennie Garth: Know your heart, know the risks. CNN: How did that experience, and learning more about heart disease, change the way you looked at exercise and nutrition? Janney: I've lost 15 (to) 20 pounds since the summer. I've been doing Pilates three days a week, and I have three dogs, which gets me out walking every single morning. It's been nice to slim down and bump up the exercise. She was sometimes oppressed by the thought that the only prospect before her, was a melancholy one of long years of struggles against poverty, and all the grievous evils of dependence. Her brother Charles, who was a year younger than herself, tried with some success to cheer her; he was of an active, enterprising disposition, full of hope and cheerfulness. This disposition subjected him to frequent disappointments, but his father had wisely guarded against their bad effects by forming in him strong habits of perseverance. Charles had been intended by his father for the same business as himself, and he had therefore never been removed from under his parent's eye. It was well now for the whole family that Charles had been so carefully trained. His natural disposition, his acquired habits, and his sense of responsibility, joined to his strong affection for his sisters, made him the object on which Jane fixed her best hopes for the future prosperity of the family. Charles encouraged her hopes, and expressed confidence in his ability to maintain himself at present, and to assist the younger ones when a few years should have matured his powers of usefulness. Jane and Charles anxiously desired some conversation with Mr Barker, the kind friend who had taken them into his house; and were very glad when he invited them, the day after the funeral, to a consultation on the state of their affairs. He told them that it was his intention always to treat them with perfect openness, as it had been their father's custom to do. He was the more inclined to do so, from the knowledge that they were worthy of his confidence, that they possessed prudence beyond their years, and that whatever exertions they might make, would be more efficient if they knew perfectly what they had to do, what objects were to be accomplished, and on what sources they were to depend. Mr Barker told them that when the affairs were all settled, their income, he feared, would not exceed eighty or ninety pounds a year. That he thought the first object ought to be to give the younger children such an education as would fit them for supporting themselves when they were old enough: that for this purpose the assistance of friends would be required for a few years, and that he knew of some who were willing to assist, believing, from the good principles of the children, that their assistance would be well bestowed, and that their endeavours would be in time rewarded by the usefulness and happiness of those who now required their care. Jane acquiesced in Mr Barker's proposal, but expressed her hope that they might not be separated. The one thing that she desired more than any other, was, to remain with, and watch over the little ones, and be as far as possible a mother to them.

Their paper examined how changing physical and chemical parameters of the deposit, and changing processing methods through the life of a project can influence the environmental impact. This method was also applied by Pell et al. (2019a) for the Bear Lodge project in USA. The results highlighted the environmental impact changes over the life-of-mine and the positive relationship between decreasing grade and increasing global warming impact. This work also highlighted that this relationship is not consistent among the different mineralogies at the deposit. A major limitation of current LCA methodology for REE production is that it is difficult to compare results across studies because of variation in system boundaries used, source and quality of life cycle inventory (LCI) data, different allocation procedures, and the use of different databases and life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods. In particular, most LCA studies use simple average black-boxes to represent high-level aggregated processes when compiling the LCI such as with Weng et al. (2016). Although the results from these studies can be useful for communicating aggregated impacts to non-specialist audiences, using this approach may not provide the resolution needed to identify particular impacts as it cannot capture the details and interconnected nature of materials processing systems. Carrying out an LCA at the early stages of a project can inform choices that are made later during the development of the project even though the LCA results might have relatively high uncertainties (see Fig. 1). Some work has even examined the inclusion of LCA in long term mine scheduling which takes place at a very early stage of a mining project (Pell et al., 2019b). The approach presented in this paper highlights how early-stage LCA based on a scoping or pre-feasibility study can be realised by generating a mineral process simulation-LCA model. This can be used to inform choices of processing routes, energy sources and waste management and can be continuously updated throughout project development. Recent studies, aiming to develop an indicator framework for the environmental sustainability benchmarking of metallurgical industry products, have already highlighted that it is possible to integrate detailed mineral processing simulations with LCA (Ronnlund et al., 2016a, 2016b; Reuter et al., 2015). Once a model has been developed it is possible to update processing efficiencies, update grade and mineralisation data following drilling campaigns, or replace specific modules to reflect changes in the project. Fig. 1 highlights the advantage of including environmental data early in the project development stage. The planning phase offers the greatest opportunity to minimize the environmental, capital and operating costs of the ultimate project, while maximizing the operability and profitability of the venture. But the opposite is also true: no phase of the project contains the potential for instilling technical or fiscal disaster into a developing project that is inherent in the planning phase. At the start of the conceptual study, there is a relatively unlimited ability to influence the cost of the emerging project.

As I sat in the grand, if slightly worn, drawing room of Government House, sipping tea from delicate china cups, I couldn't help but feel a sense of awe in the presence of this unflappable man. The Falklands War may have been a brief but brutal conflict, but Sir Rex's spirit remained unbroken, his wit and humor still razor-sharp. He regaled us with stories of his time as a Spitfire pilot, of the thrill of flying sorties over the skies of Europe, and of the camaraderie that bound him to his fellow airmen. But it was his time in the Falklands that truly brought out the twinkle in his eye. He spoke of the islanders, whom he had grown to love and respect, and of the Argentine invasion, which had brought his tenure as governor to an abrupt and unexpected end. "It was a bit of a shock, I must say," he chuckled, "to find myself facing a bunch of heavily-armed soldiers on the doorstep. But I wasn't about to let them get the better of me." As he spoke, I couldn't help but think of the famous photograph, taken just days after the invasion, of Sir Rex standing tall, his ceremonial hat firmly in place, as he faced down the Argentine general. It was an image that had become synonymous with British pluck and defiance, and one that would be etched in the nation's collective memory for generations to come. Despite the chaos and uncertainty of those tumultuous days, Sir Rex remained steadfast, a beacon of calm in the midst of turmoil. And when the war finally came to an end, and the Falklands were liberated, he was there to welcome back the islanders, to reassure them that their way of life would continue, and to oversee the rebuilding of their shattered community. As I prepared to leave, Sir Rex walked me to the door, his eyes twinkling with mischief. "You know, I never thought I'd say this, but I rather enjoyed the Falklands," he said, with a sly grin. "It was a bit of an adventure, really. And I must say, I rather fancy another posting like that. Anywhere else would be a bit dull, don't you think?" I laughed, and nodded in agreement. For Sir Rex Hunt, the Falklands had been a defining moment, a chance to prove himself in the face of adversity, and to emerge victorious. And as I walked out into the bright sunlight, I couldn't help but feel that this tiny, ebullient man had left an indelible mark on history.

As they sat down to eat, Tommy Frigo couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. He had always been the odd one out, the outsider, and this trip was supposed to be a chance for him to break free from his mundane suburban existence. But now, with James's recent heartbreak and the looming uncertainty of their futures, he couldn't shake the feeling that this trip was going to be a disaster. "So, what's the plan, guys?" he asked, trying to sound casual, but his voice came out strained. James shrugged, his eyes fixed on the plate of manicotti in front of him. "We'll figure it out. We'll make it work." Tommy nodded, but his mind was already racing with worst-case scenarios. What if they got lost in Europe? What if they ran out of money? He didn't want to be the one to ruin the trip, but he couldn't help but feel like he was stuck in a bad dream. As they ate, the conversation turned to their plans for after graduation. James talked about his dreams of becoming a writer, while Brad rambled on about his plans to start his own business. Tommy listened, feeling like an outsider, like he didn't belong. After dinner, they decided to take a walk around the neighborhood, enjoying the warm summer evening. As they strolled, Tommy couldn't help but feel like he was stuck in a rut. He was tired of the same old routine, tired of the same old friends. He wanted to break free, to see the world, to experience something new. As they walked, they stumbled upon a group of kids having a party in the park. The music was loud, the beer was flowing, and the laughter was contagious. Tommy felt a pang of longing, a desire to be a part of something bigger than himself. James, sensing his friend's unease, turned to him and said, "Hey, Frigo, what's wrong?" This idea of infusing our homes with intentional magic brings such a richness to our mundane routines. Imagine transforming common chores-like washing dishes or sweeping floors-into sacred rituals, serving not just to clean and tidy, but to nurture the very essence of your space. Erin encourages us to create an atmosphere that resonates with tranquility, and her insights into home deities, ranging from the playful household spirits to the more serious, protective entities, provide a lovely framework for us to establish our own connections. As the pages of this book unfold, you'll find rituals designed to align with the changing seasons, fostering an awareness of the natural cycles around us. It's almost poetry in motion how the cycles of the moon and the flow of the seasons can guide us in our home practices. For instance, setting up an autumnal altar with seasonal offerings, igniting a shared sense of gratitude amongst family members, or lighting candles not just for ambiance but for welcoming blessings into your home. All of these practices bring life back to the walls that shelter us. Let's talk about the idea of "sacred space." It's easy, in our busy lives, to overlook the importance of creating environments purposely infused with love and warmth. A clutter-free kitchen, a well-cared-for garden, or an inviting living room nook can become havens for relaxation and creativity when infused with intention. One of my favorite takeaways from Erin is her emphasis on sensory experiences-those rich moments of aromas, textures, and colors that speak to our souls. The simple act of cooking a family recipe, for example, becomes a magical experience when you throw in a little gratitude for the ancestors who passed it down, whispering blessings over the pot as you stir. Moreover, the book dives into the realm of spells for the household. Whether it's crafting a simple ward against negativity at the entrance or creating a charm for harmony among family members, we find that our intentions can take physical forms. I particularly loved her approach to imagination in spell work, suggesting that we visualize the energy we want to manifest in our homes. It's like becoming the artist of your own living experience, coloring outside the lines, if you will! Erin also doesn't shy away from discussing the more practical aspects of home magic. There's a chapter dedicated to organizing your space and the powerful influence of decluttering-not just physically but energetically. Clearing out those cabinets or closets filled with things we no longer need can be a transformative act that opens up new energies, making room for positivity and abundance. It's a reminder that our outer worlds often reflect our inner states. As we edge closer to the festive season, it's a perfect time to bring these concepts to the forefront of our preparations. Hosting gatherings, wrapping gifts with care, and setting intentions for the new year can all be infused with this home magic. Whether you're lighting candles for a winter solstice gathering or preparing a special dish, let each action resonate with joy and intention. So, dear listeners, as I embark on my holiday preparations, I hope you feel inspired to welcome this magic into your own spaces as well. Let's make this holiday season not just a time of celebration but a true manifestation of home, where love, laughter, and intention create a sanctuary for all. Stay tuned for more musings, and may your home be ever enchanting!

He gave permission for the marriage, and allowed his ward to accept an offer of 2000 pounds down, and a further sum of 5000 pounds on her husband's death. The wedding took place; but, ere long, all seemed changed. The husband became morose, harsh, overbearing. He quarreled with the servants, grumbled at his father-in-law, and neglected his wife. His mistress found out that she had married a monster - a fiend in human form! But she loved him too well to leave him, though she could hardly bear to stay with him. At length she determined to tell her father how matters stood. She went to see him, and related the whole story. Her father listened attentively, then said - "I think I can put you right again." He went himself to the house where his daughter lived, and entered into conversation with her husband. The interview lasted some hours, and ended by Vaughan consenting to go abroad with his father-in-law, who, having business in France, was going to Paris. They sailed from Dover, and arrived safely in Boulogne. The next morning they breakfasted together, and parted forever. A little later, the worthy Mr. Bliss returned home, bringing back his daughter with him. She was happy in her home, and in her husband's memory, and lived happily ever after. As for Vaughan, he reached Calais, where he met a friend. This friend was an officer in the French service, and knew the roads well. Vaughan joined him, and they travelled together till they came to Rheims. Here Vaughan left him, saying that he must visit a relative residing near Amiens. It was agreed between them that Vaughan should meet his companion at Lyons, and proceed thence to Marseilles. After staying some days at Amiens, Vaughan, instead of taking the route to Lyons, turned off towards the Swiss frontier. Once across, he proceeded to Geneva, and then to Turin. From Turin he wrote to his old acquaintance in London, telling him to come to him if possible. He received an answer in due course, stating that the correspondent would do so, and, in the meanwhile, giving news of his own affairs. It appeared that, immediately on hearing of Vaughan's disappearance, Mr. Bliss had gone to the Bank of England to ascertain whether any drafts had been issued upon him since he left town. The officers informed him that several had been presented, and paid. On examination of the drawer's books, these were found to have been signed in the same manner as those previously written by Vaughan. Mr. Bliss hastened to his lawyer, and obtained a warrant against Vaughan. Meantime, the latter had heard nothing of his former friend, and, becoming impatient, went to Milan. Here he fell ill, and remained in bed for three weeks. During his illness, he made acquaintances among his fellow-patients, and learned from them that an Englishman had recently passed through Milan. They described him, and Vaughan recognized him as his old comrade. Vaughan got better, and started in search of his friend, whom he soon discovered in Venice. He told him what had happened, and asked his advice. The other advised him to return to England at once, and give himself up. Vaughan consented to do so. They crossed to Trieste, and proceeded by Vienna to Frankfort-on-the-Main. Here they separated, each travelling alone, and Vaughan arrived at Dover without meeting any adventure. He reported himself to the authorities, and was conveyed to London. He was tried, convicted, and sentenced to death.

Mechanical cleaning is performed by rotating brushes or scrubbing devices mounted on the tubesheets, which remove the deposit layer through abrasion. However, this method requires the plant to be shut down, is costly and generates wear particles that can cause further fouling problems (Vepsalainen, 2010). Recently, in order to address the aforementioned limitations of current steam generator cleaning technologies, an innovative method based on the use of ultrasonic waves was proposed by Zhang et al. (2017). The authors reported that when the frequency of the incident acoustic wave is tuned so that the resonance frequency of the steam generator shell matches the frequency of the incident wave, strong oscillations of the shell occur, which result in enhanced fluid motion near the shell wall and consequent improvement in the efficiency of mass transport between the shell wall and the fluid flowing over the shell wall. As a consequence, the removal of fouling deposits becomes more efficient. The implementation of the above-mentioned concept in industrial applications, however, presents some challenges. First, while the theory of cavitation bubble dynamics is rather mature, the effects of ultrasound propagation in fluids containing solid particles and/or suspended gases have not yet been investigated sufficiently. Second, the presence of solid debris in the system might interfere with the transmission of ultrasound energy, thus requiring appropriate measures to prevent signal attenuation. Third, a fundamental issue is whether the fluid dynamic effects generated by the interaction between ultrasound and a solid surface can be efficiently exploited for removing deposits from the surface. This work aims at addressing these three points. To this end, we first focus on the development of numerical models able to predict the behavior of ultrasound in liquids containing suspended solids. These numerical models will be implemented in a numerical code that will be employed for the design and optimization of an experimental apparatus aimed at investigating the effect of ultrasound on the removal of CRUD deposits from simulated fuel rods. Modelling the behaviour of ultrasound in liquids containing suspended solids SANTONASTASO, MARCO During the operation of light water reactors, various corrosion products typically termed CRUD (Chalk river unidentified deposit) gradually accumulate on surfaces exposed to coolant flow, particularly on fuel rods and steam generator tubing. CRUD deposition might results in multiple undesired consequences. For example, due to its porous structure, CRUD deposited on fuel rods can absorb the boron dissolved into the coolant for reactivity control, generating issues with the power management of nuclear systems. Axial offset anomalies in power density and CRUD-induced power shifts are well-known examples of this problem (Zou et al., 2013). Once present on heat-transferring surfaces, such as reactor fuel rods and steam generator tubes, CRUD provides additional thermal resistance, reducing the effectiveness of heat transfer and/or inducing surface overheating (Cinosi et al., 2011). A particularly effective cleaning technology currently available to remove CRUD deposits from nuclear fuel rods relies on cavitation, which is the formation of gas or vapor cavities in a liquid triggered by a reduction in local pressure. When the reduction in local pressure is induced via ultrasound, the phenomenon is referred to as ultrasonic cavitation. Ultrasonic cavitation cleaning has been used industrially for decades, particularly for cleaning mechanical tools and components, surgical instruments and electronic equipment (Mason, 2016). The object to be cleaned is placed in a chamber that is filled with a suitable liquid solution and equipped with ultrasound-generating transducers that produce high frequency pressure waves in the solution. During the rarefaction of a pressure wave, the rapid decrease in pressure triggers the formation of microscopic cavitation bubbles, which then collapse during the subsequent compression wave.

To consider when evaluating the role of ruminants in both human health and environmental sustainability. One major point often overlooked in these discussions is the fact that ruminants can play a significant role in carbon sequestration. When managed properly, grazing animals can help restore grasslands, which ultimately store carbon in the soil while fostering biodiversity. By allowing nature to thrive through more sustainable farming practices, we can cultivate a harmonious relationship between animal agriculture and the environment. It's crucial to recognize that the quality of the meat and dairy products we consume matters just as much as the quantity. Grass-fed beef, for instance, generally comes from cattle that lead happier, healthier lives and produce meat that is richer in omega-3 fatty acids compared to their grain-fed counterparts. This aligns with a growing body of research that indicates not all meat is created equal and that the benefits of consuming pasture-raised, nutrient-dense animal products extend beyond individual health to encompass broader environmental considerations. Moreover, addressing misconceptions about meat and health is paramount. The narrative linking red meat consumption to chronic diseases like cardiovascular disease and cancer often lacks context and nuance. The source of meat, its processing, and the individual's overall dietary pattern profoundly influence health outcomes. For instance, consumption of processed meat may be associated with certain health risks, but unprocessed meat sourced from healthy animals can be a part of a nutritious diet. Nutrients found in meat, such as high-quality protein, iron, and B-vitamins, play critical roles in our overall health, suggesting that vilifying all animal products is not only unreasonable but potentially harmful. Transitioning to a more holistic view, it's essential to advocate for sustainable practices that promote both ecological balance and personal health. The conversation should not be limited to the dichotomy of plant versus animal products but should instead embrace a regenerative approach that recognizes the benefits of both food groups. By encouraging sustainable livestock management, we can significantly reduce the environmental impact of our food systems while still supporting human health. In light of this evidence, we should broaden the discourse to include conversations about how to improve livestock farming practices. Initiatives aimed at reducing methane emissions from ruminants-like supplementing animal feed with seaweed or ensuring better grazing techniques-can yield promising results, and these should be included in our discussions about sustainability and meat consumption. Let's also not forget the cultural and social dimensions of food. Meat often plays a vital role in many cultures' culinary traditions, providing not only nourishment but also community and identity. By acknowledging these factors, we enhance our conversations around food and health, steering them toward inclusivity rather than division. In summary, while the debate about animal agriculture's environmental impact is critical, it's equally important that we approach this subject with a balanced perspective. As we embrace various nutritional frameworks, let us ensure that we elevate the discourse around sustainable practices and the potential for healthier food choices, acknowledging the complexity of our food systems. Sustainable eating should be about finding common ground while promoting health for individuals and the planet alike. So, as you navigate your own dietary choices, remember that knowledge is power, and understanding the nuances of this intricate subject will enable you to make informed decisions to safeguard your health and well-being. Thank you for tuning into today's session, and let's continue our journey towards a healthier future together.

The 28 LMBs were established in 1899 and had powers to levy local property taxes, to decide on the provision of local services (sewer connections, bathhouses, parks, libraries, dairies and milk shops, etc.) and to take out loans to finance capital expenses on the security of future property taxes. Within the statutory boundaries, the LMBs had significant fiscal autonomy and the elected representatives of the councils could decide on the level, composition and the timing of key fiscal variables. All councillors were elected every three years. The franchise before the First World War was based on property tax payment and restricted to men; we refer to it as taxpayer suffrage. The Representation of the People Act (sometimes referred to as the Fourth Reform Act) in 1918 eradicated the tax payment requirement at all levels of government (including for the LMBs) and introduced almost equal and universal suffrage.5 This quasi-natural experiment allows us to study the opportunistic political budget cycle under two different suffrage regimes.6 Besides adding new historical evidence to the debate on the opportunistic political budget cycle, our study contributes directly to two more specific strands of literature.7 Firstly, it significantly enhances our understanding of fiscal retrenchment and taxpayer democracy in Britain. Until 1918, voting rights in local elections linked representation to the prompt payment of the local property tax (known in Britain as the rate) such that only local taxpayers had the right to vote. This had intriguing implications for the relationship between the size of the electorate and local public finance. In particular when the balance of power shifted to small-scale, middle class taxpayer-voters, demands were made for retrenchment and economy rather than fiscal expansion, despite apparently large social returns on public investment in local public goods (Hennock, 1963, 1973; Wohl, 1983; Szreter, 1988, 1997). As documented by Aidt et al. (2010), this generated a negative relationship between spending on local public goods and the extension of the franchise.8 We add to this by studying how opportunistic political budget cycles operate in an environment with taxpayer-voters. This restricted franchise is compared to the regime of universal suffrage, where the pivotal voter often does not contribute much to the local tax base. Secondly, our study contributes to the fast expanding research on the conditional political budget cycle initiated by Persson and Tabellini (2003), Brender and Drazen (2005), Shi and Svensson (2006), Alt and Lassen (2006a,b) and Alt and Rose (2007) amongst others, and recently surveyed by de Haan and Klomp (2013). The general point here is that the size and nature of the political budget cycle are conditional on the political and economic environment. They depend, amongst other factors, on economic conditions (e.g., the level of income), the institutional framework (e.g., the level of corruption, the type of election or political system), and the monitoring framework (e.g., fiscal transparency and quality of the press).

The Rue St. Gingolphe is within a stone's-throw of the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, and in the very centre of a remarkably cheap and yet respectable quarter. Thus there are many young men occupying apartments in close proximity - and young men do not mind much what they smoke, especially provincial young men living in Paris. They feel it incumbent upon them to be constantly smoking something - just to show that they are Parisians, true sons of the pavement, knowing how to live. And their brightest hopes are in all truth realised, because theirs is certainly a reckless life, flavoured as it is with "number one" tobacco, and those "little corporal" cigarettes which are enveloped in the blue paper. The tobacconist's shop is singularly convenient. It has, namely, an entrance at the back, as well as that giving on to the street of St. Gingolphe. This entrance is through a little courtyard, in which is the stable and coach-house combined, where Madame Perinere, a lady who paints the magic word "Modes" beneath her name on the door-post of number seventeen, keeps the dapper little cart and pony which carry her bonnets to the farthest corner of Paris. The tobacconist is a large man, much given to perspiration. In fact, one may safely make the statement that he perspires annually from the middle of April to the second or even third week in October. In consequence of this habit he wears no collar, and a man without a collar does not start fairly on the social race. It is always best to make inquiries before condemning a man who wears no collar. There is probably a very good reason, as in the case of Mr. Jacquetot, but it is to be feared that few pause to seek it. One need not seek the reason with much assiduity in this instance, because the tobacconist of the Rue St. Gingolphe is always prepared to explain it at length. French people are thus. They talk of things, and take pleasure in so doing, which we, on this side of the Channel, treat with a larger discretion. Mr. Jacquetot does not even wear a collar on Sunday, for the simple reason that Sunday is to him as other days. He attends no place of worship, because he acknowledges but one god - the god of most Frenchmen - his inner man. His pleasures are gastronomical, his sorrows stomachic. The little shop is open early and late, Sundays, week-days, and holidays. Moreover, the tobacconist - Mr. Jacquetot himself - is always at his post, on the high chair behind the counter, near the window, where he can see into the street. This constant attention to business is almost phenomenal, because Frenchmen who worship the god of Mr. Jacquetot love to pay tribute on fete-days at one of the little restaurants on the Place at Versailles, at Duval's, or even in the Palais Royal.

Differences of 1-4% between indoor and outdoor measurements using the same chain of traceability performed at the same laboratory were observed (Shimokawa et al., 1987), which confirms the observations made in the computational study of Shimokawa, et al. (1986). At that time, the measurement uncertainties using the global (normal) sunlight method were typically in the range of 2.5-3.7% for the short-circuit current (Emery and Osterwald, 1989). Indoor laboratory calibrations of reference solar cells using only direct normal incidence irradiation provide uncertainties of 0.4% (k = 2, expanded uncertainty 95%) (Winter, et al., 2014). Since the indoor primary calibrated reference cells are often used as irradiance sensors for secondary calibrations of other PV devices such as modules using global outdoor irradiation conditions or simulated sunlight, the relatively high impact of angular effects is not negligible. This leads to the conclusion that, if not considered, uncertainties due to angular effects contribute significantly to the total measurement uncertainty budget for global sunlight methods. Furthermore, spectral dependencies of the sky radiance (Bullrich et al., 1952) are only negligible for devices without differing angular-dependent spectral responsivities. Emery and Osterwald (1988) devised a generalized equation for this problem and incorporated it into the uncertainty budget of outdoor measurements under global sunlight. The dependence of the responsivity of PV devices on polarization, spectrum, reflection and absorption losses, as well as on light trapping effects, is discussed elsewhere (Shimokawa, et al., 1986; Seibert, 1968; Dennler, et al., 2007; Gjessing and Marstein, 2014; Beal, et al., 2014; Potter, et al., 2015; Smeets, et al., 2015; Geisemeyer, et al., 2017; Plag, et al., 2017a). A more recent publication (Mullejans, et al., 2005a) reports reduced measurement uncertainties of 1% (k = 2, expanded uncertainty 95%) for measurements of the short-circuit current using the global sunlight method traceable to the world radiometric reference (WRR). Mullejans et al. proposed using the global sunlight method reference for the primary calibration of photovoltaic reference cells. Their analysis of measurement uncertainties assumed an "ideal cosine response" (Mullejans, et al., 2005b). The differences from the cosine responsivity observed in Plag, et al. (2017a) and Geisemeyer, et al. (2017) for different solar cell types encouraged us to investigate the effect of diffuse light on solar cells in depth by means of a computational study. Therefore, we focus in this paper on how angular effects introduced by different angular responsivities influence PV device measurements; we also focus on the impact of direct, diffuse and ground reflected irradiation components of solar irradiance on these measurements. It is worth mentioning that the experimental characterization of the detectors' responsivity and of the sky spectral radiance requires considerable efforts. While the computation of an angular mismatch is trivial for direct irradiance, the diffuse and ground-reflected irradiance components require knowledge of the radiance distribution.
