Along the valleys of the numerous creeks and bayous that empty their waters into the Ohio, the soil was of a rich alluvium, where in the early Spring the back waters from the Ohio covered thousands of acres of farm and timber lands, and in receding left the land plastered with a coat of river sand and clay which greatly added to the soil's productivity. One who owned a farm on these bottoms was considered quite fortunate. Here the corn stalks grew like saplings, with ears dangling one and two to a stalk, and as sound and heavy as green blocks of wood. The heavy rains washed the loam from the hills and deposited it on these bottoms. Years ago, when the rolling lands were cleared, and before the excessive rainfall had washed away the loose surface, the highlands were considered most valuable for agricultural purposes, equally as valuable as the bottoms now are. Farther back from the river the more rolling the land became, until some sixteen miles away it was known as the hills, and here, long before I was born, the land had been very valuable. Large barns and fine stately houses - now gone to wreck and deserted - stood behind beautiful groves of chestnut, locust and stately old oaks, where rabbits, quail and wood-peckers made their homes, and sometimes a raccoon or opossum founded its den during the cold, bleak winter days. The orchards, formerly the pride of their owners, now dropped their neglected fruit which rotted and mulched with the leaves. The fields, where formerly had grown great crops of wheat, corn, oats, timothy and clover, were now grown over and enmeshed in a tangled mass of weeds and dew-berry vines; while along the branches and where the old rail fences had stood, black-berry vines had grown up, twisting their thorny stems and forming a veritable hedge fence. These places I promised mother to avoid as I begged her to allow me to follow the big boys and carry their game when they went hunting. In the neighborhood and throughout the country there had at one time been many colored farmers, or ex-slaves, who had settled there after the war. Many of them having built up nice homes and cleared the valley of tough-rooted hickory, gum, pecan and water-oak trees, and the highlands of the black, white, red or post oak, sassafras and dogwood. Similar results were obtained in a generalized stochastic framework with many compartments, that performed efficiently provided the number of state variables was not too high (Lopez-Garcia and Kypraios, 2018). van Kleef et al. (2017) proposed a deterministic compartmental model to assess how hand hygiene intervention may prevent infections by both drug resistant and drug sensitive bacteria. The model captured the transmission of strains in both hospital and community settings. In the former, transmission was assumed to occur through contaminated hands of healthcare workers (HCW) and once hand hygiene was performed, the contamination was cleared. They further assumed that resistant strains are better adapted to the hospital environment and sensitive strains are better adapted to community environment, based on the presence and absence of drug pressure in the two environments. They found that hand hygiene intervention targeting only one of the environments strongly affects the better-adapted strain. Moreover, the flux of patients between community and hospital environments maintained the frequency of the sensitive strain, while the hand hygiene limited the spread of the resistant strain. Recently, mathematical models have been addressing the importance of hospital networks on the spread of healthcare-associated infections. Donker et al. (2012) used an agent-based model to study the spread of a nosocomial infection on the British hospital network. Using data from the health care system on patient admissions, discharges and transfers for each hospital, they estimated the probability that a patient carries the infection from one hospital to another. This estimate takes into account several factors: the probability of acquiring the infection which depends on the length of stay; the probability of transmitting the infection, which depends on the length of stay following readmission; and the probability of being infected upon readmission. They showed that in order to contain the spread of infection, the hospitals must be seen as part of a connected network and not only as an isolated unit. Karkada et al. (2011) presented a network model based on the national information of direct ICU patient transfers in the USA. In order to analyse various control strategies, they allocated arbitrary units of infection control to the hospitals. Each unit was assumed to reduce the transmission probability by 25% and if a hospital received more than one unit, the reduction was cumulative. They compared three different strategies for unit allocations in the network: random allocation, specific allocation given by the degree-centrality (a measure of how many hospitals are directly connected to the focal hospital by patient transfer) and specific allocation given by the betweenness-centrality (a measure of how often the shortest network path between two hospitals passes through the focal hospital).

It is important to note here that the will is passive. The will does not dictate the desires of an agent. The will is simply the faculty of choice. As such, the will cannot choose contrary to its strongest desire, because the strongest desire comes from the nature. Now, back to the discussion of the gift of faith. If the nature dictates the desires, then the desires dictate the choices of the will, then how is it possible to say that faith is a gift? If faith is a gift, then faith must come from outside of man. How could the nature produce faith when the nature is sinful? In other words, how could the nature produce faith as a desire when the nature is sinful? And if faith is a desire, then how could the nature produce faith as a desire when the nature is sinful? If the nature is sinful, and the nature dictates the desires, and the desires dictate the choices of the will, then there is no way that man could possibly receive faith as a gift. Man has no ability to choose faith, since he cannot choose contrary to his strongest desire. Therefore, the only way faith could be received as a gift would be if the nature was changed into something other than sinful. And the only way this could occur would be if God Himself intervened and changed the nature of man. But this is precisely what Calvinism teaches. This is the TULIP doctrine of Total Depravity. Man's nature is so corrupt that it is incapable of choosing faith, unless God intervenes and changes the nature of man. This is the Calvinistic understanding of the total depravity of man. In fact, this is exactly what the Westminster Confession says, and exactly what John Calvin taught. And this is what the Reformers taught. This is also what the early church fathers taught. The Reformers were not innovators, but rather they returned to the teaching of the Church Fathers, who were not innovators either. They were innovators in the sense that they re-instituted the doctrines of grace after the church had abandoned them. But the doctrines of grace did not originate with Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, Knox, Cranmer, etc., but they originated with Augustine and the early church fathers. I believe the Reformers and the early church fathers are correct. The Bible clearly teaches that man is unable to choose faith, unless God Himself intervenes and changes the nature of man. Instead I said something jumbled about missing her and how hard it would be. "Well, It's not like we're dating," she said. "Oh..." My heart tore in two "Well, er, that's what I told everyone else" People like me should have been born mutes. Her sudden, shocked reaction woke up a latent cynic burried deep inside my innocent shell. For the first time I began to realize that romance had a darker side, the side that was rough and crinkled and inhabited the whole of reality. I quickly made some joke to cover up my blunder, passing the whole statement off as some sort of failed attempt at humor, and never spoke about it to her again. But the movie romantic in me was not killed that day. He reasserted himself just a short day later, before I left that sleepy NH town for good. I bought a small, heart shaped locked for Kayden and made a special trip to her house to give it to her. She was quite surprised and looked like she wanted to say something more. There's a part of me that wants to believe she was ready to confess her feelings for me. In reality, she just probably thought I was crazy. Sweet, but crazy. Sadly, I was so overwhelmed with the Kayden affair that I missed it entirely. Then again, one also has to consider that I did move away and had absolutely no opportunity to develop any sort of romance with the lovely Sarah #1. Romance from this point out fluxuated between being something fantastic and something gut-wrenching. Yet, the allure of that bustling atmosphere with its mingling scents of roasted coffee and fresh pastries, mingled seamlessly with the chatter of patrons and staff alike, tugged at Clyde's senses. There was a vibrancy that drew him in, a magnetic pull that made him forget the humdrum routine of his job for a fleeting moment. As he stood near the exit contemplating his next move, a barista, her apron slightly askew, caught his eye. She glanced up from her workbench, where she arranged delicately crafted pastries like pieces of art. "Hey, you look lost, buddy. Looking for a caffeine fix?" she offered, her voice bright and inviting. Clyde hesitated, his mind racing through images of his responsibilities waiting for him back in the limo, the couple still nestled inside, and the delicate child, untouched by the mundane fatigue of adulthood. But something in the barista's friendly demeanor made him want to linger just a bit longer. "Uh, I'm just passing through, really. I've got a couple of folks I'm driving." She nodded, unfazed. "Well, these pastries won't drive themselves, you know. They're fresh out of the oven. Perfect with a latte," she said, pointing to a chocolate croissant, its flaky exterior gleaming temptingly. Clyde glanced at the pastries, then back at her. "You really recommend them?" "Absolutely. You're missing out if you don't at least try one!" Her enthusiasm was infectious, and before he could think twice, he found himself stepping closer to the counter. "What's your name, buddy? You don't strike me as a regular here," she queried, as she slid the buttery croissant into a small white paper bag. "Clyde," he responded, realizing he had yet to leave a mark on this busy establishment in all his rides past. Usually, he was the unseen hand that ferried people from A to B, an afterthought, a mere cog in the vast machine of the city. "Well, Clyde, consider this your introduction," she said, handing him the bag. "And I'm Tara, in case you want to drop by again and avoid the rut of your usual run," she replied, her smile warm and welcoming. "Thanks, Tara. I might just take you up on that offer." Clyde chuckled, feeling a hint of camaraderie build between them, however fleeting. There was a spark in that moment, a reminder of the lively banter he often missed during the monotony of his day-to-day. "Good luck with your customers!" she called as he stepped back toward the exit, bag in hand. "Yeah, and you with those pastries," Clyde replied, glancing back before he slipped outside. The chilly air hit him like a wave, invigorating him once again. Returning to the limo, he contemplated the croissant nestled in the bag, wondering how something so small could represent a sudden shift in his day. As he pulled the door open, he was greeted by the playful giggles of the little girl. "Daddy! Open it!" she squealed, tugging at her father's sleeve, her excitement contagious. He smiled, watching the father fumble with the box while the mother leaned back, eyes sparkling with warmth. Perhaps today wouldn't just be another day. With that thought swirling in his mind, Clyde found himself wishing for small moments of joy - the kind that sneaked up on you when you least expected them.

As the seasons passed, Violet's gaze would often wander beyond the hills, to the distant woods that lay hidden from view. She would imagine the rustling of leaves, the chirping of birds, and the soft filtering of sunlight through the trees. Her imagination would run wild, conjuring up tales of adventures and escapades, of brave knights and fair maidens, of hidden treasures and secret glades. But as the sun began to set, casting long shadows across the street, Violet's thoughts would return to the present, and her eyes would fall upon the Bible, now worn and dog-eared from countless readings. The words within its pages had become her solace, her comfort, and her guide. She would read of love and loss, of hope and redemption, and find solace in the promises of a brighter tomorrow. The stories of the prophets, the wisdom of the psalms, and the parables of Jesus had become her constant companions, her friends in a world that seemed to be moving further and further away from her. As the months went by, Violet's hair grew longer, her face paler, and her eyes more sunken. Her once-bright smile had faded, replaced by a quiet resignation, a sense of acceptance that had settled upon her like a shroud. The children still came to visit, bringing their flowers and their stories, but even their laughter and chatter seemed to fade into the background as Violet's thoughts turned inward. The turret window, once a symbol of her isolation, had become her refuge, her sanctuary. She would sit for hours, lost in thought, her gaze fixed on some distant point beyond the hills, her heart heavy with longing. The world outside seemed to be moving on without her, leaving her behind in a sea of memories, of what-ifs, and of maybes. And yet, even in the midst of her sorrow, Violet found a strange, quiet beauty. The way the sunlight filtered through the stained glass windows, casting kaleidoscopic patterns on the floor. The sound of the wind rustling through the leaves of the trees outside. The gentle touch of a summer breeze on her skin. These small, fleeting joys became her lifeline, her connection to a world that seemed to be slipping away from her grasp. As the seasons passed, Violet's story became a testament to the human spirit, a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there is always hope, always a glimmer of light to guide us through the darkness. And though her body may have been confined to that small, turret-shaped window, her heart and mind roamed free, soaring on the wings of imagination, and finding solace in the beauty of the world around her.

But let's expand our understanding of the concept of the "friend zone" beyond just romantic entanglements. You see, the friend zone can manifest in so many facets of life. It can inhabit our relationships with acquaintances, family members, colleagues, and even ourselves. There's a profound irony in this: often we confine ourselves, maybe even subconsciously, into a limited understanding of connection, thinking a relationship must strictly adhere to certain labels or expectations. In doing so, we miss out on the richness that comes with simply allowing relationships to unfold as they are meant to, with their own unique rhythms and dynamics. Now, I want to delve into the importance of friendship itself. Isn't it beautiful how God designed us to be relational beings? In Genesis, we see that God declared, "It is not good for man to be alone." This speaks volumes about the need for companionship and community. Friendship should be celebrated! It's a divine gift that enriches our lives, provides support in our trials, and amplifies our joy in times of celebration. However, as we navigate our friendships, we must be mindful-are we putting people in boxes, limiting them to where we feel comfortable? The friend zone can often breed frustration, misunderstandings, and hurt feelings, especially when we impose our expectations onto others. Think about it: how many times have you found yourself feeling neglected or even betrayed because a friend didn't act the way you anticipated they would? Perhaps they didn't prioritize your friendship in the way you thought they should. It's in these moments that we need to take a step back and examine what we might be bringing to the table. And I want to be clear-friendship isn't simply about reciprocity; it's about grace, deep understanding, and unconditional love. It's about nurturing and uplifting one another rather than keeping score. When we start to function from a place of expectation, it can lead us down a path of disappointment. Instead, let's allow ourselves to approach these relationships with open hands and open hearts. I also want to highlight the importance of boundaries in friendships. Boundaries aren't mean; they show that you value both yourself and the other party involved. Boundaries create space for us to grow and flourish as individuals while allowing relationships to deepen organically. Sometimes we find ourselves in friendships that have stalled or become stagnant, and it's essential to have those honest conversations, reevaluating where we stand and mutually deciding how we can be there for one another moving forward. So as we consider the lessons offered by the friend zone, let's ask ourselves some probing questions. Are we putting conditions on our friendships? Are we stifling relationships by holding on too tightly? Or, conversely, are we letting relationships drift unnoticed, taking our friendships for granted? Today, as we dive deeper into this theme, I invite each of you to reflect. Reflect on your friendships-what do they mean to you? How can you nurture them better? After all, friends are treasures, and every moment spent together is an opportunity to cherish, grow, and learn. Let this series inspire us to shift our perspectives, to embrace the complexities, and to cultivate relationships rooted not in fear or expectation, but in love, vulnerability, and honesty. Thank you for journeying with us.

This inhomogeneity is significant among different climate regimes, even among the glaciers in a close neighbourhood (Horton et al., 2006). The rate of glacier retreat depends on both large-scale and time-invariant factors, and small-scale and time-dependent factors (Burlando et al., 2002; Khadka et al., 2014). Geographical, topographical and climatic conditions act at large scales and relatively stable, whereas the size, location of glaciers and study period of research are at a small spatial scale and time dependent (Bolch, 2007; Marshall, 2014). The processes of melt water from glaciers draining to the catchment outlet are very complex. Glaciologists and hydrologists have made many efforts to describe and model them by employing glaciological methods and hydrological methods or by integrated knowledge. The methods used can be categorised into three types: glaciological, hydrological and interdisciplinary approaches. From a glaciological point of view, it is essential to simulate response of glaciers to climate change and contribution to streamflow by glacier wastage. This approach mainly uses models to relate meteorological measurements to accumulation and ablation rates on the glacier surface. These mass balance models vary in complexity, including conceptual models and or more complicated models based on the energy balance (Gottlieb, 1980; Arnold et al., 1996; Klok and Oerlemans, 2002; Hock, 2005) and models for ice dynamics (Greuell, 1992; Hubbard et al., 1998; Jouvet et al., 2009). They have been validated by in-situ glacier measurements, such as surface mass balance or ice thickness change. Then glacier mass loss can be compared with discharge downstream of the glacier (Kotlarski et al., 2010). However, glacier melt water is only a raw volume input into the hydrological system, similar to rainfall. The discharge is further modified by, e.g. evaporation and groundwater storage. Therefore, the direct comparison leads to an overestimation of glacier contribution to discharge (Kaser et al., 2010), unless contributions from non-glacierised areas are also considered. Many diverse approaches have been used in developing hydrological models for a better representation of snow processes and ice melting (Bergstrom, 1976; Shrestha et al., 2012; Wrede et al., 2013). The models mainly use the meteorological data, satellite data of snow cover and climate scenarios to study effects of climate change on glaciers (Khadka et al., 2014; Jasper et al., 2004). Among the models, the Snowmelt Runoff Model (SRM) (Khadka et al., 2014; Immerzeel et al., 2009) and the HBV model (Mayr et al., 2013; Hagg et al., 2006; Akhtar et al., 2008) are widely used. However, these studies did not take into account the change in the glacier area to the imposed climatic changes. Although these studies provide valuable insights into the possible range of the future options, they suffer from a large uncertainty about the plausibility of the future evolution of glaciers (Immerzeel et al., 2012). This limits the time scale over which the results could apply.

In addition, the identification of highly interconnected hubs of intramodular communication can provide insight into the role of particular regions in the maintenance of normal brain functioning. Here we report the results from our recent study using a graph theoretic approach to characterize the modular organization of the resting-state brain connectivity network in schizophrenia patients and matched controls (Su et al., 2014). We used resting-state fMRI data collected from 20 chronic SCZ patients and 19 age-matched healthy control subjects. Using independent component analysis, we first identified a set of 16 intrinsic connectivity networks (ICNs) that were similar across groups. These ICNs included several well-known default mode (DMN), attentional (AN), sensorimotor (SMN), fronto-parietal (FPN), salience (SN) and visual (VN) networks, as well as two novel ICNs: one that consisted mainly of the medial temporal lobe structures and another that comprised primarily subcortical structures (see Fig. S1). The similarity between the ICNs of the two groups was confirmed by a permutation test. Next, we mapped the inter-network connectivity patterns onto the corresponding structural connectome obtained from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) scans performed on the same subjects, and assessed the overall consistency between functional and structural connectivity using a correlation-based metric. We found that the functional connectivity pattern of each ICN was significantly correlated with its corresponding structural connectivity pattern, confirming the validity of our method. Finally, we constructed undirected graphs based on the inter-network connectivity matrices of both patient and control groups, and used the Louvain algorithm to detect communities in each group. The resulting modular organization of the functional connectivity network was consistent with previous reports in the literature, showing that the DMN, AN, SN, SMN and VN formed separate communities, while the FPN was not clearly assigned to any single community. We then compared the modular organization of the two groups using a modularity-based dissimilarity measure. This revealed significant differences in the functional connectivity of three ICNs: the DMN, SN and FPN. Specifically, the DMN showed decreased within-community connectivity in patients relative to controls, whereas the SN and FPN showed increased within-community connectivity in patients. Further analysis indicated that these changes in the functional connectivity of the DMN, SN and FPN did not reflect changes in their respective structural connectivity, suggesting that they may be related to altered dynamics of the functional networks. Together, our findings suggest that abnormal functional connectivity in schizophrenia may manifest itself in reduced segregation of some networks and enhanced segregation of others, resulting in an overall reorganization of the functional connectivity network. He lingered at the window of the book store, looking with envious eyes at the display of new books. He was well known by the bookseller, for he was a frequent visitor, and, once in a while, he made a purchase; however, to day he must not spend too much time "browsing" among books. He would, however, just slip around to Twenty-fifth street and take a look at the secondhand store there. Not to buy shoes, of course, but sometimes there were other interesting things there, especially books. Ah, look here! Spread out on a table on the sidewalk in front of this second-hand store was a lot of books, a hundred or more - books of all kind - school books, history, fiction, all of them in good condition, some only a little shopworn, others just like new. Dorian Trent eagerly looked them over. Here were books he had read about, but had not read - and the prices! Dickens' "David Copperfield", "Tale of Two Cities", "Dombey and Son", large well-printed books, only a little shopworn, for thirty-five cents; Thackeray's "Vanity Fair", twenty-five cents; books by Mrs. Humphrey Ward and Margaret Deland; "Robinson Crusoe", a big book with fine pictures. Dorian had, of course, read "Robinson Crusoe" but he had always wanted to own a copy. Ah, what's this? Prescott's "Conquest of Peru", two volumes, new, fifty cents each! Dorian turned the leaves. A man stepped up and also began handling the books. Yes, here were bargains, surely. He stacked a number together as if he desired to secure them. Dorian becoming fearful, slipped the other volume of the Conquest under his arm and made as if to gather a number of other books under his protection. He must have some of these before they were all taken by others. The salesman now came up to him and asked: "Find something you want?" "O, yes, a lot of things I like" replied Dorian. "They're bargains." Dorian needed not to be told that. "They're going fast, too." "Yes, I suppose so." His heart fell as he said it, for he realized that he had no money to buy books. He had come to town to buy shoes, which he badly needed. He glanced down at his old shoes. They were nearly falling to pieces, but they might last a little longer. If he bought the "Conquest of Peru" he would still have two dollars left. Could he buy a pair of shoes for that amount? Very likely but not the kind his mother had told him to get, the kind that were not too heavy or "stogy" looking, but would be "nice" for Sundays. He held tightly on to the two books, while Dickens and Thackeray were still protectingly within his reach. What could he do? Down there in Peru there had been a wonderful people whom Pizarro, the bad, bold Spaniard had conquered and abused.

The development of solar energy has been a crucial aspect of reducing our reliance on fossil fuels and mitigating the effects of climate change. With the increasing energy demands of humanity, it is essential to explore and utilize renewable energy sources, such as solar energy, which is available in abundance and has the potential to meet the world's energy needs. The sun provides an enormous amount of energy to the Earth, with approximately 8 x 10^18 kWh of energy arriving at the surface every year, which is roughly 8000 times greater than the world's energy demand (Roth, 2005). The cost of solar modules has decreased significantly in recent years, mainly due to technological advancements and government support. This has led to a rapid growth in the installation of photovoltaic (PV) systems, with the total installed capacity increasing from 23 GW in 2009 to 117 GW in 2014 (REN21, 2015; IEA, 2014). The decreasing investment costs and technological advancements have also led to a significant increase in the efficiency of solar modules, with some examples showing an increase of 40-90% in the total installed capacity with a 40% decrease in investment costs per year (REN21, 2015; Jager-Waldau et al., 2011; Jager-Waldau, 2013, 2011). Silicon-based crystalline solar modules are the most widely used type of solar module worldwide. However, they are sensitive to temperature fluctuations, which can negatively impact their performance. One effective method of enhancing the performance of solar modules is to cool them down, as water is capable of releasing significant amounts of heat. In this study, a vaporizing cooling system was designed to investigate the effects of cooling on the performance of solar modules. Several factors can influence the efficiency of utilizing solar energy, including temperature fluctuations caused by daily temperature changes and global irradiation (Skoplaki and Palyvos, 2009; Alami, 2014). In Hungarian climatic conditions, the temperature of solar modules can reach 60-70 C during hot days, which can significantly reduce their energy production. However, this issue can be addressed by various cooling technologies (Chandrasekar et al., 2015). According to Bahaidarah et al. (2013, 2016) and Zaoui et al. (2015), the performance of photovoltaic modules is strongly dependent on the temperature of operation. Therefore, it is essential to develop effective cooling systems to mitigate the negative impact of temperature fluctuations on solar module performance. ATRA has been widely used in the treatment of various cancers, including acute promyelocytic leukemia, and has shown promising results in inhibiting cancer cell growth and inducing differentiation. Recent studies have also demonstrated that ATRA can target cancer stem cells in various types of cancer, including breast, lung, and colon cancer. Interestingly, ATRA has been shown to downregulate the expression of CD133 and CD44, two well-known markers of gastric cancer stem cells. Furthermore, ATRA has been reported to inhibit the self-renewal and tumorigenicity of cancer stem cells, suggesting its potential in targeting gastric cancer stem cells. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effect of ATRA on multiple populations of gastric cancer stem cells, including CD133+ and CD44+ cells. We used a combination of in vitro and in vivo experiments to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of ATRA in targeting gastric cancer stem cells. Our results showed that ATRA significantly inhibited the growth and self-renewal of both CD133+ and CD44+ gastric cancer cells, and induced their differentiation into non-cancerous cells. Moreover, ATRA treatment significantly reduced the tumorigenicity of gastric cancer stem cells in a xenograft mouse model. To further explore the underlying mechanisms, we analyzed the expression of key stemness genes, including Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog, in gastric cancer stem cells treated with ATRA. Our results showed that ATRA downregulated the expression of these genes, indicating that ATRA may inhibit the stemness of gastric cancer stem cells by targeting these key transcription factors. In addition, we investigated the effect of ATRA on the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of gastric cancer cells, which is a critical process involved in cancer metastasis. Our results showed that ATRA inhibited the EMT of gastric cancer cells, as evidenced by the downregulation of mesenchymal markers, such as vimentin and N-cadherin, and the upregulation of epithelial markers, such as E-cadherin. Overall, our study demonstrates that ATRA can target multiple populations of gastric cancer stem cells, including CD133+ and CD44+ cells, and inhibit their growth, self-renewal, and tumorigenicity. Our findings suggest that ATRA may be a promising therapeutic agent for the treatment of gastric cancer, and provide new insights into the development of novel strategies for targeting gastric cancer stem cells. Further studies are needed to explore the clinical application of ATRA in gastric cancer therapy. In conclusion, gastric cancer is a fatal and aggressive disease that requires urgent attention and innovative therapeutic strategies. Cancer stem cells, including gastric cancer stem cells, play a crucial role in the initiation, recurrence, and metastasis of cancer. Targeting cancer stem cells, particularly multiple populations of cancer stem cells, may provide a promising approach for improving the therapeutic efficacy of gastric cancer treatment. Our study demonstrates the potential of ATRA in targeting multiple populations of gastric cancer stem cells, and provides new insights into the development of novel therapeutic strategies for gastric cancer treatment.

Visitors here can walk the same grounds where rituals were performed, feeling connected to a lineage stretching back centuries. The allure of Raiatea goes beyond its historical significance; it is the gateway to endless exploration. Boating enthusiasts can navigate the calm waters, exploring the nooks and crannies of this enchanting paradise at their leisure. 6. Huahine. Known as the "secret island," Huahine remains a secluded gem, preserving the Polynesian essence and offering a respite away from bustling tourist trails. Made up of two islands, Huahine Nui and Huahine Iti, connected by a single bridge, this island duo is rich with ancient history and a slower pace of life that invites introspection and relaxation. The island possesses a certain mystique with its expansive archeological sites and traditional fishing villages that dot its coastline. A sense of timelessness pervades Huahine, where ancient legends are etched into the very fabric of the land. The gentle currents of its azure lagoons are ideal for discovering the marine wonders beneath, from vibrant coral gardens to gentle encounters with manta rays. The village of Maeva offers a glimpse into the island's storied past, where remnants of stone fish traps and sacred sites evoke the spiritual depth of this land, holding stories whispered through generations. Huahine, effortlessly combining celestial beauty with cultural richness, remains a haven for those seeking serene seclusion intertwined with the deep roots of Polynesian culture.

The scarlet fever scare was now a thing of the past, and the boys went back to Putnam Hall, to participate in the annual encampment, as told of in "The Rover Boys in Camp." "It will be the outing of our lives," said Tom. "We can just take it easy, and float, and float, and float." The arrangements for the outing were quickly completed. With the Rover boys went their old school chums, "Songbird" Powell, who was always making up doggerel which he called poetry; Hans Mueller, already introduced, and Fred Garrison. A band of dark- complexioned musicians, clad in red trousers, black waistcoats heavily embroidered in sombre colors, and round fur caps, played odd airs upon the deck; while bevies of laughing women, almost all pretty in their light summer gowns, alighted from coupes and barouches, descended the flight of steps leading to the river, and crossed the plank to the boat, with little coquettish graces and studied raising of the skirts, allowing ravishing glimpses of pretty feet and ankles. The defile of merry, witty Parisiennes, with their attendant cavaliers, while the orchestra played the passionate notes of the Hungarian czardas, resembled some vision of a painter, some embarkation for the dreamed-of Cythera, realized by the fancy of an artist, a poet, or a great lord, here in nineteenth century Paris, close to the bridge, across which streamed, like a living antithesis, the realism of crowded cabs, full omnibuses, and hurrying foot-passengers. Prince Andras Zilah had invited his friends, this July morning, to a breakfast in the open air, before the moving panorama of the banks of the Seine. Very well known in Parisian society, which he had sought eagerly with an evident desire to be diverted, like a man who wishes to forget, the former defender of Hungarian independence, the son of old Prince Zilah Sandor, who was the last, in 1849, to hold erect the tattered standard of his country, had been prodigal of his invitations, summoning to his side his few intimate friends, the sharers of his solitude and his privacy, and also the greater part of those chance fugitive acquaintances which the life of Paris inevitably gives, and which are blown away as lightly as they appeared, in a breath of air or a whirlwind. Count Yanski Varhely, the oldest, strongest, and most devoted friend of all those who surrounded the Prince, knew very well why this fanciful idea had come to Andras. At forty-four, the Prince was bidding farewell to his bachelor life: it was no folly, and Yanski saw with delight that the ancient race of the Zilahs, from time immemorial servants of patriotism and the right, was not to be extinct with Prince Andras. Hungary, whose future seemed brightening; needed the Zilahs in the future as she had needed them in the past. "I have only one objection to make to this marriage," said Varhely; "it should have taken place sooner." But a man can not command his heart to love at a given hour. When very young, Andras Zilah had cared for scarcely anything but his country; and, far from her, in the bitterness of exile, he had returned to the passion of his youth, living in Paris only upon memories of his Hungary. He had allowed year after year to roll by, without thinking of establishing a home of his own by marriage.

But even we can be caught out by clever marketing and unclear labelling. It's not just vegetarians who are affected, either. Anyone with dietary restrictions or preferences, whether it's gluten-free, halal, or kosher, deserves to know exactly what they're consuming. The lack of transparency in food labelling is a widespread problem. Take, for example, the popular snack, Quavers. The cheese flavour variety contains no actual cheese, instead relying on a blend of milk protein and flavour enhancers. Similarly, the 'meat' in some popular sandwiches is actually a mixture of reconstituted chicken protein and water. It's not just the ingredients that are misleading - the nutritional information can be just as deceptive. Some breakfast cereals, for instance, claim to be high in fibre, but the fibre content comes from added artificial ingredients rather than whole grains. And what about the 'whole grain' label itself? It can be slapped on a product even if it contains as little as 3% whole grain content. The food industry's defence is that they're not breaking any rules, and that all the information is available to consumers - if they take the time to read the small print. But that's not good enough. Shoppers have a right to know what they're buying, and companies have a responsibility to be honest and transparent about their products. The solution is simple: clearer labelling and more stringent regulations. If a product doesn't contain the ingredient it's named after, it shouldn't be allowed to claim it does. And nutritional information should be presented in a clear, easy-to-understand format, rather than hidden in tiny print on the back of the packet. Until then, consumers will continue to be misled, and the food industry will continue to profit from their deception. It's time for change, and it's time for companies to come clean about what's really in their products. In the meantime, shoppers can take matters into their own hands by being more vigilant about what they buy. Check the ingredients, read the labels, and don't be afraid to contact the manufacturer if you're unsure. And if you're really concerned, consider switching to products from companies that prioritize transparency and honesty. The power is in our hands, and it's time we started using it. By demanding better from the food industry, we can create a more honest and transparent market, where consumers know exactly what they're getting - and what they're not getting.

Batman swiftly follows, their boots skidding over the polished marble of the museum's floor as they pursue the mammoth vehicle. "We've got to stop him before he reaches the water mains," Batman warns, his voice a resolute reminder of the stakes at hand. Freeze, within his colossal but cumbersome contraption, glances back through frosted over glass at the oncoming duo. "Fools," he growls, turning his attention back to the task at hand. With a flick of his wrist, levers are pulled, gears groan, and the drill powers up once more, the noise deafening. Outside, Gotham's skyline looms ahead, a witness to the impending chaos as the drilling truck bursts from the confines of the museum. Traffic screeches to a halt, horns blaring in frustrated dissonance as drivers witness the mechanical behemoth impose its will on the crowded streets. Batman leaps onto the back of the machine, his grappling hook a spider's web of intention over the icy metal. Robin follows, his acrobatics a blur beside the steadier form of his mentor. "Time for a crash course in cold justice," Robin shouts over the din, his enthusiasm unwavering in the face of danger. Batman nods, focused. "Stop him from reaching the reservoir," he commands. "I'll override the controls." Inside, Freeze senses them, his scanners picking up their life signs. With a cold smile, he mutters, "Let's see how well you dance on ice." His fingers fly over switches and buttons, the cryogenic systems activating within the truck, chilling the air to sub-zero temperatures. Robin moves first, slipping through openings, his approach a combination of parkour and kinesthetic intuition. He lands near the controls, fingers already working to undo Freeze's modifications. But the villain was ready. The deck beneath Robin's feet erupts into frost, threatening to engulf him. Batman, meanwhile, wrestles with a panel, sparks flying as he works to dismantle it. Focus etched on his face, the need to protect the city pushing him onward. Freeze, with his grip tightening on the diamond, watches them, his anger palpable. "This city's fate is sealed," he declares, the drilling truck's vibrations matching the tremor in his steely voice. But Batman and Robin are undeterred. They are more than just Gotham's champions; they're family, their teamwork a symphony of strength against the cold despair Freeze offers. "Robin! Now!" Batman's voice is the signal; Robin flips a master switch. The truck shudders, the icy grip on its systems relinquishing as control returns to the heroes, their resolve as unyielding as the Bat-signal's guiding light in Gotham's night.

My life was a series of cycles too, stretching from one dreary task to another, much like a second-rate hamster in an endless wheel. Each tick of the office clock was a personal metronome counting out the rhythm of my mediocrity. Beneath the harsh fluorescent lights, I drowned in the monotony, surrounded by the cacophony of clacking keyboards and interwoven telephone rings-a symphony of despair, punctuated by the occasional outburst from Janice. I sipped my tepid coffee, now as stale as my career prospects, and considered the fact that being ordinary had always been inevitable. I was like a paperclip-useful, perhaps, but easily replaceable. Rochelle's birthday had been the only highlight of the year so far. Even that small joy had been tarnished by my own incapacity to muster anything more than a meager contribution to the office birthday fund. Not like Rochelle would notice my absence, but still, it was symbolic. A nod to the veneer of camaraderie we all wore like cheap cologne. Just as these thoughts spiraled into a chasm of self-pity, the name Henry Helms shot through my memories like an errant bullet. The revelation was as abrupt as it had been back then-a name dropped in passing, like a pebble into a deep well. The repercussions were swiftly collapsing circles that threatened to engulf everything in which I merely subsisted. Helms had been digging up dirt, sifting through the societal refuse that others turned a blind eye to. He was on the cusp of unleashing truths that the power elite feared. Five assassination attempts. The tally stuck in my mind, a grim ledger spiraling toward some irrevocable conclusion. I was no stranger to danger lurking at the edges of my humdrum existence. The danger was like storm clouds visible on a distant horizon. Immensely real, yet far enough to almost be ignored. Almost. But Wesley Gibson, the sound of my own name never stopped resonating like a warning siren in an otherwise silent night. A spectral promise of potential that seemed almost absurd in the monotonous reality of my day-to-day survival-except it wasn't. Somewhere, beneath layers of averageness and the numbing predictability of the office circus, something was stirring, something as fresh as over-brewed ambition masked in beige-toned normalcy. I leaned back in my chair, hands stretching lazily above my head, a gesture more out of habit than defiance. My mind danced between the deciding pulses of nothingness and action. I thought of Cathy with her perfunctory nods of greetings and Barry's laughter that grated my nerves. The illusion of kinship was dissolving as I sat there, etching out threads of personal consequence in my workplace universe. A decision needed to be made-not later, not tomorrow, but like everything in my life, it would demand its due before the stark indifference of today ended. Janice's voice was now a distant echo, drowned by the tidal force of newfound resolve. The cycles had to break, just like business cycles. It was no longer a choice but an imperative. And maybe, just once, I wouldn't be the paperclip, bent into submission. Maybe, just for once, I could be the binder-in control, anchoring the chaos into coherence.

It's as if the urgency of the moment has finally given people the courage to shed the euphemisms and speak plainly about the realities of abortion. For Cynthia Nixon, this shift is long overdue. As she puts it, "We've been dancing around this issue for far too long, using language that's too polite, too vague, too sanitized. We need to call it what it is: a medical procedure that can be a matter of life and death." Cynthia's own story, of course, is deeply personal. Her mother's experience with illegal abortion is a testament to the dangers of criminalizing women's bodies. But it's also a reminder that the fight for reproductive rights is not just about abstract principles or political ideologies - it's about real people, real lives, and real bodies. As we sit down to talk, I ask Cynthia about the moment she decided to share her mother's story with the world. "It was a moment of reckoning," she says. "I realized that I had been given a platform, and I had a responsibility to use it to speak truth to power. My mother's story is not unique, but it's one that needs to be told. We need to humanize this issue, to put faces and names to the statistics and the rhetoric." Cynthia's campaign for governor may not have been successful, but it marked a turning point in the way we talk about abortion. It showed that even in the most unlikely of places - the world of politics - we can find courage, vulnerability, and honesty. And it reminded us that the fight for reproductive rights is not just about winning elections or passing laws - it's about creating a culture that values women's lives, women's bodies, and women's autonomy. As our conversation winds down, I ask Cynthia what she hopes people take away from her story, from her mother's story. "I hope they understand that this is not just about abortion," she says. "It's about the fundamental human right to make decisions about our own bodies, our own lives. It's about dignity, autonomy, and justice. And it's about time we started talking about it in a way that's honest, raw, and unapologetic." The coat hanger, that stark and haunting symbol of the pre-Roe era, is a reminder of what's at stake. But it's also a reminder of the power of storytelling, of the power of women's voices, and of the power of truth-telling. As Cynthia Nixon so eloquently puts it, "We don't need to put tablecloths and doilies on these issues. We need to call them what they are, and we need to fight for a world where every woman can live with dignity, respect, and autonomy."

"He does not need me, but he may - he will one day; and then I shall be ready. But now - " Old Soolsby's face turned away. His house overlooked every house in the valley beneath: he could see nearly every garden; he could even recognise many in the far streets. Besides, there hung along two nails on the wall a telescope, relic of days when he sailed the main. The grounds of the Cloistered House and the fruit-decked garden-wall of the Red Mansion were ever within his vision. Once, twice, thrice, he had seen what he had seen, and dark feelings, harsh emotions, had been roused in him. "He will need us both - the Egyptian will need us both one day," he answered now; "you more than any, me because I can help him, too - ay, I can help him. But married or single you could help him; so why waste your days here?" "Is it wasting my days to stay with my father? He is lonely, most lonely since our Davy went away; and troubled, too, for the dangers of that life yonder. His voice used to shake when he prayed, in those days when Davy was away in the desert, down at Darfur and elsewhere among the rebel tribes. He frightened me then, he was so stern and still. Ah, but that day when we knew he was safe, I was eighteen, and no more!" she added, smiling. "But, think you, I could marry while my life is so tied to him and to our Egyptian?" "I hardly thought you would wait for me, Claude. You are very patient." "I would wait twice seven years for only one look at your face," he rejoined. "Would you?" interrogated the girl wearily. "I would not wait so long even for a fairy prince." She sat down on the heather-covered bank, and took off her hat. She fanned herself with it for a few minutes, and then flung it carelessly among the flowers. "You do not seem very enraptured at seeing me, Hyacinth," said the young lover reproachfully. The girl sighed wearily. "I do not believe I could go into a rapture over any thing in the world," she broke out. "I am so tired of my life - so tired of it, Claude, that I do not believe I could get up an interest in a single thing." "I hope you feel some little interest in me," he said. "I - I - I cannot tell. I think even bitterest pain would be better than the dead monotony that is killing me." She remembered those words in after years, and repented of them when repentance was in vain. "Surely you might smile now," said Claude. "I hope you do not find sitting by my side on this lovely evening monotonous." She laughed, but the laugh had no music in it. "No, I cannot say that I do; but you are going away soon, you tell me, and then the only gleam of sunshine in my life will fade, and all will be darkness again." A central heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) system is widely used in large buildings, such as office buildings, commercial buildings and shopping centres [18]. The HVAC systems are the largest energy end use in the non-residential sector [3] where inefficient operation and maintenance of the HVAC system can cause energy wastage, customer complaints, poor indoor air quality and even environmental damage [19]. In order to achieve energy efficiency in buildings, the energy optimisation of HVAC systems is particularly important [20] where the energy performance of such systems is affected by operating conditions as well as time sensitivity to a building's heating and cooling energy needs. According to Cho et al. [20] an energy evaluation methodology based on quantifying the energy consumption characteristics of HVAC systems may be used by engineers and designers to assess the effectiveness and economic benefits of HVAC systems. Electric lighting is one area where energy savings are possible at reasonable cost in new buildings as well as in retrofit projects. According to Dubois and Blomsterberg [21] some barriers to these energy savings may be related to the difficulty to switch-off lights at night due to extended office hours, user-acceptance issues related to the proposed low light levels or to the occupancy switch-off and daylight dimming control systems. The UK government is committed to an 80% reduction in CO2 emissions by the year 2050 [5]. According to the UK Green Building Council [9] there is almost twice as much potential for cost-effective carbon mitigation in the built environment in comparison to any other sector. The UK government has begun targeting the non-domestic sector with increasingly stringent building regulations and methods of measuring as-built and operational performance, such as energy performance certificates (EPCs) and display energy certificates (DECs) [22]. Although these initiatives are likely to improve the performance of buildings detailed knowledge of the non-domestic building stock is still limited [23]. Practically, energy consumption in non-domestic buildings is a very complex organisational issue due to the heterogeneity of activities (for e.g. as lecture halls, laboratories, and offices) that take place as well as the energy services such as HVAC, domestic hot water (DHW), lighting, refrigeration and food preparation [3,6]. Achieving a balance poses a challenge: on the one hand, to consume energy to satisfactorily meet the energy needs of users and maintain comfort standards and on the other hand, to minimise energy consumption through effective organisational energy management [12]. Universities in the UK consume significant amounts of energy [24,25] and according to new legislation [26], most of the UK's colleges and universities are now required to report on their energy use and improve their efficiency. The energy demand behaviour in university buildings are less well understood than other non-domestic buildings including schools and offices [27,28]. Reducing energy use is impossible without good data on which to make management and investment decisions [9].

Slack began its life as a quick-and-easy tool created so Butterfield, Henderson and the team could communicate with one and other while they built the real project, a game called Glitch. When Glitch just wasn't happening, they gave up. But kept working on Slack. They'd previously worked together on another project, a online mulitplayer title called Game Neverending. Here too they created a tool to help with the game's development. Again, the game failed, but the tool remained - it became Flickr, a photo-sharing site eventually bought by Yahoo for $40m. It's this ability to snatch success from the jaws of failure that breeds great companies in Silicon Valley, Henderson says. "One of the things that's pretty obvious as a Brit when you move to California is that the isn't a lot of cynicism here. "The British attitude towards failure is 'oh you're going to fail, you may as well not try'. "That just doesn't exist here." On the wall in the SoftTech VC office is a poster celebrating the venture capital firm's 10th anniversary. It's covered with the logos of the companies in which SoftTech has invested millions. "Onwards and upwards," reads a scribbled message next to the logo for fitness tracker firm FitBit. Venture capital is the lifeblood of any start-up ecosystem, and there's more of it here than anywhere else. It's a big gamble throwing money at ideas when you know most are destined to fail. And yet, just shy of $60bn was spent doing just that in the US last year. Andy McCloughlin looks after $100m-worth of that kitty. He's been a partner at SoftTech VC since March 2015. His job is to whittle through the pitches from eager entrepreneurs at a rate of about 10 a week, settling on a privileged few who'll get what they call "early stage" funding. The idea is to invest "just" a few million for a small stake in a company that might hit the big time. More often than not, they don't - but the ones that do soar and make it worth it. That balance of risk to reward puts off British money, McLoughlin tells me. "[Silicon Valley] is just this magical place where people have made money and rather than disappearing into the Cotswolds like perhaps people used to do in the UK, they're staying very active in the ecosystem and putting that money back in. "Success begets success, and we just see this continuous virtuous cycle." McLouglin's route to Silicon Valley is also a troubling indicator for the UK tech industry. He co-founded Huddle, a workplace document-sharing and collaboration business, in 2006. When the time came to raise serious money, he felt he had no choice but to relocate to San Francisco (though the company still has a significant presence in London).

In the ample chimney of that which served for the common room, was burning a bright flame of pine knots; for, although it was the middle of summer, the sun sank so early behind the hills, and the evenings were so chilly, that the warmth was necessary, and the light from the small window cheered the laborer returning late from his work. An old man sat by the chimney, evidently resting from the labors of the day. He was bent by time, but his brilliant eye and his flowing gray locks gave a certain refinement to his appearance, beyond that which his homely garments would warrant. A woman, apparently as aged as himself, sat by the little window, catching the last rays of evening, as they were reflected from her white cap and silvery hair. Before her was a table on which lay a large Bible. She had just placed her spectacles between the leaves, as she closed it and resumed her knitting. These two formed a picture full of the quiet repose of old age. But there was another in the room, - a youth, apparently less than twenty, kneeling before the flaming pine, over the leaves of a worn volume that absorbed him wholly. The ruddy flame imparted the glow of health to a countenance habitually pale. Over his dark, enthusiastic eye was spread a clear and noble brow, so smooth and polished that it seemed as if at seventy it would be as unwrinkled as at seventeen. His piercing eye had that depth of expression that indicates dark passions or religious melancholy. He was slender in form, and very tall; but a bend in the shoulders, produced by agricultural labor, or by weakness in the chest, impaired somewhat the symmetry of his form. They had been silent some moments. The young man closed his worn volume, an imperfect copy of Virgil, and walked several times, with hurried steps, across the little room. At length he stopped before the woman, and said, "Mother, let me see how much your frugal care has hoarded. Let me know all our wealth. Unless I can procure another book, I cannot be prepared for the approaching examination. If I cannot enter college the next term, I never can. I must give up all hope of ever being any thing but the drudge I am now, and of living and dying in this narrow nook of earth." "No, no, my son," answered the woman; "if my prayers are heard, you will be a light and a blessing to the church, though I may not live to see it." The young man sighed deeply, and, taking the key she gave him, he opened an old-fashioned chest, and, from a little cup of silver tied over with a piece of leather, he poured the contents into his hand. In recent years, there has been a growing recognition of the need to better understand the complex relationships between protected areas, recreation, and local communities. This is particularly important in developing countries, where protected areas are often established with the primary goal of conserving biodiversity, but may also have significant potential to generate economic benefits for local communities (Adams et al., 2004). However, the benefits of protected areas are not always evenly distributed, and local communities may bear significant costs associated with conservation efforts, such as restrictions on land use and access to natural resources (Borrini-Feyerabend et al., 2013). In order to optimize the economic benefits of protected areas, it is essential to understand the preferences and behaviors of visitors. This can be achieved through the use of stated preference surveys, which ask respondents to indicate their willingness to pay for specific attributes of protected areas, such as scenic beauty, wildlife viewing opportunities, or recreational facilities (Hanley et al., 2001). Travel cost models can also be used to estimate the economic value of recreation in protected areas, by analyzing the relationship between the cost of travel and the number of visitors (Neher et al., 2013). In addition to understanding visitor preferences, it is also important to consider the role of protected areas in supporting local economies. This can be achieved through the development of sustainable tourism initiatives, which aim to maximize the economic benefits of tourism while minimizing its environmental and social impacts (Fennell, 2008). Sustainable tourism can provide a range of benefits, including job creation, income generation, and infrastructure development, as well as promoting cross-cultural understanding and environmental awareness (Honey, 2008). However, the development of sustainable tourism initiatives in protected areas is not without its challenges. One of the key issues is the need to balance the economic benefits of tourism with the conservation goals of protected areas (Buckley, 2009). This requires careful planning and management, to ensure that tourism activities do not harm the environment or disrupt the conservation of biodiversity (Newsome et al., 2013). Another challenge is the need to ensure that the benefits of tourism are equitably distributed among local communities, and that they are not concentrated among a small elite (Ashley, 2006). In conclusion, the economic benefits of recreation in protected areas are significant, and can play an important role in supporting local economies and promoting biodiversity conservation. However, realizing these benefits requires careful planning and management, to ensure that protected areas are designed to align with visitor preferences, and that the benefits of tourism are equitably distributed among local communities. By adopting a sustainable tourism approach, protected areas can provide a range of benefits, including job creation, income generation, and infrastructure development, while also promoting cross-cultural understanding and environmental awareness. The use of lignocellulosic biomass as a feedstock for anaerobic digestion (AD) has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential to produce energy-rich methane gas. The annual global production of dry biomass exceeds 2.00 1011 t, making it a promising feedstock for biogas production (Kumar et al., 2008). The biodegradation of lignocellulosic biomass depends on its chemical structure, primarily on the cellulose content, hemicellulose, lignin, and C/N ratio (Karthikeyan and Visvanathan, 2013). Residue grass is a type of lignocellulosic biomass that can be profitably used for the production of bioenergy in biorefineries (Nimmanterdwong et al., 2017). The average production of 500 / 600 m3 of biogas per t of VS can be achieved from the AD of residue grass (Mattioli et al., 2017). The methane content of the generated biogas ranges between 52% and 56%, similar to maize silage (L.E.E. SARL, 2018), which is often used in biogas plants (Bull, 2008). The use of riverbank grass as a feedstock for AD has also shown promising results. Boscaro et al. (2018) found that the higher biomass yields could be achieved in low-nature quality areas and nutrient-rich soils. The advantages of using riverbank grass include its high cellulose content, which can increase the biogas yield, and its low C/N ratio, which can reduce the need for additional nutrients (Boscaro et al., 2018). In addition to residue grass and riverbank grass, other types of lignocellulosic biomass can also be used for AD. For example, agricultural waste, such as corn stover and wheat straw, can be used as a feedstock for biogas production (Kumar et al., 2008). The use of agricultural waste for AD can reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills and can also provide a renewable source of energy. The use of lignocellulosic biomass for AD has several advantages over other types of biomass. For example, it can produce a higher biogas yield than other types of biomass, such as animal manure (Neshat et al., 2017). Additionally, lignocellulosic biomass can be used as a carbon-neutral feedstock, which can help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions (Karthikeyan and Visvanathan, 2013). However, there are also some challenges associated with the use of lignocellulosic biomass for AD. For example, the pretreatment of the biomass can be difficult and expensive, and the biodegradation of the biomass can be slow (Karthikeyan and Visvanathan, 2013). Additionally, the use of lignocellulosic biomass can also produce a higher amount of CO2 emissions than other types of biomass (Neshat et al., 2017). In conclusion, the use of lignocellulosic biomass as a feedstock for anaerobic digestion has several advantages and disadvantages. The advantages include the potential to produce a higher biogas yield than other types of biomass, the ability to use a carbon-neutral feedstock, and the potential to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills.

PFPs can be classified into two large groups -PFPs and -PFPs, based on the structures utilized to form a membrane-integrated pore ( -helices or -barrels) and these mechanisms can be classified with a high rate of accuracy through the use of bioinformatics (Dal Peraro and van der Goot, 2016). -PFPs potentially provide a diverse source of new insecticidal proteins for commercial pest control in a wide variety of crops. Safety of -PFPs in crops used for food and feed is demonstrated by the safe use of a binary toxin complex that includes Cry35Ab1, a Toxin 10 family -PFP. Cry35Ab1 works together with a non- -PFP partner protein Cry34Ab1 to control coleopteran pest species such as corn rootworms, yet this binary protein complex is safe for humans and animals as evidenced by its narrow activity spectrum, digestibility, empirical mammalian safety data, and safe use on millions of acres in the U.S. annually since 2006 (Juberg et al., 2009; Moar et al., 2017). -PFP safety is also supported by the presence of these proteins in safely consumed foods including: spinach, cucumber, wheat, and fish such as cod and tilapia (Moar et al., 2017). A variety of insects can cause significant damage to cotton crops. Currently, commercial cotton varieties expressing Bt proteins provide excellent control of traditional cotton pests such as lepidopteran insects, but have limited efficacy for control of hemipteran insects that are emerging as economically important pests of cotton in the United States. The Bt protein Cry51Aa2 was shown to have insecticidal activity against two hemipteran pests in cotton; Lygus lineolaris and Lygus hesperus (Baum et al., 2012). Cry51Aa2 is a member of the expansive ETX MTX2 -PFP protein family and accordingly shares a similar structure (Fig. 1) and general functional similarity with a number of other insecticidal Cry proteins and ETX MTX2 members. Millions of pounds of biopesticides that contain the -PFPs Cry60Aa1 and Cry60Ba1 from Bt israeliensis and the -PFPs BinB, MTX2, and MTX3 from Lysinobacillus sphaericus have been widely used to control mosquitoes in the U.S. and have been extensively used in potable water to control disease vector mosquitoes and blackflies in Africa (Moar et al., 2017). This demonstrates their history of safe use and strongly supports the safety of this structural class of insecticidal proteins for use in GM crops. Although Cry51Aa2 is a member of the ETX MTX2 -pore forming protein family (Moar et al., 2017), this protein has significant sequence divergence from other ETX MTX2 family members, enabling its specificity and limiting its activity spectrum (Bachman et al., 2017), thereby limiting its potential to impact non-target organisms. Enhancing control of Lygus pests to a commercial level of efficacy was achieved through selected amino acid modifications (i.e. selective substitutions and deletions) to the Cry51Aa2 protein, which substantially increased the insecticidal activity of the resulting variant Cry51Aa2.834 16 relative to the wild-type Cry51Aa2 protein (Gowda et al., 2016).

Say you are in the country; in some high land of lakes. Take almost any path you please, and ten to one it carries you down in a dale, and leaves you there by a pool in the stream. There is magic in it. Let the most absent-minded of men be plunged in his deepest reveries-stand that man on his legs, set his feet a-going, and he will infallibly lead you to water, if water there be in all that region. Should you ever be athirst in the great American desert, try this experiment, if your caravan happen to be supplied with a metaphysical professor. Yes, as every one knows, meditation and water are wedded for ever. But here is an artist. He desires to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting bit of romantic landscape in all the valley of the Saco. What is the chief element he employs? There stand his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as if a hermit and a crucifix were within; and here sleeps his meadow, and there sleep his cattle; and up from yonder cottage goes a sleepy smoke. Deep into distant woodlands winds a mazy way, reaching to overlapping spurs of mountains bathed in their hill-side blue. But though the picture lies thus tranced, and though this pine-tree shakes down its sighs like leaves upon this shepherd's head, yet all were vain, unless the shepherd's eye were fixed upon the magic stream before him. Go visit the Prairies in June, when for scores on scores of miles you wade knee-deep among Tiger-lilies-what is the one charm wanting?- Water there is not a drop of water there! Were Niagara but a cataract of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, upon suddenly receiving two handfuls of silver, deliberate whether to buy him a coat, which he sadly needed, or invest his money in a pedestrian trip to Rockaway Beach? Why is almost every robust healthy boy with a robust healthy soul in him, at some time or other crazy to go to sea? Why upon your first voyage as a passenger, did you yourself feel such a mystical vibration, when first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the old Persians hold the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it a separate deity, and own brother of Jove? Surely all this is not without meaning. And still deeper the meaning of that story of Narcissus, who because he could not grasp the tormenting, mild image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and was drowned. But that same image, we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

The similarity in structure and position across different taxa has led to the suggestion that apical organs might be homologous, but this hypothesis is still a topic of ongoing debate (Nielsen, 2005a; Raff, 2008; Sly et al., 2003). A thorough understanding of the developmental genetic mechanisms underlying apical organ formation and function is essential to resolve this question. Recent studies have shed light on the molecular mechanisms controlling apical organ development in a few model organisms. For example, in the sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, the transcription factor Six3 is required for the specification of apical organ precursors (Cameron et al., 2006). Similarly, in the mollusk Patella vulgata, the Wnt/ -catenin signaling pathway has been implicated in the formation of the apical organ (Kempf et al., 1997). These findings suggest that conserved developmental genetic mechanisms might be involved in the formation of apical organs across different taxa. However, the conservation of developmental genetic mechanisms does not necessarily imply homology. The same signaling pathways and transcription factors can be co-opted for different purposes in different organisms, a phenomenon known as developmental gene regulatory network (dGRN) co-option (Davidson and Erwin, 2006). Therefore, it is crucial to integrate molecular data with morphological and phylogenetic analyses to infer the evolutionary relationships between apical organs. Phylogenetic reconstructions have revealed that apical organs are present in a wide range of animal groups, but their distribution is not universal. For example, apical organs are absent in some deuterostomes, such as vertebrates and tunicates (Nielsen, 2012). This patchy distribution could be due to secondary loss or modification of apical organs in certain lineages. Alternatively, it is possible that apical organs evolved independently in different animal groups, a scenario supported by the presence of distinct apical organ morphologies and functions across taxa. In conclusion, the question of whether apical organs share a common evolutionary origin remains an open one. While similarities in structure, position, and developmental genetic mechanisms suggest a possible homology, the patchy distribution and diverse functions of apical organs across different animal groups argue against a simple, universal explanation. Further studies are needed to resolve this question, including comparative analyses of apical organ development and function across a broader range of taxa, as well as more detailed phylogenetic reconstructions of animal relationships. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the evolution of apical organs will provide valuable insights into the development and diversification of animal life cycles.

On our campus, we built shanties and held protests, teach-ins and sit-ins. During that time, it seemed not only useless, but inappropriate to continue to got to class, study, exercise, wash and eat. Every quotidian act felt like a slide toward co-optation. The need to be political was so total and unremitting that it seems fitting to use the word "a calling" with its religious connotations. I feel that calling again now. And yet, I am acutely aware that the Iraq situation falls rather conviently for me. Having recently decided to become a political theorist, what better opportunity than a political crisis to define myself and my work? Because of the convenience of the issue to my career aspirations, I am doubly suspicious of my ability to interpret evidence. Am I selecting what I want to see (whether consciously or unconsciously the effect seems to be the same)? Am I denying any evidence that contradicts my interpretation? What evidence would have to appear for me to change my mind about the situation? Moreover, what is the appropriate response given my reservations regarding my calling? I want to be careful to neither abandon the call nor invent a myth of urgency to suit my own illusions or interests. "Mieux vaut avoir tort avec Sartre, que raison avec Aron!" (Better to be wrong with Sartre than right with Aaron!" is a mantra that frequently sounds in my head. It's a phrase that political activists chanted in France during the uprisings in 1968. The question was whether to support Communism with Jean Paul Sartre, a communist, or oppose it with Raymond Aron, a conservative. Sartre, a charismatic public figure and persuasive writer, won "blind" support for communism in the face of mounting evidence that Russia and other communist states were abusive, totalitarian regimes. Aron, who had evidence on his side, failed to communicate his criticisms of communism to those who were "called" to politics with Sartre, mostly because Aron was a "square". The lesson I have drawn from this scenario is that it is difficult and important to be both receptive and critical of ALL evidence - evidence that supports and undermines my current position. I don't think that it is possible, nor desirable, to live a life free of opinion (although it is an interesting exercise to try). I believe, however, that I - like most people - hold too many opinions, arrive at them hastily and cling to them tenaciously. Perhaps in general it is useful to our survival that we are tenacious and complacent. It seems to me, however, that at times our quality of life and survival are threatened by complacency.

"Why not? What can I do better with it?" "Live here, man! live here! - as I do at Temple Grove. You will never find another residence like it. To be sure, it wants some additions, and would require a few thousand pounds to put it into perfect repair; but it is worth the expense. No, don't sell it; only marry, and bring a young lady here, who will love the very walls because she lives within them." "My dear sir, I am not inclined to marry; besides, even if I were, I doubt whether I should choose to reside here. I have seen enough of the world to feel the necessity of living in it. A retired life is well enough for men whose minds are made up, whose habits are fixed, and whose opinions are settled. But I want excitement, and I must seek it where it is most easily found. I feel myself again a boy, with all the boyish thirst for novelty, adventure, and pleasure; and the world is the best school for the sort of education I desire." "You are right," said Cleveland, thoughtfully; "it is the best school for the education you desire. I was about to advise you differently; but perhaps I ought rather to congratulate you. For you are now in the prime of life, and you have youth, health, wealth, and talents. Your father's death has removed all obstacles to your enjoyment of these advantages, and you are free to follow the bent of your own inclination. If you prefer London to the country, you are quite right. If you wish to travel, you are equally wise. Do whatever you please; and depend upon it, you will find yourself happy." "But, my dear sir, I have not said that I wished to be happy." "Not wish to be happy!" repeated Cleveland, in surprise. "No; I wish to be amused. Happiness implies rest; amusement, motion. I wish to keep my mind constantly occupied, and, above all things, to avoid reflection. I wish to learn something new every day, and to forget something old. I wish to lead a gay, active, stirring life, and to leave happiness alone till I grow old and tired of everything else." "What a strange theory!" exclaimed Cleveland. "Is this the result of your travels? Is this the wisdom you have brought back from your wanderings?" "It is the only wisdom that suits my temper, and the only philosophy that does not revolt my understanding. Why, my dear sir, if I wished to be happy, I must first ask myself, 'What is happiness?' And then I should discover that, according to my notions, happiness consists in the perpetual gratification of desires. Now, how many of our desires are it possible to gratify? Take ambition, for instance. How often does it happen that the ambitious man attains the object of his wishes, and finds himself miserable afterwards? Look at the great conquerors and heroes of history. They have attained the end of their career, and what follows? Disappointment, satiety, disgust. Caesar, after conquering the world, killed himself in despair. Napoleon, having realized his wildest dreams of power, languished in exile. Alexander wept because there were no more worlds to subjugate. And so with the other passions. Love, when satisfied, becomes indifference; jealousy, envy, revenge, hatred, are appeased and die away, leaving a void behind them. Then comes remorse, the terrible avenger of crime; and regret, the sad companion of misfortune.
