Two years later, Mavis and their two children, together with domestic staff from Government House, were sheltering in friends' homes in Stanley while battle raged, and her portly husband was facing the invaders - incredibly - with a pistol. Everything that had led to this moment was astonishing, both militarily and diplomatically. First, the cynical FO had sent him there expecting this comfortable, mature family man to convince the islanders that their best interests would be served if they drifted away from Britain (7,000 miles away) and accepted Argentine sovereignty just across the water. Successive British governments, anxious to divest themselves of what they knew was potential trouble, had been considering relinquishing the British Dependency since the mid-Sixties. Argentina, of course, had been claiming sovereignty for 150 years. The Foreign Office saw Hunt as the ideal man, as he put it, 'to gain the islanders' confidence and talk them into accepting a lease-back solution with Argentina'. What happened, instead, was that Sir Rex found himself sympathising with their wish to remain British. As he wrote in his memoir, My Falkland Days: 'I had previously determined that if it should ever reach the stage that the FCO instructed me to pursue a policy that I believed to be against the best interests of the Falkland islanders, I should have no alternative but to resign.' Defiant: Sir Rex pictured with the Duke of York (left) who fought during the Falklands conflict as a naval helicopter pilot in 1982 and with then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and her husband Sir Denis after the war in which Britain reclaimed them from Argentina (right) Sir Rex held discussions with the 1,800 islanders who made their feelings very clear: they were British and wanted to stay British. For his part, Hunt saw it as his moral duty to represent their views to London, not London's views to them. As long as they wanted to stay British, their rights were the same as any other British people. Back at the Foreign Office, there was near apoplexy. Hunt had 'gone native'. It wasn't long before the then Tory Defence Secretary, John Nott, was announcing the withdrawal of the British Antarctic survey ship, the Endurance. It was ostensibly part of defence cuts, but the islanders saw it as a first indication of British withdrawal. Whether or not it really was an invitation to the Argentine navy, as they suspected, on March 19, 1982, a party of Argentine 'scrap metal merchants' landed on South Georgia, a tiny British island 800 miles east of the Falklands, and hoisted an Argentine flag. Rex was not only governor, he was also commander-in-chief of the Falklands, so he ordered a unit of Marines to remove them. To his astonishment, this was countermanded in London by Foreign Secretary Lord Carrington. On March 31, the Foreign Office learned that an Argentine fleet had set sail for the Falkland Islands with orders to seize them.

The challenges associated with the valorization of lignin are multifaceted, and the development of efficient and sustainable conversion pathways is crucial for the widespread adoption of lignin as a feedstock for the production of fuels and chemicals. One of the primary obstacles is the complex structure of lignin, which is composed of a mixture of aromatic and aliphatic compounds, making it difficult to convert into valuable products. Additionally, the variability in lignin composition and amount across different biomass sources can affect the efficiency and yield of conversion processes. Despite these challenges, researchers have made significant progress in developing novel conversion technologies and strategies to valorize lignin. For instance, the use of ionic liquids as solvents has been shown to be effective in dissolving and depolymerizing lignin, allowing for the production of a range of chemicals and fuels. Similarly, the application of enzymes and microorganisms has been explored as a means of breaking down lignin and releasing its constituent monomers. Another promising approach is the use of catalytic processes, such as hydrogenolysis and hydrolysis, to convert lignin into valuable chemicals and fuels. These processes involve the use of metal catalysts or enzymes to break down the lignin molecule into smaller fragments, which can then be further converted into desired products. For example, the hydrogenolysis of lignin has been shown to produce a range of aromatic compounds, including phenol and guaiacol, which can be used as building blocks for the production of a variety of chemicals and materials. In addition to these technological advancements, the development of sustainable and scalable production processes is critical for the widespread adoption of lignin as a feedstock. This includes the use of biomass feedstocks that are readily available and cost-effective, as well as the development of efficient and low-energy conversion processes. Furthermore, the integration of lignin conversion processes with other biorefinery operations, such as cellulose and hemicellulose conversion, can help to create a more sustainable and circular bioeconomy. The valorization of lignin has the potential to play a significant role in the transition to a more sustainable and renewable energy future. As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of climate change and energy security, the development of innovative and sustainable conversion technologies for lignin is critical. By leveraging the unique properties of lignin and the advances in biotechnology and catalysis, we can unlock the potential of this abundant and renewable resource and create a more sustainable and circular bioeconomy.

It has been widely demonstrated that an algorithm performing well in one lake or type of lake may not prove transferable to another lake or another type of lake and vice versa (Kallio et al., 2001; Matthews, 2011; Odermatt, Gitelson, Brando, & Schaepman, 2012), and site-specific and regional validation is therefore very important. Several of the algorithms listed above have been evaluated individually and in various combinations in terms of their retrieval performance for a number of parameters and for diverse lake conditions. Binding, Greenberg, Jerome, Bukata, and Letourneau (2010) applied the C2R, FLH, and MCI algorithms, with and without the "smile effect" (caused by slight variation in centre wavelength for a given band across the MERIS field-of-view (Bourg, D'Alba, & Colagrande, 2008)) correction and Improved Contrast between Ocean and Land (ICOL) processors applied, to evaluate chl-a retrieval from MERIS imagery of Lake of the Woods (Canada/USA) during an intense algal bloom, and also compared these with the standard MERIS algal 2 product. A validation of the C2R, EUL and BL processors' atmospheric correction, IOPs and water quality constituents (chl-a, gelbstoff absorbance, and total suspended matter) was carried out over several European and African lakes by Koponen et al. Odermatt, Pomati, et al. (2012) report validation results of C2R, EUL and FUB WeW with ICOL applied for Greifensee (Switzerland), including the consideration of in situ measurements at various depths and locally-tuned coefficients relating neural network retrieved pigment absorption to chl-a concentration. Gege and Plattner (2004) investigated the performance of MERIS standard L2 products over Lake Constance (Germany), and Matthews et al. Their exploration into the variability within lithic assemblages reveals how different populations adapted to their respective ecological niches, highlighting the significant regional differences that characterize the eastern African landscape. This adaptability underscores the role of environmental pressures in shaping not only the material culture of early humans but also their social structures and interactions. These dynamics further illustrate how technological innovations, from the inception of blade technology to specialized toolkits, were sporadically adopted and modified based on local circumstances, reinforcing the idea of a mosaic of cultures coexisting across vast expanses of the African continent. Concurrently, the work of Hovers and Bar-Yosef (2006) posits that as climatic conditions fluctuated, so too did the lifeways of early Homo sapiens, leading to innovations that may reflect increased social complexity. Their investigation into the stratigraphic contexts of various MSA sites demonstrates that environmental alterations played a role in the multidimensional development of human behavior, often leading to the emergence of new technological forms aimed at meeting the demands of shifting resources. This perspective compels us to reconsider simplistic narratives of evolutionary linearity, favoring instead a model where hominin adaptability is intertwined with cultural and technological progression-a model characterized by local experimentation and intergroup exchanges that enriched the regional tapestry of human life. Collectively, these studies coalesce into an understanding that apparent technological uniformities could mask deeper undercurrents of diversity enriched by environmental context and geographic nuance. More importantly, such a comprehensive examination of the MSA stone tool record pushes us toward a broader contemplation of the social networks that underpinned these technological practices. The exchange of ideas, knowledge, and materials among various groups, hinted at through the presence of similar tool types across geographically separate sites, suggests that early Homo sapiens were not isolated cultural entities but, rather, participants in a shared, albeit complex, web of interactions. Moreover, as we continue to explore the implications of these findings, attention also turns to the role of climate in driving population migrations and dispersals. The cyclic nature of arid and humid phases in eastern Africa created regions of both opportunity and challenge for early humans as they sought food and resources. Such climatic variability undoubtedly influenced migratory patterns, allowing certain groups to capitalize on favorable periods while compelling others to adapt, innovate, or seek refuge in more hospitable areas. In light of this, the examination of paleoenvironmental data becomes indispensable to deciphering the intricate relationship between human behavior and the environment. Integrating climate records into our assessments of MSA lithic variability broadens our understanding of how external factors shaped not only the technological identities of early populations but also their cultural affiliations. As we sift through the rich interplay of archaeology, environmental science, and genetics, we begin to envision a more nuanced understanding of Homo sapiens' evolution, one that acknowledges both the vibrant diversity of early technological practices and the profound interconnectedness of emerging human societies. The task ahead involves a collaborative effort to deepen our knowledge of the past, continually refining our frameworks to account for an ever-expanding dataset that showcases the complexities of human heritage across the ages.

The intricate interplay between domestic resource efficiency initiatives and consumer practices encapsulates a myriad of practices that shape our daily lives. Understanding this relationship necessitates a closer examination of the underlying frameworks that dictate how interventions are conceived and executed. Importantly, it highlights the need for a comprehensive approach that transcends superficial technical adjustments and delves into the sociocultural contexts that frame domestic behaviors (Hargreaves et al., 2010). For instance, effective engagement strategies must consider not only the technological installations or behavioral nudges that are implemented but also the social networks through which ideas about resource use are disseminated. Peer influence has emerged as a significant determinant of how individuals adopt resource-efficient practices (Rogers, 2003). When households observe their neighbors and friends embracing sustainable technologies or practices, it can spark interest and motivate similar actions. Therefore, initiatives must cultivate these social ties, leveraging community dynamics to support and enhance collective action towards sustainability. Furthermore, the evaluative frameworks used in these interventions must evolve to account for the complexities of human behavior in relation to environmental challenges. Traditional metrics of success, which often focus solely on quantifiable reductions in resource consumption, may not adequately reflect the multifaceted impacts of initiatives (Stern et al., 2016). Instead, evaluations that capture shifts in social norms, values, and broader lifestyle changes towards sustainability will provide a richer understanding of effectiveness. This necessitates a participatory approach to monitoring, whereby feedback loops are established, allowing participants to voice their experiences and insights, thus informing ongoing project refinements. Equally critical is the role of narrative in shaping perceptions of domestic resource efficiency initiatives. The stories told around resource usage-the motivations behind certain behavioral choices and the emotional undercurrents associated with them-can significantly influence public attitudes toward sustainability (Fischer, 2000). By framing these initiatives within compelling narratives that resonate with individuals' identities and aspirations, advocates can foster deeper connections to resource efficiency practices. Bridging personal values with environmental responsibility has the potential to catalyze profound behavioral transformations and promote sustained engagement. Institutional structures also play a pivotal role in shaping the trajectory of domestic resource governance. The intricate web of policies, regulations, and stakeholder engagements imbues initiatives with legitimacy and direction. When governance organizations align their mission with community values, there is a propensity for greater trust and collaboration (Ostrom, 1990). As such, transparent communication and inclusive policy-making processes are essential to ensure that the design and implementation of resource efficiency initiatives reflect the needs and aspirations of diverse communities. Moreover, the localization of initiatives can further fortify these connections. Tailored interventions that consider regional characteristics, cultural practices, and local economies are likely to resonate more deeply with participants. By weaving resource efficiency into the fabric of local identity and heritage, communities may feel more empowered to enact change. The concept of 'place-making' in developing sustainable practices underscores the importance of contextual relevance (Tansley, 1935), suggesting that when individuals see resources as integral to their community's identity, they may be more inclined to adapt their behaviors accordingly. In sum, the pathway towards achieving effective domestic resource efficiency initiatives lies beyond mere technological solutions or behavioral nudges. It involves a multifaceted understanding of the sociocultural landscape, characterized by community engagement, participatory evaluation, compelling narratives, supportive institutional frameworks, and localized practices. By prioritizing these elements, we create a fertile ground for nurturing the aspirations of communities and fostering sustainable, meaningful change. Understanding these dynamics not only enriches our approach to resource governance but also marks a significant step towards harmonizing environmental sustainability with the lived experiences of individuals and communities alike.

In addition to novelty-seeking and cue-conditioning influences, the tendency to preferentially process cues related to the object of addiction (attentional biases) is also an important feature that characterizes disorders of addiction (Ersche et al., 2010; van Hemel-Ruiter et al., 2013; Wiers et al., 2011). The influence of emotional stimuli on attentional processes is widely reported both in healthy and clinical samples (Yiend, 2010). Attentional biases towards substance-related stimuli have been found in substance-use disorders for alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, opiates and cocaine (Cox et al., 2006). Moreover, a direct association between highly arousing sexual pictures and attentional interference has also been found in healthy individuals, which seems to be influenced by sexuality-related attitudes and sexual motivation (Kagerer et al., 2014; Prause et al., 2008). We have previously extended these findings to individuals with compulsive sexual behaviour (CSB) using a dot-probe task (Mechelmans et al., 2014). With increasing access to the Internet, there is growing concern regarding the potential for excessive use. A study that assessed the predictive power of several types of Internet applications (gaming, gambling, email, etc.) on the development of compulsive Internet use suggested that online sexually explicit stimuli have the highest potential for addictive/compulsive use (Meerkerk et al., 2006). Online explicit stimuli are vast and expanding, and this feature may promote escalation of use in some individuals. For instance, healthy males viewing repeatedly the same explicit film have been found to habituate to the stimulus and find the explicit stimulus as progressively less sexually arousing, less appetitive and less absorbing (Koukounas and Over, 2000). However, subsequent exposure to a novel explicit film segment increases the levels of sexual arousal and absorption to the same previous levels prior to habituation, suggesting important roles for novelty and habituation. Imaging studies have identified a specific network for the neural processing of sexual stimuli in healthy humans, comprising the hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens, orbitofrontal, occipital and parietal areas (Wehrum et al., 2013; Wehrum-Osinsky et al., 2014). This neural network, which is independent of general emotional arousal, is found both in men and women although men show overall stronger activations than women, which might be indicative of a stronger sexual responsivity in men. The same neural network activates for stimuli conditioned sexual arousal, with a gender effect in the same direction (Klucken et al., 2009). In our study, we assess novelty, attentional bias and cue-conditioning to online explicit sexual material in individuals with CSB. These processes are highly relevant to substance-use disorders and may also be relevant to CSB. Online sexually explicit stimuli have significant potential for compulsive use, and CSB is relatively common, occurring in 2-4% in community and college-based young adults and in psychiatric inpatients (Grant et al., 2005; Odlaug and Grant, 2010; Odlaug et al., 2013). CSB is associated with significant distress, feelings of shame and psychosocial dysfunction.

Through these and other studies, variations in these parameters had been shown to produce different extents in their abilities to influence coaxial jet flows. The parallel effort reported in New and Tsioli [18], on the other hand, focused upon the influence of inclined exits on freely-exhausting coaxial jets, where only effects due to variations in the incline-angle and/or velocity-ratio were considered at that point. In that study, fundamental flow dynamics of inclined coaxial jets were elaborated through a series of laser-induced fluorescence and particle-image velocimetry tests. A primary jet at a Reynolds number of Re = 2500 was used, where the coaxial jet area-ratio remained constant at (D2/D1)2 = 2.25, and velocity-ratios of U2/U1 = 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 were examined. Flow visualizations showed that the primary jet underwent regular oscillations about the incline-plane when velocity-ratio reached 1.0 and beyond, similar to single-stream inclined jets examined by Webster and Longmire [29] earlier. The result was a distinctive "serpentine"-shaped primary jet outline, first described by Webster and Longmire [29]. This phenomenon is due to jet oscillations produced by mutual interactions between inclined ring-vortices along both the primary and secondary jet shear layers. Visual evidence gathered during that study also indicated that the natures of jet oscillations at velocity-ratios of 1.0 and 2.0 were fundamentally different. Furthermore, as a result of the jet oscillations, the primary jet was found to deflect towards the longer nozzle length regions in a consistent manner with the extent of deflection increasing with the velocity-ratio and incline-angle used. While New and Tsioli [18] had shed light upon the influences of the incline-angle and velocity-ratio in driving the underlying flow mechanisms in inclined coaxial jets, the role of area-ratio in inclined coaxial jets remains unresolved. In coaxial jets, the area-ratio directly impacts upon the extent of mutual interactions between the primary and secondary jet shear layer ring-vortices. While sufficiently small area-ratio coaxial jets produce intense mutual interactions that may lead to "lock-in" effects even in the near-field [9,25], it is expected that larger area-ratio coaxial jets are less likely to reproduce such behaviour. Any physical increase in the annular gap size should in theory serve to separate the two different trains of shear layer ring-vortices more and reduce the extent of mutual vortical interactions. Within the context of inclined coaxial jets here, this line of argument raises several outstanding questions. Firstly, how will the behaviour of primary and secondary jet ring-vortices differ in inclined coaxial jets with an area-ratio larger than that used by the preceding study? And secondly, what are the effects of velocity-ratio and incline-angle variations upon inclined coaxial jets with a larger area-ratio?

Furthermore, the low dose required for insect control results in negligible exposure levels to humans and animals. For example, when compared with natural constituents in foods such as potato glycoalkaloids (GAs), the concentration of Cry1Ab protein in corn grain is up to 10,000-fold lower than GA concentrations in potatoes (Margaretten et al., 1996; Herman et al., 2002). The Cyt1Aa protein was first described by Wu and Federici (Wu and Federici, 1993). It is a 25 kDa monomeric protein that forms cation-selective channels upon insertion into lipid bilayers (Butko et al., 1999). Cyt1Aa does not share sequence similarity with any other Bt toxin and it lacks the N-terminal signal peptide characteristic of most secreted bacterial proteins (Butko et al., 1999). This protein shares some features with -helical peptides such as melittin, alamethicin, and magainin (Li et al., 1996b). Like these peptides, Cyt1Aa inserts into biological membranes causing disruption of the membrane structure. However, unlike these peptides, Cyt1Aa forms oligomers on the membrane surface before inserting into the phospholipid bilayer (Butko et al., 1999; Li et al., 1996a). Once inserted into the membrane, Cyt1Aa causes cell lysis via colloid osmotic shock resulting from an influx of water through the ion-permeable channel created by the protein (Butko et al., 1999). The mechanism of action of Cyt1Aa is different from that of the typical Bt toxins, which require receptor-binding for its mode of action (Bravo et al., 2007). While Cyt1Aa binds weakly to the same receptors as those of Cry11Aa and Cry4Ba, it is capable of killing mosquitoes in the absence of these receptors (Chen et al., 2009). Cyt1Aa is toxic to mosquito larvae but shows no toxicity toward mammals or other vertebrate cells (Wu and Federici, 1993). Molecular characterization studies show that the gene encoding Cyt1Aa is located downstream of the cry4Aa gene (Thorne et al., 1986). Transcription of the cyt1Aa gene initiates at the end of the cry4Aa gene, suggesting that both genes are transcribed together as one polycistronic transcript (Angsuthanasombat et al., 1992). The cyt1Aa gene encodes a protein of 249 amino acids with a predicted molecular weight of 27.7 kDa. The N-terminal region of the protein contains a putative secretion signal peptide of 23 amino acid residues. Cleavage of the signal peptide produces the mature protein consisting of 226 amino acids with a calculated molecular mass of 24.9 kDa (Angsuthanasombat et al., 1992). Cyt1Aa is active against Lepidoptera, Diptera, Coleoptera, and Hymenoptera (Butko et al., 1999). The highest level of activity is observed against Aedes aegypti mosquito larvae, where the LC50 value is approximately 30 ng/mL (Butko et al., 1999).

The ears were short and delicately made, the eyes well-placed, the distance to the angle of the jaw long - in brief, it was that short head of small volume and large brain space which speaks most eloquently of hot blood. As her expert eye ran over the rest of the body she sighed to think that such a creature had come to such an end. There was about him no sign of life save the twitch of his skin to shake off flies. Certainly this could not be the horse she had been advised to see and she was about to pass on when she felt eyes watching her from the steep shadow of the shed which bordered the corral. Then she made out a dapper olive-skinned fellow sitting with his back against the wall in such a position of complete relaxation as only a Mexican is capable of assuming. He wore a short tuft of black moustache cut well away from the edge of the red lip, a moustache which oddly accentuated his youth. In body and features he was of that feminine delicacy which your large-handed Saxon dislikes, and though Marianne was by no means a stalwart, she detested the man at once. For that reason, being a lady to the tips of her slim fingers, her smile was more cordial than necessary. "I am looking for Manuel Cordova," she said. "Me," replied the Mexican, and managed to speak without removing the cigarette. "I'm glad to know you." she answered. "I am Marianne Jordan." At this, Manuel Cordova removed his cigarette, regardless of the ashes which tumbled straightway down the bell-mouthed sleeve of his jacket; for a Mexican deems it highly indecorous to pay the slightest heed to his tobacco ashes. Whether they land on chin or waistcoat they are allowed to remain until the wind carries them away. "The pleasure is to me," said Cordova melodiously, and made painful preparations to rise. She gathered at once that the effort would spoil his morning and urged him to remain where he was, at which he smiled with the care of a movie star, presenting an even, white line of teeth. Marianne went on: "Let me explain. I've come to the Glosterville fair to buy some brood mares for my ranch and of course the ones I want are the Coles horses. You've seen them?" He nodded. "But those horses," she continued, checking off her points, "will not be offered for sale until after the race this afternoon. They're all entered and they are sure to win. That would put them above my reach and I can only pray that the miracle will happen - a horse may turn up to beat them.

In Europe, however, efforts towards a similarly comprehensive WUI framework have been fragmentary. Differing national policies and varying levels of resources allocated to wildfire management contribute to a disparate approach across the continent. While countries like Spain and Portugal have implemented significant measures to monitor and manage WUI zones, others lag behind, hampered by financial constraints and less frequent fire occurrences. Addressing this inconsistency remains a pressing challenge for European policymakers, as the threat of wildfires grows increasingly acute under changing climatic conditions. The urgency to establish a pan-European strategy is underpinned by the recent surge in extreme weather events, with prolonged droughts and heatwaves creating an environment ripe for uncontrolled fires. This climate shift places both natural and human systems under severe stress, catalyzing a vicious cycle where increased fire activity leads to further degradation of ecosystems, reducing their resilience and recovery potential. Within this context, the role of local communities becomes ever more critical, as they are often the first responders when a fire erupts at the WUI. Empowering these communities with knowledge, resources, and robust evacuation plans would inevitably bolster the collective capacity to mitigate fire impacts. Furthermore, technological advancements offer promising opportunities to enhance wildfire management practices. The integration of satellite imagery and drones provides detailed, real-time data that can significantly elevate surveillance and early warning systems. When combined with sophisticated modeling tools, these technologies enable scientists to predict fire spread and behavior with improved accuracy, assisting in strategic firefighting operations. However, despite these technological leaps, the effectiveness of fire management ultimately hinges on human factors-collaboration, communication, and commitment among stakeholders at local, national, and European levels. Public awareness and education campaigns stand out as pivotal components of a comprehensive fire management strategy. Engaging residents in fire risk reduction activities, such as creating defensible spaces and adopting fire-resistant landscaping, can dramatically decrease the vulnerability of WUI areas. Additionally, tailoring information to specific communities, taking into account cultural and socio-economic contexts, ensures that awareness efforts resonate and compel collective action. Such grass-root initiatives are most successful when supported by governmental policies that incentivize and facilitate community involvement. Simultaneously, research into alternative land use practices offers insights into sustainable interfacing between urban expansion and rural abandonment. Promoting agroforestry and sustainable grazing on underutilized lands not only curbs the encroachment of flammable vegetation but also sustains biodiversity and rural livelihoods. Policymakers must strive to integrate these insights into land management frameworks, fostering resilience through adaptive and multi-functional landscapes. In conclusion, the wildland-urban interface in Europe represents both a challenge and an opportunity for transformative action in forest fire management. As climate pressures mount, a unified and holistic approach becomes imperative to safeguard human lives, property, and natural ecosystems. By leveraging technological innovations, enhancing cross-border collaboration, and fostering community resilience, Europe can forge a path forward in mitigating wildfire risks. This endeavor calls for the commitment of all societal levels, intertwining policy, practice, and scientific research into an agile, adaptive strategy that will protect its diverse landscapes for generations to come.

Specifically, a short variant allele (S-allele) of the 5-HTTLPR has been associated with increased anxiety and depression relative to a long variant (L-allele), although there are inconsistent findings (Munafo et al., 2008; Risch et al., 2009; Schinka et al., 2004). Importantly, the effect of the S-allele appears to be further enhanced when individuals experience stressful life events (Caspi et al., 2003; Kendler et al., 2005). However, recent meta-analytic work has failed to find support for this gene x environment interaction (Risch et al., 2009). Nevertheless, several studies using neuroimaging methods have found associations between the 5-HTTLPR genotype and neural circuitry implicated in emotion processing (Canli and Lesch, 2007; Hariri et al., 2002; Heinz et al., 2005). Although these imaging-genetics studies have focused mainly on amygdala reactivity to aversive stimuli, other structures within fronto-limbic pathways have also been implicated (Heinz et al., 2005). One such structure is the hippocampus, which plays an important role in memory consolidation and retrieval, and is involved in the regulation of the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis through glucocorticoid feedback (Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991; McEwen, 1998). Hippocampal dysfunction has been observed in major depressive disorder (Bremner et al., 2000; Sheline et al., 1996) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Bremner et al., 1995; Bremner et al., 2003a,b). Moreover, the hippocampus expresses high levels of 5-HTT receptors (Lesch et al., 1993b), making it a potential site for modulation of mood-related behaviors by 5-HTTLPR. Consistent with this hypothesis, a recent study showed that the 5-HTTLPR S-allele was associated with decreased gray matter volume in the subiculum, a subregion of the hippocampus (Pezawas et al., 2005). Moreover, reduced hippocampal volumes were recently reported in carriers of the 5-HTTLPR S-allele who had experienced childhood trauma (Frodl et al., 2010). Such structural changes could potentially affect the functional connectivity of the hippocampus with other regions in the limbic system and prefrontal cortex. However, few studies have examined how 5-HTTLPR affects hippocampal functional connectivity. One exception is a recent resting-state fMRI study showing that the 5-HTTLPR S-allele was associated with greater connectivity between the left hippocampus and the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (Chen et al., 2012). This finding suggests that 5-HTTLPR might influence hippocampal connectivity with prefrontal regions. Given the role of the IFG in cognitive control of emotion (Ochsner and Gross, 2005; Ochsner et al., 2002; Wager et al., 2008), the finding raises the possibility that 5-HTTLPR might also modulate hippocampal functional connectivity during the processing of emotionally salient information. To test this hypothesis, we used fMRI to examine whether the 5-HTTLPR S-allele is associated with altered hippocampal functional connectivity during an emotion-processing task. Participants performed a standard face-matching task (Hariri et al., 2002) while undergoing fMRI scanning.

But the love for my family eclipses any attachment to material things. It's such a simple truth, yet in those frantic moments, it felt crushingly complicated. How easy it is to lose sight of what truly matters when flames rage and smoke suffocates the air. I could hear my heart pounding, the rush of adrenaline coursing through my veins like a tidal wave. How on earth could I articulate all that? Even now, while I sit typing, I feel the tremor of that night fanning the embers of fear within me. As the fire trucks finally arrived, their sirens piercing through the chaos, I watched those brave souls jump into action, some rushing with hoses while others scrambled to assess the situation. For a second, there was a sliver of hope-a glimmer that maybe this nightmare could get under control. But then the realization settled over me; it was too late for hope. We had already lost so much. Jim came back with the milk and the good water, his face streaked with worry, yet I knew he was trying to put on a brave front for the girls. They were nestled beside each other on the couch, watching their favorite shows, but I could tell their innocence had been shattered. How can one explain to little minds that material possessions can vanish in an instant while love remains steadfast? I felt a rush of guilt for helplessly thrusting them into a whirlwind of chaos. They had only wanted a normal, happy Easter, a day filled with egg hunts and laughter. Instead, their world had spun on its axis. "Hey, how about I make some hot chocolate?" Jim said, trying to lure them back into the present, and it warmed my heart to see him so effortlessly navigate these turbulent waters. There he was, reminding us all that life, though marred with uncertainty, still offered small pockets of comfort. The steam rising from the mugs would perhaps act as a balm to our fraying nerves. Or so I hoped. Jim disappeared into the kitchen, and I took a deep breath, allowing my thoughts to travel down a different path. Perhaps we wouldn't be able to return to the life we knew, but maybe this was a turning point-a chance to reconsider our lives, to rebuild stronger and more united than ever. It took some convincing to talk myself into that sentiment, but I really believed somewhere deep down that we would find a way. **Maybe this fire was not just destructive but also a catalyst for change.** The girls started giggling again, and suddenly, the atmosphere lightened just a bit. That joyful sound, as innocent as it was, became a song of hope, and I found myself wanting to cradle this moment and freeze it in time. At that very instant, in a very real way, their laughter was more valuable than any material possession we could ever own. The events of this week had thrown us into the fiery abyss, yet in its wake, they had ignited awareness. We were alive; we were together. And as I sat there clenching my cup, I felt the warmth of the hot chocolate against my palm, and the cool breeze wafting through the open windows stirred something hopeful within me.

The degree of machine utilization and the ability to fully utilize the machine build volume for batch production is also included in existing AM cost models [16]. In typical case studies, the cost of producing components with AM is calculated and compared to the cost of conventional manufacturing using break-even point analysis [20]. For example, a customizable automotive plastic gripper part is used to demonstrate that AM is more cost-effective in producing components with many variations because injection molding requires costly tools for every product alternative [11]. In another case study, part consolidation was used to compare the cost-effectiveness of AM with injection molding. This investigation was based on an electric component that was redesigned to capitalize on the design freedom of AM [21]. Similarly, a slightly modified metal stainless steel hot air blower was shown to be more cost-effective to produce with AM than conventional manufacturing after applying part consolidation [19]. The machine utilization rate and build volume rate (BVR) are relevant metrics of productivity of metal PBF systems [22]. Best in class commercial PBF systems are capable of producing parts with build volume rates up to 27.78 mm3/sec [23]. Material cost dominates the cost of production at build volume rates above 20 mm3/sec [15]. In a case study presented by Kretzschmar et al. [15], the material costs accounted for 63% of the total cost per part at high BVRs. The remaining costs are related to machine and labor, which are responsible for 26% and 11% of the final unit cost, respectively [5]. The exact cost distributions are highly dependent on specific AM designs, machines, and materials. Nevertheless, the high relevance of material cost in high productivity scenarios applies to all metal PBF systems. The cost of parts produced with metal PBF systems in industrial settings is therefore primarily determined by the high price of the machinery and metallic powder materials. Therefore, production cost can only be decreased by either reducing the need of material from the original design (e.g. part weight reduction through DfAM), or by enhancing the productivity rates of the machines (e. g. set-up times, full utilization of the build volume and increased build volume rates to obtain higher productivity). The principal objective of this research is to study the impact of lattice structure design on the economics of metal PBF. This research provides an overview of cost reduction limits and saving potentials for the AM of end-use components using metal PBF. The work is limited to study productivity issues of DfAM using lattice structures and topology optimization; and therefore, it does not perform an in-depth study of the technical feasibility and mechanical performance analysis of lattice designs. The implementation of lattice structures requires careful examination to ensure manufacturability and that the functional requirements of the product remain fulfilled in real engineering applications.

"The past whispers its truths to the present, and in its echoes, I find clarity. We are descendants of those who fought against neglect and injustice, and it is our duty to breathe life into their legacies. No, if I must reclaim my vision, I must first see through the eyes of those who walked before me; their stories are the menu from which we feast." Stillness enveloped us, wrapping around our words like a shawl that both comforts and constrains. I thought of the countless souls I had seen rise and fall, of the laughter that had punctured the darkness like stars piercing the night sky. In those moments, I glimpsed the finest truth: the brilliance of existence lies in conflict, in the ebb and flow of our shared humanity. "Then let us kindle that fire, Inkosi," he urged, his enthusiasm igniting my spirit. "Let us breathe life into the tales that have been pushed aside into the corners of forgotten rooms. For it is through our words that we reclaim the power stripped from us. But know this-like snuff, or the deepest truths of our story, it must be handled with reverence. Each utterance can carry the weight of both grief and liberation." And so we continued, like the river carving its path through the rock, relentless and unwavering, each word an echo, a reminder, a mourning and a celebration. What began as a recounting slowly transformed into a profound dialogue, steeped in our shared understanding of the intertwined destinies of our people, the binding threads of existence from which no one could extricate themselves. It was here, in the embrace of the past, that I found the resilience to step boldly into the future.

This produces additional GHG emissions that offset the initial emission reductions. This mechanism is known as the rebound effect, first described by Jevons (1866) and later by Saunders (1992) and the Khazzoom-Brookes Postulate which states that increased energy efficiency leads to increased energy consumption. The rebound effect has been seen in practice in car-free households in Vienna (Ornetzeder et al., 2008). Rebound effects can arise either from efficiency improvements that make a good or service cheaper or from changing the pattern of consumption leading to lower costs, known as sufficiency strategies. There are three main types of rebound effects; direct (re-spending on the same good or service as the one where money is saved), indirect (re-spending on other goods and services) and various macroeconomic effects (how the effect of the efficiency improvement or changed consumption distributes throughout the economy) (Greening et al., 2000). Since Jevons (1866), researchers have known that efficiency improvements are subject to rebound effects. However, recent studies have shown that sufficiency strategies also are subject to rebound effects (Figge et al., 2014). In the discussions of a transition to a circular economy, overcoming rebound effects of efficiency and sufficiency strategies is pointed out as a key challenge (Ghisellini et al., 2016). If rebound effects are not overcome, the last resort is to reduce economic activity on the macro level (Figge et al., 2014). Previous rebound effect studies often analyze the impacts of one or a few behavioral actions, rather than lifestyle changes. Grabs (2015) found GHG emission rebound effects of 49% from changing to a vegetarian diet. Briceno et al. (2005) found indirect rebound effects of 42-49% from car-sharing schemes. Chitnis et al. (2013) found direct and indirect rebound effects in the range of 5-15% from energy efficiency improvements by UK households. Font Vivanco et al. (2014) found rebound effects in the range of 3-5% when changing from a conventional car to a plug-in hybrid electric passenger car. Chitnis and Sorrell (2015) found combined direct and indirect rebound effects of energy efficiency improvements by UK households to be 41%, 48% and 78% for measures involving domestic gas use, electricity use and vehicle fuel use respectively. Studies on rebound effects from complete lifestyle changes are less common. Chitnis et al. (2014) found combined direct and indirect rebound effects of 15-35% for different combinations of household actions. Rebound effects were lowest for measures affecting domestic energy use and largest for reducing food waste. Druckman et al. (2011) found combined indirect and direct rebound effects from three efficiency measures to be 34%, which dropped to 12% when restricting re-spending to goods and services with low GHG intensities. Alfredsson (2004) found CO2 rebound effects of 238% for "green" food consumption, 12% for "green" travel and 19% for "green" housing. An overall "green" consumption pattern resulted in 14% rebound using a "green" re-spending scenario.

"Sir?" I ventured, trying to keep my tone respectful despite the chaos around us. "How do I get to Fort Sedgewick?" The major's expression turned stern, his eyes narrowing. "You think I'm going to give you a map and compass? You're a soldier, not a lost puppy. You'll figure it out. Just get there. And don't come back until you've seen what you came for." I nodded, feeling a surge of determination. I was going to see the frontier, no matter what it took. And I was going to make it back in one piece. As I turned to leave, the major called out after me. "And Dunbar?" "Yes, sir?" I replied, turning back. "You're not just a soldier, you're a soldier of the United States Army. You're not just fighting for your country, you're fighting for your fellow man. Don't forget that." I saluted, feeling a sense of pride and purpose wash over me. I was going to make a difference, no matter what lay ahead. I made my way back to my quarters, my mind racing with thoughts of the journey ahead. I would have to be careful, though. The frontier was a treacherous place, full of hostile Native Americans and rugged terrain. But I was ready for it. I was John J. Dunbar, and I was going to see the frontier. As I packed my gear, I couldn't help but think of the major's words. I was fighting for something bigger than myself, something that went beyond the boundaries of my own little world. I was fighting for the future, for the chance to make a difference in a world that often seemed too big and too overwhelming. I finished packing, slung my rifle over my shoulder, and headed out into the unknown. The sun was setting, casting a golden glow over the landscape. I felt a sense of excitement and trepidation as I set off into the wild blue yonder. As I walked, I couldn't help but think of the major's words again. "You're not just a soldier, you're a soldier of the United States Army. You're not just fighting for your country, you're fighting for your fellow man." I repeated them to myself, trying to commit them to memory. I walked for hours, the sun dipping lower and lower in the sky. I could see the outlines of trees in the distance, their branches stretching out like skeletal fingers. I quickened my pace, my heart pounding in my chest. As the darkness closed in, I spotted a figure in the distance. It was a Native American, dressed in buckskin and feathers. He was standing tall, his eyes fixed on me. I slowed to a stop, my hand on the hilt of my sword. The Indian didn't move, didn't flinch. He just stood there, watching me. I could feel his eyes on me, boring into my very soul. I swallowed hard, trying to keep my nerves steady. And then, in a flash of movement, he vanished. I was left standing there, my heart still racing. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself down. I was on the frontier, and I was on my own.

They do this by initially creating a sense of belonging and specialness, making you feel indispensable in their world. You feel like the center of their universe, the missing piece to their puzzle. They might shower you with attention, gifts, and compliments, drawing you closer with every gesture, every loving word. This initial stage is intoxicating. You are their hero, their confidant, the one they have been waiting for all their life. But this euphoria is short-lived. Once they sense your dependence, they start to withdraw that affection, slowly and methodically, akin to a magician pulling a disappearing act. This withdrawal is strategic. It leaves you questioning, doubting yourself, wondering what went wrong. What did you do? What changed? The sudden shift hits you like a cold wave, and you scramble desperately to regain that initial affection. This is where the hook embeds itself deeply, where the cycle of bait-and-switch begins. They start to devalue you, subtly at first. The compliments turn to critiques. Your accomplishments, which once dazzled them, now seem to annoy them. The connection you once shared begins to crumble, overshadowed by disdain and condescension. Yet amidst this chaos, they throw you crumbs of affection to keep you tethered. These intermittent moments of kindness rekindle your hope, the belief that things will go back to how they once were. But this hope is fleeting, designed to keep you ensnared. The duality of their behavior leaves you in a state of confusion, akin to a roller coaster of emotions. This constant up-down creates an emotional addiction, making you chase their approval, tirelessly working to restore the relationship to its glorified beginning. In essence, this technique is not only a guise but a power play. The narcissist maintains control, ensuring you're walking on eggshells, perpetually seeking their favor. This emotional leverage grants them the upper hand while rendering you powerless. The once vibrant, confident person you were begins to erode under the weight of manipulative tactics. Slowly, your world starts revolving around their needs, their moods dictating your reality. Understanding this pattern is crucial. Recognizing the bait-and-switch can be the first step toward healing and reclaiming your self-worth. It is a painful realization, accepting that the person you loved never truly existed, but merely a facade woven with deceit and manipulation. There is strength in awareness. By naming their strategies, you can begin to dismantle their control over your life and start setting boundaries that protect your emotional well-being. Healing from such entrapment requires introspection and self-care. Engaging in activities that foster your sense of identity, surrounding yourself with supportive individuals who validate your experiences, and possibly seeking professional guidance can aid in piecing together the fragments of your self-worth. Remember, the true enemy in this dynamic is the manipulation, not you. With time and effort, you can learn to trust yourself again, shedding the remnants of the narcissist's influence and stepping into a space where you are valued, respected, and-most importantly-free.

Recent advancements in the field emphasize the importance of accounting for both angular and spectral deviations when evaluating PV device performance under realistic operational conditions. There is a growing recognition that conventional models, which often rely on simplified assumptions, may underestimate these complexities, potentially leading to inaccuracies in performance predictions and efficiency calculations. A significant body of research has aimed to refine these models by incorporating more detailed atmospheric and ground-reflection characteristics. For instance, the role of spectral sky radiance and its angular distribution has been explored in various settings, highlighting the intricacy of accurately predicting PV performance in different geographical locations and throughout various seasons (de la Parra et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2018). These studies underscore the necessity of updating current measurement and calibration techniques to incorporate a more nuanced understanding of these factors, especially in light of their profound impact on device efficiency. Furthermore, particular attention has been devoted to the interaction between spectral albedo and device orientation, particularly for bifacial modules. These devices, which can capture light from both sides, are especially sensitive to ground-reflected irradiance, making the accurate assessment of albedo a critical factor in performance evaluation (Gu and Yuan, 2015; Kandilli et al., 2017). Recent methodologies involve sophisticated models that simulate solar spectrum variations across different surface types, providing more accurate predictions of bifacial module performance under diverse environmental conditions (Marion et al., 2017). This renewed focus on more accurately accounting for spectral and angular variances has significant implications for PV system design and optimization. Engineers and researchers must consider these factors when designing systems, selecting materials, and determining installation angles, all of which could profoundly affect energy yield. Additionally, policymakers and industry leaders are increasingly aware of the need for enhanced standards and guidelines that reflect these advanced understandings, as they are essential for promoting the widespread adoption and deployment of solar technologies (Sengupta et al., 2018). Efforts to develop and refine tools that effectively model these complex interactions continue to gain momentum, with various institutions dedicating resources to both theoretical and empirical research. Future research directions may include the exploration of machine learning algorithms to improve model predictive capabilities, especially in handling large datasets ranging from multi-spectral satellite data to real-time ground measurements (Yang et al., 2019). In conclusion, addressing the intricacies associated with spectral and angular effects remains paramount in the quest to enhance the precision of performance assessments for photovoltaic devices. As soon as we arrived at St. Catherineas monastery we were off to climb Mt. Sinai. It took us about four hours. It was a very difficult hike, especially since I was carrying my heavy camera bag. But I could not leave it behind because the sunrise was going to be spectacular. The first hour of the hike was steep but manageable. Then we came to what they call the steps of repentance. They are 750 steps carved into the rock face. Some of them were almost knee high. At times I thought my legs were going to give out from under me. But I persevered. Then the last leg of the journey was more steep rocky terrain. I was so happy when I finally reached the top. It was worth every painful step. It was freezing cold and windy at the summit. A few of us huddled together and watched the sun rise. What an amazing feeling to be at the top of Mt. Sinai watching the sun come up. I was literally at the top of the world. I felt so close to God and Moses and the burning bush. I really did feel as though I was walking in the footsteps of history. That morning was a spiritual awakening for me. After we got down from the mountain we went into St. Catharineas Monastery. It was founded in the fourth century and built around the site where the burning bush was located. The chapel of the burning bush still stands today. In the sixth century Emperor Justinian ordered the fortification of the monastery due to attacks from nomadic tribes. The building of the monastery has protected the oldest continually used church in Christendom. It is a Greek Orthodox Church and they do not allow women inside unless they cover themselves completely. I had a scarf with me so I was able to go in. The church was stunningly beautiful. All of the walls were covered with paintings and mosaics. The altar was huge and covered in gold leaf. There was a door behind the altar that led to the chapel of the burning bush. Unfortunately no photography was allowed. You will just have to take my word for how magnificent it was. On our way out of the complex we saw a camel train coming through. Camels are such odd looking creatures. Their heads look so small compared to the rest of their bodies. It was interesting to see the Bedouins riding their camels. They looked like they belonged in another era. After the monastery visit we went to Dahab, which means gold in Arabic. This town is situated right on the Gulf of Aqaba and is famous for its diving, snorkeling, and windsurfing. It was a sleepy little beach town. We ate lunch at a place on the beach. I had fresh calamari that was caught that morning. It was delicious. While we were eating lunch the waiter brought out a huge platter of fruit. There must have been fifteen different kinds of fruit on it. He then proceeded to cut each piece of fruit individually for everyone. It was the best tasting fruit I have ever eaten. I guess everything tastes better near the sea. I can't wait until tomorrow when I get to snorkel again!

The immobilisation of sulfate bearing radioactive waste poses technical challenges for vitrification and traditional cementing processes. The presence of sulfate during vitrification causes phase separation in borosilicate glass [1], and in the case of Portland cement-based materials it can promote microstructural changes in the long term [2-4], such as expansion and cracking through the process of internal sulfate attack, which may result in the loss of matrix integrity and the release of radionuclides into the environment. If sulfate-containing nuclear waste is not treated and encapsulated effectively, it can also interact with any Portland cement-based backfill or structural concrete used in a nuclear waste repository, potentially causing decay of the repository structure through sulfate attack processes. Asano et al. [5] proposed a method for the solidification/stabilisation of sulfate-rich aqueous low level wastes using Ba(OH)2 and blast furnace slag (BFS), derived from the iron making industry, via a two-step process to produce cement-like solid monoliths. In their method, a sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) (simulated waste) solution was mixed with Ba(OH)2 in a first step, stabilising the sulfate ions through the precipitation of the highly insoluble phase barium sulfate (BaSO4) and releasing sodium hydroxide (NaOH) as a by-product of this reaction. This was followed by a second step where the BaSO4 and NaOH-containing slurry was blended with slag to produce a cementitious grout. Mobasher et al. [6] published a proof-of-concept of a one-step process to produce solid wasteforms with comparable chemistry to those assessed by Asano et al. [5] for immobilisation of sulfate bearing aqueous waste, formulating Ba(OH)2-Na2SO4-BFS cementitious grouts. This study demonstrated that in the one-step process, in-situ precipitation of BaSO4 particles and chemical reaction between the slag and NaOH (also referred to as alkali-activation) take place simultaneously, with the remnant Ba(OH)2 and Na2SO4 interacting with the slag to form a hardened binder. A single-step approach has advantages from an operational point of view, compared with that proposed by Asano et al. [5], as reduced manipulation of the radioactive aqueous waste is desirable. Formation of barium sulfate in cementitious wasteforms is advantageous as it can enhance their radiation shielding properties due to the high atomic number of barium [7], and potentially promote co-precipitation of radionuclides such as 90Sr that can be present in the aqueous nuclear waste [8]. In our previous study, Ba(OH)2-Na2SO4-slag composite wasteforms were characterised after six months of curing [9], and the results confirmed the formation of the low solubility salts BaSO4 and BaCO3 along with a calcium aluminosilicate hydrate (C-A-S-H) type phase, as the main reaction products.

Despite the fact that extensive studies have been carried out to solve the mass transport limitations on MECs from double-chamber using separators to membrane-less MECs, none of these studies were focused on the usage of biocatalysts in both anode and cathode. Rozendal et al. (2008) began a comprehensive biocatalysts study of a MEC by deploiting three step start-up procedure and polarity reversal method in accordance to turn the electrochemically activated-bioanode into biocathode for hydrogen production. Years after, with the same setup, Jeremiasse et al. (2010) studied the first full biological MECs by combining both bioanode and biocathode in which both oxidation and reduction processes was performed by electrochemically active microorgansms. The same study was also performed by Liang et al. (2014) to test the effect of bicarbonate and cathode potential on the three step start-up biocathode. In their results, the study was focused on the hydrogen-producing biocathode and its performance based on a range of applied potentials providing little information on the bioanodes. It was assumed that the bioanode could supply sufficient current required for biocathodes to generate hydrogen. Lately, simpler start-up procedure was adapted for enriching autotrophic hydrogen-producing biofilm which making the utilisation of both bioanode and biocathode in a same system more reliable and easier (Batlle-Vilanova et al., 2014; Jourdin et al., 2015; Zaybak et al., 2013). But once again, the studies were half-cell experiments only focused on biocathode and not information was reported on the anode. Other advantages of using biocathode MECs were also demonstrated in wastewater treatment to remove inorganic substance such as sulphate, nitrate and heavy metals by supplying electrons from an external power supply. However, those studies only involved inorganic reduction reactions without generating any hydrogen (Cheng et al., 2012; Coma et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014). Although information was included on how bioanode react during the polarisation test on one of the studies, the biocathode was meant for sulphate reduction instead of hydrogen production (Coma et al., 2013). The minimal electrical potential that is required to drive the reaction is 0.13 V. However, more energy is required (>0.13 V) due to overpotentials to overcome energy barriers in the system (Rozendal et al., 2006). Thermodynamically, this voltage is relatively smaller required to derive hydrogen from water electrolysis compared to 1.21 V at neutral pH. Meanwhile, it could go up to 1.8-2.0 V for water electrolysis under alkaline condition due to overpotential at the electrodes (Liu et al., 2005). Secondly, the robustness of anode should be considered for better MEC performance as it could limit the current supply to cathode (Kumar et al., 2017; Rago et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2010). Weak anode with more positive open-circuit potential tends to perform poorly in supporting cathode reduction reaction when a fixed voltage was applied between the electrodes (Wang et al., 2010).

Acting Administrator Dan Tangherlini has pledged to reform the agency's practices, including implementing new policies on conferences and events. However, critics say that more needs to be done to address the agency's culture of wasteful spending. "The GSA's problems go far beyond just a few bad apples," said Senator Claire McCaskill, a Democrat from Missouri. "We need to see real reform and accountability, not just lip service. Northrup found himself at the crossroads where, five minutes before, he had stood, and there, in plain sight of any one not marked by Fate for a turning-point, was a sign-board in perfectly good condition, stating the fact that if one followed the direction, indicated by a long, tapering finger, for three miles, he would come to Heathcote Inn, "Open All the Year." "The girl must take me for a fool, or worse!" thought Northrup. Then he was conscious of a feeling that he had left something behind him in that room he had just invaded. But no! His gripsack was securely fastened on his back, his walking stick was in his hand, his hat upon his head. Still he felt that lack of something. "It's the air!" Northrup sniffed it. "I'm as hungry as a wolf, too. Hungry as I used to be twenty years ago." Northrup was twenty-seven. "Lord! what a day." It was a day with which to reckon, there was no doubt about that. An autumn day of silence, crispness, and colour. Suddenly, something Manly had said came hurtingly into Northrup's consciousness: "... or a woman's face!" Then, because of the day and a certain regained strength, Northrup laughed and shook off that impression of having left something behind him and set off at a brisk rate on the road to the inn. He soon came to the lake. It lay to the right of the road. The many-coloured hills rose protectingly on the left. All along the edge of the water a flaming trail of sumach marked the curves where the obliging land withdrew as the lake intruded. "I might be a thousand miles from home," Northrup thought as he swung along. In reality, he had been only a week on his way and had taken it easy. He had made no plans; had walked until he was weary, had slept where he could find quarters, and was doing what he had all his life wanted to do, and which at last Manly had given him courage to do: leave the self that circumstances had evolved and take to the open trail, seeking, as Manly had figuratively put it, his real self. During his long illness reality seemed to have fallen from his perceptions - or was it unreality? He knew that he must find out or he could never again hope to take his place among men with any assurance. As far as he could he must cut himself off from the past, blot out the time-honoured prejudices that might or might not be legitimate. He must settle that score! Northrup was a tall, lean man with a slant of the body that suggested resistance. His face, too, carried out the impression. The eyes, deep set and keenly gray, brooded questioningly when the humour of a situation did not control them.

"They're finding out about these sites through their friends, not by reading about them online, so it's really difficult for parents to stay ahead of the curve." The National Crime Prevention Council recently released a report that found nearly one-third of American teens reported being bullied in the past year. Among those surveyed, 31% used cell phones to bully others, and more than half of the respondents said they used instant messenger. As technology evolves, so do the ways people use it to harm others. According to the report, 30% of teens surveyed said they've been harassed online. And while bullying has always existed, technology has made it easier to spread rumors, share photos and videos, and harass victims with greater reach and permanence. Bullying can happen anywhere - at home, at school or in cyberspace. For example, someone could post a picture of a victim on Instagram and ask followers to comment on how ugly or stupid the person looks. Or, a student could send threatening texts or emails to a classmate. What's worse? A recent survey conducted by Common Sense Media found that only 25% of parents talk to their kids regularly about their Internet activities. And when asked what would make them feel safe online, 60% of kids polled said having a parent talk to them about the dangers of the Internet would help. "It's really important for parents to understand the different places where kids are going, and also just as importantly, the reasons behind why they're going there," said Delaney Ruston, director of the film "Screenagers" and founder of Screenagers.org. "Are they really interested in the content of the site, or is it just something else?" Parents need to keep track of their kids' activities online, said Susan Newman, a social psychologist and author of several books, including "Little Things Long Remembered: Making Your Children Feel Special Every Day." "Kids aren't just going to tell you. You have to monitor their activity. Bert surrendered the child, who looked up into the bearded face of the rough fellow, then rested her head on his breast, and went to sleep at last. It made his heart thrill as he felt her little head against his breast. He never had held a child in his arms before. "Say, Bert, reckon I'm a purty fair picture of a fam'ly man, now, eh? Throw in a couple o' twists more o' hay - " Bert stirred up the fire. "Well, now the little one is off, what's up over to the Norsk's? Wha' d'ye bring the child for?" he asked at last. "Because she was the only livin' soul in the shanty." "What?" His face was set in horror. "Fact." "Where's the Norsk?" "I don't know. On the prairie somewhere." "An' the mother?" "She's - " Here the little one stirred slightly as he leaned forward, and Ans said, with a wink, "She's asleep." He winked significantly, and Bert understood what the sleep was. "Be a little careful what y' say - jes' now; the little rat is listenin'. Jest say relative when y' mean her - the woman, y' know." "Yes, sir," he resumed after a moment; "I was scart when I saw that house - when I knocked, an' no one stirred 'r come to the door.
