We get there and it's packed, which is awesome, because I love sitting down when I'm feeling like I'm going to die. And then, we get seated and I'm like, "Yes, I'm going to make it through this." But then, I look over and see Harry Potter sitting next to us. I'm not even kidding, it was like I had stumbled into a real-life fantasy novel. The kid was dressed to the nines in a striped shirt and everything. I was like, "This is amazing, I'm going to die, but at least I'm going to die with Harry Potter." But then, the kid gets up and leaves, and it's like, "Oh no, the magic is gone." And then, the ugliest people start pouring in. I mean, this one hostess had a watch on her arm that was like a crime against humanity. It was a pink, rhinestoned square that took up half her arm, and I was like, "I don't know if I can handle this." And then, we finally get seated, and I'm like, "Okay, this is it, I'm going to make it through this." But then, this psycho girl starts staring at me the whole time. I'm like, "What is wrong with you, lady? Can't you see I'm trying to eat my pasta and recover from food poisoning?" She was really creepy, and I was like, "I'm going to get out of here as soon as I can." But then, the waitress comes over, and I'm like, "Thank God, someone normal." And then, she tells us it's going to be a few minutes, and I'm like, "What, are you kidding me? I'm going to die over here." But then, she comes back, and we order our food, and I'm like, "Okay, this is it, I'm going to make it through this."

Wu et al. [22] explored the role of Au particles supported on mesoporous silica on the reaction mechanism, showing the activation of O2 molecules by gold, providing active surface oxygen species. All these studies demonstrate the critical role of nano size gold particles in the oxidation of cyclohexane. Tsukuda and coworkers extensively explored the catalytic activity of supported Aun nanoclusters in oxidation reactions [15,17,23,24]. Carbon supported Aun(SG)m clusters (n = 5, 10, 18, 25, 39, 1/2 85)(G = glutathione), after ligand removal, were all active in the aerobic oxidation of cyclohexane to cyclohexanol and cyclohexanone, but with a volcano-type dependence with a maximum at n = 39 [17]. This clearly shows how a difference in cluster size of several atoms affects the catalytic activity. In a study of benzyl alcohol oxidation with extended cluster size (n = 2, 25, 38, 144, 330) Au144 exhibited the highest activity [23]. The size dependence was ascribed to differences in the geometric structure of the various clusters. For example, Au25(SR)18 has an icosahedral Au13 core, protected by characteristic long staples (-SR-Au-SR-Au-SR-) [25,26]. In contrast, Au144(SR)60 has a hollow icosahedral Au114 core, in this case protected by short staples (-SR-Au-SR-) [27,28] (Fig. 1). The thiolate ligands on the clusters influence also the catalytic properties [10,24]. Generally, the ligands are considered to poison the active Au sites [3,10]. Consequently, the ligands are often removed by oxidative thermal pretreatments to produce more accessible Au surface [29]. Metal oxides are commonly used as supports to stabilize the cluster core structure during pretreatment and reaction conditions. The influence of the ligand coverage around the gold core on the activity in cyclohexane oxidation was studied by Zhang et al [30] using Au38(SR)24 clusters supported on CeO2 and Al2O3. Pretreated catalysts were more active than untreated ones, once more showing that the removal of thiolates creates more active sites. Despite identical thermal treatments, Au38 clusters supported on CeO2 were more active than the ones on Al2O3 with higher K/A selectivity. This suggests different cluster-support interactions for CeO2 and Al2O3. For Au25 clusters, support effects were also studied by Fang et al. [31], using hydroxyapatite (HAP), TiO2 (P25), activated carbon (AC), pyrolyzed graphene oxide (PGO) and fumed SiO2. It was found that certain supports (like HAP and TiO2) effectively prevented the sintering of Au nanoclusters during pretreatments, due to the strength of Au-support interaction, whereas cluster growth occurred for AC; PGO; and SiO2. In contrast, Ma et al. [32] and Das et al. [33] reported that no sintering occurred for Au25 and Au144 supported on a different kind of mesoporous silica upon thiolate ligand removal (again ascribed to a strong interaction between Au and silica). Therefore, the current study of the stability of clusters supported on TiO2 or SiO2 should clarify the contradicting previous observations [31-33].

This seemingly innocuous order has turned into a mammoth environmental challenge-an emblem of shortsighted policymaking cloaked in a veneer of cultural tradition. The officials might argue for the revival of traditional crafts, but what they conveniently overlook is the ecological burden and the hidden motives of their decisions. The contracts for supplying these pots likely fill the coffers of a select few, those with connections to the officials, rather than genuinely supporting local artisans. The irony is palpable. In urban settings, educated citizens see through these ploys, but their voices are mere whispers drowned by the overwhelming silence of the rural majority, for whom participation in the political process is but a ceremonial exercise. This conundrum extends beyond mere policy decisions. Political leaders with questionable integrity, charting the course for millions, are elected based more on perceived legacy and manipulated narratives rather than verified competence or intentions. The veneer of democracy, unfortunately, seems to be just that-a fragile facade that hides rooms rife with obfuscation and self-interest. While technology and the internet have penetrated even into the most remote locales, the education system laggingly churns out young minds unprepared to sift through the barrage of misinformation. Without critical thinking skills, even access to information becomes futile, creating a fertile ground for manipulation. Hope rests with the burgeoning youth population demanding accountability through every available medium. Social media emerges as an unlikely ally, offering a platform where the truth struggles to find its way but sometimes does. Even in its imperfections, social media might yet become the catalyst for change, sparking debates and shining light into these dark crevices of governance. Consider the plight of a villager, living on the fringes of the national consciousness, sending his children to subpar schools, trusting in the promises sung out during election campaigns. These children are the future arbiters of democracy, saddled with the responsibility of discerning integrity from pretense. The stakes are high, and the clock never pauses. With each passing election, with each successive regime, the burden of educated choice becomes increasingly difficult to bear, threatening the very foundation of the democratic ideals espoused in the constitution. Thus, as an observer, one must ask: is it possible to mend this systemic disrepair without overhauling the sociopolitical infrastructure? Can India, in its sprawling diversity and complexity, reconfigure its approach to grooming future leaders in an environment that breeds transparency and accountability? Certainly, the challenges are immense, yet the capacity for reinvention lies within the same spirited dynamism that drove the country's original struggle for independence. Such introspection and resolve must originate from within, mobilizing not only the intelligentsia but the grassroots-those very rural constituents who remain the fulcrum of democratic sway. To transcend this undulating sea of adversity, India's path may demand an audacious reevaluation of educational priorities, a reframing of political dialogue, and a sincere commitment to bridging communication chasms. In that conviction, perhaps, lies the promise of a true democracy, one where the machinations of governance reflect the aspirations and wisdom of an enlightened populace.

It's interesting because you know, I had this thought that it would be easy to say empathy is something that everybody needs and wants and it's a skill that everybody could benefit from developing and that's certainly true. And yet, when I started talking to these corporate leaders about why they wanted to develop empathy, it wasn't always because they felt that it was important for themselves personally. Although I did get that sense from some of them. Some of them were concerned about burnout among their employees and what they perceived as lack of loyalty among their employees. And I think part of the reason for that is that there has been a shift in the way that people relate to each other in the workplace, and the way that companies relate to their employees and the way that employees relate to companies and especially with the pandemic. There's a lot of fear and uncertainty and it's hard to keep people motivated and engaged when there's so much anxiety and fear around us. And so what they want to do is they want to create a culture of trust and safety where people feel safe enough to open up and express themselves and be vulnerable with each other without fearing judgment or reprisal and that's what they hope will lead to greater loyalty and retention and productivity and profitability. And so they want to develop skills of listening and curiosity and vulnerability and compassion and self-awareness and all those things that go along with empathy and I think what's interesting is that they don't realize that what they want is to develop skills of emotional intelligence, which is different than empathy. Empathy is feeling someone else's emotions as if they were your own. Emotional intelligence is having the awareness and the tools to navigate relationships with other people. So that's what we're working on together. Okay, okay, so let's dive deeper into that a little bit. Can you tell me what what you mean by emotional intelligence versus empathy? Sure, sure. Well, the definition of emotional intelligence is the ability to understand and manage your own emotions and recognize the emotions of others and it includes skills like self-awareness, social awareness, self-management and relationship management and empathy is one aspect of emotional intelligence. The ability to feel another person's emotion as if it were your own. It's an instinctual response. We feel it automatically and it doesn't require any conscious effort on our part. It's a natural response. Whereas emotional intelligence requires that we make an active choice to use the skills that we have developed. And so I think that sometimes when people hear the word empathy they think that it means feeling sorry for somebody or feeling pity or feeling sadness for them. And I think what I'm trying to convey to them is that actually empathy is feeling what they feel. You know, it's feeling what they feel. Not necessarily feeling bad for them. Okay, and and how do you do that? How do you teach somebody how to feel what somebody else feels. Because I know that sounds like a strange question. But yeah, exactly. I mean, I'm I'm curious, you know, what are the steps? Yeah, so it's funny because I have noticed that when I teach this stuff to groups of people who are already interested in personal development and spirituality and things like that. They tend to be very receptive and they're often surprised at how quickly they pick it up and how easily they can access this capacity within themselves. And yet when I try to teach this to people who are not particularly interested in personal growth or spirituality, they seem to struggle with it.

"Try?" repeated the Younger Man. "Yes! Try!" "What do you suggest?" "Why - oh, I don't know!" answered the Older Man vaguely. "Anything! Anything! Any one thing will do! Just try anything!" "Try anything?" queried the Younger Man blankly. "Why, yes! Why shouldn't you try anything?" "Of course, I should!" "Then go ahead and try it!" "What?" "Try anything!" "I see!" "You'll find it quite interesting!" "How?" "Why, I assure you, sir, that when you get right down to brass tacks, it's astonishing how little you need in order to make yourself happy! You can make yourself perfectly contented with absolutely nothing!" "Nothing?" echoed the Younger Man. "Not a blessed thing! Not a solitary thing! Nothing! Absolutely nothing!" "Aha!" chuckled the Younger Man. "Ah, well, that's good enough for me!" "For you?" "Yes! For me!" "Haven't you got any ambition?" asked the Older Man. "Ambition?" scoffed the Younger Man. "Ambition! "Accomplish? Accomplish? What does that mean? To accomplish? To do what? To accomplish what?" "To do something useful - to make money - to succeed - to win - to conquer - to become somebody!" "Ought to amount to something?" echoed the Younger Man. "Amount to something? Amount to something? Where in the name of heaven could I possibly amount to anything? I'm a nobody! Mechanical cleaning via high-pressure water blasting, on the other hand, is time consuming and has limited environmental sustainability because it requires large amounts of water that needs to be treated afterwards. To date, the possibility of using in situ cavitation to remove CRUD deposits from nuclear systems has received little consideration. It is well known that, when a liquid flow accelerates, the static pressure decreases. If the static pressure falls below the local liquid vapor pressure, then cavitation occurs. Being triggered by a reduction in local pressure related to the liquid flow itself, this type of cavitation is normally referred to as hydrodynamic cavitation. Since hydrodynamic cavitation could in principle be triggered, via proper tuning of the operating conditions, around regions of flow acceleration where CRUD deposition occurs, the possibility of using hydrodynamic cavitation to remove CRUD deposits from nuclear systems becomes apparent. In fact, it is worth noting that CRUD deposition can be enhanced by fluid flow and it is known to increase strongly around regions of flow acceleration, such as through flow holes in steam generator tube support plates (McGrady et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017). A previous study (Kim and Bang, 2016) showed that orifice-induced hydrodynamic cavitation directed at a previously deposited target was capable of partially removing CRUD-like deposits over short time periods. However, the possibility of removing CRUD deposit from an orifice itself, being similar in structure to constrictions such as those found between steam generator tube support plates, has not been previously considered and is what motivated the present investigation. The aim of this work is to explore the possibility of using hydrodynamic cavitation in nuclear systems for short time periods to effectively remove CRUD. In this study, tests were performed on CRUD deposited micro-orifices to assess the possibility of removing CRUD by hydrodynamic cavitation. CRUD removal from within the micro-orifices was monitored as a function of time of exposure to cavitating flow, showing that a few minutes exposure could reduce the volume of CRUD deposit by 80-90% with no detectable damage to the metal surface. The use of microfluidics systems to recreate nuclear plant operating conditions while using a simplified experimental set-up is an effective approach recently developed by McGrady et al. (2017a), and motivated the use of micro-orifices for the present work. Though preliminary and restricted to small-scale microfluidics test systems, our results suggest that hydrodynamic cavitation may be used in nuclear systems for short time periods to effectively reduce CRUD build-up within and surrounding constricted areas, possibly in synergy with the other CRUD removal techniques previously discussed. Even though our results seem encouraging, it is worth remembering that the present work is just a proof-of-concept carried out with a simplified, though representative, experimental setup. The actual implementation of hydrodynamic cavitation cleaning in nuclear systems would require further investigation and extensive assessment.

In addition, their analysis assumed that there were no economies of scale associated with transporting greater quantities of CO2 over longer distances. More recently, a report published by the International Energy Agency (IEA) Greenhouse Gas R&D Programme (IEAGHG) on the techno-economic evaluation of CO2 transport indicated that pipeline diameter was also a key driver of cost (International Energy Agency Greenhouse Gas R&D Programme, 2011). A similar finding was reported by Zhang et al. (2006) who found that transport costs decrease with increasing pipeline diameters. The IEAGHG report concluded that the distance between the CO2 source and the storage location was the primary factor affecting the cost of CO2 transport, but did not address other factors such as pipe diameter and pressure drop along the pipeline. The IEAGHG report also noted that, while transport costs vary based on geographic region, they represent only a fraction of the overall cost of implementing CCS (International Energy Agency Greenhouse Gas R&D Programme, 2011). With respect to storage, several studies have focused on identifying the major cost drivers associated with CO2 injection and storage within different types of geologic formations including saline aquifers, coal seams, and depleted oil and gas reservoirs (Benson et al., 2004; Hovorka, 2007; Buscheck et al., 2012). These studies have generally agreed that the two main factors influencing storage costs are: (1) the type of geologic formation selected for CO2 storage (e.g., deep saline formations, depleted oil and gas fields, unmineable coal beds); and (2) the location of the storage reservoir relative to the CO2 source (Hovorka, 2007; Buscheck et al., 2012). Additional considerations include the number of wells required to inject the desired amount of CO2, the depth of the reservoir, and the cost of the monitoring program necessary to ensure safe storage of CO2 (Buscheck et al., 2012).

Chuck kneels beside the cooling body, eyes scanning the wreckage of a life once vibrant, now reduced to pulp and echoes. The scar tissue on Eddie's knuckles, a testament to countless battles, glimmers under the harsh fluorescents. He shivers, not from the cold, but the lingering ghost of chaos thrumming in the air. The Killer was here, and he had no mercy. Detective Ames stands nearby, a frown carved deep into his gravelly features, eyes taking in every detail with the predatory focus of a seasoned hunter. This one's bad, even by his standards. "Three, huh?" he grumbles, voice like crushed rocks. "It's like he's making a collection." Chuck rises, slipping the scarf back into his coat pocket. "Eddie was a good fighter," he muses aloud, not to anyone in particular, but the room that holds too many secrets. "Maybe too good." Ames grunts in agreement, turning the thought over. "What's the motive then? Jealousy? Or does somebody have a serious chip on their shoulder against boxers?" Chuck kicks at the remnants of a broken stool, scattered like bones along the stained floor. "Could be personal. Or hell, maybe he's just crazy, a twisted artist painting in blood." The image is unsettling, but it brings a bitter chuckle to his lips. They'd seen worse, yet nothing quite this raw. The moon watches them from the cracked window, pale and indifferent. Its light spills over the ring, illuminating the shattered remnants of brutality. This dance of shadows and suffering, it's a stage, and the Killer seems to revel in the darkness, leaving his victims as gruesome masterpieces. Suddenly, a noise stirs. The faint sound of footsteps outside the gym. Both men freeze, ears attuned to the murmur of danger. Ames motions for silence, and they creep towards the door, hearts pounding. Could it be him, returning to witness his handiwork? The Killer, the artist of pain? The door creaks open to reveal Ernie, the cornerman, eyes wide with disbelief and sorrow. "I heard," he stammers, breathless. "I came as soon as I could, but... Eddie..." Chuck nods, a heavy hand on Ernie's shoulder. "Yeah, Ernie. He's gone." There's no sugarcoating the truth, not when it spills like entrails across the canvas. Ernie's face crumples, a man cast adrift without his champion. "I should've stayed," he whispers, regret like acid in his voice. "I shouldn't have left him." "Don't blame yourself," Ames interjects, steel tempering his tone. "This guy, he's... he's something else. Ain't nothing you or anyone could have done." But the guilt lingers, thick in the air, mingling with the stench of sweat and despair. It's another night in a city that sometimes feels as though it devours dreams, growing fat on the failures of the innocent. Together, they stand in silence, three men-one alive, one dead, one grieving-bound by the brutal hand of fate and the haunting promise of vengeance. Beneath the indifferent moon, shadows remain long after the blood dries, echoing the steps of a puppet master pulling strings in an endless night.

The popularity of SLES is mainly due to economic reasons (relatively low price compared to other surfactants), technological aspects (good performance at low concentrations and possibility to achieve the desired product consistency - viscosity - by adding sodium chloride, which also brings economic benefits), and qualitative aspects (possibility of formulation a product with desired washing performance and foaming properties). A disadvantage in use of this surfactant is related to its relatively high potential to induce skin irritation reactions by creating strong ionic bonds with the epidermal proteins [1,2,9,12-17]. For this reason, cosmetic manufacturers are constantly looking for new solutions to reduce the negative impact of SLES on the skin. A number of methods to achieve this effect have been elaborated. For example, the formulations may be enriched with additional substances such as polymers, proteins and it's hydrolysates [18-28], plant extracts and oils [29-33]. Alternatively, delicate surfactants or their mixtures may be used (e.g. anionic with nonionic and amphoteric or cationic types) [1,5,34-38]. Structures arising in such systems, e.g. surfactant and polymer combinations, or the formation of mixed micelles in systems containing different types of surfactants, decrease the adverse effects caused by washing compounds on the skin. A frequently used method of reducing the adverse skin effects caused by anionic surfactants is the incorporation of a cationic surface-active compound into the product. Among an extensive range of cationic surfactants, the most widely used group in the cosmetic industry comprises ammonium chlorides (e.g. cetrimonium chloride) as well as various types of ammonium derivatives referred to as polyquaterniums, or cationic silicone derivatives. Disadvantages of these substances include their relatively high potential to produce skin and eye irritation, and adverse effects on the natural environment. These compounds are classified as toxic to aquatic organisms with long-term effects. In addition, they may have a corrosive effect on the skin and cause eye damage. As a result, a need arose to develop a cationic surfactant without any adverse effects on human health nor to the natural environment [1-5,9]. In the course of development efforts, a special interest was focused on the cationic amphiphilic polymer called Guar Hydroxypropyltrimonium Chloride. It is being obtained from guar gum (polysaccharide - galactomannan), a substance of natural origin produced from the seeds of the plant Cyamopsis Tetragonoloba [39]. The production process of the cationic derivative includes a quaternization reaction of guar flour with (3-chloro-2-hydroxypropyl) trimethylammonium chloride. The chemical structure of cationized guar gum is shown in Fig. 1. Unlike the commonly used cationic surfactants, Guar Hydroxypropyltrimonium Chloride has no adverse impact on the natural environment or human health, and it may serve as a sustainable raw material alternative to substances such as Polyquaternium-7. At present, the substance is used as a conditioning ingredient in hair conditioners and 2-in-1 shampoos.

For inclusion, eligible studies had to have relevant area-level indicators and associations with mortality presented, include populations consisting of people with severe mental illness, and have an effect size for the association of the area-level indicator with mortality outcomes. We excluded ecological studies. A total of 1281 studies were identified, which were screened by abstract or full text for possible inclusion. A total of eight studies were identified as relevant. Six focused on all-cause mortality of which one study also included deaths from natural and unnatural causes, and the other two studies focused on suicide. The studies also assessed area-level exposures across international settings, which included Ethiopia (two studies), China (one study), Taiwan (one study), UK and devolved countries (two studies), and Canada (two studies). Across all studies, irrespective of area-level associations, people with severe mental illness had increased mortality compared with reference groups without severe mental illness. Associations with area-level indicators and mortality outcomes followed differing patterns, dependent on context. There were mixed findings across studies examining the effect of urbanicity on mortality outcomes in severe mental illness. This included one study suggesting an increased risk of death in urban compared with rural areas (from Ethiopia), one study indicating an increased risk in rural compared with urban areas (from China), and two studies suggesting no association (from Canada and Ethiopia). Four out of five retrieved studies supported residency in more deprived areas being associated with elevated mortality in people with severe mental illness. However, in one study from a nationally representative sample from the UK, the investigators reported that people with severe mental illness resident in more deprived areas had a lower risk of suicide than people resident in less deprived areas. No studies were identified that assessed the association of ethnic density or social fragmentation with mortality in severe mental illness. Added value of this study This study is the first to systematically assess a range of neighbourhood-level exposures and, specifically, ethnic density, with mortality in severe mental illness. The study was situated in a geographically defined, ethnically diverse, urban location in the UK. We found strong support for the observation that, for certain ethnic minority groups with severe mental illness, mortality risks (especially for deaths from all causes and natural causes) are lower in areas of higher own-group density relative to white British people with severe mental illness. Other area-level indicators (social fragmentation, urbanicity, and area-level deprivation) as assessed in this study were not associated with excess mortality in severe mental illness. Our findings build on a previous analysis that had shown that risks of all-cause, natural-cause, and unnatural-cause mortality were lower in most UK ethnic minority groups with severe mental illness compared with a white British reference group with severe mental illness. The present study suggests that the ethnic density of the area where ethnic minority groups with severe mental illness reside might have an important role in modifying mortality risks.

The scent of freedom mingled with the faint aroma of a distant espresso bar, tickling his senses and lifting his spirits. The city was abuzz, cars honking impatiently, pedestrians darting like restless birds-all oblivious to the legend among them, newly untethered and daringly resurrected. Behind him, Cesar and Antony followed in his wake, the latter grinning devilishly, his eyes narrowed with mischief. "Hawk, my man," Cesar called, his voice imbued with a hint of uneasy camaraderie, "we've got ourselves a fine little venture lined up. Something that'll have folks talking 'bout the great Hawk again." Hawk turned sharply, his eyes gleaming with the mirth of a man unfazed by danger, but he arched an eyebrow, ever the skeptic. "You boys never learned, did you? It's a new era. I play by different rules now." Antony laughed, a sound reminiscent of clinking coins or the shuffling of a king's deck. "Different rules? Aren't you tired of preaching from the righteous book? World's not changing, my friend, only the faces who run it." Hawk's lips twitched upward in subtle acknowledgment of the truth. His fingers brushed against the canvas bag Cesar thrust into his hands, filled with what Hawk guessed was several volumes measured in intrigue and risk. "We're talking art, Hawk," Cesar insisted, sounding like a peddler of fine dreams on a sunny boulevard, "Stuff legends are made of. Da Vinci, to be exact. Your kind of game." Hawk tilted his head, curiosity piqued beneath layers of cynicism formed like sediment over years of escapades. "Da Vinci, you say. What's the catch?" Antony slung an arm around Hawk's shoulders, pulling him into a conspiratorial huddle. "Old man Moretti is sitting on a goldmine, a stash of inkworks no one's laid eyes on for centuries. Da Vinci's lost sketches, they say." "Dusty designs and doodles?" Hawk smirked, pausing dramatically. "Is this what the world thinks I've been pining for? I'm flattered, truly." Cesar leaned in, urgency in his voice now. "These aren't just doodles, Hawk. They're the key to... well, let's call it 'immense influence.' Don't you feel it? The thrill? You're the only one who can pull this off." Hawk's eyes darted between the duo, assessing more than words-unspoken promises, potential disaster. The sun dipped below the horizon, painting the skyline in bruised violets and passionate reds. He could sense the electricity in the air, the very elements daring him to rejoin the dance of deft deception. "I'll play," he declared finally, the decision as firm as eternity's whisper, "but on my terms. We keep it clean, no bloodshed. I'm not returning to the cages you found me in." "Agreed," Antony stated, the eagerness of an acolyte learning from a sage. They moved, a triad of shadowy figures merging with the city's nightly tapestry, Hawk leading with considerable grace and audacious poise. Above, stars winked conspiratorially, part of the eternal show, guiding Hawk on his freshly paved path-into history, infamy, and the beauty that comes alive only in the dark.

Flewitt Linear friction welding (LFW) is a solid-state joining process that is used for the fabrication of near-net-shape, titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V, aerospace components [1,2]. This is primarily due to the significant cost savings can be achieved when compared to other manufacturing techniques [2,3]. The process also offers many advantages over traditional fusion welding methods [2,3], including excellent mechanical properties, avoidance of melting and very low defect rates. During LFW one workpiece is oscillated relative to another whilst under a compressive force. Despite being one continuous process, LFW is said to occur over four [4-6] phases: Phase 1 - initial phase. Contact exists between asperities on the two surfaces to be joined and heat is generated due to friction - see Fig. 1(a). The asperities soften and deform, increasing the true area of contact between the workpieces. Negligible axial shortening (burn-off) perpendicular to the direction of oscillation is observed during this phase. Phase 2 - transition phase. The material plasticises and becomes highly viscous causing the true area of contact to increase to 100% of the cross-sectional area - see Fig. 1(b). The heat conducts back from the interface plasticising more material and the burn-off begins to occur due to viscous material expulsion. Phase 3 - equilibrium phase. The interface force, thermal profile and burn-off rate reach a quasi-steady-state condition and significant burn-off occurs through the rapid expulsion of viscous material from the interface. Phase 4 - deceleration phase. The relative motion is ceased and the workpieces are aligned. In some applications an additional forging force may also be applied. Despite the benefits, LFW has experienced limited industrial implementation. One of the reasons for this is due to a lack of fundamental scientific understanding [7]. The rapid nature of the process and the fact that the interface of the workpieces cannot be observed during welding particularly inhibits increased understanding. Computational models offer a pragmatic method to understand what is happening during the rapidly evolving process. Various authors have developed two [1,6-16] and three [15,17-25] dimensional (2D/3D) computational models.

Q: But why is that, Daddy? A: Because they're the ones who refuse to play nice with us and insist on keeping their system. Q: So if we look the other way at cruel dictators who aren't directly confrontational, that makes it okay to just ignore their actions? A: Exactly! It's all about geopolitics, sweetheart. Q: Geopolitics? A: Yes, it's the art of political maneuvering on a world stage. Q: So we just choose which dictators to care about? A: It's more strategic than that, my dear. We make choices based on our national interests, you see. Q: What's a national interest? A: Good question. It means what's best for America, whether that's protecting jobs, securing resources, or forming alliances. Q: But how does invading Iraq help America? A: Well, it sends a message! A message that we won't tolerate threats, and it opens up markets for our businesses. Q: So, there's money involved? A: It's always about the money, kiddo. Wars are expensive, but the post-war reconstruction contracts? Those are gold. Q: Contracts? Like the ones we sign at home? A: Precisely! Only these are multi-million dollar deals to rebuild what we bombed. Q: So, we destroy to create? A: A bit cynical, isn't it? But you see, in politics, sometimes destruction is the first step toward rebuilding a better future. Q: How do we know they'll use the money to rebuild? A: Well, we trust the process, darling. Sometimes it takes a little faith. Q: It sounds like a gamble. A: Life is a gamble, sweetie. Just like hoping that no one checks the books on how the money is being spent. Q: Isn't that dishonest? A: You're learning how to navigate this complicated world! And yes, in politics, things aren't always black and white. Sometimes gray is where the power lies. Q: So we could invade other places if we thought it was in our interest? A: In theory, yes. But we have to be careful-there's a balance, and we don't want to overextend ourselves. Q: Overextend? A: That's when you take on more than you can handle. Like if you tried to eat an extra-large pizza all by yourself. Q: But if we had the manpower, why not? A: Because then you'd end up sick to your stomach, and we wouldn't want that now, would we? Q: So what's the difference between a country and a pizza? Q: So, what you're saying is that international relations are like pizza toppings? A: You got it! Some combinations are delicious while others can turn stomachs. Q: And if we try to force our favorite toppings on everyone else? A: Then we might just end up with a food fight, possibly sparking wars of a different sort. Q: This is a lot to take in, Daddy. A: I know, kiddo. The world's a messy place, but you're learning the nuanced dance of diplomacy, even if it seems more like a slapstick routine right now!

The residents of Stockwood Park are on high alert, fearing that the influx of caravans from Dale Farm will only continue to grow. With around 20 families already setting up camp, there are reports that up to 40 more are on their way, bringing the total to a staggering 60. The 100-hectare site, which neighbors a golf course, horse riding center, and various other outdoor pursuits venues, has been overrun with mobile homes, leaving residents feeling frustrated and concerned. "I used to look out of my bedroom window and see a beautiful park," said one neighbor. "Now it's caravans. I'm sure the gypsies won't cause trouble. Let's hope it stays that way." However, the situation is far from ideal, with many residents feeling that the police and local council have been slow to respond to the situation. A spokesman for Luton Borough Council said that the council was made aware of the encampment and immediately started the standard legal procedure for eviction. "We expect to move them on very soon," he said. However, the travellers seem to be digging in, with one resident claiming that they have nowhere else to go. "We came to Luton because we've been here before," said Flint Devons, 29, who has lived at Dale Farm for seven years. "The word has now spread back to Dale Farm. There'll be 20 to 40 more caravans coming from Dale Farm. We have nowhere else to go." The situation is a repeat of the battle that has been playing out at Dale Farm for the past decade, where the travellers have been in a long-standing dispute with Basildon Council over planning permission. The travellers claim that they own the land, but only have permission to occupy half of it. The rest of the site is strewn with mobile homes, and the council has been trying to evict them for years. The High Court has intervened, ruling that the proposed measures "may go further" than the terms of the enforcement notices. The travellers have been given a temporary reprieve, but it's unclear how long this will last. As the situation continues to unfold, residents of Stockwood Park are left to wonder what the future holds. Will the council be able to evict the travellers, or will they be forced to find a new home elsewhere? Only time will tell.

However, there is an undeniable allure to the notion that, perhaps, elements of our existence are woven into a larger tapestry, one where threads intersect in ways we may not immediately comprehend. In that respect, I find myself balancing on the precipice between skepticism and wonder, weary of a perspective that entirely discounts the spontaneous eruption of serendipity. The idea of purpose can be deceptive, often masquerading as certainty when, in truth, our quests for meaning are anything but linear. Consider this notion: every tall tale we tell, every laugh we share, every tear shed bears the weight of countless preceding moments. Life, in this sense, resembles a sprawling maze, intricate and layered, where even fleeting encounters leave imprints upon the soul. I think of the faces I catch on the street-a stranger's smile, a brief exchange of glances-all of which could be perceived as random yet become catalysts for introspection and change. Are they not but flickering reminders that we are all part of an inexplicable web? In the dull hum of daily life, one might dismiss such moments, yet, I believe they carry significance beyond their mundane appearances. This brings to mind the distinct humanity within the tapestry of existence. It is far too easy to view oneself as an isolated incident, a solitary entity adrift in this vast cosmos. However, the connections we forge, whether profound or subtle, may reveal a deeper design beneath the surface chaos. Could it be that the universe conspires to interlock our paths, a kind of celestial choreography where intention and coincidence sway gently in sync? And while it is comforting to think that each encounter serves a specific purpose, I also revel in the thought that we possess the autonomy to assign our own meanings. Consider the artistic lens through which life can be viewed. Art often mirrors the chaos of existence-brush strokes of unpredictability mingle with deliberate intentions, creating a mosaic reflective of the human experience. Aren't our lives, too, muddled with both chaos and intention? Each choice we make, each rejection we face, might simply be the paintbrush's stroke carrying us toward an unforeseen revelation. Perhaps it isn't solely about predestination or free will, but rather the interplay of both, an intricate dance that propels us forward, nudging us through the unfolding plot of existence. I find solace in creativity, a realm where experience meets profound possibility. When I write, I often feel caught between embracing structure or surrendering to spontaneity, a microcosm of the broader existential struggle. The blank page is an open invitation-do I allow the muse to guide me, or do I attempt to sculpt something with the particular shape I've envisioned? In this interplay, I glean wisdom: creation thrives not in rigid confines but in the fluid movement between control and abandon. So what does it mean to rest upon the knife's edge of fate and free will? Beyond the philosophical musings, I find that accepting our inherent uncertainty can be liberating. To navigate life with the understanding that we are both a product of our myriad experiences and active participants in crafting our narrative, to me, feels profoundly human. In the end, one must ask: does the search for purpose bind us or set us free?

So yes, while I might endeavor to understand what drives my colleague to act in ways that seem curved and sharp, I also remind myself that my response matters. The antidote to cycle of negativity can often be found in compassion and kindness-kindness not just towards others, but also towards oneself. It's the simple act of recognizing our shared humanity and the understanding that we're all walking this labyrinth of life, trying to navigate through our personal storms. I contemplate how transformative it is when one breaks up the cycles of negativity-not merely becoming a vessel for kindness, but allowing it to echo through all interactions. Each of us possesses the power to cultivate positivity, to extend a hand or a kind word, even to those who seem intent on throwing shadows. Such is the beauty of human connection; when viewed through the lens of compassion, even the darkest moments can reveal a glimmer of light. And therein lies the challenge-a challenge I fully embrace, for within the embrace of empathy lies the true essence of growth. I am learning and I am hopeful, and I choose to walk this path with grace.

Though the origin of that strange sound had yet to be discovered, it had bonded the two boys in a faithful friendship through which their courage and curiosity propelled them into adventures they never anticipated. Now, as they rode across the sun-baked plains, their spirits were lighter, despite the concern over Bob's missing knife. The bright expanse stretched before them, a boundless ocean of waving grass under an arching azure sky, where clouds floated lazily as if set adrift by an unseen hand. The afternoon sun cast long shadows of horse and rider, dancing across the terrain as Frank and Bob conversed in their saddle-bound reverie. "You know, Bob," Frank mused, breaking the peaceful rhythm of hoofbeats, "there's talk of that old abandoned mine up near Hawk's Peak. Some people say things vanish into thin air up there. Not that I'm suggesting your knife did, but it's a curious notion." Bob chuckled, shaking his head slightly. "I doubt a ghost mine would know what to do with a good honest knife from Kentucky. But it does stir the imagination, doesn't it? Perhaps we should take a ride up there, if for nothing else, for the sake of satisfying our curiosity." "That or for a good tale to tell by the fireplace," Frank grinned. It was well known that old stories, whether spun around mysteries or entailed brave feats, were just as much the sinews of frontier life as tending cattle or mending fences. Pushing the thought aside, at least for the moment, Bob shifted the conversation. "Still, it makes you wonder how something just disappears like that. I keep thinking there's some clue I'm missing. If only I could remember." "Well, until you do," Frank said optimistically, "we might as well be on the lookout for bigger things than knives and ghostly whispers. There's the world to explore, and places neither of us have yet claimed." "Dad did mention a certain silver mine," Bob remarked, his voice edging with intrigue, "tucked somewhere in the folds of the Chisos Mountains. He spoke of old prospects and new rumors. Maybe we ought to take a gander in that direction, see what we find." "Sounds like a plan!" Frank exclaimed, his excitement palpable. "There's more than one kind of treasure to be found in this world. And who knows? We might even stumble upon something worth writing about in far more than dusty journals." With visions of looming peaks and forgotten tales weaving through their thoughts, the boys urged their horses faster. The sunlight danced upon their backs as they headed toward an uncertain horizon, its promises as vast and variable as the plains they so loved. Their ride was an emblem of youthful hope and a testament to the unyielding bond that made all of life's adventures more worthwhile when shared. Yet deep down, even amidst the thrill of possibilities ahead, the mystery of the lost knife simmered at the edges of Bob's mind. But for now, he felt a seed of freedom, secure in the company of his dearest friend, embraced by the wild symphony of nature, where all things seemed vividly alive. The Saddle Boys were on their way, and each mile carried the weight of stories untold and dreams yet to be lived.

I couldn't shake the sudden chill that crept over me. Was it paranoia? Was I overthinking? It felt childish to feel so territorial over a seating arrangement, but there it was: the undeniable sting of rejection. I tried to play it cool, leaning back into the couch, crossing my arms over my chest, feigning nonchalance. The movie flickered on, casting a dance of shadows and vivid colors across the living room, but my mind wasn't on the screen. Every laugh, every pointed glance, seemed magnified between Gwen and that Butters guy. Later, speaking of the evening seemed almost cathartic. Melissa, with her endless well of wisdom and cheer, nudged me during the end credits. "You seem distracted, buddy," she remarked, her eyebrows doing that thing where they knitted together just enough to express genuine concern. I shrugged, maintaining the facade that nothing more was amiss than a passing worry. "Just tired, I guess," I replied, though the lie tasted bitter on my tongue. As March dragged into its latter days, I began revisiting our interactions with a new lens. Had I been ignorant of a dynamic shift? Was it me, or had Gwen genuinely grown distant? I couldn't quite tell if I was placing the magnifying glass over nothing but smoke and mirrors. Butters and pain meds-a laughable excuse that I couldn't quite bring myself to swallow-constantly danced in my mind, though I willed myself to forget. But here's where things take another twist. One afternoon, in the warmth of early spring, I found myself on the school's soccer field. Now, I wasn't part of the team, just a casual kicker on the sidelines. There Gwen appeared, an unexpected sight against the green expanse. She wore that familiar expression of hers-a cross between excitement and contemplation. Our conversation began with the usual trifles, but eventually, the elephant in the room could no longer be ignored. I finally mustered the courage to ask, "Are we still...us?" The question hovered awkwardly, the air tense with unsaid words. Gwen paused, and for a moment, I regretted breaking the fragile thread of normalcy. But then she spoke, her words delicate yet steady. "I think we've changed. People do that, you know?" Her voice was a mix of vulnerability and certainty, painting a picture of resolutions formed over restless nights. "I care about us, about you. But I need to figure out who I am outside of this... connection." It didn't feel like an end, not yet. More like a bookmark in an ongoing story where both characters need to wander within separate paragraphs before joining again-perhaps. With that, I started to understand. The journey of 'us' perhaps required side quests of self-discovery-an alignment of hearts that first needed space to beat independently. And so, we parted ways on that field with an unspoken promise, a handshake of understanding. Despite the unpredictability of the dating game, a new chapter loomed: one of patience, growth, and acceptance. Maybe, just maybe, this was what the flawed, chaotic, heartbreakingly beautiful game was all about.

Humans are important environmental agents (Steffen et al., 2007; Price et al., 2011), with anthropogenic processes (e.g., as discussed above, vegetation removal, infrastructure development, groundwater abstraction) existing in every inhabited region of the world. Anthropogenic processes may influence the occurrence, frequency or intensity of natural hazards. Identifying and understanding anthropogenic processes and their spatio-temporal relevance is therefore of importance when (i) assessing the potential of natural hazards occurring, (ii) developing holistic multi-hazard frameworks for a given region, and (iii) determining possible disaster risk reduction (DRR) measures. As an example of the influence of anthropogenic processes on natural hazards, consider a slope that is susceptible to landslides. Multiple anthropogenic processes could change the extent to which it is susceptible to slope failure and thus increase or decrease the overall likelihood of a landslide occurring or its size. Examples of some anthropogenic processes that are known to increase landslide susceptibility include vegetation removal, changes in agriculture, implementation of development projects, construction unloading and inadequate drainage (Alexander, 1992; Glade, 2003; Sarkar and Kanungo, 2004; Tarolli and Sofia, 2016). Road construction, which may involve one or more of these anthropogenic processes, is noted to increase landslide susceptibility close to roads both during and after construction (Montgomery, 1994; Devkota et al., 2013; Brenning et al., 2015). Many other instances of anthropogenic processes influencing natural hazards are described in the literature, with examples referred to throughout this paper. If anthropogenic processes trigger the occurrence of particular natural hazards, these 'primary' natural hazards may in turn trigger secondary natural hazards, generating a network of natural hazard interactions (cascade) with the anthropogenic process as the source trigger. Furthermore, anthropogenic processes may also increase or decrease the likelihood of a particular natural hazard interaction, i.e., the coupling relationship between a primary and secondary natural hazard. For example, an earthquake or heavy rain can trigger many thousands of landslides, with the number of triggered landslides related to anthropogenic processes such as road construction and vegetation removal (Glade, 2003; Owen et al., 2008; Brenning et al., 2015). The widespread prevalence of anthropogenic processes and their ability to accelerate or decelerate natural hazard processes strongly suggests that understanding the 'hazardousness' of a region (Hewitt and Burton, 1971; Regmi et al., 2013) cannot be done effectively without taking these processes into consideration. Analysing these important networks of interactions can assist in the development of holistic multi-hazard frameworks. This paper is organised as follows: Section 2 on anthropogenic processes presents background information, describes in detail the anthropogenic processes examined here, their interactions, and possible mechanisms by which they might interact with natural hazards. Section 3 presents the results of a review to identify and visualise the triggering relationships between anthropogenic process types and natural hazards. Section 4 presents a methodology for assessing and visualising the influence of anthropogenic processes on the interactions between natural hazards, through catalysis and impedance relationships.

The application of LCA to REE projects has provided valuable insights into the environmental impacts associated with REE production. However, there is still a need for further research to address the complexities and uncertainties involved in REE production. One of the key challenges in conducting LCA studies on REE projects is the limited availability of data, particularly for projects in the early stages of development. This lack of data can lead to uncertainties in the results, making it difficult to draw conclusions about the environmental performance of REE production. To address this challenge, researchers have developed various methods to estimate the environmental impacts of REE production. For example, some studies have used surrogate data from similar projects or industries to estimate the environmental impacts of REE production (Weng et al., 2016). Others have used scenario analysis to explore the potential environmental impacts of different production scenarios (Schreiber et al., 2016). Another challenge in conducting LCA studies on REE projects is the complexity of the production process. REE production involves multiple stages, including mining, beneficiation, and separation, each of which can have significant environmental impacts. Additionally, the production of REE often involves the use of energy-intensive processes, which can contribute to greenhouse gas emissions and other environmental impacts. To address these challenges, researchers have developed more detailed and nuanced models of REE production. For example, some studies have used process-based models to estimate the energy and material requirements of REE production (Marx et al., 2018). Others have used system dynamics models to explore the dynamic interactions between different stages of REE production and their environmental impacts (Haque et al., 2014). Despite these advances, there is still a need for further research to improve our understanding of the environmental impacts of REE production. In particular, there is a need for more detailed and comprehensive LCA studies that take into account the complexities and uncertainties involved in REE production. Additionally, there is a need for more research on the social and economic impacts of REE production, as well as the potential risks and benefits of different production scenarios. In terms of policy and regulation, there is a need for governments and organizations to develop more comprehensive and coordinated approaches to managing the environmental impacts of REE production. This could involve the development of more stringent environmental regulations and standards, as well as the provision of incentives for companies to adopt more sustainable production practices. In conclusion, the application of LCA to REE projects has provided valuable insights into the environmental impacts associated with REE production. However, there is still a need for further research to address the complexities and uncertainties involved in REE production. Additionally, there is a need for more comprehensive and coordinated approaches to managing the environmental impacts of REE production. By addressing these challenges, we can work towards more sustainable and responsible production of REE, which is critical for the development of clean energy technologies and other applications.

This intricate linkage between climate modeling and hydrological forecasting is pivotal, as it facilitates the understanding of how modifications in climate parameters influence hydrological systems and flood risks (Koussis et al., 2012). Within this framework, the accuracy of projections hinges significantly upon the robustness of the climate models utilized, making it imperative to continually refine their parameters and validate their outputs against observed data. The complexities inherent in river basin responses to changing precipitation patterns, coupled with human influences such as land-use changes and water management practices, add layers of difficulty to this already intricate endeavor (Bennett et al., 2013). Emerging studies have underscored the necessity of localized approaches to flood risk management, recognizing that hydrological responses can be profoundly affected by regional characteristics including topography, soil saturation levels, and urbanization (Hirsch et al., 2014). Therefore, the development of adaptive management strategies that incorporate real-time data and predictive modeling can enhance the resilience of communities vulnerable to flooding. By integrating hydrological modeling with decision-support systems, planners can create more precise forecasts of potential flood events, tailoring responses and mitigations to the unique needs of specific areas (Vaughan et al., 2012). In tandem with these technical advancements, public engagement plays a crucial role in fostering a culture of preparedness and environmental stewardship. Communities that are well-informed about flood risks are often better equipped to respond proactively, thereby mitigating potential damages and loss (Tapsell et al., 2002). Educational initiatives that emphasize the significance of sustainability practices, such as the preservation of wetlands and reforestation, can further enhance the natural capacities of landscapes to manage excessive rainfall and flooding (Palmer et al., 2010). Moreover, interdisciplinary approaches are essential as they ensure that historical land-use decisions and planning paradigms are reconsidered within the context of climate change. The historical reliance on flood insurance and traditional engineering solutions must be reassessed, with an emphasis on nature-based solutions that prioritize ecological integrity alongside infrastructural resilience (Pitt, 2008). Examples from around the world illustrate the potential success of such initiatives, where restored floodplains and urban green spaces have demonstrated capacity to attenuate flood peaks and improve water quality (Aldridge et al., 2015). Simultaneously, the socio-economic implications of flooding must not be underestimated. Economically disadvantaged communities often bear the brunt of climate change impacts, faced with limited resources to recover from catastrophic events. Thus, equitable flood management strategies must be prioritized to ensure that vulnerable populations receive adequate support (Schwerdtle et al., 2018). Policymakers must be mindful that climate adaptation is not merely a technical challenge, but also a moral imperative to protect those most at risk. As the realities of climate change continue to unfold, the intersection of science, policy, and community will dictate the future trajectory of flood resilience efforts. Continued investment in research, infrastructure, and education is required to foster adaptability and ensure that societies are not rendered vulnerable by the very changes that necessitate a collective response. In conclusion, while climate models provide us with critical projections, the integration of those projections into effective management strategies will ultimately determine the resilience of vulnerable regions against the impending tide of hydrological extremes-an escalating challenge that we must confront with both urgency and foresight.

Despite the mounting evidence of the detrimental effects of air pollution on public health, the implementation of low emission zones (LEZs) has been met with limited research on their impact on air quality and health outcomes. This knowledge gap is particularly concerning, given the increasing trend of urbanization and population growth, which is expected to further exacerbate air pollution in cities. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive review of the existing literature on the effects of LEZs on air quality and health, with a focus on the European context. Our search strategy yielded 25 studies that met the inclusion criteria, including both observational and experimental studies published between 2009 and 2017. The majority of the studies were conducted in Europe, with a focus on the United Kingdom, Germany, and France. The studies employed a range of methodologies, including regression analysis, time-series analysis, and cohort studies, to examine the impact of LEZs on air quality and health outcomes. The results of our review suggest that LEZs can have a significant impact on reducing air pollution, particularly particulate matter (PM) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2), in urban areas. A study in the UK found that the introduction of an LEZ in London led to a 12% reduction in PM10 concentrations and a 15% reduction in NO2 concentrations. Similarly, a study in Germany found that the introduction of an LEZ in Berlin led to a 10% reduction in PM10 concentrations and a 12% reduction in NO2 concentrations. In terms of health outcomes, our review found that LEZs were associated with a range of benefits, including reduced respiratory symptoms, improved lung function, and reduced hospital admissions for respiratory diseases. A study in France found that the introduction of an LEZ in Paris was associated with a 10% reduction in hospital admissions for respiratory diseases. Another study in the UK found that the introduction of an LEZ in London was associated with a 5% reduction in respiratory symptoms in children. Our review also found that the effectiveness of LEZs in improving air quality and health outcomes varied depending on the specific design and implementation of the scheme. For example, studies that implemented LEZs with stricter emission standards and more effective enforcement mechanisms tended to have greater impacts on air quality and health outcomes. Additionally, studies that included a combination of measures, such as traffic management and public transportation improvements, tended to have more comprehensive benefits. Overall, our review suggests that LEZs can be an effective tool in reducing air pollution and improving public health, particularly in urban areas. However, the effectiveness of LEZs also depends on the specific design and implementation of the scheme, and further research is needed to better understand the optimal design and implementation of LEZs to maximize their health benefits.

As I sat in the jeepney, sweating bullets, I couldn't help but feel a sense of frustration wash over me. The driver, a gruff old man with a bushy mustache, looked at me with a mixture of curiosity and annoyance. "Ano ba 'to, miss?" he asked, eyeing the giant bamboo trunks precariously balanced on the rear seat. I took a deep breath and explained, for what felt like the hundredth time, that I needed to get them to my new house in Bacoor. He grunted and muttered under his breath, but eventually relented, agreeing to take me to the edge of town for a hefty fee. As we bounced along the rough roads, I couldn't help but think about the absurdity of it all. I, a 40-year-old paralegal, struggling to move a living room set into a small house in the 'burbs. It was a far cry from the glamorous life I had envisioned for myself when I started law school all those years ago. But life had a way of humbling you, and I had learned to adapt. When we finally arrived at the edge of town, I hauled out my wallet and paid the driver, who grudgingly helped me unload the trunks. As I watched him drive away, I couldn't help but feel a sense of trepidation. What was I getting myself into? The house was supposed to be mine, but the owner was still away, and I had no idea what kind of shape it was in. I had seen the pictures, of course, but pictures could be deceiving. What if it was a dump? What if it was infested with cockroaches and rats? I took a deep breath and squared my shoulders. I had come this far, after all. I had worked hard to get to this point, and I wasn't about to let a little thing like uncertainty hold me back. I trudged up the path, my eyes scanning the exterior of the house for any signs of trouble. It looked...fine. A bit dusty, maybe, but fine. I pushed open the creaky front door and stepped inside, my eyes adjusting to the dim light. The interior was surprisingly clean, if a bit musty. I made my way upstairs, my heart pounding in my chest. The second floor was just as I had hoped - two small rooms, a balcony with a lovely view of the street below. I could already imagine myself sipping coffee on that balcony, watching the sun rise over the rooftops. But as I began to unpack the trunks, I realized that I had underestimated the task. The bamboo trunks were heavier than they looked, and the stairs were steeper than I remembered. I was sweating and panting by the time I finally got everything unpacked, but it was worth it. I had done it. I had moved into my new home, and it was all mine. For now, at least.

It is the greatest mistake," he said to me yesterday, "to talk of the Republic of Letters. Every author who wins a name is a sovereign in his own domain, be it large or small. Woe to any republican who wants to dethrone me!" Somehow or other, when M. Savarin thus talks I feel as if he were betraying the cause of, genius. I cannot bring myself to regard literature as a craft, - to me it is a sacred mission; and in hearing this "sovereign" boast of the tricks by which he maintains his state, I seem to listen to a priest who treats as imposture the religion he professes to teach. M. Savarin's favourite eleve now is a young contributor to his journal, named Gustave Rameau. M. Savarin said the other day in my hearing, "I and my set were Young France; Gustave Rameau and his set are New Paris." "And what is the distinction between the one and the other?" asked my American friend, Mrs. Morley. "The set of 'Young France,'" answered M. Savarin, "had in it the hearty consciousness of youth; it was bold and vehement, with abundant vitality and animal spirits; whatever may be said against it in other respects, the power of thews and sinews must be conceded to its chief representatives. But the set of 'New Paris' has very bad health, and very indifferent spirits. Still, in its way, it is very clever; it can sting and bite as keenly as if it were big and strong. Rameau is the most promising member of the set. He will be popular in his time, because he represents a good deal of the mind of his time, - namely, the mind and the time of 'New Paris.'" Do you know anything of this young Rameau's writings? You do not know himself, for he told me so, expressing a desire, that was evidently very sincere, to find some occasion on which to render you his homage. He said this the first time I met him at M. Savarin's, and before he knew how dear to me are yourself and your fame. He came and sat by me after dinner, and won my interest at once by asking me if I had heard that you were busied on a new work; and then, without waiting for my answer, he launched forth into praises of you, which made a notable contrast to the scorn with which he spoke of all your contemporaries, - except indeed M. Savarin, who, however, might not have been pleased to hear his favourite pupil style him "a great writer in small things." I spare you his epigrams on Dumas and Victor Hugo and my beloved Lamartine. Though his talk was showy, and dazzled me at first, I soon got rather tired of it, even the first time we met.

On the side nearest the castle, a little behind the front level of the house, was an "outshot," a little wing built to the side, which formed the kitchen, upon the ever-open door of which the corner window of the common family sitting room kept up a vigilant inspection. A plentiful number of bed-chambers up-stairs were reached by a good stair-case, and a gallery which encircled the hall; the architecture was of the most monotonous and simple regularity; so many windows on one side soberly poising so many windows on the other. The stair-case made a rounded projection at the back of the house, which was surmounted by a steep little turret roof, blue-slated, and bearing a tiny vane for its crown, after the fashion of the countryside; and this, which glimmered pleasantly among the garden fruit trees when you looked down from the top of the hill - and the one-storied projection, which was the kitchen, were the only two features which broke the perfect plainness and uniformity of the house. But though it was July when this history begins, the flush of summer - and though the sunshine was sweet upon the trees and the water, and the bare old walls of the castle, there was little animation in Norlaw. The blinds were drawn up in the east room, the best apartment - though the sun streamed in at the end window, and "the Mistress" was not wont to leave her favorite carpet to the tender mercies of that bright intruder; and the blinds were down in the dining-room, which nobody had entered this morning, and where even the Mistress's chair and little table in the corner window could not keep a vicarious watch upon the kitchen door. It was not needful; the two maids were very quiet, and not disposed to amuse themselves. Marget, the elder one, who was the byrewoman, and had responsibilities, went about the kitchen very solemnly, speaking with a gravity which became the occasion; and Janet, who was the house-servant, and soft-hearted, stood at the table, washing cups and saucers, very slowly, and with the most elaborate care, lest one of them should tingle upon the other, and putting up her apron very often to wipe the tears from her eyes. Outside, on the broad stone before the kitchen door, a little ragged boy sat, crying bitterly - and no one else was to be seen about the house. "Jenny," said the elder maid, at last, "give that bairn a piece, and send him away. There's enow of us to greet - for what we're a' to do for a puir distressed family, when aince the will o' God's accomplished this day, I canna tell." "Oh, woman, dinna speak! he'll maybe win through," cried Jenny, with renewed tears. Marget was calm in her superior knowledge.

The European Union uses energy policy to make sure that three objectives are met: (i) to safeguard secure energy supplies to ensure reliable provision of energy; (ii) to ensure that energy providers operate in a competitive environment that ensures affordable prices for consumers; and (iii) to stimulate sustainable energy consumption, and to lower greenhouse gas emissions, pollution and fossil fuel dependence [6]. In The Netherlands energy policy is defined as "the entire set of policy measures and instruments to assure reliable, affordable and clean supply of energy carriers, on the short run and the long run, to spur sustainable, economic development of economies on both the macro, meso and micro level" ([4]: 17). Some of the objectives of energy policy in the three examples mentioned appear value driven and may be contested. In sum, energy policy concerns the set of policy instruments that are used to ensure reliable, affordable, clean energy provision, and spur economic development. Given the importance energy policy has for the functioning of economies and society, it might be expected that energy policy would attract considerable academic attention. For academic journals such as Energy Policy this is most certainly true. However, one might wonder whether this also applies to social science disciplines studying the very government interventions in the energy domain. It is here that we argue that the academic discipline of policy studies has much to offer to energy studies. Given recent academic attention to issues like energy transition, renewable energy and low carbon strategies, scholars of policy studies would potentially have lots to study, analysing (different forms of) energy policies and their implications for energy markets, and providing advice to policy-makers on how to (re-) design energy policies. In such studies, they can make use of the abundant theories of the policy process1 addressing issues such as agenda-setting, policy implementation, and capacity building. We argue that this would enrich interdisciplinary energy research. We feel that policy studies can add something new providing advice to policy makers on designing energy policies and analysis of the impact and effects of energy policies that have been implemented. In a preliminary exploration we noticed that although a journal like Energy Policy indeed includes articles addressing studies in which the authors used concepts related to theories of the policy process (e.g. [7-12]). Inspection of the journal's published articles however suggests that the majority of articles published are economic in nature, using quantitative models to establish the impacts of energy policies (both ex ante and ex post), with little room for the use and elaboration of theories of the policy process and theories of governance.2 This article originates from a debate in an academic energy policy research network,3 in which the authors participate. During the debate the question was raised what theoretical concepts of the policy studies' discipline can contribute to multidisciplinary energy research.

Eva Morrison was acquainted with all this story, except the fact of his financial collapse, and she had no idea that all he possessed in the world was some fifteen hundred dollars in the Mobile bank. "You mustn't give up. You mustn't bury yourself," she persisted. "Why not? It's as good a life as any, maybe. I was born here in Alabama, you know-took my first diploma in Montgomery. I know the piney-woods country, the big swamps, the bayous and the great rivers, and the queer, good, primitive people. I'll drive a flivver over the sand roads, and hunt wild turkeys and never get my fees." She saw through his affected lightness, and looked at him gravely, her chin on her hands. "Your hand will get better. Your surgery will come back." "Never, or perhaps in years, and what good then? A surgeon has to keep in constant practice, like a pianist." Failing to find him at his hotel, persistent Destiny tried again, and a page summoned Lang to the telephone. He was away only a minute, and came back with an odd smile. "A call. A patient-the owner of a yacht out in the harbor somewhere." Eva made a delighted gesture, beaming suddenly. "I declined, of course," he added. "I referred them to another physician. I'm not practicing in Mobile." "But you might-you could-you're qualified!" Eva exclaimed, bitterly disappointed. "You must be mad! A yachtsman-likely a millionaire! They've heard of your reputation even here." "But I tell you I don't want to practice in Mobile, or in any of these towns!" Lang exclaimed, again in sudden irritation. "I dare say they have heard of me. The doctors here know my name, and I don't want to face their sympathy for my comedown. I had enough of that in Boston-the men who had always hated me, been jealous of me, coming with their crocodile sympathy, hoping that I'd soon be fit again, and praying that they'd seen the last of me. I'd sooner bury myself, as you say." He checked himself, quivering, angry and ashamed at his lack of control. Sick nerves know no reason. He looked at Eva Morrison again, wondering once more how she had come so deeply into his confidence, this girl of twenty, pretty as a picture, indeed, looking at him now with grieved brown eyes. But he had known her less than a month, and what could she understand, after all? She had been a passenger on the steamer that he boarded at Boston for Mobile. He had not remembered her at first; he did not want to know anybody; but in the inevitable companionship of shipboard she reminded him of past acquaintance.

Mr. Warton," said my governess, "you know we have had many serious conversations about the necessity for proper correction in case Miss Lucille should continue so inattentive to her studies, to-day she has failed in everything, and I am certain that unless her energies are sharpened up by the stinging smart of the rod she will go from bad to worse; I am so averse to wield the birch myself, and would much prefer that her papa should take in hand the serious whipping she ought to have." Papa.-"Lucille, you hear what Miss Birch says, (I noticed him cast most excited and amorous looks towards the governess as he spoke), she has been most forbearing with you, and interceded with me many times to save your bottom, and even now cannot bring herself to lift her own hand to make you smart a little; it must indeed be a serious fault to induce her to ask me to use the rod, but, 'Spare the rod and spoil the child,' has always been a maxim with me; lay her across your lap, Miss Birch, and pull up her clothes, whilst I get the rod out of the table drawer." Miss Birch, with heaving bosom, and quite a deep blush upon her face.-"I feel as ashamed at baring her naughty posteriors as if I was going to suffer the degradation and humiliation myself, but come, Lucille dear, you must bear it, and I hope you will be a better and more diligent girl in future." Then catching me by the wrist, as I stood by her side covered with confusion, she tried to lay me across her knees, but I struggled and screamed, "No! No!! No!!! I won't be whipped! Oh! Oh!! dear papa, do forgive me this time!" my face quite crimson and streaming with tears. Papa, having got out the rod, a fine switch of long thin birch twigs, tied up with velvet and silk ribbons at the handle,-"Come! Come!! Lucille, this resistance will only make it worse for you." As he seized and threw me on the governess's lap, Miss Birch securing my head well under her left arm, speedily pulled up dress and skirts, till my fat little bottom was exposed in a tight fitting pair of drawers, my legs being left to kick about, although I was quite firmly secured, and to all intents quite helpless, and my toes could scarcely touch the ground. I could hear papa whisking the birch about, and then he said, "That will do famously, Miss Birch, keep her head and shoulders well down as you hold up her skirts; much as I pity my darling little Lucille, I must do my duty and make her smart for her idleness in school."
