All these young people were great chums, and all were having a good time. They had left New York City by rail and then had boarded the steamer Cleveland at Cincinnati. On the boat they had met Mr. Stanhope, and soon afterward they had become acquainted with Captain Tait, a veteran of many years' experience on the river. The captain had invited the boys and girls to go on a pleasure cruise down the mighty stream, and they had accepted the invitation gladly. As yet the party had seen little of the river, but already they had had several adventures. One of these had occurred at Cairo, Illinois, where they had encountered a band of desperadoes known as the Black Bandits. Another adventure had happened at Cape Girardeau, Missouri, where they had lost Dora and Frank, only to find them again at St. Louis, Missouri. And now here they were, making their way down the river toward Memphis, Tennessee. "Look! Look!" suddenly cried Sam Rover. "See how close that lumber raft is getting!" He pointed to the big raft, which was moving rapidly down the middle of the channel. "Yes, it's coming closer," answered Dick. "Let me see - what is that over there?" "I believe it's another raft," said Tom. "That looks like it, Tom," said Hans. "But why should dem two rafts be running so close togedder?" "There must be something wrong with the pilot of the second raft," answered Dick. "He ought to know better than to run so close to our houseboat." "We're far enough away from the shore to make throwing bricks impracticable." "Then what can we do about it?" asked Sam. "Wait till the raft gets a bit nearer and then let me use the megaphone," answered Dick. "I'll tell the fellow on the other raft to stay clear of us." "Good idea!" cried Tom. "Now, then, hold your breaths," went on Dick. "Here comes the chance!" A few moments later the two rafts drew alongside each other. "Hey, you on the other raft!"

For better success in drought tolerance breeding, the traits of choice need to be causal rather than the effect (Kashiwagi et al., 2006a) and an integrator of the responses to events across the whole life cycle e.g., transpiration efficiency (TE) and partitioning coefficient (Krishnamurthy et al., 2013a,b). Crop models help in dissecting the grain yield into its components that can be considered more generic and organizationally close to the yield. One such model splits the grain yield as a function of three component traits, viz, crop growth rate, reproductive duration and partitioning coefficient (Duncan et al., 1978; Williams and Saxena, 1991) that are easy to measure in large populations. Also the components of this model are shoot-based and are amenable for selection through other surrogate traits. Crop growth rate (C) is an integrated expression of both transpiration and transpiration efficiency. Recognition of its importance for drought tolerance, breeding for C had been extensively practiced in wheat and groundnut (Calderini et al., 1997; Wright et al., 1993). Large-scale field measurements of transpiration and transpiration efficiency are cumbersome. Therefore, surrogate traits for transpiration such as leaf area index (LAI) (Fageria et al., 2010) and canopy temperature depression (CTD) (Fuchs and Tanner, 1966; Jackson et al., 1981; Fuchs, 1990; Jones, 1992; Jones et al., 2002, 2009; Rebetzke et al., 2013) and for transpiration efficiency, carbon isotope discrimination, specific leaf area index and SPAD chlorophyll meter readings were sought to breed for in various legume crops (Comstock and Ehleringer, 1993; Sheshshayee et al., 2006; Thompson et al., 2007; Nageswara Rao et al., 2001; Bindu-Madhava et al., 2003; Kashiwagi et al., 2006a; Arunyanark et al., 2008). High heritability and a weak response to environmental variation of harvest index (HI) (Hay, 1995) had made HI suitable as a major trait for improving yield stability under DS. However, HI alone had not been considered as a yield determining trait for selection as high yields under DS were the product of interaction of both C and HI. An independent selection for HI alone was considered to pose the danger of selecting entries with a poor plant biomass potential (poor C) (Wallace et al., 1993). Therefore, success in selecting for high yield under DS requires a simultaneous selection for both C and HI. HI is a product of two components; i.e. the reproductive duration (Dr) and the rate of partitioning (p) to grains (Duncan et al., 1978; Williams and Saxena, 1991; Gallagher et al., 1976; Scully and Wallace, 1990; Krishnamurthy et al., 1999). Terminal DS in chickpea, as in many other crops, is known to reduce the growth duration, especially the reproductive phase (Krishnamurthy et al., 2013a). Chickpea growing environments experience a ceiling to the reproductive growth duration due to progressively increasing terminal DS and heat stress at the final stages of reproductive growth, requiring an increased p, thereby providing the plants to escape the later stress stages with less adverse effects on the yield formation (Krishnamurthy et al., 2013a).

"But it was something of an adventure to get away from the island in the canoe after those wild Indians came hunting us." "You bet we had some lively moments, didn't we, fellows?" cried the twin brother of Bobolink. "If we were sure of getting the same kind of welcome this time I'd vote for going to Lake Tokala again." "Oh, pshaw!" scoffed Jack, "you know perfectly well that the Indians never saw us, or they would have given chase." "Perhaps so; but don't forget how they fired into the air after we paddled off from the shore." "It was a big bluff, all right enough," admitted Bobolink, "but it sounded pretty convincing to our ears." "Say, if you want to hear a story about the Indians," ventured Tom Betts, "just ask my dad to tell you about the time he went out West as a young fellow, and spent two years among them. He says they were the most savage lot he ever struck." "Then let's give him a chance to spin his yarn before we go camping, and he'll get the benefit of the first-class entertainment," suggested Bluff Shipley. "Of course, but we're wasting valuable time talking here instead of skating," declared Jack. "Come along, boys, let's have a race across the pond. I'll start you off." "Wait till I catch my breath, Jack," begged Bluff Shipley, panting. "I'm not built for speed, you know." "Oh, come on! Don't be a softy," urged the other, laughing. "We're not racing a mile, only a hundred yards." "Maybe so," said the slow-moving lad, "but that's far enough for me. I always want to save myself for the finish." "And don't forget that you're the man who started the race," reminded Jack. "Aren't you ashamed of yourself, Bluff Shipley?" "Not a bit," retorted the other, "because I'm the best judge of my own capabilities." "As a rule you're right, too," added Bobolink, smiling. "Bluff is a splendid marksman, and a mighty fine shot with a rifle. He's also a very handy fellow to have along when you need someone to steady your nerves." "Oh, shut up, Bobolink, because I believe you're jealous because I can shoot better than you can." "Me, jealous? Not on your life!" exclaimed the twin brother. "I'm willing to admit that you're the better marksman, but you ought to remember that I'm a crack shot myself." "All right, then, Bobolink," challenged Bluff Shipley, "let's settle this question once and for all. I'll wager a dollar that I can beat you in shooting at a target fifty feet away." "Done!" agreed the other instantly. "You're on!" "Who's backing you?" demanded Tom Betts, sharply. "Don't care who backs me," replied Bobolink, coolly. "Let's make the bets between ourselves, without outside help. You're on, Bluff." "Then I'm on, too," added Jack Stormways. "There's no doubt about it," continued Bobolink, "that Bluff is the best shot in the troop, and I'm willing to stand up to him any time." "You're all right, Bobolink," said the twin brother, grinning. "I know you're game, and I've no kick coming against you."

As the list continues, a curious pattern emerges-a tapestry woven from societal anxieties about what content is appropriate for impressionable minds. The reactions speak volumes about cultural shifts and the growing sensitivity surrounding media portrayals. One need only glance at the details of the complaints to gain insight into what outrages parents and caregivers today. Take CBeebies' famed show, Get Well Soon. With its cheerful puppetry and medical-themed discussions, the intent is to educate and alleviate children's fears about health issues. Yet, it garnered 65 complaints for allegedly breaching 'generally accepted standards'-a phrase that encapsulates the struggle between creative freedom and the careful vetting of content destined for young audiences. Perhaps the ongoing discussions surrounding these complaints reflect a broader cultural responsibility for the health and wellbeing of children, a topic that extends beyond just mere entertainment. Blue Peter, a beloved children's staple, found itself embroiled in its own storm after a segment depicting a goat being slaughtered during an Omani religious ceremony in 2007 drew shock and dismay. So rooted in tradition, yet so foreign to many audiences, the incident highlights the sensitive nature of cultural representation on screens intended for children. Fierce debates ensued about whether this served as an educational moment or a stark example of insensitivity. The peculiar case of Bratz on ITV1 underscores another strain of discontent, with its use of the term 'spaz' igniting fervor among viewers who found it deeply offensive. Claiming the word as derogatory and harmful, the complaints reflected a rising awareness of how language shapes perceptions of disability and difference. This aligns with contemporary movements pushing for inclusivity and sensitivity, demanding that even children's programming needs to reflect compassionate narratives that build rather than diminish respect for diversities. Rastamouse, a charming character created to engage young viewers through reggae music and vibrant storytelling, too faced scrutiny, though the nature of the complaints differed. Cited as a focus of complaints due to its portrayal of a community living in harmony, some felt the messages were too simplistic, failing to address the complexities of societal issues. Yet this show invites discussions that plague adults-what does it mean to simplify narratives for children, and where do we draw the line between being educational and being overly prescriptive? And then there's My Parents Are Aliens, posing the whimsical notion of otherworldly guardians trying, sometimes disastrously, to navigate the terrain of mundane human life. It drew fire for issues seen as trivial at first blush; what seemed to be harmless fun raised eyebrows concerning depictions of parenting styles that may not align with conventional views. This epitomizes the tension between creative liberty and parental expectations: Should the purpose of children's programming be merely to entertain, or should it hold an inherent responsibility to reflect societal norms? While this landscape of children's television evolves, the ramifications of these complaints suggest a pressing dialogue about the nature of childhood, identity, and the values we impart through the screens that dominate young lives. As media continues to shape the hearts and minds of new generations, the careful balancing act between creative expression and social conscience appears more relevant than ever. Each complaint tells a story, revealing not just concerns about specific portrayals, but a wider commentary on the values we embrace as a society striving for a greater understanding in an ever-diversified world.

Ruth had rehearsed the scene in her mind countless times, yet the choreography of emotions failed to align. She shifted her weight from one foot to the other, the hardwood floor beneath her feet serving as a grounding presence, a tangible reminder that this was her reality. Ruth's heart skipped in her chest; there they were, the women whose presence threatened to alter the fabric of her life irrevocably. A moment of hesitation flickered between them, a silent acknowledgement of the void that years of separateness had created. Then she smiled, a tentative curving of lips, and stepped forward with a hand outstretched. "Ruth, my dear," she said, voice gentle yet carrying the weight of bygone years and missed connections. Ruth swallowed, mimicking the gesture, feeling awkward as their hands met in a clasp that was neither familial nor entirely foreign. It was an introduction, fraught with history unshared. Beside her stood the sister-her sister-whose existence had been a revelation, a puzzle piece that didn't quite seem to belong to the picture of her life until now. Her name was Anne; Ruth had learned this much through hesitant, late-night talks with her father. "Hello, Ruth," Anne said, her voice emitting a warm tremor, as if understanding that this connection, tentative as it was, held the promise of something precious. Ruth managed a nod, her mind whirling, wondering how to bridge an ocean of difference. Words felt heavy, cumbersome, unsuitable for the gravity of the moment. "Ruth, I think you and Anne will have much to discuss," he ventured, as if trying to sketch the outline of a shared future in the air around them. Ruth nodded again, mechanically, feelings unnameable pressing down on her like the humid air before a storm. "Yes, of course," she replied, voice as steady as she could manage, betraying none of the turmoil roiling within. They stood that way, a tableau of new beginnings, the echo of trunks and travelers' haste fading into the background. An awkward trio, bound by blood yet separated by the chasms time had carved; they were poised at the dawn of a new chapter they collectively dreaded and anticipated. As Ruth stood amidst this familial tableau, she knew challenges lay ahead-an unlearning and relearning of life as she had known it. And it was here, in the stillness of an unresolved moment, on the threshold of change, that Ruth Erskine took her first, halting steps into an uncharted future.

The questions raised by Pakistanis echo a broader international debate: What, indeed, are the ethical implications of deploying drones in sovereign territories without explicit consent, and what precedents might such actions set? The discourse surrounding drone use is a tapestry woven with threads of national security, sovereignty, and human rights. As more nations develop these capabilities, a tangled web of alliances, hostilities, and geopolitical maneuvers unfurls across the global stage. Take, for instance, the burgeoning drone program in China. While the United States grapples with the morality and legality of its drone operations, China is rapidly expanding its own fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles. The balance of power is shifting, and with it, the rules of engagement in modern warfare. Unlike conventional forces, drones operate with a semblance of stealth, shifting the traditional paradigms of risk and reward in military action. This evolution warrants a reexamination of international law, particularly as it pertains to the rules of warfare established in bygone eras. Russia, too, is no stranger to this unmanned revolution. With its own fleet advancing in sophistication, Russia's strategic calculations are influenced by its tense relationships with neighboring countries and its broader global aspirations. In this climate, drones serve not just as instruments of war, but as symbols of technological prowess and national strength. However, the proliferation of drone technology also heightens the risk of falling into the wrong hands. Non-state actors, rogue nations, and terrorist organizations might soon leverage this technology for nefarious purposes, triggering unprecedented security dilemmas. Meanwhile, ethical consideration looms large over this domain. As drones increasingly engage in targeted killings, they bring to the fore the question of accountability. If a drone strike results in civilian casualties, who bears the responsibility? Can there be transparency in an operation shrouded in secrecy? These are not mere hypotheticals but pressing questions that demand answers from policymakers and military leaders worldwide. The narratives of those who have suffered loss due to such strikes remain powerful testimonies against the impersonal nature of drone warfare. Yet, some argue that drones, when deployed prudently, can reduce casualties and collateral damage compared to conventional warfare. Proponents assert that precision technology allows for more accurate targeting and less risk to military personnel. This argument, however, is counterbalanced by the psychological impact on those living beneath the drones' unyielding gaze. The constant threat of strikes can foment fear, anxiety, and resentment among civilian populations, potentially driving recruitment for militant groups rather than quelling it. As the conversation surrounding these issues evolves, it is imperative to foster dialogue that transcends borders. A robust framework for regulation and oversight, established through international cooperation, might mitigate the potential for misuse while promoting accountability and transparency. Such a framework could help ensure that the poignant concerns raised by Senator Rand Paul and others are duly addressed, acknowledging the complex realities of modern conflict. In an increasingly uncertain world, the challenge lies in balancing the strategic advantages of drone technology with the ethical and legal imperatives that safeguard humanity's collective conscience.

However, while control participants develop elevated anticipatory SC in the few seconds prior to selecting cards from bad decks, VMPFC patients do not (Bechara et al., 1996). However, findings for these "anticipatory skin conductance responses" ("SCR) are not consistent. Bechara and Damasio (2002) reported variance in the "SCRs of healthy participants who were poor performers in the IGT, with some developing anticipatory markers as would be predicted but this did not facilitate advantageous play, yet some studies find elevated "SCRs only in the highest performing sub-groups of participants (e.g., Carter & Smith Pasqualini, 2004; Crone, Somsen, Van Beek, & Van der Molen, 2004). Crone et al.'s (2004) moderately performing group, showed lower "SCRs but improvement in deck selections across the game; indicating learning can take place in the absence of somatic markers. Another challenge comes from Suzuki, Hirota, Takasawa, and Shigemasu (2003) who found no difference between anticipatory SC on early and later trials - failing to provide support for anticipatory markers developing as the game progresses and subsequently guiding behaviour in the IGT. The structure of the reward and punishment schedule - as distinct from each deck's expected value (i.e., mean loss/gain) - has been suggested as an alternative explanation for elevated "SCRs found for bad decks. Modifying the good decks to have the higher rewards and punishments (but still an overall net gain), Tomb, Hauser, Deldin, and Caramazza (2002) found greater "SCRs prior to selecting from good decks; the opposite of what the SMH predicts. Tomb et al. (2002) suggested somatic markers were driven by the immediate action being taken, rather than by longer-term outcomes. Yen, Chou, Chung, and Chen (2012) modified the IGT to test whether "SCRs were due to differences in expected value (EV) or differences in the riskiness of the decks. They found that anticipatory SC marked the preferred choices across different stages of learning in the game; greater for the high-risk bad deck early on, then greater for low-risk good deck later in the task. Chiu et al. (2008) also adapted the IGT to create the Soochow gambling task: the good and back decks had the same EVs as in the original IGT, but punishments occurred on 4/5 cards in the good decks and only 1/5 times in the bad decks. Chiu et al. (2008) found that participants chose more from the bad decks, suggesting that the frequency of gains and losses took precedence over EV. If conscious awareness of advantageous play can occur before "SCRs develop, this would negate the need to use somatic states to guide decision making. Bechara, Damasio, Tranel, and Damasio (1997) measured SCRs during the IGT but also assessed participants' knowledge about the decks at points throughout the game to determine when participants became aware of the best strategy for advantageous play. The assessment of conscious knowledge led Bechara et al. to describe four conceptual stages in the game: 'pre-punishment', 'pre-hunch', 'hunch' and 'conceptual' stage.

As he tied the last bundle, his eye fell upon a cluster of red berries which grew close to the ground beside him, and he stooped to pick one. But, before he touched it, the bird flew away, and he watched its flight with a sigh of regret. "I wish I could go where you are going," said he, "for the world seems very dull to me." "Maybe you will go some time," returned the robin, perching on the fence close to Josiah. "You seem to be a good boy, and you may be taken somewhere else than this old place." "You don't know what you say," replied Josiah, shaking his head sadly. "I am sure I shall never get out of this. Mother has told me many times that I am a cripple, and must stay here always; and father says I can do nothing but mind the cows, and gather herbs for medicine. They won't let me do anything else. If I tried to work in the field, my legs would give way under me, and I should fall down and hurt myself. So I must stay here and be good, or else they will whip me." The robin shook her wings vigorously and made a little noise of impatience. "Why do you talk like that?" she asked. "If your mother is right, why do you think you are not a cripple?" Josiah looked surprised. "Because I am not crippled," he answered promptly. "My legs do not shake much, and sometimes I can run a little without falling. Father does not see how strong I am, and so he thinks I cannot work. But I can work just as well as any other boy, only I cannot run fast enough to keep up with the others. When I try to, I feel weak and tired. Sometimes I wonder whether my legs will ever grow strong enough to carry me away from this old place." "Do you want to leave it?" asked the robin. "Yes, indeed!" replied Josiah eagerly. "I hate this old farm! It is so lonely. There is nothing to do except to take care of the cows, and to help mother with the work. I wish I could play with other boys, and go to school, and learn something besides how to make medicines." "That is all very well," returned the robin, "but I doubt if you will ever go away from here unless you behave better than you have done." "Oh, I'm sure I'll behave better!" exclaimed Josiah earnestly. "Mother says I am always getting into mischief. She does not understand how hard it is for me to keep still, and not run around and play like other boys. And when I do get into trouble, father beats me till I cry. Then mother gets angry with him for whipping me, and he grows cross, and we quarrel. I wish they would both be kinder to me. Perhaps I might learn to be a better boy if they were not always scolding me." "Well, maybe you will find a chance to go away sometime," said the robin, as she fluttered off the fence and began to hop about on the ground, looking for worms. "But remember that you must mind your parents, and do whatever they tell you. Don't get into mischief, or you will lose your chance." "I'll try to be good," promised Josiah, "and perhaps I will go away after all."

The angles of the bands were found to vary with the bearing type, e.g. ball or cylindrical roller bearings, within the ranges mentioned above [7,13], however no details on how they were related were provided by the researchers. WEBs mainly form in highly stressed zones and the density of WEBs increases with the rolling cycles [7]. LABs start to form after about 100 million cycles followed by HABs that occur after about 500 million cycles [9]. However Mitamura et al. found HABs formed before LABs under high contact pressure of 4.6 GPa and 5.5 GPa [4]. LABs have been described as disc-shaped regions of ferrite bordered by unusual narrow elongated features that were not broken during tempering [7,8] thus had been referred to as lenticular carbides [6,7]. LABs have been reported as 5-30 1/2m long, 0.1-0.5 1/2m thick bands with 0.5-10 1/2m spacing between them [5,9]. Thicker bands (up to 2 1/2m thickness) have also been reported [16,18]. HABs are longer, thicker bands compared to LABs [9,16,17,21,23]. They are typically about 100 1/2m long, 10 1/2m thick and the spacing between the bands varies from 5 to 50 1/2m [9]. Swahn et al. [9] were able to show from their TEM analysis that HABs consist of heavily deformed ferrite with about 0.2 1/2m cell size. Beswick et al. [25] were the first and only group who found a crystallographic {1 1 1} texture had developed in regions of the altered microstructure using the X-ray pole figure technique and the analysis of diffraction intensity maximum variation with depth. Their results suggested that this texture was formed by dynamic recrystallisation. Unfortunately no further analysis has been performed to confirm. However these findings have been considered paradoxical and thus ignored by others [24]. Martin et al. [7] showed both WEBs and lenticular carbides in a LOM image of a bearing race in Nital etched condition, where WEBs appeared white while lenticular carbides were dark and thin. However, Swahn et al. [9] and Osterlund et al. [5] claimed that the white parts are lenticular carbides and the dark thin structures are ferrite based on their TEM results. Lenticular carbides attached to LABs have been proposed to be formed by plastic deformation (flattening) of the primary spheroidised carbides [18]; or due to carbide dissolution in the LAB and precipitation at the edge of the LAB in the form of lenticular carbides [8,26]. Zwirlein [20] and Swahn et al. [9] suggested that LABs consist of ferrite particles surrounded by carbon-rich (carbide-like) zones.

He looked curiously at the pictures, the photographs, the bronze statuettes, the china figures, the glass cases filled with rare shells, the books, the music, the flowers, the ferns, the birds, the very furniture. It was all strange to him, and he felt the strangeness of it. He had never been in such surroundings before. He tried to put himself in imagination in the place of the man who lived here, and he could not conceive how he would feel. He was conscious of a vague discomfort. It was not that he was afraid of the people whom he was soon to meet. But something was wrong. He did not belong here. He belonged to the sea, to the wind, to the sand and spray, to the sun and stars. Here was no place for him. This was a house, while he was but a sailor. He was used to the stormy sea, to the ship that rolled and pitched and plunged through the water. What was this flat floor? How could feet stand upon it? It was not natural. There was nothing to hold the body upright. He leaned forward and tested it with his fingers. He ran his hand along it and felt its smoothness. He knew that it was wood, that it was painted, that it was hard and firm. But why paint wood? Why paint anything? Did not nature make things beautiful enough without painting? He wondered what the paint was made of. It certainly was not oil, nor was it varnish. No, it was some sort of paste. He could tell that because his finger tips told him so. And then he remembered that the ship's deck was painted, and he recalled that the paint was called anti-fouling, and that it kept off the barnacles and weeds. It was not for beauty. Then what was it for? To keep the wood from rotting, perhaps. Yes, he was sure it was that. The house was built of wood, and the wood had to be protected from decay. He was puzzled by the fact that the wood did not decay. He had seen many trees lying around on the beach, and he had noticed that the wood rotted quickly after the tree died. It was not so with the houses. They lasted forever. He wondered why. Was it because the wood was different? Or was it because the houses were painted? He concluded that it was the latter, and he resolved to ask the man who owned this house about it. The man was reading a letter. He appeared to be absorbed in it. He seemed to have forgotten the sailor standing behind him. The sailor waited patiently. He wanted to talk to the man, but he dared not speak until spoken to. He knew better than to break in upon another person's thoughts. He had learned that lesson well, and he had learned also the value of patience. He was patient, but he was anxious. He wanted to know what the man was thinking about. He wanted to hear what he was saying. He wanted to join in the conversation. He wanted to tell the man about the voyage, about the terrible storm, about the rescue of the crew, about the gold he had won, about everything. He wanted to explain to the man that he had come ashore to visit him, that he had known him ever since childhood, that he had been sent by the captain to deliver the money. He wanted to show the man the letter from the captain, and to prove to him that he was the bearer of the gold.

As they hastily gobbled down their breakfast, laughter and chatter filled the air. The aroma of coffee wafted through the room, mingling with the rich scent of fried ham. Bill, whose ambitions for the day were grand, turned to Bob between mouthfuls, "What do you think we'll find at the market today? I hear it's quite the spectacle!" Bob, still focused on the last bite of his biscuit, replied, "Oh, I reckon it's going to be a kaleidoscope of colors, sounds, and smells-just like the stories they tell back home. Nothing like eating something that hasn't seen the inside of a can." The thought prompted a collective groan from the other boys, but Mr. Waterman could not help but smile at their enthusiasm. "Just remember," he advised, "that markets in foreign lands can be overwhelming for a tender mindset. It's best to approach it as an adventure, not merely a shopping expedition." There was a moment of silence, as the gravity of Mr. Waterman's advice sank in, before it was broken by the raucous laughter of Bill, who was merely mimicking the twists and turns of a dodgy market vendor's pitch. After breakfast, they donned their day's attire, each boy seeking to embody the spirit of a daring explorer. Bob fluttered his hands dramatically, declaring himself the Captain of Exploration, destined to uncover the secrets of the marketplace. The others delighted in playacting his tales, embellishing them with exaggerated gestures and silly imitations. As they rushed down the stairs and out the door, the morning sun bloomed brightly over the small town, casting long shadows that danced as the boys hurried along. Upon reaching the market square, a vibrant tableau greeted them. Stalls brimming with exotic fruits, colorful textiles, and trinkets that glimmered in the sunlight created a bustling kaleidoscope. Lively banter in the street mingled with the calls of vendors hawking their wares. "By all that's holy! Look at that!" exclaimed Bill, pointing to a particularly ostentatious display of brightly dyed woven baskets. "We could fill those with all the treasures we discover!" Pud, more intrigued by a vendor's display of mangoes, practically hopped from one foot to the other, "I want to try one! Can we?" Mr. Waterman encouraged their pursuits. "Remember, fellows, a good traveler is not just one who seeks out novelty, but one who also savors it." With those words echoing in their ears, the boys dispersed, eager to immerse themselves in the vibrant market scene, each setting off to discover his own adventure. As Bob and Bill navigated through the throng, it became clear that every corner promised a new find-a glinting bracelet, a basket of fragrant spices, or even something as simple yet delightful as handmade pastries that tempted their senses. The exuberance of the day enveloped them, and for a moment, they were untethered, the worries of home and school forgotten amidst the thrill of discovery. But as they wandered further, the atmosphere began to change ever so slightly. The lively chatter shifted to an undercurrent of anxious whispers, and the vibrancy around them turned into a tapestry of uncertainty. Bob looked at Bill, raising an eyebrow. "Do you feel that?" "What?" Bill replied, intrigued but distracted by a large ruby glistening among the wares, "I just want to see what this is worth!" "No, not that. Look." They turned to observe a group of people lingering at the far end of the marketplace, their expressions solemn. The laughter and cheers seemed distant now, fading like an echo. "Something's off," Bob noted, his adventurous spirit dampening slightly. "Let's check it out." And with that, the boys strode toward the gathering crowd, unaware that their quest for discovery was about to twist into something far deeper than mere curiosities.

Of Stonewall's antecedents I know very little. I only know that, in a moderate way, he was wealthy, and that he had no immediate family ties. He was somewhere near thirty years of age, and held the diploma of one of our oldest universities. But he was not, in a general way, sociable, and I never knew him to attend any of the reunions of his former classmates, or to show the slightest interest in any of the events or functions of society, although its doors were open to him through some distant relatives who were widely connected in New York, and who at times tried to draw him into their circle. He would certainly have adorned it, but it had no attraction for him. Nevertheless he was a member of the Olympus Club, where he frequently spent his evenings. But he made very few acquaintances even there, and I believe that except myself, Jack Ashton, Henry Darton, and Will Church, he had no intimates. And we knew him only at the club. There, when he was alone with us, he sometimes partly opened up his mind, and we were charmed by his variety of knowledge and the singularity of his conversation. I shall not disguise the fact that we thought him extremely eccentric, although the idea of anything in the nature of insanity never entered our heads. We knew that he was engaged in recondite researches of a scientific nature, and that he possessed a private laboratory, although none of us had ever entered it. Occasionally he would speak of some new advance of science, throwing a flood of light by his clear expositions upon things of which we should otherwise have remained profoundly ignorant. His imagination flashed like lightning over the subject of his talk, revealing it at the most unexpected angles, and often he roused us to real enthusiasm for things the very names of which we almost forgot amidst the next day's occupations. There was one subject on which he was particularly eloquent - radioactivity; that most strange property of matter whose discovery had been the crowning glory of science in the closing decade of the nineteenth century. None of us really knew anything about it except what Stonewall taught us. If some new incomprehensible announcement appeared in the newspapers we skipped it, being sure that Edmund would make it all clear at the club in the evening. He made us understand, in a dim way, that some vast, tremendous secret lay behind it all. I recall his saying, on one occasion, not long before the blow fell: "Listen to this! Here's Professor Thomson declaring that a single grain of radium contains in its padlocked atoms energy enough to lift a million tons three hundred yards high. Professor Thomson is too modest in his estimates, and he hasn't the ghost of an idea how to get at that energy.

As the Sea Ranger plowed through the growing waves, the brothers' conversation was interrupted by the creaking and groaning of the wooden hull, and the howling of the wind as it began to pick up speed. The sky above seemed to darken by the minute, and the brothers exchanged a glance, their faces set with determination. "We'll ride this out," Tom said, his voice steady and firm. "We've been through worse, remember?" Jack nodded, his eyes fixed on the horizon. "Yeah, but this is Lake Huron, not the Caribbean. These storms can be a lot nastier." Tom nodded in agreement. "I know, but we're not going to let a little bad weather stop us. We're almost to Alpena, and then we can find shelter and wait out the storm." The Sea Ranger shuddered and lurched, throwing the brothers off balance. Tom quickly regained control, his hands firm on the wheel. "Hold on, Jack," he shouted above the din of the storm. "We're going to take a hit!" The boat bucked and heaved, the waves crashing over the deck in great green swells. The brothers clung to the rail, their faces set against the wind and rain. The storm raged on, its fury unabated, but the Sea Ranger held steady, her engines purring smoothly beneath them. As the hours passed, the storm showed no signs of abating. The brothers huddled together, their eyes fixed on the horizon, their ears ringing from the constant roar of the wind. But Tom's eyes never left the sea, his hands never wavering on the wheel. "We're almost there," he shouted above the din of the storm. "Just a little farther!" The Sea Ranger surged forward, her engines roaring as she battled through the waves. The brothers held on tight, their hearts pounding with excitement and fear. And then, suddenly, the storm began to subside, the winds dying down, the waves calming. The brothers looked at each other, their faces set with relief and exhaustion. They had made it. They had ridden out the storm and were safe in the harbor at Alpena. As they steered the Sea Ranger towards the shore, Tom turned to Jack and grinned. "Well, that was fun," he said, his voice dripping with sarcasm. Jack laughed, his eyes shining with relief. Ameeta Phull, 34, who lives in Chigwell, Essex, with husband Navin, 39, a chartered accountant, also went all out for her baby shower last summer. She had been planning her first child since she discovered she was pregnant six months earlier. 'It was something I'd always dreamed of doing,' she explains. Ameeta wanted a baby shower that was 'glamorous, fancy and memorable', and that's what she got. The cost of hiring a ballroom at a local hotel, along with food, drink, decorations, entertainment and gifts, came to 5,000. 'I didn't want anything too girly or flowery because I don't like those things,' says Ameeta, who works part-time for an IT company. 'I wanted everything to look elegant, stylish and sophisticated.' And that meant a black-and-gold theme. Ameeta and her friend Sunita Patel, 35, who lives nearby, planned every detail. 'We scouted around London for venues and we looked at the menus and price lists for caterers,' says Ameeta. 'When we saw the prices, we decided to do our own catering. Another reason why many British women are keen to splash out on a baby shower is that they see it as an opportunity to celebrate a milestone in their life, as well as marking the arrival of a new family member. 'In Britain, we don't tend to get together to mark a pregnancy,' says Dr Laura Morgan Roberts, a psychologist and academic at Harvard Business School. 'But in the U.S., people often throw a baby shower as a way of recognising a woman's transition to becoming a mother.' In addition, Dr Roberts says, a baby shower can make women feel less isolated during pregnancy, which may explain why American women attend them more frequently than Britons. 'Women in the U.S. have a stronger sense of community and support networks, which means they're likely to have bigger families and more frequent contact with relatives and friends,' she adds. 'This makes them more likely to have a baby shower.' For Mel, the baby shower was about sharing the excitement of her impending arrival with her nearest and dearest. 'It was a chance to let go of any anxieties I might have had about giving birth, and to talk about how I imagined my labour and delivery would go,' she says. 'And it gave me time to reflect on my life so far and where I wanted to go next.'

The selection of product ingredients is a crucial aspect in the formulation of cosmetic products, as it ensures both safety-in-use and quality of the formulated product. In recent years, there has been a growing trend towards the use of natural origin surfactants, such as alkylpolyglucosides, in the cosmetic industry. These surfactants have been shown to be gentler on the skin and hair, and have a lower environmental impact compared to traditional synthetic surfactants. Additionally, the incorporation of active substances, such as oils and plant extracts, can enhance the sensory properties of the product and provide additional benefits to the consumer. One of the most popular washing compounds used in body wash cosmetics is the anionic surfactant Sodium Laureth Sulfate (SLES). However, SLES has been shown to have some drawbacks, including skin irritation and dryness. As a result, manufacturers are increasingly turning to alternative surfactants, such as cocamidopropyl betaine, which is derived from coconut oil and has been shown to be gentler on the skin. The use of cationic surfactants in cosmetic products has also been increasing in recent years. These surfactants are known for their ability to bind to the hair and skin, providing a range of benefits including moisturization, conditioning, and antistatic properties. Cationic surfactants are often used in combination with anionic surfactants to create a balanced formula that provides both cleansing and moisturizing properties. In addition to their use in cosmetic products, cationic surfactants have also been used in a range of other applications, including pharmaceuticals, household cleaning products, and industrial applications. In pharmaceuticals, cationic surfactants are used as emulsifiers and solubilizers, while in household cleaning products, they are used as detergents and disinfectants. In industrial applications, cationic surfactants are used as wetting agents and foaming agents. Despite their many benefits, cationic surfactants can also have some drawbacks. For example, they can be irritating to the skin and eyes, and can also be toxic to aquatic organisms. As a result, manufacturers must carefully consider the potential risks and benefits of using cationic surfactants in their products. In conclusion, cationic surfactants are a widely used class of compounds that have a range of applications in the cosmetic, pharmaceutical, and industrial sectors. Air is the most common gas mixture used in two-phase flow as it is omnipresent and easy to store and handle. In RED the use of water/air sparging has been studied by Vermaas et al. (2013) using profiled membranes that integrate the membrane and spacer functionality. During the experiment, the stack with air sparging as the antifouling strategy maintained a low pressure drop over the full duration of the experiment (67 days) in comparison to the stack without any antifouling strategy. Unfortunately, the authors only investigated the effect of two-phase flow using profiled membranes and did not consider the effectiveness of this approach in stacks with separate membranes and spacers. Profiled membranes are however not yet commercially available and the use of separate membranes and spacers in RED is initially foreseen for large-scale applications. Usually, woven net-spacers are used in RED to keep the membranes separated and create flow channels, since these are commercially produced and are in general thinner than extruded spacers. However, woven net-spacers are not desirable when using two-phase flow approaches as the gas introduction easily breaks the net-spacer structure, thus blocking the feed flow compartments. Although the use of air bubbles in net-spacer filled channels with low liquid flow velocities is used in other membrane processes, such as NF and RO, one of the major drawbacks is that the introduction of air in the system results in the presence of undesired stagnant bubbles (Willems et al., 2009). These stagnant bubbles reduce the active membrane surface area available for water permeation (Willems et al., 2009) and ion diffusion in RED (Hatzell and Logan, 2013). Additionally, in RED the presence of stagnant bubbles in the stack induces an increase of the stack ohmic resistance, thus reducing the gross power density output of the system. In other words, the presence of stagnant bubbles reduces the amount of energy that potentially can be harvested (Hatzell and Logan, 2013). Although air is a very versatile choice for two-phase flow, it has a relatively low solubility in water (0.023 g/L at 1 atm at 25 C, calculated using Henry's law) (Burton et al., 2013). This low solubility does not only limit the effectiveness of two-phase flow cleaning, it also increases the formation of stagnant bubbles. Carbon dioxide (CO2), which has a solubility in water two orders of magnitude higher than that of air in water (1,27 g/L at 1 atm at 25 C, calculated using Henry's law), is considered to be much more effective (Burton et al., 2013; Carroll et al., 1991). Ngene et al., 2010 investigated the use of CO2 as antifouling strategy in reverse osmosis with spacer-filled channels. CO2 was dissolved in water at a pressure higher than the working pressure used in the membrane process, meaning that upon entrance of the membrane module, the water was supersaturated in CO2. This provokes CO2 bubbles to nucleate due to depressurization.

And as we all know now, Hip Hop took off, and kept growing and growing until it reached the point where it is today. A billion dollar industry and still going strong. And while the music has changed drastically since 1996, the fan base remains loyal to the genre. It's become a way of life, a lifestyle. From clothing lines, to video games and movies, Hip Hop has taken over pop culture, even though it's been around for nearly four decades now. The early days of rap music were pretty much limited to the East Coast and West Coast regions of the United States. In the early 80as the Bronx, New York became the epicenter of Hip Hop. Soon after the rest of the world started to take notice, especially Europe. It wasn't long before the UK embraced the sounds of American Hip Hop. Many British MCs took the sounds of NYC and flipped it to fit the needs of the British youth. But by the mid-90as, the sound had evolved into a new style of its own. While the US was still trying to figure out which direction it wanted to go in, the Brits had already found theirs. Grime music was born. Not unlike the US, the UKs music scene was segregated. There was dancehall, garage, drum n bass, dubstep etc. Grime was the most popular form of music at the time. It was also the most accessible, due to the fact that it was played on pirate radios stations. These radio stations would broadcast music from various genres but mainly grime. They would play anything that sounded good, regardless of who made it. This allowed up-and-comers to gain exposure without having to sign any contracts with record companies. Grime was so successful that it eventually spread throughout England. By the late 90as, grime could be heard everywhere. It was no longer confined to London. This was due to the fact that grime DJs were playing their sets at clubs and parties all over Britain. As grime grew in popularity, more and more rappers began to emerge. Some of the biggest names include Skepta, Wiley, JME, Dizzee Rascal, and Stormzy. These guys were making noise and starting to break through onto the national stage. However, there was one problem. The music industry was slow to catch on. They weren't ready for grime. They didn't understand it and they didn't want to promote it. So instead, they tried to force feed us watered down versions of hip-hop. They called it Urban Music. It was a joke. We knew it and they knew it. But we were stuck with it because that's all the major labels would put out. It was a sad state of affairs. But thankfully, things have changed. Nowadays, grime is being recognized for what it is. There are several grime artists signed to major labels. And there are even more independent labels putting out great grime music. The future looks bright for grime. If you haven't heard it yet, check out some of the best grime albums released in the last decade. You won't regret it.

As I stood there, lost in the fog and my own musings, the red-faced man's sudden appearance startled me, and I turned to regard him with a mixture of curiosity and annoyance. He was a sturdy fellow, with a thick beard and a gruff demeanor, and he seemed to be in a state of high agitation. He paced back and forth across the deck, muttering to himself and gesticulating wildly with his arms. I watched him with growing fascination, wondering what could be the cause of his distress. Presently, he paused in his pacing and approached me, his eyes fixed intently on mine. "You're a writer, ain't ya?" he demanded, his voice low and urgent. I nodded, taken aback by his sudden interest in my profession. "I knew it," he exclaimed, his face lighting up with excitement. "I can always tell. You've got the look of a man who's seen the depths of human suffering." I was taken aback by his words, but I nodded politely, intrigued by his intensity. "I've written a few things," I admitted, trying to downplay my own literary ambitions. The red-faced man nodded vigorously, his eyes gleaming with a fervent light. "I knew it," he repeated. "I've got a story to tell, and I need someone to write it down. It's a tale of the sea, of adventure and danger and heroism. It's a story that'll make your blood run cold and your heart sing." I was skeptical, but the man's enthusiasm was infectious. I found myself drawn into his orbit, caught up in the whirlwind of his passion. "Tell me more," I said, my curiosity getting the better of me. And so he did, launching into a tale of shipwrecks and mutiny, of storms and sea monsters. His words poured out in a torrent, carrying me along on a tide of imagination and excitement. I listened, entranced, as the fog swirled around us, hiding the world from view. As he spoke, I felt the fog begin to clear, at least in my mind. I saw the possibilities, the drama and the romance, the heroism and the tragedy. I saw the story unfolding before me, like a canvas waiting to be filled with color and life. And I knew, in that moment, that I had to write it down, to capture the essence of this wild and wonderful tale. The red-faced man finished his story, his chest heaving with exertion. I nodded, my mind racing with ideas and inspiration. "I'll write it," I said, my voice firm and decisive. "I'll write it, and it'll be a story for the ages." The man grinned, his face creasing with pleasure. "I knew you'd see it," he said, clapping me on the back. "I knew you'd be the one to bring my story to life." And with that, our partnership was formed, a partnership that would take us on a journey across the seas, and into the very heart of adventure itself.

Aspects of predictive coding models of AON function (Keysers and Perrett, 2004; Kilner et al., 2007a, 2007b; Gazzola and Keysers, 2009; Schippers and Keysers, 2011; Tipper et al., 2015), predicated on the use of perceptuomotor maps to predict and interpret observed actions (Lamm et al., 2007; Schubotz, 2007; Urgesi et al., 2010) may help resolve these seemingly discrepant findings concerning the relationship between action familiarity and engagement of sensorimotor cortices. This framework proposes a Bayesian comparison of predicted and observed actions, creating a reciprocally modulated network comprising premotor cortex (including the inferior frontal gyrus), inferior parietal lobule, and posterior temporal cortices (middle and superior temporal gyri). Activity in this network serves to minimise differences between observed and predicted actions. When observing a less familiar action, predictions (feedback signals from frontal -> parietal -> temporal cortices) are lacking or are under informed, and thus do not match incoming information about the observed action (feedforward signals from temporal -> parietal -> frontal cortices), which equates to high prediction error. This could result in robust AON engagement for highly unfamiliar actions, as the influence of feedforward/perceptual activity is heavily relied upon. When viewing an action that is highly familiar, however, predictions generated by the network should be much more precise, thus minimising prediction error. The minimising of prediction error could also manifest as robust AON engagement, this time due to the strength of feedback signals projecting posteriorly (which were weaker when movements were unfamiliar and prediction error was higher; see also Cross et al., 2012). The reciprocal nature of exchanging prediction error signals between core AON nodes allows for the explanation of robust AON engagement for both familiar or unfamiliar actions, relative to actions of an intermediate level of familiarity (illustrated in Fig. 1B 1). It is important to note as well that while this Bayesian framework has been most fully developed in the realm of action observation, it also has been applied to action execution, formally known as active inference (Friston, 2005). As several authors have now suggested, a predictive coding account of action familiarity and AON engagement could manifest as a quadratic, or U-shaped, function (Cross et al., 2012; Liew et al., 2013). However, as identified within the predictive coding literature (Kilner et al., 2007a, 2007b; Friston, 2005), a system that relies on Bayesian comparisons would need to continually update predicted movements in relation to actual movements. For example, when observing an expert guitarist playing a scale (a familiar sequence of actions for both novice and expert guitarists), the player may use all her fingers to achieve this goal. As such, the actions performed by an expert guitarist to play a scale might look much different to those performed by a novice guitarist to play the same scale (i.e., a novice might use fewer fingers and/or transition between notes more awkwardly), even though the musical outcome (playing a scale) remains the same.

For the U.S., human activity likely has increased N loads to the coast by approximately 4 to 8-fold (Howarth et al., 2002). Nonpoint sources are the dominant inputs of N and phosphorus (P) to most U.S. surface waters, but in urban areas, while diffuse sources affect a larger number of streams, point sources contribute >50% of the N and P mass reaching rivers (Carpenter et al., 1998; Preston et al., 2011). P tends to be elevated in urban areas due to point-source sewage inputs and because of fertilizer and manure usage in agricultural areas (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2016). N is the largest pollution problem in U.S. coastal waters and one of the greatest threats to the ecological functioning of these ecosystems (Howarth et al., 2000; National Research Council, 2000) although elevated P concentrations in near-shore coastal waters are common (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2016). Relatively few national-scale assessments have addressed the changes in water quality in rivers and streams that flow to coastal waters. A comprehensive assessment of nutrient enrichment and eutrophic conditions in U.S. estuaries was published by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in 1999 (Bricker et al., 1999), followed by a similar assessment in 2007 (Bricker et al., 2007) that included information about N and P loading to estuaries. However, assessment of the change in eutrophic condition for individual estuaries in the second assessment was impeded by reduced reporting and a change in the data collection method (Bricker et al., 2007). The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) has conducted regular assessments of coastal marine waters and the results are published in four National Coastal Condition Reports (NCCR) that assess the overall condition of U.S. coastal waters, but do not provide individual estuary results. (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2012). In 2010 and 2015, the USEPA conducted National Coastal Condition Assessments (NCCA) using a statistical survey of U.S. nearshore coastal waters during the summer and concluded that P was the most widespread stressor to nearshore water quality (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2016). Riverine inputs dominate nutrient loading to coastal waters (National Research Council, 2000; Sharples et al., 2017). Therefore, determining the trends in nutrient and sediment loading from streams is critical to understanding whether progress is being made in reducing nutrient loads and whether differences in trends are evident between sites with different land use and nutrient sources. This study focuses on recent trends in nutrient and sediment loads in rivers and streams that flow to coastal waters of the conterminous U.S., including the Great Lakes. We focused on results from individual sites, rather than aggregated regional fluxes, to better understand where nutrient and sediment loads were increasing or decreasing as well as the land-use factors contributing to those changes. Understanding national trends in surface-water quality is a primary goal of the U.S. Geological Survey's (USGS) National Water Quality Assessment project (NAWQA).

Legends surrounding the Isle of Demons swirled like fog over the Atlantic, fueled by tales spun from the imaginations of seafarers who braved the tumultuous waters of the North. Sailors spoke of grotesque beasts that inhabited the island, creatures that were said to haunt the shores and terrorize any who dared approach. These fears were likely compounded by the treacherous conditions sailors faced on their voyages through the icy waters, leading to reports of phantom islands arising from the mist and then fading away. Accounts of encounters with the Isle of Demons were so vivid that they sparked interest and curiosity among cartographers and adventurers alike. The origins of the Isle of Demons can be traced back to a 16th-century expedition by French explorer Jacques Cartier, who, in his quest for a passage to the riches of Asia, sailed close to the coast of what is now Canada. His crew's tales of a foreboding land filled with strange beasts and swirling mists fueled the fears of subsequent explorers. The island, marked on charts and maps, became a dreaded destination; one that mariners would plot a course around, avoiding its supposed terrors at all costs. Yet, as explorers pushed the realm of understanding further, whittling the globe down to a more accurate representation, the Isle of Demons began to fade from the annals of cartography. The great maritime cartographers of the 17th century, recognizing the absence of any tangible evidence for its existence, began to erase the phantom isle from their maps. The tide of discovery also swept away many other fictitious landmasses. Although the island itself fell from favor, it serves as a monument to the power of storytelling intertwined with exploration. In an age when maps were interlaced with mystery and myth, the notion that a place could exist even without evidence became a compelling theme of human creativity. Perhaps one of the most intriguing instances of this phenomenon was that of San Borondon. This fabled island was said to be located just off the northern coast of the Canary Islands, tantalizing explorers with promises of lush greenery and abundant resources. Local legend offered that it emerged from the sea only to vanish again, leaving traces of its existence in the minds of those who sought it. In the early 16th century, tales of San Borondon captivated the imaginations of sailors, inspiring quests that would span generations. Each voyage into the treacherous waters surrounding the islands would add another layer to the legend, bolstered by anecdotal reports of sightings and fantastical descriptions. However, like its kin, San Borondon too succumbed to the tides of time, ultimately slipping into the obscurity of myth. As navigation improved and scientific reasoning began to overshadow the whimsical narratives of yore, the belief in phantom islands shifted from a widespread truth to mere folklore. Cartographers replaced the allure of the unknown with tangible realities, meticulously documenting each coastline and contour of the earth's surface. Nevertheless, the allure of these spectral islands remains firmly rooted in the annals of adventure. They stand as a testament to the human spirit's boundless curiosity and the shadows of the past that dance amid the waves-mysteries tangibly robust yet ethereally elusive, forever holding our fascination. Even today, as one gazes at the illuminated screens of digital maps, it is an echo from these tantalizing tales that lingers, reminding us of a time when the world was still riddled with enigmas waiting to be uncovered. These phantom realms, although faded from the maps of our modern world, continue to inhabit the liminal spaces of history, half-glimpsed in a realm of dreams and faded memories.

You would be amazed at how many things can be fixed without professional help.

When it is possible to know it is your business to find out, and if you cannot find out you must say you don't know. It is moral cowardice, injurious to yourself, not to own your ignorance; and you may also be misleading, or unintentionally deceiving, someone else." "How might the moral cowardice of not owning my ignorance be injurious to myself, father?" she asked. "Why, don't you see," he answered, "you would suffer in two ways? If the habit of inaccuracy became confirmed, your own character would deteriorate; and by leading people to suppose that you are as wise as themselves, you lose opportunities of obtaining useful information. They won't tell you things they think you know already." Evadne bent her brows upon this lesson and reflected; and doubtless it was the origin of the verbal accuracy for which she afterward became notable. Patient investigation had always been a pleasure, but from that time forward it became a principle also. She understood from what her father had said that to know the facts of life exactly is a positive duty; which, in a limited sense, was what he had intended to teach her; but the extent to which she carried the precept would have surprised him. Her mind was prone to experiment with every item of information it gathered, in order to test its practical value; if she could turn it to account she treasured it; if not, she rejected it, from whatever source it came. But she was not herself aware of any reservation in her manner of accepting instruction. The trick was innate, and in no way interfered with her faith in her friends, which was profound. She might have justified it, however, upon her father's authority, for she once heard him say to one of her brothers: "Find out for yourself, and form your own opinions," a lesson which she had laid to heart also. Not that her father would have approved of her putting it into practice. He was one of those men who believe emphatically that a woman should hold no opinion which is not of masculine origin, and the maxims he had for his boys differed materially in many respects from those which he gave to his girls. But these precepts of his were, after all, only matches to Evadne which fired whole trains of reflection, and lighted her to conclusions quite other than those at which he had arrived himself. In this way, however, he became her principal instructor. She had attached herself to him from the time that she could toddle, and had acquired from his conversation a proper appreciation of masculine precision of thought.

The first official definition of WUI was coined by the U.S. Department of Agriculture and U.S. Department of Interior (1996) as areas where interacting human structures and forest fuel come into contact. WUI mapping was developed in the USA due to the urgent need to improve risk assessment. In the USA an advanced legal forest framework and high spatial data availability facilitate cartographic map production at large scale. In North America the techniques implemented to map WUI zones are based on an evaluation of the urban density and vegetation density per km2. Census data and a national land cover map provide data sources for US studies of WUIs. At the same time, the legal framework in the US provides an analytical definition of the WUI, characterised by an urban density greater than 6.17 houses/km2 and 50% or more vegetation cover in an area of 5 km2 around the urban perimeter zone of width 2.4 km (USDA and USDI, 2001). Radeloff et al. (2005) converts this legal definition to a cartographic product by GIS analysis and presents a sensitivity analysis by doubling and halving the original threshold values expressed by law, observing that the WUI area mapping is most susceptible to the housing density threshold. However, the size and dimensions of the WUI areas are closely dependent on landscape features, landscape structure and forest fragmentation (Chas-Amil et al., 2013). Bar-Massada et al. (2013) applied different buffer zones around settlements in order to detect the relative WUI area variability. The author highlighted that the spatial extension of a WUI area is defined by the combination of several regional landscape features. Peters et al. (2013) produced a WUI map that considered the housing density and vegetation value as expressed by the legal framework to calculate the fire probability for the WUI areas using a moisture index. Theobald and Romme (2007) compared a WUI map with the wildfire hazard and verified that more than 65% of WUI areas in the US are located in areas labelled as having a 'severe fire regime'. However, a detailed WUI map at the local scale in North America can also be useful without making any reference to national spatial data infrastructures. For this propose, Cleve et al. (2008) published a local WUI map for a small community of California (Napa County) from aerial photographs with 15 cm spatial resolution. In recent years, WUI mapping approaches have also been developed in Europe (Galiana-Martin, 2012), though at the large scale it is a complicated by the heterogeneous laws and administrative organisations and the scarcity of standardised geo-data. Wadsworth et al. (2008) discuss the difficulties in reconciling semantic differences between land cover maps generated for different purposes and following diverse class definitions. The current European approaches to mapping and classifying the WUI have in common that they analyse the landscape characteristics defined by urban settlement and vegetation.

Although the strains varied by their alleles and DNA repair backgrounds, there was substantial redundancy among some strains to permit the recovery of some of the same classes of mutations. In the time since the publication of OECD TG471, the database of Salmonella mutagenicity assay data has expanded to >10,000 compounds, and the storage of those data in searchable, electronic databases now permits analyses that were not possible 25 years ago. Thus, it was considered both sensible and timely to review whether the recommended strain battery is consistent with current experience. To this end, we posed three questions. (1) Although TA100 is derived from TA1535 and generally detects more mutagens than TA1535, does TA1535 detect any mutagens that are not detected by TA100? Both strains detect base-pair substitutions at the same GC base pairs; however, TA100 contains pKM101, which confers error-prone DNA repair. (2) Because there is a choice to use one of either Salmonella TA1537, TA97 or TA97a for detection of frameshift mutagens, are these strains truly equivalent? (3) Because there is a choice to use one of either E. coli WP2 uvrA, E. coli WP2 uvrA pKM101, or Salmonella TA102 for detection of base substitutions at AT base pairs, are these strains truly equivalent? We addressed these questions by first obtaining data from one of three sources: (1) two commercial electronic databases containing mutagenicity data on >10,000 compounds from the open literature, (2) anonymized, proprietary data from a pharmaceutical company, and (3) generating test data ourselves where literature data were unsuitable for comparison. We then performed a series of pairwise comparisons of various compounds in the strains using the qualitative calls of the authors (who generally did not use statistical analyses and who mostly used a 2- or 3-fold rule) to determine if any agents were mutagenic in only one strain of the pair being compared. Where possible we also evaluated whether a compound that was mutagenic in only one of the related strains was also mutagenic in any other OECD-recommended strains or other commonly used genotoxicity assays. In addition to using the study calls reported by the authors, which were almost exclusively based on non-statistical analyses, we also addressed the three questions above quantitatively by calculating linear regressions and determining the slopes (mutagenic potencies) over the linear portions of the dose-response curves, using a trend-test (P 0.05) for significance. This analysis was limited to chemicals where we had access to suitable dose-response data. In addition, we also checked if strains preferentially detected compounds of certain chemical classes or structures.
